intros.text: Flipped Learning is an educational approach in which the conventional order of  receiving knowledge is reversed.  In flipped learning, the initial stage of receiving  knowledge starts before attending class, when students study the teacher-assigned  materials and complete their assignments. Afterwards they enter class to reinforce what  they have covered prior to class (Flipped Learning Network, 2014).  Researchers and  teachers have successfully implemented flipped learning in different courses from  various disciplines and areas, requiring skills practice or mere recitation of content. For  example, flipped learning has been incorporated in algebra, biology, computer  programming, engineering, information and communications technology (ICT), medical  education, and multimedia production.  In the area of English as a foreign language (EFL), flipped learning has been  implemented to improve students’ knowledge of English idioms (Chen Hsieh, Wu, &  Marek, 2017); and to promote students’ active learning in terms of becoming more  willing to communicate, enhancing their speaking skills, and increasing their  satisfaction with the flip approach (Hung, 2017). The effects of flipped learning have  also been investigated in other EFL-related areas, such as: English speaking (Li &  Suwanthep, 2017), English writing (Ahmed, 2016), reading comprehension (Abaeian & Samadi, 2016), English pronunciation (Zhang, Du, Yuan, & Zhang, 2016), and  translation (Shu, 2015).  Flipped learning changes the role of learners and instructors.  Hung (2017) recommended an acquisition-rich environment where students can benefit from both  fluency and accuracy.  This suggests that teachers should design syllabi which cover  both meaning negotiation and linguistic instruction.  This study endeavours to  investigate the extent to which teaching English grammar through flipped learning can  affect the EFL learners’ performance by examining the following research questions: 1. Were there any statistically significant differences between the flipped learning  group (FLG) and the traditional instruction group (TIG) regarding their English  grammar performance? 2. How did the FLG perceive English grammar learning through flipped learning?

intros.text:
The teaching of English grammar to learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) has long presented challenges, particularly when instruction relies heavily on teacher-centred approaches that leave little class time for meaningful application of concepts. In traditional classrooms, students often spend the bulk of their lessons passively receiving information, with practice and consolidation relegated to individual homework completed without immediate support. In recent years, however, educators have increasingly explored alternative instructional models that reverse this arrangement in order to make learning more active and interactive. One such approach is flipped learning, in which learners engage with course content individually before class and then apply and reinforce that knowledge collaboratively during class time (Flipped Learning Network, 2014).

A growing body of research suggests that flipped learning can be beneficial across a range of language skills. Studies have reported positive effects on speaking (Li & Suwanthep, 2017; Hung, 2017), writing (Ahmed, 2016), pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016), and translation competence (Shu, 2015). Others have found that flipped instruction can enhance learners' motivation and idiomatic knowledge (Chen Hsieh et al., 2017), while cooperative and interactive classroom techniques more generally have been shown to support comprehension and engagement (Abaeian & Samadi, 2016). This literature indicates that shifting the initial exposure to content outside the classroom frees valuable in-class time for discussion, clarification, and application under the teacher's guidance.

Despite this promising evidence, comparatively little research has focused specifically on the effect of flipped learning on English grammar acquisition among entry-level EFL university students, and questions remain about how such learners perceive the approach. The present study addresses this gap by investigating whether flipped learning is more effective than traditional instruction in teaching English grammar to first-year university students in Taiwan, and by examining how these learners perceive their grammar learning through flipping. In doing so, it seeks to contribute practical insights into the implementation of flipped learning in EFL grammar instruction and its potential to foster active, autonomous learning.

intros.text:
The teaching of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) has increasingly embraced instructional models that shift responsibility from teachers to learners. Among these, flipped learning has attracted considerable attention as an approach that combines face-to-face and online instruction to enhance student performance (Osguthorpe & Graham, 2003). In a flipped classroom, teachers make course materials available before class so that students can prepare independently and then use valuable class time to apply, discuss, and reinforce what they have learned. This restructuring of when and how learning takes place has been championed as a means of fostering active engagement and learner autonomy.

A growing body of research reports positive effects of flipped learning across various English language skills. Studies have shown gains in speaking (Li & Suwanthep, 2017; Hung, 2017), writing (Ahmed, 2016), pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016), translation competence (Shu, 2015), and idiomatic knowledge (Chen Hsieh et al., 2017). These findings collectively suggest that flipped learning enables teachers to design varied strategies and activities that influence student learning both inside and outside the classroom (Flipped Learning Network, 2014).

Despite this expanding literature, most investigations have concentrated on productive skills or vocabulary, while the teaching of English grammar through flipped learning remains comparatively under-explored, particularly in EFL contexts where learners have limited exposure to English. Grammar is fundamental to accurate communication, yet few studies have examined whether the two-stage design of flipped learning—individual preparation followed by collaborative in-class work—can effectively reinforce grammatical knowledge among entry-level university learners. There is also a need to understand how such learners perceive this comparatively unfamiliar approach.

To address these gaps, the present study investigates the effect of flipped learning on the English grammar of first-year Taiwanese university students. It compares a flipped learning group with a traditional instruction group over a treatment period, and it examines learners' perceptions of grammar learning through flipped instruction. The study is guided by two research questions concerning grammar performance differences between the groups and learners' attitudes towards the flipped approach.

intros.text:
The pursuit of effective instructional methodologies remains a priority in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, as traditional lecture-based approaches often struggle to keep pace with the evolving needs of learners (Chen Hsieh et al., 2017). To address these challenges, educators have increasingly turned to flipped learning, a pedagogical model that reverses the traditional instructional sequence by shifting direct instruction from the group space to the individual space. According to the Flipped Learning Network (2014), this approach allows for a more dynamic use of classroom time, moving the focus from passive reception to active application. 

Recent empirical evidence suggests that flipped learning can significantly enhance various linguistic competencies. For instance, studies have demonstrated its effectiveness in improving EFL speaking skills (Li & Suwanthep, 2017) and writing proficiency (Ahmed, 2016). Beyond these productive skills, the model has shown promise in specialized areas such as English pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016) and translation competence (Shu, 2015). Furthermore, the integration of technology-driven flipped classrooms has been linked to increased student satisfaction and a greater willingness to communicate (Hung, 2017). By requiring students to engage with materials independently before class, the flipped model encourages them to transition from being mere knowledge consumers to active knowledge providers, thereby fostering greater learner autonomy.

Despite these positive findings across various domains of language acquisition, there is a need to further examine how this model specifically impacts the mastery of English grammar, which is often perceived as one of the most challenging aspects of EFL learning. While some research indicates that flipped classrooms can outperform traditional instruction in grammar and vocabulary acquisition, more data is needed to understand student perceptions and the overall efficacy of this approach in a university setting. Therefore, the present study aims to evaluate the effect of flipped learning on the grammar performance of first-year university students and to explore their perceptions of this instructional shift.

intros.text:
In recent years, the landscape of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction has been significantly influenced by the integration of technology to enhance learner performance. Among the most prominent innovative approaches is flipped learning, a pedagogical model that reverses the traditional instructional sequence by shifting direct instruction from the group learning space to the individual learning space (Flipped Learning Network, 2014). By providing materials online before class, this approach encourages students to take greater responsibility for their learning, allowing classroom time to be repurposed for active application and deeper cognitive engagement.

Previous research has demonstrated the efficacy of flipped learning across various linguistic domains. For instance, studies have shown its positive impact on the development of speaking skills (Li & Suwanthep, 2017), writing proficiency (Ahmed, 2016), and English pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016). Furthermore, the model has been found to enhance translation competence (Shu, 2015) and increase overall learner motivation and idiomatic knowledge (Chen Hsieh et al., 2017). Despite these promising results in skill-based areas, there remains a need for further empirical evidence regarding the specific impact of flipped learning on the acquisition of English grammar, particularly among first-year university students who are transitioning to higher education environments.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the effect of flipped learning on EFL learners' grammar performance compared to traditional instructional methods. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether a flipped approach leads to statistically significant improvements in grammar test scores and to explore students' perceptions of this learning experience. To achieve this, a quasi-experimental design was employed involving 132 university students divided into a flipped learning group and a traditional instruction group. The findings of this study provide insights into the effectiveness of the flipped model in teaching grammar and offer pedagogical implications for EFL practitioners seeking to foster learner autonomy and cooperative learning in the classroom.

intros.text:
The integration of technology in English language teaching has transformed traditional pedagogical approaches, with flipped learning emerging as a prominent model. Flipped learning, also known as inverted classrooms or blended learning, restructures the educational process by shifting direct instruction to the individual learning space and moving group activities to the group learning space (Shih & Tsai, 2017). This approach requires students to engage with course materials, such as videos and texts, prior to class, allowing face-to-face time to be dedicated to active learning, problem-solving, and deeper cognitive engagement (Osguthorpe & Graham, 2003). While the potential of flipped learning to enhance learner autonomy and interaction is widely acknowledged, its specific efficacy in teaching English grammar to EFL learners requires further empirical investigation.

Previous research has demonstrated the benefits of flipped learning across various language skills. For instance, Li and Suwanthep (2017) found that flipped classrooms significantly improved EFL students' speaking abilities in a Thai university context. Similarly, Ahmed (2016) reported positive outcomes in writing proficiency among Saudi female university students. Zhang et al. (2016) and Shu (2015) further supported these findings, highlighting improvements in pronunciation and translation competence, respectively. However, while studies by Kang (2015) have touched upon grammar and vocabulary, there remains a need to examine how flipped learning specifically impacts grammatical accuracy and learner perceptions in a structured university setting. Furthermore, the role of the teacher and the nature of in-class interactions within this framework warrant closer attention, as emphasized by the Flipped Learning Network (2014).

Despite the growing body of literature, gaps persist regarding the comparative effectiveness of flipped learning versus traditional instruction in grammar acquisition, particularly for non-English majors at the freshman level. This study aims to address these gaps by investigating the effect of a 10-week flipped learning program on EFL learners' grammar performance. Additionally, it seeks to explore students' perceptions of this pedagogical approach. By comparing a flipped learning group with a traditional instruction group, this research contributes to the understanding of how restructuring learning spaces can foster grammatical development and learner autonomy in the EFL context.

intros.text:
In the rapidly evolving landscape of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction, pedagogical approaches that leverage technology to enhance learner autonomy and engagement have gained significant attention. Among these, flipped learning has emerged as a promising model, redefining the traditional classroom dynamic by shifting direct instruction from the group learning space to the individual learning space. This approach allows class time to be repurposed for interactive, higher-order cognitive activities, theoretically fostering deeper understanding and skill application. As noted by the Flipped Learning Network (2014), the efficacy of this model relies on the flexible environment it creates for students to learn at their own pace before engaging in collaborative tasks during face-to-face sessions.

Empirical research has increasingly validated the potential of flipped learning across various EFL domains. For instance, Li and Suwanthep (2017) demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing speaking skills among university students, while Ahmed (2016) reported significant improvements in writing proficiency. Similarly, Zhang et al. (2016) found that flipped classrooms outperformed traditional modes in teaching pronunciation, and Shu (2015) highlighted gains in translation competence. These studies collectively suggest that flipping the classroom can positively influence language acquisition by promoting active participation and learner responsibility. However, despite these encouraging findings, the specific impact of flipped learning on the acquisition of English grammar—a foundational yet often challenging component of EFL curricula—remains less explored in the context of non-English major university students. Furthermore, while quantitative gains have been documented, there is a need for further investigation into learners' perceptions regarding this pedagogical shift, particularly concerning their engagement with online materials and in-class discussions.

To address this gap, the present study examines the effect of flipped learning on EFL learners' grammar performance and their perceptions of the learning experience. Adopting a quasi-experimental design, this research compares a flipped learning group with a traditional instruction group over a ten-week period. The study aims to determine whether the flipped model yields statistically significant improvements in grammar proficiency and to explore students' attitudes toward the approach. The findings offer valuable insights for educators seeking to integrate technology-enhanced pedagogies into grammar instruction, potentially transforming the teacher's role from a knowledge provider to a facilitator of autonomous learning.

intros.text:
In many EFL contexts, grammar remains a central component of university English courses because it supports learners’ accuracy in comprehension and production. Yet grammar instruction is often delivered through teacher-fronted explanation followed by individual practice, a sequence that can limit opportunities for interaction, clarification, and meaningful use during class time. As digital platforms have become increasingly available, language teachers have begun to reconsider how classroom time can be reorganized so that learners encounter input before class and use face-to-face sessions for guided practice and collaboration.

Flipped learning offers one such reorganization. In this approach, students first engage with instructional materials—often videos, readings, and online exercises—outside the classroom, and class time is then devoted to discussion, problem solving, peer support, and teacher feedback. The Flipped Learning Network (2014) characterizes effective flipped learning as a flexible, learner-centred environment in which direct instruction is moved from the group space to the individual space. Such a model has potential value for EFL learners because it can increase preparation, encourage responsibility for learning, and create more time for communicative and collaborative work. However, students may need support in adapting to the more active role expected of them.

Previous studies have reported positive effects of flipped learning in several areas of English language learning. Ahmed (2016) found that a flipped classroom improved EFL learners’ writing performance and attitudes, while Chen Hsieh et al. (2017) showed gains in idiom learning and motivation through flipped instruction supported by online interaction. Similar benefits have been reported for speaking (Li & Suwanthep, 2017; Hung, 2017), pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016), and translation competence (Shu, 2015). Research on cooperative learning also suggests that structured peer interaction can enhance language learning by requiring learners to share knowledge and take responsibility for group understanding (Abaeian & Samadi, 2016).

Despite this growing evidence, comparatively less attention has been paid to the use of flipped learning for teaching EFL grammar, particularly among lower-proficiency first-year university students. The present study therefore investigates whether flipped learning improves learners’ English grammar performance more than traditional instruction and explores students’ perceptions of learning grammar through a flipped model.

intros.text:
Grammar remains a central component of EFL instruction because it supports learners’ ability to express meanings accurately in speaking and writing and to understand texts beyond the word level. In many university English courses, however, grammar is still taught through teacher-fronted explanation followed by exercises completed after class. Although this sequence can transmit rules efficiently, it often leaves limited classroom time for interaction, clarification, and guided application, especially for lower-proficiency learners who need repeated opportunities to notice, practise, and receive feedback on form.

Flipped learning offers an alternative organization of instructional time. In this approach, learners first encounter course content individually, usually through online materials before class, and classroom time is then used for collaborative practice, problem solving, and teacher-supported discussion. The Flipped Learning Network (2014) characterizes effective flipped learning as a flexible, learner-centred environment in which direct instruction is partly moved outside class so that group space can be devoted to active learning. Such a model may be particularly relevant to EFL contexts, where students often need both input and meaningful opportunities to use English with peers.

Previous research has reported positive effects of flipped learning in several areas of English language learning. Ahmed (2016) found that flipped instruction improved EFL writing and students’ attitudes towards learning, while Li and Suwanthep (2017) showed gains in undergraduate EFL speaking. Chen Hsieh et al. (2017) reported enhanced idiom learning and motivation through a flipped oral training course, and Hung (2017) found that flipped classrooms supported speaking development and willingness to communicate. Other studies have suggested benefits for pronunciation (Zhang et al., 2016), translation competence (Shu, 2015), and grammar and vocabulary learning (Kang, 2015). These findings indicate the potential of flipped learning to increase preparation, engagement, and responsibility for learning.

Nevertheless, relatively little classroom-based evidence has focused specifically on EFL grammar learning at the freshman university level, and learners’ perceptions of studying grammar through a flipped sequence remain underexplored. The present study therefore investigates whether flipped learning leads to greater improvement in English grammar than traditional instruction and examines how students perceive the flipped grammar-learning experience. Using a quasi-experimental design with first-year university students in Taiwan, the study compares pre- and post-test grammar performance between a flipped learning group and a traditional instruction group and surveys the flipped group’s views of online materials, in-class discussions, the teacher’s role, and perceived learning benefits.

intros.text: In teaching oral communication, there are multiple key factors including fluency,  pronunciation, interaction and turn-taking (Thornbury, 2011). Grammar is also an  important factor which differentiates spoken from written English (Carter & McCarthy,  2017) through the provision of unique linguistic features  Spoken English has also been  influenced by new technological developments such as real-time communication  platforms and the development of corpora.  In the Chinese context in which the study reported here is set, the Higher Education  Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee has set the following basic  requirements for university English oral communication teaching: The university students should be able to have simple and multi-rounds of English conversations,  make comments on familiar topics, and have simple discussions on the topics related to their  study and future job. The language should be clear in structure. The intonation, tone and grammar  should meet the basic communicative norms. They should be able to have basic conversation  skills. (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014, p. 6) There are also more advanced requirements according to the same document, which  require students to acquire oral communicative competence on complex topics and  activities, such as conference presentations and sales promotions (Higher Education  Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014)  Against this background, this article aims to explore the teaching of English oral  communication in the Chinese university context by investigating the main barriers and  challenges for oral communication skills development; the students’ perceptions of oral  English communication topics, resources and activities; and the routes for improvement  in oral English communication courses.  For the purposes of this paper, barriers refer to  problems students encounter in the learning process, whereas challenges are the problems  they face when attending their oral English classes.

intros.text:
The ability to communicate orally in English is increasingly valued in China, where growing numbers of undergraduates seek to enhance their language competence beyond the requirements of their core disciplines. One route to this goal is the English minor programme, in which students from a wide range of scientific and humanities backgrounds pursue additional English study alongside their compulsory college English courses. Yet, despite the popularity of such programmes, comparatively little is known about how these learners experience the learning of spoken English, particularly the obstacles they encounter and the kinds of teaching that would best support them.

Developing oral communicative competence has long been a central concern of applied linguistics and language pedagogy. Methodological thinking has evolved from grammar-translation and audiolingualism towards communicative language teaching (Thornbury, 2005), while ongoing work on spoken grammar has highlighted the interactive, co-constructed nature of everyday talk and its implications for classroom practice (Carter & McCarthy, 2015). Teaching speaking is nevertheless demanding, requiring attention to speech production, fluency, automaticity, turn-taking and the management of interaction (Thornbury, 2005). In the Chinese context, technological developments and new resources have also been drawn into English teaching to support learners' engagement and practice (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014).

Although much research has examined approaches to teaching speaking and the factors that shape learners' willingness and ability to communicate, the specific perspectives of English minor undergraduates in China remain under-explored. Their motivations, self-perceptions, and the barriers and challenges they perceive have received little empirical attention. This article addresses that gap by investigating, through surveys administered at the start and end of an oral English communication course, how such learners perceive the obstacles they face, their preferences for topics, activities and resources, and the improvements they would recommend. In doing so, it aims to inform both theory and practice in oral English communication teaching for this and comparable learner populations.

intros.text:
The ability to communicate orally in English is widely recognised as central to the goals of English language education, and teaching speaking has long attracted the attention of researchers and practitioners alike. Speaking is a complex skill involving speech production, conceptualisation, articulation, self-monitoring, fluency and the management of interaction (Thornbury, 2005). It also draws on linguistic, psycholinguistic, sociolinguistic and discourse knowledge, all of which learners must coordinate in real time. Understanding how such competence develops, and what helps or hinders learners, is therefore of considerable pedagogical importance, particularly as spoken corpus research continues to reshape our view of conversational grammar and its place in language teaching (Carter & McCarthy, 2015).

In the Chinese context, English is increasingly taught not only to specialists but also to large numbers of non-specialist learners through initiatives such as college English and, more recently, English minor programmes. Technology has expanded the range of resources available, from e-mail to multimedia and online materials, that can support spoken English learning (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014). Yet the teaching of spoken English in China continues to face persistent problems, including examination-oriented practices and limited opportunities for authentic communication.

Despite the substantial body of research on approaches to teaching oral communication and on the factors influencing speaking development, relatively little attention has been paid to the growing population of English minor undergraduates, whose needs and perceptions remain under-explored. Insufficient is known about how these learners themselves perceive the barriers and challenges they encounter in improving their spoken English, or about their preferences regarding topics, activities and resources.

To help address this gap, the present study investigates the perceptions of English minor undergraduates enrolled in an oral English communication course at a Chinese university. It examines the barriers and challenges they perceive, their preferences for teaching topics, activities and resources, and their suggestions for improvement, thereby offering empirical evidence to inform both theory and practice in oral English communication teaching in China.

intros.text:
Developing oral communicative competence is a central goal of English language teaching, yet it remains one of the most challenging aspects of language acquisition in higher education. According to Thornbury (2005), teaching speaking at the university level is particularly complex because it requires students to integrate linguistic, sociolinguistic, and discourse knowledge while managing real-time speech production, fluency, and interaction. Traditionally, pedagogy has been heavily influenced by written standards; however, recent shifts in applied linguistics emphasize the need for a distinct approach to spoken grammar, acknowledging that conversational language is interactive, co-constructed, and non-sentence-based (Carter & McCarthy, 2015). 

In the Chinese university context, the integration of information technology has offered new avenues for enhancing language learning, such as the application of e-mail and other digital tools to supplement classroom instruction (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014). Despite these technological advancements and the shift toward communicative language teaching, many students continue to struggle with the transition from theoretical knowledge to practical oral application. While much research has focused on English majors, there is a relative dearth of empirical evidence regarding the specific experiences of English minor undergraduates—students who pursue English as a secondary specialization alongside other disciplinary studies.

This group of learners often faces unique barriers and challenges that can hinder their oral proficiency. Understanding their perceptions of the learning process is essential for developing more effective, tailored curricula. Consequently, the present study aims to investigate the perceived barriers and challenges faced by English minor undergraduates in a Chinese university, as well as their preferences regarding teaching topics, activities, and resources. By addressing these factors, the study seeks to provide practical insights for improving the delivery of oral English communication courses in similar academic settings.

intros.text:
Developing oral communicative competence is a central goal in English language teaching, as the ability to speak fluently and accurately is vital for successful interaction in global contexts. In university settings, teaching speaking is particularly challenging because students' existing knowledge and experiences significantly influence their output (Thornbury, 2005). To address this, scholars have highlighted the importance of moving beyond written standards toward a pedagogy based on spoken grammar, which is inherently interactive and co-constructed (Carter & McCarthy, 2015). In China, the integration of information technology, such as the use of e-mail in college English teaching, has been explored to enhance learning outcomes (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014).

While substantial research has examined the general difficulties of learning spoken English in China—such as a lack of linguistic knowledge and confidence—much of this work has focused on English majors or general college English students. However, insufficient is known about the specific perceptions of English minor undergraduates regarding the barriers and challenges they face. This particular group often balances specialized disciplinary studies with English language acquisition, yet their unique needs and perceptions remain under-researched.

To contribute towards filling this gap in the literature, the current study investigates the barriers and challenges encountered by English minor undergraduates in a Chinese university, as well as their perceptions of oral communication teaching. Specifically, the study addresses three research questions: (1) What do these students perceive as the main barriers and challenges to developing spoken English skills? (2) What are their perceptions of spoken English teaching topics, activities, and resources? (3) What suggestions for improvement do they offer based on their course experience? By providing empirical evidence, this study aims to offer practical implications for the design and delivery of oral English curricula in the Chinese higher education context.

Carter and McCarthy (2015) emphasize that spoken grammar is distinct from written standards, being non-sentence-based, co-constructed, and highly interactive. Unlike English majors, these students undertake English courses alongside their primary disciplines, often with limited prior exposure to formal speaking training. Consequently, their perceptions of barriers, challenges, and pedagogical needs may differ significantly from those of major students.

Existing literature suggests that factors such as linguistic knowledge, confidence, and learning environments heavily influence speaking ability development. However, insufficient is known about how English minor undergraduates specifically perceive these factors. This study aims to address this gap by investigating the barriers and challenges English minor undergraduates face in improving their oral English communication skills. Furthermore, it explores their perceptions of teaching topics, activities, and resources within a Chinese university setting. By examining these elements, the study seeks to provide empirical evidence to inform theory and practice in oral English communication teaching for this under-researched demographic.

intros.text: Oral communication has become a central goal of English language teaching in higher education, particularly in EFL contexts where learners may have limited opportunities to use English outside the classroom. Speaking requires more than knowledge of vocabulary and grammar; it involves fluency, accuracy, interactional management, pronunciation, pragmatic awareness and the ability to negotiate meaning in real time (Thornbury, 2005). Developments in spoken corpus research have also shown that everyday spoken English differs in important ways from written models traditionally emphasized in language teaching, suggesting the need for pedagogies that attend to the interactive and co-constructed nature of spoken grammar (Carter & McCarthy, 2015). At the same time, technological and multimedia resources have expanded the possibilities for oral English teaching, including in Chinese college English classrooms (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014). In China, the development of students’ communicative competence has received increasing attention alongside more established emphases on reading, writing and examination performance. However, many university students still experience difficulty in developing spoken English because of limited practice opportunities, lack of confidence, insufficient linguistic resources and classroom conditions that do not always support sustained interaction. Previous research has examined oral English teaching among English majors, non-English majors and learners in various Chinese and international EFL settings, identifying the importance of communicative tasks, interactional competence, appropriate feedback, learner motivation and supportive learning environments. Yet English minor undergraduates constitute a distinctive group: they are not English majors, but they voluntarily pursue additional English study and may have specific expectations for oral communication courses. Their perceptions of barriers, classroom challenges, preferred topics, learning activities and resources remain under-explored. Understanding these perceptions is important for designing oral English courses that are responsive to learner needs and realistic institutional conditions. This study therefore investigates English minor undergraduates’ experiences of an oral English communication course at a Chinese university, focusing on perceived barriers and challenges, preferences for teaching content and resources, and suggestions for improving course design and post-course practice.

intros.text:
Oral communication has become a central concern in English language teaching because successful participation in academic, professional and intercultural settings increasingly depends on learners’ ability to speak English intelligibly, fluently and appropriately. In EFL contexts such as China, university students often receive substantial instruction in reading, writing and test-oriented language knowledge, yet opportunities for sustained spoken interaction may be limited. Teaching speaking therefore requires attention not only to pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, but also to fluency, interactional management, confidence and the ability to use language across topics and situations.

Research on spoken English has shown that speaking is a complex skill involving conceptualisation, formulation, articulation, monitoring, repair, automaticity, fluency and turn-taking (Thornbury, 2005). Developments in spoken grammar have further demonstrated that everyday spoken language differs in important ways from written norms, being interactive, co-constructed and often non-sentence-based (Carter & McCarthy, 2015). These insights have implications for pedagogy, particularly for courses that aim to move learners beyond written accuracy towards communicative competence. In China, policy and pedagogical discussions have also encouraged the integration of information technology and diverse resources into College English teaching (Higher Education Institution College English Teaching Advisory Committee, 2014), while classroom research has explored communicative, interactional and technology-enhanced approaches to developing oral competence.

Nevertheless, much remains to be understood about the specific needs of English minor undergraduates. This group differs from English majors and general College English students: they invest additional time in English study while pursuing primary degrees in other disciplines, and their learning needs may combine general communicative goals with academic, cultural and career-related motivations. Despite growing work on oral English teaching in Chinese universities, relatively little empirical evidence is available on how English minor students themselves perceive the barriers, classroom challenges, topics, activities and resources associated with learning spoken English.

To address this gap, the present study investigates an oral English communication course for English minor undergraduates at a Chinese university. It examines students’ perceived barriers and challenges in improving spoken English, their preferences regarding topics, teaching activities and learning resources, and their suggestions for course improvement and post-course practice. By foregrounding learners’ perspectives, the study aims to inform more responsive oral English curriculum design for English minor programmes in China.

intros.text: This article presents a quantitative study that seeks to establish how discursive means of self-mention are represented in research sections of the leading universities in Estonia and the United Kingdom (the UK), respectively.  Research sections of university websites serve as digital artifacts that are used to communicate, disseminate and promote research (Tomášková 2015).  Typically, the university’s research communication on its website involves discursive means of self-mention, i.e. how the university refers to itself on the website.  The specific aim of this study is to identify and juxtapose self-mentions in the research sections of the university websites in Estonia and the UK.  This study is grounded in the theoretical premises of self-mention in academic discourse that are formulated by Hyland (2001, 2008) and the construal of the Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles of the English language in the sense postulated by Kachru (1985).  According to Kachru (1985), the Inner Circle of English is represented by the countries where English is the mother tongue, e.g., the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Ireland. In the Inner Circle, English is “a mother tongue that is passed on to infants naturalistically across generations” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159). In the countries of the Inner Circle, English is used in a normative manner as a linguistically codified and socially accepted set of norms or standards that are regarded as norm-providing to the Outer and Expanding Circles (Bolton 2006; Kachru 1985). The Outer Circle is associated with the speakers of English as the second language (ESL) in the former British colonies (e.g., India, Jamaica, Singapore, etc.), where “English is only one of the community languages in what are clearly multilingual societies” (Bolton 2006: 3) In contrast to the Outer Circle, the English language in the Expanding Circle of English does not have an official or semi-official status. The Expanding Circle is theorised to be associated with English as an international language in those countries where English is taught as a Foreign Language, or EFL (Bolton 2006: 3). English in the Expanding Circle is assumed “to be exonormative in that speakers, educators, and policy-makers have traditionally looked to American or British models for linguistic norms” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159-160). Arguably, the use of English in the Expanding Circle is norm-dependent, since EFL speakers need to be provided with a model or a codified norm of English associated with the Inner Circle (Bolton 2006). The aforementioned characteristics of the Expanding Circle of English could be illustrated by the case of Estonia. Whilst English does not have an official status there, the importance and prestige of the English language increases in today’s Estonia (Lazdiņa, Marten 2019) due to the country’s participation in the “collective West”, as a member-state of the EU, NATO, OECD and other international organisations that use English as a lingua franca (Jurkynas 2020). In addition, the use of the English language in Estonia is facilitated by an increased number of international students at Estonian universities (Soler, Björkman, and Kuteeva 2018). After Estonia regained its independence after nearly 50 years of Soviet occupation, the teaching and learning of English have aligned with the practices that are found in the West (Alas, Liiv 2009: 20).  Given the increase in international co-operation and university mobility, Estonian universities maintain and regularly update websites in English (van Doorslaer, Loogus 2020; Virkus 2008).  Presumably, English-mediated university websites in Estonia could be regarded as digital discursive artifacts that construe university-specific narratives associated with a variety of aspects, i.e. the presentation of the university’s structure, university’s identity, university student life, enrollment, and research activities.  In this regard, it should be noted that university websites in Estonia and the UK alike could be theorised as a complex multimodal discursive space, where verbal and non-verbal discursive means are employed in order to achieve the pragma-communicative goals of promoting the university to the public (Tomášková 2015).  It could be assumed that, by serving the aforementioned pragmacommunicative aims, the use of the English language on the English-mediated university websites reflects the realities of the Circles of English, as well as the cultural, educational, and socio-economic realities. Consequently, the discursive means of self-mention on the university websites might differ, due to the disparities between a university that is situated in a country of the Expanding Circle of English (e.g., Estonia) and a university in the UK that belongs to the Inner Circle of English.  Currently, however, little is known about whether or not self-mentions are linguistically similar and/or different on the English-mediated university websites in the Expanding Circle of English (e.g., Estonia) and the Inner Circle of English (e.g., the UK). Furthermore, there are no prior studies that investigate self-mentions in the research sections of Estonian university websites in order to compare their use with that of the UK’s university websites  The present study seeks to address this under-represented issue.  This article is structured as follows. First, I will provide a review of the current literature associated with self-mention in academic writing in English and in computer-mediated discourse in section 2. Then, I will introduce and discuss the present study with its research questions, corpus, methodology, and results, and provide a detailed discussion of the major findings in section 3. Finally, the article will be concluded with the summary of the results in section 4

segments.text: According to Kachru (1985), the Inner Circle of English is represented by the countries where English is the mother tongue, e.g., the UK, USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, and Ireland. In the Inner Circle, English is “a mother tongue that is passed on to infants naturalistically across generations” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159). In the countries of the Inner Circle, English is used in a normative manner as a linguistically codified and socially accepted set of norms or standards that are regarded as norm-providing to the Outer and Expanding Circles (Bolton 2006; Kachru 1985). The Outer Circle is associated with the speakers of English as the second language (ESL) in the former British colonies (e.g., India, Jamaica, Singapore, etc.), where “English is only one of the community languages in what are clearly multilingual societies” (Bolton 2006: 3) In contrast to the Outer Circle, the English language in the Expanding Circle of English does not have an official or semi-official status. The Expanding Circle is theorised to be associated with English as an international language in those countries where English is taught as a Foreign Language, or EFL (Bolton 2006: 3). English in the Expanding Circle is assumed “to be exonormative in that speakers, educators, and policy-makers have traditionally looked to American or British models for linguistic norms” (Bruthiaux 2003: 159-160). Arguably, the use of English in the Expanding Circle is norm-dependent, since EFL speakers need to be provided with a model or a codified norm of English associated with the Inner Circle (Bolton 2006).

segments.text: The aforementioned characteristics of the Expanding Circle of English could be illustrated by the case of Estonia. Whilst English does not have an official status there, the importance and prestige of the English language increases in today’s Estonia (Lazdiņa, Marten 2019) due to the country’s participation in the “collective West”, as a member-state of the EU, NATO, OECD and other international organisations that use English as a lingua franca (Jurkynas 2020). In addition, the use of the English language in Estonia is facilitated by an increased number of international students at Estonian universities (Soler, Björkman, and Kuteeva 2018). After Estonia regained its independence after nearly 50 years of Soviet occupation, the teaching and learning of English have aligned with the practices that are found in the West (Alas, Liiv 2009: 20).  Given the increase in international co-operation and university mobility, Estonian universities maintain and regularly update websites in English (van Doorslaer, Loogus 2020; Virkus 2008).

intros.text:
The proliferation of digital communication has transformed the ways in which institutions present themselves to the world. Universities, in particular, increasingly rely upon their official websites to project an image, communicate with a range of stakeholders, and promote their achievements to prospective students, researchers, funders, and the wider public. Within this context, the university website has come to constitute a distinct genre of computer-mediated discourse (CMD), one that is 'unified by a common communicative purpose – presenting the institution and promoting it' (Tomášková 2015: 79). The discursive means by which universities accomplish this presentational and promotional work, however, remain relatively underexplored, especially where the research-related activities of institutions are concerned. The present study addresses this gap by examining one specific and rhetorically significant device – self-mention – in the research sections of the websites of two leading European universities.

Self-mention, understood as an explicit reference to the author or authors by means of markers such as I / my and we / our (Hyland & Tse 2004), has attracted sustained scholarly attention within applied linguistics and discourse studies. Hyland (2001) has demonstrated that far from being neutral or self-effacing, academic writing routinely encodes information about its authors, and that the first person pronoun functions as 'an important rhetorical device which allows writers to emphasise their contribution to the academic debate and construct an authoritative discoursal self' (Martínez 2005: 175). Indeed, Hyland (2001: 209) argues that any form of 'writing carries information about the writer, and the conventions of personal projection, particularly the use of first person pronouns, are powerful means for self-representation'. The theoretical concern with authorial self-representation has deep roots in the seminal works of Bakhtin, Foucault, and Ivanič, in which authorial presence is situated within the relations between self and others, between the author's voice and the audience, and between the writer and the writer's identity. These insights, while originally developed in relation to literary and academic texts, extend naturally to other forms of written discourse, including the increasingly consequential domain of institutional communication online.

While a substantial body of scholarship has examined self-mention in the genre of academic writing in English (Hyland 2008), its use in CMD has received comparatively little attention. The existing studies that do address self-mention in digital settings suggest that pronominal choices vary considerably across contexts and communicative purposes. Research into internet-based university courses indicates that students' social presence is often realised through the first person singular pronoun I, whereas studies of research project websites reveal that we is the most frequent form of self-mention, referring variously to a project, an institution, or a group of researchers (Lorés-Sanz & Herrando-Rodrigo 2020). Analyses of English-mediated tourist websites in Spain similarly show that self-mentions are 'almost entirely displayed through the use of the first person plural, which helps to enhance the notion of a community or group of people' (Malenkina & Ivanov 2018: 212). By contrast, a contrastive study of business websites in Spain and the United States found that American websites are marked by a substantially more frequent use of the first person singular than their Spanish counterparts (Pérez 2014). These findings hint that the deployment of self-mention may be sensitive not only to genre but also to broader linguistic and cultural factors, including the status of English in the community from which the discourse originates.

Such cross-cultural variation invites interpretation through the lens of Kachru's (1985) influential model of World Englishes, which conceptualises the language as a system of Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles. The Inner Circle comprises countries such as the United Kingdom, where English is the norm-providing native language; the Expanding Circle includes countries such as Estonia, where English functions as a foreign language increasingly used for international academic and professional purposes. Although the model has been subject to critique for its reliance on political and historical categories rather than sociolinguistic realities (Bruthiaux 2003), it continues to offer a useful heuristic for comparing English-mediated discourse across settings. The distinction is especially pertinent to higher education in the Baltic region, where universities negotiate a complex interplay between national languages and English as a vehicle of internationalisation (Soler et al. 2017; van Doorslaer & Loogus 2020). Estonia, in particular, has developed language and translation policies that prioritise the national language while pragmatically accommodating international audiences through English-language institutional communication (van Doorslaer & Loogus 2020).

Despite this growing interest, no state-of-the-art study has examined the use of self-mention in the research sections of university websites in the UK and Estonia – representatives, respectively, of the Inner and Expanding Circles of English. It is against this backdrop that the present study is situated. It investigates how self-mention is represented in the research sections of the official websites of the University of Cambridge and the University of Tartu, which in 2020 were ranked as the leading universities in their respective countries (Times Higher Education 2020). It is hypothesised that there may be quantitative differences in the use of self-mention depending on whether the institution is associated with the Inner Circle or the Expanding Circle. At the same time, it is not precluded that the University of Tartu, as a prestigious and well-established institution with extensive discursive practices in CMD, might display patterns similar or identical to those of Cambridge (Bolton 2006). Two research questions guide the inquiry: first, what are the most frequent discursive means of self-mention in the research sections of the two universities' websites; and second, are there differences or similarities in the frequency of self-mention use between the two institutions? In pursuing these questions, the article aims to contribute new empirical knowledge about the intersection of self-representation, institutional promotion, and the varieties of English employed in academic CMD.

intros.text:
The manner in which authors represent themselves in written discourse has become a topic of considerable interest among applied linguists and discourse analysts. Central to this line of inquiry is the notion of self-mention, which is understood as an explicit reference to the author or authors by means of self-mention markers such as I / my and we / our (Hyland, Tse 2004). Such markers are generally regarded as genre-specific (Hyland 2008), and in the genre of academic discourse in English they typically involve the first person pronouns (Hyland 2001; Ivanič 1998), which function as 'an important rhetorical device which allows writers to emphasise their contribution to the academic debate and construct an authoritative discoursal self' (Martínez 2005: 175). Indeed, as Hyland (2001: 209) argues, any form of 'writing carries information about the writer, and the conventions of personal projection, particularly the use of first person pronouns, are powerful means for self-representation'. The current interest in authorial self-representation, in the sense postulated by Hyland (2001, 2008), draws upon the seminal works of Bakhtin (1986), Foucault (1988), and Ivanič (1998), in which the authorial presence is situated within the co-ordinates of self and others, of the author's voice and the audience, and of the writer and the writer's identity respectively.

Whilst there is now a substantial body of research that elucidates the use of self-mention in the genre of academic writing in English (Hyland 2008; McGrath 2016), self-mention in computer-mediated discourse (CMD) has attracted comparatively less scholarly attention (Malenkina, Ivanov 2018). Following Herring and Androutsopoulos (2015), CMD is understood here as a form of human communication produced by 'transmitting messages via networked or mobile computers, where 'computers' are defined broadly to include any digital communication device' (Herring, Androutsopoulos 2015: 127). Recently, however, a growing number of studies have begun to examine how self-mention operates in a variety of web-based settings, including online teaching and learning (Zhu, Herring, Bonk 2019), research project websites (Lorés-Sanz, Herrando-Rodrigo 2020), tourist websites (Malenkina, Ivanov 2018), and business websites (Pérez 2014). Zhu, Herring, and Bonk (2019) demonstrate that students' social presence in Internet-based university courses is often manifested through the first person singular pronoun I. In contrast, Lorés-Sanz and Herrando-Rodrigo (2020) find that we is the most frequent form of self-mention on research project websites, where it may refer to a project, an institution, or a group of researchers. Similarly, Malenkina and Ivanov (2018) report that self-mentions on English-mediated official tourist websites in Spain are 'almost entirely displayed through the use of the first person plural' (Malenkina, Ivanov 2018: 212), whilst Pérez (2014) shows that business websites in the USA are characterised by a markedly more frequent use of the first person singular than their Spanish counterparts.

A further dimension relevant to the study of self-mention in CMD concerns the varieties and status of English worldwide. The present study is informed by the model that represents English as a system of Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles (Kachru 1985; see also Bruthiaux 2003; Bolton et al. 2006). This distinction is of particular interest in national contexts such as Estonia, where universities negotiate the interplay between the national language and English as an international language of research and higher education (Soler et al. 2017; van Doorslaer, Loogus 2020). University websites themselves constitute a distinctive genre of CMD, unified, as Tomášková (2015: 79) observes, by 'a common communicative purpose – presenting the institution and promoting it', and shaped by culture-specific and language-specific features.

Although research on self-mention in CMD is expanding (Lorés-Sanz, Herrando-Rodrigo 2020; Malenkina, Ivanov 2018; Pérez 2014; Zhu, Herring, Bonk 2019), relatively little is known about how self-mention is deployed on the sections of university websites that present the respective institution's research activities (Lorés-Sanz, Herrando-Rodrigo 2020). In particular, to the best of the author's knowledge, there are no studies that examine the use of self-mention in the research sections of websites belonging to leading universities in the United Kingdom, as a representative of the Inner Circle of English, and Estonia, which is associated with the Expanding Circle. This is a notable gap, given both the promotional communicative purpose of such websites and the potential influence of the differing status of English across the Circles on the discursive means of self-representation.

Accordingly, the present study sets out to investigate how self-mention is represented in the research sections of the official websites of the University of Cambridge (UC) in the UK and the University of Tartu (UT) in Estonia, both of which are currently ranked as the leading universities in their respective countries (Times Higher Education 2020). It is hypothesised that there would be quantitative differences in the use of self-mention depending on whether a university is associated with the Expanding Circle (Estonia) or the Inner Circle (the UK). At the same time, it is not precluded that UT, as a prestigious and well-established institution with extensive discursive practices of CMD and access to norm-bearing English (Bolton et al. 2006), might display patterns of self-mention similar to those of UC. To address these premises, the study is guided by two research questions: first, what are the most frequent discursive means of self-mention in the research sections of the websites of UC and UT; and second, are there differences and/or similarities in the frequency of self-mention use between UC, as a representative of the Inner Circle, and UT, as a representative of the Expanding Circle? Drawing on a corpus of research-section texts collected from the two universities' websites, the study employs a quantitative analysis, including normalisation of the data and a one-way analysis of variance, in order to reveal new information about self-mention on university research websites in Estonia and the UK.

intros.text:
The global expansion of the English language has led to its adoption as the primary medium for international academic communication and institutional promotion. In the context of higher education, university websites serve as critical digital interfaces where institutions construct their public identities and project their research capabilities to a global audience. As these institutions seek to increase their international visibility and attract researchers and students, the language policies they adopt—specifically regarding the use of English—reflect a complex interplay between global standards and local cultural identities (Soler et al., 2017). In Estonia, for instance, the use of English in higher education is often a pragmatic response to globalization and the need to accommodate an international audience while maintaining national linguistic priorities (van Doorslaer & Loogus, 2020). This linguistic landscape is further shaped by the institutional drive to standardize proficiency and evaluation to ensure competitiveness in a global market (Alas & Liiv, 2009).

To understand the sociolinguistic dynamics of English worldwide, scholars have frequently employed the model of the Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles proposed by Kachru (1985). According to this framework, the Inner Circle comprises countries where English is the primary native language (e.g., the UK), while the Expanding Circle includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language for international communication (e.g., Estonia). While this model has been criticized for its historical and political foundations and its tendency to overlook internal variation within locales (Bruthiaux, 2003), it remains a useful shorthand for analyzing how different linguistic backgrounds influence the discursive practices of English-mediated communication (Bolton et al., 2006).

One of the most significant discursive markers of authorial identity in any written text is self-mention. Defined as an explicit reference to the author or authors through markers such as 'I', 'my', 'we', or 'our', self-mention allows writers to project their presence and establish a specific relationship with the reader (Hyland, 2001). In academic discourse, these markers are not merely grammatical choices but rhetorical devices used to emphasize contributions to a field and construct an authoritative professional self (Hyland, 2001). Because the conventions of personal projection are powerful means of self-representation, the choice between the first-person singular ('I') and the first-person plural ('we') often reflects genre-specific expectations and cultural norms (Hyland, 2008).

With the rise of computer-mediated discourse (CMD), the study of self-mention has expanded beyond traditional research articles to include digital platforms. University websites, as a specific genre of CMD, are characterized by a dual purpose: they must provide factual information about the institution while simultaneously promoting its brand and prestige (Tomášková, 2015). The integration of Web 2.0 technologies has further transformed how universities communicate, shifting toward more interactive and socialized forms of online presence (Virkus, 2008). Within these digital spaces, the way an institution refers to itself—whether as a collection of individual experts or as a unified collective entity—can signal different institutional values and cultural orientations.

Despite the abundance of research on self-mention in traditional academic writing, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding its use in the research-specific sections of university websites. While some studies have explored self-mention in online courses or general business websites, the specific discursive strategies used by leading research universities to present their scientific activities remain under-examined. There is particular interest in whether these strategies differ based on the university's position within Kachru's circles. For example, the preference for individualised versus collective self-representation may be influenced by the cultural and linguistic conventions of the Inner Circle versus the Expanding Circle of English.

Given this gap, the present study aims to investigate and compare the patterns of self-mention in the research sections of the official websites of the University of Cambridge (UK) and the University of Tartu (Estonia). These two institutions represent the leading universities in their respective countries and serve as representatives of the Inner and Expanding Circles of English, respectively. By employing a quantitative analysis of self-mention markers, this research seeks to determine whether there are statistically significant differences in how these universities project their authorial identity in a digital environment.

It is hypothesised that the use of self-mention will vary according to the circle of English associated with the institution, reflecting distinct culture-specific and language-specific presentational purposes. Specifically, it is expected that the UK-based institution may exhibit different preferences for first-person pronouns compared to the Estonian institution, though it is also possible that a convergence toward global academic norms may result in similar patterns. To explore these possibilities, the study addresses two primary research questions: First, what are the most frequent discursive means of self-mention in the research sections of the websites of the University of Cambridge and the University of Tartu? Second, are there significant differences or similarities in the frequency of self-mention use between these two universities, reflecting their respective positions in the Inner and Expanding Circles of English?

intros.text:
The proliferation of digital communication has fundamentally transformed the way academic institutions project their identity and engage with global stakeholders. In the contemporary higher education landscape, university websites serve as primary interfaces for institutional promotion, acting as multimodal landscapes that unify a common communicative purpose: presenting the institution to the world and promoting its academic prestige (Tomááková, 2015). Within these digital spaces, the research section is of particular importance, as it communicates the university's intellectual contributions, its capacity for innovation, and its standing within the global scientific community. Consequently, the linguistic choices employed in these sections are not merely functional but are strategic rhetorical tools used to construct a specific institutional persona.

One of the most significant rhetorical devices in the construction of authorial presence is self-mention. Defined as the explicit reference to the author or authors through markers such as 'I/my' or 'we/our', self-mention allows writers to emphasize their contributions to a discourse and construct an authoritative discoursal self (Hyland & Tse, 2004; Martínez, 2005). In the realm of academic discourse, Hyland (2001) argues that the use of first-person pronouns is a powerful means of self-representation, signaling the writer's identity and their relationship with the audience. Because any form of writing carries implicit information about the writer, the conventions governing personal projection are essential for understanding how authority and community are negotiated in professional texts.

Historically, much of the scholarship on self-mention has focused on traditional academic genres, such as research articles (Hyland, 2001, 2008; McGrath, 2016). However, the shift toward computer-mediated discourse (CMD) has opened new avenues for linguistic inquiry. CMD, which encompasses human communication transmitted via networked digital devices (Herring & Androutsopoulos, 2015), demands a different set of rhetorical strategies than print-based academic writing. Recent studies have begun to explore self-mention in various CMD contexts, including online teaching and learning (Zhu, Herring & Bonk, 2019), business websites (Pérez, 2014), and tourist portals (Malenkina & Ivanov, 2018). These inquiries suggest that the choice between the first-person singular ('I') and plural ('we') often reflects broader cultural and professional norms. For instance, Pérez (2014) found a prevalence of 'I' on US business websites compared to those in Spain, suggesting that self-representation in CMD is influenced by national and cultural orientations.

Such variations in language use can be analyzed through the lens of World Englishes, particularly the model proposed by Kachru (1985), which categorizes the spread of English into the Inner, Outer, and Expanding Circles. The Inner Circle comprises countries where English is the primary native language, such as the United Kingdom, while the Expanding Circle includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language for international communication, such as Estonia. While the Kachruvian model has been critiqued for its political and historical foundations (Bruthiaux, 2003), it remains a useful shorthand for identifying broad patterns in the use of English globally (Bolton et al., 2006). In the context of Estonia, the role of English in higher education has become increasingly prominent as universities seek internationalization while simultaneously maintaining national linguistic identities (Soler et al., 2017; Lazdińa & Marten, 2018). The tension between global English standards and local cultural backgrounds often manifests in the way Estonian institutions translate and present their activities to an international audience (van Doorslaer & Loogus, 2020).

Despite the growing body of research on self-mention in CMD, a significant gap remains in our understanding of how these markers are used specifically within the research sections of university websites. While some studies have touched upon research project websites (Lorés-Sanz & Herrando-Rodrigo, 2020), there is a lack of comparative data addressing the discursive differences between universities in the Inner Circle and those in the Expanding Circle. Specifically, it remains unclear whether the promotional and presentational goals of leading universities lead to a convergence in the use of self-mention, or if distinct culture-specific and language-specific preferences persist. To date, no comprehensive study has contrasted the research-related digital discourse of a leading UK institution with that of a leading Estonian institution to determine how authorial presence is constructed across these different linguistic circles.

The present study aims to fill this gap by investigating the representation of self-mention in the research sections of the official websites of the University of Cambridge (representing the UK/Inner Circle) and the University of Tartu (representing Estonia/Expanding Circle). By employing a quantitative analysis of these two corpora, the research seeks to answer two primary questions: First, what are the most frequent discursive means of self-mention used on these websites? Second, are there significant differences or similarities in the frequency of these markers between the Inner Circle and Expanding Circle representatives?

It is hypothesized that while both universities may utilize certain common markers to signal a professional research community, there will be quantitative differences rooted in their respective positions within the circles of English. Specifically, the study explores whether the University of Cambridge employs a more personalized, 'I-centered' narrative—consistent with Inner Circle preferences—compared to the more collective 'we-centered' approach likely found at the University of Tartu. By addressing these questions, this study offers a contextualized account of how prestigious universities use self-mention to balance institutional authority with accessibility in a digital environment. The following sections of the article are organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed review of the literature on self-mention and CMD; Section 3 describes the corpus, methodology, and results; and Section 4 discusses the findings and presents the final conclusions.
