intros.text: In the last 40 years, vocabulary has reached an unforeseen position within the field  of  Second  Language  Acquisition  after  years  of  grammar  supremacy  (Boers  and  Lindstromberg  2009;  Meara  1980;  Milton  and  Fitzpatrick  2014;  Nation  2001;  Schmitt  2010).  Starting  within  the  movement  of  regeneration  towards  exploring  aspects  other  than  grammar  in  language  learning,  vocabulary  was  considered  central to mastering a second language  For this reason, a large body of research on  aspects  directly  related  to  vocabulary  learning,  such  as  frequency  (Coxhead  2000;  Nation  2001;  Schmitt  2010),  testing  (Laufer  and  Nation  1999;  Meara  2010;  Schmitt,  Schmitt  and  Claphman  2001)  or  the  implications  of  word  knowledge  (Anderson and Freebody 1981; Meara 1996a), has been carried out. In this context, studies on vocabulary learning strategies emerged as a response to the need to understand how vocabulary is learnt. Language learning strategies had already been explored for nearly twenty years from a psycholinguistic perspective (Bialystok 1978; O’Malley and Chamot 1990; Oxford 1990) when they started to be applied to vocabulary  This field of study aimed at identifying the most beneficial actions or behaviours that language learners took when learning a new language and  their  findings  had  already  materialized  into  a  number  of  taxonomies  and  principles.  Language  learning  strategies,  and,  consequently,  vocabulary  learning  strategies, seem to be teachable actions and their selection seems to be influenced by  a  number  of  different  aspects,  such  as  the  foreign  language  studied  or  the  language learning approaches used.  It is in line with this latter idea that the present study has been conceptualized, as  it  can  clearly  be  used  to  approach  the  new  language  teaching  proposals  put  forward  in  recent  times.  In  the  last  fifteen  years,  a  new  language  learning  approach  has  come  to  Spain.  This  approach,  known  as  Content  and  Language  Integrated Learning (CLIL), promotes the use of a foreign language as a vehicle of communication in content subjects. To achieve full development of contents and language,  new  teaching  techniques  are  proposed  and  new  objectives  are  set.  In  the case of vocabulary learning, research has shown that the use of CLIL seems to benefit  vocabulary  development.  Therefore,  if  there  is  a  modification  in  the  way  language  is  conceived  and  this  resonates  with  the  vocabulary  learnt,  could  it  be  that CLIL also affects the way learners learn vocabulary?  This  paper  is  organized  as  follows.  First,  it  deals  with  theoretical  aspects  regarding  vocabulary  learning  strategies  and  their  possible  relation  to  CLIL,  including  a  short  account  of  what  CLIL  involves.  After  that,  the  methodology  followed will be explained.  To do so, the research questions, the sample, and the instruments will be detailed. Then, the data obtained from the Vocabulary Learning Strategies questionnaire (adapted from Schmitt 1997) are presented, administered to  two  groups  of  year  9  secondary  school  learners  from  Extremadura  (a  CLIL  group and a mainstream EFL [English as a Foreign Language] group). These data are  examined,  looking  at  the  difference  in  the  selection  of  vocabulary  learning  strategies between both group

intros.text:
The acquisition of vocabulary has long been recognised as a cornerstone of foreign language learning, with lexical competence considered essential to the full mastery of a second or foreign language (Meara, 1980; Nation, 2001). Word knowledge is a multidimensional construct that encompasses not only recognising and recalling meanings but also using words appropriately in receptive and productive modes (Laufer & Nation, 1999; Milton & Fitzpatrick, 2014). Given the sheer volume of lexis that learners must acquire, and the impossibility of teaching every item explicitly, considerable attention has been directed towards the strategies learners deploy to discover and consolidate word meanings for themselves. The study of vocabulary learning strategies emerged from broader research on language learning strategies (Bialystok, 1978; O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990) and has since generated a rich body of work devoted to identifying, classifying and understanding these strategies (Schmitt & Schmitt, 1993; Schmitt, 2010; Nation, 2001).

Within this line of enquiry, a central concern has been to explain what governs learners' selection of particular strategies. It is widely acknowledged that strategy choice is shaped by a range of factors relating to learners' language background, their individual characteristics, and the instructional context in which they learn. Two aspects of the teaching context have attracted particular attention: the nature of the language task and the language teaching method. While a good deal of research has examined how strategy use varies across tasks associated with the four skills, comparatively little work has explored the influence of the broader instructional approach on the actions learners take to learn vocabulary.

This gap is especially salient in light of the spread of Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) across Europe. In CLIL settings, foreign languages are used as the medium for teaching curricular content, so that language development becomes a vehicle for, rather than the exclusive goal of, learning. Research conducted in Spain has repeatedly reported lexical advantages for CLIL learners over their mainstream English as a Foreign Language (EFL) counterparts (Agustín-Llach & Canga Alonso, 2016; Canga Alonso, 2015), although such differences may be at least partly attributable to the greater amount of exposure to English that CLIL programmes afford. Crucially, most of this research has concentrated on learning outcomes—the vocabulary learners come to know—while neglecting the processes and strategies through which that knowledge is built. Where CLIL learners' strategy use has been examined, strategies have generally been approached from a communicative perspective, as devices for compensating for gaps in knowledge, rather than as tools for facilitating vocabulary learning.

The present study addresses this shortfall by shifting the focus from the learning product to the learning process. Rather than measuring how much vocabulary CLIL and mainstream EFL learners know, it investigates whether and how the instructional approach shapes the vocabulary learning strategies that secondary-school learners select. Drawing on data from 138 Year 9 learners in Extremadura, and adapting Schmitt's (Schmitt & Schmitt, 1993) widely used taxonomy, the study pursues two questions: whether secondary-school learners show a preference for particular vocabulary learning strategies, and whether their selection of strategies differs according to the type of instruction they receive. In so doing, it seeks to develop and compare distinct learner profiles and to consider their implications for vocabulary development.

intros.text:
Vocabulary has long been acknowledged as a cornerstone of foreign language learning, and its mastery is now widely regarded as essential to achieving full command of a second language (Laufer & Nation, 1999; Meara, 1980; Schmitt, 2010). Within this broad concern, considerable attention has been devoted since the 1990s to the strategies learners deploy to acquire and consolidate new lexical items (Gu & Johnson, 1996; Nation, 2001; Schmitt & Schmitt, 1993). The study of vocabulary learning strategies grew out of the incorporation of strategic competence into the notion of communicative competence (Canale & Swain, 1980) and, subsequently, from the transfer of the concept of learning strategies from psychology into applied linguistics (Bialystok, 1978; O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). As the field matured, the focus shifted from communicative tactics for overcoming gaps in knowledge towards the actions learners take to manage and facilitate their own learning, and vocabulary learning strategies came to be defined as the mechanisms and steps used to discover, retain, recall and use new words (Jimu00e9nez Catalu00e1n, 2003).

Much of this research has pursued two lines of enquiry: the identification and classification of strategies into taxonomies, of which Schmitt's (1997) remains the most widely used, and the exploration of the factors that shape strategy selection. It is generally accepted that the choice of vocabulary learning strategies is conditioned by learners' background, individual characteristics and the teaching context (Oxford & Nyikos, 1989). Within the teaching context, two elements have received particular attention: the demands of the language task and the language teaching method. A considerable amount of work has examined how strategy use varies across tasks aimed at developing the four skills (Bialystok, 1981; Vandergrift, 1997). To the best of my knowledge, however, most of this effort has concentrated on skill-specific tasks, while comparatively little research has addressed the impact of a more general and arguably more influential variable: the overall language teaching approach.

This gap is especially salient in relation to Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), an approach that has spread rapidly across Europe and that uses the foreign language as the medium for teaching academic content. Studies conducted in the Spanish context have repeatedly reported that CLIL learners tend to outperform their mainstream EFL counterparts in vocabulary size (Agustu00edn-Llach & Canga Alonso, 2016; Canga Alonso, 2015; Castellano-Risco, 2018). Yet this research has focused almost exclusively on the learning product—the words learners know—while neglecting the process, that is, how the implementation of CLIL affects the very actions learners take to learn vocabulary. Where CLIL learners' strategies have been examined at all, they have generally been approached from a communicative perspective, as devices for compensating for lack of language rather than as tools for facilitating learning (Azkarai & Imaz Aguirre, 2016; Martu00ednez Adriu00e1n et al., 2019).

The present study seeks to fill this gap by shifting the focus from vocabulary known to vocabulary learning strategies used, and by comparing the strategy profiles of CLIL and mainstream EFL secondary-school learners. It addresses two questions: whether these learners show a preference for particular vocabulary learning strategies, and whether their selection differs according to the type of instruction to which they are exposed. In doing so, it also reconsiders the internal coherence of Schmitt's (1997) taxonomy in light of empirical data.

intros.text:
The acquisition of a comprehensive vocabulary is widely recognised as a fundamental pillar for achieving mastery of a foreign language (Meara, 1980; Nation, 2001). Because lexical competence is critical for communicative success, researchers have long sought to understand the mechanisms learners employ to acquire, retain, and retrieve new words. Central to this investigation is the concept of language learning strategies, which emerged from broader theories of strategic competence and second language acquisition models that distinguish between obligatory learning processes and optional strategies selected by the learner (Bialystok, 1978; O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). Within this framework, vocabulary learning strategies (VLS) refer to the specific actions students take to determine the meaning of unknown words and consolidate that knowledge in long-term memory (Nation, 2001).

Extensive research has been dedicated to identifying and classifying these strategies, with taxonomies such as those proposed by Schmitt (1993) providing a structured way to analyse how learners engage with lexical input. While some studies have highlighted the efficacy of morphological awareness—such as the use of prefixes and suffixes—in enhancing reading comprehension and vocabulary growth (Anderson et al., 1981), others have explored the role of repetition, dictionary use, and social interaction in the learning process (Schmitt, 1993; Nation, 2001). It is generally acknowledged that the selection of these strategies is not random but is influenced by various factors, including learner characteristics, the nature of the linguistic task, and the instructional environment (Oxford & Nyikos, 1989).

In recent years, the European educational landscape has seen the rise of Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), an approach where a foreign language is used as the medium for teaching non-language subjects. CLIL aims to integrate language development with academic content, potentially offering a more immersive and cognitively demanding environment than traditional English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction. While previous research has indicated that CLIL learners often outperform mainstream EFL learners in terms of vocabulary size and general proficiency (Canga Alonso, 2015), there is a paucity of research examining how this specific instructional approach influences the *process* of learning—specifically, the selection of vocabulary learning strategies.

Most existing studies on strategy use in CLIL have focused on communicative strategies used to compensate for linguistic gaps rather than the cognitive and metacognitive strategies used to acquire new lexicon. Consequently, there remains a gap in the literature regarding whether the systemic differences between CLIL and EFL environments lead to distinct learner profiles in terms of VLS. The present study seeks to address this gap by comparing the vocabulary learning strategies employed by secondary-school learners in CLIL and mainstream EFL programmes. By doing so, this research aims to determine if the instructional approach significantly impacts the strategies learners choose to develop their lexical competence.

intros.text:
The acquisition of a robust vocabulary is widely recognized as a cornerstone of achieving full mastery of a foreign language (Meara, 1980; Nation, 2001). Consequently, a substantial body of research has emerged focusing on vocabulary learning strategies—the specific actions and mechanisms students employ to discover the meaning of unknown words and retain them in long-term memory. This field has evolved significantly since the late 20th century, transitioning from a broad conceptualization of strategic competence as a means of compensating for communication breakdowns (Canale & Swain, 1980) to a more nuanced understanding of learning strategies as cognitive tools used to control the learning process (O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). Central to this evolution has been the development of taxonomies, most notably that of Schmitt (1997), which provides a comprehensive framework for classifying the diverse ways learners approach lexical acquisition.

While previous research has extensively explored the relationship between strategy selection and specific linguistic tasks—such as reading or listening—little attention has been paid to the impact of the overarching language teaching approach. In the European context, the implementation of Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has revolutionized instructional practice by using a foreign language to teach academic content. While existing studies have frequently demonstrated that CLIL learners outperform mainstream English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in terms of vocabulary size (Canga Alonso, 2015), it remains unclear whether these gains are a direct result of the CLIL methodology or simply a consequence of increased exposure to the target language. Furthermore, while some studies have touched upon CLIL learners' strategies, they have predominantly viewed them from a communicative perspective—as tools to overcome a lack of knowledge—rather than as systematic learning strategies designed to facilitate lexical growth.

Therefore, there is a pressing need to investigate how the instructional framework specifically influences the selection of vocabulary learning strategies. The present study aims to fill this gap by comparing the strategy profiles of secondary-school learners in CLIL and mainstream EFL programs. Specifically, the research seeks to answer two primary questions: first, whether secondary-school learners show a general preference for specific vocabulary learning strategies; and second, whether the selection of these strategies differs significantly depending on the type of instruction the learners are exposed to. By moving beyond the final learning product (vocabulary knowledge) to examine the learning process itself, this study offers a contextualized account of how different teaching approaches shape the cognitive actions learners take to acquire new words. The findings may provide valuable implications for the development of teaching materials and instructional strategies tailored to the needs of diverse learner profiles.

intros.text:
Since the 1990s, vocabulary learning strategies (VLS) have emerged as a central topic in applied linguistics, reflecting a broader shift towards understanding the cognitive processes underlying second language acquisition (O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). Initially conceptualized as part of strategic competence within communicative competence models (Canale & Swain, 1980), the focus has gradually shifted from compensatory communication tactics to specific actions learners take to control their own learning processes (Wenden & Rubin, 1987). This evolution coincided with a growing recognition of the pivotal role vocabulary plays in achieving language proficiency (Laufer, 1990; Nation, 2001). Consequently, VLS are now defined as the specific mechanisms and actions employed by learners to discover meanings, retain words in long-term memory, and utilize them effectively (Jiménez Catalán, 2003). 

Despite the substantial body of research identifying and classifying these strategies, such as Schmitt’s widely adopted taxonomy (1997), significant gaps remain regarding the factors influencing their selection. While scholars have acknowledged that strategy use is contingent upon learner characteristics and language background (Oxford & Nyikos, 1989), less attention has been paid to the impact of the instructional context. Existing literature has predominantly explored the relationship between strategies and specific language tasks, such as reading or listening (Bialystok, 1981; Vandergrift, 1997), or the efficacy of the strategies themselves (Gu & Johnson, 1996). However, the influence of the broader language teaching approach on the selection of VLS remains underexplored. 

This gap is particularly relevant in the context of Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), an educational approach that has gained significant traction in Europe over recent decades. Unlike traditional English as a Foreign Language (EFL) programs, where the primary goal is language development, CLIL utilizes the foreign language as a medium for teaching academic content (Coyle, 2007). This shift in focus has been shown to yield benefits in lexical development, with studies indicating that CLIL learners often outperform their mainstream EFL peers in vocabulary size (Agustín-Llach, 2012; Canga Alonso, 2015). Nevertheless, much of this research has focused on the learning product—the vocabulary acquired—rather than the learning process. Specifically, it remains unclear how the distinct pedagogical environment of CLIL influences the specific strategies learners employ to acquire this vocabulary. 

While some studies have examined CLIL learners' strategy use, they have often viewed strategies through a communicative lens, focusing on how learners overcome communication breakdowns rather than how they facilitate vocabulary learning (Martínez Adrián et al., 2019). Furthermore, previous comparisons often confound the variable of instructional approach with the variable of exposure time, as CLIL learners typically receive significantly more input (Castellano-Risco, 2018). To address these limitations, this study investigates the selection of vocabulary learning strategies among secondary-school learners in Spain, comparing those in CLIL programmes with those in mainstream EFL settings. By isolating the impact of the instructional approach, this research aims to determine whether the pedagogical context shapes the strategic profiles of learners. Specifically, it seeks to answer two research questions: (1) Do secondary-school learners show a preference for specific vocabulary learning strategies? and (2) Does the selection of these strategies differ depending on the type of instruction learners are exposed to? The findings provide critical insights into how instructional design influences learner autonomy and strategic behaviour in vocabulary acquisition.

intros.text:
Vocabulary learning has long been recognized as a critical component of second language acquisition, with lexical competence often cited as a prerequisite for successful communication. In recent decades, research has increasingly focused on the mechanisms learners employ to acquire and retain new words, shifting attention from mere vocabulary size to the processes underlying vocabulary development. This shift has given rise to the study of vocabulary learning strategies (VLS), defined as the specific actions learners take to discover, retain, and recall new vocabulary. Since the 1990s, a substantial body of research has conceptualized and investigated these strategies, drawing on frameworks from cognitive psychology and applied linguistics (O'Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). Prominent taxonomies, such as Schmitt's (1997), have provided structured ways to categorize these strategies into groups like determination, social, memory, and cognitive strategies, offering a foundation for empirical inquiry.

Despite the extensive literature on VLS, much of the existing research has concentrated on identifying which strategies are used or how they correlate with proficiency levels. Less attention has been paid to the contextual factors that influence the selection of these strategies, particularly the language teaching approach. While studies have explored how specific tasks—such as reading or listening—affect strategy use (Bialystok, 1981; Vandergrift, 1997), the impact of broader instructional methodologies remains under-examined. This gap is particularly relevant in the context of Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL), an approach that has gained significant traction in European educational systems. CLIL integrates language learning with content subject instruction, thereby increasing learners' exposure to the target language in authentic contexts. Although CLIL has been shown to positively impact vocabulary size (Agustín-Llach & Canga Alonso, 2016; Canga Alonso, 2015), the extent to which this instructional model influences the specific strategies learners employ to acquire vocabulary remains unclear.

Existing studies comparing CLIL and mainstream English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners have primarily focused on outcomes, such as vocabulary breadth or grammatical accuracy, rather than the learning processes themselves. Furthermore, previous investigations into CLIL learners' strategies have often examined communicative strategies used to overcome breakdowns in interaction, rather than the cognitive and metacognitive strategies used for vocabulary acquisition. Consequently, there is a need to investigate how the distinct pedagogical environment of CLIL shapes the selection of vocabulary learning strategies compared to traditional EFL instruction.

This study aims to address this gap by examining the vocabulary learning strategies employed by secondary-school learners in two different instructional contexts: CLIL and mainstream EFL. Specifically, it seeks to answer two research questions: (1) Do secondary-school learners show any preference for specific vocabulary learning strategies? and (2) Does the selection of vocabulary learning strategies differ depending on the type of instruction learners are exposed to? By comparing the strategy profiles of 138 learners, this research provides insights into how instructional approaches influence vocabulary learning behaviors. The findings offer implications for vocabulary pedagogy, suggesting that teaching methods may play a pivotal role in shaping the strategic competence of language learners.

intros.text:
Vocabulary knowledge is widely recognised as a central component of second and foreign language learning. Without sufficient lexical resources, learners’ ability to comprehend input, express meanings, and participate in academic or communicative tasks is severely constrained. For this reason, vocabulary has moved from a relatively marginal position in language teaching research to a core area of inquiry concerned not only with how many words learners know, but also with the depth, organisation, and use of that knowledge (Coady, 1996; Laufer & Nation, 1999; Milton & Fitzpatrick, 2014; Nation, 2001; Schmitt, 2010). Research on vocabulary size and levels has provided valuable tools for assessing lexical development (Meara, 2010; Schmitt et al., 2001), while work on academic vocabulary and lexical approaches has shown the importance of selecting, recycling, and processing words in meaningful ways (Boers & Lindstromberg, 2009; Coxhead, 2000). However, knowing which words learners acquire is only one part of the picture. It is also necessary to understand how learners attempt to learn, remember, and use new vocabulary.

This concern links vocabulary research to the broader field of language learning strategies. Early models of second language learning emphasised that learners differ not only in aptitude, exposure, or motivation, but also in the optional procedures they use to process and store linguistic information (Bialystok, 1978). Subsequent work on learning strategies highlighted the role of deliberate actions through which learners regulate their learning, solve problems, and compensate for gaps in knowledge (O’Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). Within this framework, vocabulary learning strategies can be understood as the specific techniques learners employ to discover the meaning of unfamiliar words, consolidate them in memory, retrieve them when needed, and integrate them into language use (Nation, 2001; Schmitt & Schmitt, 1993). These strategies may include analysing word parts, using dictionaries, asking others for help, repeating or writing words, creating associations, using imagery, or encountering words through media and reading.

A major contribution to this area has been the classification of vocabulary learning strategies. Schmitt and Schmitt (1993) and later Schmitt (1997) organised strategies according to whether they are used for discovering meanings or consolidating known words, and according to the cognitive, metacognitive, memory, determination, and social processes involved. Such taxonomies have been influential because they offer researchers and teachers a practical framework for describing learners’ strategic behaviour. Nevertheless, strategy use is not fixed. Learners’ choices may vary according to age, proficiency, language background, task demands, instructional experience, and the opportunities for language use provided by the learning environment. For instance, strategies based on morphological analysis may be especially relevant when learners are encouraged to attend to prefixes, suffixes, roots, and word families (Anderson et al., 1981), whereas strategies based on repetition or word lists may reflect more traditional classroom routines.

One instructional context in which vocabulary learning may be shaped in distinctive ways is Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL). In CLIL programmes, a foreign language is used as a medium for learning curricular content, thereby increasing learners’ exposure to the language and placing vocabulary in meaningful subject-based contexts. In contrast with mainstream EFL instruction, where language itself is the primary object of study, CLIL requires learners to use English to access information, understand explanations, interact with teachers and peers, and complete academic tasks. This difference may affect not only the amount of vocabulary acquired, but also the strategies learners develop for dealing with unfamiliar lexis. Learners in CLIL settings may be expected to rely more on contextual inference, lexical analysis, interaction, and exposure to authentic or semi-authentic input, whereas mainstream EFL learners may depend more heavily on translation, repetition, or decontextualised memorisation.

Although CLIL research has frequently reported advantages in learners’ vocabulary development, less attention has been paid to the strategic processes that may underlie these outcomes. In particular, it remains unclear whether learners exposed to CLIL and those in mainstream EFL programmes differ in the vocabulary learning strategies they report using. Addressing this issue can contribute to a more process-oriented understanding of lexical development and can inform vocabulary pedagogy in both bilingual and foreign language classrooms. The present study therefore investigates the vocabulary learning strategies reported by Spanish secondary-school learners, comparing students enrolled in CLIL programmes with peers receiving mainstream EFL instruction. Specifically, it examines learners’ general preferences for particular strategies and explores whether the type of instructional programme is associated with different patterns of strategy selection.

intros.text:
Vocabulary knowledge is widely recognised as a central component of second and foreign language development. Without a sufficiently large and well-organised lexicon, learners’ ability to comprehend input, express meanings, and participate in academic or everyday communication is seriously constrained. For this reason, vocabulary has occupied a prominent place in second language acquisition and language teaching research, with studies addressing vocabulary size, depth of word knowledge, productive lexical ability, and the pedagogical conditions that foster lexical growth (Coady, 1996; Laufer & Nation, 1999; Milton & Fitzpatrick, 2014; Nation, 2001; Schmitt, 2010). Alongside this concern with lexical outcomes, increasing attention has been paid to the processes through which learners acquire, store, retrieve, and use new words.

One important line of enquiry has focused on vocabulary learning strategies, understood as the actions and techniques learners employ to discover the meaning of unfamiliar lexical items and to consolidate them for later use. This interest emerged from broader work on language learning strategies, in which learners were viewed as active agents who make choices about how to process input, practise language, and compensate for gaps in knowledge (Bialystok, 1978; O’Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990). In the specific domain of vocabulary, strategy research has attempted to identify the procedures learners use when encountering new words, to classify these procedures, and to evaluate their perceived usefulness. Schmitt and Schmitt (1993), for instance, distinguished strategies for initially discovering word meaning from those used to remember and practise known meanings, a distinction later developed in Schmitt’s taxonomy of vocabulary learning strategies.

Research in this area has shown that learners do not select strategies randomly. Their choices may be shaped by individual characteristics, proficiency level, previous learning experiences, task demands, and the instructional context in which language learning takes place. Some strategies, such as repetition, dictionary use, word lists, inference from context, or analysis of word parts, have been reported frequently in earlier studies, although their usefulness may vary depending on the learners’ first language, age, level of proficiency, and learning goals. Moreover, approaches to teaching may encourage particular ways of engaging with vocabulary. A classroom centred on explicit language practice may promote strategies different from those fostered in contexts where learners use the foreign language to access subject content.

Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) provides a particularly relevant context in which to examine this issue. In CLIL programmes, a foreign language is used not only as an object of study but also as a medium for learning curricular content. This dual focus increases learners’ exposure to the target language and may require them to engage with vocabulary in more varied, contextualised, and cognitively demanding ways than in mainstream English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction. Previous research has often reported advantages for CLIL learners in aspects of lexical development, yet much of this work has concentrated on vocabulary outcomes, such as the number of words known, rather than on the strategic behaviour that may underlie vocabulary learning.

Thus, although vocabulary learning strategies have been extensively investigated, comparatively little is known about whether learners exposed to different instructional approaches select different strategies for learning vocabulary. In particular, the possible effect of CLIL, as opposed to mainstream EFL instruction, on secondary-school learners’ strategic choices remains underexplored. Addressing this gap can contribute to a better understanding of how teaching contexts shape lexical learning processes and may also inform classroom practices aimed at promoting more effective vocabulary development.

The present study examines the reported use of vocabulary learning strategies by secondary-school learners in Spain and compares the strategy profiles of learners enrolled in CLIL programmes with those following mainstream EFL instruction. Specifically, it asks whether learners show preferences for particular vocabulary learning strategies and whether these preferences differ according to instructional approach. To this end, CLIL and EFL learners completed a vocabulary learning strategies questionnaire adapted from Schmitt’s taxonomy, and their responses were analysed both at the level of individual strategies and broader strategy groupings.

intros.text: Mobile apps have the potential to support collaboration in the task  of documenting and conserving endangered languages, even in places where network  connectivity is limited or nonexistent. Apps can support diverse tasks: collecting  metadata, recording linguistic performances, eliciting responses to prompts, tracking documentary workflows, and so forth. In particular, the touch-screen interface is  helpful for crafting tools that support diverse forms of collaboration.  There is scarcely need to elaborate on the utility of mobile apps, but what of  their potential for supporting fieldwork?  One approach is for a user to download  and operate a language app autonomously and undertake remote language work.  This is a form of crowdsourcing (Malone et al. 2010).  However, we are concerned  not with anonymous crowds but rather small-scale personalised interactions with  local participants in remote locations.  There are no off-the-shelf solutions and little  market for product-like solutions.  Instead, we propose a new form of practice that  integrates purpose-made tools with new tool-using interactions.  Designing and deploying apps for remote indigenous communities presents  unique challenges. Aside from the logistical factors, we must deal with the fact that  technology designs are usually based on assumptions shaped by mainstream audiences. There is a need to establish design ideas and processes leading to tools and  artefacts that make sense for local people and, ultimately, will contribute towards  the agendas and aspirations of local people. We describe a collection of bespoke  apps intended to support collaborative knowledge work with members of the local  community, and a documentary activity to elicit speech data and speaker judgements. We discuss our evolving understanding of this situated interaction design  activity, where fieldworkers, technologists, and community members each have a  vital role to play. Then we  describe the situation in the far north of Australia where our language work takes  place (§3), and establish a grounding for technology/activity design (§4). The following two sections describe the hardware and software components of our ‘BushPi’ solution (§5, 6). We offer a discussion with a focus on the prospects and requirements  of replicating this work elsewhere (§7), and conclude by highlighting the need for  further work on interdisciplinary collaborations (§8)

intros.text:
Fieldwork in linguistics and language documentation is fundamentally collaborative, drawing together researchers and community members to observe, record, and elicit language data (Samarin 1967; Bernard & Gravlee 2014). Increasingly, digital technologies promise to enhance this work through systematisation, automation, and the distribution of tasks. Computer-supported cooperative work has been proposed as a framework for language documentation workflows (Hanke 2017), and crowdsourcing approaches have shown how the intelligence of many participants can be harnessed to accomplish tasks at scale (Malone et al. 2009). Yet much of this promise depends on assumptions - reliable connectivity, individual device ownership, and access to specialised infrastructure - that do not hold in many of the environments where documentary work is most urgently needed.

Remote Indigenous communities in Australia present precisely such a challenge. Telecommunications infrastructure falls far short of that available in urban centres (Papandrea 2010), and many locations lack cellular coverage or reliable power altogether. At the same time, Aboriginal Australians are enthusiastic adopters of mobile technology, using smartphones widely to create and share media (Carew et al. 2015; Featherstone 2013). This combination - familiarity with devices coupled with an absence of network access - motivates a search for self-contained solutions that can support collaborative, concurrent work without depending on the Internet.

Designing such solutions raises questions that go well beyond engineering. Cross-cultural technology design carries the risk of importing flawed assumptions or projecting the designer's own values onto very different audiences (Sun 2012). Established practices of requirements elicitation and user testing (Stone et al. 2005) sit uneasily with the ethics and relational protocols of Indigenous research in Australia (Brereton et al. 2014; Christie 2013). We therefore place engagement and reciprocity first, treating technology prototypes not as finished products but as probes for building relationships and exploring what might work (Hutchinson et al. 2003; Soro et al. 2016; Taylor 2020).

In this article we describe our efforts to support collaborative fieldwork with the Bininj people of West Arnhem Land, speakers of Kunwinjku. We developed BushPi, a portable, battery-powered server and Wi-Fi hotspot, together with Sandboard, a platform for short-lived custom field-tool apps. Across a series of visits we iterated these tools in situ, working alongside community members. We found that custom toolmaking delivers the benefits of digital collaboration tailored to the specific needs of the environment and community. Crucially, however, we argue that it is activity design - the human interactions the tools support - rather than the technology itself that must be foregrounded, placing fieldworkers in the driving seat of innovation in digital fieldwork practice.

intros.text:
Field researchers have long assembled resources into ad hoc processes and workflows to observe, record, and elicit language data (Samarin 1967; Crowley 2007; Bernard & Gravlee 2014). Increasingly, digital technologies promise to systematise and automate these workflows, offering greater efficiency and enabling documentation at a scale that would otherwise be impossible (Liberman 2006). The field of computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW; Grudin 1994), well established in human-computer interaction research, has inspired proposals for computer-supported language documentation (Hanke 2017), and mobile devices in particular have shown enduring promise as tools for data collection on the move (Pascoe et al. 2000). Methodological innovations such as Basic Oral Language Documentation (Bird 2010; Reiman 2010) and their mobile reimplementations, including Aikuma and its successors (Bird et al. 2014; Adda et al. 2016), have demonstrated how local knowledge holders can contribute meaningfully when specialised tasks are appropriately deferred and distributed. Distributed, crowdsourcing-like arrangements can harness the collective effort of many participants (cf. Malone et al. 2009), and applications such as the Dialekt app (Goldman et al. 2014) illustrate the potential of coordinating contributions across many devices.

Yet much of this promise rests on an assumption that is untenable in many field settings: reliable network connectivity. Internet-based crowdsourcing systems are ill suited for remote locations that lack dependable access (Fuchs-Kittowski & Faust 2014), and the telecommunications infrastructure available in Australia's remote Indigenous communities falls far short of that found in urban centres (Papandrea 2010). Moreover, mainstream technology design carries the risk of projecting the values and assumptions of outsiders onto communities whose practices differ markedly (Sun 2012), a problem that established human-centred and participatory design processes only partly address (Muller & Kuhn 1993; Brereton et al. 2014). It remains unclear how digital field tools can be designed and deployed to support genuinely collaborative work under such constraints, and how fieldworkers themselves should relate to the technology they use.

This paper addresses these questions by describing our efforts to support collaborative fieldwork through custom-made mobile apps and portable network infrastructure. Working with the Bininj people of West Arnhem, in remote communities of far northern Australia, we developed BushPi, a self-contained battery-powered server, and Sandboard, a platform for short-lived field tools, and iterated a series of apps in situ over repeated visits. We adopt a research-through-design approach (Zimmerman et al. 2007), placing engagement, reciprocity, and human interaction ahead of the technology itself. We argue that custom toolmaking offers tailored benefits for the specific needs of a community and environment, but that it is activity design, not the technology, that must be foregrounded, positioning fieldworkers as the drivers of innovation in digital fieldwork practice.

intros.text:
The documentation of endangered languages often relies on traditional fieldwork methods of observing, recording, and eliciting, which are frequently organised into ad hoc workflows to suit specific project goals (Samarin, 1967; Bernard & Gravlee, 2014; Crowley, 2007). Despite the potential for digital technologies to increase efficiency through systematisation, many of these processes remain manual, limiting the scale of language documentation (Liberman, 2006). While computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW) has advanced office automation, its application to language conservation is still developing (Grudin, 1994; Hanke, 2017). Efforts to automate large-scale workflows have been attempted, but sustainability remains a challenge (Dunham et al., 2014).

Mobile devices offer a promising avenue for enhancing fieldwork, moving beyond simple data collection to support inclusive, community-based workflows (Pascoe et al., 2000; Bird, 2010). Recent innovations, such as the Aikuma app and the Image-Gesture-Voice method, demonstrate how mobile tools can facilitate complex documentary tasks (Bird et al., 2014; Bettinson & Bird, 2018). Furthermore, the concept of 'crowdsourcing'—harnessing collective intelligence to distribute tasks among many participants (Malone et al., 2009)—presents an opportunity to scale data collection. However, most crowdsourcing systems rely on stable internet connectivity, which is often unavailable in remote field locations (Fuchs-Kittowski & Faust, 2014).

In Australia's remote Indigenous communities, telecommunications infrastructure is often unreliable, necessitating self-contained digital solutions (Papandrea, 2010; Vitos et al., 2017). While Aboriginal Australians are often enthusiastic adopters of mobile technology (Featherstone, 2013; Shaw et al., 2014), the design of tools for these contexts requires a participatory approach that prioritises reciprocity and cultural protocols over standard requirements elicitation (Brereton et al., 2014; Muller & Kuhn, 1993). This suggests a need for 'technology probes'—prototypes used to establish relationships and explore design spaces (Hutchinson et al., 2003; Soro et al., 2016).

In this article, we describe the development and deployment of a portable network infrastructure and a suite of custom mobile apps used in collaborative fieldwork with the Bininj people of Arnhem Land. By focusing on research-through-design, we explore how custom toolmaking can be tailored to the specific needs of a community and its environment. We argue that the success of digital fieldwork depends less on the technology itself and more on the design of the activity, placing the fieldworker and community members at the centre of innovation.

intros.text:
Digital technologies offer significant potential for enhancing the efficiency of linguistic fieldwork through the systematisation and automation of data collection. The concept of computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), while well-established in human-computer interaction research, has traditionally focused on large-scale office automation rather than the unique demands of field environments. However, applying these principles to language documentation can distribute tasks among multiple knowledge holders, reducing the reliance on a single researcher and increasing the scale of documentation (Hanke, 2017). In recent years, mobile devices have emerged as versatile tools for 'on the move' data collection, evolving from early personal digital assistants (Pascoe et al., 2000) to sophisticated apps that implement inclusive workflows like Basic Oral Language Documentation (Bird, 2010; Reiman, 2010). 

Despite these advancements, many existing digital tools rely on stable internet connectivity for crowdsourcing and data synchronization (Fuchs-Kittowski & Faust, 2014). In remote regions, such as the Indigenous communities of northern Australia, telecommunications infrastructure often falls far short of urban standards (Papandrea, 2010). This creates a critical gap: there is a pressing need for self-contained, portable network solutions that support collaborative work and secure data centrally under extreme conditions. Furthermore, standard technology design often follows a rigid process of requirements elicitation and user testing (Stone et al., 2005) that may project outsider values and ignore the specific cultural protocols and social dynamics of Indigenous communities. To move beyond a purely instrumental view of technology, more research is needed into participatory design processes that prioritize reciprocity and relationship-building over mere usability.

This article describes the development and deployment of the BushPi/Sandboard platform—a custom, battery-powered server-in-a-box and a suite of tailored mobile apps—used during collaborative language work with the Bininj people in Arnhem Land, Australia. By adopting a research-through-design (RTD) methodology, we explore how custom toolmaking can be iterated alongside community members to better suit the social and environmental context of the field. We demonstrate that while custom apps can significantly facilitate collaborative documentary tasks, the success of such tools depends more on the design of the human activity than the technology itself. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses the design of digital field tools and activity theory; Section 3 details the BushPi hardware and Sandboard architecture; Section 4 presents the specific apps deployed; and Section 7 provides a discussion on the implications for interdisciplinary fieldwork.

intros.text:
Digital technologies offer transformative potential for language documentation and fieldwork, particularly in remote or resource-constrained environments. While mobile devices have long been used for 'on the move' data collection (Pascoe et al. 2000), their integration into collaborative workflows remains underexplored, especially where internet connectivity is unreliable or absent. Traditional field methods rely heavily on individual researcher effort, limiting scalability (Liberman 2006). Although computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW) has revolutionised office automation (Grudin 1994), its application to language documentation has been sporadic and often unsustainable (Hanke 2017). Existing tools like Aikuma and SayMore demonstrate promise (Bird et al. 2014; Hatton 2013), yet they often presuppose individual device use and stable network access—conditions rarely met in remote Indigenous communities.

In Australia’s far north, telecommunications infrastructure is severely limited (Papandrea 2010), necessitating self-contained, offline-capable solutions. Aboriginal Australians are enthusiastic technology adopters when tools align with their social practices (Featherstone 2013), yet mainstream app design frequently overlooks collective interaction patterns prevalent in Indigenous communities (Sun 2012). This misalignment risks imposing individualistic technological paradigms onto collaborative cultural practices. Moreover, typical technology design cycles—requirements elicitation, development, testing—are often incompatible with Indigenous research ethics, which prioritise reciprocity, relationship-building, and community ownership (Brereton et al. 2014; Christie 2013). Ethnographic and participatory design approaches are better suited to navigate these complexities (Blomberg et al. 1993; Muller & Kuhn 1993).

This paper presents a research-through-design project conducted in collaboration with the Bininj people of West Arnhem Land. Our goal was to develop custom mobile applications and portable network infrastructure to support collaborative language work in contexts lacking reliable internet. We deployed a bespoke server-in-a-box (BushPi) and a suite of field tools (Sandboard apps) across two locations: the township of Gunbalanya and the remote homeland of Kabulwarnamyo. Through iterative co-design with community members, we explored how technology could mediate collective knowledge production while respecting local social norms and ethical protocols.

Our findings reveal that custom toolmaking yields significant benefits when tailored to specific environmental and cultural needs. However, we argue that technological innovation alone is insufficient; activity design must be foregrounded. Fieldworkers, not technologists, should drive the adaptation and evolution of digital tools. This aligns with broader calls for interdisciplinary collaboration in language technology (Bird 2020; Le Ferrand et al. 2020) and echoes Malone et al.’s (2009) framework for harnessing collective intelligence—where task design, motivation, and coordination mechanisms are as critical as the technology itself. By placing human interaction at the centre, we demonstrate a pathway toward sustainable, ethically grounded digital fieldwork practices.

intros.text:
Mobile technologies have increasingly become central to contemporary fieldwork, offering the potential to streamline data collection and facilitate collaborative practices even in remote environments. In domains ranging from ecology to anthropology, handheld devices enable researchers to capture, store, and share information in real-time. However, the efficacy of these tools often depends on reliable network infrastructure, a resource that remains scarce in many Indigenous and rural communities. While 'computer-supported cooperative work' (CSCW) has long been established in human-computer interaction research, its application to fieldwork—particularly in linguistically diverse, low-connectivity contexts—remains underexplored. 

The concept of collective intelligence, as outlined by Malone et al. (2009), provides a useful framework for understanding how distributed groups can achieve complex tasks through coordinated effort. Their 'genome' of collective intelligence highlights the importance of defining who performs tasks, why they do so, and how work is accomplished. Yet, applying these principles to fieldwork requires more than simply deploying off-the-shelf applications; it demands a reimagining of how technology mediates human interaction in situ. Existing digital tools often prioritise efficiency and automation, reflecting the demands of office-based workflows rather than the relational and ethical complexities of cross-cultural research. 

In remote Indigenous communities, such as those in northern Australia, telecommunications infrastructure is frequently unreliable or absent. This necessitates self-contained solutions that operate independently of external networks. Furthermore, the design of such tools must account for local cultural practices, including preferences for group-based activities and the importance of reciprocity in research relationships. Standard participatory design approaches may inadvertently impose external values or overlook the nuanced ways in which community members engage with technology. 

This study addresses these challenges by developing a custom mobile platform—comprising portable network infrastructure and bespoke field apps—deployed in collaboration with the Bininj people of West Arnhem Land. Through iterative design and co-located fieldwork, we explore how purpose-built digital tools can support collaborative language documentation in extreme environments. Our findings suggest that while custom toolmaking offers significant benefits, it is the design of activities, rather than the technology itself, that drives successful innovation. We argue that foregrounding human interaction and placing fieldworkers in the driving seat of technological adaptation is essential for ethical and effective digital fieldwork practice.

intros.text:
Language fieldwork has always depended on collaboration: researchers, speakers, interpreters, teachers, and community organisations jointly shape what is recorded, how it is understood, and what it becomes useful for. Yet many of the everyday workflows of documentary and descriptive linguistics remain organised around the labour of a small number of specialists, often with the visiting researcher functioning as the bottleneck for recording, elicitation, metadata creation, and data management. Digital tools promise to redistribute some of this work, increasing efficiency and participation while supporting new forms of language documentation and language development. Internet-based models of collective intelligence and crowdsourcing show how distributed tasks can be coordinated at scale (Malone et al., 2009), but such models presuppose connectivity, stable infrastructure, and task designs that may not fit the social and ethical realities of fieldwork.

These assumptions are particularly problematic in remote Indigenous Australia, where telecommunications access is uneven and where research is governed by protocols of relationship, reciprocity, permission, and local authority. Mobile devices are widely familiar in many Aboriginal communities, especially for creating, viewing, and sharing media, but this familiarity does not automatically translate into successful app-based fieldwork. Tools designed for individual users, constant connectivity, or decontextualised data collection may fail to support the collective, place-based, and interactional character of language work. For fieldworkers, the challenge is therefore not simply to bring existing digital methods into the field, but to design activities and technologies together in ways that are robust, intelligible, locally appropriate, and ethically accountable.

This article explores that challenge through the development and deployment of a portable platform for collaborative fieldwork in West Arnhem Land, northern Australia. Working with Bininj partners in connection with Kunwinjku language activities, we built BushPi, a battery-powered local server and Wi-Fi hotspot, and Sandboard, a suite of custom mobile web apps for documentary and elicitation tasks. The apps supported activities such as talking about photos, recording information about people, eliciting spoken words, and confirming lexical identity in speech recordings. Because the system operates without Internet access and stores data locally, it provides a practical alternative to cloud-dependent collaboration while making data location and transfer more tangible.

Our central concern, however, is not the technical platform in isolation. We ask what custom mobile tools make possible when they are treated as part of evolving fieldwork activities rather than as finished products to be imposed on users. Across a series of visits, app use revealed preferences for group-based participation, multi-operator interaction, immediate discussion, and learner-directed explanation—features that sometimes ran counter to the efficiency assumptions embedded in crowdsourcing-like task designs. We argue that the main contribution of custom toolmaking lies in the design knowledge generated through situated use. In remote collaborative fieldwork, innovation must be led by fieldworkers and community members, with technology serving the activity rather than defining it.

intros.text:
Fieldwork has always been collaborative, even when the tools of field research have foregrounded the work of the individual researcher. Linguists and other fieldworkers depend on local experts to observe, interpret, record, translate, correct, and evaluate knowledge in context. In contemporary language documentation, however, the amount of data that can be collected, organised, and processed is often constrained by the extent to which such work must pass through a single researcher or a small specialist team. Digital tools offer an apparent remedy: they can distribute tasks, regularise workflows, and make it possible for many people to contribute to a shared documentary activity.

The broader digital world has shown the productivity of collective systems in which tasks are divided across participants and coordinated through networked infrastructure. Accounts of collective intelligence, for example, emphasise the design choices involved in deciding who performs a task, why they participate, what is accomplished, and how contributions are coordinated (Malone et al., 2009). Similar possibilities are attractive for language work, where recording, elicitation, checking, annotation, and metadata collection can in principle be shared across multiple participants. Mobile devices are especially promising because they are portable, familiar to many users, and equipped with cameras, microphones, touchscreens, and local storage.

Yet the conditions of linguistic fieldwork differ sharply from the settings for which most networked collaborative systems are designed. Many field sites have unreliable electricity, limited or non-existent internet connectivity, harsh environmental conditions, and locally specific protocols governing participation, knowledge, and data access. In remote Indigenous communities in northern Australia, these constraints are not incidental technical obstacles but central features of the design context. Moreover, a tool that appears efficient from the perspective of data collection may fail if it does not fit local practices of interaction, learning, authority, reciprocity, and collaboration. This raises a practical and methodological problem: how can mobile technologies support collaborative fieldwork in places where ordinary web infrastructure is unavailable, while remaining responsive to the social organisation of field activities?

This article addresses that problem through a research-through-design account of custom mobile app development for language-related fieldwork in West Arnhem Land, northern Australia. Across repeated visits, we used these tools in workshops and field sessions, observed how participants interpreted and adapted the tasks, and iterated the designs in response.

Rather, it is the design of activities in which people, tools, relationships, and research goals are brought into workable alignment.

intros.text: Recent studies investigating language acquisition and processing in children have highlighted the roles of cognitive individual differences.  With specific reference to long-term learning, two main strands of research have emerged. The first strand has considered declarative and procedural learning ability as behavioral correlates of declarative and procedural long-term memory (for a metaanalysis of these associations, see Hamrick, Lum, & Ullman, 2018). The second strand has focused on differences in implicit statistical learning, broadly characterized as the largely implicit1 ability to track and learn co-occurrence patterns from repeated exposure to sensory input in different modalities (Perruchet & Pachton, 2006; for reviews, see Kidd, Donnelly, & Christiansen, 2018, and Williams, 2020).  The present study mainly considered the relationship between child second language (L2) learning and cognitive individual differences from the perspective of the declarative/procedural model of learning and memory, but relevant child studies within the implicit statistical learning framework were also considered in the literature review and in the discussion.

intros.text: How children learn language has long been linked to the interplay between the memory systems that underpin learning more generally. According to the declarative/procedural model (Ullman, 2015), declarative memory supports the fast learning of lexis and idiosyncratic forms, whereas procedural memory subserves the acquisition of rule-based patterns in morphosyntax and phonology. Because these systems follow distinct maturational trajectories, the model predicts a comparatively greater reliance on procedural learning in childhood and an increasing role for declarative learning from adolescence onward. Growing evidence suggests that both first and second language learning are tied to general-purpose learning systems (Hamrick et al., 2018), and that implicit and statistical learning may reflect a common mechanism (Christiansen, 2019; Perruchet & Pacton, 2006; Williams, 2020). Yet individual differences in these abilities remain understudied in children (Kidd et al., 2018), and no study has examined how declarative and procedural learning abilities relate to child second language (L2) learning. The present study addresses this gap by investigating cognitive predictors of L2 comprehension and syntactic learning in 8- to 9-year-old children.

intros.text: Aptitudes for procedural and declarative learning have been identified as important predictors of second language (L2) outcomes, yet most relevant studies have been conducted with adults or have relied on aptitude batteries not validated for children (Hamrick et al., 2018). Neurocognitive models such as the declarative/procedural model (Ullman, 2015) posit distinct roles for the two long-term memory systems in language acquisition and, given their divergent maturational trajectories, predict a greater reliance on procedural learning in early childhood. Implicit statistical learning, closely related to procedural learning, has similarly been tied to general-purpose neurocognitive mechanisms underpinning both first (L1) and second language (Christiansen, 2019; Kidd et al., 2018; Williams, 2020). However, child studies to date have overwhelmingly examined L1 outcomes, and no study has yet investigated how declarative and procedural learning abilities predict L2 learning in children. The present study addresses this gap, examining whether these cognitive abilities predict 8- to 9-year-old children's learning of word order, case marking, and online sentence comprehension in a novel miniature language.

intros.text: The mechanisms underlying second language (L2) acquisition are often debated, specifically whether language is learned through dedicated systems or general-purpose neurocognitive mechanisms (Hamrick et al., 2018). A prominent framework in this area is the declarative/procedural model (Ullman, 2015), which posits that declarative memory handles lexis and idiosyncratic forms, while procedural memory is specialized for rule-based morphosyntax. Because these systems follow different maturational trajectories—with procedural memory maturing earlier in childhood than declarative memory—this model predicts a greater reliance on procedural learning in early childhood L2 acquisition. While adult studies have shown a shift from declarative to procedural processing as input increases, research on children has focused primarily on first language outcomes. Consequently, there is a lack of experimental evidence regarding how these cognitive aptitudes predict L2 learning in children. This study aims to elucidate the roles of declarative and procedural learning abilities in the initial stages of novel language acquisition in 8- to 9-year-old children.

intros.text: Understanding the cognitive predictors of language acquisition is central to elucidating how individual differences shape linguistic outcomes (Kidd et al., 2018). Within the declarative/procedural model, it is posited that procedural memory is specialized for rule-based morphosyntax, while declarative memory handles lexis and idiosyncratic forms (Ullman, 2015). While evidence suggests that general-purpose learning systems underpin both first (L1) and second language (L2) acquisition (Hamrick et al., 2018), and that implicit learning mechanisms are vital for tracking structural regularities (Williams, 2020; Christiansen, 2019), research has predominantly focused on adults or L1 outcomes in children. Consequently, the relative roles of declarative and procedural abilities in child L2 acquisition remain largely unexplored. The current study aims to address this gap by examining how these cognitive abilities predict the learning of word order, case marking, and online sentence comprehension in 8- to 9-year-old children exposed to a novel miniature language. By doing so, this research seeks to determine if children rely more heavily on procedural systems during early L2 exposure.

intros.text: The role of cognitive abilities in language acquisition has long been a central topic in applied linguistics and cognitive science. Recent work emphasizes the importance of individual differences in learning mechanisms, particularly the distinction between declarative and procedural memory systems (Kidd et al., 2018; Hamrick et al., 2018). While the declarative/procedural model posits that procedural memory is crucial for rule-based morphosyntax, evidence regarding its predictive power in child second language (L2) acquisition remains scarce. Most existing studies focus on adults or employ measures not fully validated for children (Rogers et al., 2017). Furthermore, the relationship between implicit statistical learning and procedural learning remains theoretically debated (Christiansen, 2019; Perruchet & Pacton, 2006). Given that procedural memory matures earlier than declarative memory in childhood, understanding how these systems interact during early L2 exposure is vital. This study investigates the role of declarative and procedural learning abilities in the initial stages of L2 acquisition among typically developing children. Using a miniature language paradigm, we examine whether these cognitive predictors influence word order learning, case marking, and online sentence comprehension. By addressing these gaps, we aim to elucidate the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying child L2 learning and compare them with adult patterns.

intros.text: Understanding the cognitive mechanisms that underlie second language (L2) acquisition is a central goal in applied linguistics and cognitive psychology. While individual differences in cognitive aptitude have been extensively studied in adult L2 learning, the specific role of long-term memory systems in child L2 acquisition remains largely unexplored. The declarative/procedural model posits that distinct memory systems support different aspects of language learning, with procedural memory implicated in rule-based grammar and declarative memory in lexical knowledge. Although this model has gained traction in adult research, its predictions for children—who exhibit different developmental trajectories for these systems—are less clear. Furthermore, while some studies have linked procedural learning to child first language (L1) outcomes, no research has yet examined how declarative and procedural learning abilities predict child learning of a novel L2. To address this gap, the present study investigated the extent to which declarative and procedural learning abilities predict morphosyntactic learning and online sentence comprehension in 8- to 9-year-old children exposed to a miniature language. The results offer initial evidence that procedural learning ability plays a significant role in early child L2 acquisition, potentially emerging earlier than in adults.

intros.text: Children often achieve high levels of second language (L2) attainment given sufficient exposure, yet the cognitive mechanisms supporting their earliest learning remain poorly understood. Recent accounts emphasize that language acquisition draws on domain-general learning systems, including declarative memory for rapid association learning and procedural memory for gradually extracting sequential and rule-based regularities (Ullman, 2015; Hamrick et al., 2018). These systems follow different developmental trajectories, raising the possibility that children’s L2 learning may rely less on declarative learning and more on procedural or implicit statistical learning than adult L2 learning (DeKeyser, 2012; Christiansen, 2019). Although individual-differences research has increasingly linked learning abilities to language outcomes (Kidd et al., 2018), most evidence comes from child first language or adult L2 studies, leaving child L2 acquisition underexplored. This gap is important because early exposure may reveal whether children recruit procedural resources before the extended practice typically required in adults. The present study therefore investigates whether declarative and procedural learning abilities predict 8- to 9-year-old children’s comprehension and morphosyntactic learning during initial exposure to a novel miniature L2.

intros.text: Understanding why children differ in the earliest stages of second language (L2) learning is central to theories of language acquisition and to accounts of age-related variation in L2 outcomes. Recent work has increasingly linked language learning to domain-general memory and learning systems, including declarative memory, procedural memory, and implicit statistical learning (Perruchet & Pacton, 2006; Hamrick et al., 2018; Christiansen, 2019; Williams, 2020). The declarative/procedural model predicts that rule-based aspects of grammar should rely particularly on procedural memory, whereas declarative memory should support rapid learning of associations and may become more influential later in development (Ullman, 2015). Individual-differences research has also shown that cognitive variation can illuminate mechanisms of acquisition and processing (Kidd et al., 2018). However, evidence on declarative and procedural predictors of L2 morphosyntax comes mainly from adults, and child research has focused primarily on first language outcomes. Thus, it remains unclear whether children’s early L2 syntactic learning and sentence comprehension are predicted by the same cognitive systems. The present study addresses this gap by examining whether declarative and procedural learning abilities predict 8- to 9-year-old Italian-speaking children’s learning of word order, case marking, and aural comprehension in a novel miniature language.

intros.text: Children’s learning of academic skills is supported by domain-general cognitiveabilities such as attention and working memory (Borella, Carretti, & Pelgrina,2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole, Pickering, Knight, & Stegmann, 2004),but the impact of these abilities on language learning is unclear. For determiningthe impact of cognitive ability on language development, longitudinal studiesare relevant because these can reveal the temporal ordering of events. Previouslongitudinal research focusing on children has shown that cognitive ability pre-dicts language (Ekerim & Selc ̧uk, 2018; Weiland, Barata, & Yoshikawa, 2014;White, Alexander, & Greenfield, 2017) and that language predicts cognitiveability (Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn, Willoughby, Vernon-Feagans, Blair, & TheFamily Life Project Key Investigators, 2016). Other studies have also observeda bidirectional relationship between language and cognitive ability (Bohlmann,Maier, & Palacios, 2015; Slot & Suchodoletz, 2018) or found no relationshipbetween the two (Gooch, Thompson, Nash, Snowling, & Hulme, 2016; Loni-gan, Allan, Goodrich, Farrington, & Phillips, 2017)  Not only have the findingsbeen inconsistent but conclusions regarding the impact of cognitive ability onone language have not necessarily generalized to the other language of thetested participants (Lonigan, Lerner, Goodrich, Farrington, & Allan, 2016; Tse& Altarriba, 2014).  Therefore, the present study investigated relationships be-tween bilingual immigrant children’s cognitive ability and vocabulary in boththe minority (Turkish, Tarifit) and majority (Dutch) languages.  Data were col-lected three times at yearly intervals, starting when the participants were 5 or6 years old. At all three testing times, receptive vocabulary in both languageswas measured as well as working memory and attention to estimate the impactof cognitive ability on the participants’ receptive vocabulary skills.

intros.text:
Children's vocabulary development is shaped by a multitude of factors, among which the quality and quantity of language input feature prominently (Hoff, 2006; Unsworth, 2016). Yet children exposed to comparable input differ in how much and how deeply they learn, pointing to the contribution of child-internal factors. Domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly attention and working memory, are thought to underpin this variation because they enable children to process linguistic input efficiently, retain information in an accessible state, and focus on what is relevant while suppressing distractors (Baddeley, 2003; Cowan, 2014; Diamond, 2013). Such abilities also support fast mapping, whereby children pair new words with referents by selecting and inhibiting lexical competitors (Carey & Bartlett, 1978; Yoshida et al., 2011). These processes are known to matter for academic learning more broadly (Borella et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole et al., 2004).

Although many studies link performance on executive function tasks to language outcomes, longitudinal evidence remains inconclusive. Some studies report that executive function predicts later vocabulary (Weiland et al., 2013; White et al., 2017; Ekerim & Selcuk, 2017), whereas others find bidirectional relationships in which language also predicts cognition (Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn et al., 2016; Slot & von Suchodoletz, 2018; Bohlmann et al., 2015). Crucially, very few longitudinal studies have included bilingual children, and only one examined both languages, yielding null results (Lonigan et al., 2015).

The present study addresses this gap by investigating whether domain-general cognitive ability predicts the receptive vocabulary of bilingual immigrant children in both their languages. Using a longitudinal, within-subjects design with children of Turkish and Moroccan descent in the Netherlands, we assessed working memory, selective attention, and executive attention alongside receptive vocabulary in the majority (Dutch) and minority (Turkish, Tarifit) languages at three annual intervals. Cross-lagged analyses allowed us to examine the directionality and stability of these relationships across the two languages.

intros.text:
Vocabulary development is a multicausal process in which environmental input and children's own characteristics jointly shape outcomes. Among these characteristics, domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly attention and working memory, are thought to play a central role because they enable children to process linguistic input as it unfolds, keep information accessible, and modulate fast mapping (Cowan, 2014; Diamond, 2013). Working memory and attention have repeatedly been linked to the acquisition of academic skills (Borella et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole et al., 2004), and a growing body of research demonstrates associations between children's executive function performance and their language outcomes (Weiland et al., 2013; White et al., 2017).

Despite this theoretical expectation, empirical findings remain inconclusive. Longitudinal studies capable of establishing temporal precedence report divergent patterns: some find that executive function predicts vocabulary unidirectionally (Weiland et al., 2013; Ekerim & Selcuk, 2017; White et al., 2017), whereas others observe bidirectional relationships in which language also predicts cognition (Bohlmann et al., 2015; Fuhs & Day, 2011; Slot & von Suchodoletz, 2018), and still others find no effect (Lonigan et al., 2015). Crucially, only two of these longitudinal studies explicitly examined bilingual children, their outcomes disagreed, and only one considered both languages.

Little is therefore known about whether cognitive ability influences bilingual children's vocabularies differently across their two languages. To address this gap, the present study investigated whether working memory, selective attention, and executive attention predict receptive vocabulary in the majority (Dutch) and minority (Turkish, Tarifit) languages of immigrant children. Sixty-nine bilingual children were tested three times at annual intervals, and cross-lagged correlational and regression analyses established the directionality of relationships. We expected cognitive ability to predict vocabulary growth, while acknowledging that the differing acquisition dynamics of the two languages might yield differential patterns.
