intros.text:
Domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly executive functions such as working memory and attention, are thought to play a critical role in the acquisition of academic skills (Borella et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole et al., 2003). In the realm of language development, these functions support the processing of environmental stimuli, enabling children to efficiently encode relevant information and maintain it in an accessible state to facilitate word learning and fast mapping. While the importance of linguistic input is well-documented, children vary in their capacity to process this input, suggesting that cognitive resources may independently contribute to vocabulary growth.

Empirical evidence regarding the relationship between executive function and vocabulary remains inconclusive. Some longitudinal studies suggest a unidirectional path where cognitive ability predicts later vocabulary knowledge (Weiland et al., 2013; White et al., 2017), while others indicate bidirectional relationships where verbal ability also supports the development of executive functions (Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn et al., 2016; Slot & Suchodoletz, 2018). Furthermore, research involving bilingual children has yielded mixed results; for instance, Bohlmann et al. (2015) found that self-regulation predicted majority-language vocabulary, whereas Lonigan et al. (2015) found no such link between inhibitory control and vocabulary in either language.

The present study aims to clarify these relationships by investigating whether cognitive ability influences receptive vocabulary development in both the majority (Dutch) and minority (home) languages of bilingual immigrant children. Using a longitudinal within-subjects design, we examine the directionality and stability of these associations over a two-year period. We specifically hypothesize that cognitive abilities will predict vocabulary growth, with potential differences between the two languages arising from distinct acquisition dynamics, learning contexts, and the relative dominance of the majority language in the school environment.

intros.text:
Domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly executive functions such as attention and working memory, are considered vital for the acquisition of academic skills (Borella et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole et al., 2003). These higher-order functions support the processing of environmental stimuli, enabling children to efficiently encode and retain linguistic input, which is essential for fast mapping and vocabulary growth. While the role of environmental input is well-documented, significant individual differences in cognitive capacity suggest that domain-general abilities independently contribute to language development (White et al., 2017; Weiland et al., 2013).

Despite this theoretical consensus, empirical evidence regarding the longitudinal relationship between cognitive ability and vocabulary remains inconclusive. Some studies indicate that executive function predicts vocabulary (Weiland et al., 2013; White et al., 2017), while others observe bidirectional relationships where verbal ability also supports cognitive development (Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn et al., 2016; Slot & Suchodoletz, 2018). Furthermore, few studies have explicitly examined this relationship in bilingual children, and results among this population are inconsistent; for instance, Lonigan et al. (2015) found no significant link between inhibitory control and vocabulary, whereas Bohlmann et al. (2015) observed a predictive effect for majority-language vocabulary.

The present study aims to clarify whether cognitive ability influences receptive vocabulary development in both the majority and minority languages of bilingual immigrant children. Using a longitudinal within-subjects design with children of Turkish and Moroccan descent in the Netherlands, we examine the directionality and stability of these relationships over a two-year period. We hypothesize that cognitive abilities will predict vocabulary growth, particularly in the majority language (Dutch), due to the intentional and explicit nature of second-language learning. The results may provide insight into how the context and timing of acquisition modulate the impact of cognition on bilingual language development.

intros.text:
Domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly executive functions such as working memory and attention, are increasingly recognized as critical factors in children’s language development. These higher-order cognitive processes support goal-oriented behavior and the efficient processing of environmental stimuli (Diamond, 2013; Miller & Cohen, 2001). While the role of environmental input in vocabulary acquisition is well-established (Hoff, 2006), individual differences in cognitive capacity may determine how effectively children utilize this input. Specifically, attention and working memory facilitate the encoding of relevant linguistic information and the retention of new words in an accessible state (Cowan, 2014; Engle et al., 1999). Consequently, children with superior cognitive resources may acquire vocabulary more rapidly than their peers.

Although cross-sectional studies consistently link executive functions to language outcomes (Gathercole et al., 2004; White et al., 2017), longitudinal evidence regarding the directionality of this relationship remains mixed. Some research suggests that cognitive abilities predict later vocabulary growth (Weiland et al., 2013; Ekerim & Selcuk, 2017), while other studies report bidirectional effects, where language skills also support the development of executive functions (Bohlman et al., 2015; Slot & Suchodoletz, 2018). This inconsistency highlights the need for further investigation, particularly within bilingual populations where language learning contexts vary significantly. Previous studies involving bilingual children have yielded conflicting results; for instance, Lonigan et al. (2015) found no predictive effect of inhibitory control on vocabulary, whereas Bohlman et al. (2015) observed that self-regulation predicted expressive vocabulary in the majority language.

The current study addresses these gaps by examining the longitudinal relationship between cognitive ability and receptive vocabulary in bilingual immigrant children learning both a minority (home) and majority (school) language. Using a three-wave longitudinal design with Turkish-Dutch and Tarifit-Dutch bilinguals aged 5 to 8, we investigated whether working memory and attention predict vocabulary development over time. We hypothesized that cognitive ability would predict subsequent vocabulary growth, particularly in the majority language where learning is often more explicit and contextually supported. Furthermore, we explored whether these effects differ between the home and majority languages, considering the distinct acquisition dynamics and input contexts associated with each.

intros.text:
The role of domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly executive functions, in early language development has garnered significant attention in applied linguistics and developmental psychology. Executive functions, encompassing working memory and attentional control, are higher-order cognitive processes that facilitate goal-oriented behavior and are thought to underpin the acquisition of academic skills (Diamond, 2013; Miller & Cohen, 2001). These cognitive mechanisms are theorized to support language learning by enabling children to process environmental stimuli efficiently, retain information, and focus on relevant linguistic input while inhibiting distractors (Cowan, 2014; Hoff, 2006). Consequently, variations in cognitive capacity may explain individual differences in vocabulary development, acting alongside contextual factors such as language input and socioeconomic status.

Despite the theoretical consensus that cognitive ability supports language growth, empirical evidence regarding the directionality and specificity of this relationship remains mixed. Longitudinal studies have yielded inconsistent findings: some report that executive functions predict later vocabulary (Weiland et al., 2013; White et al., 2017), while others suggest bidirectional relationships where language skills also foster cognitive development (Bohlman et al., 2015; Slot & Suchodoletz, 2018). Furthermore, research focusing specifically on bilingual children is scarce. While Lonigan et al. (2015) found no predictive effect of inhibition on vocabulary in Spanish-English bilinguals, Bohlman et al. (2015) observed that self-regulation predicted English vocabulary. Crucially, few studies have examined whether these cognitive predictors operate differently for majority versus minority languages, a distinction that may be influenced by the context and explicitness of learning environments.

This study investigates the influence of cognitive ability on bilingual children’s receptive vocabulary in both their home language and the majority language. Using a longitudinal design with three annual assessments, we examined whether working memory and attention predict vocabulary growth in Dutch and home languages (Turkish, Tarifit) among immigrant children in the Netherlands. By employing cross-lagged analyses and controlling for fluid intelligence and parental education, this research aims to clarify the directionality of these relationships and determine if cognitive effects differ between languages.

intros.text:
Vocabulary development is a central component of children’s early language and school success, and it is shaped by both environmental and child-internal factors. For bilingual immigrant children, vocabulary growth is especially complex because input is distributed across a majority language used in school and society and a minority language used primarily at home. Although quantity and quality of language exposure are known to matter, children may also differ in how efficiently they process linguistic input. Domain-general cognitive abilities, particularly working memory and attention, are plausible contributors because they support the encoding, maintenance, and selection of information during learning (Gathercole et al., 2003; Borella et al., 2010). These abilities are often discussed as part of executive functioning, a set of processes that underpins goal-directed behavior and is associated with later academic achievement (Duncan et al., 2007). 

A growing body of research has examined links between executive functioning and language in early childhood, but findings remain mixed. Some longitudinal studies suggest that executive function predicts later receptive vocabulary (Weiland et al., 2013) or broader language outcomes (White et al., 2017), whereas others report bidirectional relations between self-regulation and vocabulary or stronger effects of language on later executive functioning (Bohlmann et al., 2015; Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn et al., 2016; Slot & von Suchodoletz, 2018). Evidence from bilingual children is particularly limited. Studies with language-minority preschoolers have shown associations between inhibitory control and some academic skills, but not consistently with vocabulary in both languages (Lonigan et al., 2015). Moreover, bilingual proficiency itself has been linked to attentional control and working memory, especially in the second language (Tse & Altarriba, 2014), raising questions about directionality.

The present study investigates whether working memory, selective attention, and executive attention predict receptive vocabulary development in bilingual Turkish–Dutch and Tarifit–Dutch immigrant children. Using three annual measurement waves, we examine cross-lagged relations between cognition and vocabulary in Dutch, the majority language, and in the children’s home language, allowing us to test whether cognitive effects differ across bilingual children’s two developing vocabularies.

intros.text:
Vocabulary growth in the early school years is central to children’s educational trajectories, and it is especially consequential for bilingual children who must develop lexical knowledge in both a home language and the majority language of schooling. Although the quantity and quality of language input are widely recognized as major determinants of vocabulary development, children also differ in domain-general cognitive abilities that may shape how efficiently they encode, select, maintain, and use linguistic information. Executive functions, including attention and working memory, are therefore likely to be relevant to word learning because they support goal-directed processing in complex environments and have been linked to academic and language-related outcomes (Borella et al., 2010; Duncan et al., 2007; Gathercole et al., 2003).

Previous research has provided evidence for associations between executive functioning and language development, but the direction and specificity of these relations remain unsettled. Some longitudinal studies suggest that executive function predicts later receptive vocabulary (Weiland et al., 2013) or broader language outcomes (White et al., 2017), whereas others report bidirectional relations between language and self-regulation or executive function (Bohlmann et al., 2015; Slot & von Suchodoletz, 2018) or effects from verbal ability to later executive functioning (Fuhs & Day, 2011; Kuhn et al., 2016). Studies including bilingual or language-minority children are fewer, and their findings are mixed: inhibitory control has not consistently predicted vocabulary in both languages (Lonigan et al., 2015), while proficiency in a second language has been associated with attentional control and working memory (Tse & Altarriba, 2014). Thus, it remains unclear whether domain-general cognitive ability contributes longitudinally to bilingual children’s vocabulary growth, whether such effects are similar in the majority and minority languages, and whether attention or working memory is most relevant.

The present study addresses these issues by following Turkish-Dutch and Tarifit-Dutch bilingual immigrant children in the Netherlands across three annual measurement waves. Receptive vocabulary was assessed in Dutch and in the home language, and cognitive ability was measured through tasks tapping visuospatial working memory, selective attention, and executive attention. Using cross-lagged correlations and follow-up regression analyses controlling for prior vocabulary, fluid intelligence, verbal short-term memory, and parental education, the study examined whether cognitive ability predicts later vocabulary, whether vocabulary predicts later cognitive ability, and whether these relations differ across the children’s two languages.

intros.text: Helping learners to gain a wide range of vocabulary knowledge is a fundamental issue for improving their general language proficiency globally, and no less so in classes teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) in China (Silver, Hu, & Iino, 2002).  Discussion often focuses on the comparative merits of intentional learning and of incidental learning, where learners unintentionally “pick up” vocabulary knowledge when they are focused on understanding the meaning of the language input (Hulstijn, 2001). Whereas vocabulary gains tend to be smaller for the latter (Laufer & Girsai, 2008), perhaps because learners’ attention is on global meaning rather than on individual vocabulary items, pedagogical activities can be used alongside a focus on meaning to enhance the salience of items (Sharwood Smith, 1991) and hence noticing (Schmidt, 1990) and thence vocabulary learning (Laufer, 2005).  The extent to which learners of different proficiency levels in a second language (L2) benefit from different types of attention-enhancing pedagogical activities is, however, underexplored, particularly in relation to aural input and the role of the first language (L1).  A consideration of those issues is important, not only from a pedagogical perspective, but also within models of L2 vocabulary acquisition in which the L1 functions differently at different levels of proficiency (Jiang, 2002, 2004; Kroll & Stewart, 1994).  This study therefore investigated the impact of L2 learners’ preexisting vocabulary knowledge (PVK) and listening proficiency on their vocabulary learning from attention-enhancing activities in the form of different types of vocabulary explanations after listening: no explanations (NE), explanations in the L2, codeswitched explanations,and those that give contrastive focus-on-form (CFoF) information.

intros.text:
Vocabulary can be acquired not only through reading but also through listening, yet how much is learned from aural input, and under what conditions, remains less well understood. A recurring concern is the role of learner proficiency, whether in the form of general proficiency, prior vocabulary knowledge, or listening proficiency specifically. Because vocabulary breadth is positively related to listening comprehension, learners with larger vocabularies might be expected to acquire more words from spoken input; however, the relationship between vocabulary knowledge and listening is more complex than that between vocabulary and reading, and some learners comprehend well despite modest lexical knowledge. This suggests that listening proficiency, as distinct from vocabulary size, may itself shape how much is learned from aural input.

What is learned may also depend on the type of support offered. A lexical focus-on-form approach (Laufer, 2005) can enhance vocabulary learning by drawing attention to lexical items and prompting deeper processing, in line with the involvement load hypothesis (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). Contrastive form-focused instruction, which highlights crosslinguistic similarities and differences, has proven especially valuable (Laufer & Girsai, 2008). Studies comparing L2-only and codeswitched explanations (Tian & Macaro, 2012; Lee & Levine, 2020) have produced contradictory findings regarding proficiency effects, partly because proficiency has typically been treated as a categorical rather than continuous variable, obscuring subtle interactions.

The present study revisits the data of Zhang and Graham (2019), in which Chinese secondary school learners received L2, codeswitching, contrastive focus-on-form, or no vocabulary explanations during listening. Whereas that study treated learners' preexisting vocabulary knowledge and listening proficiency as covariates, we treat them as continuous predictors and examine how they interact with instructional condition and time to shape short- and long-term vocabulary learning through listening.

intros.text:
The acquisition of vocabulary through spoken input has attracted growing interest in recent years, yet it remains substantially less well understood than vocabulary learning through reading. A recurring finding in the literature is that gains from listening tend to be lower than those from reading (Vidal, 2011), and that listening may primarily develop earlier-acquired aspects of vocabulary knowledge such as form recognition. How much learners gain, however, may depend on their level of proficiency, whether general proficiency, prior vocabulary knowledge, or listening proficiency specifically. Existing vocabulary knowledge might be expected to shape learning through spoken input, given that vocabulary breadth correlates with listening comprehension, yet findings across studies have been contradictory, partly because the relationship between vocabulary knowledge and listening is more complex than that between vocabulary knowledge and reading, with learners drawing on factors beyond word knowledge when interpreting speech.

Vocabulary learning during listening can also be enhanced through a lexical focus-on-form approach (Laufer, 2005), in which the salience of items is heightened to increase noticing (Schmidt, 1990) and involvement load (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). Different forms of teacher explanation—including second-language, codeswitched, and contrastive crosslinguistic explanations (Kroll & Stewart, 1994; Jiang, 2002)—may prompt differing degrees of processing and hence learning.

A small number of studies have examined how such explanations interact with learner proficiency, but they have treated proficiency as a categorical rather than continuous variable, losing potentially subtle variance, and have paid little attention to school settings. Consequently, the role of proficiency and its interaction with explanation type remains unclear. Returning to data from Zhang and Graham (2019), the present study therefore examined how preexisting vocabulary knowledge and listening proficiency, treated as continuous predictors, interact with test time points and four types of vocabulary explanation among Chinese secondary-school learners of English.

intros.text:
While significant research has explored vocabulary acquisition through reading, the extent to which learners acquire vocabulary through listening remains less understood. Evidence suggests that learning gains from listening are typically lower than those from reading (Vidal, 2011) and often limited to early-acquired aspects of knowledge, such as form recognition (van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013a). These outcomes may be influenced by learner proficiency, yet findings are contradictory; some research suggests that larger vocabulary sizes facilitate further acquisition (Peters & Webb, 2018), while others find no such effect (Rodgers, 2013). This discrepancy may stem from the complex relationship between vocabulary knowledge and listening comprehension, as L2 listeners often rely on non-lexical cues to interpret spoken input (van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013b).

To enhance learning, a lexical focus-on-form approach can increase the salience of target items, promoting noticing (Schmidt, 1990) and deeper processing. According to the involvement load hypothesis, retention is higher when tasks require greater 'need,' 'search,' and 'evaluation' (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). Different instructional supports, such as L2 explanations, codeswitching (CS), or contrastive focus-on-form (CFoF), may prompt varying levels of involvement. While previous research has examined these interventions, many studies have relied on categorical proficiency groupings, potentially obscuring subtle effects (Aiken & West, 1991). Furthermore, the specific interaction between preexisting vocabulary knowledge (PVK), listening proficiency, and instructional type remains under-researched, particularly in school settings. The current study addresses this gap by re-examining data from Zhang and Graham (2019) to explore how PVK and listening proficiency interact with different types of post-listening vocabulary explanations to influence short- and long-term learning.

intros.text:
The acquisition of vocabulary through listening is a vital component of second language development, yet it has received significantly less research attention than vocabulary learning through reading. While the importance of input is well-established, scholars have noted that learning gains from listening are typically lower than those from reading, often limited to the recognition of forms rather than deeper levels of knowledge. To enhance these outcomes, researchers have proposed lexical focus-on-form approaches (Laufer, 2005), which utilize input enhancement to increase the salience of target items and promote noticing (Schmidt, 1990). Such enhancement can be achieved through various instructional supports, including L2 explanations, codeswitching (CS), or contrastive focus-on-form (CFoF) approaches that highlight crosslinguistic differences. According to the involvement load hypothesis (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001), the effectiveness of these methods may depend on the degree of cognitive effort—specifically evaluation—prompted in the learner.

However, it remains unclear how individual differences in learner proficiency interact with these instructional conditions. Previous research has yielded contradictory findings regarding whether preexisting vocabulary knowledge (PVK) or general proficiency predicts learning gains. Furthermore, many studies have relied on categorical proficiency groupings, potentially masking subtle effects that continuous variables might reveal. There is also a dearth of research specifically examining the distinct roles of PVK versus listening proficiency in school settings.

Addressing these gaps, the present study utilizes data from a group of Chinese EFL learners to explore the complex interplay between PVK, listening proficiency, and four types of vocabulary explanation (L2, CS, CFoF, and no explanation). The study aims to determine the extent to which these predictors influence vocabulary learning and how their impact varies across different instructional conditions.

intros.text:
The extent to which vocabulary knowledge can be acquired through listening has received less research attention than is the case for reading. While reading is often associated with higher vocabulary gains, listening may develop earlier-acquired aspects of vocabulary knowledge, such as form recognition, rather than high levels of meaning recognition and recall (van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013a). Furthermore, the amount of learning through listening appears to depend on learners' proficiency levels, specifically general proficiency, prior vocabulary knowledge, or listening proficiency. For instance, Vidal (2011) found that lower proficiency learners retained very few words from spoken input, possibly because they were hampered by difficulties in segmenting words from the speech stream. Existing vocabulary knowledge might also influence learning gains, as vocabulary breadth is positively correlated with listening proficiency (Stæhr, 2008). However, findings remain contradictory; while some studies suggest learners with larger vocabulary sizes acquire more words from aural input, others report no effect of vocabulary knowledge on learning gains (Rodgers, 2013).

These inconsistencies may reflect the complex relationship between vocabulary knowledge and listening comprehension. Although correlations exist, they are generally lower than those reported for reading (Stæhr, 2008). Consequently, L2 listeners may draw on factors other than vocabulary knowledge, such as contextual information, when interpreting spoken input (van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013b). This suggests that listening proficiency may be a distinct and crucial factor in vocabulary learning through listening, separate from preexisting vocabulary knowledge (PVK). Additionally, the type of listening activity and the support offered can enhance vocabulary learning. A lexical focus-on-form approach, which heightens the salience of lexical items, can increase noticing (Schmidt, 1990; Laufer, 2005). Different forms of input enhancement vary in the 'involvement load' they prompt (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001), potentially leading to different learning outcomes.

Previous studies have explored various forms of input enhancement, including L2 explanations, codeswitching (CS), and contrastive focus-on-form (CFoF). Zhang and Graham (2019) found that CFoF was significantly more effective than L2 or CS explanations for vocabulary learning through listening. However, that study treated learners' PVK and listening proficiency as covariates rather than primary predictors. Furthermore, many studies have used proficiency as a categorical variable, which may obscure subtle effects. The current study addresses these gaps by reanalyzing data from Zhang and Graham (2019) to explore the interaction between PVK, listening proficiency, and instructional conditions, treating proficiency as a continuous variable.

intros.text:
Acquiring vocabulary through listening has received less research attention than reading, yet it remains a vital component of second language development. While reading often yields higher levels of vocabulary gain, listening may develop earlier-acquired aspects of knowledge, such as form recognition (van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013a). However, the extent to which vocabulary is developed through listening depends on learner proficiency and the type of instructional support provided. Previous research suggests that vocabulary learning from listening is influenced by general proficiency, prior vocabulary knowledge (PVK), or specifically listening proficiency (Vidal, 2011). For instance, lower proficiency learners often retain fewer words from spoken input due to difficulties in segmenting the speech stream. Conversely, some studies indicate that vocabulary knowledge correlates positively with listening comprehension (Stæhr, 2008), though this relationship is complex and sometimes contradictory (Rodgers, 2013).

To enhance vocabulary learning, researchers have explored various forms of input enhancement, such as lexical focus-on-form (Laufer, 2005) and the provision of explanations (Tian & Macaro, 2012; Zhang & Graham, 2019). Zhang and Graham (2019) found that contrastive focus-on-form (CFoF) explanations were more effective than second-language (L2) or codeswitching (CS) explanations for short- and long-term vocabulary retention. However, in that study, learners' PVK and listening proficiency were treated merely as covariates rather than primary predictors. Furthermore, existing studies often categorize proficiency levels, potentially obscuring subtle effects that continuous variables might reveal (Aiken & West, 1991). Consequently, there is a need to investigate the interaction between continuous measures of PVK and listening proficiency with different types of instructional explanations.

The current study addresses this gap by re-analyzing data from Zhang and Graham (2019) to explore how PVK and listening proficiency interact with four types of post-listening vocabulary explanations: L2, CS, CFoF, and no explanation (NE). Specifically, this research asks: (1) To what extent does vocabulary learning through listening vary according to learners' PVK and listening proficiency? and (2) To what extent does the impact of different types of post-listening vocabulary explanation vary according to learners' PVK or listening proficiency? By treating proficiency as continuous variables, this study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of the factors influencing vocabulary acquisition through aural input.

intros.text:
Vocabulary growth is central to second language (L2) development, yet the conditions under which learners acquire vocabulary from spoken input remain less well understood than those supporting learning from written input. Listening is a particularly demanding medium for vocabulary learning because speech is transient and learners’ attention is usually directed primarily toward message comprehension rather than toward individual lexical forms. From a focus-on-form perspective, therefore, spoken vocabulary input may need to be made salient if learners are to notice, process, and retain unfamiliar items (Schmidt, 1990; Sharwood Smith, 1991; Laufer, 2005). Such enhancement may be especially relevant in instructed EFL contexts, including Chinese secondary classrooms, where teacher-led listening activities and vocabulary explanations form an important part of English learning (Silver et al., 2002). 

A further issue concerns the kind of lexical support that best promotes learning through listening. Explanations in the L2 may encourage processing within the target language, whereas codeswitching to the first language (L1) may reduce comprehension demands and support form–meaning mapping, particularly for less advanced learners whose L2 lexical representations remain closely linked to L1 translations (Kroll & Stewart, 1994; Jiang, 2002; Chen, 2004). A contrastive focus-on-form approach, in which L1–L2 similarities and differences are made explicit, may generate deeper processing by requiring learners to evaluate lexical meanings and uses across languages. This possibility is consistent with the involvement load hypothesis, which links stronger vocabulary retention to greater task-induced need, search, and especially evaluation (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001; Hulstijn, 2001). 

However, learners are unlikely to benefit uniformly from such instructional options. Preexisting vocabulary knowledge may affect how much of the input is understood, while listening proficiency may determine learners’ capacity to segment, interpret, and exploit spoken language for lexical learning. The present study therefore investigates how these two learner factors interact with different post-listening vocabulary explanation conditions—L2, codeswitching, contrastive focus-on-form, and no explanation—in shaping short- and longer-term vocabulary learning through listening.

intros.text:
Vocabulary learning from aural input is an important but comparatively underexplored dimension of second language development. In many EFL classrooms, listening activities are not only used to build comprehension but also provide opportunities for learners to encounter, notice, and consolidate new lexical items. Yet spoken input is transient, and learners’ attention during listening is typically directed toward meaning rather than toward individual word forms. For this reason, the conditions under which listening promotes vocabulary learning, and the learner characteristics that make such learning more or less likely, merit close investigation.

Research on vocabulary acquisition has shown that input alone may be insufficient unless learners’ attention is drawn to lexical form and meaning (Laufer, 2005; Schmidt, 1990; Sharwood Smith, 1991). The involvement load hypothesis further suggests that tasks requiring greater need, search, and especially evaluation can promote deeper processing and stronger retention (Hulstijn & Laufer, 2001). In vocabulary explanation during listening, such processing may be encouraged through second-language explanations, principled codeswitching, or contrastive focus on form, where L1–L2 similarities and differences are made explicit. Theoretical accounts of bilingual lexical representation also suggest that the value of L1 support may vary with learners’ proficiency and lexical development, because L2 words may initially be mediated through L1 translations before more direct conceptual links are established (Kroll & Stewart, 1994; Jiang, 2002; Chen, 2004).

Although previous studies have examined vocabulary learning through listening and the effects of different instructional supports, less is known about how preexisting vocabulary knowledge and listening proficiency jointly shape learning outcomes. Moreover, proficiency has often been treated categorically, which may obscure more subtle interactions between learner variables and instructional conditions. Addressing this gap, the present study revisits classroom data from Chinese senior-secondary EFL learners and investigates how vocabulary learning through listening varies according to learners’ prior vocabulary knowledge, listening proficiency, and four post-listening explanation conditions: L2 explanations, codeswitching, contrastive focus on form, and no vocabulary explanation.

intros.text: Implicit learning (IL)1 refers to the process of learning without intention, and even without awareness of what has been learned. It is regarded as a basic form of learning that makes a major contribution to the acquisition of many motor, perceptual, and cognitive skills, not least the ability to speak a first or second language.  The focus here will be on IL of structural regularities. Can structurespecific activity be detected in the brain during IL tasks? If so, do the brain regions involved vary according to the nature of the regularities to be learned or the domain in which they are instantiated? Do the results of imaging studies tie in with what is known about IL after various types of brain damage?  As in neuroscience more generally the ultimate aim is to understand how and where specific computational functions are carried out in the brain. By studying the brain correlates of IL of structural regularities of different types and in different tasks perhaps we can approach a true science of learning.  Of course, studying IL of real-world skills is immensely challenging, not only because of the time scales over which it occurs, but also because of the difficulty of being able to isolate learning of specific structural regularities from other features of the input, being able to prove that structural generalizations have been learned (for which a perfect record of inputs and outputs is necessary), and being able to prove that any learning is not affected by the participants’ prior knowledge. Hence a number of laboratory IL paradigms have been developed that provide convenient vehicles for studying the acquisition of pure structural regularities in artificial systems. This review will focus on three such paradigms: artificial grammar learning (AGL), sequence learning, and statistical learning. Typically they involve short training periods of between 2 and 20 minutes (though some AGL studies have trained participants over days), the stimuli are devoid of any meaning, the underlying structural regularities are unlike any that the participants are likely to have encountered before, are generally unlike those found in natural domains like language, and the stimuli are stripped of all the other cues to structure that might occur in real-world learning situations. Such tasks have certainly proved extremely useful in establishing that there is such a thing as IL, in exploring its potential limits, individual differences and interactions with other learning processes. They also provide convenient vehicles for examining the brain systems involved in IL, either through brain imaging, brain stimulation, or the study of brain damaged patients. But do they have anything to do with natural language, or with natural language learning? intros.text:
Understanding how humans acquire the intricate structural regularities of natural language remains one of the central challenges of the language sciences. Because the acquisition of grammar occurs largely without conscious effort or explicit instruction, especially in first language acquisition, researchers have long been drawn to the notion that language learning is underpinned by implicit learning (IL): the ability to become sensitive to structure in the environment without intention and, at least in part, without awareness. Over the past several decades, an influential body of experimental work has attempted to capture this capacity in the laboratory using a family of related paradigms—artificial grammar learning (AGL), sequence learning, and statistical learning. Each of these methods exposes participants to structured input and then measures whether they have become attuned to the underlying regularities, typically without being able to articulate what those regularities are. Collectively, these paradigms have been taken to offer a window, albeit a restricted one, on the mechanisms that support natural language learning (Batterink et al., 2019).

The appeal of these paradigms is understandable. They are controlled and replicable, they permit precise manipulation of the input, and they appear to tap learning processes that operate outside of awareness. Yet the extent to which they genuinely model natural language acquisition is far from obvious. AGL, sequence learning, and statistical learning experiments typically provide relatively limited exposure to their target structures; they employ meaningless stimuli such as letter strings, spatial locations, nonsense syllables, or abstract shapes; and the structures they instantiate—finite state grammars, repeating spatial sequences, or triplets defined by transition probabilities—do not necessarily correspond to the properties that many linguists regard as diagnostic of natural language, such as hierarchical organization, nonadjacent dependencies, and grammatical categories. This raises a fundamental question: do these laboratory paradigms actually engage the same brain systems that support the processing and acquisition of natural language, or do they recruit more generic or task-specific mechanisms that happen to yield behavioral sensitivity to structure?

Neuroscience offers a means of addressing this question directly. If the paradigms used to study IL rely on the same neural machinery as natural language, then the brain regions that respond to structural regularities in these tasks should overlap with those known to support language processing. Conversely, divergences may reveal the limits of these paradigms as models of language learning, as well as clues about the specific computational contributions of different brain systems. Previous reviews have considered the balance between learning-related changes in modality-specific perceptual systems and more supramodal regions across the various implicit and statistical learning paradigms (Batterink et al., 2019; Frost, Armstrong, Siegelman, & Christiansen, 2015; Uddén & Männel, 2018). While visual and auditory paradigms do sometimes produce learning-related changes within sensory cortices, the most prominent discussion in the literature has centered on a small number of supramodal regions that appear to carry out generic computational functions across modalities: the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), which encompasses Broca's area and is strongly associated with syntactic processing; the basal ganglia (BG), subcortical structures increasingly implicated in sequencing and rule-based processing; and the hippocampus (H), a central component of the declarative memory system.

Each of these regions carries a distinct set of theoretical commitments. The function of LIFG in language is itself contested, having been attributed variously to hierarchical structure building (Friederici, 2002), to a generic unification or sequence-processing role (Hagoort, 2013), and to working memory or cognitive control demands (Rogalsky & Hickok, 2011; Novick, Trueswell, & Thompson-Schill, 2005). The BG have been characterized both as a procedural engine for rule-based language processing and learning (Ullman, 2001) and as a general sequencing device (Lieberman, 2007), though their precise role remains debated. The hippocampus, classically tied to explicit, declarative memory, has traditionally been assumed to contribute to IL tasks only through contamination from conscious knowledge. Adjudicating between these accounts requires converging evidence from multiple sources.

The aim of this review is therefore to draw together evidence from three complementary methodologies—functional brain imaging, brain stimulation (TMS and tDCS), and the study of the effects of brain damage (in Broca's aphasia, Parkinson's disease, and amnesia)—in order to identify the main brain regions that show sensitivity to structural regularities across implicit learning paradigms. Imaging localizes activity in the healthy brain, while stimulation and lesion studies establish whether that activity is causally necessary for learning. By triangulating across these approaches, and organizing the discussion around AGL, sequence learning, and statistical learning in turn, this review considers what these paradigms reveal about the functions of LIFG, BG, and H, and how those functions relate to the neural basis of natural language processing and learning.

intros.text:
The idea that much of language is learned without intention or awareness has long animated research in language acquisition, and it has motivated an enormous body of experimental work designed to capture such learning in the laboratory. Over recent decades, three paradigms in particular have flourished as putative models of the processes that underlie natural language learning: artificial grammar learning, sequence learning, and statistical learning. Each appears to offer a window, albeit a restricted one, onto how learners become sensitive to structural regularities in their input. In artificial grammar learning, participants are exposed to strings generated by a finite state grammar and then make grammaticality judgments on novel items using intuition; in sequence learning, they respond to repeating stimulus sequences whose structure they cannot report; and in statistical learning, they segment recurring units from continuous streams on the basis of transition probabilities alone. The popularity of these methods reflects an assumption that the computations they engage are broadly the same as, or at least closely related to, those recruited during the acquisition and processing of natural language.

Yet there is reason to question how far this assumption can be taken. These paradigms typically provide relatively little exposure, use meaningless stimuli such as letters, syllables, tones, or nonsense shapes, and do not necessarily target the structural properties—hierarchical constituency, nonadjacent dependencies, and word classes—that many regard as the defining characteristics of natural language. If the paradigms differ so markedly from natural language in their content and in the amount of exposure they afford, then it becomes an open empirical question whether they engage the same brain regions as natural language processing and learning. Answering that question is important because, insofar as these paradigms do recruit the neural machinery of language, they promise a tractable means of investigating how the brain extracts structure from experience; insofar as they do not, inferences drawn from them about natural language learning may be misplaced.

Neuroscientific methods offer a way to address this question directly. Functional imaging reveals which brain regions are active when learners process structured material, brain stimulation techniques such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation can establish whether a given region plays a causal role, and studies of brain damage—in Broca's aphasia, Parkinson's disease, and amnesia—can indicate whether particular regions are necessary for learning. Previous reviews have surveyed this literature and have considered the balance between learning-related changes in modality-specific systems and in supramodal systems that appear to perform generic computations across modalities (Batterink et al., 2019; Frost, Armstrong, Siegelman, & Christiansen, 2015; Uddén & Männel, 2018). Discussions in this area have converged on three supramodal regions as being of particular interest: the left inferior frontal gyrus, encompassing Broca's area, which has been associated with syntactic structure building, unification, control, and working memory; the basal ganglia, a set of subcortical structures increasingly implicated in sequencing and rule-based processing; and the hippocampus, classically the seat of declarative and episodic memory but increasingly linked to implicit and relational learning.

What remains unclear, however, is how coherent the picture from these different sources of evidence really is. Imaging findings are not always consistent with one another, and their alignment with the results of brain stimulation and brain damage studies has rarely been examined systematically across the three learning paradigms simultaneously. Nor has sufficient attention been paid to whether the learning under investigation is genuinely implicit, since many studies rely on grammaticality judgment tasks and few employ rigorous tests of awareness. There is therefore a need to bring together the imaging, stimulation, and lesion evidence, region by region and paradigm by paradigm, in order to establish what can and cannot be concluded about the neural bases of implicit learning and its relationship to language.

The aim of this review is to use data from brain imaging, brain stimulation, and the effects of brain damage to identify the main brain regions that show sensitivity to structural regularities in implicit learning paradigms, and to consider the relationship of these regions to natural language processing and learning. Focusing on the left inferior frontal gyrus, the basal ganglia, and the hippocampus, the review evaluates the consistency of the evidence within and across the artificial grammar, sequence, and statistical learning literatures, and asks what functions these regions might perform. In doing so it will suggest that, rather than mapping discrete functions onto isolated regions, it may be more appropriate to view implicit learning as emerging from the cooperative activity of interconnected networks whose more primitive computations provide the bedrock upon which natural language learning is built.

intros.text:
Over the past several decades, research into the cognitive mechanisms of implicit learning has flourished, driven largely by the development of artificial grammar, sequence learning, and statistical learning paradigms. These experimental frameworks are designed to isolate the ability of the human brain to extract structural regularities from the environment without conscious intention or explicit awareness. In the field of applied linguistics and second language acquisition, these paradigms are of particular interest because they are thought to offer a window into the implicit processes that underlie natural language acquisition. By stripping away the complexities of meaningful communication and focusing on abstract patterns, researchers can investigate how learners acquire the underlying rules of a system—whether those rules are simple linear associations or complex, branching dependencies.

Despite their utility, these paradigms are not without limitations. Most implicit learning tasks provide relatively limited exposure to stimuli, often employ meaningless strings of letters or syllables, and do not necessarily target the specific hierarchical structures characteristic of natural human languages. This raises a fundamental neuroscientific question: do these experimental paradigms engage the same brain regions and neural circuits as the processing and learning of natural language? If artificial grammar learning (AGL) or statistical learning relies on fundamentally different neural architecture than natural language acquisition, then the inferences drawn from these paradigms regarding linguistic competence may be limited.

To address this question, it is necessary to move beyond behavioral data and examine the neural substrates of implicit learning. Previous reviews have explored the tension between modality-specific systems—such as the visual and auditory cortices—and supramodal systems that perform generic computational functions across different types of input (Batterink et al., 2019). Among these supramodal regions, three areas have emerged as primary candidates for the coordination of implicit structural learning: the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), the basal ganglia (BG), and the hippocampus (H). The LIFG, which encompasses Broca's area, is strongly associated with syntactic processing and the construction of hierarchical representations in natural language. The basal ganglia, as part of the procedural memory system, are often viewed as a general sequencing engine capable of automating rule-based processing. Meanwhile, the hippocampus, central to the declarative memory system, is typically associated with explicit recollection but may also play a role in the early stages of pattern extraction and relational encoding.

Establishing a causal link between these brain regions and implicit learning requires a multifaceted approach. While functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can identify sites of increased blood flow during learning or judgment tasks, it provides only correlational evidence. To establish causality, researchers employ brain stimulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), which can temporarily disrupt or enhance the activity of specific regions. Furthermore, the study of brain-damaged patients—such as those with Broca's aphasia, Parkinson's disease (affecting the basal ganglia), or amnesia (affecting the hippocampus)—provides critical evidence regarding which regions are indispensable for the acquisition of implicit structure.

This review aims to synthesize data from brain imaging, brain stimulation, and neuropsychological case studies to identify the primary brain regions sensitive to structural regularities in implicit learning paradigms. By comparing the neural activity observed in artificial grammar, sequence, and statistical learning tasks with known patterns of natural language processing, we seek to clarify the relationship between experimental implicit learning and the actual acquisition of language. In doing so, we will consider whether the brain employs a set of domain-general mechanisms for extracting regularity, or whether certain regions are specialized for the unique complexities of linguistic structure. Ultimately, this analysis will help determine the extent to which our current models of implicit learning can be generalized to the multifaceted process of natural language learning.

intros.text:
Over the past several decades, research into the neural mechanisms of implicit learning has flourished, driven largely by the development and application of artificial grammar, sequence learning, and statistical learning paradigms. These methodologies are of central importance to the field of applied linguistics and cognitive neuroscience because they offer a critical, albeit restricted, window into the implicit processes that underlie the acquisition of natural language. By stripping away the complexities of semantic meaning and communicative intent, these paradigms allow researchers to isolate how the human brain detects and internalizes structural regularities, such as transition probabilities and hierarchical dependencies, without the learner's conscious awareness.

Considerable theoretical attention has been paid to the balance between modality-specific and supramodal systems in these processes. For instance, while visual and auditory paradigms often reveal changes in sensory processing areas, much of the literature has focused on supramodal regions that perform generic computational functions across different modalities (Batterink et al., 2019). Among the most prominent of these are the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), the basal ganglia (BG), and the hippocampus (H). The LIFG, which encompasses Broca's area, is strongly associated with syntactic processing in natural language, though its precise role—whether as a domain-specific center for hierarchical structure building or a general-purpose unification space for sequential processing—remains a subject of intense debate. Similarly, the basal ganglia are often viewed as a procedural engine supporting automatic, rule-based processing, while the hippocampus is traditionally linked to the declarative system and episodic memory.

Despite the volume of research, a significant gap remains in our understanding of the extent to which these artificial paradigms actually engage the same neural architecture as natural language learning. Most implicit learning studies utilize meaningless stimuli, provide relatively limited exposure, and do not necessarily target the types of hierarchical structures characteristic of human grammar. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the activation of regions like the LIFG in artificial grammar tasks reflects the same structural computations used in natural language, or if such activation is merely a byproduct of increased cognitive control and working memory demands during the judgment of nonsense strings. Furthermore, there is a persistent lack of alignment between neuroimaging data—which often show widespread activation—and evidence from brain stimulation and lesion studies, where the necessity of specific regions for implicit learning is less consistent.

To address these inconsistencies, the present review aims to synthesize data from brain imaging, brain stimulation (such as TMS and tDCS), and the study of brain damage (including Broca's aphasia, Parkinson's disease, and amnesia) to identify the primary brain regions sensitive to structural regularities in implicit learning paradigms. Specifically, this article seeks to evaluate the relationship between these identified regions and the processes involved in natural language processing and learning. By triangulating findings across these diverse methodologies, we can better determine whether the neural bases of implicit learning are modular or whether they operate as part of a dynamic, interconnected network.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. First, we examine the role of the LIFG and adjoining regions, contrasting results from artificial grammar learning with those of natural phrase structure grammars. Second, we analyze the contributions of the basal ganglia and the hippocampus, exploring the traditional distinction between procedural and declarative systems. Third, we review evidence from sequence and statistical learning to assess how different levels of structural complexity modulate neural activation. Finally, we discuss how these findings converge to suggest a shift from a modular view of the brain toward a network-based perspective on implicit language acquisition.

segments.text: Despite the volume of research, a significant gap remains in our understanding of the extent to which these artificial paradigms actually engage the same neural architecture as natural language learning. Most implicit learning studies utilize meaningless stimuli, provide relatively limited exposure, and do not necessarily target the types of hierarchical structures characteristic of human grammar. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the activation of regions like the LIFG in artificial grammar tasks reflects the same structural computations used in natural language, or if such activation is merely a byproduct of increased cognitive control and working memory demands during the judgment of nonsense strings.

segments.text: To address these inconsistencies, the present review aims to synthesize data from brain imaging, brain stimulation (such as TMS and tDCS), and the study of brain damage (including Broca's aphasia, Parkinson's disease, and amnesia) to identify the primary brain regions sensitive to structural regularities in implicit learning paradigms. Specifically, this article seeks to evaluate the relationship between these identified regions and the processes involved in natural language processing and learning.

segments.text: The remainder of this article is organized as follows. First, we examine the role of the LIFG and adjoining regions, contrasting results from artificial grammar learning with those of natural phrase structure grammars. Second, we analyze the contributions of the basal ganglia and the hippocampus, exploring the traditional distinction between procedural and declarative systems. Third, we review evidence from sequence and statistical learning to assess how different levels of structural complexity modulate neural activation. Finally, we discuss how these findings converge to suggest a shift from a modular view of the brain toward a network-based perspective on implicit language acquisition.

intros.text:
Over the past decades, research employing artificial grammar, sequence learning, and statistical learning paradigms has flourished, not least because these methods appear to offer a window, albeit with a restricted view, on implicit learning processes underlying natural language learning. But these paradigms usually provide relatively little exposure, use meaningless stimuli, and do not even necessarily target natural language structures. So the question arises whether they engage the same brain regions as natural language. The aim of this review is to use data from brain imaging, brain stimulation, and the effects of brain damage to identify the main brain regions that show sensitivity to structural regularities in implicit learning paradigms and to consider their relationship to natural language processing and learning.

Previous reviews have considered the balance between learning-related brain changes in modality-specific and supramodal systems across different implicit and statistical learning paradigms (Batterink et al., 2019; Frost, Armstrong, Siegelman, & Christiansen, 2015; Udd´ en & M¨ annel, 2018). Visual paradigms have sometimes, but not consistently, revealed learning-related changes in visual processing areas of the brain (e.g., occipital cortex, and even V1), and, as we shall see, auditory statistical learning has revealed changes in brain areas associated with spoken language processing (e.g., left superior temporal gyrus, LSTG). Here the primary focus will be on supramodal regions: Areas that seem to perform some generic computational functions across modalities. This corresponds to the emphasis in discussions of this research in the literature, where the most prominent regions are the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), basal ganglia (shortened here to BG), and hippocampus (shortened here to H).

Syntactic processing is strongly associated with LIFG, which encompasses Broca's area (i.e., Brodmann' s areas [BA] 44/45, and adjoining BA 47). However, there has been much debate over the actual function of LIFG in sentence processing. Some argue that it is involved in building syntactic representations as classically conceived, that is, as involving hierarchical structure and nonadjacent dependency relations (Friederici, 2002). Others argue that it constitutes a general unification space for structure building during sequential processing (Hagoort, 2013). Others argue that in fact LIFG involvement in sentence processing reflects working memory demands (Rogalsky & Hickok, 2011), or that it is primarily engaged in order to resolve syntactic or semantic ambiguity (Hsu, Jaeggi, & Novick, 2017; January, Trueswell, & Thompson-Schill, 2009; Tyler, Cheung, Devereux, & Clarke, 2013), resolve competition between alternatives (Schnur et al., 2009), or that it engages whenever general control demands increase (Novick, Trueswell, & Thompson-Schill, 2005; van de Meerendonk, Rueschemeyer, & Kolk, 2013). The domain-specificity of LIFG is also disputed. From a control perspective the involvement of LIFG in nonlinguistic conflict resolution, such as in the Stroop task, has been emphasized (Hsu et al., 2017; January et al., 2009; van de Meerendonk et al., 2013). From a structure-building point of view LIFG has been implicated in, among other things, music perception (Patel, 2003) and it has been suggested that LIFG is a 'hub' that engages with other representational systems to effect either control or structure building in different domains (Hsu et al., 2017; Patel, 2003). Others have argued that there is language specialization within the LIFG region, with syntactic structure building functions localizable to BA 44 and 45 (Fedorenko, Duncan, & Kanwisher, 2012; Hagoort, 2014), or possibly specifically BA 44, with BA 45 implicated in semantic combinatorics (Schell, Zaccarella, & Friederici, 2017). In the studies reviewed here, when LIFG is referred to it can be assumed that this at least includes BA 44.

Imaging studies have explored the brain areas that are involved in adult explicit learning of natural phrase structure grammars (PSGs) under experimental conditions (Bahlmann, Schubotz, & Friederici, 2008; Hauser, Hofmann, & Opitz, 2012; Musso et al., 2003; Opitz & Friederici, 2003, 2004, 2007). As a shorthand, these will be referred to collectively as the explicit PSG studies. Only one of these studies used actual natural languages (Musso et al., 2003), whereas the others used PSGs (e.g., Brocanto) that generated strings of meaningless nonsense words like aaf plox glif rufi aak boke gum , the structure of which corresponds to the natural language sequence determiner-noun-verbadverb-determiner-adjective-noun. These grammars contain the equivalent of word classes: Either two or four nonsense words were assigned to the noun and verb categories depending on the study (Opitz & Friederici, 2003, 2004). In all of these studies, the participants were trained under explicit learning conditions; for example, they cycled between presentation of examples and grammaticality judgment (GJ) with feedback under instructions to work out the rules of the language. Such procedures encourage active hypothesis formation and testing; learning is intentional and leads to conscious knowledge. These studies have found that, in grammaticality judgment tasks (GJTs), following training there is higher activation to nongrammatical (NG) than grammatical (G) items in LIFG and also adjoining areas of the left ventral premotor cortex (vPMC) and the frontal operculum (FOP). Some studies have gone further and identified activity in the phylogenetically older vPMC or FOP regions with processing and learning of local, adjacent dependencies, and activity in the more recently evolved LIFG with processing and learning of nonadjacent dependencies and hierarchical structure (Bahlmann et al., 2008; Opitz & Friederici, 2007; Wilson et al., 2015; Wilson, Marslen-Wilson, & Petkov, 2017). These studies at least tell us that, following explicit training, meaningless material that is structured in a language-like way can engage similar brain areas as natural language in the performance of a GJT. The question is whether, and for what other kinds of structures, LIFG and related regions are also engaged in IL situations, and what this might tell us about the function of these regions.

The BG are a group of subcortical structures that include the caudate nucleus and putamen. They constitute a relatively primitive part of the brain and it was initially thought that they are primarily involved in basic movement control and motor learning. But, more recently, their role in cognitive functions, and even language, has come to the fore. It has become apparent that BG are connected to many cortical areas. There are loops connecting putamen to motor cortex, the head of the caudate to the prefrontal cortex (including BA 47; Dominey, Inui, & Hoen, 2009), and the body and tail of the caudate to visual and auditory cortices (Lim, Fiez, & Holt, 2014; Seger, 2008). With regard to function, Ullman (2001) has stressed the role of BG in a procedural (as opposed to declarative ) system that supports automatic, and implicit, rule-based language processing and learning. Lieberman (2007) regards BG as a general sequencing engine that in relation to language 'can form a potentially infinite number of different sentences by reordering, recombining, and modifying a finite set of words using a finite set of linguistic rules' (p. 51). This focus on subcortical structures in relation to language processing may seem surprising, and invites the idea that language was made possible by an adaptation of preexisting motor systems (Lieberman, 2007). Given the importance of this claim, it is not surprising that the precise role of BG in language processing is debated. There is neuroimaging evidence that BG is involved in purely syntactic, as opposed to semantic, processing (Moreno, Limousin, Dehaene, & Pallier, 2018; Moro et al., 2001). However, other researchers appear to limit its role to ancillary functions, rather than core syntactic processing. It has been argued that BG may be particularly active when expectations are violated, a preferred interpretation suppressed, and controlled processes (in frontal cortex) need to be engaged to effect a repair, as happens in garden-path sentences, for example (Mestres-Miss´ e, Bazin, Trampel, Turner, & Kotz, 2014; Mestres-Miss´ e, Turner, & Friederici, 2012; Sambin et al., 2012). These control functions seem similar to those attributed to LIFG, reinforcing the idea that these regions work closely together. In the context of morphological processing and word recognition, it has been argued that BG are only involved in late stage processing and that the essential syntactic and morphological computations are carried out elsewhere (Longworth, Keenan, Barker, Marslen-Wilson, & Tyler, 2005). It will be interesting to see the extent to which BG are involved in performing IL tasks given that they usually tap into the very early phases of learning, prior to the acquisition of automaticity, and do not obviously entail reanalysis and repair processes.

BGandthelargerprocedural system are classically contrasted with a declarative system that supports explicit learning and knowledge. H is a central component of the declarative system and is known to be essential for episodic memory (the conscious recollection of experiences; Squire, 1992). Damage to H is associated with amnesia, that is, the inability to recall the recent past, and more relevant here, the apparent inability to form new memories. Various kinds of IL and memory are relatively intact in amnesia leading to the assumption that the declarative and procedural learning systems are dissociable. For this reason, studying amnesic performance on IL tasks is usually used as a means of assessing procedural learning without contamination from explicit knowledge.

Hippocampal functions are not typically related to structural aspects of language processing. However, studies of explicit learning of the artificial language Brocanto have found that left hippocampal activity showed a decreasing trend from being greater than baseline at the start of training to being below baseline at the end (Opitz & Friederici, 2003, 2004). Opitz and Friederici (2004) nuance this by showing that the decreasing trend is associated with manipulations of similarity rather than rule application, and Hauser et al. (2012) show that in post-training GJT, the (in this case right) hippocampus is related to similarity-, rather than rule-, based processing. The decreasing trend in hippocampal activity over training contrasts with the increasing trend in LIFG in the same studies (Opitz & Friederici, 2003, 2004). These studies therefore reveal the changing balance between similarity- and rule-based processing in the course of acquisition, at least as evidenced in the performance of GJs (for related evidence based on individual differences and electrophysiology see Morgan-Short, Faretta-Stuttenberg, Brill-Scheutz, Carpenter, & Wong, 2014; Tanner, Inoue, & Osterhout, 2014; Tanner, McLaughlin, Herschensohn, & Osterhout, 2013). This shift might suggest a competitive relationship between declarative memory-based and procedural rule-based systems (Ullman, 2004). Indeed, there is evidence in favor of mutual exclusivity of the electrophysiological indices of these processes (in the form of P600 and N400 effects) in classroom language learning (Tanner et al., 2013). On the other hand, using a similar artificial language training method to Opitz and Friederici (2003), an fMRI study by Kepinska, de Rover, Caspers, and Schiller (2018) found no evidence for functional connectivity between LIFG and H, implying independent contributions of these systems. Bear in mind that these studies all used explicit training paradigms. On the standard view, one would not expect to find hippocampal involvement in IL situations unless there is contamination from explicit memory processes.

intros.text:
Over the past few decades, research into implicit learning has flourished, driven by the hope that experimental paradigms such as artificial grammar learning (AGL), sequence learning, and statistical learning might offer a window onto the mechanisms underlying natural language acquisition. These methods are particularly attractive because they appear to capture the incidental, often unconscious, extraction of structural regularities that characterizes first language learning. However, a critical question remains: do these artificial paradigms, which typically employ meaningless stimuli and provide limited exposure, engage the same neural substrates as natural language processing? The aim of this review is to synthesize data from brain imaging, brain stimulation, and patient studies to identify the primary brain regions sensitive to structural regularities in implicit learning and to evaluate their relationship to natural language. 

The literature has largely focused on three supramodal regions: the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG), the basal ganglia (BG), and the hippocampus (H). The LIFG, encompassing Broca’s area, is strongly associated with syntactic processing in natural language, though its precise function—whether hierarchical structure building, unification, or cognitive control—remains debated (Friederici, 2002; Hagoort, 2013; Rogalsky & Hickok, 2011). The BG, traditionally linked to motor control, are increasingly viewed as central to procedural learning and rule-based language processing (Ullman, 2001; Lieberman, 2007). Conversely, the hippocampus is the cornerstone of the declarative system, supporting explicit memory and episodic recall (Squire, 1992). While these regions are often contrasted as procedural versus declarative systems, recent neuroimaging suggests they may interact dynamically during learning. 

Despite the proliferation of studies, the field faces significant challenges. First, there is often a poor alignment between imaging results in healthy participants and behavioral outcomes in patients with brain damage. For instance, while fMRI studies consistently show BG involvement in sequence learning, patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) often perform unimpaired on similar tasks, raising questions about the necessity of this region or the role of compensatory mechanisms. Similarly, hippocampal activation is frequently observed in implicit learning contexts, yet amnesic patients often show preserved learning, challenging the assumption that hippocampal contributions reflect explicit memory. Second, methodological variations across studies—such as differences in stimulus presentation (sequential vs. whole string), task demands (judgment vs. passive listening), and the complexity of the underlying grammars—complicate functional interpretation. 

Furthermore, the extent to which implicit learning in these paradigms truly isolates unconscious processes is frequently unclear. Many studies rely on grammaticality judgment tasks (GJTs), which may inadvertently engage explicit strategies or working memory, particularly in the LIFG. While some research has attempted to rule out awareness through subjective measures or by using tasks where grammaticality is irrelevant (e.g., liking judgments), inconsistencies persist. 

This review addresses these gaps by triangulating evidence from three distinct methodologies: functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to identify activation patterns, brain stimulation (TMS/tDCS) to establish causal links, and patient studies (Broca’s aphasia, PD, amnesia) to assess necessity. By examining these regions across AGL, sequence learning, and statistical learning paradigms, we aim to clarify whether the neural mechanisms of implicit learning overlap with those of natural language or represent distinct, domain-general processes. Ultimately, understanding the interplay between these systems is vital for determining whether the brain regions identified in artificial tasks are indeed the building blocks of human language learning.

These methods are particularly attractive because they appear to capture the incidental, often unconscious, extraction of structural regularities that characterizes first language learning.
