intros.text:
Implicit learning is usually understood as the acquisition of knowledge about structural regularities in the environment without the intention to learn and without full awareness of what has been learned. It has long been assumed to play a central role in language acquisition, where learners become sensitive to phonological, lexical, morphological, and syntactic patterns that are far too numerous and probabilistic to be taught or consciously inferred one by one. For this reason, experimental paradigms such as artificial grammar learning, serial reaction time or sequence learning, and statistical learning have become influential tools for investigating learning mechanisms that may also support natural language learning. In artificial grammar learning, participants are exposed to strings generated by a finite-state system and later classify new strings as grammatical or ungrammatical, often despite being unable to verbalize the rules. In sequence learning, participants become faster at responding to structured sequences than to random ones, typically without being able to report the sequence. In statistical learning, participants extract recurring units from continuous streams on the basis of distributional regularities such as transitional probabilities. Together, these paradigms appear to offer experimentally tractable windows onto the capacity to learn structure from exposure.

At the same time, the relationship between these laboratory paradigms and natural language learning remains uncertain. The stimuli used in implicit learning experiments are often highly reduced: letters, tones, syllables, shapes, or spatial locations rather than meaningful words and sentences. Exposure is usually brief, the structures are simpler than those found in natural languages, and the tasks used to reveal learning—especially grammaticality judgments—may themselves recruit decision, memory, or control processes that are not identical to learning. Moreover, statistical learning is not always implicit in the strict sense: Participants may be instructed to find words or patterns, and the products of learning may become consciously accessible even if the computations that generated them were not. Batterink et al. (2019) therefore argue for a careful distinction between experimental paradigms and the awareness status of the knowledge acquired, suggesting that “implicit learning” should be reserved for learning without awareness, which may occur across different paradigms. This distinction is especially important when interpreting neuroscientific evidence, because the same task may involve implicit sensitivity to structure, explicit memory for exemplars, working memory, prediction, and response selection.

A central question, then, is whether the brain systems recruited in artificial grammar, sequence, and statistical learning overlap with those involved in natural language processing and learning. If these paradigms genuinely capture mechanisms relevant to language, one might expect them to engage regions known to participate in linguistic structure building, sequential prediction, or memory-based learning. Three regions or systems have been especially prominent in this debate. The left inferior frontal gyrus, including Broca’s area, is strongly associated with syntactic processing, although its precise contribution is contested: It has been linked to hierarchical structure building, unification, working memory, cognitive control, and conflict resolution. The basal ganglia have traditionally been associated with motor control and procedural learning, but have also been implicated in sequencing, prediction, reinforcement learning, and aspects of grammatical processing. The hippocampus, by contrast, is classically associated with declarative and episodic memory, and is often treated as supporting explicit rather than implicit learning; nevertheless, increasing evidence suggests that it may also contribute to relational encoding, rapid association formation, and abstraction of regularities without awareness.

Neuroscientific methods offer complementary ways of evaluating these possible contributions. Functional neuroimaging can identify regions whose activity changes as learners process structured rather than unstructured input, grammatical rather than ungrammatical strings, or familiar rather than novel sequences. Brain stimulation methods such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation can test whether perturbing a region changes learning or later performance. Studies of patients with focal or system-specific damage—such as Broca’s aphasia, Parkinson’s disease, or amnesia—can provide further evidence about whether a region is necessary for particular forms of learning. Yet these methods do not always converge. A region may be active in healthy participants but not necessary when damaged, either because other regions compensate or because the task can be solved in more than one way. Conversely, patient deficits may reflect broader task demands rather than the loss of a specific learning computation. Procedural differences across studies, including whole-string versus sequential presentation, passive exposure versus feedback-based training, and implicit versus explicit instructions, further complicate interpretation.

The aim of this review is to examine what current evidence from brain imaging, brain stimulation, and neuropsychological studies reveals about the neural bases of implicit learning, with particular attention to its relevance for natural language. The review focuses on artificial grammar learning, sequence learning, and statistical learning because these paradigms have generated the most substantial neuroscientific literature on sensitivity to structural regularities. Rather than assuming that a single implicit learning system underlies all such tasks, the review considers how different brain regions contribute under different task conditions, how these contributions align or fail to align across methodologies, and whether the computations revealed are plausibly related to those required for language. The broader goal is to move beyond simple mappings between paradigms and brain modules, and toward an account of implicit learning as the product of interacting neural systems whose roles vary with structure, modality, awareness, and task demands.

intros.text:
Implicit learning is widely assumed to be one of the foundations on which language learning rests. Natural languages present learners with patterned distributions of sounds, words, morphemes, and syntactic dependencies, many of which are acquired without explicit instruction and often without conscious access to the regularities that have been learned. For this reason, experimental paradigms such as artificial grammar learning, serial reaction time sequence learning, and statistical learning have become central tools for investigating how humans detect structure in complex input. These paradigms appear to offer a controlled way of examining learning from exposure: participants encounter patterned material, often incidentally, and later show sensitivity to its structure despite being unable to verbalize the relevant rules or regularities.

The appeal of these paradigms for language research is clear. Artificial grammar learning studies ask whether learners can acquire constraints over novel symbol strings; sequence learning studies examine sensitivity to ordered dependencies; and statistical learning studies show that learners can segment continuous streams by tracking distributional cues. Together, these methods seem to capture component processes that may contribute to first and second language acquisition, including the extraction of sequential regularities, the formation of chunks, and the abstraction of structural relations. Recent neuroscientific work has therefore sought to identify the brain systems that support such learning, and to determine whether these systems overlap with those implicated in natural language processing. Reviews of this literature have emphasized that implicit and statistical learning are not supported by a single isolated mechanism but by interactions among declarative and nondeclarative memory systems, with learning-related effects observed across cortical and subcortical regions (Batterink et al., 2019).

Yet the relationship between laboratory implicit learning and natural language learning remains uncertain. The stimuli used in many experiments are deliberately impoverished: strings of letters, tones, syllables, visual shapes, or spatial locations that lack meaning, communicative function, and the rich multilayered structure of real language. Exposure is often brief, sometimes lasting only minutes, and the target regularities may be much simpler than those found in phonology, morphology, or syntax. Moreover, what counts as “implicit” varies across studies. Some experiments rely on incidental exposure and post hoc awareness checks; others instruct participants to search for patterns or repeatedly alternate exposure with testing, thereby encouraging explicit strategies. Consequently, it is not always clear whether the neural activity observed in these tasks reflects implicit learning itself, the expression of acquired knowledge in a judgment task, explicit memory, working memory, cognitive control, or some combination of these processes.

This uncertainty is particularly important because several brain regions prominent in implicit learning research also have established or debated roles in language. The left inferior frontal gyrus, including Broca’s area and adjoining frontal opercular regions, is strongly associated with syntactic processing, but its precise contribution has been interpreted in different ways: as hierarchical structure building, combinatorial unification, working memory, conflict resolution, or domain-general control. The basal ganglia have been linked to procedural learning, sequencing, prediction, and aspects of morphosyntactic processing, but they are also involved in motor control, reinforcement learning, and feedback-based categorization. The hippocampus is classically associated with declarative memory and explicit recollection, yet increasing evidence suggests that it can contribute to relational encoding, sequence learning, and the extraction of regularities even when awareness is limited. Thus, the very regions that might connect implicit learning paradigms to language are multifunctional, and their activation does not by itself establish that language-like learning mechanisms are being engaged.

A further difficulty is methodological. Functional neuroimaging can reveal where activity changes during exposure to structured input or during later grammaticality, familiarity, or preference judgments, but it cannot by itself show whether a region is necessary for learning. Brain stimulation and patient studies provide stronger causal evidence, but they often use procedures that differ from imaging studies in stimulus presentation, task demands, amount of exposure, and measures of awareness. As a result, findings across methods do not always align. A region may be active in healthy participants but damage to that region may leave performance intact, perhaps because the task is simple enough for other systems to compensate, or because the patient version of the task changes the learning problem. Conversely, impairments may emerge only when the regularities are complex, probabilistic, noisy, or require integration across stimulus dimensions.

The present review addresses this problem by examining neuroscientific evidence from artificial grammar learning, sequence learning, and statistical learning with a focus on three supramodal regions repeatedly implicated in the literature: the left inferior frontal gyrus/frontal operculum, the basal ganglia, and the hippocampus. Rather than treating brain imaging findings in isolation, the review triangulates evidence from functional imaging, brain stimulation, and studies of neurological patients, including individuals with agrammatism, Parkinson’s disease, and amnesia. Its aim is to identify which regions show sensitivity to structural regularities under implicit learning conditions, to evaluate whether these regions are necessary for performance, and to consider how their functions relate to natural language processing and learning. In doing so, the review argues for a cautious interpretation of overlap between implicit learning tasks and language: such overlap is informative, but only when task demands, awareness, structural complexity, and interactions among neural systems are taken into account.

intros.text: Oral fluency, the “flow, continuity, automaticity, or smoothness of speech” (Koponen & Riggenbach, 2000, p. 6), is a prime characteristic of successful language communication that has recently become central to many studies of second language acquisition (SLA).  Investigating fluency helps researchers to understand how a second language (L2) is processed, produced, and acquired  In addition, exploring fluency enables them to examine some abstract dimensions of SLA, including implicit knowledge, proceduralization of newly learned structures, and automatization of the processes of speech production (Loewen & Sato, 2018; Paradis, 2009; Suzuki & DeKeyser, 2017). For this reason, fluency is often examined in relation to other aspects of language processing and performance  The current study belongs to this body of research in aiming to investigate the relationship between fluency and use of formulaic language.  The interest in this relationship is built on psycholinguistic research evidence suggesting that use of formulaic language reduces the amount of language planning and processing, and therefore facilitates oral production (see Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018, for a review).  One line of research in this area has focused on the use of multiword sequences (MWSs)—combinations of words that appear together highly frequently in a target language (Garner & Crossley, 2018)—and on its relationship with proficiency (e.g., Nattinger & DeCarrico, 1992; Pawley & Syder, 1983; Wood, 2015; Wray, 2002; see Granger, 2018, for a review). Findings suggest that more proficient L2 users have a better command of MWSs in terms of range, frequency, and sophistication (e.g., Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle & Crossley, 2015; Paquot, 2019). The findings also indicate that use of MWSs is related to oral fluency (Boers, Eyckmans, Kappel, Stengers, & Demecheleer, 2006; Stengers, Boers, Housen, & Eyckmans, 2011; Tavakoli, 2011; Wood, 2009, 2010).  Although the existing research evidence highlights the relationship between fluency and MWSs, no study thus far has examined this relationship systematically across a range of assessed levels of proficiency to see if there is a linear relationship between the two.  Understanding the relationship between MWSs and fluency at different levels of development is important for the study of SLA in shedding light on the processes of speech production.  In addition, such knowledge can help the language testing discipline to develop a valid assessment of learner phraseological knowledge and its relationship to fluency at different levels of proficiency.  The current study aimed to contribute to these areas by investigating, both quantitatively and qualitatively, the relationship between MWSs and fluency in 56 participants at four levels of proficiency assessed via the speaking paper of the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP).

intros.text:
The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) production has attracted growing attention in second language acquisition (SLA) research, largely because of the processing advantages that phraseological knowledge is thought to confer. Formulaic language—a broad category encompassing idioms, collocations, phrasal verbs, binomials, and lexical bundles or n-grams (Wray, 2002; Wood, 2015)—is widely assumed to be stored and retrieved more efficiently than freely generated word combinations (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018). This retrieval efficiency has been theorized to free up the attentional resources that speakers need in order to attend to other aspects of language processing, thereby facilitating more fluent oral production (Pawley & Syder, 1983; Boers et al., 2006). Since Pawley and Syder's (1983) seminal observation that native-like fluency depends on a vast store of memorized phrases, researchers have increasingly viewed knowledge of MWSs as central to the development of oral proficiency (Nattinger & DeCarrico, 1992).

Much of the empirical work on this relationship has, however, concentrated on written production, where a consistent picture has emerged: more proficient writers make greater use of high-frequency collocations and, in some studies, of strongly associated, lower-frequency combinations (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018). Corpus-based studies of speech have begun to complement this literature, showing that oral proficiency is positively related to the proportion and frequency of target-like n-grams, though the relationship between proficiency and n-gram association strength remains far less clear (Kyle et al., 2017; Garner & Crossley, 2018). A smaller set of studies has looked specifically at the link between MWSs and oral fluency, reporting positive associations between formulaic language use and both perceived and temporal fluency (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Wood, 2009).

This body of work is nonetheless limited in important respects. Several studies have relied on very small samples or on participants drawn from a narrow band of proficiency, constraining the generalizability of their findings (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Wood, 2009). Moreover, fluency has often been assessed through subjective ratings, and where objective measures have been used, they have typically captured only a single dimension—usually speed—rather than the multifaceted construct of utterance fluency, which comprises speed, breakdown, and repair (Kormos, 1999). Given the field's move toward more objective and fine-grained measurement of oral ability, there is a clear need for studies that examine how different aspects of fluency relate to distinct measures of MWS use across a range of proficiency levels.

The present study addresses these gaps by investigating the relationship between oral fluency and the use of MWSs among 56 learners across four proficiency levels, using a validated speaking test and corpus-based n-gram measures of frequency, proportion, and association. In doing so, it aims to provide a more comprehensive account of how the lexical demands of L2 speech relate to fluency at different stages of oral development.

intros.text:
The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) learning and use has attracted growing attention among researchers in recent years, largely because of the important part such sequences play in language processing and production (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Wray, 2002). MWSs—combinations of words that recur with high frequency in a target language, ranging from idioms and collocations to lexical bundles and n-grams—are widely believed to offer L2 speakers quick and cost-effective access to correct language, thereby freeing up the attentional resources needed for other aspects of speech production (Boers et al., 2006; Kormos, 2006; Pawley & Syder, 1983). Because MWSs can be retrieved as holistic units, they are theorized to reduce processing load, particularly at the formulation stage of speech production, and thus to facilitate fluent speech (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018; Wood, 2015).

Given this theoretical motivation, a substantial body of research has explored the relationship between MWS use and L2 proficiency. However, the majority of these studies have focused on written production, typically through essay-writing tasks (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018). Findings from this line of work suggest that more proficient writers tend to have richer phraseological knowledge and better control of MWSs. A smaller set of studies, notably those employing corpus-based frequency, proportion, and association measures, has begun to examine oral production (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle et al., 2017), showing that orally proficient speakers produce a greater number of targetlike sequences.

A further group of studies has specifically addressed the link between oral fluency and formulaic language, generally reporting positive relationships (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Tavakoli, 2011; Wood, 2009). Nonetheless, this emerging evidence is limited in several important respects. First, many of these studies drew on very small samples or on participants spanning only a narrow range of proficiency levels, which constrains the generalizability of their findings. Second, fluency in earlier work was often assessed through subjective ratings, whereas the field of language testing is increasingly moving toward more objective measurement of L2 ability. Third, those few studies that did employ objective measures tended to capture only a single dimension of fluency—typically speed—leaving the multifaceted nature of the construct largely unexplored. Consequently, it remains unclear how different aspects of fluency relate to different types of MWS use across the proficiency continuum.

The present study addresses these gaps by examining the relationship between oral fluency and MWS use across four proficiency levels, using objective, corpus-based n-gram measures alongside fine-grained measures of speed, breakdown, and repair fluency. Drawing on speaking test data from 56 learners, we ask (a) to what extent n-gram proportion, frequency, and association relate to proficiency level, and (b) to what extent these measures are associated with the three dimensions of oral fluency. In doing so, we aim to offer a more comprehensive, quantitative and qualitative account of how phraseological competence relates to fluent L2 speech.

intros.text:
The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) acquisition has become a focal point of research due to their significant impact on language processing and production. MWSs, which encompass a diverse range of lexical strings including idioms, collocations, phrasal verbs, and lexical bundles, are thought to be processed more efficiently than infrequent word combinations (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018). From a psycholinguistic perspective, the ability to retrieve these sequences as holistic units rather than assembling them from individual words is believed to reduce the cognitive load on a speaker's attentional resources, thereby facilitating greater automaticity and oral fluency (Kormos, 2006). 

Empirical evidence has generally supported the link between phraseological knowledge and L2 proficiency. Much of this research has focused on written production, where higher-proficiency writers typically demonstrate a richer and more accurate use of MWSs (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018). In the domain of oral production, recent corpus-based studies have shown that orally proficient speakers produce a greater number of target-like n-grams (Kyle & Crossley, 2015) and that the proportion of these sequences increases as proficiency develops (Garner & Crossley, 2018). Furthermore, some studies have specifically linked the use of formulaic sequences to perceived oral proficiency (Boers et al., 2006) and objective measures of speed fluency (Wood, 2009). 

Despite these insights, several gaps remain in the current literature. First, many existing studies have relied on small sample sizes or restricted proficiency ranges, limiting the generalizability of their findings. Second, the measurement of fluency has often been based on subjective human ratings (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011), which may lack the objectivity required for rigorous language testing research. Third, while speed fluency has been examined, fewer studies have explored the relationship between MWSs and other critical dimensions of utterance fluency, such as breakdown (pausing) and repair (self-correction). To address these limitations, it is necessary to employ objective, multi-dimensional measures of fluency alongside frequency-based n-gram indices.

The present study aims to investigate the relationship between the use of MWSs and oral fluency across four proficiency levels (Low B1 to C1). Using data from the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP), we employ a frequency-based approach to identify n-grams through the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Lexical Sophistication (TAALES; Kyle et al., 2017). Specifically, the study seeks to determine: (1) the extent to which MWSs—measured by proportion, frequency, and association strength—relate to general oral proficiency levels, and (2) the extent to which these n-gram measures are associated with specific dimensions of oral fluency, namely speed, breakdown, and repair.

intros.text:
The use of multiword sequences (MWSs)—combinations of words that co-occur with high frequency in a target language—has attracted significant attention in second language acquisition (SLA) research due to its vital role in language processing and production (Garner & Crossley, 2018). From a psycholinguistic perspective, MWSs are thought to be processed differently from infrequent strings, offering processing advantages that enable speakers to produce utterances more fluently by freeing up attentional resources for other aspects of production, such as monitoring and articulation (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018). Consequently, a larger repertoire of formulaic language is often viewed as a key mechanism for reducing cognitive load during the formulation stage of speech (Kormos, 2006).

Empirical evidence has consistently highlighted the relationship between phraseological knowledge and L2 proficiency. While the majority of research has focused on written production (e.g., Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Kyle & Crossley, 2015), recent studies have begun to explore oral performance. For instance, Kyle and Crossley (2015) found that orally proficient speakers produce a greater number of target-like sequences. Similarly, research specifically targeting oral fluency has shown positive correlations between MWS counts and perceived fluency (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011) or objective speed measures (Wood, 2009, 2010).

Despite these insights, the existing evidence remains limited. Many previous studies relied on small sample sizes or restricted proficiency ranges, potentially limiting the generalizability of their findings. Furthermore, several studies relied on subjective human ratings of fluency, which lacks the objectivity sought in contemporary language testing (Tavakoli et al., 2017). While some objective measures have been employed, they often focused on a single dimension of fluency, such as speed, neglecting the complexities of breakdown and repair processes.

Addressing these gaps, the current study examines the relationship between MWSs and a multifaceted construct of oral fluency—comprising speed, breakdown, and repair—across four proficiency levels (Low B1 to C1). Using the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Lexical Sophistication (TAALES; Kyle et al., 2017), we employ frequency-based n-gram measures to objectively analyze the spoken output of 56 learners taking the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP). The study is guided by two primary research questions: first, to what extent does the use of MWSs (measured through proportion, frequency, and association) relate to general proficiency levels? Second, to what extent are these n-gram measures associated with specific dimensions of oral fluency? By combining quantitative n-gram analysis with qualitative inspection, this research aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how phraseological competence contributes to the flow and continuity of L2 speech.

intros.text:
The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) acquisition has gained significant attention in applied linguistics, particularly regarding their contribution to oral proficiency. MWSs, a catch-all term for recurrent word combinations such as collocations, idioms, and lexical bundles, are theorized to facilitate language processing by allowing speakers to retrieve longer units of language holistically rather than constructing them word-by-word (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Jeong & Jiang, 2019). Psycholinguistic research suggests that MWSs are processed differently from infrequent strings, offering processing advantages that free up attentional resources for other aspects of production, such as articulation and monitoring (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018; Skehan, 2009). This theoretical framework posits that a larger repertoire of formulaic language reduces cognitive load, thereby enhancing oral fluency (Kormos, 2006; Levelt, 1989).

Oral fluency is a complex construct often characterized by temporal features and disfluency markers. Segalowitz (2010) distinguishes between cognitive, utterance, and perceived fluency, with utterance fluency being the most objectively measurable through acoustic analysis. Skehan (2003) further delineates fluency into three dimensions: speed (flow and continuity), breakdown (pauses and silences), and repair (monitoring and self-correction). These dimensions reflect different stages of the speech production process, with speed indicating automaticity, breakdown signaling formulation difficulties, and repair reflecting monitoring processes (Kahng, 2014; Tavakoli & Skehan, 2005).

Empirical evidence supports a positive relationship between MWS use and L2 proficiency. Studies on written production consistently show that higher-proficiency writers employ richer phraseological knowledge (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger & Bestgen, 2014). In the realm of oral proficiency, recent corpus-based studies have demonstrated that L2 speakers produce a greater proportion of target-like bigrams and trigrams as proficiency increases (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle & Crossley, 2015). Furthermore, specific investigations into oral fluency have found significant correlations between the frequency of MWSs and both perceived and objective measures of fluency (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Wood, 2009, 2010). For instance, Wood (2009, 2010) reported that improvements in speed fluency measures were accompanied by an increase in MWS usage.

Despite these findings, the existing literature presents several limitations. First, many studies rely on subjective fluency ratings rather than objective, fine-grained acoustic measures (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011). Second, sample sizes in fluency-focused studies are often small, and the range of proficiency levels examined is restricted, potentially limiting the generalizability of results (Wood, 2009, 2010). Third, while previous research has explored the relationship between MWSs and general proficiency, fewer studies have systematically investigated how specific aspects of fluency (speed, breakdown, repair) relate to different measures of MWSs (frequency, proportion, association strength) across a broad spectrum of proficiency levels. Addressing these gaps is essential for understanding the nuanced role of phraseology in L2 speech production.

The current study aims to address these limitations by examining the relationship between oral fluency and MWS use across four proficiency levels (Low B1 to C1). Utilizing data from the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP), we analyze objective measures of fluency alongside corpus-based measures of MWSs. Specifically, this study investigates: (1) the extent to which MWS use relates to general oral proficiency levels, and (2) the extent to which MWS use is associated with specific dimensions of oral fluency (speed, breakdown, and repair). By integrating quantitative analysis with qualitative insights, this research seeks to provide a comprehensive picture of how phraseological competence contributes to oral fluency in L2 speakers.

intros.text:
The role of multiword sequences (MWSs) in second language (L2) acquisition has attracted increasing attention from researchers, particularly regarding their potential contribution to oral proficiency and fluency. MWSs, defined as combinations of words that co-occur frequently in a target language, encompass various forms such as idioms, collocations, and lexical bundles (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Jeong & Jiang, 2019). Theoretical accounts suggest that the use of MWSs facilitates speech production by reducing cognitive load, thereby freeing attentional resources for other aspects of language processing (Kormos, 2006; Skehan, 2009). This processing advantage is often linked to the holistic retrieval of prefabricated chunks, which allows speakers to produce language more efficiently than constructing utterances word-by-word.

While the relationship between phraseological knowledge and oral proficiency is well-established in theory, empirical evidence regarding its specific link to oral fluency remains less clear. Previous studies have primarily focused on written production, demonstrating that higher proficiency writers tend to use a richer variety of MWSs (Bestgen & Granger, 2014; Kyle & Crossley, 2015). In the domain of speaking, recent corpus-based studies have confirmed that oral proficiency is positively correlated with the frequency and proportion of target-like n-grams (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle & Crossley, 2015). However, these studies often relied on holistic proficiency ratings rather than objective measures of utterance fluency.

A limited number of studies have specifically investigated the link between MWSs and oral fluency. Boers et al. (2006) and Stengers et al. (2011) found significant correlations between MWS counts and perceived fluency ratings. More recently, Wood (2009, 2010) utilized objective temporal measures, such as speech rate, and reported that improvements in fluency were accompanied by an increase in the use of MWSs. Despite these findings, the existing literature presents several limitations. First, many studies employed small sample sizes or restricted proficiency ranges, potentially limiting the generalizability of the results (Boers et al., 2006; Stengers et al., 2011; Wood, 2009). Second, the measurement of fluency in earlier work often relied on subjective judgments, whereas contemporary language testing research emphasizes the need for objective, fine-grained measures of utterance fluency (Tavakoli, Nakatsuhara, & Hunter, 2017; Thomson, Boers, & Coxhead, 2017). Furthermore, previous investigations have typically examined only one aspect of fluency, such as speed, neglecting the triadic framework of speed, breakdown, and repair proposed by Skehan (2003).

To address these gaps, the current study examines the relationship between the use of MWSs and oral fluency across four distinct proficiency levels (Low B1 to C1). Utilizing data from the Test of English for Educational Purposes (TEEP), we analyze objective measures of fluency—including articulation rate, pause frequency, and repair frequency—and correlate them with corpus-based measures of MWSs, specifically n-gram proportion, frequency, and association strength. This study aims to provide a more nuanced understanding of how phraseological competence contributes to the mechanics of oral fluency in L2 speech production.

intros.text:
A central challenge for second language (L2) speakers is to produce speech that is not only accurate and appropriate but also fluent. In applied linguistics and language testing, oral fluency is commonly understood as the smooth, rapid, and continuous delivery of speech, reflected in temporal features such as speed, pausing, and repair behavior. Fluency is also closely tied to the efficiency of speech processing: speakers must conceptualize messages, select lexical and grammatical forms, and articulate them under real-time pressure. One source of such efficiency may be learners’ command of multiword sequences (MWSs), including collocations, lexical bundles, and other recurrent word combinations. Formulaic language has long been argued to support fluent expression because stored or highly familiar sequences can reduce processing demands during speech production (Wray, 2002; Wood, 2015). Classic accounts of native-like selection and fluency similarly emphasize speakers’ reliance on prefabricated or semi-prefabricated strings rather than fully novel word-by-word assembly (Pawley & Syder, 1983).

The psycholinguistic rationale for linking MWSs to fluency is compelling. If recurrent strings such as I think that, a lot of, or in the case of are processed more efficiently than less familiar combinations, they may help speakers allocate attentional resources to planning, monitoring, and articulation. Research on formulaic processing suggests that frequent sequences enjoy processing advantages in both comprehension and production (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018). From a skill-acquisition perspective, repeated exposure and practice may contribute to automatization and proceduralization, enabling learners to retrieve and deploy larger units with less effort (Paradis, 2008; Suzuki & DeKeyser, 2017). For L2 speakers, whose lexical networks and phraseological repertoires are typically less developed than those of first language users, such sequences may be especially valuable as resources for maintaining speech flow.

Empirical work has generally supported a positive relationship between formulaic language and oral proficiency. Boers et al. (2006) found that learners who used more formulaic sequences were perceived as more orally proficient, and Stengers et al. (2011) reported similar associations across target languages. Wood (2009) further suggested that focused instruction in formulaic sequences can contribute to more fluent narrative performance. However, much of this evidence has relied on subjective ratings or relatively small samples, and studies have not always distinguished among different dimensions of fluency, such as speed, breakdown, and repair. At the same time, corpus-based research has made it possible to operationalize MWS use more objectively through n-gram measures of frequency, proportion, and association strength. Such measures have shown that L2 learners’ phraseological production develops over time and relates to proficiency (Garner & Crossley, 2018; Kyle et al., 2017), while writing research indicates that frequency and association measures may capture different aspects of phraseological competence (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018).

Despite these advances, the extent to which objectively measured MWS use is associated with objectively measured oral fluency remains insufficiently understood. This gap is particularly important for language testing, where fluency is routinely assessed but the lexical and phraseological basis of fluent performance is less often specified. The present study therefore investigates the relationship between MWSs and oral fluency in performances from a standardized academic speaking test across four proficiency levels. Using corpus-based bigram and trigram indices and temporal measures of speed, pausing, and repair, it examines whether more proficient and more fluent speakers make different use of target-like recurrent word combinations.

intros.text:
Oral fluency is a central dimension of second language (L2) speaking ability and a key concern in language teaching, assessment, and second language acquisition research. Fluent speech is not simply fast speech; it reflects the speaker’s capacity to produce language with appropriate speed, limited disruption, and effective monitoring. For this reason, contemporary fluency research commonly distinguishes speed fluency, breakdown fluency, and repair fluency, each of which is assumed to index different aspects of the speech production process. Understanding what linguistic resources support these aspects of fluency is therefore important for both theories of L2 speech production and the assessment of spoken proficiency.

One resource that has attracted sustained attention is formulaic language, often discussed in terms of lexical phrases, formulaic sequences, lexical bundles, collocations, or multiword sequences (MWSs). MWSs can be broadly understood as recurrent combinations of words that are stored, processed, or used as relatively conventionalized units. Early accounts of native-like selection and fluency emphasized the importance of prefabricated language in producing idiomatic and fluent speech, and subsequent work has argued that formulaic language reduces processing load by allowing speakers to retrieve larger stretches of language more efficiently than if each word had to be generated independently (Pawley & Syder, 1983; Wray, 2002; Wood, 2015). Psycholinguistic evidence further suggests that frequent sequences may enjoy processing advantages over less frequent strings (Siyanova-Chanturia & Van Lancker Sidtis, 2018), a claim that is compatible with models of speech production in which lexical retrieval, grammatical encoding, articulation, and monitoring compete for limited attentional resources (Kormos, 1999; Paradis, 2008).

Empirical research has provided growing support for a link between phraseological competence and L2 proficiency. In writing, corpus-based studies have shown that learners differ from native speakers in their use of collocations and lexical bundles, often relying heavily on high-frequency combinations while underusing less frequent but strongly associated collocations (Durrant & Schmitt, 2009; Granger, 2018). In speaking, Boers et al. (2006) found that counts of formulaic sequences correlated with perceived oral proficiency, and Stengers et al. (2011) reported similar associations across different target languages. More recent corpus-based work has examined n-gram development in spoken L2 production and has shown that learners’ use of bigrams and trigrams changes over time, with proficiency predicting growth in some indices of n-gram frequency and proportion (Garner & Crossley, 2018). These developments have been facilitated by computational tools such as TAALES, which allow researchers to calculate indices of n-gram frequency, proportion, and association strength in relation to large reference corpora (Kyle et al., 2017).

Nevertheless, the relationship between MWSs and oral fluency remains insufficiently specified. Many previous studies have relied on subjective ratings of fluency or overall oral proficiency rather than objective temporal measures. Others have used small samples, restricted proficiency ranges, or have focused mainly on speed fluency, leaving open the question of how MWSs relate to pausing and repair phenomena. It also remains unclear whether different properties of MWSs—how frequent they are, how strongly their component words are associated, and how much of a speaker’s output they constitute—relate in the same way to different dimensions of utterance fluency.

The present study addresses these issues by examining the association between MWS use and oral fluency in performances from a standardized academic English speaking test. It investigates learners across four proficiency levels, from Low B1 to C1, and analyzes MWSs through corpus-based bigram and trigram measures of proportion, frequency, and association strength. Oral fluency is measured objectively in terms of articulation rate, mid- and end-clause pausing, and repair frequency. The study asks, first, how n-gram measures relate to proficiency level, and second, how these measures are associated with speed, breakdown, and repair fluency. In doing so, it aims to provide a more fine-grained account of the role of MWSs in L2 spoken performance and to inform both phraseological research and speaking assessment.

intros.text: Asking varying levels of questions within the cognitive domain is not an innate skill, even if you grew up in a  Socratic educational context. This view is first agreed by Nappi’s argument emphasizing the planning of questions (2017, p.38), “developing questions that are scaffolded ---beginning with recall and working up to analysis, synthesis,  and creation— requires careful planning” when she studied questioning in developing critical thinking skills. The view is also supported by the emphasis of “designing questions” (p. 179) in Sun’s study (2012) on the relationship between  teacher questioning and student learning.  The view is especially true with English as a second language (L2) pre-service teachers called learner teachers in this study. A majority of them come from non-Socratic educational contexts in which  they are trained to ask questions in classrooms. Instead, they are praised to be silent and obedient to teacher authority.  This lack of questioning instruction is documented in the classroom “silence” or “reticence” studies where their participation behaviors are questioned (Jackson, 2002; Xia, 2009). It is further evidenced in the zero training finding  from the pre-questionnaire of this study and in the current call for training teacher questioning behaviors (Davoudi &  Sadeghi, 2015; Dös et al, 2016).  Questioning is such a fundamental scaffolding strategy in teaching that shapes language learning and teaching paths.  Teacher instruction cannot proceed without teacher questioning as Celce-Murcia, Brinton and Snow (2014) stated “70%  of class time consists of the teacher talking or asking questions” (p. 345). In the past decades, the problem of  questioning has invited rich empirical investigation into types of teacher questions (Brock, 1986; Cotton, 1988; Döş et  al, 2016; Nunan, 1990), functions of questions in various discourses (Freed & Ehrlich, 2010; Koshik; 2010), and functions of teacher questions (Döş et al, 2016; McCormick & Donato, 2000; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2011) in L2  language classrooms. It has also examined the relationship of L2 teacher questioning and student learning (Sun, 2012; Toni & Parse, 2013; Wu, 1993) including teacher beliefs (Farrell & Mom, 2015). These studies have collected teacher questions and conducted systematic content analysis to reveal the scaffolding functions of questions in contexts.  However, limited research has directly investigated the development of L2 teacher questioning, a fundamental  component of the teacher strategic competence (Canale & Swain, 1980). Relevant interventional research to develop L2 teachers’ awareness of questioning strategy seems missing from the current literature, though Brown and Lee (2015)  strongly advocated, “teachers need to develop a repertoire of questioning strategies for the purpose of initiating and  sustaining interaction” (p. 262).  In addition, the ongoing call for contextualizing L2 learning and teaching (LarsenFreeman, 2018; Ortega, 2009), including teacher questioning behaviors (Davoudi & Sadeghi, 2015; Dös et al, 2016), recreates research currency and focus that this study intends to investigate.  The present study investigates the problem from the focus of developing L2 advanced learner teachers’ awareness of forming varying levels of questions according to the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) and constructing Divergent Questions through applying planned and intensified restructuring activities  The study design is  informed by the social-cognitive perspective of strategy learning (Cohen, 2010; Cohen & Macaro, 2007; O’Malley & Chamot, 1990; Oxford, 1990, 2011, 2017).  It attempts to develop learner teachers’ awareness of questioning strategies  through explicit instruction, engaging interactions, and contextualized restructuring and productive activities (DeKeyser,  1997, 2007; Ellis, 2002; Mackey, 2006, 2008; Ortega, 2009; Schmidt, 1990, 1995). Specifically, it operationalizes the framework of the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001, pp. 67-68; shortened for Revised  Taxonomy) to develop questioning strategies at six levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and  Create.  In the study, the participants are called learner teachers because English is their L2 and they concurrently  develop L2 competence in the English context while learning to become effective teachers, which further justifies why  the study is simultaneously situated in learner strategic competence development and teacher education

intros.text:
Questioning lies at the heart of academic instruction, functioning both as a tool for eliciting student engagement and as a mechanism for scaffolding cognitive development (Hall & Verplaetse, 2000; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2010). Skilled teachers deploy questions strategically, adjusting their cognitive demand, wait time, and phrasing to advance learning and to build productive relationships with students (Sun, 2012; Farrell & Mom, 2015). Yet the ability to ask varying levels of questions within the cognitive domain is not an innate skill. This is especially true for English as a second language (L2) learner teachers, many of whom grew up in educational cultures that did not emphasize a Socratic tradition of inquiry and who therefore received limited explicit instruction in questioning during their prior schooling. When such learner teachers enter teacher training programs, they are expected to design and pose purposeful classroom questions, but the questioning education that would empower them to do so has often been missing.

The research literature offers considerable insight into questioning, but it also reveals a persistent gap. A substantial body of first language (L1) English research has examined how children develop questioning ability, whether through training, modeling, or games (Blank & Covington, 1965; Zimmerman & Pike, 1972; Nelson & Earl, 1973; Lindfors, 1999). A parallel line of inquiry has analyzed the forms and functions of questions in institutional discourse, showing that context shapes how utterances come to function as questions (Ehrlich & Freed, 2009; Koshik, 2009). Still other studies have investigated the relationship between teacher question types and learner responses, though with strikingly inconsistent findings: some report that display or lower order questions elicit richer responses (Wu, 1993; Cotton, 1989), while others conclude that referential or higher order questions generate more interactive and complex output (Brock, 1986; Nunan, 1990). Within L2 acquisition, McDonough and Mackey (2006, 2008) demonstrated that adult EFL learners' question formation develops when learners produce forms in their own way rather than merely mimicking them, underscoring the value of productive, contextualized practice. What remains conspicuously underexplored, however, is explicit instruction in questioning strategies for the teachers themselves. At the same time, L2 strategy research has moved toward valuing learners' strategic investment while cautioning that strategy use cannot be reduced to context-free taxonomies of self-reported behaviors (Cohen & Macaro, 2007; Oxford, 1992, 2017; Ortega, 2009). Adults, moreover, learn differently from children, thinking more analytically about the learning process and often benefiting from explicit strategy instruction (Grenfell & Macaro, 2007). These insights suggest that developing L2 learner teachers' questioning is best approached not through decontextualized drilling but through contextualized, restructured, and noticed practice grounded in a social-cognitive perspective (DeKeyser, 1997, 2007; Schmidt, 1990).

The present study responds to this need by operationalizing the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) to develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of questioning strategies. Divergent Questions (DQs) are understood as questions posed from new perspectives on the same content focus (McKenzie, 2005; Morgan & Saxton, 1991). Through an eight-week quasi-experimental design featuring intensive restructuring activities and a Question-Question Game, the study taught learner teachers to ask questions across the six levels of the cognitive domain and to generate divergent questions, using content they already knew to contextualize the learning process. Two research questions guide the inquiry: (1) To what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers' awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions? and (2) To what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction raise learner teachers' awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions?

intros.text:
Questioning lies at the heart of classroom interaction and academic inquiry. The capacity to formulate questions that span the full range of the cognitive domain—from remembering and understanding to analysing, evaluating, and creating—is central to effective teaching, yet it is far from an innate ability. This is especially true for English as a second language (L2) learner teachers, many of whom enter teacher training programs having received little or no explicit instruction in how to ask questions purposefully and strategically. For these teachers, developing awareness of questioning strategies is a demanding cognitive and linguistic task that intertwines their command of English with their emerging pedagogical repertoire.

Research on questioning has accumulated across several distinct traditions. Within first language (L1) English contexts, a substantial body of interventional studies examined how children develop questioning ability through training, modelling, and awareness-raising (Blank & Covington, 1965; Zimmerman & Pike, 1972; Nelson & Earl, 1973). Later work analysed how children use questioning to make sense of the world, uniting the forms and functions of inquiry in authentic texts (Lindfors, 1999). A parallel line of work in language learner strategy research established that learners invest strategically in acquiring language skills (Cohen & Macaro, 2007; Oxford, 1992), though critical reviews have cautioned that L2 strategic behaviour should not be reduced to decontextualised taxonomies of self-reported processes (Ortega, 2009). Studies of teacher questioning have compared display and referential questions and their effects on classroom discourse, producing notably inconsistent findings: while some report that referential questions elicit more elaborate responses (Brock, 1986; Nunan, 1990), others conclude that display and closed questions are more effective in eliciting student responses in particular contexts (Wu, 1993; Cotton, 1989). Research on the functions of questions in institutional discourse has further shown that context and institutional structure shape what counts as, and how one performs, a question (Ehrlich & Freed, 2009; Koshik, 2009). Studies of teacher questioning as scaffolded assistance similarly foreground its interactive role in supporting learning (Hall & Verplaetse, 2000; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2010).

Despite this breadth, the development of adult L2 teachers' own questioning ability remains strikingly under-investigated. Adults, unlike children, approach language learning more analytically and are frequently the subjects of strategy instruction research (Grenfell & Macaro, 2007), yet interventional work has focused overwhelmingly on question formation as a syntactic developmental task rather than on the cognitive levels and purposes of questioning. McDonough and Mackey (2006, 2008), for example, demonstrated that productively using a question form is more beneficial for development than mimicking it, but their participants were EFL undergraduates rather than learner teachers who need such development most acutely. Survey and content-analytic studies have exposed teachers' lack of specific questioning strategies and revealed persistent misconceptions about convergent, divergent, and cognitive-level question types (Sun, 2012; Döş et al., 2016). These findings have generated repeated and explicit calls for the teaching of questioning strategies and for in-service and pre-service training programs to strengthen teachers' classroom questioning behaviours (Döş et al., 2016; Davoudi & Sadeghi, 2015). To date, however, no experimental study has taught L2 learner teachers questioning through the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), and interventional research on developing L2 teacher questioning is scarce. Learner teachers educated in non-Socratic contexts, who receive limited questioning instruction in their prior schooling, therefore need contextualised training to catch up on the questioning education they have missed.

The present study addresses this gap. It reports an eight-week quasi-experimental study that operationalises the Revised Taxonomy to develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of questioning strategies—specifically, formulating questions at varying cognitive levels and generating Divergent Questions for scaffolding purposes—through intensive restructuring activities and a Question-Question Game. Guided by principles of contextualisation (Ortega, 2009), restructuring (DeKeyser, 1997, 2007), and noticing (Schmidt, 1990), the study pursues two research questions: (1) to what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers' awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions, and (2) to what extent can such instruction raise their awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions? In doing so, the study offers new empirical and pedagogical directions for L2 teacher training in questioning.

intros.text:
Effective classroom questioning is a cornerstone of pedagogical practice, yet the ability to elicit varying levels of cognitive engagement is not an innate skill. This is particularly evident among second language (L2) learner teachers, who often struggle to move beyond basic information retrieval to foster higher-order thinking. Within the field of applied linguistics, substantial research has explored learner "strategic investment" in acquiring language skills, such as grammar and vocabulary (Brown & Lee, 2015; Cohen & Macaro, 2007), often drawing on the pioneering work of Oxford (1990) regarding learning strategies. However, as Ortega (2009) noted, these strategic behaviors should not be reduced to simple taxonomies without considering the specific contexts in which they are employed. For L2 learner teachers, the context is often one of limited explicit instruction in questioning strategies during their own prior education.

Historically, questioning research was well-established in first language (L1) English contexts, focusing on training children through modeling, praise, and games (Blank & Covington, 1965; Nelson & Earl, 1973; Zimmerman & Pike, 1972). Later work by Lindfors (1999) emphasized "languaging," uniting the structures and functions of questioning to make sense of the world. Despite these advances in L1 contexts, there remains a significant gap regarding adult L2 learners and teachers. Adults process language learning more analytically than children (Grenfell & Macaro, 2007) and often require explicit instruction to compensate for a lack of Socratic education in their native contexts.

Recent efforts to address this gap have focused on various dimensions of questioning. McDonough and Mackey (2006, 2008) investigated the development of question formation through syntactic priming and communicative activities, finding that the productive use of forms is more beneficial than mere mimicry. Other scholars have examined the functions of questioning within institutional discourses, such as L2 writing conferences (Koshik, 2009), suggesting that academic discourse is structured around fundamental levels of cognitive interrogation. Furthermore, the relationship between teacher questioning and learner outcomes has been widely debated. While some research suggests that referential, higher-order questions elicit more interactive responses (Brock, 1986; Nunan, 1990), other studies in specific contexts, such as Hong Kong, found that display questions were more effective in eliciting responses (Wu, 1993), echoing findings by Cotton (1988).

Despite the importance of these dynamics, many L2 teachers still lack specific strategies to engage students cognitively. Sun (2012) highlighted a lack of purposeful academic questioning, noting that without explicit training, teachers struggle to change their behaviors. More recent evidence from Döş et al. (2016) revealed a significant mismatch between teachers' self-reported questioning levels and their actual practice, suggesting widespread misconceptions about convergent and divergent questions. This necessitates a call for structured in-service and pre-service training (Davoudi & Sadeghi, 2015).

To address this need, the present study employs a quasi-experimental design to develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of questioning strategies. Utilizing the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), the study provides explicit instruction on formulating varying cognitive levels of questions and creating Divergent Questions (DQs)—defined as questions that offer new perspectives on the same content focus (McKenzie, 2005; Morgan & Saxton, 1991). By contextualizing this training through content familiar to the participants, the study aims to empower learner teachers with targeted scaffolding competence. Specifically, this research seeks to answer the following questions:

1. To what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers' awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions?

2. To what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction raise learner teachers' awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions?

intros.text:
Teacher questioning is a fundamental pedagogical tool that shapes classroom discourse, influences learner engagement, and facilitates cognitive development. In the context of second language (L2) education, the ability to formulate varied and cognitively demanding questions is not an innate skill, particularly for L2 learner teachers who may lack prior exposure to Socratic questioning traditions. While research on questioning strategies has been extensive in first language (L1) contexts, focusing on children's development and teacher practices (Blank & Covington, 1965; Lindfors, 1999), there remains a significant gap in understanding how L2 learner teachers can be explicitly trained to develop these strategies. This is especially critical given that adults learn differently than children, often requiring explicit instruction on forms and structures to compensate for missed educational opportunities (Grenfell & Macaro, 2007).

Previous studies have highlighted the importance of questioning in L2 contexts. For instance, McDonough and Mackey (2008) investigated question formation among Thai EFL undergraduates, finding that productive use of questioning forms was more beneficial than simple repetition. Similarly, Wu (1993) and Sun (2012) examined the relationship between teacher questions and learner attitudes, noting that while some lower-order questions are effective, there is a need for strategies that promote cognitive engagement. However, these studies often focus on the functions of questions or their impact on learners rather than the development of the teachers' own questioning awareness. Recent work by Döş et al. (2016) revealed that many teachers hold misconceptions about question types and cognitive levels, strongly calling for training programs to address these gaps. This aligns with Davoudi and Sadegh (2015), who reviewed experimental studies and emphasized the need for in-service programs to strengthen classroom questioning behaviors.

The theoretical framework for developing questioning strategies often draws on cognitive taxonomies. Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) Revised Taxonomy provides a robust structure for categorizing questions based on cognitive processes, ranging from remembering and understanding to analyzing, evaluating, and creating. This framework is particularly relevant for L2 teacher training as it allows for the operationalization of questioning levels and the design of targeted interventions. Despite its potential, few studies have experimentally taught L2 learner teachers questioning strategies using this taxonomy. Most existing research has focused on L1 contexts or general teacher practices, leaving the specific needs of L2 learner teachers largely unaddressed.

Furthermore, the role of context in strategy development cannot be overlooked. Ortega (2009) argued that L2 learning strategies should not be reduced to simple taxonomies but must be contextualized to the learners' prior educational experiences. For L2 learner teachers coming from non-Socratic educational backgrounds, explicit instruction that contextualizes questioning strategies within their known content is essential. This approach empowers them with scaled scaffolding competence, allowing them to bridge the gap between their prior knowledge and the new skills required for effective questioning. The concept of "languaging" (Lindfors, 1999), which unites questioning forms and functions, further supports the need for training that integrates structure and purpose.

Despite the wealth of research on questioning, there is a lack of interventional studies specifically designed to develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of questioning strategies. While studies like those by Cohen and Macaro (2007) and Oxford (1990, 2017) have explored learner strategies broadly, the specific domain of teacher questioning remains under-researched in L2 contexts. This study aims to fill this void by investigating the extent to which explicit questioning strategy instruction, grounded in the Revised Taxonomy, can develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of formulating varying levels of questions and divergent questions. By employing a quasi-experimental design with pre- and post-tests, questionnaires, and qualitative data, this research seeks to provide empirical evidence on the effectiveness of such training. The findings have significant implications for teacher education programs, suggesting that explicit, contextualized instruction can effectively enhance the questioning capabilities of L2 learner teachers, thereby improving their future classroom practices and student outcomes.

intros.text:
Teacher questioning is a cornerstone of effective pedagogy, serving as a primary vehicle for scaffolding learning, eliciting student responses, and fostering critical thinking. In the context of English language teaching (ELT), the ability to formulate varying levels of questions is not merely a linguistic skill but a complex cognitive strategy that requires explicit development. While the importance of questioning in classroom discourse has been widely acknowledged, the specific strategies employed by second language (L2) learner teachers to formulate these questions remain under-researched. This study addresses the gap in understanding how L2 learner teachers can be trained to develop awareness of questioning strategies, specifically focusing on the cognitive levels defined by the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001).

Research on questioning strategies has a long history, particularly within first language (L1) contexts. Early studies by Blank and Covington (1965) and Zimmerman and Pike (1972) examined the effects of training and modeling on children's questioning behaviors. Later, Lindfors (1999) emphasized the concept of "languaging," uniting questioning forms and functions to understand how learners make sense of the world. However, this body of research has largely focused on child development in L1 settings. In contrast, the questioning development of adult L2 learners, particularly those training to become teachers, has received less attention. Grenfell and Macaro (2007) argue that adults learn differently from children, often requiring explicit instruction on the forms and structures of language to catch up on educational experiences they may have missed. This distinction is crucial for L2 learner teachers who may not have grown up with Socratic educational traditions.

In the domain of L2 teacher education, the focus has often shifted from form to function. McDonough and Mackey (2008) investigated question formation among Thai EFL undergraduates, finding that productive use of questioning forms through syntactic priming was more beneficial than simple repetition. Similarly, Wu (1993) and Nunan (1990) explored the relationship between question types (display vs. referential) and student interaction, though findings have been inconsistent. Wu (1993) found that display questions were more effective in a Hong Kong context, contradicting earlier conclusions by Brock (1986) and Nunan (1990) that referential questions elicit more complex responses. More recently, Döş et al. (2016) highlighted a significant mismatch between teachers' self-reported questioning levels and their actual classroom practices, noting widespread misconceptions about convergent and divergent question types. They called for explicit training in questioning strategies for both pre- and in-service teachers. This call resonates with Davoudi and Sadegh (2015), who, after reviewing decades of research, emphasized the need for in-service programs to strengthen classroom questioning behaviors.

Despite these calls for intervention, there is a scarcity of experimental studies explicitly teaching questioning strategies to L2 learner teachers. Most existing literature focuses on observing teacher behaviors or correlating questioning styles with student outcomes, rather than developing the teachers' own cognitive awareness of questioning levels. Furthermore, while the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001) provides a robust framework for categorizing cognitive processes, its application in training L2 teachers to formulate questions across these levels is rarely operationalized. Sun (2012) noted that teachers often lack specific strategies to foster cognitive engagement, yet failed to recognize that designing purposeful academic questions requires explicit training. Without such training, teachers may remain unaware of the cognitive levels they are targeting, limiting their ability to scaffold student learning effectively.

To address this gap, the present study investigates the extent to which explicit instruction in questioning strategies can develop L2 learner teachers' awareness of formulating varying levels of questions and divergent questions. Drawing on the Revised Bloom's Taxonomy, this quasi-experimental study employs an eight-week intervention involving intense restructuring activities and a "Question-Question Game" to scaffold participants' questioning skills. By comparing the experimental group with a control group through pre- and post-tests, questionnaires, and question journals, this research aims to determine if explicit training can shift teachers' questioning behaviors from lower-order to higher-order cognitive levels. The study seeks to contribute to the field by providing empirical evidence on the effectiveness of such training and offering new directions for teacher education programs in non-Socratic contexts.

intros.text:
Questioning is a central practice in language classrooms because it organizes interaction, elicits learner thinking, checks comprehension, and scaffolds participation in meaning making. In communicative approaches to second language teaching, classroom discourse is expected to move beyond transmission of information toward purposeful interaction in which learners negotiate meaning, formulate ideas, and use language for academic and social purposes (Canale & Swain, 1980; Brown, 2001). Teacher questions are therefore not merely grammatical interrogatives; they are pedagogical tools that can shape the quality of learner response, the direction of classroom talk, and the cognitive level at which content is explored (Hall & Verplaetse, 2000; Davoudi & Sadeghi, 2015). For learner teachers preparing to teach English as a second or foreign language, developing the ability to ask purposeful questions is thus an important component of professional competence.

Research on teacher questioning in ESL/EFL classrooms has long shown that question type matters, though findings have not always been consistent. Brock (1986) reported that referential questions generated richer learner discourse in adult ESL classes, whereas Wu (1993), working in the Hong Kong ESL context, found that display and closed questions were more effective in eliciting responses than referential and open questions. Nunan (1990) similarly cautioned against treating closed or display questions as inherently unproductive, arguing that their pedagogical value depends on classroom goals and institutional purposes. These findings suggest that effective questioning cannot be reduced to simple binaries such as display/referential or closed/open. Rather, teachers need strategic awareness of how question forms, functions, contexts, and cognitive demands interact.

More recent work has reinforced this need for strategic and contextualized understandings of questioning. Questions in institutional discourse perform varied functions and are shaped by local activity types, participant roles, and interactional goals (Freed & Ehrlich, 2009). In educational settings, questions may convey information, diagnose learner understanding, direct attention to errors, or scaffold learning processes (Koshik, 2009; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2010). Studies of teacher questioning practices in EFL contexts have also indicated that teachers may lack explicit awareness of the cognitive levels or purposes of the questions they ask. Döş et al. (2016), for example, found mismatches between teachers’ self-reported use of convergent and divergent questions and the researchers’ analysis of those questions, leading them to call for direct training in questioning strategies. Similarly, Sun (2012) argued that students value questioning practices that create a relaxed, respectful, and cognitively engaging classroom environment, but such practices require teachers to know how to design questions intentionally.

This issue is especially important for second language learner teachers who are themselves operating across linguistic, academic, and cultural systems. Many L2 graduate students and teacher candidates come from educational contexts where overt classroom questioning, Socratic dialogue, or verbal participation has not been emphasized. Research on East Asian students in English-medium academic settings, for instance, has shown that reticence and limited oral participation may be shaped by sociocultural, affective, cognitive, and pedagogical factors rather than by linguistic proficiency alone (Jackson, 2002; Xia, 2009). If learner teachers have had limited experience asking questions in prior schooling, they may need explicit opportunities to notice, analyze, and practice questioning as a teachable strategy. Such a need aligns with broader research on language learning strategies, which views strategies as conscious, purposeful actions that can be developed through instruction, practice, and reflection (Oxford, 1992, 2016; Cohen, 2018).

The present study approaches teacher questioning as a strategic, learnable practice that can be developed through explicit instruction and repeated restructuring. From a skill acquisition perspective, explicit knowledge requires meaningful and sustained practice in order to become usable in performance (DeKeyser, 1997, 2007). From a noticing perspective, learners must attend to features of language and discourse before they can modify their use of them (Schmidt, 1990). In the case of questioning, this means that learner teachers may benefit from being made aware of question levels, question functions, and divergent ways of approaching the same content. The Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy provides a useful framework for this purpose because it distinguishes cognitive levels—Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create—and specifies processes associated with each level (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001). It can therefore help learner teachers connect linguistic forms of questions with pedagogical purposes and cognitive demands.

Despite extensive research on classroom questioning, relatively few studies have experimentally examined how L2 learner teachers can be taught to formulate questions across cognitive levels and from divergent perspectives. Existing research has investigated teacher question types, student responses, interactional functions, and attitudes toward questioning, but less attention has been given to intervention-based training that helps learner teachers become aware of their own questioning habits and expand their repertoire. To address this gap, the present quasi-experimental study investigates whether explicit instruction based on the Revised Taxonomy can develop L2 TESOL learner teachers’ awareness of strategies for asking varying levels of questions and divergent questions. Specifically, it asks: to what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers’ awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions, and to what extent can such instruction raise their awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions?
