intros.text:
Questioning is central to classroom interaction, instructional scaffolding, and the development of learners’ thinking in second and foreign language education. In communicative language teaching, teachers’ questions do more than check comprehension; they organize participation, direct attention to form and meaning, elicit learner output, and create opportunities for negotiation and reflection. Because teacher questioning shapes what learners are invited to notice, say, explain, justify, and create, it has long been treated as an important pedagogical strategy in ESL and EFL classrooms (Brock, 1986; Nunan, 1990; Wu, 1993). It is also closely connected to the broader goal of developing communicative competence, in which learners need opportunities to use language for meaningful academic and social purposes (Canale & Swain, 1980; Brown, 2001).

A substantial body of research has examined the types and functions of classroom questions. Earlier studies often distinguished display from referential questions or closed from open questions, investigating how these types affected learner responses. Brock (1986) reported that referential questions could generate more extended ESL classroom discourse, whereas Wu (1993), working in the Hong Kong ESL context, found that display and closed questions were more effective than referential and open questions in eliciting responses. Nunan (1990) cautioned against interpreting question types too narrowly, arguing that teacher questions need to be understood in relation to institutional purposes and classroom agendas. More recent work has extended this focus to questioning as institutional discourse, showing that questions perform context-sensitive functions in educational and professional encounters (Ehrlich & Freed, 2009; Koshik, 2009). In ESL classrooms, teacher questions have also been conceptualized as scaffolded assistance that can support learners’ participation and meaning-making (Hall & Verplaetse, 2000; Yaqubi & Mozaffari, 2010).

Research has further linked questioning to higher-order cognition and learning. Cotton (1989) reviewed classroom questioning as a major instructional practice, and Davoudi and Sadeghi’s (2015) systematic review showed that questioning can facilitate critical thinking, reading comprehension, writing ability, metacognitive development, and subject-matter learning. Taxonomies of educational objectives have provided teachers with tools for designing questions at different cognitive levels. In particular, the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy distinguishes cognitive processes such as remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), offering a principled way to examine whether classroom questions primarily elicit recall and comprehension or invite analysis, evaluation, and creation. For language teachers, such a framework can make questioning strategy more visible and teachable.

Despite this importance, asking purposeful questions at varied cognitive levels is not necessarily an intuitive skill, especially for second language learner teachers whose prior educational experiences may not have emphasized Socratic inquiry, classroom verbal participation, or explicit questioning practice. Studies of East Asian and other international students in English-medium academic contexts have shown that participation is shaped by sociocultural, affective, linguistic, and pedagogical factors (Jackson, 2002; Xia, 2009). Learner teachers from such backgrounds may be advanced users of English and knowledgeable about language teaching, yet still have limited awareness of how to formulate questions that move beyond understanding-level prompts or yes/no structures. This concern is consistent with research on language learning strategies, which emphasizes that strategic behavior can be made more effective through conscious, contextualized instruction and practice (Oxford, 1992, 2017; Cohen, 2018). It also aligns with skill acquisition perspectives suggesting that productive, repeated, and structured practice is necessary for developing complex L2 abilities (DeKeyser, 1997, 2007).

Although research on teacher questioning is extensive, relatively little empirical work has experimentally examined how L2 learner teachers can be trained to develop awareness of questioning strategies. McDonough and Mackey (2006, 2008) demonstrated that productive use of question forms through interaction and syntactic priming can support ESL question development, but their focus was on learners’ grammatical development rather than on teacher questioning as a pedagogical strategy. Farrell and Mom (2015) explored teacher questions through reflective practice, and Döş et al. (2016) found that teachers may hold misconceptions about convergent and divergent questions and about cognitive levels of questioning. Sun (2012) likewise highlighted students’ preference for varied teacher questioning strategies and called attention to the need for questions that promote cognitive engagement. However, there remains a need for intervention studies that explicitly teach L2 learner teachers to formulate questions across cognitive levels and to develop divergent questions from multiple perspectives.

To address this gap, the present quasi-experimental study investigates whether explicit questioning strategy instruction based on the Revised Bloom’s Taxonomy can develop L2 TESOL learner teachers’ awareness of formulating varying levels of questions and divergent questions. In this study, questioning strategy is understood as a conscious effort to formulate cognitive interrogations at different levels and to plan divergent interrogations through intentionally selected structures, functions, and cognitive processes. The study asks: To what extent can explicit questioning strategy instruction develop learner teachers’ awareness of strategies to formulate levels of questions? To what extent can such instruction raise their awareness of strategies to develop divergent questions? By examining pre- and post-test questions, questionnaire responses, question journals, and comparisons with a control group, the study aims to contribute evidence for integrating explicit, contextualized questioning strategy training into L2 teacher education.

intros.text: Today’s world is strongly influenced by Media with the emergence of new technology, new  forms of global and intercultural communication have also arisen, leading to new forms of  translation.  Audio-visual translation (AVT) is “a discipline that is much more than mere transfer  of pictures, music, sounds and other non- verbal elements are also involved in the process,  making it a kind of multi-semiotic transfer” (Au, 2009, p. vii). Dubbing and subtitling are the  most common types of AVT. Dubbing is a form of interlingual audio-visual translation that  presumes a transformation of the soundtrack of the source language into the soundtrack of the  target language with the intention of having it distributed in countries where the original  language is not their native tongue (Cintas, 2009) while subtitling is the presentation of a  translation dialogue in a film in the form of caption usually placed at the bottom of the picture  or on the screen (Szarkowska, 2005).  Since the 1990s, the presence of television channels in the Arab world, and the  significant increase in communication, in addition to the amount of time spent in front of  screens have led to the purchase of a huge number of foreign programs in an attempt to attract  viewers. Not understanding a foreign language is the major obstacle that prevents audiences  from enjoying these television programs and films. Subtitling and dubbing are the mechanisms  which facilitate the interpretation of international programs and films.  In the field of AVT, one  of the most challenging tasks is translating animated cartoons, which can play a vital role in  children’s emotional and social development and education, and have a direct influence on their  cognition and behaviour (Ghilzai, Alam, Ahmad, Shaukat, & Noor, 2017). Additionally,  religious beliefs have been also outlined to be influenced to a large degree. Dubbing and  subtitling are the major forms of animated cartoons translation. Each one of them interferes to a certain degree with the original version to make it sound real, interesting and enjoyable to the  target audience.  Translators usually show great concern when they render a certain work for the Arab  audience to protect their identity and culture.  It is often believed that national identity is  culturally diverse, connected to issues related to race and ethnicity and manifested in a  particular language and culture (Venuti, 2005).  Throughout the course of translation, as  different new areas are drawn into sharp focus, identities are lost, allowing ways for new ones.  This is why translators take strong caution when approaching subjects that are considered  unacceptable like religion, humour, and taboos that often constitute a major challenge for  translators.  Those subjects are discussed thoroughly in this paper. In this study, the researchers  have classified cultural constraints into three categories, namely, religious remarks, jokes and  humour of proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks in this paper refer to any unacceptable  offensive religious reference that has been included in Family Guy. Jokes and humour of proper  nouns refer to cross-cultural names that have been used in a humorous context. This paper also  investigates taboos, which can be defined as immoral or explicit content that is deemed  inappropriate by the target audience.  According to Allan (2001, p. 148), “tabooed words are  those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts” The reason behind this classification is that religion might be the number one red zone  for almost all societies and cultures.  The followers of a particular religion do not tolerate  mockery or disdain of their beliefs nor invading the sacredness of their religion. Therefore,  when a popular television show provokes the audience by offending their religion for creating  controversy, the translator shall avoid rendering such provocative utterances by resorting to one  of the translation strategies.  Jankowska (2009) examined how comedy elements are translated  in animated films and found that the target text contains fewer humorous elements than the  source texts. This is due to the translators’ lack of knowledge of how cultural humorous  references could be rendered. The second category, jokes and humour of proper nouns, shows  how a translator can deliver an item that is well known to the source culture but not the target  culture, without losing the humorous effect. The third category, taboos, is included owing to  the fact that the explicit rendition of taboos often comes as shocking and unpleasant, let alone  that conveying an idea that is acceptable by a particular society to a more conservative one  might taint the identity and customs of it.  The purpose of this study is to investigate and identify the strategies translators opted  for while subtitling cultural constraints in an American animated sitcom, Family Guy, into  Arabic. This objective is examined via the following research question. -What are the strategies used by the subtitlists of Family Guy to: A: translate unacceptable religious remarks? B: reflect the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns on the target audience? C: render taboos into Arabic?

intros.text:
The proliferation of foreign television programmes across the Arab world has made audio-visual translation an increasingly significant field of enquiry. Since television screens first entered Arab homes, the subtitling and dubbing of foreign animation have grown steadily, bringing with them the need for stricter control and ethical supervision of the language that reaches viewers (Díaz Cintas, 2009). Animated series, in particular, occupy an unusual position: while animation is frequently associated with children, a substantial number of contemporary animated sitcoms are produced for adult audiences and rely heavily on satire, irony, and culturally embedded humour. This tension is significant because cartoons and animated programmes have been shown to exert considerable influence on the language and behaviour of their viewers, especially the young (Ghilzai et al., 2017). Consequently, translators working into Arabic are expected not only to transfer linguistic meaning but also to act as cultural gatekeepers who mediate between the values of the source culture and those of the target audience.

Among the animated sitcoms broadcast in the Arab world, the American series Family Guy stands out as a particularly demanding case for the translator. Created by Seth MacFarlane, the show is built around provocative and irreverent humour that repeatedly engages with sensitive matters such as sex, alcohol, religion, and politics. What functions as ordinary comic material for its original American audience may be received with concern and caution, or outright rejection, in Arab societies whose ideological and religious frameworks differ markedly from those of the West. Film translation possesses a strong potential to shape the beliefs and opinions of its audience, arguably more than other forms of translation, which is precisely why questions of censorship and appropriateness become so pressing in this context. The translator of Family Guy is therefore confronted with content that not only resists straightforward linguistic transfer but also collides with the deeply held convictions of the receiving community.

The relationship between translation and culture lies at the heart of this challenge. National identity is culturally diverse, bound up with race and ethnicity, and expressed through a particular language and culture (Venuti, 2005); in the process of translation, identities may be lost and reshaped as new cultural material is brought into focus. It is for this reason that translators exercise strong caution when approaching subjects deemed unacceptable, and it is this caution that motivates the present study. Because translation and culture cannot be separated, the transfer of cultural aspects during subtitling can be extremely challenging, and at times impossible, given the wide gap that may exist between source and target cultures. Film translation in particular carries the power to influence audiences profoundly (Szarkowska, 2005), which places a heavy responsibility on the subtitler to render content in a manner that is both intelligible and culturally acceptable.

For the purposes of this study, the cultural constraints that emerge in subtitling Family Guy into Arabic are grouped into three broad categories: religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks refer to any offensive or unacceptable religious reference contained in the show; jokes and humour of proper nouns concern cross-cultural names deployed within a humorous context; and taboos are understood as immoral or explicit content deemed inappropriate by the target audience. Following Allan (2001, p. 148), tabooed words may be defined as ‘those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts’. This threefold classification is deliberate. Religion arguably constitutes the foremost ‘red zone’ for most societies, since adherents of a faith rarely tolerate mockery of their beliefs or intrusion upon what they hold sacred. Humour, meanwhile, poses distinct difficulties, as comic references familiar to the source culture may lose their effect when transferred; indeed, earlier research has shown that target texts tend to contain fewer humorous elements than their source texts, partly because translators lack the means to render culturally specific humour (Jankowska, 2009). Taboos are included because the explicit rendition of sexual or otherwise indecent content can be experienced as shocking and unpleasant, and because conveying an idea acceptable in one society to a more conservative one risks tainting the latter's identity and customs.

Despite the growing body of scholarship on audio-visual translation into Arabic, relatively little attention has been paid to Family Guy, notwithstanding its notoriety and the intensity of the cultural clashes it provokes. This study seeks to address that gap by investigating and identifying the strategies that subtitlers adopt when confronting cultural constraints in the Arabic version of the programme. In doing so, it draws on the cultural approach to translation, which treats the translated text not as a mere replica of the source but as a product shaped by the norms, history, and ideology of the receiving culture. Specifically, the study is guided by the following research question: what are the strategies used by the subtitlers of Family Guy to (A) translate unacceptable religious remarks, (B) reflect on the target audience the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns, and (C) render taboos into Arabic? By answering these questions, the study aims to illuminate the vital role that the target audience's ideology and culture play in determining which constraints govern the translation process.

intros.text:
The proliferation of satellite television, digital streaming platforms, and DVD distribution across the Arab world has dramatically increased Arab audiences' exposure to foreign audiovisual content, particularly animated series and sitcoms originally produced for Western markets. As foreign animation reached Arab homes, the demand for subtitled and dubbed versions grew steadily, imposing on translators a heavier responsibility to mediate not only between two languages but also between two markedly different value systems. Translating such content is therefore far more than a linguistic exercise; it involves careful negotiation of cultural, religious, and ideological sensitivities that shape what is acceptable for a target audience. Audiovisual translation, in this sense, has become a central concern for both scholars and practitioners who recognise that the choices made in subtitling can either preserve or distort the identity and cultural integrity of the receiving community (Díaz Cintas, 2009; Szarkowska, 2005).

Culture and translation are inseparable. Since translation is the outcome of cultural interchange, the translator must act as a cultural mediator who conveys meaning across communities that hold divergent customs, beliefs, and norms. This mediating role becomes especially delicate in film and television translation, which has a powerful capacity to legitimise the ideas and behaviours it represents. As Szarkowska (2005) observes, film translation carries considerable influence over the perceptions and attitudes of its viewers, and this influence is amplified in the case of younger audiences who look to television as a model of what is natural and acceptable. Cartoons and animated programmes, in particular, have been shown to affect the language and behaviour of their viewers (Ghilzai et al., 2017), which raises the stakes for translators working with material that addresses sensitive subject matter. The originality of the voice preserved in subtitles keeps the raw feeling of the source culture intact, yet it simultaneously confronts the target audience with references and values that may clash with their own.

The difficulty of maintaining an equivalent effect while respecting the target culture has attracted considerable scholarly attention. Studies of dubbing and subtitling have examined how register, style, and tone are handled across languages, showing that translators must sift through multiple layers of verbal, aural, and visual meaning to preserve coherence (Jankowska, 2009). Others have explored the transfer of humour, noting that comedy elements frequently diminish in the target text because translators lack ready means of rendering culture-bound references. National identity, as Venuti (2005) argues, is culturally diverse and manifested through a particular language and culture, and it is precisely this identity that translators seek to protect when approaching subjects considered unacceptable by the receiving community. Among the most challenging of these subjects are religion, humour built around proper names, and taboo language, each of which constitutes a recognised category of cultural constraint. Taboo words, as Allan (2001) notes, are those regarded as offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts, and their treatment varies enormously from one society to another.

Despite the growing body of research on audiovisual translation from English into Arabic, most existing studies have concentrated on feature films, children's movies, and a limited set of widely examined animated productions such as The Simpsons, Shrek, and Mulan. To the best of the researchers' knowledge, little or no attention has been paid to the Arabic subtitled version of Family Guy, an American animated sitcom that repeatedly courts controversy through its treatment of sex, alcohol, religion, and politics. Because the show deliberately provokes its audience by mocking religious figures, employing culturally specific humour, and deploying explicit taboo language, it presents an unusually rich site for examining how Arab subtitlists negotiate deeply sensitive material. This gap is significant: while previous work has documented individual strategies such as euphemism, omission, and explanation, no study has systematically mapped how these strategies are distributed across the distinct categories of religious remarks, humour surrounding proper names, and taboos within a single controversial series aimed at adult audiences.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the cultural constraints involved in subtitling Family Guy into Arabic and identifying the strategies translators adopt to overcome them. Drawing on the cultural approach to translation and the associated manipulation theory, which frames the translator as a rewriter capable of altering the source text to secure social acceptance in the target culture, the study classifies cultural constraints into three categories: unacceptable religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboos. Adopting a qualitative, corpus-based analysis, it compares the Arabic subtitled version screened on OSN networks with the original English broadcasts, provides back translation for each example, and examines the strategies used to render the most controversial and highly rated episodes. Specifically, the study seeks to answer a single overarching research question concerning the strategies used by the subtitlists of Family Guy to translate unacceptable religious remarks, to reflect the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns on the target audience, and to render taboos into Arabic. In doing so, the study aims to illuminate the vital role the target audience plays in determining which constraints govern translation, and to offer insights that may enhance the quality and cultural appropriateness of English-to-Arabic subtitling more broadly.

intros.text:
The proliferation of global media and the widespread availability of television screens in Arab homes have led to a significant increase in the subtitling and dubbing of foreign animation. This trend has brought diverse cultural perspectives into the Middle Eastern domestic sphere, yet it has simultaneously imposed stricter controls and ethical supervision over the language used in these translations. As audiovisual translation serves as a bridge between disparate worldviews, the translator often finds themselves navigating a complex landscape of linguistic and ideological tensions. The process is not merely a matter of lexical substitution but is deeply intertwined with the preservation of national identity, which is often viewed as a culturally diverse construct connected to race, ethnicity, and manifested through a specific language and culture (Venuti, 2005). Consequently, translators often exhibit great caution when rendering works for Arab audiences to protect their identity and cultural integrity from perceived intrusions or offenses.

Within the realm of audiovisual translation, the challenges are multifaceted. As noted by scholars such as Jorge Díaz Cintas (2009), new trends in the field require a sophisticated understanding of how to balance the source text's intent with the target culture's norms. This is particularly evident in the translation of animated series, which, despite their often-childlike appearance, can exert a profound impact on the language and behavior of viewers (Ghilzai et al., 2017). In the context of subtitling, the translator must account not only for the spoken word but also for visual cues and sound effects, often acting as a cultural mediator who explains what the target audience may not inherently understand. The power of film translation lies in its ability to shape perception, yet this power is limited by the necessity of maintaining social acceptance within the receptor culture (Szarkowska, 2005).

One of the most significant challenges arises when the source material contains elements that clash violently with the ideologies of the target audience. The American animated sitcom Family Guy serves as a prime example of such a clash. Known for its provocative nature, the series frequently addresses sensitive matters including sex, alcohol, religion, and politics. Because it employs a brand of humor that often pushes boundaries, it is viewed with concern and caution in the Arab world. For the subtitlist, the goal is to maintain a degree of fidelity to the original version to keep the content engaging and enjoyable, while simultaneously ensuring that the translation does not violate the sacred or social norms of the target society. This delicate balance requires a strategic approach to what can be termed "cultural constraints"—a set of ideologies and prohibitions that a society deems unacceptable or indecent.

In this study, the researchers have classified these cultural constraints into three primary categories: religious remarks, jokes and humor revolving around proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks encompass any offensive or unacceptable religious references that could be perceived as blasphemous or disrespectful. Given that religion is often the most sensitive "red zone" in Arab societies, the followers of these faiths generally do not tolerate mockery or the invasion of the sacredness of their beliefs. When a show like Family Guy provokes controversy by offending religious sensibilities, the translator must employ specific strategies—such as omission or deletion—to avoid inciting hostility. This aligns with findings by Jankowska (2009), who noted that target texts in animated films often contain fewer humorous elements than source texts due to the difficulties of rendering culture-specific references.

Similarly, jokes and humor based on proper nouns present a unique hurdle. Humorous effects often rely on wordplay or cultural familiarity with specific people, brands, or entities that may be entirely unknown to the Arab viewer. The challenge here is to deliver the humor without losing the intended effect or requiring excessive cognitive effort from the audience. Finally, the study investigates taboos, defined as immoral or explicit content deemed inappropriate by the target audience. As Allan (2001) suggests, tabooed words are those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent depending on the context. In a conservative society, the explicit rendition of such content can be shocking and may be seen as taining the customs and identity of the community.

Ultimately, the purpose of this study is to investigate and identify the specific strategies translators adopted while subtitling these cultural constraints in Family Guy into Arabic. By analyzing how the subtitlists managed the tension between the provocative nature of the American sitcom and the conservative values of the Arab world, this research seeks to answer the following questions:

What are the strategies used by the subtitlists of Family Guy to:

A: translate unacceptable religious remarks?

B: reflect the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns on the target audience?

C: render taboos into Arabic?

intros.text:
The proliferation of audio-visual translation has become a cornerstone of global cultural exchange, with subtitling and dubbing serving as the primary vehicles for making foreign-language media accessible to international audiences. In the Arab world, the increasing prevalence of foreign animation on television screens has heightened the demand for high-quality translation that not only bridges linguistic gaps but also navigates the complex interplay between source and target cultures. This process is rarely a neutral transfer of meaning; rather, it is a sophisticated negotiation of values. As Venuti (2005) suggests, national identity is inherently tied to linguistic and cultural manifestations, and the act of translation often involves a tension between preserving the source identity and adapting the text to fit the local contingencies of the target audience.

Subtitling, in particular, is often preferred over dubbing due to its cost-effectiveness and its ability to maintain the raw emotional impact of the original audio. However, the subtitlist faces a multifaceted challenge: they must synchronize text with visual and aural cues while ensuring that the content remains acceptable within the ideological framework of the receptor culture. When translating from English into Arabic, this challenge is amplified by significant ideological clashes. The Arab world is characterized by a conservative social fabric where religion, morality, and tradition play a central role in shaping public discourse. Consequently, translators often exercise strict control and ethical supervision over the language used in subtitles to protect the target audience's identity and prevent the introduction of concepts deemed offensive or indecent.

Previous research has extensively explored the general challenges of audio-visual translation and the strategies used to mitigate cultural gaps. For instance, Jankowska (2009) investigated the translation of comedy in animated films, noting that humorous elements are frequently lost or reduced in translation due to the translator's difficulty in rendering culture-specific references. Other scholars have highlighted the power of film translation to influence beliefs and the necessity of manipulating texts to achieve social acceptance in the target culture. However, much of the existing literature on English-Arabic subtitling has focused on feature films or children's media, where the constraints are often predictable. There remains a paucity of empirical research focusing on adult-oriented animated sitcoms, which intentionally push the boundaries of social propriety through satire and irony.

One of the most prominent examples of such boundary-pushing media is the American animated sitcom *Family Guy*. The show is renowned for its provocative use of cutaway gags and its willingness to address sensitive topics, including religion, politics, sex, and taboo subjects. Because the show's humor often relies on the mockery of sacred figures or the explicit depiction of immoral acts, it presents a unique set of cultural constraints for the Arabic subtitlist. To date, little to no academic attention has been paid specifically to the Arabic subtitled version of *Family Guy*, despite its availability on major networks like MBC and OSN. This represents a significant gap in the literature, as the show provides a fertile ground for analyzing how manipulation theory is applied in real-time to resolve extreme cultural and ideological conflicts.

Addressing this gap, the present study aims to investigate and identify the specific strategies employed by translators when subtitling cultural constraints in *Family Guy* into Arabic. The researchers categorize these constraints into three primary domains: religious remarks, jokes and humor revolving around proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks refer to offensive references to the divine or sacred figures, which are often viewed as 'red zones' in Islamic and Arab societies. Jokes involving proper nouns include wordplay on names of famous personalities or brands that may be unfamiliar or inappropriately rendered in the target culture. Finally, taboos are defined as immoral or explicit content—often sexual or vulgar in nature—that is deemed shocking or indecent by the target audience (Allan, 2001).

To achieve this objective, the study seeks to answer the following research questions:
1. What strategies are used by subtitlists to translate unacceptable religious remarks?
2. How is the humorous effect of jokes revolving around proper nouns reflected for the target audience?
3. Which strategies are employed to render taboo language into Arabic?

By analyzing a selected corpus of episodes from the OSN network, this research intends to demonstrate how the ideology of the target audience dictates the translation process. It is hypothesized that the translators rely heavily on omission and euphemism to ensure cultural compatibility, effectively acting as cultural mediators who rewrite the source text to align with the norms of the Arab world. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the broader understanding of the 'Manipulation School' of translation and provide practical insights for subtitlists and translation trainees working across disparate cultural landscapes.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows: The next section provides a detailed review of related literature on audio-visual translation and the cultural approach. The methodology section describes the selection of the *Family Guy* corpus and the analytical procedures used. This is followed by the findings and discussion, where the three categories of cultural constraints are analyzed with specific examples. Finally, the paper concludes with a summary of the results and recommendations for future research and professional practice.

The third category, taboos, is included because the explicit rendition of such content often comes across as shocking and unpleasant. intros.text:
In the contemporary era of global media consumption, the subtitling and dubbing of foreign animation in Arabic have experienced significant growth since television screens reached Arab homes. This expansion imposes stricter control and ethical supervision of the language used, necessitating a critical examination of the cultural constraints inherent in the translation process. Audio-visual translation (AVT) has become a vital field of study, particularly as it bridges the gap between diverse linguistic and cultural communities. As noted by Díaz Cintas (2009), new trends in audiovisual translation highlight the increasing complexity of rendering foreign content for local audiences, where the translator must navigate not only linguistic barriers but also deep-seated cultural ideologies. The power of film translation, as suggested by Szarkowska (2005), lies in its ability to shape perceptions, making the choices made by translators particularly consequential in conservative societies. 

The translation of animated sitcoms presents unique challenges, especially when the source material addresses sensitive matters such as sex, alcohol, religion, and politics. These themes are often viewed with concern and caution in the Arab world, where national identity is culturally diverse and connected to issues of race, ethnicity, and religious belief, as manifested in a particular language and culture (Venuti, 2005). Throughout the course of translation, as different new areas are drawn into sharp focus, identities are often lost, allowing ways for new ones to emerge. Consequently, translators show great concern when rendering works for the Arab audience to protect their identity and culture. It is often believed that translators take strong caution when approaching subjects considered unacceptable, such as religion, humour, and taboos, which often constitute a major challenge in the translation process. These subjects are discussed thoroughly in this paper, as they represent the core cultural constraints that demand specific translation strategies.

Previous research has established the significance of cultural context in translation. Jankowska (2009) examined how comedy elements are translated in animated films and found that the target text often contains fewer humorous elements than the source texts. This reduction is frequently attributed to the translators' lack of knowledge regarding how cultural humorous references could be rendered effectively. Similarly, the translation of register, style, and tone in dubbing and subtitling has been explored, revealing that translators must sift through multiple layers of meaning within the context of verbal, non-verbal, aural, and visual signs to establish coherence (Jankowska, 2009). However, despite the growing body of literature on AVT, there remains a gap in understanding how specific cultural constraints are managed in the subtitling of adult-oriented animated sitcoms into Arabic. While studies have investigated the impact of cartoon programs on children's language and behavior (Ghilzai et al., 2017), fewer studies have focused on the intricate negotiation of adult humor and taboo subjects in shows like Family Guy. 

Furthermore, the definition of tabooed words as those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent when used in certain contexts (Allan, 2001) underscores the necessity for translators to employ specific strategies to mitigate cultural shock. The cultural approach to translation, which emphasizes the cultural influence of translation in the receptor language, suggests that translation is independent literature rather than a sheer replica of the source texts. This approach pushes translation towards a broad cultural context, drawing on cultural backgrounds, history, and norms. Yet, it remains unclear how these theoretical frameworks are practically applied when translating a show that explicitly mocks religious figures and utilizes explicit language, such as the American animated sitcom Family Guy. The show, known for its satire and cutaway gags, frequently addresses sensitive topics that clash with the ideological values of the target Arab audience. 

This study aims to address these gaps by investigating and identifying the strategies translators opted for while subtitling cultural constraints in Family Guy into Arabic. Specifically, the research focuses on three main categories of cultural constraints: religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboos. Religious remarks refer to any unacceptable offensive religious reference included in the show, while jokes and humour of proper nouns refer to cross-cultural names used in a humorous context. Taboos are defined as immoral or explicit content deemed inappropriate by the target audience. The reason behind this classification is that religion might be the number one red zone for almost all societies, and followers of a particular religion do not tolerate mockery or disdain of their beliefs. Therefore, when a popular television show provokes the audience by offending their religion, the translator must avoid rendering such provocative utterances. 

To achieve this objective, the study examines the following research questions: What are the strategies used by the subtitlists of Family Guy to translate unacceptable religious remarks? How do they reflect the humorous effect that revolves around proper nouns on the target audience? And how do they render taboos into Arabic? By analyzing the Arabic subtitled version of Family Guy, this study seeks to provide a contextualized account of the translation strategies employed to navigate these cultural constraints. The findings of this study could play a great role in showing the state of today's translation practices and the vital role the target audience plays in determining the appropriate constraints on translation that go in line with their ideology and culture. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader understanding of how ideology shapes the translation process in the Arab media landscape.

intros.text:
The rapid circulation of audiovisual products across linguistic and cultural borders has made audiovisual translation a central mode of intercultural communication. Subtitling and dubbing, in particular, have enabled television programmes, films, and animated series to reach audiences far beyond their original production contexts. As Díaz Cintas (2009) notes, audiovisual translation is no longer a marginal practice but a dynamic field shaped by technological, commercial, and sociocultural developments. In the Arab world, the expansion of satellite television, streaming platforms, DVDs, and online circulation has considerably increased exposure to English-language media. This growth has also intensified the need for Arabic subtitles that are not only linguistically comprehensible but also culturally acceptable to diverse Arab audiences.

Subtitling differs from other forms of translation because the translator works under technical and semiotic constraints. The subtitlist must condense spoken dialogue into written text while taking into account timing, screen space, image, sound, gesture, accent, and viewers’ processing speed. Meaning in audiovisual texts is produced through the interaction of verbal and non-verbal signs; consequently, the subtitlist cannot treat dialogue as an isolated written script. Jankowska (2009) argues that audiovisual translators must negotiate register, style, tone, and the multiple layers of meaning created by visual and aural cues. These challenges become more complex when the source text contains humour, profanity, religious references, sexual innuendo, or culturally specific allusions, all of which are frequent in contemporary American animation aimed at adults.

Film and television translation also has cultural and ideological power. Szarkowska (2005) draws attention to the influence of translated screen products in shaping viewers’ perceptions of other cultures, values, and social practices. This influence is particularly important in the case of animated programmes, which may be perceived as light entertainment or even as suitable for younger viewers despite containing adult themes. Research on cartoon programmes has shown that animation can affect children’s language and behaviour, which makes the translation of animated content an ethically sensitive practice in many societies (Ghilzai et al., 2017). Although Family Guy is produced primarily for adult audiences, its animated format, comic style, and wide circulation mean that Arab subtitlers may still approach it with caution, especially when it is broadcast on television or made accessible in family viewing contexts.

Culture is one of the most decisive factors in this process. Translation is not a neutral transfer of words from one language into another; rather, it is an act of rewriting shaped by the target culture’s expectations, ideologies, institutions, and norms. Venuti (2005) links translation to questions of national identity, arguing that translated texts participate in the formation, negotiation, and sometimes destabilisation of cultural identities. In the Arabic context, subtitlers often work within a cultural environment in which religion, family values, modesty, and public decency are treated as important social principles. As a result, translators may manipulate, soften, omit, or explain source-text material in order to make the translated product acceptable to its intended audience.

The American animated sitcom Family Guy provides a particularly rich case for examining such cultural constraints. Created by Seth MacFarlane, the programme is well known for its satirical treatment of religion, politics, sexuality, race, celebrity culture, and popular media. Its humour frequently depends on cutaway gags, intertextual references, taboo language, and references to public figures or brands that are immediately recognisable to many American viewers but may be obscure, offensive, or culturally inappropriate for Arab audiences. The show often derives comic effect from violating expectations and social norms; however, what functions as humour in the source culture may be received as disrespectful, confusing, or unacceptable in the target culture. This makes Family Guy an illuminating object of study for English–Arabic subtitling.

Among the most problematic areas in translating such material are religious remarks, proper-name-based humour, and taboo expressions. Religious references are especially sensitive because religion occupies a central place in Arab societies and because mockery of God, prophets, scriptures, or religious communities is generally regarded as offensive. A literal rendering of irreverent religious jokes may therefore create serious cultural and ideological tension. Humour based on proper names poses a different type of problem. Names of celebrities, politicians, brands, films, or fictional characters may carry strong associations for source-language viewers, but those associations may not be shared by target-language audiences. The subtitler must decide whether to retain the name, add guidance, explain the reference, or replace it with a more accessible equivalent. Taboo language, including sexual references, swear words, and vulgar references to body parts, is another recurrent challenge. Allan (2001) defines taboo words as those considered offensive, shocking, or indecent in particular contexts; such words are especially delicate in Arabic media, where directness in sexual or obscene expression is often avoided.

The present study investigates the strategies used in subtitling cultural constraints in Family Guy into Arabic. It focuses on how the Arabic subtitles respond to three categories of culturally problematic material: unacceptable religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboos. By analysing selected episodes from the Arabic subtitled version and comparing them with the English source text, the study seeks to identify the subtitling strategies employed to negotiate the gap between the American source culture and the Arab target culture. Specifically, it asks what strategies are used to translate religiously offensive remarks, how proper-name-based humour is rendered in a way that preserves or explains its comic effect, and how taboo expressions are handled in Arabic subtitles. In doing so, the study contributes to research on audiovisual translation, English–Arabic subtitling, and the role of ideology and cultural acceptability in shaping translated media texts.

intros.text:
Audiovisual translation has become an increasingly central area of translation studies as films, television series and animated programmes circulate rapidly across linguistic and cultural borders. Subtitling and dubbing are no longer merely technical means of making foreign productions intelligible; they are cultural practices through which meanings, identities and values are negotiated for new audiences. In the Arab world, the expansion of satellite television, streaming platforms and imported entertainment has intensified the need for careful English–Arabic audiovisual translation, particularly when foreign programmes contain material that conflicts with local religious, social or moral expectations. Because subtitles are displayed directly to viewers and often accompany the original soundtrack, subtitlists must decide not only how to render words, but also how to mediate potentially sensitive images, jokes, references and ideologies within severe spatial and temporal constraints.

Subtitling is especially demanding because it operates within a multimodal text in which speech, image, music, gesture, timing and audience expectations interact. As Díaz Cintas (2009) notes, audiovisual translation involves more than the transfer of verbal language; it requires attention to the semiotic complexity of the screen text. Similarly, Jankowska (2009) argues that subtitlers and dubbers must process several layers of meaning, including register, style, tone and the relationship between verbal and non-verbal signs. These demands become more difficult when the source text depends on humour, wordplay, culture-specific allusions or offensive language. In such cases, the translator may be required to preserve the communicative effect of the original while also respecting the ideological and cultural boundaries of the target audience.

The relationship between translation and culture is particularly significant in English–Arabic subtitling. Translation is not a neutral substitution of linguistic forms; it participates in the construction, protection and transformation of cultural identities. Venuti (2005) emphasizes that translation is implicated in national and cultural identity formation, since translated texts can either reinforce local values or introduce competing foreign ones. In conservative reception contexts, this ethical dimension becomes highly visible. Arab subtitlists frequently encounter references to sex, alcohol, profanity, religion and politics that may be acceptable or humorous in the source culture but inappropriate, offensive or disturbing in the target culture. Consequently, their decisions often involve omission, mitigation, explanation or reformulation rather than literal transfer.

Animation and animated sitcoms are particularly relevant to this issue. Although animation is sometimes associated with children, many contemporary animated series are written for adults and contain satire, sexual innuendo, political mockery, taboo language and religious irreverence. At the same time, cartoons and animated programmes can influence viewers’ language and behaviour, especially younger audiences who may be exposed to them through television or online platforms (Ghilzai et al., 2017). This dual status of animation—as a popular entertainment form and as a vehicle for potentially controversial content—places additional responsibility on translators and broadcasters. The problem is intensified when an adult animated programme is imported into a cultural environment where animation may still be perceived by some viewers as suitable for family viewing.

Family Guy is a useful case through which to examine these issues. The series is an American animated sitcom known for its satirical treatment of religion, politics, race, sexuality, celebrity culture and popular media. Its humour often relies on cutaway gags, sudden intertextual references, parody, taboo expressions and deliberate violation of social norms. Such features make the programme entertaining for many source-language viewers but highly challenging for Arabic subtitling. Religious references may be perceived as blasphemous; sexual or obscene expressions may breach norms of public decency; and jokes based on proper names, celebrities, restaurants, films or political figures may fail to produce humour if the target audience lacks the necessary background knowledge. Thus, subtitling Family Guy into Arabic requires continuous negotiation between fidelity to the source text and acceptability in the target culture.

Previous research has examined several aspects of audiovisual translation, including the translation of style and tone in subtitling and dubbing (Jankowska, 2009), the power of film translation in shaping reception (Szarkowska, 2005), and the cultural implications of translation for national identities (Venuti, 2005). Studies have also addressed humour transfer, taboo language and the treatment of culture-specific references in audiovisual contexts. However, despite the growing body of work on audiovisual translation and on English–Arabic subtitling, relatively little attention has been given to the Arabic subtitled version of Family Guy and to the specific strategies used to overcome its cultural constraints. This is a notable gap because the series combines several problematic categories in a single text: irreverent religious humour, jokes built around proper names and culture-specific knowledge, and explicit taboo language. Examining how these categories are handled can provide insight into the practical operation of ideology, censorship and cultural mediation in Arabic subtitling.

The present study therefore investigates the cultural constraints involved in subtitling selected episodes of Family Guy into Arabic. It focuses on three categories that are especially sensitive in the Arab reception context: unacceptable religious remarks, jokes and humour that revolve around proper nouns, and taboo expressions. Religious remarks are understood here as references that may be considered offensive or disrespectful toward God, prophets, sacred figures or religious beliefs. Jokes and humour based on proper nouns refer to humorous instances involving names of people, celebrities, brands, films or cultural entities whose comic effect depends on source-culture knowledge. Taboos refer to words or expressions considered indecent, immoral or inappropriate in particular contexts; as Allan (2001) observes, taboo words are those regarded as offensive, shocking or indecent when used in certain situations.

Accordingly, the study aims to identify the strategies adopted by Arabic subtitlists when rendering these culturally constrained elements. More specifically, it asks how the subtitlists translate unacceptable religious remarks, how they attempt to reproduce the humorous effect of jokes involving proper names, and how they deal with taboo expressions in a way that is acceptable to Arab audiences. By analysing examples from the Arabic subtitles of Family Guy, the study contributes to research on audiovisual translation by showing how cultural, religious and ideological considerations shape translation choices. It also offers practical implications for subtitlers, translation trainers and audiovisual translation agencies seeking to balance communicative effectiveness with cultural appropriateness in English–Arabic subtitling.

intros.text: THE IMPORTANCE OF LISTENING comprehension ability in second language (L2) learning is uncontroversial given the current pedagogical emphasis on achieving communica- tive competence. Such approaches to language teaching underscore the need to practice listen- ing skills with the main goal of comprehension, which is usually operationalized in terms of per- formance on a test.  Vandergrift and Goh (2012) explained that this view of listening as a product predominates most language classrooms today but does not take into account the importance of “teaching them [learners] how to process and manage input” (p. 13).  The product approach to listening comprehension, perhaps, reflects our lack of understanding of this construct. Indeed, historically speaking, scant attention has been di- rected toward defining listening comprehension and empirically testing variables (e.g., learner or text related) assumed to facilitate or hin- der the process of L2 listening comprehension (Vandergrift & Baker, 2015).  Numerous factors are argued to influence the difficulty of L2 listening (e.g., Bloomfield et al., 2010; Imhof & Janusik, 2006), such as passage characteristics (e.g., length of passage, linguistic complexity, speed of speech), listener charac- teristics (e.g., second language proficiency, first language [L1] listening ability, prior knowledge), and listening contexts or testing conditions (e.g., formal or informal real-life listening, time limi- tations, number of exposure times).  However, as pointed out by Vandergrift & Goh (2012), while “knowledge of these factors and how they hinder or facilitate successful comprehension is impor- tant for informed teaching of L2 listening ( ...) there is still very little research to provide empiri- cal evidence for a causal relationship” (p. 57).  The present study thus seeks to contribute to the L2 listening strand of research by empirically exam- ining the impact of two passage characteristics— speech rate and utterance length—and one listener characteristic—L2 oral proficiency—on the listening comprehension of Spanish as a second language. In doing so, we provide recom- mendations to best inform pedagogical practices on developing L2 listening skills and materials.

intros.text:
Listening comprehension plays a central role in second language (L2) acquisition, yet it remains one of the least understood and least researched of the four skills (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). Unlike reading, aural comprehension unfolds in real time, requiring listeners to segment a continuous speech signal and construct meaning under considerable temporal pressure. For L2 learners, this challenge is compounded by underdeveloped automaticity, limited linguistic knowledge, and a heavier reliance on effortful, controlled bottom-up processing. As a result, learners frequently report difficulty comprehending speech, and the variables that shape this difficulty are only beginning to be systematically disentangled (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Vandergrift & Baker, 2015).

Among these variables, speech rate has long been identified as a decisive temporal factor in L2 decoding, and learners routinely cite fast delivery as a major source of comprehension difficulty. However, empirical findings on the impact of accelerated speech are mixed, with some studies reporting clear detriments to comprehension and others reporting negligible effects. A second potentially influential variable, utterance length, has been defined and operationalized inconsistently across studies—in seconds, minutes, syllables, words, or sentences—and has often been confounded with passage type or syntactic complexity, yielding contradictory results. A third variable, L2 proficiency, is widely assumed to affect the strategies learners use and the knowledge sources they can access, yet it too has been operationalized in disparate ways, rarely through standardized measures.

Crucially, these three variables have seldom been examined together, despite theoretical reasons to expect that they interact: lengthier or faster input may tax working memory more heavily for less proficient listeners, while higher proficiency may buffer against such demands. The present study addresses these gaps by isolating sentence length in terms of syllables, controlling for syntactic complexity, and measuring proficiency with a standardized oral proficiency test. Focusing on native English-speaking learners of L2 Spanish, it investigates how speech rate, utterance length, L2 oral proficiency, and their interactions influence listening comprehension, thereby contributing to a fuller understanding of the complex, multivariate nature of L2 listening (Goh & Vandergrift, 2021).

intros.text:
Listening comprehension plays a central role in second language (L2) acquisition, yet it has long been considered the Cinderella of the four communication skills in terms of both research attention and pedagogical practice (Bloomfield et al., 2010). This relative neglect is striking given that listening occupies more time than any other communication skill and that its importance in the real world continues to grow with the proliferation of new media. Importantly, listening comprehension has recently been identified as a significant predictor of overall language learning, underscoring the need to better understand the variables that shape it (Vandergrift & Baker, 2015).

Listening is a complex, dynamic process that draws simultaneously on bottom-up decoding of the speech signal and top-down application of context and prior knowledge (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Goh & Vandergrift, 2021). Because L2 listeners often possess underdeveloped automaticity, they rely more heavily on effortful, controlled processing, which makes them especially vulnerable to features of the aural input such as speech rate and utterance length. Yet, despite the assumption that both accelerated speech and lengthier passages hamper comprehension, the empirical picture remains inconsistent. Studies of speech rate report mixed findings, and much of the research has examined L1 or L1-accented speech rather than L2 listening comprehension per se. Similarly, investigations of passage length have yielded inconclusive results, in part because length has rarely been isolated from confounds such as syntactic complexity and passage type.

A further complication is that L2 proficiency, itself operationalized in disparate ways, may moderate these effects, yet few listening studies have employed standardized measures of proficiency. To date, no study has systematically examined how speech rate, utterance length, and L2 oral proficiency jointly influence listening comprehension in L2 Spanish. The present study addresses these gaps by manipulating speed and syllable-based length while controlling for syntactic complexity, and by adopting a standardized oral proficiency test. In doing so, it seeks to clarify the roles and interactions of these variables in the complex process of L2 Spanish listening comprehension, offering implications for pedagogy and materials design.

intros.text:
Listening is a multifaceted and dynamic skill that involves the simultaneous operation of bottom-up processes, such as the segmentation of speech signals, and top-down processes, which leverage prior knowledge and context (Bloomfield et al., 2010). Despite its critical role in second language (L2) acquisition, listening has often been marginalized in both pedagogical practice and empirical research (Bloomfield et al., 2010). For L2 learners, the process of constructing meaning from aural input is frequently hindered by a lack of automaticity, forcing a reliance on conscious, controlled processing that can easily overwhelm cognitive resources. 

Several variables are thought to contribute to the difficulty of L2 listening comprehension. Speech rate is a primary temporal variable; accelerated speech can degrade the ability of learners to decode input in real time, though the extent of this impact may vary depending on the target language and the listener's proficiency. Similarly, the length of an utterance may tax working memory, increasing the likelihood that a listener will miss subsequent information if earlier segments are not successfully processed. While some research suggests that longer passages are more challenging, findings remain inconsistent due to confounding factors such as syntactic complexity and varying operationalizations of "length."

Furthermore, L2 proficiency—whether measured globally or through specific domains like oral proficiency—is a significant predictor of listening success. Higher proficiency typically allows learners to process larger chunks of information and employ more efficient strategies (Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). However, there is a persistent need for more research utilizing standardized measures of proficiency to provide objective data on how these learner variables interact with speech characteristics. 

Accordingly, the present study investigates the influence of speech rate (normal vs. fast), utterance length (short vs. long), and L2 Spanish oral proficiency on listening comprehension among native English speakers. Specifically, it examines how these variables and their interactions affect the ability of learners to accurately recall L2 Spanish sentences.

intros.text:
Listening is a complex, dynamic skill encompassing neurological, linguistic, semantic, and pragmatic processing (Rost, 2016). It requires the simultaneous operation of bottom-up decoding of the speech signal and top-down application of prior knowledge and context (Vandergrift & Goh, 2012). Despite its centrality to language acquisition and its prevalence in real-world communication, listening has often been marginalized in research and pedagogy compared to other language skills (Bloomfield et al., 2010). 

L2 listening difficulties often stem from a lack of automaticity, forcing less proficient learners to rely on conscious, controlled processing (Segalowitz, 2003). Consequently, factors such as speech rate and utterance length can heavily tax cognitive resources. While previous research suggests that accelerated speech generally degrades L2 comprehension (Griffiths, 1990), findings remain inconsistent, and the precise impact of delivery speed on L2 listening comprehension—as opposed to mere speech perception—is not well documented. Similarly, the effect of utterance length remains inconclusive due to confounding variables such as syntactic complexity and varying operationalizations of length (Sonnleitner et al., 2018). Furthermore, while L2 proficiency is known to be a strong predictor of listening success (Vandergrift, 2006), there is a paucity of studies employing standardized assessments to objectively measure this variable (Rubin, 1994).

Addressing these gaps, the present study investigates the interaction between speed of delivery, length of utterance, and L2 oral proficiency in L2 Spanish listening comprehension. Specifically, the study seeks to answer: To what extent do speech rate (normal vs. fast), utterance length (short vs. long), L2 Spanish oral proficiency, and their interactions influence comprehension? By employing a standardized oral proficiency test and controlling for syntactic complexity, this research aims to clarify how proficiency moderates the effects of temporal and structural variables. The findings may offer critical implications for the design of listening materials and the development of pedagogical strategies to foster automaticity in L2 learners.

intros.text:
Listening, defined as encompassing neurological, linguistic, semantic, and pragmatic processing, is a complex, dynamic skill involving both bottom-up and top-down processes (Rost, 2016; Vandergrift & Goh, 2012). While aural processing is complex in both first (L1) and second languages (L2), L2 listeners often face greater difficulties due to underdeveloped automaticity in the target language (Buck, 2001). Native listeners typically process input automatically, allowing for parallel, recursive processing of bottom-up and top-down cues. In contrast, less proficient L2 listeners rely on more conscious, controlled processing, often struggling with phonemic segmentation and linguistic knowledge required to construct meaning (Segalowitz, 2003; Vandergrift, 2007). This reliance on controlled processing, combined with limited linguistic knowledge, can lead to missed information, particularly when speech is delivered rapidly or when working memory is taxed by lengthier utterances (Vandergrift, 2007; Bloomfield et al., 2010).

Speech rate has long been identified as a critical variable in L2 listening comprehension. Perceived speed can significantly impact listeners' judgments of task difficulty, with learners frequently citing fast speech as a barrier to understanding (Flowerdew & Miller, 1992; Révész & Brunfaut, 2013). However, empirical findings on the precise impact of accelerated speech on L2 listening comprehension remain inconsistent. While some studies suggest fast speech detrimentally affects comprehension (Griffiths, 1990, 1992), others find no significant difference between average and fast rates (Griffiths, 1992). These mixed results suggest that speech rate may interact with other variables, such as utterance length or listener proficiency. Similarly, while lengthier passages are assumed to increase listening difficulty, research findings are inconclusive, often confounded by variables like syntactic complexity or passage type (Moyer, 2006; Rupp et al., 2001).

L2 proficiency is also a major predictor of listening ability, influencing the strategies listeners employ and the knowledge sources they access (Lee & Cai, 2010). Yet, few studies utilize standardized tests to measure proficiency, often relying on instructor judgment or course level (Rubin, 1994; Bloomfield et al., 2010). Furthermore, the interaction between proficiency, speech rate, and utterance length remains underexplored. The present study addresses these gaps by investigating the influence of speech rate (normal vs. fast), sentence length (short vs. long), and L2 oral proficiency on listening comprehension in L2 Spanish. Using discrete sentences to control for complexity, this research aims to clarify how these variables interact to impact the listening performance of upper-level Spanish learners.

intros.text:
Listening comprehension is a complex, dynamic skill that is central to successful second language (L2) acquisition and communication. Despite its critical role in language learning, listening has often been neglected in both research and pedagogical practice (Bloomfield et al., 2010). The process involves the interplay of bottom-up decoding of the speech signal and top-down application of context and prior knowledge (Vandergrift & Goh, 2012). While native listeners process input automatically, L2 listeners often struggle due to underdeveloped automaticity and limited linguistic resources, which constrain their ability to process rapid or lengthy aural input efficiently.

Several variables are posited to influence L2 listening performance, including speech rate, utterance length, and learner proficiency. Speech rate, in particular, has been identified as a significant temporal variable in L2 decoding (Griffiths, 1990). While accelerated speech is generally assumed to hinder comprehension, empirical findings remain inconsistent. Some studies suggest that fast speech significantly degrades performance (Griffiths, 1990), while others find no difference between normal and fast rates (Griffiths, 1992). These discrepancies may stem from unexamined interactions between speed and other variables, such as the length of the utterance. Similarly, the impact of passage length on comprehension is unclear, with studies reporting mixed results depending on how length is operationalized and whether confounding variables like syntactic complexity are controlled (Moyer, 2006; Rupp et al., 2001).

Furthermore, the role of L2 proficiency in moderating these effects is critical yet often overlooked. Although proficiency is a known predictor of listening ability (Vandergrift, 2006), few studies have utilized standardized measures to examine how proficiency levels interact with acoustic variables like speed and length. Most existing research relies on instructor judgment or non-standardized assessments, limiting generalizability (Rubin, 1994). Additionally, the specific interplay between speech rate, sentence length, and oral proficiency in L2 Spanish remains underexplored.

This study addresses these gaps by investigating the influence of speech rate (normal vs. fast), sentence length (short vs. long), and L2 oral proficiency on listening comprehension in L2 Spanish. Using a standardized proficiency test and controlled sentence stimuli, the research aims to clarify how these variables interact to affect comprehension. By isolating these factors, this study contributes to the understanding of the cognitive processes involved in L2 listening and offers implications for pedagogy and materials development.

intros.text:
Listening comprehension is central to second language (L2) development and everyday communication, yet it remains one of the least understood and least explicitly taught language skills. Unlike reading, listening requires learners to process transient input in real time while coordinating acoustic-phonetic decoding, lexical access, syntactic parsing, semantic integration, and pragmatic interpretation. Current accounts of L2 listening emphasize the joint contribution of bottom-up and top-down processing, as well as learner variables such as vocabulary knowledge, working memory, auditory discrimination, and metacognitive awareness (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). Because L2 listeners often lack the automaticity available to first language listeners, relatively small changes in the speech signal or in the linguistic demands of the input may have disproportionate effects on comprehension.

Two input-related variables that have repeatedly been associated with listening difficulty are speech rate and utterance length. Learners frequently identify fast speech as a major obstacle, and prior research generally suggests that accelerated delivery can reduce L2 listening performance. However, findings are not uniform, partly because studies have differed in how speed was operationalized and because speech rate has often been examined in passages that also vary in length, complexity, or discourse type. Utterance length is similarly under-specified in the literature. Longer passages are assumed to place greater demands on memory and processing, but previous work has defined length in different ways and has sometimes confounded it with syntactic complexity, redundancy, or genre (Bloomfield et al., 2010). Consequently, the independent and combined effects of speech rate and length on L2 listening comprehension remain unclear.

Learner proficiency may further condition these effects. More proficient listeners are expected to process larger units of speech more efficiently and to draw on richer linguistic knowledge, whereas less proficient listeners may rely more heavily on effortful word-by-word decoding. Research has shown that L2 proficiency contributes to listening ability, but standardized measures of proficiency are not always used, limiting comparability across studies. Recent pedagogical work also underscores the need to understand how learners manage listening processes so that instruction can move beyond comprehension checks toward helping learners learn to listen (Goh & Vandergrift, 2021).

The present study addresses these issues in the context of L2 Spanish by examining how speech rate, sentence length, and L2 oral proficiency influence learners’ sentence-level listening comprehension. By manipulating rate and length while controlling lexical familiarity and syntactic complexity, and by using a standardized measure of Spanish oral proficiency, the study seeks to clarify whether these variables independently or interactively shape L2 Spanish listening outcomes.

intros.text:
Listening comprehension is central to second language (L2) learning and use, yet it remains one of the most demanding skills for learners and one of the least fully understood in applied linguistics. Successful listening requires rapid coordination of bottom-up decoding of the speech stream with top-down use of linguistic, contextual, and prior knowledge (Bloomfield et al., 2010; Vandergrift & Baker, 2015). For L2 listeners, this coordination is often constrained by less automatized phonological, lexical, and syntactic processing, making real-time comprehension especially vulnerable to characteristics of the input and to individual learner differences.

Among the input variables frequently associated with L2 listening difficulty, speech rate has received sustained attention. Learners often report fast speech as a major obstacle, and empirical work generally suggests that accelerated delivery can impair comprehension. However, findings are not wholly consistent, partly because studies have differed in how they operationalize rate, whether they examine perception or comprehension, and whether they control other properties of the aural text. Utterance or passage length is another potentially important factor: longer input may place greater demands on working memory and increase the likelihood that missed information will disrupt subsequent comprehension. Yet research on length has also produced mixed results, with effects sometimes confounded by text type, syntactic complexity, or the use of naturally occurring passages rather than systematically manipulated stimuli.

Learner proficiency further complicates this picture. Proficiency is expected to influence the efficiency with which listeners segment speech, retain information, and draw on linguistic knowledge during comprehension. Previous research has shown that L2 proficiency and listening ability are related, but proficiency has often been measured through course level, teacher judgment, or nonstandardized instruments. Moreover, relatively little is known about how proficiency interacts with temporal and structural features of Spanish input, particularly for English-speaking learners listening to native Spanish speech.

The present study addresses these issues by examining the effects of speech rate, sentence length, and L2 Spanish oral proficiency on listening comprehension. Native English-speaking learners of Spanish listened to short and longer Spanish sentences presented at normal and digitally accelerated rates, with sentence length manipulated by number of syllables while syntactic complexity was controlled. Oral proficiency was measured with the standardized Versant Spanish Test, and comprehension was assessed through written L1 recall. The study asks to what extent speech rate, utterance length, oral proficiency, and their interactions predict L2 Spanish listening comprehension, thereby contributing evidence relevant to listening theory, pedagogy, and the design of aural materials.
