intros.text: CURRICULUM IS CENTRAL TO THE processes of schooling.  Recently, scholars in language education have called for more re- search and theoretical perspectives to be brought to bear on the complexity of curriculum1 in language classrooms.  In the introduction to an edited volume on critical approaches to language materials research, Gray (2013a) pointed out that the bulk of the publications on curriculum materials have focused on materials development rather than materials use, or what Eisner (2002) called curriculum enactment.2 Gray urged re- searchers to conduct “materials research” (p. 13) that asks critical and fundamental questions in analyses of curriculum content and its enactment.  In the Perspectives column (Tarone, 2014) in this journal on the significance of Guerrettaz and Johnston’s (2013) study—which examined the functions of textbooks in one English-as-a-second- language (ESL) classroom—Garton and Graves (2014) registered a similar concern and argued that “the field is generally undertheorized” (p. 654).  Contributors to this column under- scored the importance of studying curriculum materials in relation to classroom discourse, Kongji Qin 843 as featured in Guerrettaz & Johnston (2013).  Taking up these calls for research and curriculum theorizing, this article brings together perfor- mativity theory (Butler, 1990, 1997) and critical race theory (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson– Billings & Tate, 1995) to explore the relationship between language curriculum and learners’ subjectivity, drawing on a critical ethnography of immigrant adolescents’ language learning in one U.S. high school.  Specifically, this study takes a discourse analytical approach to analyze instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to understand two research questions: RQ1. How did the teacher-designed curricu- lum for vocabulary instruction in one .ESL classroom construct subjectivity for students? RQ2. How did three immigrant students in this classroom negotiate their subjectiv- ity in relation to the curriculum con- tent  The focal participants, Tiger, Chris, and Abdullah, 3 are from Taiwan, Malawi, and Libya, respectively. This analysis explores their nego- tiation of racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities through language use during a vocabulary activity. By subjectivity, I mean “our conscious and unconscious sense of self as medi- ated through symbolic forms [such as language]” (Kramsch, 2009, p. 18). It is “the particular ways in which a person gives meaning to themselves, others, and the world” (Davies & Banks, 1992, p. 2). In this poststructuralist theorizing of self, a person is a subject, in the sense that as a social being we are subject to various forms of symbolic constraints and forces, such as normative ways of understanding gender, race, and learners. The analytic foci of this study—the construction of subjectivity by curriculum texts and learn- ers’ subjectivity negotiation during curriculum enactment—are prompted by Kramsch’s (2009) argument that learners’ subjectivity, or their sense of self as a subject, is an integral aspect of language learning and needs to be attended to in language education research and practice.  The goal of this analysis is twofold: The first goal is to make a conceptual contribution to lan- guage curriculum research by bringing in a post- structuralist lens of performativity.  Performativity theory highlights the power of language in con- stituting subjectivity and social realities (Kramsch, 2009; Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Departing from the traditional, technical view of curricu lum as a linguistic resource for language learn- ing and of language instruction as a tool for de- veloping students’ linguistic and communicative competence, this poststructuralist lens views lan- guage learning as a process intertwined with the construction of learners’ subjectivity, that is, their sense of being and becoming a certain kind of learner and individual (Davies, 2014). It allows re- searchers to ask how curriculum texts and class- room talks around the curriculum constitute lan- guage learners’ subjectivity  The second goal is to illuminate the interactional process in which cur- riculum is taken up and appropriated by the three immigrant adolescent participants for subjectivity negotiation. The issues involved at the nexus of curriculum, learning, and subjectivity are compli- cated for immigrant youths like the participants in this study. Understanding their discursive negoti- ation of self in language classrooms is of critical relevance as current debates around immigration and displacement are often mired with racism, xenophobia, and nationalist ideologies (Greene, 2018).

intros.text:
In the current U.S. sociopolitical climate, immigrant youths increasingly find themselves navigating racialized, gendered, and religious discourses that shape how they are perceived and how they come to understand themselves. Under intensifying immigration enforcement and heightened xenophobia (Greene, 2018), immigrant adolescents contend not only with the demands of learning a new language but also with the powerful discourses that position them as racialized and minoritized subjects. Schools, and language classrooms in particular, are important sites where these young people learn to speak and, in speaking, negotiate who they can become. Yet how learners' subjectivities are constructed through and negotiated in relation to language curriculum remains underexplored, especially when we take seriously the constituting power of language itself.

Language curriculum has long been theorized as a body of linguistic knowledge to be transmitted, as a socioculturally situated process of enactment, or as an ideologically inflected artifact that reproduces existing inequalities (Eisner, 2002; Garton & Graves, 2014; Gray, 2013). Studies informed by the critical ideological perspective have shown how curriculum materials perpetuate ideologies through the exclusion or misrepresentation of gender, sexuality, and social class (Gray, 2013). Complementary research on curriculum enactment has demonstrated that materials frequently function as the de facto curriculum, providing emergent rather than intended affordances for learning and use, and that teachers and students bring their identities and lived experiences into their interactions with curricular texts (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013; Tarone, 2014). What these two productive lines of inquiry have largely left unexamined, however, is the question of subjectivity: how curriculum content and its enactment constitute the kinds of subjects that learners are called upon to become, and how learners negotiate those subject positions in the moment-to-moment life of the classroom.

A poststructuralist perspective offers a way of addressing this gap by reconceptualizing the relationship between curriculum and the learner. Drawing on performativity theory, I understand language not merely as a referential tool for communication but as a constitutive force that brings subjectivities into being (Butler, 1990; Pennycook, 2004). From this vantage point, gender, and indeed subjectivity more broadly, is performative: it is produced through the repeated stylization of utterances and acts within highly regulatory frames of normative discourse. Scholars have taken up this insight to reimagine language learning as a process of subject formation in which learners are 'pressed' by discourses and yet retain the capacity to appropriate, contest, and reinterpret them (Butler, 1997; Kramsch, 2009; Miller, 2012). Read through this lens, curriculum becomes a cultural artifact that constructs subject positions for learners, and its enactment becomes a discursive and performative space in which subjectivities are negotiated (Davies & Banks, 1992; Gray, 2013). Integrating performativity theory with critical race theory (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995) allows me to view immigrant youths as racialized subjects who are read through intersecting discourses of race, gender, and religion, and who use classroom talk to produce themselves as particular kinds of learners and persons.

Building on this theorization, the present study examines how a teacher-designed vocabulary curriculum, and one routinized language practice within it, constructed subjectivity for three immigrant adolescents in a U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, and how these youths negotiated their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to that curriculum. Drawing on data from a critical ethnography, I analyze instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to address two questions: how did the vocabulary curriculum, particularly its sentence-starter language practice, construct learners' subjectivities; and how did the immigrant students negotiate their subjectivities through classroom talk around the curricular content? As the analysis will show, the sentence starters, ostensibly designed as scaffolding tools, carried an implicit goal of interpellating students to become 'good learners,' while the focal students appropriated, subverted, or conformed to this and other prevailing discourses in ways shaped by discourses of racialized masculinity originating far beyond the classroom walls.

In what follows, I first review existing conceptualizations of language curriculum and studies of curriculum content and enactment. I then elaborate the theoretical framework, integrating performativity, subjectivation, and critical race theory. After describing the study's methods and settings, I present my analysis of curriculum as a discourse of subjectivation and of the three students' subjectivity negotiations, before considering the implications of this poststructuralist theorization for the research and practice of language education.

intros.text:
Language curriculum sits at the heart of language education, shaping not only what learners come to know but also, more subtly, who they are invited to become. Current understandings of curriculum are closely tied to the field's evolving views of language, learning, and pedagogy (Garton & Graves, 2014; Tarone, 2014), and can be understood as informed by three theoretical orientations: a linguistic cognitive perspective that treats curriculum as a body of linguistic knowledge to be transmitted and mastered; a social contextual perspective that foregrounds curriculum as a negotiated process of enactment situated within sociocultural contexts of teaching and learning; and a critical ideological perspective that maintains curriculum is politically and ideologically endorsed and often reproduces existing power relations. Scholars working within the last of these have shown how curriculum content, especially in commercially published materials, can reproduce inequalities and normative ideologies through exclusion or misrepresentation, whether of culture, gender, social class, or sexuality (Gray, 2013). Others have shown that curriculum enactment is a dynamic, negotiated process in which materials frequently afford emergent rather than intended possibilities for language use, and in which teachers and students bring their identities and lived experiences into classroom interaction (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013).

Despite the richness of these two lines of inquiry, both the analysis of curriculum content and the study of curriculum enactment have, with few exceptions, paid little attention to learners' subjectivity. The dominant framing has been Marxist, examining how ideologies are reproduced in curriculum texts, rather than how curriculum texts constitute subjectivities for learners. A notable exception is Gray's (2013) analysis of ELT textbooks, which showed that narrative texts constructed particular subject positions for learners in ways aligned to prevailing ideologies. Yet what remains underexamined is how curriculum, and the interactions built around it, constructs subject positions for students and how students, in turn, negotiate those positions in the moment-to-moment life of the classroom. This is a significant gap, particularly for minoritized and immigrant youth, whose classroom participation is entangled with racialized and gendered discourses that circulate far beyond the classroom walls.

Addressing this gap requires a theoretical vocabulary that connects language, discourse, and subjectivity. Performativity theory offers such a lens, positing that subjectivity is constituted through repeated linguistic and bodily acts within regulatory normative frames (Butler, 1990; Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Coupled with Butler's (1997) account of subjectivation, in which power is understood as productive rather than merely repressive, this perspective invites a shift from a referential view of classroom language use toward an ontological one that asks how students use classroom talk to produce themselves as particular kinds of learners and persons (Kramsch, 2009). Integrating performativity theory with critical race theory (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995) further allows immigrant youths to be understood as racialized subjects, read through racial ideologies coupled with essentializing gender stereotypes. While prior sociolinguistic and applied linguistic research has examined how immigrant youths perform identities through language, racialized subjectivities and their entanglement with curriculum content have not been foregrounded.

Extending these two lines of research, and building on feminist poststructuralist work on the constituting power of school discourses (Davies & Banks, 1992), the present study brings a poststructuralist perspective to bear on the relationship between curriculum and the learner. It marries the critical ideological and social contextual approaches by theorizing curriculum and its enactment through a lens of criticality while reimagining these foci through a poststructuralist theorization of language, discourse, and the learner. Drawing on data from a critical ethnography in one U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, this classroom discourse study analyzes instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to address two questions: how a teacher-designed vocabulary curriculum, centered on a routinized sentence-starter language practice, constructed subjectivity for students; and how three immigrant adolescents negotiated their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to that curriculum content. The analysis illustrates how the sentence starters, designed as scaffolding tools, served an implicit goal of constituting students as 'good learners,' and how the focal students appropriated them to challenge, subvert, or conform to prevailing discourses. In doing so, this article argues that curriculum can constitute a discursive and performative space in which students negotiate subjectivity and meaning in relation to power, and considers the implications of this theorization for research and practice.

intros.text:
In the field of English language teaching, the language curriculum is often conceptualized as a neutral blueprint for linguistic acquisition or a set of pedagogical tools designed to facilitate communicative competence. However, from a critical perspective, curriculum is never neutral; it is a site of political and ideological struggle where certain forms of knowledge are privileged over others (Apple, 2004). While extensive research has examined how curriculum materials reproduce ideologies of race, gender, and class through misrepresentation or erasure (Gray, 2013), relatively little attention has been paid to the relationship between the curriculum and the constitution of the learner's subjectivity. Most studies of curriculum enactment focus on the 'classroom ecology' and the affordances provided by materials for language learning (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013), yet they often overlook how the very act of engaging with a curriculum can be a process of subjectivation—the making of a subject through the internalizing of power and normative discourses (Butler, 1997).

This gap is particularly salient for immigrant adolescents in the United States, who enter the classroom as racialized and gendered subjects. For these learners, the school is not merely a place of academic instruction but a space where they must navigate endemic racism and rigid social hierarchies (Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995; Delgado & Stefancic, 2001). The tension between their lived experiences and the institutional expectations of the school often manifests in their classroom discourse. While some scholars have explored how immigrant youths perform identity through language (Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004), there is a need to further investigate how this performativity intersects with the formal curriculum. When learners are pressed to adopt specific subject positions—such as the 'good learner'—they may conform, resist, or subvert these positions to negotiate their own sense of self within a regulatory frame (Butler, 1990; Davies & Banks, 1992).

Drawing on a poststructuralist framework, this study views language curriculum as a discursive and performative space. By integrating performativity theory with critical race theory, I examine how curriculum does not just teach a language but actively constitutes the subjects who use it. Performativity allows us to move beyond an essentialist view of identity to an ontological understanding of language use, where students produce themselves through repeated acts and utterances aligned with or against dominant discourses (Miller, 2012). This approach is crucial for understanding how minoritized students, who are often read through essentializing racial and gender stereotypes, use classroom talk to navigate their positions of power and marginality.

This article analyzes data from a critical ethnography conducted in a U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, focusing on three immigrant adolescent boys. Specifically, I examine a routinized vocabulary activity employing 'sentence starters'—scaffolding tools designed to assist in language production. Through an analysis of instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews, I explore two primary research questions: First, how does the teacher-designed vocabulary curriculum construct learners' subjectivities? Second, how do immigrant adolescents negotiate their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to this curricular content?

By analyzing the 'telling cases' of three students from diverse backgrounds—Taiwan, Malawi, and Libya—this study illustrates how the curriculum serves an implicit goal of interpellating students into a narrow definition of the 'good learner.' The findings reveal that students do not passively receive these subject positions; instead, they appropriate the curricular space to challenge, subvert, or conform to prevailing discourses. In doing so, this research highlights the constitutive power of language in the classroom and argues for a reimagining of curriculum as a permeable space for subjectivity negotiation. Ultimately, this study contributes to a broader scholarly effort to understand the intersections of language, power, and becoming in the lives of immigrant youths, urging educators to recognize the profound impact of discursive subjectivation on the process of learning.

intros.text:
The language curriculum in second language education is often conceptualized as a neutral blueprint for linguistic acquisition—a structured sequence of grammatical patterns and communicative functions designed to move students toward proficiency. However, scholarship has increasingly recognized that curriculum is not merely a technical document but a cultural artifact embedded with ideological commitments (Gray, 2013). In the United States, the intersection of language learning and the immigrant experience is particularly fraught, as students must navigate not only the challenges of a new language but also the pervasive effects of racialization and systemic inequality (Greene, 2018). Consequently, understanding how curriculum operates within the lived experience of immigrant youth is vital for developing more equitable pedagogical practices.

Existing research on language materials has extensively documented how curricula can reproduce social hierarchies through the misrepresentation or erasure of marginalized identities. Scholars have highlighted the persistence of gender norms and the invisibility of LGBT issues in English Language Teaching (ELT) textbooks, arguing that such materials often uphold heteronormative and neoliberal ideologies (Gray, 2013). Simultaneously, studies on curriculum enactment have shifted focus toward the 'classroom ecology,' exploring how teachers and students co-construct meaning and how materials provide emergent affordances for learning (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013). Some critical studies have shown that students engage in oppositional resistance when confronted with alien or dominant discourses inscribed in their textbooks, using the classroom as a site to negotiate their identities.

Despite these contributions, there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the relationship between the language curriculum and the learner's subjectivity. While much attention has been paid to how curriculum reflects ideologies or how identity shapes language use, few studies have examined how the curriculum itself acts as a performative force that constitutes the student as a specific kind of subject. In other words, there is a need to move beyond a referential view of curriculum to an ontological one, investigating how the structured practices of the classroom 'press' students into particular subject positions.

This study addresses this gap by employing a poststructuralist lens to examine the relationship between language curriculum and the subjectivity of immigrant adolescents. Drawing on performativity theory, which posits that subjectivity is produced through the repeated stylization of acts and utterances (Butler, 1990), and Critical Race Theory (CRT), which asserts that racism is endemic to the U.S. educational experience (Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995; Delgado & Stefancic, 2001), I investigate how a specific routinized vocabulary activity—the use of sentence starters—functions as a space for subjectivation. The aim of this research is twofold: first, to uncover how the teacher-designed curriculum constructs a discourse of the 'good learner,' and second, to analyze how three immigrant adolescents negotiate their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to these curricular constraints.

Using data from a critical ethnography in a U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, including instructional materials, audiovisual recordings of classroom interactions, and semi-structured interviews, this article analyzes the performative tension between the 'master' discourse of the curriculum and the students' agency. I argue that while the curriculum attempts to interpellate students into a narrow definition of academic success, the students frequently appropriate, subvert, or conform to these discourses to navigate their own social realities. By theorizing curriculum as a discursive and performative space, this study seeks to shift the focus of language education from the transmission of linguistic competence to the understanding of how learners produce themselves through classroom discourse.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. I first detail the theoretical framework, integrating performativity and critical race theory. I then describe the ethnographic methodology and the participants involved. The subsequent sections present the analysis of the vocabulary curriculum's subjectivation goals and the students' specific instances of subjectivity negotiation. Finally, I discuss the implications of these findings for research and practice in language education.

intros.text:
In the field of English language teaching (ELT), the relationship between curriculum and learner subjectivity remains a critical yet underexamined dimension of language education. While extensive scholarship has explored curriculum content and enactment, few studies have attended to how language curriculum constitutes learners' subjectivities through the discursive and performative spaces of the classroom. This article addresses this gap by examining the relationship between language curriculum and learners' subjectivity through a poststructuralist perspective, specifically drawing on performativity theory and critical race theory. By integrating these frameworks, the study seeks to understand how curriculum, classroom interaction, and subjectivity negotiation intersect for immigrant adolescents in a U.S. secondary multilingual classroom.

Current conceptualizations of language curriculum are often shaped by three theoretical orientations: the linguistic cognitive perspective, which views curriculum as an external body of knowledge to be transmitted; the social contextual perspective, which emphasizes curriculum enactment as a sociocultural process; and the critical ideological perspective, which posits that curriculum reproduces inequality and power relations (Graves, 2016; Richards, 2013). While critical scholars have illuminated how curriculum texts reproduce ideologies—such as heteronormativity (Gray, 2013a) and neoliberalism (Chun, 2013)—they have largely overlooked how subjectivity is constituted by these texts. One notable exception is Gray's (2010) analysis of ELT textbooks, which demonstrated how narrative texts construct subject positions aligned with neoliberal ideologies. However, the dynamic process of subjectivity negotiation in classroom discourse remains largely untheorized.

To address this gap, this study brings a poststructuralist perspective to the analysis of curriculum and classroom interaction. Performativity theory, rooted in Austin's (1962) speech act theory and expanded by Butler (1990, 1997), offers a productive lens for connecting language and subjectivity. Butler argues that subjectivity is constituted through repeated linguistic and bodily acts within regulatory frames, a process she terms subjectivation. In educational contexts, students are 'pressed' to submit to discourses of being a 'proper' student, mastering practices regulated by institutional power to be recognized as legitimate subjects (Davies, 2006; Youdell, 2011). This ontological view shifts the focus from language as a communicative tool to language as a constitutive force that produces social realities and subjectivities (Kramsch, 2009; Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004).

Furthermore, this analysis integrates critical race theory to understand immigrant youths as racialized subjects. Critical race theorists (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995) argue that racism is endemic and permeates everyday experiences, particularly for people of color in the United States. When juxtaposed with performativity theory, this perspective allows for an understanding of how minoritized individuals are subject to racial discourses that legitimize racial hierarchies. Immigrant youths, such as the participants in this study, often navigate intersecting discourses of race, gender, and schooling that position them as racialized subjects. While previous research has examined how immigrant youths perform identities through language (e.g., Rampton, 1996; Jaspers, 2006; Dávila, 2019a, 2019b), few have foregrounded the entanglement of these performances with curriculum content.

Drawing on data from a critical ethnography, this study analyzes instructional materials, classroom interactions, and interviews to understand how a teacher-designed curriculum for a routinized vocabulary activity constructed subjectivity for three immigrant adolescents. Specifically, it examines how sentence starters, designed as scaffolding tools, served an implicit goal of constituting students as 'good learners' and how the students appropriated these tools to challenge, subvert, or conform to prevailing discourses. By viewing curriculum as a discursive and performative space, this article illustrates how students negotiate subjectivity and meaning in relation to power within and beyond classroom discourses. The findings contribute to a poststructuralist theorization of curriculum with implications for research and practice in language education, urging a shift from viewing curriculum as a neutral vehicle of knowledge to recognizing its constitutive power in shaping learners' subjectivities.

intros.text:
Language curriculum has traditionally been conceptualized through three primary orientations: the linguistic cognitive, the social contextual, and the critical ideological perspectives. While the linguistic cognitive view treats curriculum as a transmissive body of knowledge to be mastered (Richards, 2013), and the social contextual perspective frames it as a process of co-construction within sociocultural contexts (Graves, 2008), the critical ideological approach emphasizes the political and contested nature of educational content (Apple, 2004; Gray, 2013a). Extensive research within this critical tradition has illuminated how curriculum materials reproduce ideologies and inequalities through exclusion or misrepresentation, such as the erasure of LGBT issues (Gray, 2013b) or the reinforcement of gender norms (Lee, 2014). Furthermore, studies on curriculum enactment have demonstrated that classroom interactions are dynamic processes where teachers and students negotiate the ideologies embedded in texts (Canagarajah, 1993; Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013). Despite these significant contributions, existing scholarship on language curriculum—with few exceptions—has largely overlooked the specific relationship between curriculum and learners' subjectivity. While Gray (2010) noted that textbook narratives can construct subject positions aligned with neoliberal ideologies, there remains a paucity of research examining how curriculum texts and their enactment actively constitute the subjectivities of immigrant adolescents in multilingual classrooms.

This gap is particularly salient given the complex intersection of race, gender, and migration status that characterizes the experiences of many immigrant youth in U.S. schools. Critical race theorists (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995) have long argued that racism is endemic to U.S. society and permeates educational institutions. Yet, the mechanisms through which curriculum discourses intersect with racialized and gendered subjectivities remain under-theorized. To address this, the present study draws on a poststructuralist perspective that integrates performativity theory with critical race theory. Performativity theory, as developed by Butler (1990, 1997), posits that subjectivity is not a pre-existing essence but is constituted through repeated linguistic and bodily acts within regulatory frameworks. In the context of education, this implies that students are "subjected" to discourses of being a "good learner" and must perform specific utterances and acts to be socially recognized (Davies, 2006; Youdell, 2011). By applying this lens, language use in the classroom can be understood not merely as a communicative tool for learning, but as an ontological process of subject formation.

However, the application of performativity theory to language education has often focused on adult learners or general identity negotiation, with limited attention to how curriculum-specific discourses shape the racialized and gendered subjectivities of immigrant adolescents. While scholars like Miller (2012) and Pennycook (2004) have explored the constitutive power of language, fewer studies have examined how specific curricular artifacts, such as sentence-starter activities, function as sites of subjectivation. Moreover, the interplay between these curricular discourses and the broader societal discourses of racism and heteronormativity requires further investigation. This study seeks to occupy this niche by examining how a teacher-designed vocabulary curriculum constructed subjectivity for three immigrant adolescents and how these students negotiated their racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to the curriculum content. Specifically, it asks: (1) How does the language curriculum construct learners' subjectivities? and (2) How do immigrant adolescents negotiate their subjectivities in relation to the curricular content and prevailing discourses?

Drawing on data from a critical ethnography conducted in a U.S. secondary multilingual classroom, this analysis explores the sentence-starter language practice as a discursive and performative space. The study finds that while the curriculum was designed to scaffold linguistic development, it implicitly served to interpellate students into a narrowly defined "good learner" identity. The focal students, however, did not passively accept this positioning; instead, they appropriated, challenged, or subverted the curriculum to negotiate their identities in response to intersecting pressures of race and gender. These findings illustrate the constitutive power of curriculum and highlight the need for a poststructuralist theorization of language education that attends to the subjective dimensions of learning. The remainder of this article presents the theoretical framework, methodology, and detailed analysis of how curriculum functions as a space for subjectivity negotiation, concluding with implications for research and practice.

intros.text:
In the United States, immigrant adolescents learn English at a moment when immigration, race, religion, and belonging are intensely contested in public life. Anti-immigrant policies and enforcement practices have heightened fear in immigrant communities (Greene, 2018), while racialized discourses continue to shape how young people of color are read in schools. For multilingual immigrant youth, then, classroom language use is never only a matter of vocabulary, grammar, or communicative competence. It is also bound up with questions of who they are allowed to be, how they are recognized by others, and what kinds of learner, racial, gendered, and national subject positions become available or foreclosed in everyday classroom interaction. This article examines these issues by asking how a seemingly routine language curriculum becomes a space in which immigrant adolescents negotiate subjectivity and learning.

Curriculum has long been understood as more than a neutral plan for instruction. Educational theorists have argued that curriculum embodies decisions about what knowledge counts, whose knowledge is legitimized, and what forms of social life schools are designed to reproduce (Eisner, 2002). In language education, however, curriculum and instructional materials are still often approached primarily as resources for organizing linguistic input, structuring classroom tasks, and supporting acquisition. Recent research on materials has complicated this view by showing that textbooks and teacher-designed materials participate in classroom ecologies, shaping interaction in emergent and sometimes unintended ways (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013; Tarone, 2014). Garton and Graves (2014) similarly call for closer attention to how materials function in actual classrooms rather than as static pedagogical objects. These studies have helped move the field beyond a purely instrumental view of materials, yet the relationship between language curriculum and learners’ subjectivity remains underexplored.

Critical scholarship on language teaching materials has demonstrated that curricular texts are ideological artifacts. Studies have shown how English language teaching materials may reproduce heteronormativity, consumerism, neoliberal individualism, and racialized or gendered forms of representation (Gray, 2013; Gray, n.d.). Such work is important because it reveals how curriculum participates in broader relations of power. Yet much of this research has focused on representation in texts rather than on how learners take up, resist, or rework subject positions through classroom discourse. If curriculum is ideological, it is also interactional and performative: its meanings are enacted, negotiated, and sometimes disrupted as teachers and students speak through and around it. Understanding curriculum in this way requires attention not only to what materials represent but also to what they do in the production of classroom subjects.

A poststructuralist perspective offers a productive framework for such an inquiry. From this view, language does not merely express preexisting identities; it helps constitute them. Butler’s theory of performativity argues that subjectivities such as gender are produced through repeated acts and utterances within regulatory discourses (Butler, 1990, 1997). In language education, performativity has been used to rethink classroom language practices as constitutive actions that sediment, appropriate, and produce language and subjectivity (Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Kramsch (2006, 2009) similarly emphasizes the symbolic and subjective dimensions of language learning, arguing that multilingual learners must find and negotiate subject positions across languages and discourses. These perspectives shift the analytical focus from language as a tool for communication alone to language as a site of becoming.

This shift is especially important in research with immigrant youth, whose subjectivities are shaped by intersecting discourses of race, gender, language, religion, and nation. Critical race theory reminds us that race remains central to the organization of schooling and everyday life in the United States (Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995; Delgado & Stefancic, 2001). Immigrant adolescents are not simply “English learners”; they are racialized subjects whose classroom participation may be read through stereotypes about Blackness, Asianness, Arabness, masculinity, academic ability, and linguistic difference. A poststructuralist analysis informed by critical race theory can therefore illuminate how immigrant youth negotiate not only schooled identities but also racialized and gendered ways of being.

This article investigates these processes in one U.S. secondary multilingual classroom. Drawing on critical ethnographic data, I analyze a routinized vocabulary activity built around teacher-designed sentence starters. Although the sentence starters were intended to scaffold academic vocabulary use, they also repeatedly positioned students as particular kinds of “good learners” who value tests, grades, preparation, and school compliance. I then examine how three immigrant adolescent boys—Tiger, Chris, and Abdullah—appropriated, conformed to, and challenged these curricular discourses in classroom interaction. By bringing together curriculum analysis, classroom discourse analysis, performativity theory, and critical race theory, the study advances a view of language curriculum as a discursive and performative space: a site where language learning and subjectivity negotiation are inseparable.

intros.text:
Language curriculum is never a neutral container of linguistic forms. In classrooms, curricular texts and routines organize what counts as legitimate knowledge, shape patterns of participation, and offer learners particular ways of being recognized as students, speakers, and social subjects. This issue is especially consequential in multilingual classrooms serving immigrant youth, whose language learning unfolds amid racialized, gendered, and institutional discourses that extend well beyond the classroom. In the United States, immigrant communities have been increasingly positioned through public discourses of surveillance, exclusion, and threat (Greene, 2018), making it urgent to understand how school practices may reproduce, interrupt, or rework such positionings in everyday interaction.

Research on language teaching materials and curriculum has shown that materials play a central role in organizing classroom discourse and learning opportunities. Guerrettaz and Johnston (2013), for example, demonstrated that materials can become the de facto curriculum of a course and that their affordances emerge through classroom ecology rather than through teachers’ intentions alone. Calls for a research agenda on materials have similarly emphasized the need to examine how materials are used, interpreted, and taken up in classroom interaction (Garton & Graves, 2014; Tarone, 2014). At the same time, critical scholarship has shown that language curriculum and materials often carry ideological assumptions about culture, gender, sexuality, class, and the ideal learner. Gray’s work on ELT materials, for instance, has illuminated how heteronormativity and neoliberal subject positions can be embedded in apparently ordinary textbook content (Gray, 2013). Such studies make clear that curriculum does not merely support language instruction; it also participates in the social production of meanings, values, and norms.

Yet the relationship between language curriculum and learner subjectivity remains insufficiently theorized. Much research has examined what ideologies are represented in materials or how materials structure interaction, but less attention has been paid to how curriculum may constitute learners as particular kinds of subjects and how students negotiate those subject positions through classroom talk. This gap matters because language classrooms are not only sites where students acquire vocabulary, grammar, or communicative competence; they are also spaces where students learn, resist, appropriate, and perform socially available ways of being. A poststructuralist perspective is useful here because it treats language not simply as a representational system but as constitutive of social reality and subjectivity.

Performativity theory provides a particularly productive lens for examining this constituting power of language. Butler’s (1990, 1997) work shows that subjectivity is formed through repeated acts and utterances within regulatory discourses; subjects become intelligible by citing norms that precede them, even as such norms may be reworked in performance. Applied to language education, performativity has enabled scholars to examine classroom language practices as actions that sediment, appropriate, and constitute language and learner subjectivities (Miller, 2012; Pennycook, 2004). Kramsch (2006, 2009) similarly argues for attention to the multilingual subject and to symbolic competence, foregrounding learners’ ability to navigate the symbolic and subjective dimensions of language use. From this perspective, curricular language practice is not only practice in saying something correctly; it is also practice in becoming recognizable as a certain kind of learner and person.

A focus on immigrant adolescents also requires attention to race and racialization. Critical race theory maintains that race remains central to the organization of U.S. society and education and that racism is ordinary rather than exceptional (Delgado & Stefancic, 2001; Ladson-Billings & Tate, 1995). When brought together with performativity theory, critical race theory allows for an analysis of how immigrant youth are constituted through racialized and gendered discourses and how they may contest, inhabit, or redirect those discourses in classroom interaction. Such an approach avoids treating identity as a stable attribute that learners bring into classrooms; instead, it asks how subjectivities are produced in relation to language, curriculum, power, and interaction.

This study examines the relationship between language curriculum and learners’ subjectivity in one U.S. secondary multilingual classroom. Drawing on data from a critical ethnography, it analyzes a routinized vocabulary activity—the teacher-designed sentence-starter language practice—to ask how curricular texts constructed subject positions for students and how three immigrant adolescent boys negotiated racialized, gendered, and schooled subjectivities in relation to those curricular discourses. By integrating performativity theory with critical race theory, the study conceptualizes curriculum as a discursive and performative space: a space in which language learning, classroom participation, and subjectivity negotiation are mutually constituted. In doing so, it contributes to research on language curriculum and materials by shifting attention from what curriculum represents or affords to what curriculum does to learners’ possibilities for being and becoming.

intros.text: IN THE FIELD OF LANGUAGE TEACHING and learning, the term ‘classroom materials’ has long functioned as shorthand for text-based instruction inside walled classrooms (Tarone, 2014).  In recent years, research on materials use in language teaching and learning contexts has expanded in scope to address the wide variety of textual (e.g., books, maps, handouts), physi- cal (e.g., realia, cuisenaire rods), and virtual (e.g., websites, podcasts, video and audio recordings) supports that teachers and learners draw on to promote learning and development.  Neverthe- less, this increasingly diverse body of scholarship has yet to address the role of the most significant language resource available land.  For many Indigenous peoples, land is not only the physical space where and with which humans and their lan- guages have grown and changed, but it is also sig- nificant for keeping time, organizing knowledge, and structuring Indigenous lifeways (McKenzie, 2020)—relations that are typically kept apart from language in research on language learning and teaching materials (LLTMs) and materials use. The field of Indigenous language reclamation, however, holds language and land together as part of a ‘decolonial intervention’ (Leonard, 2019) aiming to disrupt the social structures at the root of language shift. While reclamation ‘practices’ can resemble the efforts that are typi- cally associated with language revitalization (e.g., documentation, policy making), the overall aim of remaking relations with and through language is a deliberate turn toward epistemologies and ontologies that delink (Mignolo, 2007) from colo- nial structural thinking.  In the underrepresented context of Indigenous language reclamation in the Upper Midwest region of the United States, local land is central to ways of knowing and being; thus it is also central to learning.  A land-centered paradigm offers significant insights into socioma- terial engagements among language learners and the natural world, particularly for Indigenous language teaching and learning contexts.  This deliberately interdisciplinary study (i.e., applied linguistics, Indigenous studies, linguistic anthropology) brings Indigenous perspectives of language and land into dialogue with LLTMs and materials use research in order to clarify and ex- pand conceptions of materials as both emergent and dynamic.  We look to local land as an al- ternative representation of ‘classroom materials’ and examine the relationships enacted and em- bodied among young bilingual Ojibwe learners, first-speaker Elders, and land in a naturally oc- curring ecology—the forest beyond the classroom walls. The land-based reclamation context for this study shifts us from institutionalized spaces to the woods, from instructor–student hierarchy to flat- tened peer–Elder–nature relations, and from fab- ricated instructional resources to nature and the environment.  Though grounded in highly spe- cific ‘localness,’ this research resonates across a wide range of sociomaterial language learning en- gagements as it reimagines learning in relation to place and space.

intros.text:
Research on language learning and teaching materials (LLTMs) has increasingly recognized that materials are not static objects but dynamic resources whose meanings emerge through use in particular classroom ecologies (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013; Tarone, 2014). Yet much of this scholarship remains bound to conventional classroom settings and to Western paradigms that treat language as decontextualized content to be mastered. In contexts of Indigenous language reclamation, such paradigms are not only insufficient—they can be actively harmful, reproducing the very colonial logics that reclamation efforts seek to undo (Makoni & Pennycook, 2007; McKenzie, 2020; White, 2006). Indigenous scholars, educators, and allies have long argued that (re)learning an ancestral language for the purpose of restoring linguistic and cultural continuity 'in place' requires distinct pedagogies, motives, and materials (Hinton, 2011; Leonard, 2019; Smith, 2012).

For young bilingual Ojibwe learners in the Upper Midwest of the United States, the natural world—local, rural, and reservation land—is central to ways of knowing and being, and thus central to learning. In many reclamation settings, purpose-built curricula and materials are scarce, and teacher-learners must rely on community knowledge, local resources, and creative, bootstrapped methods to engage learners meaningfully (Hinton, 2003; Meek & Messing, 2007). Land itself, we argue, functions as one of the most significant of these resources. Unlike a textbook, however, land is not a static object; it is a dynamic, living text with its own history of resilience through settler colonial occupation and extraction. This distinction matters, because reclamation is not simply about recovering pieces of linguistic code but about restoring the relationships—among generations and between humans and the more-than-human world—through which the language traditionally lived (Bang & Marin, 2015; Simpson, 2014; Tuck, McKenzie, & McCoy, 2014).

Central to this reorientation is the dissolution of the nature-culture boundary, which feminist and Indigenous scholars alike identify as a foundational force of colonial modernity (Lugones, 2010; Deloria, 1979; Kawagley, 1993). Delinking from colonial conceptions of language (Mignolo, 2007) invites us to see language as a mediator of human-human and human-nonhuman relations, and to attend to the multimodal, embodied, and sensory work through which meaning is co-constructed on land. Drawing together Indigenous perspectives of relationality, sociomaterial theory (Fenwick, 2015), and Goodwin's (2013) notion of co-operative action and substrate, this study examines the intra-actions among land-based 'materials,' an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth on local forestland.

By analyzing intergenerational forest walks, we ask: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials? In answering this question, we reposition land not merely as context or as inert material, but as an interlocutor—a living, dynamic participant in the co-construction of knowledge—and we consider the implications of this reframing for materials use research and for the wider field of applied linguistics.

intros.text:
For young bilingual Ojibwe learners in the Upper Midwest of the United States, the natural world—local, rural, and reservation land—is far more than a backdrop to language learning. It is central to ways of knowing and being, and thus central to learning itself. In contexts of Indigenous language reclamation, the goal is not simply to master a linguistic code but to restore the intergenerational and place-based relationships through which language was traditionally transmitted and lived. This distinctive orientation has led Indigenous scholars, educators, activists, and allies to insist that reclamation requires pedagogies and paradigms that differ markedly from those typically employed in TESOL, bilingual education, or world language classrooms (Leonard, 2019; McKenzie, 2020; White, 2006).

Within applied linguistics, research on language learning and teaching materials has begun to recognize that materials cannot be understood in isolation from their situated use (Tarone, 2014). Ecological approaches, in particular, have shown how materials play emergent roles within dynamic systems of classroom relationships (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013). Yet materials research remains heavily anchored in classroom settings and in a 'language-as-content' paradigm that risks treating language as a contained object to be objectified and mastered. In many Indigenous reclamation contexts, state-of-the-art materials are scarce, and existing resources often reproduce colonial framings of language rather than Indigenous ways of knowing (Meek & Messing, 2007). Teacher-learners consequently rely on community knowledge, local resources, and land itself to engage students meaningfully (Hinton, 2011). Despite this, remarkably little usage-based research examines how such materials are actually deployed and taken up in situated interaction, particularly in Indigenous language settings.

This gap is more than a scholarly oversight. Reclamation efforts aim to close a sociohistorical and sociocultural tear rooted in settler colonialism, and a central mechanism of that colonization is the nature-culture boundary that separates humans from the natural world (Bang & Marin, 2015). For applied linguistics, desettling this boundary means returning language to its natural environment and recognizing language as a mediator of human-nonhuman relationships. Recent work on land-based pedagogy and Indigenous relationality treats land not as a static text but as a dynamic, living participant—a teacher that structures countless relationships (Simpson, 2014). To pursue an approach that delinks from colonial conceptions of language (Mignolo, 2007), we draw together Indigenous perspectives of relationality, sociomaterial orientations to learning, and analyses of co-operative action.

Building on these traditions, the present study examines the intra-actions among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth on local forestland. We ask: what kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials? In doing so, we reimagine land as emergent, living, participatory materials—indeed, as an interlocutor—and consider what such a view offers materials research and Indigenous language pedagogy alike.

intros.text:
Ecological approaches to language learning and materials use increasingly represent educational settings as complex, dynamic systems, applying relational perspectives from the natural world to the classroom. In the context of Indigenous language reclamation—specifically for bilingual Ojibwe learners in the Upper Midwest of the United States—the natural world is not merely a setting, but a significant language learning resource unto itself. For these communities, local land is central to ways of knowing and being, making it an indispensable element of the reclamation process. However, much of the existing scholarship on language learning materials has been dominated by a 'language-as-content' paradigm, which often treats language as a static object or a set of discrete skills to be mastered (Tarone, 2014). This Western, colonial framework frequently isolates language from its situated use, creating curricular enclosures that may reinforce colonial dominance rather than supporting Indigenous ontological perspectives.

Indigenous scholars and educators have long argued that reclaiming an ancestral language requires pedagogies and paradigms that differ fundamentally from those employed in TESOL or mainstream bilingual education (White, 2006). True reclamation involves restoring linguistic and cultural continuity 'in place,' necessitating a shift toward what Mignolo (2007) describes as 'delinking' from colonial epistemic frameworks. This requires a move away from seeing language as a code to be acquired and toward viewing it as a process of sustaining relationality (Henne-Ochoa et al., 2020). Such a shift allows for the recognition of land-based pedagogy, where learning occurs through active engagement with the environment (Simpson, 2014), and where the natural world functions as an emergent set of teaching materials.

Despite the importance of land-based learning, there is limited research on how nonhuman elements actually function as materials within the interactional flow of Indigenous language reclamation. By integrating Indigenous perspectives of relationality with sociomateriality, we can begin to see the land not as a static backdrop, but as an active participant in the co-construction of knowledge. This study seeks to expand the role of materials in applied linguistics by examining the 'intra-actions' among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth on local forestland. By treating land as an interlocutor, we aim to highlight how relational, consensual engagement with the environment structures language learning.

Accordingly, this study is guided by the following research question: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials?

intros.text:
In recent years, there has been a growing recognition of the role that instructional materials play in shaping classroom discourse and facilitating second language acquisition (Tarone, 2014). Within the field of applied linguistics, materials research has traditionally focused on how textbooks and curated resources mediate learning. However, for those engaged in Indigenous language reclamation, the nature and purpose of 'materials' are fundamentally different. Indigenous scholars and educators have long argued that the reclamation of ancestral languages requires pedagogies and paradigms that diverge from the Western-centric models typically found in TESOL or bilingual education (Hinton, 2011; White, 2006). In these contexts, language learning is not merely the acquisition of a linguistic code, but a process of restoring cultural continuity and sovereignty 'in place.'

Despite the centrality of place to Indigenous ways of knowing, research on the specific materials used in reclamation contexts remains limited. Much of the existing literature continues to operate under a 'language-as-content' paradigm, which treats language as a static object to be mastered and isolates it from its situated use. This approach often overlooks the colonial history of curricular enclosures and fails to account for the creative, bootstrap methods employed by 'teacher-learners' who rely on community knowledge and local resources (Hinton, 2003, 2011). There is a pressing need to delink from these colonial conceptions of language (Mignolo, 2007) and to develop a research framework that recognizes language as a process of sustaining relationality (Henne-Ochoa et al., 2020).

To address this gap, the present study examines the role of the natural world—specifically local forestland—as a dynamic, living learning resource for young bilingual Ojibwe learners. Drawing on Indigenous perspectives of relationality and sociomateriality, we explore how land functions not merely as a backdrop for learning, but as an active interlocutor in the instructional process. We specifically investigate the 'intra-actions' among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth. This study is guided by the following research question: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials?

By analyzing intergenerational interactions 'in the wild,' this research seeks to highlight Ojibwe practices of relational consensual engagement with the environment. In doing so, we aim to expand the scope of materials research to include the natural world as an emergent pedagogical resource, offering an alternative approach to language teaching and learning that prioritizes the restoration of relationships between generations and the land. The remainder of the article is organized as follows: we first detail the theoretical framing of relationality and sociomateriality, followed by the methodology, the analysis of the findings, and a discussion of the implications for Indigenous language reclamation.

To address this gap, the present study examines the role of the natural world—specifically local forestland—as a dynamic, living learning resource for young bilingual Ojibwe learners. Drawing on Indigenous perspectives of relationality and sociomateriality, we explore how land functions not merely as a backdrop for learning, but as an active interlocutor in the instructional process. We specifically investigate the 'intra-actions' among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth. This study is guided by the following research question: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials?

By analyzing intergenerational interactions 'in the wild,' this research seeks to highlight Ojibwe practices of relational consensual engagement with the environment. In doing so, we aim to expand the scope of materials research to include the natural world as an emergent pedagogical resource, offering an alternative approach to language teaching and learning that prioritizes the restoration of relationships between generations and the land.

intros.text:
Ecological approaches to language learning and materials use represent educational settings as complex and dynamic systems by applying relational perspectives from the natural world in the classroom. For young bilingual Ojibwe learners, the natural world (i.e., local, rural, and reservation land) is a significant language learning resource unto itself. In the underrepresented context of Indigenous language reclamation in the Upper Midwest of the United States, local land is central to ways of knowing and being, thus it is also central to learning. This study examines the 'intra-actions' among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth on local forestland. Focusing on the interrelated nature of human and nonhuman elements, we rely on Indigenous perspectives of relationality and sociomateriality to expand and clarify the roles of land in Indigenous language learning for reclamation. This study highlights Ojibwe practices of relational consensual engagement with the environment and has implications for materials use research, as it underscores the significance of the natural world as emergent language learning and teaching materials.

Indigenous language learning for reclamation builds on existing research with LLTMs by placing it in dialogue with scholarship on Indigenous language reclamation and land-based pedagogy. This is important because Indigenous scholars, educators, activists, and allies have long held that learning an Indigenous language for the purpose of revitalization or reclamation requires pedagogies and paradigms that differ from those typically employed in the well-represented contexts of TESOL, bilingual education, or world language education (Hinton, 2011; Jourdain, 2013; White, 2006; Willow, 2010). This distinction is a direct outcome of an attempt to desettle colonial violence and theft, especially in terms of the academy (Pember, 2015; Smith, 2012; Spring, 2016) and points to the significance of self-determination (e.g., Marin & Bang, 2015; Tuck, 2009) and sovereignty (e.g., Engman & Stemper, 2017; Lyons, 2000) in the reclamation movement. In order to 'validate the uniqueness of Native American culture within mainstream American or Canadian culture' (White, 2006, p. 104) scholarship must attend to the 'uniqueness' of language reclamation's learning objectives—(re)learning one's ancestral language for the purpose of restoring linguistic and cultural continuity 'in place.' It also involves conducting research that addresses the differences in Indigenous language-based motives, desired outcomes, distribution of resources, and materials (Hinton, 2011). In this section, we discuss research on language learning materials and language reclamation along with relevant work on land-based pedagogy and paradigms.

In many reclamation contexts, state-of-the-art language-specific materials and curricula are rare, and existing materials can follow Western and colonial paradigms rather than Indigenous ways of knowing and using language. For instance, Meek & Messing's (2007) examination of Kaska and Mexicano-Nahuatl language teaching materials found numerous examples of colonial language framing, which reinforced colonial dominance in Indigenous language spaces. This underresourcing requires Indigenous language teachers to rely on their own community knowledge, local resources, and bootstrap methods to engage students in meaningful language and culture development (Hinton, 2011). Many of the Indigenous language teachers working in modern reclamation contexts are themselves learners of the language they are teaching. These 'teacher-learners' (Hinton, 2003) often have incredibly varied language abilities and pedagogical experiences. Importantly, these teachers are also in possession of expertise and creativity that current research paradigms centered on proficiency fail to track (Engman, 2017). For instance, Head Start teachers in British Columbia relying on the Stó:lo calendar as a literacy material for young learners (Moore & MacDonald, 2013), Ojibwe immersion teachers distributing tickets to students 'caught' speaking the language (Hermes, 2007), and Hawaiian immersion students working in taro patches (Luning & Yamauchi, 2010) demonstrate the range of materials and curriculum development that teacher-learners may include in pedagogies for reclamation. Yet, research on the specific ways in which these materials are deployed and taken up in context is limited, particularly in Indigenous language settings (for a few examples, see Galla, 2016; Meek & Messing, 2007; Moore & MacDonald, 2013).

This gap in our understanding not only points to a need for more usage-based research on materials in Indigenous reclamation settings, but it also highlights a paradigmatic shortcoming in the literature. Materials research that isolates the language from its situated use represents a 'language-as-content' paradigm. Such an approach to language teaching has been shown to be problematic, acting as a barrier for culturally relevant education (Hermes, 2005). Thus we are cautious in our call for more research on materials use in reclamation contexts. The existing approaches, for the most part, tend to ignore the ways in which colonial education frames languages as an object (Richardson, 2011, p. 332) superseding Indigenous cultural knowledge production and creating curricular enclosures in which materials function. We worry that materials research might treat Indigenous languages as 'contained' content to be objectified and mastered. And so we are careful to call for materials research that stretches existing paradigms of language, of learning, and of the classroom.

Recent interdisciplinary work provides examples of alternative ways of understanding these phenomena. In a recent Perspectives column in The Modern Language Journal, numerous longtime Indigenous scholars and allies addressed these very concerns, exploring how ideologies of 'language as a process of sustaining relationality' (HenneOchoa et al., 2020) might look in different local community contexts around the world. The authors in this column centered their commentary around one particular form of learning that is quite common in Indigenous communities: learning by observing and pitching in (LOPI), which comes from Rogoff's work with numerous colleagues in Central America (e.g., Alcalá et al., 2014; Paradise & Rogoff, 2009; Rogoff, 2014; Urrieta, 2015). LOPI sees learning as a process that happens in intergenerational, informal learning contexts. Instead of standardized learning objectives and patented instructional practices, LOPI emphasizes collaboration and context; and it offers an alternative to the decontextualizing functions of classroom-based language learning.

Guerrettaz & Johnston's (2013) study of materials use in one ESL class offers an example of how existing research frames might be stretched within a classroom. Their study of the use of a text in an English-as-a-second-language (ESL) class employed an ecological approach that centered systems of relationships in the 'classroom ecology' to better understand the role(s) that a given material can play in a given space. Though there are few points of resonance between a study of an ESL textbook and Ojibwe youth on a walk in the woods, one reported finding stands out: the occasional tendency among learners in Guerrettaz & Johnston's study to perceive the textbook as a human participant. 'The materials were sometimes portrayed as if they were, or represented, human participants with a will and a purpose' (Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013, p. 785). Guerrettaz and Johnston theorized this behavior as representing how materials can serve as a proxy for their designers as well as for other physically absent parts of the classroom ecology. This raises new questions such as what or who 'counts' as a participant, and what elements of a given ecology are considered 'present' or 'absent.' By shifting the focus to relationships, an ecological approach attends to context and the dynamic interactions among different elements therein.

Importantly, ecological thinking has long been central to Indigenous language researchers as well (e.g., Meek, 2011; Nicholas, 2011; Simpson, 2014; Smith, 2012; Wilson & Kaman¯ a, 2001, 2009). The idea that Indigenous language initiatives are 'never just [emphasis in original] about language' (May, 2006, p. 302) brings us back to the original, restorative purpose of language reclamation. Indigenous language teachers are not working to simply teach their youth and community members an additional 'code' (i.e., language-as-content paradigm). They are aiming for a restoration of fluency in a cultural medium that naturally supports and is supported by other cultural practices and ways of knowing in a complex, living ecology. In this way, language is seen as alive, just as the land-Mother Earth-is also alive. The land can be 'read' as a book may be read, but unlike a book, it is not a static object. Land is a dynamic, living text with its own history of resilience through settler colonial practices of occupation and extraction. Thus, the gap in the literature is more than a scholarly oversight. Reclamation efforts aim to close a sociohistorical and sociocultural tear. Native people working for their language(s) are not only looking for the pieces of code, they are looking for the ways that it is used—how it is put together for different purposes (e.g., problem solving, relating, abstraction) in 'place.' Thus, a study of land-as-materials returns the ecological approach to its unique place in the systems of the natural world.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics, the role of materials in language learning has long been a subject of critical inquiry. Research has traditionally focused on how textbooks, digital resources, and other artifacts function within the classroom ecology to mediate interaction and support acquisition. However, recent scholarship has begun to question the adequacy of these frameworks when applied to contexts of Indigenous language reclamation. For young bilingual Ojibwe learners in the Upper Midwest of the United States, the natural world—specifically local, rural, and reservation land—is not merely a backdrop for instruction but a significant language learning resource unto itself. In these underrepresented contexts, local land is central to ways of knowing and being, and thus it is also central to the learning process. This study examines the 'intra-actions' among land-based materials, an Ojibwe Elder, and immersion school youth on local forestland to expand and clarify the roles of land in Indigenous language learning.

Existing research on language learning materials often operates within a 'language-as-content' paradigm, treating language as an object to be mastered through standardized curricula. While this approach has informed much of the TESOL and bilingual education literature, it often fails to capture the unique pedagogical objectives of Indigenous language reclamation. As scholars such as Hinton (2011) and White (2006) have noted, reclamation requires paradigms that differ from those typically employed in mainstream education, aiming instead to restore linguistic and cultural continuity 'in place.' Furthermore, materials research that isolates language from its situated use can reinforce colonial framings that objectify Indigenous languages. Consequently, there is a pressing need to understand how materials are deployed in reclamation settings that prioritize relationality over proficiency.

Recent interdisciplinary work suggests that ecological approaches to language learning may offer a more robust framework for understanding these dynamics. By applying relational perspectives from the natural world, researchers can view educational settings as complex, dynamic systems. For instance, ecological thinking has long been central to Indigenous language research, where language is seen as alive, much like the land. Yet, despite the growing recognition of the importance of place-based education, little is known about the specific ways in which the natural environment functions as an active interlocutor in Indigenous language learning. While studies have examined the use of textbooks or community resources, the ontological status of the land itself as a dynamic, living text remains underexplored in the literature.

This study addresses this gap by focusing on the interrelated nature of human and nonhuman elements in an intergenerational, land-based context. Relying on Indigenous perspectives of relationality and sociomateriality, we investigate the 'intra-actions' that occur when Ojibwe youth and an Elder engage with the forest. Specifically, we ask: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials? By analyzing these interactions, this study highlights Ojibwe practices of relational consensual engagement with the environment. The findings underscore the significance of the natural world as emergent language learning and teaching materials, offering implications for materials use research and the broader project of sustaining relationality in language education.

intros.text:
Research on language learning and teaching materials has increasingly challenged the assumption that materials are inert supports for instruction. Rather than functioning merely as containers of linguistic content, materials participate in classroom discourse, organize attention, mediate relationships, and shape opportunities for learning (Tarone, 2014; Guerrettaz & Johnston, 2013). Ecological and sociomaterial approaches have been especially useful for showing how language learning emerges through dynamic relations among people, objects, histories, bodies, and places. Yet much of this work has been developed in institutional second-language settings, where the material world is often represented by textbooks, worksheets, screens, or other designed artifacts. Less attention has been paid to contexts in which the most consequential materials for language learning are not manufactured for classrooms at all, but are encountered in place.

This issue is particularly significant for Indigenous language reclamation. Indigenous language learning is not simply the acquisition of an additional code; it is part of broader efforts to restore intergenerational, cultural, political, and land-based continuities disrupted by settler colonialism (Hinton, 2011; Leonard, 2019; McKenzie, 2020). For Ojibwe and many other Indigenous communities, language is inseparable from relations with land, water, plants, animals, ancestors, and future generations. Accordingly, pedagogies for reclamation must be understood in relation to sovereignty, self-determination, and the decolonizing work of delinking from colonial epistemologies that reduce language to an object of mastery (Mignolo, 2007; Smith, 2012). If language is a practice of sustaining relationality, then the places where those relations are made and renewed are not peripheral learning environments; they are central to what is being learned.

Land-based pedagogies offer one response to this challenge. Indigenous scholars have long argued that land is not a backdrop for human activity but a living teacher and participant in knowledge making (Deloria, 1979; Kawagley, 1993; Simpson, 2014). Empirical work on Indigenous families’ and youths’ engagements with the natural world has likewise shown that interaction on land can transform presumed relations between humans and nonhumans, particularly when Indigenous languages mediate attention, naming, observation, and inquiry (Bang & Marin, 2015). Such work unsettles the nature–culture divide that has structured colonial education and invites applied linguistics to reconsider what counts as language, materials, participation, and learning.

The present study examines Ojibwe learner language in interaction on and with naturally occurring materials during an intergenerational walk in local forestland. Focusing on two bilingual Ojibwe youth and an Elder, we analyze how talk, gesture, gaze, movement, touch, and environmental features come together in episodes of “reading land.” We ask: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials? By treating land not only as context or text but as an interlocutor in sociomaterial intra-action, this study contributes to research on materials use, Indigenous language reclamation, and land-based pedagogy.
