intros.text:
Language learning materials are never merely neutral supports for instruction. They organize participation, mediate attention, and help constitute what counts as language, learning, and legitimate knowledge in a pedagogical setting. For this reason, materials have become an important object of inquiry in applied linguistics, particularly in work that examines how classroom discourse and second language acquisition are shaped by the texts, artifacts, and tools through which teaching and learning unfold (Tarone, 2014). Ecological approaches have further expanded this view by treating classrooms as dynamic systems of relations in which materials, teachers, learners, histories, and activities interact in locally consequential ways.

In Indigenous language reclamation, however, the question of materials requires a different starting point. Indigenous languages are not simply additional codes to be acquired; they are tied to sovereignty, intergenerational continuity, place, and ways of knowing that have been disrupted by settler colonialism. Scholars of decolonial and Indigenous language work have therefore called for approaches that delink from colonial assumptions about language as an object separable from land, people, and practice (Mignolo, 2007; Leonard, 2019; McKenzie, 2020). In many reclamation settings, moreover, conventional language-specific materials are limited, and available curricula may reproduce Western categories of knowledge rather than support Indigenous epistemologies. Teachers and learners consequently draw on community expertise, local histories, embodied practice, and the land itself as resources for language learning.

Although research has increasingly recognized the importance of Indigenous pedagogies and land-based learning, less is known about how land functions interactionally as language learning material. Existing studies of materials in use have shown that artifacts can take on complex roles in classroom ecologies, but such work has rarely examined contexts in which the “material” is not a textbook, worksheet, or designed object but a living place. It also remains unclear how language learning can be analyzed when human and nonhuman participants are understood relationally rather than hierarchically. This issue is especially important for Ojibwe language reclamation, where local land is not simply a backdrop for learning but a relative, teacher, text, and source of knowledge.

This study addresses this gap by examining Ojibwe language use during an intergenerational walk on forestland in the Upper Midwest of the United States. Drawing on Indigenous theories of relationality, sociomaterial perspectives, and interactional analysis, we investigate how an Elder, bilingual Ojibwe youth, and the land co-construct linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge. We ask: What kind of linguistic, environmental, and relational knowledge is structured through engagements with land as Ojibwe language learning materials? By analyzing land as an active contributor to meaning making, the study offers an account of materials use that is grounded in Indigenous language reclamation and that reimagines the natural world as emergent, participatory language learning material.

intros.text: WORK IN SECOND LANGUAGE (L2) pragmatics has recently broadened from a focus on learners’ ability to produce particu- lar speech acts to an investigation of learners’ ability to participate in extended discourse (see Félix–Brasdefer, 2019, for a review). Commonly taking an interactional competence (IC) per- spective (Pekarek Doehler, 2019; Young, 2019), studies have investigated a variety of interac- tional features, such as sequential organization (Al–Gahtani & Roever, 2012), preference or- ganization (Al–Gahtani & Roever, 2014, 2018), turn-taking (Cekaite, 2007; Gardner, 2007), repair (Hellermann, 2009, 2011), and topic management (Galaczi, 2014)  However, with few exceptions, English has been the target language of these studies, and no studies have investigated IC in L2 Chinese.  This study aims at filling the research gap by investigating how L2 learners of Mandarin Chinese at different proficiency levels produce the disaffiliative social action of refusal in open role plays, and what the impact of their proficiency is on the sequential organization and formatting of their refusals.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC)—the ability to deploy linguistic, sequential, and prosodic resources to accomplish social actions recognizably and in a recipient-designed manner—has become a central concern in second language (L2) research (Pekarek Doehler, 2019; Young, 2019). A growing body of work has traced how learners develop the ability to organize disaffiliative actions, such as refusals, requests, and disagreements, as dispreferred, showing that lower level learners rely on a limited, 'passe-partout' repertoire while more proficient learners fine-tune their production to context and interlocutor (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2014, 2018; Cekaite, 2007; Galaczi, 2013; Hellermann, 2009, 2011). However, this research has focused overwhelmingly on English, has rarely examined how learners adapt to different initiating actions and interlocutor status, and has largely neglected languages such as Mandarin Chinese. The present study addresses these gaps by analyzing the preference organization of refusals produced by L2 Chinese learners at three proficiency levels and native speakers across three initiating actions (invitation, request, offer) and power settings, combining conversation analysis with an interlanguage pragmatics interpretation (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2018).

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC)—the ability to deploy context-appropriate linguistic, sequential, and prosodic resources to make actions recognizable and to recipient-design talk—has become a central concern in second language (L2) research (Hall & Pekarek Doehler, 2011; Young, 2019). A growing body of cross-sectional work has shown that as proficiency increases, learners move from a limited 'passe-partout' repertoire to more diversified and fine-tuned resources, particularly in organizing disaffiliative actions such as requests, refusals, and disagreements as dispreferred (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2014, 2018; Cekaite, 2007; Galaczi, 2013; Hellermann, 2011; Pekarek Doehler, 2019). However, almost all of this research has targeted English, and little attention has been paid to how learners adapt their actions to interlocutor social status and to different initiating actions. Refusals in Mandarin Chinese, moreover, have been studied mostly from a speech-act rather than an interactional perspective. Addressing these gaps, the present study examines how L2 Chinese learners at three proficiency levels, compared to native speakers, format and organize refusals to invitations, requests, and offers across varying power settings.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC) refers to the ability of L2 speakers to collaboratively achieve intersubjectivity through context-dependent discursive practices (Young, 2019). A key dimension of IC is preference organization, where disaffiliative actions, such as refusals, are typically organized as 'dispreferred' to maintain social harmony (Pekarek Doehler, 2019). Research suggests that L2 learners often evolve from using 'passe-partout' methods toward more diverse and fine-tuned interactional tools as their proficiency increases (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2018). However, most IC research has focused on English, leaving a gap in our understanding of other target languages. While previous studies on Mandarin Chinese refusals have primarily adopted a speech-act perspective, few have examined the sequential organization of these actions in interaction. The present study addresses this gap by investigating how L2 Mandarin learners at different proficiency levels organize refusals in response to invitations, requests, and offers, and whether they adapt their responses based on the social status of the interlocutor.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC) is central to successful second language (L2) communication, as it enables speakers to co-construct meaning through context-appropriate linguistic and sequential resources (Hall & Pekarek Doehler, 2011; Young, 2019). A key component of IC is preference organization, where disaffiliative actions, such as refusals, are typically marked as dispreferred to maintain social harmony (Schegloff, 2007). While research has demonstrated that L2 learners' ability to organize dispreferred responses develops with proficiency (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2018; Pekarek Doehler & Pochon-Berger, 2011), most studies have focused on English or utilized a single initiating action. Consequently, little is known about how L2 Mandarin learners adapt their refusals to diverse initiating actions and social statuses. This study addresses this gap by investigating the preference organization of refusals across three proficiency levels in L2 Mandarin. Specifically, it examines how learners format refusals in response to invitations, requests, and offers, and whether they fine-tune these responses based on the interlocutor's social power.

intros.text: Research on second language (L2) interactional competence (IC) has increasingly shifted from non-interactive data to examining how learners manage social actions in real-time discourse. Drawing on conversation analysis (CA), scholars argue that IC involves the ability to deploy context-appropriate linguistic and sequential resources to achieve intersubjectivity (Hall & Pekarek Doehler, 2011; Young, 2019). A key area of investigation is preference organization, where disaffiliative actions like refusals are typically delayed and mitigated to maintain social harmony (Schegloff, 2007). While studies on L2 requests and refusals in English and Arabic have documented developmental trajectories linked to proficiency (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2014, 2018), research on L2 Mandarin remains limited. Existing work on Chinese refusals often relies on speech-act perspectives or cross-cultural comparisons rather than interactional analysis (Wang, 2001; Tang, 2004). Consequently, little is known about how L2 Chinese learners develop the ability to organize refusals as dispreferred or adapt them to varying social contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating preference organization in L2 Mandarin refusals across proficiency levels, examining both sequential formatting and contextual sensitivity.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC) has emerged as a vital construct in second language (L2) research, shifting focus from individual linguistic knowledge to the collaborative management of social actions. Informed by conversation analysis, IC emphasizes how learners deploy sequential and linguistic resources to maintain intersubjectivity and social harmony (Hall & Pekarek Doehler, 2011; Young, 2019). A key component of IC is preference organization, where disaffiliative actions, such as refusals, are typically delayed and mitigated to preserve relationships (Schegloff, 2007). While research has established that L2 learners develop more sophisticated dispreference markers with increasing proficiency (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2018; Pekarek Doehler, 2019), most studies focus on English or Arabic. Furthermore, existing work on L2 Chinese refusals often relies on speech-act perspectives rather than interactional analysis (Wang, 2001; Tang, 2004). Consequently, little is known about how learners of Mandarin Chinese organize refusals as dispreferred actions across proficiency levels or how they fine-tune these responses to specific initiating actions and social contexts. This study addresses these gaps by investigating the preference organization of refusals in L2 Mandarin. Using a cross-sectional design, we analyze how learners at three proficiency levels and native speakers format refusals in response to invitations, requests, and offers. We examine whether learners move from a 'passe-partout' approach to increased contextual sensitivity as their proficiency develops.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC) has become central to understanding how second language (L2) users accomplish social actions in real time, beyond producing grammatically accurate utterances. Research in this tradition shows that developing learners gradually expand the sequential, linguistic, and pragmatic resources through which they manage turn-taking, repair, alignment, and affiliation (Cekaite, 2007; Hellermann, 2011; Pekarek Doehler, 2019; Young, 2019). One important locus of IC is preference organization: speakers normally design disaffiliative actions such as refusals, disagreements, and rejections as delayed, mitigated, and accountable rather than immediate and direct. Prior studies indicate that lower-proficiency learners often rely on direct formats or limited routines, whereas more advanced learners increasingly use preliminaries, accounts, particles, and other resources to mark dispreference (Hellermann, 2009; Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2014; Félix-Brasdefer, 2019). However, most evidence comes from English or a small set of additional target languages, and little is known about how learners of Mandarin Chinese organize refusals interactionally. This study addresses that gap by examining how L2 Mandarin learners at different proficiency levels and native speakers format refusals and adapt them to initiating actions and social relationships.

intros.text: Interactional competence (IC) has become central to understanding how second language users accomplish social action in talk, not merely through grammatical resources but through sequentially situated practices for maintaining intersubjectivity and social affiliation (Pekarek Doehler, 2019; Young, 2019). One important site for such competence is preference organization: when speakers perform disaffiliative actions such as refusals, they typically delay, mitigate, account for, or otherwise format them as dispreferred. Prior L2 research has shown that learners’ ability to deploy these resources develops with proficiency, with lower-level learners often producing more direct responses and higher-level learners using a wider range of sequential and linguistic devices (Al-Gahtani & Roever, 2011, 2014; Cekaite, 2007; Hellermann, 2009). However, interactional studies of refusals remain heavily concentrated on English and a small number of other languages, while L2 Mandarin Chinese refusals have largely been examined through speech-act or cross-cultural comparisons rather than sequential analysis. It also remains unclear how learners adapt refusals to different initiating actions and status relations. This study therefore investigates how learners of Mandarin at three proficiency levels, together with native speakers, organize refusals to invitations, requests, and offers in role-play interaction.

intros.text: IT HAS BEEN SUGGESTED THAT IDENTITY IS “central to the beliefs, assumptions, values and practices that guide teacher actions both inside and outside the classroom” (Farrell, 2011, p. 55).  Interest in language teacher identity (LTI) is increasing (Barkhuizen, 2017a, 2017b), evidenced by a growing body of literature, including recent special issues in Modern Language Journal (2017) and TESOL Quarterly (2016), which highlight the importance of understanding the complex ways language teachers navigate different identities in classrooms, schools, and communities.  How ever, despite the “profound embeddedness of LTI within the research, teaching, and policy practices of (multi)lingual professionals” (Varghese et al., 2016, p. 545), the identities of experienced inservice language teachers are seldom researched (Edwards & Burns, 2016; Eren–Bilgen & Richards, 2015; Farrell, 2011).  Almost all LTI research focuses on pre-service teachers, looking at, for example, identity shifts from student to practicing teacher (e.g., Barkhuizen, 2016) or the development of teacher identities during teacher education courses (e.g., Riordan & Farr, 2015; Urzúa & Vásquez, 2008).  If understanding teaching and learning involves understanding teacher identities (Varghese et al., 2005), it is important to investigate the identities of those who make up most of the profession, that is, experienced working teachers. Equally important—and also neglected in LTI research—are the supervisors who play an influential role in the evaluation and development of these teachers.  This article therefore examines the identities constructed by in-service language teachers and a supervisor during a high-stakes event: the post-observation feedback meeting.

intros.text:
Language teacher identity (LTI) has become a vibrant field of inquiry, moving beyond static, essentialist accounts toward views of identity as multiple, dynamic, and discursively co-constructed in situated social practice (Varghese et al., 2005). Much of this work has explored how teachers narrate, imagine, and negotiate who they are across time and context (Barkhuizen, 2016, 2017), often through reflective practice and interviews (Farrell, 2011). Yet two important gaps remain. First, LTI research has concentrated overwhelmingly on pre-service teachers, leaving the identities of experienced, in-service teachers comparatively under-explored (Bilgen & Richards, 2014). Second, although the concept of 'discourse' is central to identity theory, empirical studies of situated, work-based talk are scarce, and researchers rarely examine identity as it unfolds moment by moment in institutional interaction.

One site where teachers routinely talk about themselves and their practice is the post-observation feedback meeting. Previous studies of feedback discourse suggest that supervisors typically enact powerful, authoritative identities, and the few studies addressing identity in feedback have focused on novice teachers (Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009; Riordan & Farr, 2014). Little is known about how experienced teachers and their supervisors negotiate identities in feedback talk, or how these identities shape the ambiguous purpose of feedback, poised between evaluation and development.

This article addresses these gaps by examining dyadic post-observation feedback meetings between experienced in-service English teachers and a supervisor in a Gulf-state tertiary institution. Through microanalysis of situated interaction, it asks: which identities do teachers and their supervisor make relevant during feedback talk, and what does this identity negotiation reveal about the role of feedback?

intros.text:
In recent decades, understandings of identity have shifted from a fixed, essentialist view toward a conception of identity as fluid, multiple, and discursively constituted (Varghese et al., 2005). Within language teacher identity (LTI) research, teacher identity is understood to be constructed, maintained, and negotiated to a significant extent through talk (Varghese et al., 2005; Farrell, 2011). One important, yet under-explored, site of such talk is the post-observation feedback meeting, one of the rare occasions on which teachers speak about themselves and their practice.

Although LTI has attracted growing attention, research has concentrated overwhelmingly on pre-service contexts. The few studies that explicitly examine language teacher identity in feedback talk (Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009; Riordan & Farr, 2014) all involve novice teachers, and they tend to isolate speech acts rather than trace the co-constructed, turn-by-turn nature of identity work. Consequently, very little is known about the roles, relationships, and identities negotiated between in-service teachers and their supervisors. Moreover, LTI researchers rarely engage with situated examples of naturally occurring institutional interaction, despite the insights such analysis offers.

This article addresses these gaps. Drawing on audio-recorded dyadic feedback meetings between experienced English language teachers and a supervisor in a Gulf-state tertiary institution, it uses microanalysis to examine identities of experience and power as they emerge in real-life work-based talk. The study asks which identities experienced teachers and their supervisor make relevant during feedback, and what identity negotiation reveals about the role of feedback. In doing so, it seeks to redirect attention toward in-service contexts and situated institutional interaction.

intros.text:
Language teacher identity has become a central focus of research in teacher education and professional development, moving from essentialist views toward a poststructuralist understanding of identity as contingent and discursively constituted (Varghese et al., 2005). While substantial work has explored how teachers imagine their roles (Barkhuizen, 2016) or negotiate their professional identities through narrative and reflective practice (Edwards & Burns, 2016; Farrell, 2011), much of this research has focused on pre-service teachers or the broader trajectories of teacher development (Bilgen & Richards, 2014). Consequently, there is a scarcity of research investigating the situated, work-based interaction of in-service teachers, particularly within high-stakes institutional contexts.

One critical yet under-researched site of identity negotiation is the post-observation feedback meeting. These encounters are often fraught with tension, balancing the dual and sometimes conflicting goals of teacher development and institutional evaluation. While previous studies in pre-service contexts have highlighted how teacher educators often project authoritative identities (Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009), little is known about how experienced in-service teachers and their supervisors co-construct identities of power and experience during these meetings. This article seeks to fill this gap by analyzing dyadic feedback talk in a tertiary institution in a Gulf state. By employing microanalysis of real-life discourse, the study examines which identities are made relevant and what this negotiation reveals about the actual role of feedback. Specifically, it investigates how the prioritisation of evaluative identities may compromise the institutional aim of fostering teacher development.

intros.text:
Language teacher identity has emerged as a central subject of interest within teacher education and development research (Varghese et al., 2005). Recent scholarship has increasingly moved toward viewing identity not as a fixed attribute, but as a contingent, multiple, and discursively constituted phenomenon (Barkhuizen, 2016; Barkhuizen, 2017). While significant attention has been paid to how teachers negotiate their professional roles through narratives (Riordan & Farr, 2014) or within specific ecological systems (Edwards & Burns, 2016), much of this work has focused on pre-service teachers or imagined identities. Consequently, there remains a scarcity of research investigating the identity negotiation of in-service teachers within situated, work-based interactions (Gray & Morton, 2018).

One critical yet understudied site of such interaction is the post-observation feedback meeting. Although these meetings are ostensibly designed for both evaluation and professional development (Borg, 2018), they are often experienced as high-stakes events that can influence contract renewal and career advancement. To date, few studies have empirically explored these meetings as spaces for identity negotiation, particularly in in-service contexts where power dynamics between experienced teachers and supervisors may be complex.

This article addresses this gap by examining the identities claimed and negotiated by experienced language teachers and their supervisor during dyadic feedback meetings in a Gulf-state tertiary institution. Specifically, the study seeks to identify which identities are made relevant during these interactions and what this negotiation reveals about the actual role of feedback. Through microanalysis of real-life talk, the study demonstrates how identities of power and experience are co-constructed and how these dynamics shape the evaluative nature of the feedback process.

intros.text: The rise of poststructuralist theories of language and meaning has shifted the understanding of identity from a core, essentialist view to one that is contingent, multiple, and discursively constituted (Benwell & Stokoe, 2006; Bucholtz & Hall, 2005). This article aligns with this current view, seeing identity as active and performative (Butler, 1990), something that a person does in situated social practices (Antaki & Widdicombe, 1998; Roberts & Sarangi, 1999). Talk is a primary means of identity construction, where people articulate, realize, explore, construct, verify, and challenge identities (Aneja, 2016; Varghese et al., 2005). One significant site for this negotiation is the post-observation feedback meeting. While previous research has highlighted the potential benefits of such meetings as loci for 'help-giving and receiving' (Wajnryb, 1994), they are often described as 'difficult discoursal events' (Copland, 2008) due to their ambiguous purpose. Feedback is generally agreed to serve two reasons: evaluation and development (Borg, 2018; Copland & Donaghue, 2019). However, for in-service teachers, these meetings are often realized as evaluative events with high-stakes consequences for employment and career advancement (Howard, 2016; OECD, 2013b). Research on teacher identity in feedback talk has focused almost exclusively on pre-service contexts (Urzúa & Vásquez, 2008; Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009; Riordan & Farr, 2015). Little is known about identity negotiation between in-service teachers and supervisors within work-based interaction (Gray & Morton, 2018). This article aims to fill this gap by examining identities claimed and negotiated by experienced teachers and a supervisor during post-observation feedback meetings in a Gulf state tertiary institution. By using microanalysis of discourse excerpts, this study explores how identities of power and experience are constructed and how they shape the role of feedback.

intros.text: Language teacher identity has emerged as a vital area of inquiry, shifting from essentialist views toward understanding identity as contingent, multiple, and discursively constituted (Varghese et al., 2005). In this dynamic framework, identity is not merely a fixed psychological attribute but is actively performed and negotiated through situated social practices, particularly talk (Antaki & Widdicombe, 1998; Roberts & Sarangi, 1999). While teacher identity is often explored through classroom practices or personal narratives (Barkhuizen, 2016; Farrell, 2011), the post-observation feedback meeting represents a critical, yet under-researched, site where professional identities are constructed and negotiated. These meetings serve as rare opportunities for teachers to articulate their professional selves in relation to institutional expectations (Urzúa & Vásquez, 2008). However, previous research has predominantly focused on pre-service contexts, often highlighting the tension between evaluative and developmental goals (Copland, 2008; Farr, 2011). Studies on novice teachers suggest that feedback talk is a primary means for identity construction, yet little is known about how experienced in-service teachers navigate these interactions (Riordan & Farr, 2014). Furthermore, existing literature rarely examines the reciprocal nature of identity negotiation between supervisors and teachers in high-stakes, work-based settings. This study addresses this gap by analyzing dyadic post-observation feedback meetings between experienced English language teachers and a supervisor in a Gulf state tertiary institution. Through microanalysis of discourse excerpts, this research investigates how identities of power and experience are co-constructed and how these negotiated identities shape the role and outcome of feedback. By focusing on in-service contexts, this article aims to reveal the fluid nature of institutional power and its implications for teacher development.

intros.text:
Language teacher identity (LTI) has become a central concern in applied linguistics because teachers’ professional lives cannot be understood only through knowledge, beliefs, or skills; they are also shaped by how teachers position themselves and are positioned by others in particular social and institutional contexts (Varghese et al., 2005). Recent LTI research has shown that identities are multiple, situated, and negotiated over time, whether through narratives of imagined futures (Barkhuizen, 2016), accounts of socially inclusive tutoring (Barkhuizen, 2017), teacher-researcher work (Edwards & Burns, 2016), or reflective exploration of experienced teachers’ professional roles (Farrell, 2011). Such studies have significantly advanced understandings of who language teachers are and become, but much of the field continues to rely on interview, narrative, and reflective data rather than close analysis of naturally occurring professional interaction.

Post-observation feedback meetings offer a particularly important site for investigating identity in action. They are institutional encounters in which teachers and supervisors talk explicitly about teaching, competence, standards, and professional improvement. Yet they are also potentially high-stakes events, especially for in-service teachers whose appraisals may affect contract renewal, promotion, or continued employment. Although feedback is often framed as developmental, it is frequently experienced as evaluative, and this tension is likely to shape the identities participants make relevant during talk.

Existing research on feedback discourse has focused mainly on pre-service teachers and teacher educators, including studies of novice teacher identity construction in mentoring meetings (Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009; Riordan & Farr, 2014). Far less is known about how experienced in-service teachers and supervisors negotiate identities during workplace feedback. This study addresses that gap by examining post-observation feedback meetings in a tertiary EFL institution in a Gulf state, focusing on how identities of experience and power are discursively constructed, challenged, and ratified, and what these negotiations reveal about the role of feedback in the institution.

intros.text:
Language teacher identity (LTI) has become an important area of inquiry in applied linguistics because it offers a way to understand how teachers make sense of themselves, their work, and their professional worlds. Rather than treating identity as stable or internal, much recent research views it as multiple, situated, and negotiated through social interaction and discourse (Varghese et al., 2005). Studies have examined, for example, imagined identities over time (Barkhuizen, 2016), social inclusion identities in tutoring (Barkhuizen, 2017), teacher–researcher identity negotiation (Edwards & Burns, 2016), and the professional role identities of experienced ESL teachers (Farrell, 2011). This work has shown that identity is closely connected to teachers’ histories, institutional contexts, relationships, and opportunities for professional development.

One institutional site where teacher identities may be especially consequential is the post-observation feedback meeting. These meetings are intended to support teacher learning, but they are also often tied to evaluation, appraisal, and employment decisions. Feedback talk therefore brings together issues of expertise, authority, accountability, and professional worth. Previous studies of feedback discourse have shown how novice teachers construct identities through reported speech, reported mental states, and narratives in mentoring or supervisory meetings (Vásquez & Urzúa, 2009; Riordan & Farr, 2014). However, this research has focused largely on preservice or novice teachers. Much less is known about how experienced in-service language teachers and supervisors negotiate identities in naturally occurring workplace feedback talk, particularly when feedback is both developmental and evaluative.

This article addresses that gap by examining identities constructed and negotiated during dyadic post-observation feedback meetings between experienced English language teachers and a supervisor in a tertiary institution in a Gulf state. Using microanalysis of recorded interaction, it focuses on identities of experience and power and asks: Which identities do experienced language teachers and their supervisor make relevant during feedback talk, and what does this identity negotiation reveal about the role of feedback?

These  adults need instruction that differs from a standard second language class: they need instruction in both the new language and,  simultaneously, emergent print literacy instruction. In the U.S, such ESL classes are often referred to as “ESL Literacy”, “Pre-Beginning  ESL”, or even “Level 0 ESL”, and are found in a variety of contexts: adult schools, community college non-credit programs, library  literacy programs, non-profits, community centers, refugee resettlement programs, and churches. Correspondingly, instructors of these students have reported feeling greatly unprepared to teach them, as the nuanced pedagogical  approaches in teaching first-time print literacy instruction in tandem with the new language are generally not discussed in teacher  training programs (Carter, 2020; Vinogradov & Liden, 2009; Young-Scholten, Peyton, Sosinski, & Cabeza, 2015)  Fortunately, grassroots materials for teaching L2 adult students with emergent print literacy have been developed over the decades,  and many of these can be found online. While some research has been conducted on teaching initial reading to these learners, research on the teaching of  writing is largely missing, especially at the very early stages of writing, like copying. intros.text:
Worldwide, more than 90 million U.S. adults lack adequate literacy, and vast numbers of immigrant adults arrive in new countries having had little or no opportunity for formal schooling in their first language (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012; UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2020). For these learners, becoming literate is not merely a matter of transferring existing print skills to a new script; rather, they must develop print literacy for the very first time, often while simultaneously acquiring an entirely new language. Despite the growing presence of such learners in publicly funded adult education classrooms, they remain markedly underrepresented in second language acquisition (SLA) research. As Bigelow and Tarone (2004) have argued, who we choose to study fundamentally shapes what we come to know about second language learning, and the field's reliance on easy-to-recruit, well-schooled participants has left the needs of socially excluded, low-educated adult learners largely unaddressed (Young-Scholten, 2013).

The subfield of Low-Educated Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA) has emerged to fill this gap, generating a body of practice-oriented scholarship focused on instruction, teacher preparation, and the distinctive demands facing adults with emergent print literacy (Strube, 2009; Vinogradov, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015). Much of this work has concentrated on oral skills, reading, and the professional knowledge instructors require to teach this population effectively (Carter, 2020). Comparatively little attention, however, has been paid to the earliest stages of writing development—the point at which adults must learn to hold a writing implement, form recognizable shapes, and copy text before they can compose independently.

This omission is significant. Writing, even in its most rudimentary form of copying, entails a remarkable convergence of motor, perceptual, orthographic, semiotic, and linguistic skills. Whereas L1 children typically spend years engaged in play writing and shape formation before entering formal schooling, adults new to print literacy often have had no such preparatory experience. Moreover, unlike children, these adults frequently cannot map meaning onto the words they are copying, since they are simultaneously acquiring the L2 lexicon in which those words are written. The cognitive burden entailed in what may appear to be a simple copying task is therefore considerable, and current language content standards—which reduce beginning writing to targets such as tracing or printing letters—fail to capture this complexity.

Given that ethical treatment of L2 writers requires understanding learners, placing them in suitable contexts, and providing appropriate instruction (Silva, 1997; Carter & J. M, 2020), it is essential to develop a clearer picture of how adult emergent print literacy actually unfolds. Drawing on the well-developed literature on children's orthographic and motor development as a lens, this ethnographically situated study documents four adult students, each with 0–1 year of prior formal education, as they copied classroom text over a five-month period at a Northern California adult school. Specifically, it asks: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability—copying—in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy?

intros.text:
A high level of literacy in both print and digital media is a prerequisite for participating in nearly every aspect of contemporary life, including securing employment, supporting a family, accessing healthcare, and engaging in civic activities (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012). Despite this centrality, tens of millions of adults worldwide lack adequate literacy skills, and among them are second language (L2) learners who arrive in host countries with little or no experience with formal schooling in any language (UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2020). These learners, often referred to within the field of Low-Educated Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA), face a formidable dual challenge: they must acquire a new spoken language while simultaneously developing first-time print literacy in an alphabetic writing system that may be entirely foreign to them.

Research on this population has grown steadily as immigration by adults with limited native-language schooling has increased (Young-Scholten, 2013). Scholars have documented the distinctive needs of these learners and the ways in which their literacy level shapes the trajectory of their second language acquisition (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004). A body of practitioner-oriented scholarship has likewise examined the oral skills practices, instructor training, and pedagogical knowledge required to teach this group effectively (Strube, 2009; Vinogradov, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015; Carter, 2020). Much of this work rightly cautions that we cannot hold L2 learners to the same expectations as first-language writers, nor can we assume that adults new to print literacy will follow the same path as their more educated L2 peers (Carter & J. M, 2020).

Yet, while considerable attention has been paid to oral language development and to the sociopolitical circumstances of these learners, far less is known about the earliest, most fundamental stages of their writing development. The bulk of what we understand about emergent writing derives from research on first-language children, whose acquisition of orthographic features, motor skills, and perceptual-motor integration has been mapped in some detail. Whether adults acquiring print literacy for the first time in an L2 progress along comparable trajectories remains largely unexplored. Similarly, the specific demands of copying—a foundational precursor to autonomous writing—have received little empirical scrutiny in adult L2 contexts, despite copying being one of the few writing activities accessible to learners who cannot yet read or spell. It therefore remains unclear how these learners interact with classroom text at a purely orthographic level, what starting points they bring, and how their development compares with what is known about children's emergent writing.

Addressing this gap, the present study offers a close, interactional analysis of the classroom writing of four adult L2 learners with emergent print literacy at a Northern California adult school, each reporting between zero and three years of formal L1 schooling. Over a five-month period, the researcher documented instances of copying to illuminate the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability. Specifically, the study asks: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability, copying, in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy? In doing so, the study aims to deepen our understanding of these learners' developmental process and to inform more responsive classroom practice.

intros.text:
In the field of second language acquisition (SLA), a significant portion of research has historically relied on university-educated participants, often overlooking the needs of socially excluded adult learners (Young-Scholten, 2013). This gap is particularly acute for immigrants with little to no formal schooling in their native language, who must navigate the daunting challenge of acquiring L2 proficiency while simultaneously developing basic print literacy. As Lesgold and Welch-Ross (2012) emphasize, proficient literacy in print and digital media is essential for negotiating the civic, economic, and health-related demands of contemporary life. For those entering the classroom with emergent print literacy, the process of learning to write is not merely a linguistic hurdle but a complex cognitive and physiological undertaking. 

Despite the growing population of low-educated adult second language learners, there remains a dearth of empirical research regarding the earliest stages of their writing development. This lack of specialized knowledge often leaves instructors without a research-based foundation to guide their pedagogy (Young-Scholten, 2013; Vinogradov, 2009). While some instructors have shared their perceptions and praxis in teaching emergent readers (Carter, 2020), and others have highlighted the specific skills they feel they need to support this population (Young-Scholten, 2015), there is a pressing need for interactional analyses that document how these learners actually engage with text. Furthermore, the role of literacy levels in SLA remains a critical variable that can fundamentally alter the trajectory of language acquisition (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004), yet the specific developmental markers of orthographic acquisition in adults are under-studied.

Many of the challenges faced by these learners are distinct from those of literate L2 writers, for whom the focus is often on academic composition or linguistic nuance (Carter, 2020). For the emergent adult writer, the act of copying—often viewed as a simple mechanical task—is actually a high-stakes cognitive process involving the integration of motor skills, perceptual-motor coordination, and an understanding of semiotic norms. If these learners are not provided with appropriate, research-informed instruction tailored to their specific developmental stage, they may struggle to bridge the gap between oral proficiency and written communication (Strube, 2009).

Building on the need to better understand the unique complexities of this population, the present study utilizes an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples to explore the initial stages of orthographic development. Specifically, the study focuses on the process of copying among four adult L2 learners with emergent print literacy in a Northern California adult school. The primary aim is to answer the following research question: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability, copying, in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy?

intros.text:
In the 21st century, a high level of literacy in both print and digital media is essential for navigating basic aspects of civic participation, health, and economic competitiveness (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012). Within the field of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), however, there has been a noted shift toward studying middle-class university students, which has inadvertently diminished the scholarly attention paid to socially excluded adult L2 learners (Young-Scholten, 2013). Specifically, there is a growing population of adult immigrants with little to no formal schooling in their first language (L1) who face immense challenges in acquiring the linguistic and literacy skills necessary to integrate into their new communities (Young-Scholten, 2013). The role of literacy levels in SLA is critical, as the backgrounds of the learners we study fundamentally determine the nature of the knowledge we produce (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004).

Despite the social urgency of supporting these learners, those who teach low-educated adult second language and literacy acquisition (LESLLA) students often find themselves with very little empirical SLA research to guide their praxis (Young-Scholten, 2013). While there is an increasing awareness of the need for principled training for LESLLA instructors (Vinogradov, 2009) and a need to identify the specific knowledge and skills teachers require to be effective (Young-Scholten, 2015), research into the actual developmental processes of emergent print literacy in adults remains sparse. Much of the existing pedagogical focus has remained on oral skills practices (Strube, 2009) or general instructor perceptions (Carter, 2020), leaving the cognitive and physiological trajectories of first-time adult writers under-examined. Consequently, there is a significant gap in our understanding of how adults, who lack L1 literacy, navigate the earliest stages of written production in an L2 context.

Building on the need for more nuanced research into the experiences of emergent readers and writers, this study provides insight into the complexity of writing development among adult L2 learners. Specifically, the research aims to answer the following question: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability, copying, in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy? By documenting the process of copying classroom text over a five-month period, this study seeks to determine whether adult emergent literacy follows a trajectory similar to that of L1 children, particularly regarding motor skill development and perceptual-motor integration. The findings may offer critical implications for practitioners by highlighting the cognitive demands of seemingly simple copying tasks and challenging assumptions about the baseline skills of incoming students. The remainder of the article is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the literature on emergent literacy in children and adults; Section 3 describes the ethnographic methodology; Section 4 presents the findings; and Section 5 discusses the pedagogical and policy implications.

intros.text:
The intersection of second language acquisition (SLA) and literacy development presents a complex landscape, particularly for adult learners who lack formal education in their first language (L1). While the field of SLA has long focused on linguistic competence, the specific needs of Low-Educated Adult Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA) learners have often been marginalized (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004; Young-Scholten, 2013). These learners face a unique "double hurdle": they must simultaneously acquire the linguistic code of a new language while navigating the cognitive and motor demands of alphabetic print literacy for the first time (Young-Scholten, 2015). Despite the growing number of such immigrants in global communities, research into their specific developmental trajectories remains scarce compared to studies on L1 children or literate L2 adults (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012). 

Current literature highlights the critical role of literacy in economic and social participation, yet instructional practices often fail to address the foundational skills required by this population (Carter, 2020; Strube, 2009). Teachers frequently lack the specialized knowledge to support learners who are struggling not only with English vocabulary but also with the basic mechanics of writing, such as letter formation and orthographic norms (Vinogradov, 2009). Consequently, practitioners may inadvertently make assumptions about incoming students' skills, overlooking the myriad of novel cognitive demands entailed in seemingly simple tasks like copying text. As noted in the CCCC statement on second-language writing, a deeper understanding of the challenges facing ESL students is essential for equitable instruction (Carter & J. M, 2020).

Theoretical frameworks regarding emergent literacy are well-established in the context of L1 child development, outlining stages of motor skill acquisition and orthographic awareness. However, it remains unclear whether adults new to print literacy follow a similar developmental trajectory. Do they rely on the same perceptual-motor integration processes as children, or does their adult cognition alter the acquisition of these fundamental skills? Furthermore, the interaction between emerging motor skills and the acquisition of a new linguistic script adds a layer of complexity that distinguishes adult L2 learners from their child L1 counterparts. 

This study addresses these gaps by examining the developmental process of copying skills in adult L2 English learners with emergent print literacy. Situated in a Northern California adult school, the research documents the writing practices of four adult students with 0–1 year of formal L1 education over a five-month period. By focusing on the earliest stages of orthographic development, this inquiry seeks to reveal how these learners navigate the physical and cognitive demands of writing. Specifically, the study asks: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability, copying, in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy? The findings aim to inform pedagogical practices and policy, ensuring that instruction is responsive to the diverse starting points and cognitive loads experienced by this often-overlooked population.

intros.text:
The acquisition of print literacy in adulthood, particularly within a second language (L2) context, represents a critical yet frequently overlooked domain in applied linguistics and English language teaching. For millions of adult immigrants and refugees, the ability to read and write in a new language is not merely an academic exercise but a vital prerequisite for social inclusion, economic participation, and civic engagement (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012; Young-Scholten, 2013). Despite the growing demographic of low-educated adult learners in global migration streams, research attention has disproportionately focused on literate L2 adults or children acquiring literacy in their first language (L1). Consequently, the specific developmental trajectories of adults who are simultaneously learning a new language and a new script remain poorly understood (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004; Vinogradov, 2009).

While the literature on L1 emergent literacy provides robust frameworks for understanding how children acquire writing skills, its application to adult L2 learners is often assumed rather than empirically tested. Studies of child development suggest that writing emerges through a complex interplay of motor skill acquisition, visual-perceptual integration, and the gradual internalization of orthographic norms (Puranik & Lonigan, 2011). However, the cognitive and physiological demands placed on adults who lack prior schooling are distinct. These learners must navigate the dual burden of acquiring L2 vocabulary and orthographic systems while simultaneously developing the fine motor and perceptual-motor skills required for transcription (Greenberg, 1998). Existing research on Low-Educated Adult Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA) has begun to address these challenges, yet it often prioritizes oral proficiency or broad pedagogical strategies over the granular mechanics of early writing development (Strube, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015).

A significant gap exists in our understanding of the earliest stages of this development, specifically the act of copying. Copying is often dismissed as a mechanical task, yet for an adult with emergent literacy, it entails substantial cognitive load involving shape formation, directionality, and semiotic understanding of the written page (e.g., margins, lines, orientation). Current instructional practices frequently assume that learners possess a baseline of orthographic knowledge, potentially overlooking the diverse starting points and hidden complexities inherent in first-time writing (Carter, 2020). Furthermore, the extent to which adult learners replicate the developmental trajectories observed in L1 children, such as the progression of shape production, remains unclear.

To address these gaps, this study investigates the developmental process of copying skills in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy. Situated in a Northern California adult school, the research documents the written interactions of four adult students with zero to one year of formal L1 education over a five-month period. By analyzing instances of classroom copying through an interactional lens, this study aims to answer the following question: What can an analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability and copying in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy? The findings suggest that, similar to children, these adults progress through a trajectory of written shape production reliant on motor and perceptual-motor integration. However, the variance in starting points highlights the necessity for practitioners to avoid assumptions regarding incoming skills and to recognize the myriad of novel cognitive demands entailed even within simple copying tasks.

intros.text:
Adult immigrants and refugees who enter second language classrooms with little or no prior schooling are often asked to acquire a new spoken language, a new writing system, and new classroom practices at the same time. This population, frequently discussed in the LESLLA literature as adults with low education and emergent second language literacy, remains underrepresented in second language acquisition and L2 writing research, despite the social and educational significance of their learning needs (Bigelow & Tarone, 2004; Young-Scholten, 2013). As Young-Scholten (2013) argues, much SLA research has relied on schooled and relatively privileged participants, leaving teachers of low-educated adult immigrants with limited empirical guidance for understanding how language and literacy develop when print itself is new. At the same time, adult literacy is central to participation in employment, schooling, health care, civic life, and family support, and yet research-based knowledge about effective adult literacy instruction remains insufficiently developed (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012; UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2020). 

The instructional challenges in these classrooms are substantial. Teachers must support oral English development while also introducing learners to alphabetic print, classroom routines, and the semiotic conventions embedded in worksheets, notebooks, forms, and other everyday texts. Studies and practitioner-focused work in LESLLA contexts have therefore emphasized the need for specialized teacher knowledge and principled training, rather than assuming that general ESL methods are sufficient for learners who are encountering print literacy for the first time (Strube, 2009; Vinogradov, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015). Recent work on adult emergent readers likewise suggests that teachers’ perceptions and practices are shaped by the complexity of teaching adults who may still be developing foundational print concepts alongside basic L2 proficiency (Carter, 2020). Yet, comparatively little is known about the earliest visible signs of writing development in such learners, particularly before they are able to compose independently in English.

One classroom activity that can appear deceptively simple is copying. In many beginning ESL literacy classes, learners copy letters, words, dates, dialogues, and short sentences from the board or from worksheets. For fully literate adults, copying may seem mechanical; for adults with emergent print literacy, however, it may require coordination of fine motor control, visual attention, memory, directionality, letter-shape recognition, spacing, line use, and other culturally specific conventions of written text. Because these learners are also developing English vocabulary and may not understand the words they are asked to reproduce, copying can involve a heavy cognitive burden. Understanding how adults at the earliest stages of literacy interact with classroom text can therefore reveal developmental processes that are otherwise obscured when research focuses primarily on reading outcomes, spelling, or later stages of writing.

This study examines copying as an initial component of writing development among four adult English learners in a Beginning ESL Literacy class in Northern California, each of whom reported 0–1 year of formal education in their first language. By documenting naturally occurring classroom writing over five months, the study investigates what learners’ copied texts reveal about emergent orthographic ability, including letter formation, word segmentation, paper orientation, directionality, and other semiotic norms. In doing so, it seeks to contribute to a more detailed understanding of first-time print literacy development in an L2 adult context and to inform instruction for learners whose needs are not adequately captured by models designed for either schooled L2 writers or L1 children.

intros.text:
Print literacy is central to participation in contemporary civic, educational, occupational, and health-related domains, yet large numbers of adults continue to have limited access to literacy instruction and to the social resources that literacy affords (Lesgold & Welch-Ross, 2012; UNESCO Institute for Statistics, 2020). Among these adults are immigrants and refugees who are learning an additional language while also developing print literacy for the first time. In English-dominant contexts, such learners are often placed in beginning ESL literacy classes, where they must simultaneously acquire oral English, classroom routines, alphabetic print concepts, and the motor and perceptual practices involved in writing. This population, often discussed in the Low-Educated Second Language and Literacy Acquisition (LESLLA) literature, has therefore become an important focus for applied linguistics, adult education, and teacher preparation.

Despite this importance, adults with limited or no prior schooling have historically occupied a marginal position in second language acquisition research. Bigelow and Tarone (2004) argued that what the field knows about second language acquisition depends partly on who is studied, and that literacy level itself can shape language learning processes. Similarly, Young-Scholten (2013) noted that much SLA research has relied on schooled, middle-class participants, leaving low-educated immigrant learners underrepresented even as teachers increasingly work with adults who have had little opportunity to develop literacy in their first language. This imbalance has practical consequences: LESLLA teachers report needing specialized knowledge and training to support learners whose literacy, schooling, and language-learning profiles differ substantially from those assumed in mainstream ESL pedagogy (Strube, 2009; Vinogradov, 2009; Young-Scholten, 2015). Recent work on instructors’ perceptions and praxis with adult emergent readers further suggests that teachers must often make instructional decisions in an area where empirical guidance remains limited (Carter, 2020).

One area in need of closer attention is the very earliest stage of adult L2 writing: copying. In many classrooms, copying words from a board, worksheet, or book may appear to be a simple preliminary task. However, for adults new to print, copying may require unfamiliar motor routines, visual attention to letter shape, awareness of directionality and spacing, understanding of paper orientation and margins, and emerging recognition of the Roman alphabetic system. These demands are intensified when the copied words are in a language the learner is still acquiring. Although second-language writing scholarship has emphasized the need to understand L2 writers on their own terms rather than through expectations designed for L1 writers (Carter & J. M, 2020), relatively little is known about how adults with emergent print literacy develop the orthographic and semiotic skills that make even transcription possible.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines copying practices among four adult English learners with 0–1 year of formal L1 education in a Beginning ESL Literacy class at a Northern California adult school. Drawing on classroom observations and collected writing artifacts over five months, the study asks: What can an interactional analysis of classroom writing samples reveal about the initial developmental stage of orthographic ability, copying, in L2 adult learners with emergent print literacy? By focusing closely on learners’ written interactions with classroom text, the study aims to illuminate the developmental complexity hidden within routine copying tasks and to inform more responsive instruction for adults acquiring print literacy and English simultaneously.

intros.text: Within higher education, it is important to support all students so that they can maximise their potential and achieve satisfactory  outcomes, such as grades on assessments that involve academic writing, especially when these can contribute to the overall classification of their degree course  Students, however, differ in many respects, including their background knowledge and their expectations and approaches towards studying and learnin  Specifically, students can have varying beliefs about what academic writing for  assessment could or should entail (Sanders-Reio, Alexander, Reio, & Newman, 2014; White & Bruning, 2005). Some beliefs about  academic writing have associated with students’ confidence in their academic writing abilities and also with their writing performance  (Prat-Sala & Redford, 2012; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; Zimmerman & Bandura, 1994).  Contemporary theories of learning and motivation highlight the importance of students’ confidence within their studies: higher confidence may facilitate people to apply even  more effort, to set challenging goals, and to surpass their normal performance (Bandura, 1997). Conversely, lower levels of confidence,  and/or particular beliefs about academic writing, might be limiting or less helpful within higher education. Clarifying the implications  of different beliefs could help guidance and support for students to be provided or focused  English is the main language of instruction in the United Kingdom, which may be the students’ first language  (L1) or may be the students’ second or other language (L2)  L2 students within higher education have often expressed that they have  encountered various challenges, such as feeling that they had lower academic writing abilities and fluency in English (Sheridan, 2011),  and feeling that their prior experiences in examination practices in their home country had not necessarily prepared them for the  variety of assessment genres that they encountered in the United Kingdom (Morton, Storch, & Thompson, 2015; see also: Tian & Low,  2012; Kormos, 2012).  Nevertheless, the assumption that L2 speakers of English generally encounter greater challenges in writing  academically in English than L1 speakers is highly contested; for example, concepts such as the ‘native speaker’ or the ‘international  student’ are socially constructed and essentializing. Jenkins (2011) and Turner (2010) argue, in contrast, that multilingual speakers  might outperform monolinguals because they can draw on more semiotic resources (see also: Canagarajah & Gao, 2019)  Ultimately,  considering whether or not students face challenges is not an abstracted conceptual question, and insights can be gained through  research. However, much research into students’ beliefs about academic writing has not encompassed their L1/L2 status (Baaijen,  Galbraith, & de Glopper, 2014; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; White & Bruning, 2005).  It remains unclear whether L1 and L2 students  express similar or different beliefs about academic writing and their studies, and how these different beliefs might associate with their  confidence for their studies and, more specifically, their confidence for their academic writing in English.  Given this context, this study aimed to gain new insights into whether L1 and L2 students report different beliefs about academic  writing and other aspects of studying, and how these associated with their reports of their confidence and grades. Ultimately, we  wanted to explore whether and/or where students might benefit from support, encouragement, and/or other guidance about academic  writing.  Given that academic writing and assessment genres differ widely across academic areas, the research focused on one discipline  in the social sciences/humanities: applied linguistics courses at Master’s (MA) level, which includes courses undertaken in combination with associated subjects such as language teaching. Overall, 122 students participated from across 17 universities.

intros.text:
Academic writing is central to success in higher education, yet it remains a source of considerable challenge for many students, particularly at postgraduate level where the demands of academic writing become more sophisticated and discipline-specific. Writing has been variously conceptualised as a product, as a process, and through the perspective of genre, with each of these views drawing attention to different features of what 'good' academic writing might entail (Bathia, 2004; Swales, 1990). These conceptualisations have informed a growing body of research into students' beliefs about writing, including the extent to which students see writing as involving the transmission of knowledge, a transactional process of clarifying ideas or engaging emotionally, a recursive cycle of reviewing and revising, and an orientation towards audiences (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; White & Bruning, 2005). Such beliefs may reflect not only goals or standards about what writing should be, but also the practices that students apply in pursuit of those goals.

Contemporary theories of learning and motivation, particularly social-cognitive theory, highlight the reciprocal relationships between people's beliefs, behaviours, and social environments, and especially emphasise the importance of confidence (Bandura, 1977). Higher confidence can enable students to apply greater effort, to set more challenging goals, and to persist, whereas lower confidence may be limiting in the sense that some achievable actions are not even attempted (Bandura, 1977). Students' confidence for academic writing has indeed been found to correlate positively with their writing performance and grades (Prat-Sala & Redford, 2012; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; Zimmerman & Bandura, 1994), and confidence for coursework more generally has linked with academic attainment. Beliefs about writing have similarly been associated with confidence and performance, although findings have been mixed: transmission beliefs have tended to predict lower writing quality (Baaijen et al., 2014; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014), while findings concerning transaction, recursion, and audience orientation have been more variable (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; White & Bruning, 2005).

Despite this growing interest, relatively few studies have systematically considered whether students with English as a first language (L1 students) and students with first languages other than English (L2 students) express different levels of confidence and/or hold different beliefs about academic writing. This gap is notable given that L2 students may face additional challenges when writing in English (Kormos, 2012; Morton et al., 2015; Tian & Low, 2012), and given that assessment genres, terminology, and conventions can vary considerably across educational systems, disciplines, and institutions (Itua et al., 2014; Lillis & Turner, 2001; Sheridan, 2011). Where studies have included both L1 and L2 students, any differences across language background have often not been explored (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014). At the same time, there is legitimate concern about homogenising 'international students' or portraying them as deficient, when many are in fact highly competent multilingual speakers of English as a lingua franca (Jenkins et al., 2011). Nevertheless, the transition between educational levels and between educational systems may both present challenges, since expectations and practices are likely to differ.

This study therefore aimed to gain new insights by surveying postgraduate students of applied linguistics about their confidence and their beliefs about academic writing, focusing on one field in order to reduce variability arising from differences in writing and assessment genres across disciplines. Two research questions guided the study: first, whether L1 and L2 students express similar or different beliefs about academic writing and their studies; and second, which beliefs about academic writing are associated with students' confidence for academic writing in English and their overall performance on their course. Drawing on prior research, it was hypothesised that L2 students would express lower confidence for academic writing in English than L1 students (Kormos, 2012; Morton et al., 2015; Sheridan, 2011; Tian & Low, 2012), and that transmission beliefs would be negatively associated with confidence and performance (Baaijen et al., 2014; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014). Addressing these questions may help identify areas where support could help all students maximise their potential.

intros.text:
Academic writing lies at the heart of success within postgraduate study, and the ways in which students engage with it are shaped not only by their skills but also by their beliefs and their confidence. Contemporary theories and models of learning and motivation, such as social-cognitive theory, propose reciprocal interactions between people's beliefs, behaviours, and social environments, and especially highlight the importance of beliefs such as confidence (Bandura, 1977). Higher confidence may facilitate people to apply even more effort, to set challenging goals, and to surpass their normal performance, whereas lower confidence can have a limiting effect in the sense that some actions may not be attempted even though they might be achievable. Students' confidence for academic writing has indeed positively correlated with their writing performance and grades (Prat-Sala & Redford, 2012; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014), and confidence for undertaking coursework in general has similarly linked with overall attainment.

Alongside confidence, students' beliefs about what academic writing could or should entail have attracted increasing attention. Academic writing has been variously conceptualised as a product, as a process, from a genre perspective, or as a combination of these, and this has provided a basis for more detailed research into beliefs about writing as transmission, transaction, recursion, and orientation to specific audiences (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; White & Bruning, 2005). Such beliefs may reflect goals as well as the practices that might lead to achieving them, and they can be attuned to expectations within particular disciplines, institutions, and educational contexts. However, it remains less clear whether any of these beliefs are necessarily beneficial or detrimental, and studies into the area have produced somewhat variable results. White and Bruning (2005), for instance, found that both low and high transaction beliefs associated with writing quality, while Baaijen et al. (2014) found that transmission beliefs predicted lower writing quality and Sanders-Reio et al. (2014) reported that grades negatively correlated with transmission beliefs but positively with recursion and audience orientation beliefs. These varying findings themselves point to the benefit of further research.

A further concern is the situation of students who write in English but for whom English is not a first language. Studies have suggested that such students might require further support for academic writing in English (Morton et al., 2015; Sheridan, 2011; Tian & Low, 2012), and individual difference factors, including motivation and self-efficacy, may shape their engagement with writing tasks (Kormos, 2012). Detailed case studies have shown, for example, changes from initial beliefs in fixed writing conventions towards an awareness of complexity and flexibility. Yet relatively few studies have considered confidence and beliefs about academic writing concurrently across students with English as a first language (L1 students) and students with first languages other than English (L2 students). Notably, samples in prior research have often included a mix of L1, L2, and bilingual students without exploring any potential differences across these groups (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014). It therefore remains unclear whether L1 and L2 students tend to express different levels of confidence and/or hold different beliefs about what academic writing could or should entail.

Accordingly, this study aimed to gain new insights by considering students' views about academic writing and their studies, focusing on the field of applied linguistics in order to reduce variability across writing and assessment genres. Two research questions were addressed: whether L1 and L2 students express similar or different beliefs about academic writing and their studies, and which beliefs about academic writing associate with students' confidence in academic writing in English and their overall performance. Drawing on prior findings, it was hypothesised that L2 students would express lower confidence in academic writing in English than L1 students, and that transmission beliefs would negatively associate with confidence and performance (Baaijen et al., 2014; Kormos, 2012; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014). The findings may indicate areas for attention to help ensure that all students, and L2 students in particular, can maximise their potential.

intros.text:
Academic writing is a complex undertaking that can be conceptualized as a product, a process, or a genre-based practice. While a product-oriented view emphasizes the final outcome—such as register, structure, and technical vocabulary—a process view highlights the iterative cycles of planning, composing, and revising (Hayes, 2012). From a genre perspective, writing is seen as a set of conventionalized forms of language use associated with specific discourse communities (Swales, 1990). For postgraduate students, success often depends on their ability to align their writing with these disciplinary standards and expectations (Negretti, 2017). When students are uncertain about these conventions, their confidence may decrease, potentially hindering their overall academic performance (Lillis & Turner, 2001).

Central to this process are students' beliefs and confidence. Social-cognitive theory suggests a reciprocal interaction between an individual's beliefs, behaviors, and environment, emphasizing the role of self-efficacy (Bandura, 1977, 1997). Higher confidence can motivate students to set more challenging goals and persist through difficulties, whereas lower confidence may limit their attempts to engage in beneficial writing strategies (Bandura, 1997). Indeed, research has consistently linked writing self-efficacy and general academic confidence to higher grades and better performance (Prat-Sala & Redford, 2012; Richardson et al., 2012; Zimmerman & Bandura, 1994). Furthermore, students' beliefs about the nature of writing—whether they view it as a fixed ability or a skill developed through effort—can significantly influence their motivational approach to learning (Burnette et al., 2013).

Research into students' beliefs about academic writing has identified several distinct orientations. These include transmission beliefs, where writing is seen as the accurate reporting of authority; transaction beliefs, where writing is used to refine ideas or process emotion; recursion beliefs, which view writing as an inherently iterative process; and audience orientation, which focuses on adapting the text to the reader (Sanders-Reio et al., 2014; White & Bruning, 2005). The impact of these beliefs varies; for instance, transmission beliefs have been associated with lower writing quality in some contexts (Baaijen et al., 2014), while transactional and recursive beliefs are often viewed as more beneficial for cognitive engagement and performance (White & Bruning, 2005).

Despite these insights, there is a lack of comparative research exploring these dynamics across students with English as a first language (L1) and those with first languages other than English (L2). While L2 students are often highlighted as needing additional support to meet university-level expectations (Morton et al., 2015; Tian & Low, 2012), they may also bring diverse linguistic competencies that challenge traditional notions of the 'deficient' international student (Jenkins et al., 2011). It remains unclear whether L1 and L2 students differ significantly in their confidence levels or in the specific beliefs they hold about what constitutes 'good' academic writing, and how these factors correlate with their actual academic achievement.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the beliefs and confidence of postgraduate students in the field of applied linguistics. Specifically, it seeks to answer: (1) Do L1 and L2 students express similar or different beliefs about academic writing and their studies? and (2) Which beliefs about academic writing associate with students' confidence in academic writing in English and their overall course performance? Based on prior research, it was hypothesized that L2 students would report lower confidence in academic writing than L1 students (Kormos, 2012; Sheridan, 2011) and that transmission beliefs would negatively correlate with both confidence and academic performance (Baaijen et al., 2014; Sanders-Reio et al., 2014).
