intros.text: University English as a foreign language (EFL) programs often pressure  instructors and teachers to use generic, globally published EFL textbooks for  reasons more socio-political than pedagogical (Chang, 2009).  Considering  instructors and students need to make the best of matters in EFL under those  circumstances, the present study proposes a framework that echoes Fox (2004)  arguments that a curriculum is a rhetorical accomplishment.  The discursivity to  which Fox (2004) refers can be conceptually amalgamated in a term:  curricularivity. Curricularivity is additionally informed by arguments supporting  critical approaches to EFL learning (i.e., Canagarajah, 2016; Kumaravadivelu,  1999, 2006). The approach, aimed at finding a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC), encourages reflexive praxis rooted in one’s beliefs, assumptions, and  knowledge (BAK) about language teaching (Banes, Martínez, Athanases, & Wong,  2016; Meschede, Fiebranz, Möller & Steffensky, 2017; Pennycook, 2008; Woods,  1996) that any EFL instructor can use for their respective classes. The “zone” was  inspired by Rogan’s (2007) Zone of Feasible Innovation in curriculum and  Vygotsky’s (1978) Zone of Proximal Development. In the context of Korean,  university EFL courses, the ZPC establishes a “level of potential development as  determined through problem solving under guidance” (Vygotsky, 1978, p. 86).  Instead of blindly plowing through textbook content, that often serves as the  course curriculum in many EFL programs (Richards, 2001; Tomlinson &  Masuhara, 2011), without concern for one’s students, who may feel culturally  marginalized by lesson contents that can be counter-intuitive to their cultures (i.e.,  Song, 2013; Weninger & Kiss, 2013), instructors can recontextualize textbook  content to raise the value of student language learning investment  However, as  Fredricks (2007) notes in their application of culturally relevant alterations to EFL  textbook content, a systemic framework would greatly improve the reflexive  praxis that most instructors do internally when negotiating textbook content in  EFL classes.  This study endeavors to address that gap in EFL teaching practice.

intros.text:
Textbooks occupy a central and often unquestioned position in English as a foreign language (EFL) education, functioning as pedagogical artifacts whose 'school' status lends them a legitimacy that shapes the social realities students come to accept as normal (Richards, 2001; Weninger & Kiss, 2013). This is particularly true in expanding circle contexts, such as Korea, where globally published EFL textbooks are frequently selected for university programs for reasons more socio-political than pedagogical, and where neither instructors nor students have much say in that choice (Chang, 2009; Song, 2013). Critical scholars have long warned that these materials tend to reproduce inner-circle social narratives against which all other cultures are measured, subtly 'othering' non-English speaking communities and marginalizing the very learners who consume them (Pennycook, 2008; Song, 2013). Yet while a growing body of work interrogates culture in EFL materials, much of it treats language and image separately, and comparatively little attention has been paid to the multimodal discourse in which written text and visual semiotics combine to project dominant ideologies (Weninger & Kiss, 2013).

Even fewer studies have examined how such potentially harmful narratives are negotiated 'in situ,' as instructors and students engage textbook lessons in real time. This gap is consequential because a curriculum is ultimately a rhetorical accomplishment (Fox, 2004), enacted through classroom discourse and mediated by teacher expertise and beliefs (Woods, 1996; Banes et al., 2016). Critical applied linguistics reminds us that classroom moments are always connected to broader relations of power, disparity, and difference, and that instructors can act to change, not merely reproduce, inequitable narratives (Pennycook, 2008).

Drawing on notions of feasible curricular innovation (Rogan, 2007) and Vygotskian mediation (Vygotsky, 1978), the present study proposes a two-step model for achieving a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC). Demonstrated through classroom vignettes at Chung-Buk National University in Korea, the study asks: does an instructor's understanding of curricular commonplaces, together with the power relations and ideologies embedded in the multimodal discourse of their textbooks, appear to help them achieve a ZPC, and how do their students respond?

intros.text:
The globalized spread of English has made textbooks central artifacts in English as a foreign language (EFL) education, particularly in expanding circle communities where globally published materials dominate university programs (Kachru, 1992; Richards, 2001). These textbooks are frequently adopted for reasons that are more socio-political than pedagogical, and instructors and students in Korean post-secondary programs are often pressured to use them by their departments (Chang, 2009; Song, 2013). As pedagogical artifacts, textbooks carry a legitimacy conferred by the very adjective 'school,' validating the social norms they project (Curdt-Christiansen & Weninger, 2015). Critical applied linguists have long argued that what passes for knowledge in such materials is ideologically founded and can 'other' non-inner-circle learners, marginalizing their cultures and harming their educational experience (Canagarajah, 2016; Pennycook, 2008; Song, 2013).

A growing body of work has examined how culture and ideology are represented in EFL textbooks, and some scholars have called for more dynamic, semiotic approaches to understanding how learners engage with texts and images (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). Yet while multimodal discourse has been recognized as an under-appreciated source of dominant social narratives, few studies have investigated how these narratives are negotiated 'in situ' in the classroom. Existing frameworks tend to analyze the textbook as a static object rather than as content actively reconstructed by instructors drawing on their beliefs, assumptions, and knowledge (Woods, 1996) and their understanding of curricular commonplaces (Fox, 2004).

To address this gap, the present study proposes a two-step model for achieving a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC), which requires instructors to understand both the curricular commonplaces of their EFL program and the power and ideologies within the multimodal discourse of their textbooks. Demonstrated through vignettes of two EFL courses at Chung-Buk National University in Korea, this study asks: Does an instructor's understanding of curricular commonplaces and of ideologies in multimodal textbook discourse appear to help them achieve a ZPC, and how do their students respond?

intros.text:
In university English as a foreign language (EFL) programs within expanding circle communities, the selection and implementation of textbooks are often driven by socio-political pressures rather than pedagogical needs (Chang, 2009). While textbooks are essential components of language programs (Richards, 2001), they frequently project inner-circle social realities that can marginalize the cultures of their intended audiences (Song, 2013). Critical applied linguistics emphasizes the need to connect classroom texts to broader power relations, disparities, and ideologies (Pennycook, 2008). Despite this, the multimodal discourse of EFL textbooks—where images and text merge to create meaning—remains an under-appreciated source of dominant social narratives (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). There is a pressing need for a reflexive approach to teaching that allows instructors to critically analyze these materials and adjust them to fit the local sociocultural context (Banes et al., 2016).

Drawing inspiration from Rogan's (2007) concept of a "zone of feasible innovation," which balances stagnation and unrealistic change, this study proposes a "zone of prioritized curricularivity" (ZPC). The ZPC is conceived as a rhetorical accomplishment (Fox, 2004) that enables instructors to negotiate the tension between restrictive institutional curricula and the need for culturally relevant instruction. By understanding both the curricular commonplaces of their specific program and the ideologies embedded in the multimodal discourse of their textbooks, instructors can recontextualize lessons to diminish racial othering and Anglo-centric hegemonies.

This study investigates whether the implementation of a ZPC framework helps EFL instructors in Korean university settings mitigate social injustices in textbook content while enhancing student investment. Through a multimodal interactional analysis of two university courses, the research explores how the live negotiation of textbook discourses affects student participation and learning. By doing so, it aims to provide a model for instructors in expanding circle cultures to foster a stronger L2 identity for their students without abandoning necessary linguistic goals.

intros.text:
In expanding circle communities, university English as a foreign language (EFL) programs frequently rely on globally published textbooks, often due to socio-political pressures rather than pedagogical preference (Chang, 2009; Richards, 2001). These textbooks are not merely neutral tools for linguistic instruction but are artifacts that project specific social norms and inner-circle realities (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). Consequently, they can inadvertently 'other' learners or perpetuate Anglo-centric hegemonies that marginalize the cultures of the intended audience (Canagarajah, 2016; Song, 2013). While critical applied linguistics emphasizes the need to connect classroom texts to broader power relations (Pennycook, 2008), and some studies have highlighted the cultural dominance within textbook content (Song, 2013), there remains a significant gap in research concerning how the multimodal discourse of these materials—where images and text converge to create meaning—is negotiated live in the classroom.

Despite the importance of reflexive teaching and expansive language ideologies (Banes et al., 2016), many instructors in restrictive curricula feel pressured to follow pre-set learning outcomes, often leaving the ideological implications of multimodal content unaddressed. To bridge this gap, the present study proposes a two-step model for achieving a "zone of prioritized curricularivity" (ZPC), a term adapted from the notion of feasible innovation (Rogan, 2007) and the discursivity of curriculum design (Fox, 2004). The ZPC framework guides instructors to first establish curricular commonplaces and then critically analyze the power relations embedded in the multimodal discourse of their textbooks.

Using vignettes from two EFL courses at Chung-Buk National University in Korea, this study examines how instructors use the ZPC framework to reconstruct textbook lessons in situ. Through a multimodal interactional analysis of video recordings, the research explores whether this approach helps mitigate social injustices in textbook content while enhancing student participation. The findings suggest that a ZPC can improve student investment and learning by aligning textbook delivery with the sociocultural realities of the learners.

intros.text:
In expanding circle communities, university English as a Foreign Language (EFL) programs frequently mandate the use of globally published textbooks for reasons that are often socio-political rather than pedagogical (Chang, 2009; Song, 2013). While critical studies have increasingly problematized the cultural dominance and ideological narratives embedded in these materials (Pennycook, 2008; Canagarajah, 2016), there remains a paucity of research investigating how these multimodal discourses are negotiated in live classroom settings. Textbooks, as artifacts of 'school' management, often validate specific social norms that may marginalize local cultures (Curdt-Christiansen & Weninger, 2015; Dendrinos, 2015). Consequently, the unquestioned adoption of such materials can present significant challenges for Korean university students, whose learning experiences are frequently constrained by test-driven outcomes and rigid curricular commonplaces (Ahn, 2011; Paik, 2018). 

To address the potential for social injustice within textbook lessons, this study proposes a framework for establishing a Zone of Prioritized Curricularivity (ZPC). Drawing on Rogan’s (2007) concept of a 'zone of feasible innovation' and Fox’s (2004) notion of curriculum as a rhetorical accomplishment, the ZPC model necessitates a reflexive teaching practice. This practice requires instructors to critically analyze both the curricular commonplaces of their specific EFL programs and the power relations inherent in the multimodal discourse of their textbooks. By understanding these elements, instructors can mitigate perceived injustices as they negotiate content 'in situ.' 

The present study demonstrates the application of the ZPC framework through vignettes from two EFL courses at Chung-Buk National University in Korea. It investigates how instructors recontextualized, neutralized, or omitted multimodal discourse to align with student cultural identities while maintaining linguistic objectives. Utilizing a novel multimodal interactional analysis of video recordings, the research examines proxemics, gaze, gesture, and spoken language to determine how instructors and students co-construct meaning. The findings suggest that a ZPC is achieved when instructors' efforts to reconstruct textbook lessons are met with positive student feedback, such as heightened attentiveness and enthusiastic participation. Ultimately, this study argues that the ZPC can enhance student learning in expanding circle cultures by diminishing culturally marginalizing content while raising the value of student investment in EFL learning.

intros.text:
In expanding circle communities, university English as a foreign language (EFL) programs frequently pressure instructors and students to utilize globally published textbooks for reasons that are often more socio-political than pedagogical (Chang, 2009; Song, 2013). While critical studies have increasingly underscored multimodal discourse as a significant source of dominant social narratives within these materials (Weninger & Kiss, 2013), few have investigated the live negotiation of these narratives in actual classrooms. This oversight is problematic, as the unquestioned use of EFL textbooks and the lack of critical attention to their multimodal contents can present challenges for learners, resonating with complex issues regarding cultural marginalization and identity (Pennycook, 2008; Canagarajah, 2016). 

Although textbooks are often viewed as artifacts of state-sanctioned management (Curdt-Christiansen & Weninger, 2015), instructors in contexts like Korea often adhere to restrictive curricula that prioritize declarative knowledge over functional communication (Biggs & Tang, 2007; Paik, 2018). Consequently, there is a need for a framework that allows instructors to critically analyze and recontextualize textbook content without abandoning institutional requirements. To address this, the present study proposes a two-step model for achieving a Zone of Prioritized Curricularivity (ZPC). Drawing on Rogan’s (2007) concept of a zone of feasible innovation and Connely and Clandinin’s (1988) curricular commonplaces, the ZPC informs reflexive teaching practice by necessitating an understanding of both the curricular commonplaces of a specific EFL program and the power dynamics embedded in textbook multimodal discourse.

This study investigates how two instructors at Chung-Buk National University utilized the ZPC framework to negotiate multimodal discourses in their EFL textbooks. Through a novel multimodal interactional analysis of video recordings, the research examines how instructors recontextualized, neutralized, or skipped specific multimodal elements to mitigate perceived social injustices. The findings suggest that a ZPC is achieved when instructor efforts to reconstruct lessons are met with positive student feedback, characterized by heightened attentiveness and enthusiastic participation. Ultimately, the implications suggest that a ZPC can help instructors in expanding circle cultures simultaneously improve student acquisition, diminish culturally marginalizing content, and raise the value of student investment in EFL learning.

intros.text:
In many expanding-circle contexts, university EFL curricula are shaped not only by pedagogical considerations but also by institutional, economic, and sociopolitical investments in English. In South Korea, English education policy has long positioned communicative competence as a national resource for participation in globalization, yet classroom practices often remain constrained by standardized curricula, assessment pressures, and commercially produced materials (Chang, 2009). Textbooks therefore occupy a powerful curricular position: they provide linguistic content, sequence instruction, and legitimize particular cultural representations as teachable knowledge (Richards, 2001; Tomlinson, 2011). However, globally marketed EFL textbooks may also circulate dominant cultural narratives that privilege inner-circle norms and marginalize learners’ local identities, practices, and communicative priorities (Song, 2013; Weninger & Kiss, 2013).

Critical applied linguistics urges researchers and teachers to examine how language classrooms are connected to broader relations of power, ideology, identity, and inequality (Pennycook, 2008). From this perspective, textbook use is not a neutral act of materials delivery but a situated negotiation of discourse. Culture in textbooks is especially consequential because meanings are produced through combinations of written language, images, layout, tasks, and classroom interaction. Semiotic and multimodal approaches have shown that images and texts can guide learners toward particular understandings of self and other, even when the explicit pedagogical goal appears to be linguistic competence (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). Yet while critical textbook studies have identified cultural dominance in EFL materials, less attention has been paid to how instructors and students negotiate such multimodal discourses in real time during classroom instruction.

This study addresses that gap by proposing a critical instructional framework termed a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC). Drawing conceptually on Vygotskian notions of development and Rogan’s (2007) zone of feasible innovation, the ZPC foregrounds what is pedagogically possible within a particular institutional setting. It also incorporates teacher cognition and beliefs—what Woods (1996) calls teachers’ beliefs, assumptions, and knowledge—as resources for reflexive curriculum work. The framework asks instructors first to identify the curricular commonplaces of their EFL program and then to critically examine the power relations and ideologies embedded in the multimodal discourse of assigned textbooks. Through classroom vignettes from Korean university EFL courses, the study explores whether such reflexive negotiation can diminish culturally marginalizing textbook narratives while increasing student engagement, participation, and investment in English learning.

intros.text:
Globally published EFL textbooks remain central artifacts in many university language programs, particularly in expanding-circle contexts where English is tied to mobility, employability, and national projects of globalization. In South Korea, English education policy has long positioned communicative competence as a social and economic priority (Chang, 2009), yet university EFL classrooms are often organized around prescribed textbooks, institutional syllabi, and assessment-driven expectations that leave limited room for locally responsive pedagogy. Textbooks can provide structure, continuity, and resources for language programs (Richards, 2001; Tomlinson, 2011), but they also participate in the construction of curricular realities: what counts as legitimate knowledge, desirable culture, and appropriate communicative behavior.

Critical applied linguistics has emphasized that language classrooms are never ideologically neutral spaces; they are connected to wider relations of power, identity, inequality, and desire (Pennycook, 2008). This concern is especially relevant for EFL materials, where cultural representations may privilege inner-circle norms while positioning learners’ own cultures as peripheral. Studies of EFL textbooks have shown that cultural content may reproduce dominance, otherness, or limited forms of intercultural awareness (Song, 2013), and semiotic approaches have argued that images, texts, and tasks should be examined as meaning-making ensembles rather than as isolated linguistic input (Weninger & Kiss, 2013). However, although such research has productively critiqued textbook content, less attention has been given to how teachers and students negotiate potentially problematic multimodal discourses in real classroom interaction.

This article addresses that gap by proposing a zone of prioritized curricularivity (ZPC), a critical and reflexive framework for instructors required to work with mandated EFL textbooks. Informed by curriculum theory, teacher cognition, critical pedagogy, and multimodal discourse analysis (Fox, 2004; Fredricks, 2007; Rogan, 2007; Woods, 1996), the ZPC asks instructors first to examine the curricular commonplaces of a course and then to identify power relations and ideologies embedded in textbook multimodal discourse. The study demonstrates this framework through classroom vignettes from two Korean university EFL courses using Top Notch 2. By analyzing how instructors recontextualized, neutralized, or omitted textbook content in situ, the article explores whether a ZPC can support more culturally responsive, participatory, and critically aware EFL instruction.

intros.text: English for Specific Purposes (ESP) is a method of language teaching in which the practical needs (e.g. occupational or academic) of a group of learners shape the primary focus of the course. ESP, as a general term, may be used to refer to English for Academic Purposes (EAP) and to English for Occupational Purposes (EOP).  Yet, in the literature on L2 teaching, as it is the case in this study, ESP can terminologically apply to both of these sub-types.  The most important aspect of an ESP context, no matter how it is implemented, is to meet the specific needs of learners.  Naturally, various philosophies and methodologies of L2 teaching can help formulate ESP courses  A central question that demands rigorous research is the way ESP should be configured.  Communicative methods of language teaching and formfocused methods can contribute to the application of teaching methods in ESP courses, although in practice these two methods differently approach the process of teaching  Communicative methods normally rest on the fundamental idea that L1 and L2 are in some ways equal (the L1=L2 hypothesis) (Nation, 2005). Some researchers (Macaro, 2009; Rivers, 2011; Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007) have indicated that the native language of L2 learners cannot be fully excluded from L2 classrooms. In contrast, some other studies (Davila, 2005; Tang, 2002) claimed that full exposure to L2 is not the ultimate purpose of learning a new language.  The usage of L1 as a vehicle for transferring information and a means of interaction has been a popular topic for investigation among EFL and ESP teachers.  Some argue that L1 can help the process of teaching/learning when properly employed. On the other hand, some researchers have insisted that prohibiting the use of L1 would not be conducive to the process, particularly in ESP courses (Dujmovic, 2007).  Whether or not the focus on form, accompanied by occasional uses of L1, can contribute to ESP courses is a matter that demands further investigation.  This study seeks to make a comparison between communicative methods of language teaching and form-focused language teaching in ESP courses.  These two methods of language teaching have been widely studied in the history of language teaching. However, their effectiveness in ESP courses has not been properly examined in these research projects.  This study investigates an empirical context in which two groups of management students received two different teaching treatments (communicative and form-focused).  The study, more specifically, tries to answer the question which method may better serve ESP courses and to explore further the conditions that cause the more effective method.

Yet, in the literature on L2 teaching, as it is the case in this study, ESP can terminologically apply to both of these sub-types.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has become an established branch of English language teaching, designed to meet the particular linguistic and communicative needs of learners in specific academic and professional domains. Unlike general English courses, ESP courses are shaped by the subject matter that learners study, their prior knowledge of that subject, and the specific skills they must develop. Consequently, decisions about how best to teach an ESP course cannot be separated from questions about the learners' proficiency, the nature of the discipline, and the pedagogical methods and languages employed in the classroom. Yet, while much of the ESP literature has concentrated on textbooks, needs analysis, and learners' attitudes, comparatively little attention has been paid to the methods of instruction and the role of the languages used in these courses.

One of the most persistent debates in language teaching concerns the place of the learners' first language (L1) in the second language (L2) classroom. On the one hand, a number of scholars have argued that the judicious use of L1 can support comprehension, build confidence, and facilitate the learning of new vocabulary and grammar (Dujmovic, 2007; Tang, 2002). Others have advocated a more selective and principled approach to codeswitching, suggesting that there is an 'optimal' rather than a maximal role for the L1 in the classroom (Macaro, 2009). On the other hand, the rationale underlying communicative methods holds that learners benefit from maximum exposure to the target language, and that the exclusion of the L1 encourages meaningful interaction and richer input. Rivers (2010, 2011), for instance, has questioned policies of linguistic exclusion while also examining how classroom language practices relate to learner autonomy and innovation. These competing positions raise important questions about which approach best serves ESP learners.

A parallel debate surrounds the treatment of grammatical form. Form-focused instruction, whether delivered through explicit metalinguistic explanation or more implicit techniques, has been contrasted with communicative approaches that prioritise meaning and use over the study of language as an object. Central to this distinction is the recognition that communicative competence involves more than mastery of linguistic structures (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007), and that both vocabulary and multiword expressions require deliberate as well as incidental attention (Nation, 2005; Hinkel, 2022). Whether ESP learners profit more from form-focused instruction supported by the L1, or from a communicative course conducted exclusively in the L2, remains an open empirical question, particularly given that ESP learners typically bring substantial background knowledge of their subject matter to the classroom.

Against this background, the present study compares the effectiveness of form-focused and communicative methods of language teaching in an ESP course for management students, seeking to determine which approach yields greater gains and how learners' proficiency and the nature of the subject matter influence the outcome.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has become an increasingly central concern within second language teaching, as institutions and learners alike demand courses that address particular professional and academic needs. The effectiveness of an ESP course depends on a range of decisions, among which the choice of teaching method and the language of instruction are especially consequential. A recurring debate in this field concerns whether learners profit more from communicative approaches, which prioritise meaning and maximise exposure to the target language, or from form-focused approaches, which foreground grammatical structures and sometimes admit the learners' first language (L1) as a support.

Much of the existing literature has weighed in on the role of the L1 in second and foreign language classrooms. A number of scholars have argued that the judicious use of the L1 can facilitate learning, provided it is employed selectively and appropriately (Macaro, 2009; Davila, 2005; Dujmovic, 2007). Studies conducted in various contexts have reported that drawing on the mother tongue can support vocabulary acquisition, strengthen learners' confidence, and play a facilitating role in comprehension (Tang, 2002; Nation, 2005). Others, however, have questioned linguistic exclusion policies and the pedagogical assumptions behind them, calling for a more nuanced treatment of when and how the L1 should be permitted (Rivers, 2010, 2011). At the same time, communicative competence and linguistic competence have been theorised as distinct yet interrelated goals (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007), and the teaching of grammar and multiword expressions has been shown to benefit from both explicit and implicit forms of focus on form (Hinkel, 2022).

Despite this substantial body of work, the majority of ESP research has concentrated on textbooks, learners' needs, and learners' attitudes, while the comparative effectiveness of teaching methods and the role of the language of instruction within ESP settings has received far less rigorous attention. It remains unclear whether findings about L1 use derived from general English classrooms transfer to ESP contexts, where learners typically bring rich background knowledge of the subject matter that may itself compensate for gaps in language proficiency. This uncertainty leaves practitioners without firm guidance on how to match method to course.

The present study addresses this gap by directly comparing the effectiveness of a communicative method and a form-focused method as implemented in an ESP course for management students. Two comparable groups, matched for general English proficiency and subject knowledge, were taught over twenty sessions and assessed through a pre-test and post-test. In the communicative group, meaning was emphasised and English served as the sole vehicle of instruction; in the form-focused group, grammatical structures were the focus and the L1 was used on some occasions. The findings suggest that learners with higher proficiency in both English and the subject matter may gain more from communicative instruction, and that the nature of the subject matter itself warrants consideration when selecting an ESP teaching method.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has emerged as a critical branch of language teaching, designed to meet the precise linguistic needs of learners in professional or academic fields. Central to the success of ESP courses is the selection of an appropriate pedagogical approach that balances the acquisition of linguistic accuracy with the development of communicative competence (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007). However, a persistent debate remains regarding the most effective method for achieving these goals: whether to employ a form-focused approach, which emphasizes grammatical structures, or a communicative method, which prioritizes meaning and interaction. This debate often extends to the role of the learners' first language (L1) in the classroom. While some practitioners advocate for a strict "English-only" policy to maximize L2 exposure (Davila, 2005), others argue that the strategic use of L1 can facilitate understanding and reduce learner anxiety (Macaro, 2009; Tang, 2002).

In the context of communicative language teaching, the goal is to foster autonomy and functional proficiency (Rivers, 2010). Yet, the exclusion of L1 is often questioned, as many suggest that a bilingual approach—where the native language serves as a supportive tool—can prevent the negative consequences of linguistic frustration (Dujmovic, 2007). Conversely, form-focused instruction (FFI) suggests that explicit attention to grammar is necessary for accuracy, particularly when dealing with the complex technical vocabulary and structures typical of ESP courses (Hinkel, 2022; Nation, 2005). The tension between these two orientations—focus on form versus focus on meaning—creates a challenge for ESP instructors who must decide how to present specialized content effectively.

Despite the wealth of research on ESP needs analysis and textbook design, there is a relative scarcity of empirical studies comparing the efficacy of communicative and form-focused methods specifically within ESP frameworks. Much of the existing literature focuses on general English (EFL) rather than the intersection of subject-matter expertise and language acquisition. It remains unclear whether the effectiveness of a method depends on the learners' prior proficiency or the nature of the subject matter being taught. For instance, the strategies used to teach reading in a literary context may differ significantly from those required for technical management texts (Tang, 2002).

Therefore, the present study aims to compare the effectiveness of form-focused and communicative methods in an ESP course for management students. By examining two groups of learners—one exposed to a form-focused approach utilizing L1 support and another to a communicative, L2-exclusive approach—this research seeks to determine which method leads to greater proficiency in specialized English. Furthermore, the study explores how learners' existing subject-matter knowledge and English proficiency levels influence the outcome of these instructional methods.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has become a vital area of language education, as it aims to equip learners with the precise linguistic tools required for their professional or academic domains. In the field of second language acquisition, a central debate persists regarding the most effective pedagogical approach to achieve these goals. Specifically, scholars have long debated the tension between form-focused instruction, which emphasizes the mastery of grammatical structures, and communicative methods, which prioritize meaning-making and interaction (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007). 

Central to this debate is the role of the learners' first language (L1). Some researchers advocate for an 'English-only' environment to maximize L2 exposure (Davila, 2005), while others argue that the strategic use of L1 can facilitate learning and reduce learner anxiety (Dujmovic, 2007; Tang, 2002). Macaro (2009) suggests that there is an 'optimal' use of codeswitching that can support instructional goals, and Rivers (2010) has questioned the pedagogical basis of strict linguistic exclusion in the classroom. However, the application of these general EFL principles to the specific context of ESP remains complex, as ESP learners often possess significant subject-matter expertise that may interact with their language learning process in unique ways.

Despite the proliferation of research on ESP textbooks, needs analysis, and learner attitudes, there is a notable lack of rigorous empirical investigation into the comparative effectiveness of different teaching methods within ESP courses. While general studies on communicative versus form-focused approaches exist, it remains unclear how these methods perform when the subject matter is highly specialized. Furthermore, the extent to which a learner's prior knowledge of the professional domain mitigates the need for explicit form-focused instruction or L1 support has not been sufficiently explored. Consequently, more research is needed to determine which methodology better serves the needs of ESP students given their specific proficiency levels and technical backgrounds.

The present study aims to fill this gap by comparing the effectiveness of communicative methods and form-focused methods in an ESP course for management students. Specifically, the research examines whether a communicative approach—relying exclusively on the L2—yields better outcomes than a form-focused approach that allows for occasional L1 use. By employing a pre-test and post-test design with two distinct groups of learners, this study seeks to clarify how the nature of the subject matter and the students' initial proficiency influence the success of these methodologies. The findings of this research may provide valuable insights for ESP course designers and practitioners in selecting the most appropriate instructional framework for diverse professional contexts.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has long been a central focus in applied linguistics, particularly regarding how best to tailor language instruction to meet the distinct needs of learners in specialized fields. While much research has examined ESP textbooks, learner needs, and attitudes, the specific role of teaching methods and the languages used within these courses has received less rigorous exploration. A critical debate in this domain concerns the extent to which learners' first language (L1) should be employed in the classroom versus the exclusive use of the target language (L2). On one side, scholars argue that L1 can serve as a valuable scaffold, enhancing learner confidence and facilitating the understanding of complex technical concepts. For instance, Dujmovic (2007) suggests that eliminating the mother tongue can impede learning, advocating for a bilingual approach where the L1 plays a supportive role. Similarly, Tang (2002) and Macaro (2009) have explored the optimal use of codeswitching, indicating that selective use of L1 can be beneficial in specific pedagogical contexts. 

Conversely, proponents of communicative language teaching (CLT) argue for maximum exposure to the L2 to ensure effective acquisition. Rivers (2010) questions linguistic exclusion but emphasizes the importance of pedagogical strategies that foster learner autonomy within an L2 environment. The 'English-only' classroom, as discussed by Davila (2005), posits that even grammatical explanations should be delivered in the target language to maximize input. This perspective aligns with the broader distinction between 'focus-on-forms' and 'focus-on-form' instruction. Long (1991) differentiates these approaches, noting that while traditional methods treat language as an object of study, focus-on-form draws attention to linguistic elements incidentally during communication. Ellis (2006) further elaborates on the distinction between explicit and implicit knowledge, suggesting that the method of instruction significantly impacts how these knowledge types are developed. 

Despite the theoretical divergence, empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of these methods in ESP contexts remains mixed. Some studies indicate that L1 use positively impacts confidence and lexical acquisition (Jamshidi & Naveebrahimi, 2013), while others maintain that L2 immersion is superior for long-term proficiency. The specific context of ESP, where learners often possess substantial subject matter knowledge, adds a layer of complexity to this debate. It is plausible that the interaction between learners' L2 proficiency, their technical knowledge, and the nature of the subject matter influences which method yields better results. Therefore, the present study aims to compare the effectiveness of form-focused methods, which incorporate L1, against communicative methods that rely exclusively on L2 within an ESP course for management students. By examining these variables, this research seeks to determine which approach better facilitates language acquisition in specialized contexts.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has emerged as a critical domain within applied linguistics, driven by the increasing demand for specialized language skills in professional and academic contexts. As learners engage with technical content in a second language, the pedagogical approaches employed become paramount in determining instructional effectiveness. While ESP curricula are traditionally designed around specific learner needs, the debate regarding the optimal method of instruction—specifically the tension between communicative language teaching and form-focused instruction—remains a central issue in the field. This study addresses this gap by comparing the efficacy of these two methods within an ESP framework for management students.

The theoretical underpinnings of language teaching have long oscillated between a focus on meaning and a focus on form. Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) prioritizes interaction and the functional use of language, often advocating for an 'English-only' environment to maximize target language exposure. Proponents argue that immersion in the L2 fosters natural acquisition processes and prevents reliance on the native language (L1). Conversely, form-focused instruction (FFI) emphasizes the explicit teaching of linguistic structures, often utilizing the L1 to clarify complex grammatical points or technical vocabulary. Scholars such as Macaro (2009) have explored the 'optimal' use of codeswitching, suggesting that L1 can serve as a scaffolding tool rather than a hindrance. Similarly, Dujmovic (2007) and Tang (2002) have argued that strategic use of the L1 can facilitate comprehension and reduce cognitive load in the EFL classroom. However, other researchers maintain that L1 use may undermine the consistency of communicative methods, particularly in ESP settings where professional proficiency is the ultimate goal (Rivers, 2010).

Despite extensive research on ESP textbooks and learner needs, the specific role of teaching methods and language policies within ESP courses has not been rigorously explored. While general EFL studies provide conflicting evidence regarding L1 use, the context of ESP adds a layer of complexity: learners often possess significant background knowledge in their subject matter, which may influence how they process linguistic input. Previous studies have noted that ESP courses taught by content specialists often lack pedagogical variety, yet the methodological implications of this observation remain under-researched. Furthermore, the interaction between learners' proficiency levels and the nature of the subject matter (theoretical vs. applied) suggests that a 'one-size-fits-all' approach may be inadequate. There is a need to empirically investigate whether high-proficiency learners in ESP contexts benefit more from communicative immersion or from the explicit support of form-focused instruction.

The present study aims to compare the effectiveness of form-focused and communicative methods in ESP courses for management students. By isolating the variable of instructional method while controlling for proficiency levels, this research seeks to determine which approach yields superior outcomes in terms of language acquisition and subject-matter comprehension. Specifically, the study examines two groups of learners: one exposed to a form-focused method with occasional L1 use, and another engaged in a communicative method relying exclusively on L2. The findings of this study may offer critical insights for ESP course designers, suggesting that learner proficiency and subject matter knowledge are decisive factors in selecting the most appropriate pedagogical strategy.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) has become an important component of higher education because many students need English not only for general communication but also for accessing disciplinary knowledge and participating in professional communities. Unlike general English courses, ESP instruction is expected to respond to learners’ academic or occupational needs, the discourse of a particular field, and the linguistic demands of specialized texts. In this respect, ESP course design involves decisions about content, materials, skills, and methodology. Among these decisions, the choice of teaching method is especially important, since the same technical content may be presented either through explicit attention to language forms or through meaning-oriented communicative use of English.

Debates about effective language teaching have often been framed around the relationship between linguistic competence and communicative competence. While mastery of grammar, vocabulary, and sentence structure is essential for accurate language use, learners also need opportunities to use language for meaningful purposes (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007). Communicative approaches emphasize interaction, negotiation of meaning, and exposure to the target language, and are therefore commonly associated with the development of functional language ability. In ESP contexts, such approaches may be particularly relevant because learners usually bring background knowledge of their discipline to the classroom and can use that knowledge to interpret specialized input.

At the same time, form-focused instruction remains influential in EFL and ESP classrooms. Specialized texts often contain complex grammatical structures, technical vocabulary, and discipline-specific expressions that may require direct explanation. Research on vocabulary and multiword expressions has shown that focused and deliberate instruction can support learners’ control of lexical items that are frequent or important in academic and professional discourse (Nation, 2005; Hinkel, 2022). From this perspective, explicit attention to form may help learners decode ESP texts more accurately and acquire the linguistic resources needed in their field.

A related issue concerns the role of the learners’ first language (L1). English-only instruction has frequently been defended on the grounds that maximum exposure to the target language promotes learning (Davila, 2005). However, a growing body of work has questioned strict linguistic exclusion and argued for principled L1 use in second and foreign language classrooms (Macaro, 2009; Rivers, 2010). Studies of classroom practice have suggested that the L1 can reduce anxiety, clarify difficult concepts, and facilitate comprehension, especially when learners face demanding texts or abstract content (Tang, 2002; Dujmovic, 2007). Nevertheless, excessive reliance on the L1 may limit opportunities for communication in English and reduce the amount of target-language input available to learners.

These competing positions are particularly significant in ESP courses, where learners must simultaneously process language and subject matter. Yet much ESP research has concentrated on needs analysis, textbooks, and learners’ attitudes, while comparatively less attention has been paid to the relative effectiveness of instructional methods. The present study therefore compares a form-focused ESP course, in which grammatical structures and technical vocabulary are explained with some use of Persian, with a communicative ESP course conducted exclusively in English. Focusing on management students, the study investigates which method leads to greater improvement in ESP performance and considers how learners’ English proficiency and subject-matter knowledge may influence the effectiveness of each approach.

intros.text:
English for Specific Purposes (ESP) courses occupy an important position in university language programmes because they are expected to help learners use English in relation to their academic disciplines and future professions. Unlike general English courses, ESP instruction is shaped by learners’ disciplinary needs, the discourse practices of a particular field, and the extent to which learners must access specialist knowledge through English. Consequently, the selection of an appropriate teaching method is a central concern in ESP course design, especially in contexts where learners have already acquired some subject-matter knowledge but still need support in using English to understand texts, terminology, and professional concepts.

A persistent issue in language teaching concerns whether instruction should emphasize communication and meaning or the explicit teaching of linguistic forms. Communicative approaches generally seek to maximize learners’ exposure to the target language and to encourage the use of English as a medium for classroom interaction. Such approaches are often associated with the development of communicative competence, which involves more than knowledge of grammar alone (Karimnia & Izadparast, 2007). In contrast, form-focused approaches direct learners’ attention to grammar, vocabulary, and other linguistic features, sometimes through explicit explanation and controlled practice. In ESP settings, this distinction is particularly significant because learners must simultaneously process specialized content and linguistic forms.

The role of the first language (L1) further complicates this methodological choice. English-only policies have often been promoted on the grounds that maximum exposure to the second language (L2) supports learning, and practical guides for English-only classrooms have encouraged teachers to explain even difficult points through English (Davila, 2005). However, recent discussions have questioned strict linguistic exclusion and have argued for more flexible classroom language policies (Rivers, 2010). Research on codeswitching has similarly suggested that teacher use of the L1 may be pedagogically useful when it is selective and purposeful (Macaro, 2009). Studies of L1 use in EFL classrooms have reported that the mother tongue can support comprehension, reduce anxiety, and facilitate learning, particularly when learners encounter difficult texts or unfamiliar vocabulary (Tang, 2002; Dujmovic, 2007).

Despite these contributions, the effectiveness of communicative and form-focused methods in ESP courses remains insufficiently explored. Much ESP research has concentrated on needs analysis, materials, textbooks, or learner attitudes, while fewer empirical studies have compared how different instructional methods affect learners’ achievement in discipline-specific English. It is also unclear whether findings in favour of L1 support in general EFL classrooms can be extended to ESP contexts, where learners’ subject-matter knowledge may help them infer meaning and benefit from instruction delivered entirely in English.

The present study addresses this issue by comparing a form-focused ESP course, in which Persian was used occasionally to explain grammar, vocabulary, and reading passages, with a communicative ESP course conducted exclusively in English. Two groups of Iranian management students were first tested for general English proficiency and knowledge of English for management, received different instructional treatments, and were then assessed through a post-test. By examining the relative outcomes of these two methods, the study aims to clarify whether communicative or form-focused instruction is more effective in an ESP course and to consider how learners’ English proficiency, subject-matter knowledge, and the nature of the discipline may influence methodological decisions.

intros.text: It is undeniable that the global influence of the English language is everywhere we look, whether this is in the media, education, science, tourism, or business. English has permeated all levels of society entering all kinds of domains (Seidlhofer, Breiteneder, & Pitzl, 2006) and this is even more evident in Europe.  It is the language of international communication par excellence worldwide but it has become the de facto lingua franca in Europe, where the need for intraEuropean communication pushed this language to take the position but the policies around it are still very controversial in a territory where multilingualism and language diversity is one of the main core values.  It is this current status that has awoken many relevant research topics such as linguistic imperialism,the varieties of English, linguistic diversity and conservation, or linguistic and cultural identity, which are often focused in the use of language and not so much integrated in the study of language acquisition.  Our research focuses on English language teaching in a plurilingual society and aims to propose a sustainable approach to teach a language that acts as a lingua franca using the first language to learn the second one more effectively while exalting the value of the mother tongue.  In a world populated by different “Englishes” and ruled by “nativeness,” it is a complex matter to define what English as a Lingua Franca (ELF thereafter) entails and even more so to teach it as a second language, while at the same time disassociating the language from its “original native speakers” (British or American, for instance). The English language expanded with the British Empire through the colonies, it stayed dominant through the global markets and new technologies, and it has now taken the position of a global language that no longer belongs exclusively to the native speakers.  The World Englishes model “does not appear to take into account the fact that English has acquired a new dominant function world-wide” (Mollin, 2006, p. 42) and this has inspired many different research fields within ELF. Despite the different views and understandings of ELF, the idea of the plurilithic English is the common ground, where the focus of international communication is on intelligibility across groups of English speakers of different first language backgrounds (Mckay, 2018)  However, not all scholars are on the same page in terms of defining what it actually is and what it represents.  For some, ELF is conceptualised as an umbrella term to refer to a language function (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010; House, 2003), while for others it is becoming a new variety (Jenkins, Modiano, & Seidlhofer, 2001; Seidlhofer, 2009) and focus on the characteristics of a certain group of speakers using English to communicate in an international setting. As an example, we can refer to two projects in Europe, VOICE (Vienna-Oxford International Corpus of English), led by Barbara Seidlhofer, and ELFA (English as a Lingua Franca in Academic Settings), led by Anna Mauranen, which are dedicated to investigating the nuances and common traits of English used by non-natives.  Nevertheless, we find the definition of ELF as a variety rather  incomplete.

intros.text:
The global spread of English as a lingua franca (ELF) has fundamentally altered the way we conceive of language learning, teaching, and use in the twenty-first century. English is no longer the property of its native speakers but has become a means of communication among speakers of diverse first languages across the world (Seidlhofer, 2009). This reality poses significant challenges for applied linguistics and, in particular, for how English is taught in schools, where monolingual and native-based approaches continue to dominate despite the multilingual contexts in which most learners actually operate (Seidlhofer, Breiteneder, & Pitzl, 2006). The gap between the communicative function that English performs in international settings and the ways in which it is presented in the classroom demands a critical reconsideration of established pedagogical practices.

Central to understanding ELF is the distinction between languages for communication and languages for identification proposed by House (2003), who argued convincingly against the widespread assumption that English as a lingua franca constitutes a threat to national languages and to multilingualism. Rather than displacing local languages, English can coexist with them if its function as a tool for communication is separated from its role as a marker of cultural or national identity. This distinction is not merely terminological; as Friedrich and Matsuda (2010) have shown, conceptualising ELF as a function rather than as a linguistic variety is necessary in order to capture the complexity and diversity of English today and to avoid the confusion that arises when ELF is treated as belonging to a particular group of speakers (McKay, 2018; Mollin, 2006). Understanding ELF in this way opens the door to an ecological perspective in which all the languages in a learner's repertoire, including the mother tongue, are valued as part of a broader linguistic ecosystem.

Europe offers a particularly instructive setting for examining these tensions. It is a continent of many languages and identities, historically territory-bound and linguistically segregative, yet increasingly reliant on English as a common means of communication, a situation that generates potential conflict with the ideals of societal multilingualism and individual plurilingualism (Seidlhofer et al., 2006). While the Council of Europe promotes a plurilingual and intercultural agenda through instruments such as the Common European Framework of Reference, the implementation of these guidelines varies enormously across national contexts, and the emergence of a Euro-English (Jenkins, Modiano, & Seidlhofer, 2001) coexists with widely differing attitudes towards the mother tongue and towards English itself.

Against this background, the present study proposes a plurilingual and ecological approach to English language teaching in primary school, one that draws on learners' first languages as a scaffolding tool for learning English while presenting English as a language for international communication that belongs to no single nation. We argue that such an approach can improve English learning independently of the learner's mother tongue and, at the same time, foster a positive attitude towards the languages that make up the learner's repertoire. Drawing on the initial results of an international research project conducted in three very different contexts, this paper reports on data gathered in Spain and Norway, two European countries whose contrasting language policies, proficiency levels, and understandings of English as a global language allow us to explore how plurilingual and monolingual approaches shape both learning outcomes and learners' perceptions. In doing so, we aim to demonstrate that an ecological perspective is not only compatible with but necessary for the healthy coexistence of a lingua franca and linguistic diversity in the classroom.

intros.text:
The spread of English as a lingua franca (ELF) has profoundly reshaped the way languages are used, learnt and taught across the world. English now functions as the dominant means of international communication, a status that sets it apart from any other foreign language and that has generated a substantial body of applied linguistic inquiry into its nature, its varieties and its pedagogical implications (Seidlhofer et al., 2006; McKay, 2018). Much of this discussion has centred on how best to conceptualise ELF: as a variety, a register, or a function. Friedrich and Matsuda (2010) argue that understanding ELF merely as a linguistic variety fails to capture the reality of international communication, which is always context and situation specific, while Mollin (2006) similarly questions whether ELF can be integrated into nation-based models such as Kachru's as a variety at all. Seidlhofer (2009) further stresses the common ground shared by world Englishes and ELF research, both of which assume that English belongs to all who use it. These debates matter because the way English is defined shapes the way it is taught in classrooms.

Alongside the rise of ELF, a growing awareness of multilingualism has emerged as our default reality, with monolinguals increasingly the exception. This shift has sharpened the tension between English as a language for communication and as a language for identification, a distinction articulated by House (2003), who argued against the assumption that English inevitably threatens national languages and multilingualism. Jenkins et al. (2001), in describing an emerging Euro-English, similarly point to the complex ways in which English is being reappropriated across the continent. In Europe specifically, the omnipresence of English creates a potential conflict with the ideals of societal multilingualism and individual plurilingualism (Seidlhofer et al., 2006), a conflict that European policy guidelines such as the CEFR attempt, not always successfully, to resolve.

Despite this rich literature on the status and function of ELF, comparatively little attention has been paid to how a plurilingual and ecological understanding of English can be operationalised in the primary classroom, particularly in relation to the role of the mother tongue in learning the foreign language. Existing pedagogical approaches, including the popular CLIL model, remain largely monolingual and native-based in practice, with British and American models still defining authentic materials and cultural appropriateness. Moreover, cross-national comparisons that examine how differing language policies translate into differing learner attitudes and outcomes are scarce. It remains unclear whether an approach that deliberately uses the L1 as a scaffolding tool, and that presents English as a language belonging to no single nation, can improve learning independently of the student's mother tongue.

This paper addresses that gap by proposing and testing a plurilingual and ecological approach to English language teaching in primary school. Drawing on the initial results of an international research project conducted in three very different contexts, and presenting here the first phase involving 133 Year 6 students in Spain and Norway, we compare plurilingual and monolingual teaching through written tests, an oral activity and an attitudinal questionnaire. In doing so, we distinguish between languages for communication and languages for identification, examine the language policies of the participating countries, and analyse cross-linguistic and cross-cultural perspectives. We argue that a plurilingual approach using the L1 as a connecting tool improves English learning while fostering an ecological understanding of languages in which all languages are valued within a shared linguistic ecosystem.

The global spread of English has fundamentally transformed the landscape of language education, repositioning English not merely as a foreign language tied to specific native-speaker cultures, but as a tool for international communication. This phenomenon is often conceptualized as English as a Lingua Franca (ELF), a term that describes the function English performs in multilingual contexts rather than a specific linguistic variety (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010). While some scholars view ELF as a new variety emerging within the Expanding Circle (Mollin, 2006), others emphasize that it represents a shift in ownership, where the language belongs to all who use it to achieve communicative goals (Seidlhofer, 2009). Despite this theoretical shift, pedagogy in many primary schools remains rooted in monolingual, native-based approaches that prioritize British or American norms, often neglecting the linguistic identity of the learner.

This tension between the global function of English and local identity is central to the debate on multilingualism. House (2003) distinguishes between "languages for communication" and "languages for identification," suggesting that the rise of English as a lingua franca does not necessarily threaten the vitality of native languages if a clear distinction is maintained. However, the implementation of this balance in the classroom is challenging. In Europe, for instance, the omnipresence of English creates a complex interaction between the ideals of individual plurilingualism and the practical reality of English as a dominant means of communication (Seidlhofer et al., 2006). While frameworks like the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) promote a plurilingual approach, actual classroom practices often vary wildly depending on national policies and socio-historical contexts (McKay, 2018).

To address these challenges, this paper proposes an ecological perspective on English Language Teaching (ELT). Drawing on the concept of language ecology—the study of interactions between languages and their environment—we argue for a plurilingual approach that views the mother tongue (L1) not as an obstacle, but as a vital scaffolding tool. By integrating the L1 into the learning process and presenting English as a global tool uncoupled from any single nation, educators can foster plurilingual competence while respecting the learner's identity. This approach aligns with the need for an EIL (English as an International Language) pedagogy that is sensitive to the diverse backgrounds of students (McKay, 2018).

The aim of this research is to demonstrate that a plurilingual and ecological approach to English teaching can achieve superior learning results in primary education, regardless of the students' native language. This study examines the impact of such an approach through a comparative analysis of classrooms in three distinct contexts: Norway, China, and Spain. By dividing students into control groups receiving traditional monolingual instruction and experimental groups receiving plurilingual instruction, the study analyzes how the strategic use of L1 and a focus on ELF can improve both linguistic proficiency and the students' attitudes toward their own linguistic repertoire. This paper presents the initial results from the first phase of the experiment, focusing on data from Spain and Norway to illustrate how an ecological perspective can transform ELT in primary school.

intros.text:
The global expansion of English has fundamentally altered the landscape of language education, positioning English not merely as a foreign language but as a vital tool for international communication. Within this context, English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) has emerged as a central concept, describing the function English performs in multilingual contexts to facilitate interaction between speakers of different mother tongues (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010). As the demand for communicative competence grows, there is an increasing need to move beyond traditional native-speaker models, which often treat English as a linguistic variety tied to specific national identities rather than a functional tool for global exchange (McKay, 2018; Mollin, 2006).

Recent scholarly discussions have highlighted the tension between the spread of English and the preservation of linguistic diversity. House (2003) addresses this by distinguishing between languages used for communication and those used for identification, suggesting that the role of English as a lingua franca does not necessarily threaten multilingualism. Similarly, Seidlhofer et al. (2006) argue that the omnipresence of English in Europe challenges traditional distinctions between first and foreign languages, necessitating a shift in how applied linguistics approaches language acquisition. However, despite these theoretical advancements, many classroom practices remain stubbornly monolingual and native-centric, often ignoring the learner's own linguistic repertoire and identity (Seidlhofer, 2009).

While the Council of Europe has promoted plurilingual guidelines through the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), the actual implementation of these policies varies significantly across different national contexts. In many primary education systems, there is still a lack of clarity regarding how to integrate the mother tongue (L1) effectively within the English curriculum. Many policies continue to prioritize English proficiency at the expense of the students' native languages, failing to adopt a truly ecological perspective that views all languages in a learner's environment as interconnected and equally valuable.

Consequently, there is a pressing need for empirical research that demonstrates how a plurilingual and ecological approach can be operationalized in the primary school classroom to improve learning outcomes while respecting the students' linguistic identities. To address this gap, the present study aims to demonstrate that incorporating a plurilingual approach—utilizing the L1 as a scaffolding tool—can achieve better results in English language learning independently of the students' mother tongue. This research examines the initial results of an international project conducted in Norway, China, and Spain, focusing on the first phase involving 133 students. By comparing control groups receiving traditional monolingual instruction with experimental groups receiving a plurilingual approach, the study evaluates both linguistic gains and student attitudes toward their own languages.

The article is organized as follows: first, it defines ELF within a plurilingual and ecological framework; second, it analyzes the specific language policies and educational landscapes of Spain and Norway; third, it details the methodology and results of the experimental classes; and finally, it discusses the implications of these findings for the development of an ecological perspective in English language teaching.

intros.text:
The global spread of English as a lingua franca (ELF) has fundamentally altered the landscape of language education, challenging traditional monolingual pedagogies that prioritize native-speaker norms. While English serves as a dominant tool for international communication, its teaching often remains tethered to the cultural and linguistic models of inner-circle countries, creating a tension between communicative utility and identity formation. As Friedrich and Matsuda (2010) argue, understanding ELF merely as a linguistic variety fails to capture the context-specific reality of communication, potentially hindering understanding between different varieties and creating confusion regarding the mother tongue. Instead, ELF should be conceptualized as a function rather than a fixed variety, a perspective that necessitates a shift in pedagogical approaches, particularly within primary education where language attitudes are formed. This paper proposes a plurilingual and ecological approach to English language teaching (ELT) in primary school, aiming to demonstrate that utilizing the mother tongue (L1) as a connecting tool can enhance learning outcomes and foster a sustainable understanding of language diversity.

The relationship between English and identity is increasingly complex. House (2003) distinguishes between languages for communication and languages for identification, suggesting that while English asserts its status as a language of prestige, it does not necessarily threaten multilingualism if managed correctly. However, current educational policies often fail to reflect this nuance. Despite guidelines from the Council of Europe promoting plurilingualism, many national curricula continue to prioritize English proficiency over the maintenance of local linguistic repertoires. In Europe, for instance, the implementation of these guidelines varies significantly. Norway, with its high English proficiency and curriculum emphasizing English as a global language, contrasts sharply with Spain, where English is often taught through a monolingual lens despite a rich multilingual context. These disparities highlight the need for an ecological perspective that views languages not in isolation but as interacting elements within a broader ecosystem, where the vitality of the mother tongue is preserved alongside the acquisition of a lingua franca.

This study addresses the gap between theoretical plurilingual frameworks and classroom practice. By examining the impact of a plurilingual approach on primary students in Spain and Norway, we investigate how L1 use influences English acquisition and language attitudes. The research is grounded in the premise that English teaching should not aim to create native speakers but rather ELF users who respect their own linguistic identity. This approach aligns with the ecological view of language, which considers the interactions between languages and their social environments (Haugen, 1972). It posits that acknowledging the value of the L1 and presenting English as a tool for international communication, rather than a cultural imposition, can improve learning efficiency and promote positive language attitudes.

The following sections present the initial results of an international research project involving primary students in three countries. While the full project encompasses a broader range of participants, this paper focuses on the first phase, including 133 students from Norway and Spain. Through a comparative analysis of control and experimental groups receiving traditional and plurilingual instruction respectively, we evaluate the efficacy of integrating L1 in ELT. The study not only assesses linguistic proficiency through standardized testing but also explores students' attitudes towards their mother tongue and English via surveys. Ultimately, this paper seeks to contribute to the discourse on ELF pedagogy by demonstrating that a plurilingual approach, rooted in ecological principles, can achieve better educational results independently of the student's mother tongue, thereby supporting a more sustainable and inclusive multilingual future.

intros.text:
The globalisation of English has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of language education, particularly within primary school contexts. As English assumes an increasingly dominant role as a lingua franca (ELF), the traditional paradigms of English language teaching (ELT) face significant challenges. The prevailing monolingual approach, which often prioritises native-speaker norms and suppresses the use of the learners' mother tongue (L1), is increasingly viewed as inadequate for contemporary communicative needs. Instead, there is a growing consensus that pedagogical strategies must evolve to reflect the reality of English as a tool for international communication rather than a marker of cultural identity. This shift necessitates a move towards a plurilingual and ecological perspective, one that recognises the value of all languages within a learner's repertoire.

Scholars have long debated the conceptualisation of ELF. Friedrich and Matsuda (2010) argue that understanding ELF merely as a linguistic variety fails to capture the reality of communication, which is context-specific and functional. Similarly, Seidlhofer et al. (2006) highlight the methodological challenges of uncoupling the language from its native speakers, noting that ELF is not easily separated from status and 'native' culture. Despite these theoretical advancements, classroom practices often lag behind. Authentic materials remain predominantly British or American, and native-speaker models continue to define cultural appropriateness (Seidlhofer et al., 2006). This disconnect between theory and practice creates a dichotomy between English as a language for communication and a language for identification, a distinction House (2003) suggests is crucial for maintaining multilingualism. While the spread of ELF may stimulate members of minority languages to insist on their own local language for emotional binding, the dominance of English poses risks to linguistic diversity (House, 2003; Phillipson, 2003).

In Europe, the Council of Europe has attempted to bridge this gap through frameworks like the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR), promoting plurilingualism and intercultural competence. However, the implementation of these guidelines varies significantly across national contexts. For instance, while Norway has integrated the concept of language ecology into its curriculum, emphasising the relationship between English and the native language, Spain's approach remains more ambiguous, often prioritising English proficiency over the integration of regional and national languages. This disparity suggests that while policy frameworks exist, their application is heavily influenced by local socio-linguistic realities and educational traditions. Consequently, the effectiveness of plurilingual approaches in improving English learning outcomes and fostering positive attitudes towards the mother tongue remains an area requiring empirical investigation.

While previous research has established the theoretical benefits of plurilingualism and the ecological perspective on language, there is a paucity of empirical studies examining the immediate impact of these approaches on primary school students in diverse European contexts. Specifically, little is known about how a plurilingual approach, which actively utilises the L1 as a scaffolding tool, compares to traditional monolingual methods in terms of learning outcomes and student motivation. Furthermore, the intersection of language ecology and primary ELT has not been sufficiently explored in relation to the students' perception of their own linguistic identity. Addressing this gap, the present study aims to demonstrate that a plurilingual and ecological approach to ELT can achieve better results in primary school, independently of the student's mother tongue. This article presents the initial results of an international research project conducted in Norway, China, and Spain, focusing on the first phase involving 133 students. By comparing control and experimental groups, this research seeks to analyse how the positive use of the mother tongue functions as a connecting tool in the students' communication system, ultimately contributing to a more sustainable and effective model of English language teaching.
