intros.text:
English occupies an unprecedented position in contemporary language education. In many contexts, it is no longer learned primarily for communication with native speakers, but as a shared resource among speakers with different linguistic and cultural backgrounds. This has led applied linguistics to reconsider what English is, who it belongs to, and how it should be taught. Research on English as a lingua franca (ELF) has shown that English in international communication is best understood not as a fixed native-speaker variety, but as a function performed in multilingual encounters (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010; Seidlhofer, 2009). From this perspective, successful English use depends less on conformity to British or American norms than on intelligibility, negotiation of meaning, intercultural awareness and flexible use of linguistic resources (Seidlhofer, Breiteneder, & Pitzl, 2006; McKay, 2018).

This shift has important consequences for English language teaching, particularly in primary education, where learners’ attitudes towards languages and language learning are still being formed. If English is presented as a language belonging only to native speakers and associated mainly with Anglo-American cultural models, learners may perceive it as separate from, or even superior to, their own linguistic repertoire. Conversely, if English is taught as a language for international communication, it can coexist with learners’ mother tongues and contribute to the development of plurilingual competence. House’s distinction between languages for communication and languages for identification is especially relevant here: English may serve communicative purposes across communities, while the mother tongue continues to play a central role in identity, emotional attachment and cultural belonging (House, 2003). Such a distinction allows English to be valued without displacing other languages.

A plurilingual approach to English teaching therefore challenges the traditional monolingual principle that the target language should be kept separate from learners’ first language. Rather than treating the L1 as interference, plurilingual pedagogy regards it as part of the learner’s communicative system and as a resource for comparison, scaffolding and meaning-making. This is particularly important in multilingual societies, but it is also relevant in apparently monolingual classrooms, since all learners develop language awareness by relating new linguistic knowledge to what they already know. In this sense, the use of the mother tongue in English lessons is not a retreat from communicative teaching; it is a means of supporting communication and building metalinguistic understanding.

At the same time, the global role of English raises ecological questions. The expansion of ELF can be seen either as a threat to linguistic diversity or as an opportunity to rethink language relations in more sustainable ways. An ecological perspective emphasises the interaction between languages and their social environments and warns against monocultural or monolingual models of language education. In such a perspective, the goal is not to replace local languages with English, but to promote a balanced linguistic ecosystem in which English functions as a shared communicative tool while other languages remain valued as resources for identity, learning and participation.

Although European language policy has increasingly promoted plurilingualism, classroom practice often remains shaped by monolingual assumptions and native-speaker norms. Moreover, countries that follow similar international guidelines may interpret and implement them very differently, depending on their sociolinguistic histories, educational policies and levels of exposure to English. This article examines these issues through initial findings from a broader international research project on primary English education. Focusing on schools in Spain and Norway, it compares monolingual and plurilingual approaches to teaching English and explores learners’ attitudes towards English and their mother tongue. The study aims to show that integrating the L1 into English lessons can improve learning outcomes and foster a more ecological understanding of the relationship between English and other languages.

intros.text:
The global spread of English has made English language teaching in primary education a central concern for teachers, policy makers and researchers. In many contexts, children encounter English not only as a school subject but also as a resource for international communication, digital participation and future mobility. At the same time, English is learned within already existing linguistic ecologies: learners bring to the classroom one or more home, regional or national languages through which they construct knowledge, identity and social belonging. The question for contemporary ELT is therefore not simply how early learners can acquire English more efficiently, but how English can be taught without weakening the value of the other languages that form part of their communicative repertoires.

Research on English as a lingua franca (ELF) and English as an international language has challenged native-speaker-centred assumptions in language pedagogy. ELF has been described less as a stable variety than as a function English performs in multilingual encounters (Friedrich & Matsuda, 2010; Mollin, 2006), and ELF research has emphasised ownership, intelligibility, language contact and the diverse realities of English use beyond traditional inner-circle norms (Seidlhofer, 2009; Seidlhofer et al., 2006). House (2003) further distinguishes between languages for communication and languages for identification, arguing that the communicative role of English need not constitute a threat to multilingualism if local languages continue to carry symbolic and affective value. Pedagogically, this perspective implies that English should not be presented exclusively as British or American cultural property, nor should learners’ first languages be treated as interference to be excluded from the classroom. Rather, learners may benefit from approaches that recognise the full range of their linguistic resources and prepare them to use English flexibly in intercultural communication (McKay, 2018).

Despite this theoretical shift, much primary-school ELT continues to be organised around monolingual classroom practices and native-speaker models of authenticity. The use of the mother tongue is often restricted, and plurilingualism is frequently understood as the addition of foreign languages rather than as the integrated development of a learner’s whole linguistic repertoire. This is particularly problematic in multilingual or bilingual regions where children’s L1s are not merely transitional supports but central components of identity and learning. Moreover, although European language policy promotes plurilingual and intercultural competence, its implementation varies substantially across national and local contexts. Spain and Norway, for example, both operate within broad European frameworks, yet they differ markedly in learners’ exposure to English, curricular treatment of English as an international language, and recognition of relationships between English, the mother tongue and other languages.

What remains insufficiently explored is how a plurilingual and ecological approach can be enacted in primary-school English lessons and whether the principled use of L1 can improve young learners’ English performance while also fostering a positive orientation towards linguistic diversity. More empirical classroom-based work is needed across different educational contexts, particularly with young learners, to examine whether the mother tongue can function as a scaffold for English learning and as a means of sustaining rather than displacing local linguistic identities.

This paper addresses this need by presenting initial findings from a broader international research project on plurilingual English teaching in primary education. Focusing on data from Year 6 learners in Spain and Norway, the study compares lessons taught through a monolingual English-only approach with lessons taught through a plurilingual approach in which the mother tongue is used strategically for explanation, comparison and communication. The study also considers learners’ attitudes towards English and their mother tongue in order to connect language learning outcomes with an ecological view of language education. By bringing together ELF, plurilingual pedagogy and language ecology, the paper argues that primary ELT can promote English as a shared communicative tool while affirming the continuing importance of learners’ own languages.

intros.text: Teaching English has become a widely researched and discussed priority in education, and it is in the joint interest of stakeholders and policy makers to reach the most effective outcomes  Parents of very young children are generally on the opinion that it is ideal to start as early as possible (Griva and Chouvarda 2012, Linse 2011, Purdjaková 2006). Language learning is generally believed to have wideranging benefits on the child’s personal, intellectual, educational development and future career prospects (Tekin 2015: 39). Correspondingly, Greek parents were reported to be aware of the benefits of multilingualism and have positive attitudes towards early start provided that learning materials are suitable to young learners and their specific age-related needs are taken into consideration (Griva and Chouvarda 2012: 10–11). However, it is not evident that an early start of learning foreign languages is an advantage in and of itself (Nikolov and Djigunović 2011). For instance, Hanušová and Najvar (2005) investigated the long-term effects of an early start by examining university entrance exam language test scores. They found no evidence of any relationship between test score results and the start of language learning (Hanušová and Najvar 2005: 209–210). According to a public opinion survey carried out in the Czech Republic in 2006, around 68% of the public (nonteachers, generally parents) are of the opinion that children should start learning English as a Foreign Language as early as in kindergarten (Purdjaková 2006). It is essential to note that an early start is not an essential prerequisite to successful outcomes. Eventual learning success for young learners depends on an interplay of various other factors such as continuity, language policy, classroom circumstances, curriculum, or the qualification of the teacher (Hanušová and Najvar 2005, Nikolov and Djigunović 2011, Purdjaková 2006). In spite of the key role of the teacher’s proficiency and language use in the classroom, Nikolov (2006) draws attention to the scarcity of available research focusing on the effect of teachers’ pronunciation and fluency as a major factor contributing to young learners’ language development (Nikolov 2006: 250)  However, it has recently become popular and viable to carry out research into stakeholder attitudes since it is very important to have a dialogue between parents and teachers (Linse 2011, Nikolov and Djigunović 2011).  For these reasons, it is of interest what views parents have about teachers and teacher accent when it comes to dealing with young learners.

intros.text:
The teaching of English as a foreign language to children at an early (7-12) and even at a very early (under 7) age has become increasingly widespread and accessible across the world. This trend has been driven, to a considerable extent, by parents who wish their children to acquire English skills as soon as possible in response to the demands of a globalizing world in which English functions as a lingua franca (Tekin 2015). In many contexts, from Oman to Korea and across Europe, parents make substantial financial and personal investments in the early foreign-language education of their children and are keen to ensure that early exposure will secure a future advantage (Linse 2011, Tekin 2015). As a consequence, early programmes have mushroomed, sometimes ahead of the research and policy that ought to guide them (Nikolov and Mihaljević Djigunović 2006, 2011).

Within this landscape, parents emerge as essential stakeholders in the foreign-language education of very young learners. They are typically the key decision makers who determine when, how, and in what language their children begin learning, and their beliefs and expectations shape both the provision they seek and the attitudes their children develop. It is therefore beneficial for the future of TEFL to investigate parental attitudes, so that the expectations parents hold and the outcomes that programmes can realistically deliver may be brought into alignment. Previous research, however, has repeatedly noted that parents often voice unrealistic expectations regarding the proficiency, and particularly the pronunciation, they anticipate their children will attain (Linse 2011). Parental beliefs have also been shown to vary according to demographic and sociocultural factors, including parental education, age, and language-learning background (Griva and Chouvarda 2012, Tekin 2015).

One area in which parental expectations may be especially demanding concerns the teacher, and in particular the teacher's pronunciation or accent. In many settings, native-speaker norms retain considerable prestige, and native-speaking teachers are frequently assumed to be the most desirable, yet the appropriate age at which children should begin learning remains contested (Hanušová et al. 2005, Purdjaková 2006, Nikolov and Mihaljević Djigunović 2011). Whether attitudes towards accent differ among parents who favour an earlier or later start has received little attention.

It further explores how these attitudes relate to parents' self-rated proficiency in English, their plans to move abroad, and whether their children learn English in formal or informal contexts.

intros.text:
Teaching English as a foreign language at an early (7-12) and even at a very early (under 7) age is becoming increasingly popular and accessible worldwide. This growing interest is often driven by parents, who see the demands of a globalizing world and wish to ensure their children can thrive in a future in which English plays a central role (Tekin 2015). Indeed, in many contexts, from the Gulf Region to Korea and Central Europe, parents invest heavily in their children's English education and begin this process at ever-younger ages (Linse 2011, Tekin 2015). As a result, teachers of very young learners frequently face pressure and expectations from parents regarding the nature and quality of instruction they provide.

Parents, then, are essential stakeholders in the teaching of English to young and very young learners, since it is largely the family that decides when and what language a child begins to learn and shapes the child's attitudes towards the languages studied. It follows that understanding parental attitudes is beneficial for the future of the field, allowing practitioners and policy makers to ensure that expectations and outcomes meet. A considerable body of research has addressed the age question, examining the benefits and possible threats of an early start (Nikolov and Djigunović 2006, 2011, Hanušová and Najvar 2005), while other studies have surveyed public and professional opinion about the ideal starting age (Purdjaková 2006).

A parallel strand of research has explored parental beliefs about early EFL, identifying links between attitudes and demographic factors such as maternal education, parental age, and sociocultural background (Griva and Chouvarda 2012, Tekin 2015, Linse 2011). Attitudes towards accent and native-speaker norms have likewise attracted much attention, revealing that native varieties are often accorded greater prestige while non-native, including local, accents are frequently disfavoured. However, comparatively little is known about how parents of very young learners in Hungary view the pronunciation of the teacher, and whether such attitudes vary according to the age at which parents prefer language learning to begin, their own self-rated proficiency, their plans to move abroad, or the formal or informal context in which their children learn. Addressing this gap, the present study examines the attitudes of fifty Hungarian parents of children aged 0-7 towards teacher accent and the ideal age to start learning a foreign language, drawing on an online questionnaire that included an 8-item attitude scale measuring responses towards American, British, and Hungarian pronunciation. In doing so, we aim to shed light on the extent to which native-speakerism persists among these key stakeholders.

intros.text:
The proliferation of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction for children aged 7–12 (young learners) and those under 7 (very young learners) has grown significantly worldwide (Nikolov & Djigunovćić, 2011). This trend is largely driven by parental demand, as parents increasingly view early language acquisition as a necessity for their children to succeed in a globalized society (Tekin, 2015). Because parents act as primary stakeholders and decision-makers regarding when and how their children begin their linguistic journey, their beliefs and expectations profoundly shape the educational landscape and the perceived success of early childhood programs (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012; Linse, 2011). Consequently, understanding parental attitudes is essential to ensure that pedagogical outcomes align with stakeholder expectations.

One of the most contentious issues in early EFL is the role of the teacher’s linguistic profile, specifically regarding pronunciation and accent. The phenomenon of "native-speakerism"—the preference for native-speaking teachers over non-native speakers—remains prevalent in many contexts. While some parents may prioritize native-like pronunciation to provide an "ideal" model for their children to mimic, others may value methodological competence or communicative efficiency over a specific accent. In the Hungarian context, where compulsory formal education begins at age three, there is a diverse range of early start programs, yet research on how parents perceive the pronunciation of teachers in these very early settings remains sparse.

While existing literature has explored student attitudes toward native and non-native accents (e.g., Feyér, 2015), there is a need to examine whether these preferences differ among parents based on their own linguistic backgrounds or their views on the ideal age to start learning. For instance, parents who advocate for the earliest possible start (before preschool) may hold different expectations regarding teacher pronunciation than those who prefer a start in primary school. Furthermore, demographic factors and future intentions, such as plans to move abroad, may influence the value placed on specific native varieties like British or American English.

This study aims to fill this gap by examining the attitudes of Hungarian parents toward teacher pronunciation in very early English contexts. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether parental preferences for teacher accents vary according to the preferred age of language onset, the parents' self-assessed proficiency levels, their intentions to migrate, and the formality of the educational context in which their children learn. By mapping these attitudes, the study contributes to a broader discussion on the legitimacy of non-native pronunciation and the shift toward communicative pragmatism in early childhood education.

intros.text:
Teaching English as a foreign language (TEFL) to young learners (ages 7–12) and very young learners (under 7) has seen a significant rise in popularity and accessibility worldwide. This trend is largely driven by increasing pressure from parents who view early language acquisition as a vital asset in a globalizing world (Tekin, 2015). Consequently, early childhood education programs have mushroomed across various regions, from the Gulf states to Europe (Nikolov & Djigunović, 2006). In these contexts, parents act as essential stakeholders and key decision-makers, as their beliefs and expectations often shape the educational trajectories and motivations of their children (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012; Linse, 2011). 

Within the discourse of early TEFL, much attention has been paid to the ideal age of onset and the role of the teacher. While some research emphasizes the cognitive benefits of an early start, others highlight the potential threats to first language development (Nikolov & Djigunović, 2006, 2011). A recurring point of contention is the requirement for native-speaker proficiency. In many cultures, there is a strong preference for native-speaking teachers, often rooted in the belief that they provide the most authentic pronunciation models (Linse, 2011). However, this focus on "native-speakerism" is increasingly being questioned in favor of communicative efficiency and pedagogical competence. 

Despite the abundance of research on teacher proficiency and student outcomes, there remains a gap in our understanding of how parents specifically perceive teacher pronunciation in the context of very early English. While studies have examined general parental beliefs about early EFL in places like Oman (Tekin, 2015) or Korea (Linse, 2011), few have empirically investigated the specific attitudes of parents toward different accents—such as British, American, or local varieties—and how these attitudes correlate with the parents' own linguistic backgrounds or their preferences for the age of starting instruction. 

Therefore, the present study aims to examine parental attitudes toward teacher pronunciation among Hungarian parents of children aged 0–7. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether these attitudes differ based on the preferred age of language onset, the parents' self-assessed proficiency, their plans to move abroad, and the educational context (formal vs. informal) of the child. By employing an online questionnaire and a Likert-scale attitude measure, this research intends to provide a nuanced account of the expectations parents hold regarding the "ideal" pronunciation model for very young learners. In doing so, it hopes to contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the necessity of native-speaker norms in early childhood education.

intros.text:
Teaching English as a foreign language (EFL) at an early age is becoming increasingly popular and accessible, largely driven by parental pressure and the global status of English (Tekin, 2015). Parents are essential stakeholders in the TEFL of young and very young learners, and their expectations significantly influence educational outcomes. Consequently, it is beneficial for the future of EFL to research parental attitudes to ensure that expectations and outcomes align. This study examines parental attitudes towards the teacher's pronunciation and the ideal age to start learning a foreign language.

The role of parents in foreign language education is well-documented. Research indicates that parents are key decision-makers who shape their children's learning trajectories and attitudes towards language acquisition (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012; Linse, 2011). In many contexts, including Korea and Oman, parents are willing to make significant financial investments to secure early English instruction for their children, often driven by the belief that early exposure guarantees success (Linse, 2011; Tekin, 2015). However, the efficacy of early start programs and the optimal age for beginning foreign language learning remain subjects of debate within applied linguistics (Nikolov & Mihaljević Djigunović, 2006, 2011). While some researchers argue that early exposure is crucial, others caution against the potential threats to first language development and identity (Nikolov & Mihaljević Djigunović, 2011).

A critical component of early language learning is the quality of the teacher, particularly regarding pronunciation. In the context of World Englishes and the dominance of native-speakerism, stakeholders often attribute success to native-speaking teachers (Holliday, 2005). However, the preference for specific accents, such as British or American English, varies across cultures and is often influenced by the perceived prestige of certain varieties (Balogh, 2014). In Hungary, where this study is situated, there is a growing trend towards early English, yet the attitudes of parents towards teacher pronunciation, specifically the preference for native versus non-native accents, remain under-researched. Previous studies in the region have highlighted the prevalence of 'native-speakerism' but also noted a shift towards valuing intelligibility and communicative efficiency over strict adherence to native norms (Timmis, 2002).

Despite the proliferation of early English programs in Hungary, there is a lack of empirical data regarding parental expectations concerning teacher pronunciation and the ideal starting age for very young learners. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the attitudes of Hungarian parents of children aged 0-7. Specifically, it seeks to determine whether parental attitudes towards teacher accent vary based on their preferred starting age for foreign language instruction, their own proficiency levels, and their educational contexts. By mapping these attitudes, this research contributes to a better understanding of the complex interplay between parental expectations, teacher qualifications, and early language learning outcomes.

The role of parents in shaping children's language learning trajectories is well-documented. Research indicates that parental beliefs significantly influence learners' motivation and attitudes (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012; Linse, 2011). In contexts ranging from Korea to Greece, parents are often key decision-makers, determining when and how their children begin learning a foreign language (Linse, 2011; Tekin, 2015). However, these attitudes are not uniform; they are often shaped by demographic factors and the perceived prestige of native speaker norms. In many EFL contexts, there is a prevailing tendency to favor native-speaking teachers, a phenomenon often termed 'native-speakerism' (Nikolov & Djigunović, 2011). This preference frequently extends to specific accents, with British or American varieties often viewed as superior to local or non-native varieties (Feyér, 2015).

Despite the extensive literature on accent attitudes and parental involvement, a gap remains regarding the intersection of these variables in the context of very early English learning. While studies have examined parental beliefs in various regions (Tekin, 2015; Linse, 2011), fewer have specifically investigated how parents of very young learners (aged 0–7) perceive teacher pronunciation. Furthermore, it is unclear whether these attitudes vary based on the parents' preferred age for starting instruction. Some research suggests that parents favoring an earlier start may hold different expectations regarding teacher proficiency compared to those opting for a later start (Nikolov & Djigunović, 2006). Additionally, the influence of parental proficiency and migration plans on these attitudes requires further empirical investigation.

This study aims to address these gaps by examining parental attitudes towards teacher pronunciation in the context of very early English in Hungary. Specifically, it investigates the importance parents place on native-like pronunciation versus other teacher qualities. Furthermore, it explores whether these attitudes differ among parents who prefer an early start to language learning compared to those favoring a later start. By analyzing the relationship between parental demographics, proficiency levels, and their expectations of teacher accent, this research seeks to provide insights into the evolving landscape of early EFL education and the persistence of native-speaker norms.

intros.text:
English is increasingly introduced in foreign language education at an early, and in many contexts a very early, age. This tendency is often justified by reference to children’s presumed advantages in language learning, but research has repeatedly shown that age alone does not guarantee successful outcomes; the quality, amount and continuity of input, the aims of the programme, teacher expertise and the wider learning environment are all crucial (Nikolov & Mihaljević Djigunović, 2006, 2011; Hanušová et al., 2005). Nevertheless, early English programmes have expanded rapidly across diverse EFL settings, partly because parents associate English with future educational, professional and mobility opportunities and therefore seek to provide their children with access to English as soon as possible (Tekin, 2015; Linse, 2011). In Hungary, as in many Central European contexts, foreign language learning is compulsory only later in primary school, yet kindergartens, private providers and families increasingly offer English activities before the official starting point.

Parents are therefore central stakeholders in early and very early English education. Their beliefs influence whether children start learning a foreign language, which language they learn, what type of programme they attend, and what expectations are attached to instruction. Previous studies have shown that parental beliefs about early English are shaped by educational background, language learning experience, sociocultural context and perceptions of children’s future needs (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012; Linse, 2011; Tekin, 2015). At the same time, parental expectations may not always correspond to what is pedagogically realistic or desirable for very young learners. This is especially important because young children require age-appropriate methodology, meaningful interaction and positive affective conditions rather than formal, accuracy-centred instruction.

One particularly sensitive issue concerns the pronunciation and accent of the teacher. In many EFL contexts, native speaker models continue to enjoy high prestige, and parents may assume that a native-speaking teacher, or a teacher with a British or American accent, provides the best input. Such expectations reflect wider ideologies of native-speakerism, despite extensive arguments that intelligibility, comprehensibility and communicative effectiveness are more appropriate goals than imitation of a native norm, especially in international uses of English. The issue is further complicated in early childhood education, where teachers are expected not only to provide a good linguistic model but also to understand children’s developmental needs and employ suitable methodology.

The present study investigates Hungarian parents’ attitudes towards teacher pronunciation in very early English. It focuses on parents of children aged 0–7 and examines how they evaluate native speaker status, British and American accents, Hungarian-accented English, pronunciation, fluency, comprehensibility and methodology. It also explores whether these attitudes vary according to parents’ preferred age for starting foreign language learning, self-rated English proficiency, plans to move abroad and their children’s formal or informal learning contexts.

intros.text:
English language learning is increasingly introduced before the traditional start of compulsory foreign language education, and in many contexts children encounter English not only as young learners but also as very young learners. This tendency is often driven by parental demand, as parents associate early English with future educational, social, and economic opportunities in a globalised world. At the same time, early foreign language education remains a debated field: an early start is widely believed to be advantageous, yet research has shown that its success depends on conditions such as programme quality, teacher expertise, appropriate methodology, and realistic expectations rather than on age alone (Nikolov & Mihaljević Djigunović, 2006, 2011; Hanušová et al., 2005).

Parents are central stakeholders in very early English education because they decide when and where their children begin learning, choose formal or informal learning opportunities, and often evaluate teachers and programmes according to their own beliefs about language learning. Studies from different contexts have shown that parental attitudes can influence children’s access to English and the types of provision they receive. In Korea, parents’ expectations were found to exert pressure on teachers and to combine research-informed views with more traditional beliefs about instruction (Linse, 2011). In Oman, parents were reported to be strongly aware of the perceived benefits and challenges of early EFL education (Tekin, 2015). In Greece, parents acknowledged the importance of English while also valuing broader multilingual development (Griva & Chouvarda, 2012). Such findings indicate that parental beliefs are context-sensitive and should be examined locally.

One particularly sensitive issue in English teaching is pronunciation. Native-speaker accents, especially British and American varieties, continue to enjoy prestige in many EFL contexts, even though applied linguistic research has increasingly questioned native-speaker norms and emphasised intelligibility, comprehensibility, and communicative effectiveness. For teachers of very young learners, this issue is especially important because parents may expect children to acquire “good” or native-like pronunciation from the beginning, while successful teaching at this age also requires appropriate pedagogy and an understanding of child development. The perceived value of native-speaker pronunciation may therefore affect how parents judge native and non-native English teachers, including teachers who speak English with a Hungarian accent.

Despite the growing availability of early and very early English programmes, relatively little is known about Hungarian parents’ attitudes towards teachers’ pronunciation in this age group, or about whether such attitudes vary according to parents’ preferred starting age, language proficiency, plans to move abroad, and children’s learning contexts. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates Hungarian parents of children aged 0–7 through an online questionnaire. It examines their attitudes towards teacher accent, including British, American, native-speaker, and Hungarian-accented pronunciation, and explores how these attitudes relate to selected demographic and language-learning variables. By doing so, the study aims to contribute to a more contextually grounded understanding of parental expectations in very early English education.

intros.text: As with other learner characteristics, such as motivation and learning styles, much  attention has been focused on the beliefs of second language (L2) learners, that is, “the  general assumptions that students hold about themselves as learners, about factors  influencing language learning, and about the nature of language learning and teaching”  (Victori & Lockart, 1995, p. 224). Given that L2 learning beliefs are relevant to understanding learner “expectations of, commitment to, success in, and satisfaction with”  a learning environment (Horwitz, 1988, p. 283), they are thought to be among the vital  factors that account for the experiences and outcomes of individuals’ language learning  (Kalaja & Barcelos, 2013).  L2 learning beliefs can indicate the decisions learners make  (McDonough, 1995) and may influence the ways they approach the challenge of learning  a language (Kalaja, Barcelos, & Aro, 2018). In the increasingly skill-focused mode of  English language learning promoted in the education sector in Japan (see Kubota, 2015),  such as task-based teaching (Willis & Willis, 2007), the active role is handed over to  learners. The extended discretion bestowed on learners with regard to how they should  approach learning means they have more freedom to negotiate their learning approach. In  increasingly flexible circumstances, some limiting beliefs may exercise an inhibiting effect on learner perception and behaviour and, consequently, may limit the path to  successful learning, which involves change, such as “stretching” of the learning style  (Griffiths & İnceçay, 2016; Ma & Oxford, 2014). Hence, learner expectations,  experience, and understanding of the optimal form and content of language learning have  come under greater scrutiny (Abe, 2013).  According to the literature (see, for example, Benson & Lor, 1999; Bernat & Lloyd,  2007; White, 1999), research on how students perceive and approach foreign language  learning across different contexts is essential for constructing an informed pedagogic  practice.  As learner expectations of the learning context are rooted in beliefs that are  informed by national belonging, as well as in previous experience (Horwitz, 1987), many  studies have focused on the linkage between beliefs and cultural membership (De Costa,  2011; Horwitz, 1999; Pan & Block, 2011), and between beliefs and instructional  approaches or new learning environments (Amuzie & Winke, 2009; Johnson, 1994;  Loewen et al., 2009)  However, few studies narrow the focus to specific university  disciplines, thus, there is insufficient evidence clarifying the linkage between the  precursors of students’ disciplinary choices and their conceptions of the aims and means  of language learning (Trinder, 2013).  The present study investigates whether the  antecedents that form students’ choice of university discipline might intervene in  language learning in Japanese higher education.

intros.text:
Learners' beliefs about second language (L2) learning have long attracted the attention of applied linguists because such beliefs are understood to influence learners' strategies, expectations, and ultimate success (Horwitz, 1988, 1999). Since the development of Horwitz's (1987) Beliefs About Language Learning Instrument (BALLI), a substantial body of research has documented the ways in which learners' convictions about aptitude, difficulty, the nature of language learning, and appropriate learning strategies inform their classroom behaviour (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007; Loewen et al., 2009). More recently, researchers have shown that these beliefs are not fixed but emerge, and sometimes change, in response to learners' experiences, as demonstrated in studies of study abroad (Amuzie & Winke, 2009) and self-instruction (White, 1999). Correspondingly, the field has witnessed a shift from a strictly positivist orientation, which treats beliefs as measurable mental representations, towards a contextual perspective that views beliefs as idiosyncratic and situated within particular learning communities (Benson & Lor, 1999; De Costa, 2011; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012; Kalaja et al., 2017).

Much of this research, particularly in the Japanese higher education setting, has relied on survey instruments to map the belief structures of undergraduate learners. Sakui and Gaies (1999) developed a context-specific questionnaire and identified a robust factorial structure among Japanese university students, an instrument subsequently taken up in comparable studies that consistently involved English or arts and humanities majors (Yonesaka, 2008; Yonesaka & Tanaka, 2013). These studies have established a shared belief structure among such learners, but they have paid little attention to whether students in other disciplines conceive of language learning in the same way. This gap is significant in a context where the Japanese Ministry of Education has pressed for a stronger orientation towards communicative competence (Abe, 2013; Kubota, 2015), yet where many university English programmes remain focused on receptive skills. Studies of business (Trinder, 2013) and ESP learners (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007) suggest that disciplinary context may shape how learners understand the purpose and difficulty of language learning, but engineering students remain largely unexamined.

The present study proceeds from the supposition that students' choice of tertiary subject, together with their prior schooling, may attract learners with similar individual traits, including their beliefs about L2 learning. The problem-solving, practical orientation of engineering, alongside the divergent experiences of academic and vocational high school graduates, may give rise to belief structures that differ from those documented among non-engineering majors. Using a mixed-methods design that combines Sakui and Gaies' (1999) questionnaire with narrative interview data, this study addresses two questions: (1) What beliefs do engineering students hold about English learning, and how can these beliefs be explained? and (2) Are there differences in students' beliefs according to their prior secondary education? In doing so, it seeks to raise teachers' awareness of how such beliefs may shape learning behaviour and preferred learning styles (Griffiths & İ nceçay, 2015; Ma & Oxford, 2014).

intros.text:
Learners' beliefs about second language (L2) learning are increasingly recognised as a significant individual difference that shapes how students approach the task of language study, the strategies they deploy, and ultimately their learning outcomes (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007; Loewen et al., 2009). Because beliefs can affect learning behaviour and success, understanding them is important for teachers seeking to align their instruction with the dispositions their students bring to the classroom (Horwitz, 1988, 1999). Research on this topic has broadly followed two epistemological traditions. The positivist approach treats beliefs as relatively stable cognitive representations that can be elicited through psychometric surveys such as Horwitz's (1987) Beliefs about Language Learning Instrument, whereas the more recent contextual approach highlights the emic, idiosyncratic, and transient nature of beliefs as they are constructed within particular social and institutional environments (De Costa, 2011; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012; White, 1999).

In the Japanese higher education setting, much of the work on L2 learning beliefs has operated from the positivist perspective (Amuzie & Winke, 2009; Horwitz, 1999). A seminal contribution was made by Sakui and Gaies (1999), whose survey of approximately 1,300 university students yielded a four-factor structure and has since become a recognised instrument in Japanese contexts. Subsequent studies drawing on this common format have consistently reported that university students share a broadly similar belief structure. This convergence is of particular interest given the emphasis that the Japanese Ministry of Education has placed on developing communicative competence and expanding communicative language teaching in schools (Abe, 2013; Kubota, 2015).

However, these Japanese studies have almost exclusively involved English-major and arts and humanities undergraduates. Comparatively little is known about whether the belief structures identified among such students also hold for learners in other, contrasting disciplines. Business students, for instance, have been shown to hold discipline-specific conceptions of language learning (Trinder, 2013), yet the beliefs of engineering students, whose degrees emphasise problem-solving and practical application, remain largely unexplored in this literature. It is therefore unclear whether the practical, technical orientation of engineering study is associated with a distinctive organisation of L2 learning beliefs, and whether students' prior secondary schooling contributes to any such variation.

The present mixed-methods study addresses this gap. It begins from the supposition that a given tertiary subject area, together with students' former school experience, may attract or nurture learners with similar traits, including beliefs about L2 learning. Using Sakui and Gaies' (1999) questionnaire with 253 engineering students in Japan, complemented by narrative interviews, the study asks: (1) What beliefs do these engineering students hold about English learning, and how can their beliefs be explained? and (2) Do their beliefs differ according to the secondary education they received? In doing so, the study seeks to sharpen teachers' awareness of how individual belief orientations may influence learners' behaviour and preferred learning styles.

intros.text:
Learner beliefs regarding second language (L2) acquisition are complex, multifaceted constructs shaped by a dynamic interplay of internal cognitive representations and external environmental factors (Bernat & Gvozdenko, 2005). Within the field of applied linguistics, research into these beliefs has traditionally oscillated between two epistemological poles. A positivist approach treats beliefs as stable mental traits that can be mapped through psychometric instruments, such as the Beliefs About Language Learning Instrument developed by Horwitz (1987, 1988). Conversely, a contextual approach views beliefs as idiosyncratic, transient, and socially constructed phenomena, emphasizing the emic perspective of the learner within their specific institutional and social environment (De Costa, 2011). Understanding these beliefs is critical, as they can significantly influence a learner's behavior, strategy use, and overall success in the language classroom (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012).

In the context of Japanese higher education, most studies on L2 beliefs have adopted a positivist framework, often utilizing the Beliefs about Language Learning Questionnaire developed by Sakui and Gaies (1999). A substantial body of research using this instrument has focused predominantly on university students majoring in English, revealing a relatively consistent and shared belief structure among these arts and humanities students (Riley, 2006, 2009; Yonesaka, 2008; Yonesaka & Tanaka, 2013). However, there is a paucity of research examining whether these belief structures remain consistent across different academic disciplines. Given that different tertiary subject areas may attract students with distinct individual traits and metacognitive orientations, it is plausible that students in practical, problem-solving disciplines—such as engineering—may hold different conceptions of language learning compared to their peers in the humanities (Trinder, 2013).

Furthermore, the formation of these beliefs is likely influenced by a student's prior educational trajectory. In Japan, the distinction between academic and vocational high school curricula may instill different values regarding the utility and nature of English language study. While the Japanese Ministry of Education has moved toward emphasizing communicative competence (Abe, 2013), the actual experiences of students in these different school tracks may vary significantly.

This study aims to explore the latent factorial structure of L2 learning beliefs among Japanese engineering students and to examine how these beliefs differ based on their secondary school background. Specifically, the inquiry is guided by two research questions: (1) What beliefs do engineering students have about English learning, and how can these beliefs be explained? and (2) Are there significant differences in these beliefs between students who graduated from academic high schools versus those from vocational high schools?

intros.text:
Second language (L2) learners' beliefs are inherently multifaceted constructs that are intricately informed by both internal cognitive factors and external environmental influences (Bernat & Gvozdenko, 2005). In the field of applied linguistics, these beliefs are viewed as critical individual differences that can significantly impact a learner's behavior, strategy use, and overall success in language acquisition (Horwitz, 1988; Loewen et al., 2009). Traditionally, research has operated from a positivist perspective, treating beliefs as mental representations that can be mapped via psychometric instruments (Horwitz, 1987). More recently, however, a contextual approach has emerged, emphasizing the emic perspective and viewing beliefs as idiosyncratic, context-specific phenomena constructed in relation to the learner's social and institutional environment (De Costa, 2011). 

Within the Japanese higher education context, most L2 belief research has adhered to the positivist tradition (Riley, 2006, 2009; Yonesaka, 2008). A seminal contribution by Sakui and Gaies (1999) established a four-factor structure of language learning beliefs among Japanese university students, providing a definitive instrument that has been widely adopted. Subsequent studies using this framework have consistently demonstrated that English-major students in Japan share a common L2 learning belief structure (Riley, 2006, 2009; Yonesaka & Tanaka, 2013). However, while evidence abounds regarding students in the arts and humanities, there is a notable paucity of research focusing on students in discipline-specific tertiary settings, such as engineering. Given that the problem-solving and practical nature of engineering may attract individuals with specific metacognitive traits, it remains unclear whether the belief structures of engineering majors differ from those of their non-engineering peers.

The present study aims to address this gap by exploring the latent factorial structure of language learning beliefs among 253 engineering students in Japan. Specifically, the research seeks to determine what beliefs these students hold and whether their beliefs vary according to their secondary education background—comparing those from academic high schools with those from vocational high schools. To achieve this, the study employs a mixed-methods design, utilizing the Sakui and Gaies (1999) questionnaire for quantitative analysis, supplemented by narrative interviews to capture the idiosyncratic nature of student beliefs. By identifying the unique perceptual patterns of engineering students, this research hopes to provide insights that can help foreign language teachers better align their instructional approaches with the preferred learning styles and convictions of students in technical disciplines.

The remainder of the article is organized as follows: the methodology is detailed in the following sections, followed by a presentation of the descriptive statistics and factor analysis results. Finally, the findings are discussed in relation to the students' school careers and the broader implications for L2 pedagogy.

intros.text:
Learners' beliefs about second language (L2) learning are inherently multifaceted constructs, intricately informed by both internal cognitive factors and external contextual influences (Bernat & Gvozdenko, 2005). While traditional positivist approaches treat these beliefs as stable mental representations that can be mapped through psychometric surveys (Horwitz, 1987), contemporary contextual approaches emphasize the dynamic linkage between individual learners and the institutional structures they inhabit (Barcelos, 2003; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2013). This contextual perspective views beliefs as idiosyncratic and transient phenomena, constructed in relation to the specific social environments in which learners are nurtured (Riley, 2009; Sakui & Gaies, 1999). Despite this theoretical shift, research in Japanese higher education has predominantly operated from a positivist standpoint, utilizing instruments like the Beliefs about Language Learning Questionnaire (Sakui & Gaies, 1999) to identify consistent belief structures among university students.

Extant literature indicates that English-major undergraduates in Japan share a common four-factor belief structure, as evidenced by multiple studies employing the Sakui and Gaies instrument (Keim et al., 1996; Riley, 2006, 2009; Yonesaka, 2008; Yonesaka & Tanaka, 2013). However, these findings are largely confined to humanities and arts disciplines. There remains a paucity of research examining how L2 learning beliefs manifest in non-language majors, particularly within the discipline of engineering. The problem-solving and practical nature of engineering education may attract students with distinct individual traits and metacognitive styles, potentially resulting in a unique organization of language learning beliefs. Furthermore, the influence of secondary educational background—specifically the distinction between academic and vocational high schools—on the formation of these beliefs has not been sufficiently explored within this specific tertiary context.

This study aims to address these gaps by exploring the latent factorial structure of language learning beliefs among 253 engineering students in Japan. intros.text:
Learners’ beliefs about language learning have long been recognized as a critical component in second language acquisition, significantly influencing learners' strategies, motivation, and ultimate success (Horwitz, 1987; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012). These beliefs are complex, multifaceted constructs shaped by a confluence of internal cognitive factors and external contextual influences (Bernat & Gvozdenko, 2005). While early research often treated beliefs as static mental representations amenable to positivist measurement, contemporary scholarship increasingly emphasizes the contextual nature of belief formation, viewing them as dynamic phenomena constructed through interaction with social environments and institutional structures (Barcelos, 2003; Kalaja et al., 2018). In the Japanese higher education context, the majority of studies investigating L2 learner beliefs have operated from a positivist perspective, utilizing psychometric instruments to map cognitive structures (Keim et al., 1996; Riley, 2006; Yonesaka, 2008). A seminal contribution in this area is the work of Sakui and Gaies (1999), who established a four-factor structure of language learning beliefs among Japanese university students. This instrument has since become the standard for comparative research within the field, consistently revealing a shared belief structure among English-major undergraduates across various institutions (Riley, 2009; Yonesaka & Tanaka, 2013).

However, the existing literature is heavily skewed toward students in arts and humanities disciplines, particularly those majoring in English. Consequently, there is a paucity of research concerning the belief structures of students in non-linguistic fields, such as engineering. Given that the problem-solving and practical nature of engineering education may attract students with distinct individual traits and metacognitive styles, it is plausible that their beliefs about language learning differ significantly from those of their humanities counterparts. Furthermore, while previous studies have examined the impact of study abroad or specific pedagogical interventions on beliefs (Amuzie & Winke, 2009; Trinder, 2013), little attention has been paid to how prior secondary school experiences—specifically the distinction between academic and vocational high schools—might shape the L2 learning beliefs of engineering undergraduates. Understanding these discipline-specific and career-path-derived variations is essential for tailoring instruction to diverse learner needs.

This study aims to address these gaps by exploring the latent factorial structure of language learning beliefs among 253 engineering students in Japan. Utilizing the Sakui and Gaies (1999) Beliefs about Language Learning Questionnaire, the research investigates whether the belief structure of engineering students diverges from the established four-factor model found in non-engineering majors. Additionally, the study examines potential variations in beliefs based on the students' secondary school career. To provide a richer understanding of the quantitative data, the inquiry is complemented by qualitative narrative interviews. The findings suggest that engineering students exhibit a unique five-factor belief structure and that their communicative orientation is significantly influenced by their prior educational background. These results underscore the necessity for teachers to raise awareness of how specific learner beliefs influence learning behaviors and preferred styles, ultimately informing more responsive pedagogical practices in discipline-specific EFL contexts.

intros.text:
In an era in which English is routinely framed as a global resource for academic mobility, employment and intercultural communication, English language education in Japan continues to occupy a contested position. National curriculum reforms have repeatedly emphasized communicative competence and the practical use of English, yet university students often arrive with learning experiences shaped by examinations, grammar explanation and translation-oriented instruction (Abe, 2013; Kubota, 2015). This tension is particularly salient in tertiary settings where English is compulsory for students whose major fields are not language-related. For such learners, English may be understood less as an object of disciplinary study than as a tool whose value depends on perceived relevance to future study, work or everyday communication.

One important way of understanding students’ engagement with English is to examine their beliefs about language learning. Learner beliefs have been shown to influence how students interpret classroom practices, select strategies, respond to difficulty and evaluate their own progress (Horwitz, 1988, 1999; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012). They may include assumptions about aptitude, the role of grammar, the importance of communication, the amount of effort required, and the usefulness of particular learning methods. Such beliefs are not merely incidental opinions; they form part of learners’ metacognitive knowledge and can support or constrain autonomous learning (Victori & Lockhart, 1995; White, 1999). At the same time, research increasingly views beliefs as situated and dynamic, shaped by learners’ histories, institutional contexts and imagined futures rather than as stable traits alone (Amuzie & Winke, 2009; De Costa, 2011; Kalaja et al., 2017).

Much early work on learner beliefs was advanced through survey instruments such as Horwitz’s BALLI, which made it possible to compare belief patterns across groups and instructional contexts (Horwitz, 1987, 1988). Subsequent studies have shown that beliefs can vary according to target language, educational setting and disciplinary orientation (Loewen et al., 2009; Pan & Block, 2011). In English for specific purposes and university contexts, such variation is especially important because students’ academic majors and professional aspirations may mediate what they expect from English courses. For example, business students’ beliefs about English learning have been linked to their perceptions of institutional demands and professional utility (Trinder, 2013), while research in ESP contexts has highlighted how misconceptions may affect learning behaviours and instructional design (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007).

In Japan, however, much of the accumulated evidence on university students’ beliefs has focused on English majors or arts-oriented undergraduates, leaving comparatively little known about students in engineering education. This is a notable gap because engineering is often associated with practical problem solving, technical application and future participation in international professional communities. Engineering students may therefore bring to English learning belief systems that differ from those of students whose major studies are more closely aligned with language, culture or the humanities. Moreover, their prior schooling may matter: graduates of academic and vocational high schools typically experience different curricula, institutional expectations and amounts of English instruction, which may in turn shape their orientations toward communication, translation, effort and usefulness.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating Japanese engineering students’ beliefs about learning English and by examining whether these beliefs differ according to students’ secondary school background. Using Sakui and Gaies’ questionnaire, complemented by narrative interview data, the study explores both the latent structure of beliefs within this disciplinary setting and the ways individual learning histories illuminate quantitative patterns.

intros.text:
In Japan, English occupies a prominent yet contested position in education. National policy has increasingly emphasized communicative competence, reflecting the view that English is needed for participation in a globalized world, while classroom practices and learners’ experiences often remain shaped by examination pressures, grammar translation, and limited opportunities for meaningful interaction (Abe, 2013; Kubota, 2015). For university students, these tensions are especially consequential because compulsory English courses are expected to support both general education and future professional needs. Understanding how students conceive of language learning is therefore important for designing instruction that is responsive to their expectations, motivations, and learning behaviours.

Learners’ beliefs about second or foreign language learning have long been recognized as a significant individual difference in applied linguistics. Such beliefs may concern aptitude, difficulty, the role of grammar, the value of communication, preferred learning strategies, and expectations of success (Horwitz, 1987, 1988, 1999). They are also linked to metacognition and learner autonomy, since students’ assumptions about what language learning involves can influence how they allocate effort, interpret classroom tasks, and evaluate their own progress (Victori & Lockhart, 1995; White, 1999). Research has further shown that beliefs are not fixed or context-free. They may shift through experience, such as study abroad (Amuzie & Winke, 2009), and they may be shaped by social positioning, institutional environments, and broader language ideologies (De Costa, 2011; Kalaja & Barcelos, 2012; Kalaja et al., 2017).

A substantial body of work has investigated language learning beliefs through survey instruments, most notably Horwitz’s BALLI tradition, while more recent studies have complemented psychometric approaches with contextual and qualitative accounts. In Japan, Sakui and Gaies’ (1999) Beliefs about Language Learning Questionnaire provided a locally grounded instrument for examining university students’ beliefs and has enabled comparison across studies. Subsequent research has suggested that Japanese university students, particularly those in English-related or humanities-oriented programs, may share broadly similar structures of belief about language learning. At the same time, studies in English for specific purposes and disciplinary contexts indicate that learners’ academic fields and future professional orientations can shape what they value in language learning (Bernat & Lloyd, 2007; Loewen et al., 2009; Trinder, 2013).

Despite this growing literature, relatively little is known about the beliefs of engineering students in Japanese higher education. Engineering education is often associated with problem-solving, practical application, and technical specialization, and these characteristics may attract or cultivate orientations toward learning that differ from those of students in non-engineering disciplines. Moreover, Japanese engineering students enter university through varied school careers. Some come from academically oriented high schools with relatively intensive preparation for entrance examinations, whereas others come from vocational high schools where English may have occupied a different curricular and experiential role. It remains unclear whether such prior educational pathways are reflected in students’ beliefs about English learning at university.

The present study addresses this issue by investigating the language learning beliefs of engineering students at a regional Japanese university. Using Sakui and Gaies’ questionnaire together with narrative interview data, it explores the latent structure of these students’ beliefs and examines whether beliefs differ according to previous secondary education. The study is guided by two questions: What beliefs do engineering students have about English learning, and how can these beliefs be explained? Are there differences in these beliefs between students from academic and vocational high school backgrounds? By focusing on an underexamined disciplinary group, the study contributes to a more contextualized understanding of learner beliefs and offers implications for EFL teaching in engineering education.

intros.text: Writing is a way of connecting individuals with each other in ways that carry particular  special meanings, and the process of writing is a rich collection of elements (Hyland,  2003). Specifically, Hyland (2003) points out the merits of genre-based writing, which  unlike process approaches to writing, offers students “explicit and systematic  explanations of the ways language functions in social contexts” (Hyland, 2003, p. 18).  Genre-based writing is writing based on the assumption that the features of a similar  group of texts depend on the social context of their creation and use (Hyland, 2003). It  is based on the idea that members of a community are usually able to recognize  similarities in texts they use on a frequent basis, and are able to draw on repeated  experiences with such texts to read, understand and perhaps write such texts (Hyland,  2007). As such, genre-writing enables L2 users to use language to interpret  communicative situations, combining language together with content and context. Kern and Schultz (2005) view L2 literacy, which is defined as the “reciprocal  relationships among readers, writers, texts, culture and language learning” (Kern &  Schultz, 2005, p. 382), as being a combination of social, cognitive and linguistic  practices which differ according to situational and cultural contexts. Kern (2008) emphasizes the point that texts enable learners the opportunities to position themselves  in relation to viewpoints and cultures, and to “make the connection between grammar,  discourse, and meaning, between language and content, between language and culture,  and between another culture and their own” (Kern, 2008, p. 380).  Canagarajah (2011) looks at translanguaging in writing, which can bring discourse  and rhetorical issues into focus (p. 402).  Writing is different to speaking which is more  spontaneous, and unlike the relatively spontaneous speech act, the monitored and  somewhat detached activity of writing involves strategic options and choices. Students  have to develop a critical awareness of the choices that are rhetorically more effective.  Canagarajah (2014) points out that language choice can index the author’s reshaping of  identity, subjectivity, and role, providing additional layers to voice at the microtextual  level (p. 4). In his study, Canagarajah presents a model featuring identity, role,  subjectivity and awareness with the aim of exploring how these “find amalgamation in  the textual voices of multilingual students” (p. 2). “Identity” relates to features such as  language, ethnic, and national affiliations that are part of one’s history. Canagarajah  points out that although these should not be treated as monolithic or essentialized, one  should remain open to the possibility that “students might desire to represent their  heritage with pride or draw from it positively for fashioning their voices” (p. 3). “Role” is a social category which refers to varying subject positions people are provided in  institutions such as schools, workplaces, professional communities and the family.  According to Canagarajah, the roles one plays come with expectations about the voice  one should adopt in communicative interactions. “Subjectivity” is an “ideological  construct” which indexes the discourses that shape one’s voice as they find expression  through genre conventions, communicative norms, and value systems (Canagarajah,  2014, pp. 2-3).  The learning journal has been used by many scholars and practitioners, and studies  have highlighted its usefulness in the classroom (Fox, 2000; Lee & Gyogi, 2016; Moon,  1999, 2004; Orem, 2001; Pearson-Evans, 2006; Shih, 2011; Tuan, 2010).  A learning  journal, sometimes called a learner diary, learning diary or log, is “an accumulation of  material that is mainly based on the writer’s processes of reflection” (Moon, 1999, p. 4).  The reflective learning journal has been used in various practice- and/or work-based  areas, including professional education such as nursing and teacher training (Shih,  2011). It has also been used by various scholars and practitioners in the field of  translation studies (Adab, 2000; Fox, 2000; Lee, 2015; Martinez Melis & Hurtado  Albir, 2001) and language pedagogy (Orem, 2001; Pearson-Evans, 2006; Tuan, 2010).  According to Li (1998), the journal can promote students’ critical and reflective  thinking. It has also been found that the reflective learning journal can draw students’  attention to the process of translation (Li, 1998). Lee (2015) conducted a study of  postgraduate students of translation and interpreting studies in South Korea and found  that a learning journal enabled them to analyse and review their own work and  performance, recognize change and development and also set future goals.  Considering the usefulness of the learning journal and the nature of writing, the  current study draws on data from a learning journal kept over the duration of the course  to look at the role of the learning journal in a writing classroom. Through the writing of  a learning journal in either their L1 or L2, students’ are reflecting on their learning and  L2 writing.  The current study aims to answer the following question: What role can the learning  journal play in the undergraduate writing classroom?

intros.text:
Writing is widely acknowledged to be one of the most demanding skills for learners of English as a second or foreign language (EFL/ESL) to develop. For many learners, the act of producing coherent, well-organised and grammatically accurate text in a language other than their own poses considerable cognitive and affective challenges (Tuan, 2010). Consequently, approaches to the teaching of writing have evolved considerably over recent decades, moving from a focus on the written product towards more process-oriented and, more recently, genre-based pedagogies that emphasise the social and communicative functions of writing (Hyland, 2003, 2007). Within this shift, greater attention has been paid to what learners themselves bring to the writing classroom, and to the ways in which their own reflection on the learning process might be harnessed as a pedagogical resource. It is against this backdrop that the present study explores the usefulness of the learning journal as a tool in the academic writing classroom.

The learning journal, sometimes referred to as a reflective journal, learning log or diary, has a long and well-established history as a means of promoting reflective learning and personal development (Moon, 2018). By recording their experiences, thoughts and reactions over time, learners are encouraged to look back on their own learning, to make connections between what they study and how they feel about it, and to identify areas of difficulty as well as evidence of their own progress. Journal writing has been applied in a range of educational settings, including adult ESL teacher education and classroom teaching, where it has been shown to support the improvement of practice through reflective writing (Orem, 2001), and in the recording of intercultural experiences among students studying abroad (Pearson-Evans, 2006). Across these varied contexts, the learning journal is valued not only for what it reveals to the teacher about the learner, but also for the reflective processes it stimulates in the learner.

A substantial body of work exploring the reflective learning journal has emerged within translation studies, an area of particular relevance to the present study given the disciplinary background of its participants. Reflective journals have been used to engage translation students in learning process and in critically examining their own work (Li, 1998; Fox, 2000; Shih, 2011). Lee (2014) proposed a model for using the reflective learning journal in a postgraduate translation practice classroom in South Korea, demonstrating how the journal helped students to identify their own weaknesses, to articulate the strategies they used to deal with obstacles, and to make observations about their own self-development. Subsequent work has continued to explore the reflective learning journal in the classroom more broadly (Lee & Gyogi, 2016). These studies collectively point to the value of the learning journal in promoting critical and reflective thinking and in encouraging learners to review and evaluate their own performance. However, much of this research has concentrated on translation training and on postgraduate or theory-based modules (Shih, 2011), and comparatively little attention has been given to the potential of the learning journal within the academic writing classroom itself, particularly among lower-proficiency undergraduate learners.

A further consideration in the present study concerns the language in which learners write their journal entries. In multilingual and translation-oriented contexts, the boundaries between the first language (L1) and the second language (L2) are increasingly recognised as fluid rather than fixed. Scholarship on translanguaging and codemeshing has highlighted how multilingual writers draw upon their full linguistic repertoire as a resource for meaning-making, and how such practices can be harnessed pedagogically to develop students' proficiency and metacognitive awareness (Canagarajah, 2011, 2015). Related work on literacy and the making of connections through texts has similarly argued for viewing reading, writing and related practices not as universal psycholinguistic processes but as socially and culturally embedded practices (Kern, 2008; Kern & Schultz, 2005). Allowing learners to write their reflections in either their L1 or their L2 acknowledges this multilingual reality, and raises the question of whether the reflective and pedagogical benefits of the learning journal are realised regardless of the language chosen.

The present study seeks to contribute to this discussion by examining the usefulness of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea. In this context, students who were majoring in English Interpreting and Translation, alongside another discipline, kept a semester-long learning journal, referred to as a 'study log', in which they recorded a summary of the content they had studied and offered their own subjective reflections on the class and their learning. Crucially, students were free to write in either their L1 (Korean) or their L2 (English). Through a qualitative analysis of these journals, the study investigates how students reflected on themselves as learners and, in particular, as writers. The study addresses how the learning journal, whether written in the L1 or L2, enables learners to reflect on their own writing through the act of writing. In doing so, it aims to shed light on the several purposes the journal can serve, including helping students to recognise the close relationship between reading and writing, enabling them to document their own learning process and outcomes, and allowing them to identify their weaknesses and their improvements. The unique contribution of this study lies in the insights it offers into the utility of learning journals in the under-explored context of lower-proficiency university students in Korea.
