intros.text:
The teaching of academic writing to second language (L2) learners remains one of the most demanding tasks facing language educators, not least because writing is a complex, recursive process requiring learners to attend simultaneously to organization, grammar, vocabulary and the needs of an intended reader. In recent decades, considerable attention has been directed towards pedagogical approaches that support learners in developing not only their written products but also their awareness of themselves as writers. Genre-based pedagogies, for example, have gained prominence for the way they foreground the social and communicative functions of language and complement earlier process-oriented views (Hyland, 2003, 2007). Alongside such approaches, there has been growing recognition of the value of literacy as a set of socially and cognitively situated practices, learned through apprenticeship and shaped by cultural context (Kern & Schultz, 2005; Kern, 2008), and of the intimate connections between reading and writing that learners must come to appreciate. This body of work underscores the importance of finding classroom tools that help learners reflect on, and take ownership of, their own development as writers.

One such tool is the learning journal. Journals, diaries and other forms of reflective writing have long been employed in language and teacher education as means of encouraging learners to record and interrogate their own learning experiences (Orem, 2001; Pearson-Evans, 2006; Moon, 2018). Reflective writing has been shown to promote critical and metacognitive awareness, allowing learners to articulate their concerns, identify their strategies, and observe changes in themselves over time. Within adult ESL contexts, journal writing has been used to build interaction between teachers and students and to open a window onto the learner's inner processes (Orem, 2001). More specifically, journal writing has been proposed as a means of enhancing the writing skills of EFL learners, with evidence suggesting that regular journal writing can foster writing motivation and improve writing ability while establishing closer communication between teachers and learners (Tuan, 2010).

The reflective learning journal has been explored perhaps most extensively within translation studies and translator training. Reflective and translation diaries have been used to encourage trainee translators to record their thoughts, articulate the difficulties they encounter, and consider the strategies they use to resolve translation problems (Fox, 2000; Li, 1998; Shih, 2011). Such journals have been argued to promote students' critical and reflective thinking and to draw their attention to the translation process itself, rather than merely to the finished product (Li, 1998). Lee (2014) demonstrated how a reflective learning journal in a South Korean postgraduate translation practice classroom enabled students to identify their weaknesses, describe the strategies they used to overcome obstacles, and reflect on their own self-development, ultimately proposing a model for using reflective learning journals in the translation classroom. Related work has considered how the journal functions as a space for learners to analyse and review their own work, recognise change and development, and set future goals (Lee & Gyogi, 2016). These studies collectively situate the reflective journal as a pedagogically valuable instrument, particularly for cultivating learner autonomy and metacognitive awareness. This is significant given wider interest in how multilingual writers draw upon their full linguistic repertoires, with translanguaging strategies and dialogical pedagogies shown to support voice construction and critical reflection in student writing (Canagarajah, 2011, 2015).

Despite this considerable body of research, the use of the learning journal has been examined predominantly in the context of translation training and, more generally, with postgraduate or reasonably proficient learners. Comparatively little attention has been paid to its role in the undergraduate academic writing classroom, and even less to its application with lower proficiency L2 writers. Furthermore, while previous studies have documented the benefits of reflective journals for translator trainees, there remains limited understanding of how learners at the early stages of academic writing use such journals to reflect on their own writing, particularly in a setting where students are free to write in either their first language (L1) or their second language (L2). It is therefore unclear how the journal functions as a reflective tool when learners of relatively low writing proficiency are given the flexibility to choose the language in which they record and contemplate their learning.

The present study seeks to address this gap by examining the usefulness of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea. Building on prior studies that have highlighted the advantages of reflective learning journals, this study focuses specifically on the journal's role in supporting students' reflection on their own writing. Over one semester, students in a pre-elementary level university writing course kept a learning journal, referred to as a study log, in which they summarised what they had learned and recorded their subjective reflections on the class and on their own learning, writing in either their L1 (Korean) or their L2 (English). Through qualitative, thematic analysis of these journals, the study explores how learners reflect as writers, and considers the various functions the journal serves. In doing so, it aims to offer fresh insight into the utility of learning journals for low proficiency university writers in Korea, a context that has received little attention in the existing literature.

intros.text:
The development of writing proficiency in a second language (L2) is widely recognized as one of the most challenging aspects of language acquisition. For many English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, the act of writing can be daunting, often fraught with difficulties related to linguistic competence, structural organization, and the cognitive load of composing in a non-native tongue (Tuan, 2010). To address these challenges, pedagogical approaches have evolved from focusing solely on the final product to emphasizing the process of writing. Hyland (2003) notes that genre-based pedagogies complement process views by highlighting the social role of language in written communication, while Hyland (2007) argues for a framework that integrates concept-based instruction to empower L2 writers to be more agentive and strategic. Central to this development is the notion that literacy is not a universal psycholinguistic process but a constellation of social and cognitive practices learned through apprenticeship and situated within specific cultural contexts (Kern & Schultz, 2005).

In this context, the integration of reflective practices has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing learner autonomy and metacognitive awareness. One such tool is the learning journal, which allows students to document their journey, record their struggles, and reflect on their progress. The use of journals in adult ESL contexts has been shown to improve practice through reflective writing, facilitating a dialogue between the teacher and the student (Orem, 2001). Furthermore, the act of journaling can serve as an extensive activity that increases writing motivation and fosters a closer interactive relationship between the instructor and the learner (Tuan, 2010). By engaging in regular reflection, students are encouraged to move beyond the mere execution of tasks and instead think critically about how they learn, identifying specific areas for growth and recognizing the evolution of their own skills over time (Moon, 2018).

While the benefits of reflective journals are well-documented in general language teaching, they have found significant utility in specialized fields such as translation studies. Because translation is inherently a reflective process—requiring the writer to navigate between two linguistic systems—the use of translation diaries or reflective journals helps students draw attention to the complexities of the translation process (Li, 1998; Fox, 2000). For instance, Lee (2014) explored the use of reflective journals in a South Korean postgraduate translation classroom, finding that they enabled students to record thoughts and look back on their learning process to identify weaknesses and develop personalized strategies. Similarly, Shih (2011) demonstrated that reflective journals could be successfully applied even in theory-based modules to help students bridge the gap between abstract theory and practical application.

An emerging area of interest within this discourse is the role of the students' first language (L1) in the reflective process. Traditional L2 pedagogy often prioritized English-only environments; however, recent scholarship suggests that allowing students to utilize their full linguistic repertoire—a practice known as translanguaging—can provide significant pedagogical affordances. Canagarajah (2011) argues that translanguaging strategies can be teachable, helping students develop metacognitive awareness and think more critically about their textual choices. By utilizing both L1 and L2, learners can better negotiate meaning and construct a more authentic dialogical voice in their writing (Canagarajah, 2015). This suggests that the language of reflection—whether it be the L1, the L2, or a mixture of both—may play a crucial role in how students perceive and analyze their own learning trajectories.

Despite these insights, there remains a need for further empirical research on the application of learning journals among low-proficiency undergraduate students, particularly in the specific context of academic writing in South Korea. While previous studies have focused on postgraduate translation students (Lee, 2014) or specialized translation modules (Shih, 2011), the utility of the learning journal as a tool for basic academic writing development—covering the transition from paragraphs to full essays—requires closer examination. Understanding how these students use the journal to document their learning and reflect on their writing process can provide valuable insights into the pedagogical effectiveness of the tool in a general undergraduate setting.

Therefore, the present study aims to examine the usefulness of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea. By providing students with the autonomy to write their reflections in either their L1 (Korean) or L2 (English), the study seeks to explore how students use these journals to reflect on their learning process, identify the relationship between reading and writing, and document their individual progress. Specifically, the research focuses on whether the learning journal, regardless of the language used, enables learners to identify their own weaknesses and recognize improvements in their writing habits over the course of a semester.

intros.text:
The development of academic writing proficiency is a cornerstone of success in higher education, particularly for students in English-medium contexts where the ability to produce coherent, structured, and rhetorically effective texts is essential. In the field of second language (L2) writing, there has been a significant shift toward pedagogies that emphasize the strategic and agentive nature of the writer. Hyland (2003, 2007) has highlighted the importance of genre-based approaches, which complement process-oriented views by empowering students to become more aware of the social and communicative purposes of their writing. Central to this empowerment is the development of metacognitive awareness—the ability of learners to monitor, evaluate, and regulate their own cognitive processes during the act of writing.

One pedagogical tool that has gained attention for fostering such awareness is the learning journal. Reflective writing, through journals or diaries, allows students to move beyond the mere production of a final text to a deeper engagement with the process of learning itself. In the broader context of language education, journal writing has been recognized as an extensive activity that can enhance learner motivation and foster overall writing skills (Tuan, 2010). Similarly, Orem (2001) has explored the use of collaborative and dialogue journals in adult ESL contexts to improve practice through reflection. The utility of these tools extends into specialized fields such as translation studies, where reflective diaries are used to help students navigate the complexities of translation competence (Adab, 2000; Fox, 2000). For instance, Li (1998) demonstrated that reflective journals in translation teaching promote critical thinking and draw students' attention to the intricate processes of translation. More recently, Lee (2014) proposed a model for reflective learning journals in a South Korean postgraduate translation classroom, noting that such journals allow students to document their learning process, identify personal weaknesses, and observe their own professional development. This is echoed by Shih (2011), who found that reflective journals could change students' perceptions of complex theories and facilitate learning even in non-practice-oriented modules.

Beyond the specific application to translation, the use of journals aligns with a wider call in applied linguistics to view literacy as a constellation of social and cognitive practices (Kern & Schultz, 2005). By engaging in reflective writing, students can position themselves in relation to the texts they produce and the cultures they are engaging with (Kern, 2008). Furthermore, the concept of translanguaging—where students draw on their full linguistic repertoire—suggests that allowing students to utilize both their first language (L1) and second language (L2) can be a powerful strategy for developing voice and critical awareness (Canagarajah, 2011, 2015). When students are permitted to reflect in their L1, they may be able to articulate complex subjective contemplations and metacognitive insights that they cannot yet express in the target language.

Despite these recognized benefits, much of the existing research on reflective journals has focused either on highly specialized translation contexts or on advanced learners. There remains a relative scarcity of empirical research investigating the specific utility of learning journals for low-proficiency undergraduate students in general academic writing classrooms, particularly in the East Asian context. While the general advantages of journaling are well-documented, it remains unclear how the option to switch between L1 and L2 in a learning journal specifically aids the reflective process for students who are still struggling with basic academic writing conventions. There is a need to understand whether the act of documenting one's learning—regardless of the language used—leads to tangible realizations about the relationship between reading and writing, or the identification of specific linguistic gaps.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines the pedagogical usefulness of the learning journal in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea. The primary objective is to investigate how students utilize a semester-long learning journal to reflect on their writing process and how these reflections are manifested in either their L1 (Korean) or L2 (English). Specifically, the study seeks to identify the functions that the journal serves for the learner and the extent to which it facilitates the identification of weaknesses and the documentation of progress.

To achieve this, the study employs a qualitative analysis of journals kept by students in a pre-elementary level academic writing course. By analyzing thematic patterns in the entries, the research explores the intersection of L1 and L2 reflection and its impact on the students' writing habits. It is anticipated that the findings will provide insights into how reflective tools can be integrated into L2 writing pedagogy to support low-proficiency learners in becoming more autonomous and self-aware writers. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: the Methodology section details the participants and data collection process; the Findings and Discussion section presents a thematic analysis of student reflections; and the Conclusion summarizes the pedagogical implications of the study.

segments.text:
In the broader context of language education, journal writing has been recognized as an extensive activity that can enhance learner motivation and foster overall writing skills (Tuan, 2010). Similarly, Orem (2001) has explored the use of collaborative and dialogue journals in adult ESL contexts to improve practice through reflection. The utility of these tools extends into specialized fields such as translation studies, where reflective diaries are used to help students navigate the complexities of translation competence (Adab, 2000; Fox, 2000). For instance, Li (1998) demonstrated that reflective journals in translation teaching promote critical thinking and draw students' attention to the intricate processes of translation. More recently, Lee (2014) proposed a model for reflective learning journals in a South Korean postgraduate translation classroom, noting that such journals allow students to document their learning process, identify personal weaknesses, and observe their own professional development. This is echoed by Shih (2011), who found that reflective journals could change students' perceptions of complex theories and facilitate learning even in non-practice-oriented modules.

Beyond the specific application to translation, the use of journals aligns with a wider call in applied linguistics to view literacy as a constellation of social and cognitive practices (Kern & Schultz, 2005). By engaging in reflective writing, students can position themselves in relation to the texts they produce and the cultures they are engaging with (Kern, 2008). Furthermore, the concept of translanguaging—where students draw on their full linguistic repertoire—suggests that allowing students to utilize both their first language (L1) and second language (L2) can be a powerful strategy for developing voice and critical awareness (Canagarajah, 2011, 2015).

intros.text:
In the field of English Language Teaching (ELT) and Second Language Writing (L2W), the pedagogical value of reflective practices has gained significant traction over the past few decades. Reflective writing, particularly through the use of learning journals, is increasingly recognized as a mechanism that facilitates metacognitive awareness, allowing learners to monitor their own learning processes and develop critical thinking skills. While the benefits of journaling in general language education are well-documented, its specific application within the context of academic writing classrooms, particularly for undergraduate students in East Asian contexts, warrants further investigation. This study examines the utility of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea, focusing on how students utilize these journals to reflect on their writing development.

Theoretical frameworks surrounding L2 writing have evolved from a focus on product to process, and subsequently to genre-based pedagogies. Hyland (2003, 2007) argues that genre-based approaches complement process views by emphasizing the social context of language use, empowering student writers to be agentive and strategic. Within this landscape, the learning journal serves as a bridge between the cognitive processes of writing and the social context of learning. It provides a space where learners can document their journey, moving beyond the immediate production of text to a deeper contemplation of the writing act itself. This aligns with Moon's (2018) perspective on learning journals as tools for personal development, where the act of recording experiences fosters increased understanding and skill development.

In the realm of translation studies and multilingual writing, the use of diaries and journals has also been explored. Li (1998) and Fox (2000) have highlighted the role of reflective journals in translation teaching, suggesting that they help students identify weaknesses and strategies for overcoming obstacles. Similarly, Lee (2014) proposed a model for using reflective learning journals in postgraduate translation practice classrooms, demonstrating how they allow students to record thoughts and look back on their learning process. These studies suggest that the learning journal is not merely a record of content but a tool for self-regulation and professional growth. Furthermore, Canagarajah (2011, 2015) discusses the concept of codemeshing and translanguaging, where multilingual students utilize their full linguistic repertoire. While his work focuses on the strategies students use in drafting, the learning journal offers a unique medium where students can choose to write in their L1 or L2, potentially facilitating deeper reflection without the constraint of L2 proficiency.

Despite the established benefits in translation and general language contexts, there is a need to understand how these tools function specifically in L2 academic writing classrooms for pre-elementary to intermediate learners. Luu Trong Tuan (2010) investigated the enhancement of EFL learners' writing skills via journal writing, finding benefits in motivation and skill fostering. However, few studies have explicitly examined the dual function of the journal as both a summary of learned content and a space for subjective contemplation in a Korean university context. Additionally, the role of the journal in connecting reading and writing, as well as in documenting the learning process for future review, remains an area requiring empirical evidence. Orem (2001) notes the importance of journal writing in adult ESL for improving practice through reflection, yet the specific dynamics of the Korean EFL classroom, characterized by distinct educational cultures and proficiency levels, present a unique context.

The current study addresses this gap by analyzing the learning journals of undergraduate students enrolled in an English academic writing course. The study is situated at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, where students have the option to write in either their L1 (Korean) or L2 (English). This choice is significant, as it allows for an exploration of whether the language of reflection impacts the depth of insight gained. Drawing on the work of Kern (2008) and Kern & Schultz (2005), who advocate for context-sensitive approaches to literacy that link language to other disciplines and cultures, this research investigates how the journal facilitates connections between classroom learning and personal development. The study also considers the assessment implications, echoing the calls by Melis & Hurtado Albir (2002) for better assessment instruments in training contexts, by examining how the journal serves as a form of holistic evaluation.

The primary aim of this research is to explore the usefulness of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in the academic writing classroom. Specifically, it seeks to understand how the journal enables learners to reflect on their own writing through writing, how it aids in the documentation of the learning process, and whether it helps students identify the relationship between reading and writing. By examining the qualitative data from student journals, this study aims to provide insights into the multifaceted roles these journals play, ranging from a personal diary to a strategic learning tool. The findings contribute to the broader literature on reflective practice in EFL/ESL and offer practical implications for instructors seeking to enhance student engagement and metacognitive awareness in writing instruction.

intros.text:
In the realm of second language acquisition and pedagogy, the integration of reflective practices has become increasingly central to fostering deep learning and metacognitive awareness. Among the various tools employed to facilitate this reflection, the learning journal stands out as a versatile pedagogical instrument. Learning journals, often conceptualized as a space for students to document their learning journey, record subjective contemplations, and engage in critical self-analysis, have been widely recognized for their potential to enhance learner autonomy and critical thinking skills. As Moon (2018) notes, learning journals serve not only as a record of content but also as a mechanism for personal development, allowing students to identify their own skills development and consciousness of power differentials in learning contexts. Similarly, Orem (2001) highlights the utility of journal writing in adult ESL contexts, suggesting that reflective writing can significantly improve teaching and learning practices by bridging the gap between teacher instruction and student experience.

The theoretical underpinnings of using learning journals in language education are rooted in the broader shift towards process-oriented and genre-based pedagogies. Hyland (2003, 2007) argues that genre-based pedagogies complement process views by emphasizing the role of language in written communication, empowering student writers to be agentive and strategic. This aligns with the view that literacy is not merely a set of psycholinguistic processes but a constellation of social, cognitive, and linguistic practices, as Kern and Schultz (2005) suggest. In this context, the learning journal acts as a bridge between the cognitive and social dimensions of learning, allowing students to articulate their internal processes and externalize their understanding of the writing process. Canagarajah (2011, 2015) further supports this by exploring the pedagogical affordances of translanguaging and codemeshing, suggesting that students' use of multiple languages in their reflective writing can enhance metacognitive awareness and critical thinking.

Despite the growing body of literature supporting the efficacy of learning journals, much of the existing research has focused on translation studies or higher-level proficiency contexts. For instance, Li (1998) and Lee (2014) have investigated the role of reflective journals in translation teaching, demonstrating their value in helping students identify weaknesses and develop strategies to overcome obstacles. Adab (2000) and Fox (2000) also contribute to this discourse by examining the use of translation diaries in process-oriented methodologies. However, these studies predominantly target postgraduate translation students or professional contexts, leaving a gap in our understanding of how learning journals function in undergraduate academic writing classrooms, particularly for learners with lower proficiency levels. Furthermore, while studies like Luu (2010) have explored journal writing to enhance EFL learners' writing skills, there is limited empirical evidence regarding the specific benefits of allowing students to write their journals in either their L1 or L2 within an academic writing context.

The current study addresses this gap by examining the usefulness of the learning journal as a pedagogical tool in an undergraduate academic writing classroom in Seoul, South Korea. Unlike previous studies that may have mandated the use of the target language (L2), this study allowed students to choose whether to write their journal entries in their first language (L1) or second language (L2). This flexibility is particularly relevant in the context of multilingual classrooms where translanguaging strategies are increasingly recognized as valuable resources for learning (Canagarajah, 2011). The study focuses on pre-elementary level students, a demographic often overlooked in journaling research, to investigate how the journal facilitates reflection on the writing process, documentation of learning outcomes, and identification of personal weaknesses and improvements. By analyzing qualitative data from student journals, this research aims to provide insights into the multifaceted roles that learning journals play in fostering critical reflection and self-regulated learning among low-proficiency university students. The findings of this study contribute to the existing literature by offering a contextualized account of the pedagogical utility of learning journals in a specific EFL setting, thereby extending the applicability of reflective practices to diverse educational contexts.

intros.text:
Writing in a second or foreign language is a demanding activity because it requires learners to coordinate linguistic resources, rhetorical knowledge, genre awareness, audience expectations and composing processes. In university EFL contexts, academic writing can be especially challenging for students who are still developing grammatical and lexical control but are also expected to produce organized, purposeful texts. Research on L2 writing pedagogy has therefore moved beyond a narrow concern with the final written product to include the processes through which learners plan, draft, revise, edit and make meaning. Process-oriented approaches have usefully foregrounded the recursive nature of writing, while genre-based pedagogies have emphasized that writing is socially situated and that students need explicit access to the purposes, structures and language choices associated with particular text types (Hyland, 2003, 2007). For novice academic writers, such pedagogies can help make visible the expectations that underlie successful written communication.

At the same time, writing development is not only a matter of acquiring forms or formats. It also involves becoming aware of oneself as a writer: recognizing difficulties, evaluating strategies, understanding the relationship between reading and writing, and developing confidence in the ability to produce and improve texts. Literacy in an additional language is best understood as a constellation of social, cognitive and textual practices rather than as a set of decontextualized skills (Kern & Schultz, 2005). From this perspective, students benefit when classroom practices encourage them to connect texts, experiences and reflections, and to position themselves in relation to what they read and write (Kern, 2008). Reflection is therefore central to writing pedagogy because it can help learners notice not only what they have written, but also how and why they write in particular ways.

One pedagogical tool that can support such noticing is the learning journal. Learning journals have been widely used to promote reflection, personal development and awareness of learning processes. Moon (2018) describes journal writing as a means of recording experience, revisiting it, and developing more considered understandings of learning. In language education, journals may serve multiple functions: they can be spaces for personal response, records of classroom learning, opportunities for extended writing practice, and channels of communication between learners and teachers. Orem (2001), for example, discusses journal writing in adult ESL as a reflective practice that can inform both teaching and learning. In EFL writing classrooms, journal writing has also been associated with increased motivation, greater writing fluency and improved learner–teacher interaction (Luu, 2010). These benefits suggest that journals may be particularly valuable in contexts where learners need low-stakes opportunities to use writing to think about writing.

Reflective journals have also been explored in translator education, where the need for students to articulate decision-making processes is especially apparent. Translation pedagogy has long been concerned with the assessment and development of competence, including the ability to identify problems, justify choices and evaluate outcomes (Adab, 2000; Martínez Melis & Hurtado Albir, 2002). Within this field, reflective journals and translation diaries have been used to help students document their processes and develop critical awareness of their strategies (Fox, 2000; Li, 1998). Shih (2011) shows that reflective learning journals can help translation students engage with theory and reconsider their understanding of translation concepts, while Lee (2014) demonstrates that journals in a Korean postgraduate translation practice classroom can support the identification of weaknesses, the recording of strategies and the observation of self-development. Lee and Gyogi (2016) similarly point to the classroom potential of reflective learning journals. Although these studies are situated primarily in translation education, they are relevant to academic writing because both domains require learners to attend to process, audience, textual purpose and self-evaluation.

Another important issue in journal writing is the language in which reflection takes place. In multilingual and EFL classrooms, students’ first language is often treated as separate from, or even in competition with, the target language. However, recent work on multilingual writing has challenged this separation by showing how learners draw on their full linguistic repertoires in meaning-making. Canagarajah (2011) argues that translanguaging and codemeshing can foster metacognitive awareness when students are encouraged to question choices, compare options and reflect critically on their writing. His later work further highlights the pedagogical affordances of multilingual writing for voice construction (Canagarajah, 2015). For reflective writing, allowing students to use either the L1 or L2 may be especially productive: the L2 offers additional writing practice, while the L1 may enable more nuanced personal reflection, particularly for lower-proficiency learners. Yet the pedagogical implications of permitting both languages in learning journals remain underexplored in EFL academic writing classrooms.

The present study addresses this issue by examining the use of a semester-long learning journal, called a study log, in an undergraduate English academic writing course in Seoul, South Korea. The course focused on paragraph-to-essay development and on descriptive, narrative and opinion essays, with attention to drafting, peer review, self-editing and final revision. Students were permitted to write their journals in either Korean, their L1, or English, their L2. Rather than treating the journal only as a language practice activity or an assessment instrument, the study investigates how it functioned as a pedagogical tool through which learners recorded course content, reflected on their writing processes, identified weaknesses and recognized development.

While previous research has established the value of journal writing in ESL/EFL and translation classrooms, there is still a need for qualitative classroom-based studies that show how low-proficiency university EFL students use learning journals in academic writing courses, particularly when they are free to choose the language of reflection. The current study therefore asks what kinds of reflections emerge in students’ learning journals and what pedagogical roles the journal appears to play in supporting their development as academic writers. By analyzing journal entries from an undergraduate writing class in Korea, the study contributes to discussions of reflective writing, L1/L2 use and process-oriented academic writing pedagogy.

intros.text:
Writing occupies a central place in university language learning because it requires learners not only to produce accurate texts but also to make decisions about audience, purpose, organization, genre, and voice. In EFL contexts, academic writing is especially demanding: students are often asked to compose in a language in which they are still developing linguistic resources while also learning unfamiliar conventions of academic literacy. For this reason, the teaching of writing has increasingly moved beyond the correction of finished products toward pedagogies that help learners understand writing as a process of planning, drafting, reviewing, revising, and reflecting.

Process-oriented and genre-based approaches have contributed substantially to this shift. Genre pedagogy emphasizes that writing is socially situated and that learners need explicit access to the rhetorical and linguistic resources through which texts achieve communicative purposes (Hyland, 2003, 2007). At the same time, literacy-oriented perspectives have argued that reading and writing should not be treated as isolated skills, but as connected meaning-making practices embedded in particular social, cultural, and educational contexts (Kern & Schultz, 2005; Kern, 2008). From this view, learners’ development as writers involves more than the acquisition of vocabulary and grammar; it also involves awareness of how texts work, how readers respond, and how writers position themselves in relation to tasks and audiences.

One pedagogical tool that can support such awareness is the learning journal. Learning journals provide a space in which students record what they have learned, monitor difficulties, revisit classroom experiences, and articulate personal responses to their learning. They can function as records of progress, sites of metacognitive reflection, and channels of communication between teacher and learner. Moon (2018) emphasizes the role of learning journals in personal development and reflective learning, particularly because they allow learners to move from description of experience toward deeper consideration of meaning, change, and future action. In language education, journal writing has also been associated with reflective practice, learner autonomy, and greater interaction between students and teachers (Orem, 2001). In EFL writing classrooms, regular journal writing can provide learners with additional opportunities to write and can contribute to improved motivation and writing development (Tuan, 2010).

The usefulness of journals has been explored in related areas of language and literacy education, including study-abroad learning and translation pedagogy. Diaries have been used to document learners’ experiences across cultures, providing insight into affective and developmental aspects of learning that may not be visible in formal assessment (Pearson-Evans, 2006). In translation education, reflective journals and translation diaries have been used to encourage students to examine decision-making processes, identify problems, and evaluate their own developing competence (Fox, 2000; Li, 1998; Shih, 2011). Lee (2014), for example, proposed a model for using reflective learning journals in a postgraduate translation practice classroom in South Korea and showed that journals helped students identify weaknesses, consider strategies for overcoming difficulties, observe self-development, and set goals. Such work is consistent with broader concerns in translator training that assessment and pedagogy should attend not only to final products but also to learner competence, problem-solving, and development over time (Adab, 2000; Martínez Melis & Hurtado Albir, 2002).

Research on multilingual writing has also highlighted the value of spaces where learners can draw on their full linguistic repertoires and reflect on their choices. Canagarajah (2011) showed how multilingual students’ translanguaging and codemeshing strategies in academic writing can become teachable when classroom practices encourage dialogue, feedback, and metacognitive awareness. Later work on dialogical voice construction similarly points to the pedagogical affordances of allowing multilingual student writers to negotiate voice through interaction and reflection (Canagarajah, 2015). These perspectives are relevant to EFL writing classrooms in which students may benefit from using either the target language or their first language to think through what they have learned. If the goal of the journal is reflection rather than formal performance alone, permitting L1 use may allow learners to express more complex thoughts about their writing processes, difficulties, and progress.

Despite this growing interest, the role of learning journals in undergraduate EFL academic writing classrooms remains underexplored, particularly in Korean university contexts and with students at lower levels of English proficiency. Much of the existing work on reflective journals has focused on translation studies, teacher education, adult ESL, or general reflective learning. Studies of journal writing in EFL writing have often emphasized writing practice and skill improvement, but less attention has been given to what students’ journal entries reveal about their understandings of academic writing, their awareness of the relationship between reading and writing, and their perceptions of change across a semester-long writing course. It also remains important to examine how journals function when learners are allowed to write in either their L1 or L2, since such a choice may shape the depth and character of reflection.

The present study addresses this gap by examining the pedagogical usefulness of a learning journal in an undergraduate academic writing class in Seoul, South Korea. The journal, referred to in the course as a study log, was assigned over a 16-week semester in a university English academic writing course. Students were invited to summarize what they had learned and to add personal remarks about the class, their writing, or their learning process. They were permitted to write in either Korean or English. Through qualitative thematic analysis of student journal entries, the study investigates how learners used the journal to reflect on writing, document learning, identify weaknesses and improvements, and make sense of their development as academic writers.

By focusing on students’ own reflections, this study offers a classroom-based account of how learning journals can support academic writing pedagogy in an EFL context. It suggests that the learning journal is not merely an additional writing assignment but a flexible pedagogical tool through which learners can review content, connect reading and writing, observe changes in writing habits, and articulate future goals. The study therefore contributes to discussions of reflective learning, multilingual writing pedagogy, and the teaching of academic writing in Korean higher education.

intros.text: Teaching doctoral students to become fully recognized researchers is a challenge for most university lecturers, and not much research has been conducted on it yet (Araiza, Kutugata & Pérez, 2015).  PhD training courses need to share certain principles, such as critical thinking (Laal & Ghodsi, 2012) and collaboration (Araiza et al., 2015). Moreover, collaborative learning requires the acquisition of cognitive and social skills (Le, Janssen & Wubbles, 2018).  One of the priorities for doctoral students is learning the right use of academic and disciplinary discourse, a task even more difficult when they need to use a foreign language such as English.  Writing has been the focus of most research attention at this level of studies (Ädel, 2010; Cheng, 2008; Flowerdew, 2015), but no research to our knowledge has focused on the teaching and learning of academic spoken discourse, even less on spontaneous spoken communicative events.  Conference discourse is always a great challenge for novice researchers, especially the discussion session (DS), in which, by means of generally unpredictable dialogic encounters, presenters have to convince the audience of the value of their findings and conclusions (Querol-Julián, 2011). The conference colony of spoken genres (Bhatia, 2004; Koester & Handford, 2012) needs to be effective, not only for being understood, but also for persuading the audience of the relevance of the results presented. Discourse analysis can serve as a basis for the teaching and learning of genres such as discussion sessions following conference presentations (Davies & Lester, 2016), where it is common to find an ensemble of “linguistic, visual, audio, gestural and spatial modes of meaning” (Cope & Kalantzis, 2009: 166).  Although verbal expression is often considered the most significant mode of communication, multimodality shows that all modes have the potential to contribute to meaning in the same way (Jewitt, 2013).  Nonetheless, only a few studies have focused on the multimodal nature of conference presentations.  Morell (2015) shows that effective speakers use modes that often overlap and combine to convey meaning. In the interviews held in her study, speakers recognize the need for greater awareness of the affordances of the modes available for communication, which can lead to improved performance. As Archer (2010) claims, students need to learn the several semiotic resources that make meaning, they need “to engage in the critical analysis of multimodal texts and videos, which in turn requires a detailed understanding of how such texts function to begin with” (O‟Halloran, Tan & Smith, 2015: 260). One of these functions is to persuade the audience about the relevance of one‟s research, considering that conference presentations are discipline and context dependent (Valeiras-Jurado, 2015). In general, the speakers aim at convincing the audience about the originality and value of their research, according to disciplinary rules, while they assume the responsibility for the decisions taken and the interpretations of their findings. In the same line, Wulff, Swales and Keller (2009) identified the evaluative nature of the discourse used in the DS. Evaluation refers to the aspects of the discourse that signal participants‟ attitude and engage the audience. It is used to show an appropriate professional persona and it is an important aspect of persuasive discourse. All these characteristics of conference presentations DSs are common to other spoken research genres such as research seminars and theses defences DS, in which speakers also need to persuade the audience about the value of their research. On the other hand, Clennell (1999) and Lam and Wong (2000) suggest the need for explicit teaching of conversation strategies and pragmatic awareness. However, this is not an easy task, since there are few materials that include them, and those that do are not based on authentic events. Moreover, Reese and Wells (2007) propose adopting an experiential method to teach discussion skills, using authentic materials and creating real-like learning situations. This experiential learning approach is in line with teaching pedagogies of spoken discourse (Cameron, 2001; McCarthy & Carter, 2014). Though it is an interesting approach, it does not take into account the multimodal nature of spoken academic discourse.  That is the reason why we claim the importance of teaching discussion skills from a multimodal perspective.  This may promote awareness of how the different semiotic resources employed to express meaning contribute to the development of interpersonal relations and the construction of the genre.  In this regard, much research has been conducted on “multimodal literacy” since the concept of “multiliteracies” was introduced by the New London Group (1996), as a pedagogy that “focuses on modes of representation much broader than language alone” (Cope & Kalantzis, 2000: 2).  However, the bulk of its development targets multimodal and digital texts to engage learners -generally in lower educational levels- in meaningful multimodal inquiry (Serafini, 2014; Walsh, 2010), rather than face to face interaction, as is the case in the research we have developed.  Regarding the approaches to teach genres, the Sydney school, based on Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) and the model of language development (Rose & Martin, 2012), elaborated scaffolding into an explicit methodological model that has largely been called the teaching-learning cycle. Gibbons (2002: 16) defines scaffolding as “a special kind of help that assists learners in moving toward new skills, concepts, or levels of understanding”. Most of the models following this approach (see Martin (1999, 2009) for a review of the different models) are mainly designed for primary and secondary education, and literacy teaching. It was not until the latest generation, with the Scaffolding Literacy in Academic and Tertiary Environments project (SLATE) (Dreyfus, Humphrey, Mahboob & Martin, 2015), that higher education has come into focus.  The SLATE project has been one of the sources of inspiration for the present research, though it was designed to meet a different aim, teaching and learning writing skills using web-based materials. It provided online genre-based embedded language and literacy support for undergraduate linguistics and biology students at the City University of Hong Kong. In the present study, we take as a basis genre-based pedagogy to adapt the Sydney perspective (and especially their teachinglearning cycle) in order to teach an oral interactive discourse to doctoral students. This pedagogy serves the development of our conception of learning-focused teaching (Light, Calkins & Cox, 2009).  From this perspective, learning is seen as conceptual development of student relationship with subject content, and as active-reflective construction, while the focus of teaching is “developing ways to help students improve and change their conceptual understanding” (Light et al., 2009: 29).  The objective of this research is to prove the effectiveness of an adaptation of the teaching-learning cycle pedagogical model in a course on conference academic discourse for a group of PhD students. In order to meet this objective, we pose two research questions: Q1. Are doctoral students aware of the multimodal characteristics of the DS genre and their influence on interpersonal relations? Q2. Can a scaffolded critical thinking approach help them in their learning and use of this genre?  The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. First, we present the pedagogical model we have designed; then, we introduce in the Method section the context and participants in the implementation (section 3.1), as well as the resources and data collection tools (section 3.2). In section 4, the procedure we have followed is explained as well as the findings. This section is divided into subsections presenting each of the 4 sessions used for the implementation, and a follow-up analysis we have conducted. The findings and conclusions are discussed in section 5.

intros.text:
The doctoral programme represents the final teaching-learning stage in the education system, the phase in which graduate students are transformed into autonomous researchers. This transformation is customarily associated with the ability to produce a dissertation, and much attention has consequently been devoted to the development of academic writing skills. Indeed, the teaching of research writing, particularly of the research article and its component sections, has generated a substantial body of pedagogical and descriptive research (Ädel, 2010; Cheng, 2008; Flowerdew, 2015; Bhatia, 2004). However, becoming a researcher entails much more than writing. It also involves the capacity to present, defend, and discuss one's research orally before a community of peers, most notably at international conferences where English typically operates as the vehicular language. The oral dimension of research communication has received considerably less attention than its written counterpart, and where it has been addressed, the focus has fallen almost exclusively on monologic, carefully prepared genres such as the conference presentation (Morell, 2015). The interactive spoken genres that surround and follow these presentations remain remarkably under-explored, both as objects of description and as the focus of instruction.

Among these interactive genres, the discussion session (DS) that immediately follows the delivery of a conference paper is particularly significant and particularly challenging. Unlike the presentation itself, the DS cannot be fully rehearsed in advance: presenters must respond in real time to questions, comments, and criticisms formulated by an audience that is often more experienced than they are. For novice researchers, and especially for those operating in a language that is not their first, this unpredictability is a source of considerable anxiety. The DS demands the rapid deployment of a wide range of verbal and non-verbal resources in order to construct and protect interpersonal relations, to project a credible academic identity, and to persuade the audience of the value of one's work (Konzett, 2012; Querol-Julián & Fortanet-Gómez, 2016). Yet the DS has attracted only sporadic scholarly attention. The pioneering study by Wulff et al. (2009) described the discussion sessions of a specialised conference, and subsequent work has begun to characterise their structure and, importantly, their evaluative and multimodal nature (Querol-Julián, 2011; Querol-Julián & Fortanet-Gómez, 2012, 2014, 2016). Despite this emerging interest, to the best of our knowledge the DS has rarely if ever been made the explicit focus of a systematic teaching-learning intervention, and its multimodal-in-context dimension remains almost entirely absent from pedagogical practice.

The absence of instruction in this area is problematic because the DS is not primarily a matter of grammatical accuracy or lexical range. It is a fundamentally multimodal event, in which meaning is co-constructed through the interplay of language, paralanguage, and non-verbal semiotic resources such as facial expression, gaze, head movement, and gesture (Jewitt, 2013; O'Halloran et al., 2016). Persuasion and the negotiation of interpersonal relations, which lie at the heart of the genre, are realised through ensembles of these resources rather than through words alone (Valeiras-Jurado, 2015; Camiciottoli & Fortanet-Gómez, 2015). This has significant implications for how the genre should be taught. If instruction is to be effective, learners must become aware not only of what is said but of how it is said, and of how the various modes combine to build meaning. Such an orientation aligns doctoral training with wider developments in the field of multimodal literacy and multiliteracies (The New London Group, 1996; Cope & Kalantzis, 2009; Walsh, 2010; Serafini, 2014), which have argued forcefully that communicative competence in contemporary academic and professional contexts extends well beyond the verbal. However, whereas multimodal literacy has been developed primarily in relation to visual and digital written genres (Archer, 2010), its application to interactive spoken academic genres remains largely uncharted territory.

A further consideration concerns pedagogy itself. Genre-based instruction has a long and productive tradition, particularly within the Sydney School and systemic functional linguistics, where the teaching-learning cycle has become a well-established framework for moving learners towards increasing independence in the control of a genre (Christie, 1999; Martin, 2009; Rose & Martin, 2012; Hyland, 2004, 2007). The classic versions of this cycle typically comprise stages of modelling and deconstruction, joint construction, and independent construction (Rothery, 1996; Feez, 1998; Dreyfus et al., 2016). Yet in most of these formulations the deconstruction of the genre is the responsibility of the teacher, who presents and explains its features to the learners. Moreover, the cycle has been developed overwhelmingly in relation to writing, with the analysis of context and rhetorical structure oriented towards the production of written texts. For a genre as dynamic, interactive, and multimodal as the DS, and for a group of adult learners who bring their own experience and beliefs to the classroom, there are good reasons to reconsider both the locus of deconstruction and the modal scope of analysis.

This reconsideration draws on a broader set of pedagogical principles. Collaborative learning has been shown to yield significant cognitive and social benefits, engaging learners in an active, shared process of meaning construction (Laal & Ghodsi, 2012; Le et al., 2017), and scaffolding remains central to enabling second language learners to move towards autonomy (Gibbons, 2002). At the same time, the fostering of critical and higher-order thinking, understood through Bloom's revised taxonomy as a movement from remembering towards analysing, evaluating, and creating (Krathwohl, 2002; Light, Cox & Calkins, 2009), offers a principled way of structuring learners' engagement with a genre. There is, in addition, a growing recognition that doctoral education is a site of identity formation and community building, in which students negotiate their emerging researcher identities through discourse and through participation in academic communities (Davis & Lester, 2016; Araiza et al., 2015). Instruction in spoken discussion skills has been explored in various ESL and EAP contexts (Lam & Wong, 2000; Clennell, 1999; Reese & Wells, 2007), but these efforts have not typically targeted the specific demands of the research DS, nor have they systematically incorporated multimodal awareness.

Against this background, the present paper proposes and evaluates a learner-led, genre-based pedagogy for the teaching and learning of the discussion session. Building on, but departing from, earlier versions of the teaching-learning cycle, we design a model that is learning-oriented from the outset. Its central innovation is twofold. First, we make the learners themselves responsible for the joint deconstruction of the genre, engaging them in critical and creative thinking rather than positioning them as recipients of teacher-transmitted knowledge. This deconstruction is approached from two complementary perspectives: the learners' own previous experience and predictions about the genre, and the collaborative multimodal analysis of authentic video-recorded discussion sessions. Second, we broaden the focus of analysis to embrace the multimodal, interactive, and interpersonal nature of spoken academic communication, attending to the macro level of rhetorical structure and to the micro level of lexico-grammar, paralanguage, and non-verbal features, and to how these resources work together to persuade audiences and to build professional relationships.

The model was implemented in a course on English for Research for doctoral students at a Spanish university where English is a foreign language, and its effectiveness was assessed within a naturalistic, qualitative research paradigm. Two research questions guide the study: first, whether the pedagogy raises students' awareness of the multimodal characteristics of the DS genre and of the influence of ensembles of semiotic resources on the construction of interpersonal relations; and second, whether a scaffolded, critical-thinking approach supports learners in their learning and use of this genre. In addressing these questions, the paper aims to contribute both a description of an under-researched interactive spoken genre and a transferable pedagogical proposal that may help trainers of novice researchers design courses that facilitate their access to, and acceptance within, their scientific communities.

intros.text:
Doctoral programmes constitute the final teaching-learning stage in the education system, the point at which graduate students are transformed into autonomous researchers. This transformation is customarily understood in terms of the ability to write a doctoral dissertation and to publish research articles, yet becoming a member of a scientific community entails far more than mastering the written word. Novice researchers must also learn to present their work orally and, crucially, to defend it in front of an audience of peers and more experienced scholars. As the demand for international dissemination of research grows, and as English consolidates its position as the vehicular language of academic exchange, the pressure on early-career researchers to communicate effectively in spoken academic settings has become increasingly acute. Learning to participate confidently in these settings is therefore central to the professional development of doctoral students, particularly those for whom English is a foreign language.

Academic literacy at the doctoral level has traditionally been approached through the lens of writing. A substantial body of research has examined the rhetorical organisation and disciplinary conventions of written genres such as the research article and the thesis, and has explored how these genres can be taught (Ädel, 2010; Cheng, 2008; Flowerdew, 2015). Genre-based pedagogies grounded in systemic functional linguistics, and in particular the work associated with the so-called Sydney School, have offered powerful frameworks for making the features of valued genres explicit and for scaffolding learners towards independent control of them (Martin, 2009; Rose & Martin, 2012; Dreyfus et al., 2016; Christie, 1999). The teaching-learning cycle, with its stages of modelling, joint construction and independent construction, has proven especially influential in higher education contexts (Hyland, 2004, 2007). These approaches share a common goal: to move learners progressively towards independence in producing a particular genre while the teacher gradually withdraws support.

Yet the overwhelming majority of this work has been directed at written discourse. Training in spoken academic genres has received comparatively little attention, and where it has been addressed, the interest has been concentrated largely on monologic, prepared speech such as the conference presentation itself (Morell, 2015). Studies of spoken professional and academic genres have begun to describe the linguistic and interactional features of these events (Cameron, 2001; Koester & Handford; Kramsch et al., 1994), and researchers working within English for Academic Purposes have called attention to the need to develop learners' pragmatic awareness and spoken discourse skills (Clennell, 1999; Reese & Wells, 2007). Some pedagogical work has explored the teaching of discussion and interaction skills, showing that strategy training combined with linguistic scaffolding and peer cooperation can enhance learners' participation (Lam & Wong, 2000). Nonetheless, the interactive, dialogic dimension of research communication remains markedly under-explored in the teaching literature, especially at the doctoral level.

One interactive spoken genre stands out as both highly consequential and particularly demanding for novice researchers: the discussion session that follows a conference paper presentation. Unlike the presentation, which can be rehearsed and controlled, the discussion session is unpredictable and dialogic. It requires speakers to field questions and comments in real time, to respond to criticism, to protect their own face and that of their interlocutors, and to persuade the audience of the value of their research, all while building and maintaining professional and social relations. It is precisely in this arena that novice researchers, and especially those working in a language that is not their L1, report the greatest anxiety. Existing descriptive research has documented the rhetorical and interactional structure of discussion sessions (Wulff et al., 2009), and our own prior work has examined the multimodal expression of evaluation and interpersonal meaning in this genre, showing how verbal, paralinguistic and non-verbal resources combine to construct persuasion and identity (Querol-Julián & Fortanet-Gómez, 2016). Konzett's (2012) work has similarly underscored the centrality of identity construction in these encounters. However, the discussion session has been noted repeatedly to have received little attention within the broader genre of conference presentations, and to our knowledge no pedagogical model has yet been proposed for teaching and learning it.

This gap is compounded by a second one relating to the modes through which academic communication takes place. Communication is inherently multimodal: meaning is made not only through language but through gaze, facial expression, gesture, posture, silence and paralanguage, all of which interplay in spoken interaction (Jewitt, 2013). The recognition of multimodality has reshaped thinking about academic literacy, and scholars have argued for the incorporation of multimodal perspectives into English for Academic Purposes and into writing pedagogy (Archer, 2010; O'Halloran et al., 2016; Camiciottoli & Fortanet-Gómez, 2015). The notion of multimodal literacy, however, and the closely related pedagogy of multiliteracies (New London Group, 1996; Cope & Kalantzis, 2009), has been developed overwhelmingly in relation to visual and digital genres and to written composition (Walsh, 2010; Serafini, 2013). It has rarely been extended to spoken interactive genres in which embodied resources carry decisive interpersonal weight. The study of research spoken genres, and of the discussion session in particular, from a multimodal-in-context approach thus remains remarkably limited.

A further consideration concerns how such a genre might best be taught. Genre-based teaching-learning cycles have conventionally cast the teacher as the agent of deconstruction, presenting learners with the features of the target genre. Yet doctoral students bring with them considerable experience and intellectual maturity, and contemporary understandings of learning in higher education emphasise the reflective, social and constructivist nature of the process (Chism, 2011; Gibbons, 2002). Collaborative learning has been shown to yield significant benefits for engagement and understanding (Laal & Ghodsi, 2012; Le et al., 2017), and the cultivation of higher-order thinking skills, in line with Bloom's revised taxonomy (Krathwohl, 2002), is increasingly seen as a central aim of advanced education. Doctoral classrooms are, moreover, sites in which learners actively construct their researcher identities through discourse (Davis & Lester, 2016; Araiza et al., 2015). These insights suggest that a pedagogy for the discussion session should not merely transmit generic knowledge but should engage learners as active, critical and collaborative agents in the deconstruction and construction of the genre.

Against this background, the present paper proposes and evaluates a learner-led pedagogical model for the teaching and learning of the discussion session as an interactive multimodal spoken academic genre. Building on established variants of the genre-based teaching-learning cycle (Rothery, 1996; Feez, 1998; Dreyfus et al., 2016), our proposal introduces two substantive modifications. First, it broadens the object of instruction from written monologue to an oral interactive genre while foregrounding the multimodal nature of communication, attending to verbal, paralinguistic and non-verbal resources and their interpersonal functions. Second, it makes learners, rather than the teacher, responsible for the deconstruction of the genre, and proposes that this joint deconstruction proceed from two complementary perspectives: the learners' own previous experience and predictions, and the analysis of authentic video-recorded discussion sessions. Throughout, discussion and critical thinking are deployed to move learners from lower-order to higher-order thinking skills.

The model was implemented in a course on English for Research for doctoral students at a Spanish university where English is a foreign language, and its effectiveness was investigated within a naturalistic, qualitative paradigm. In order to assess the proposal, we posed two research questions: first, whether the model fosters students' awareness of the multimodal characteristics of the discussion session and of the way ensembles of semiotic resources construct interpersonal relations; and second, whether a scaffolded critical-thinking approach can support learners in their learning and use of this genre. In addressing these questions, this study aims to offer novice-researcher trainers a concrete, replicable pedagogy for designing courses that facilitate their students' access to, and acceptance within, their scientific communities, and to contribute to a broader reconceptualisation of multimodal literacy that embraces spoken interpersonal communication.

It is precisely in this arena that novice researchers, and especially those working in a language that is not their L1, report the greatest anxiety.

intros.text:
The final stage of formal education, the doctoral programme, is designed to transform graduate students from learners into independent researchers. This evolution is traditionally associated with the mastery of written academic genres, most notably the dissertation. However, the role of a researcher extends far beyond the written word; it fundamentally involves the ability to engage in scholarly dialogue and discuss research findings within a professional community. While significant attention has been paid to the written components of academic literacy (Ädel, 2010; Flowerdew, 2015), training on spoken academic genres has remained relatively neglected. Furthermore, existing research and pedagogy regarding spoken academic discourse have focused primarily on monologic, prepared speeches, such as the conference presentation itself, often overlooking the interactive dimensions of academic exchange (Cameron, 2001; Koester & Handford, n.d.).

Among the various spoken genres used in academic settings, the discussion session (DS)—the interactive period of questioning and commenting that follows a paper presentation—is perhaps one of the most critical yet challenging for novice researchers. The DS is not merely a formality but a high-stakes communicative event where the presenter must defend their research, respond to criticism, and negotiate meaning with an audience of peers and experts. As noted by Wulff et al. (2009), these sessions are characterized by tight time constraints and high unpredictability. For doctoral students, particularly those operating in English as a foreign language, the DS represents a site of significant anxiety. The need to process complex questions in real-time while simultaneously managing the interpersonal dynamics of a professional community can be overwhelming. This is further complicated by the fact that the DS is a multimodal event; effectiveness is not derived solely from linguistic accuracy but from a complex ensemble of semiotic resources, including paralanguage, gaze, gesture, and facial expression (Jewitt, 2013; Querol-Julián & Fortanet-Gómez, 2016).

Despite its importance, the DS is rarely the subject of explicit instructional intervention. Most doctoral students are expected to acquire the necessary skills through immersion or trial and error. However, the construction of a researcher identity—a process that involves moving from a position of a student to that of a contributing member of a scientific community (Davis & Lester, 2016)—requires more than just exposure. It requires a conscious awareness of the rhetorical and pragmatic strategies used to persuade an audience and build professional rapport. The persuasive nature of the DS means that speakers must navigate a delicate balance between confidence and humility, using mitigation and evaluative language to maintain face while asserting the value of their work. When these skills are lacking, novice researchers may struggle to project the professional identity required for acceptance and integration into their field.

In recent years, the concept of "multiliteracies" has challenged traditional views of literacy by emphasizing that meaning-making occurs through multiple modes—visual, aural, embodied, and spatial (The New London Group, 1996; Cope & Kalantzis, 2009). In higher education, this shift has led to a growing recognition that academic literacy must encompass multimodal competencies (Archer, 2010; O’Halloran et al., 2016). If we accept that academic communication is inherently multimodal, then the teaching of spoken genres must move beyond the transcript and consider the embodied actions of the speaker. Multimodal Discourse Analysis (MDA) provides a framework for understanding how these non-verbal cues interact with verbal language to create interpersonal meaning. Yet, as highlighted by previous research, the application of a multimodal-in-context approach to the specific genre of the DS remains remarkably limited (Querol-Julián & Fortanet-Gómez, 2016).

To address this gap, a robust pedagogical framework is needed—one that moves beyond the simple provision of a list of "useful phrases" for discussion (Reese & Wells, 2007) and instead fosters a deep, critical awareness of the genre. Genre-based pedagogy, particularly the traditions associated with the "Sydney School," offers a promising path (Rose & Martin, 2012; Martin, 2009). The core of this approach is the teaching-learning cycle, which provides a scaffolded transition from teacher-led modelling to independent production (Dreyfus et al., 2016). By deconstructing authentic exemplars, learners can identify the rhetorical "moves" and linguistic patterns that characterize a genre, eventually allowing them to construct their own texts with greater autonomy (Bhatia, 2004; Cheng, 2008).

While the teaching-learning cycle has been widely applied to writing, its application to interactive, multimodal spoken genres presents unique challenges. To be effective in the context of the DS, the pedagogy must shift from a teacher-centered model to a learner-led one. Rather than receiving the "rules" of the genre from the instructor, students should be encouraged to actively deconstruct the discourse themselves, drawing on their own predictions and experiences and analyzing real-world data. This process aligns with the need for higher-order thinking skills (HOTS), moving students from simple recall and understanding toward analysis, evaluation, and creation. Such a critical orientation empowers novice researchers to not only imitate the genre but to manipulate its resources strategically based on the social and professional context of the interaction.

Furthermore, the social nature of this learning process is paramount. Collaborative learning—where students work together to analyze discourse and create guidelines—can reduce anxiety and mirror the communal nature of the academic environment (Laal & Ghodsi, 2012; Le et al., 2017). By engaging in joint construction, students can negotiate their understanding of what constitutes an "effective" discussion, reflecting on the interplay between identity, persuasion, and interpersonal relations. This collaborative reflection transforms the classroom into a community of practice, facilitating the transition from student to researcher.

Given this context, the present study proposes and evaluates a pedagogical model specifically designed for the teaching and learning of the interactive multimodal spoken genre of the discussion session. The model is structured around a three-stage cycle: (1) modelling and joint deconstruction, (2) joint construction, and (3) independent construction. Unlike traditional models, this approach places the responsibility for deconstruction on the learners, utilizing both their prior beliefs and the analysis of authentic video recordings to foster multimodal awareness. The primary aim of this study is to prove the effectiveness of this learner-led, scaffolded approach in helping doctoral students gain control over the verbal and non-verbal resources of the DS.

Specifically, this research seeks to answer two fundamental questions. First, to what extent does this pedagogical model increase students' awareness of the multimodal characteristics of the DS and the role of semiotic ensembles in constructing interpersonal relations? Second, can a scaffolded approach based on critical thinking and collaborative learning effectively support novice researchers in the practical application of this genre? By documenting the implementation of this model in a course for PhD students, this paper contributes to the field of English for Academic Purposes (EAP) by extending genre-based pedagogy into the realm of interactive, multimodal spoken discourse, ultimately providing a tool to help novice researchers successfully enter and navigate their scientific communities.
