intros.text:
Marketization in all public spheres, including academic discourse, has led to the increased importance of promotion. One of the promotional tools usually used in Research Articles Introductions (RAIs) is claiming centrality. In this study, we aimed to explore differences between native and non-native writers in the use of strategies for claiming centrality in Applied Linguistics RAIs. To this end, a corpus of 50 English RAIs (25 L1 and 25 L2) was analyzed in terms of the strategies used for claiming centrality. The analysis of the two sets of texts revealed that they are similar in the mean occurrence of centrality claims in general while in terms of the specific strategies used for claiming centrality, there are differences between them. The findings of this study can be used by instructors of writing courses to address promotion better as well as by article authors to report their research findings more convincingly.

When public institutions adopt the structures and practices of the market model, marketization is said to have taken place (Fairclough, 1993). Mautner (2010, 2015) has recently introduced and discussed the notion of 'market society', believing that a majority of organizations and sectors in societies have adopted the conventions and practices which are typical features of the market-based relationships. This trend has also influenced the realm of discourse, where 'ways of talking that were originally confined to the commercial world are now commonplace in the public sphere generally -in government and public administration, in education, health care, culture, sports, and many other domains' (Mautner, 2015: 1). Academia has not been an exception. Fairclough (1993) argues that academic environment has also been marketized because of the fact that universities are required to operate as businesses, selling their products to consumers. Also, Wernick (1991: vii) reports that academic discourse has been permeated by 'promotional culture', which is a typical feature of market-based practices. In recent years, publication of scientific Research Articles (RAs) has become one of the determinant factors in scholars' professional promotion. On the other hand, the degree of competitiveness in publishing papers in top tier journals continues to grow (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010). Therefore, in such a condition, scholars need to employ appropriate structural and rhetorical tools to demonstrate the value of their work and gain acceptance among other members and gatekeepers of the related disciplinary community (Martin & Perez, 2014). This is where promotionalism comes in. Through the use of discoursal and rhetorical elements which function to enhance the perceived value of one's research (Bhatia, 2005), writers promote their research to others. Bekenkotter and Huckin (1995: 43) also argue that 'today's scientists seem to be promoting their work to a degree never seen before.' For them, one of the main reasons for the increase of promotion is rooted in the current promotional culture, which is changing discoursal practices and creating hybrid genres.

Promotion can be expressed in various forms as it can be 'realized by means of those linguistic choices that seek to change or affect the opinions or behaviors of an audience in terms of positively assessing the research contribution' (Martin & Perez, 2014: 1). It has been studied as a discourse feature realized through evaluation (e.g. Hunston & Thomson, 2000), metadiscourse (e.g. Hyland, 2005), and lexicogrammatical features such as selfreference and self-citation (e.g. Afros & Schryer, 2009; Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2000, 2005). Some other strategies have also functioned as promotional elements, such as explicitly highlighting the novel contributions of the study to the discipline or commenting briefly on the findings in the introduction section (Martin & Perez, 2014). Most of the studies related to promotion have investigated the introduction sections of RAs (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Berkenkotter & Huckin, 1995; Bhatia, 2004; Lindeberg, 2004). This section has been a major focus of attention since it 'generally entails a great deal of complexity in terms of rhetorical options, among them the possibility of including promotional elements' (Martin & Perez, 2014: 2). Analyzing the rhetorical structure of introductions has proved to be the most fruitful method in order to gain an in-depth understanding of, among other things, how promotional elements are employed by the authors of RAs. Swales' (1990) seminal work on the rhetorical structure of introduction has been revolutionary in the analysis and teaching of academic writing. He came up with a model, namely the Create a Research Space (CARS) model, which has been the basis of numerous subsequent studies (e.g. Bhatia, 1993; Burgess, 2002; Fredrickson & Swales, 1994; Loi, 2010; Nwugo, 1991).

Swales' (1990) CARS model is a framework proposed to describe the organizational patterns of writing the Introduction sections in academic research articles. This model assumes that writers, in an attempt to develop an effective introduction to their research articles, follow a general organizational pattern. The model comprises three main actions referred to as 'Moves', each of which consists of a number of 'Steps' as illustrated in Table 1 and briefly explained below.

Move 1: Establishing a territory
Step 1: Claiming centrality and/or
Step 2: Making topic generalization(s) and/or
Step 3: Reviewing items of previous research

Move 2: Establishing a niche
Step 1A: Counter-claiming or
Step 1B: Indicating a gap or
Step 1C: Question-raising or
Step 1D: Continuing a tradition

Move 3: Occupying the niche
Step 1A: Outlining purposes or
Step 1B: Announcing present research
Step 2: Announcing principal findings
Step 3: Indicating RA structure

As Table 1 shows, Move 1 generally sets the ground for introducing the research topic. Step 1 of the first move is claiming centrality, which is defined by Swales (1990) as appeals through which authors argue that their research is 'part of a lively, significant or well established research area' (p. 144). In Step 2, statements are made about the current state of knowledge and the need for further investigations in the area. In Step 3, authors review one or two studies that they consider to be relevant to the establishment (Swales, 1990).

In Move 2, authors try to persuade readers that their research is important and valuable (Swales, 1990). In Step 1A, authors point out the limitations of the general research area; in Step 1B, authors develop a research problem around a gap in the literature; in Step 1C, they raise key questions in the area; and in Step 1D, authors generally pose a weaker challenge to the prior research, aiming to expand or clarify a specific research problem (Swales, 1990).

In Move 3, writers discuss the contribution and organizational structure of their paper (Swales, 1990). In Step 1A, they indicate their main purpose(s); in Step 1B, they describe the main features of their research. In Step 2, authors provide a general summary of key findings, and in Step 3, they bring statements about the structure of the remainder of the article (Swales, 1990).

Later in another book, Swales (2004) made some revisions to his model, which are minor and have not changed the basic structure. As can be seen in Table 2, the moves are roughly the same in the revised version of the model, with a minor difference in the wording of the third move. The steps have undergone relatively more changes, with some steps in the original model omitted and some others added. The order of the steps and their wordings have also been revised. However, it seems that the literature on claiming centrality has mostly favored the original model since it has specifically treated claiming centrality as a separate step in introduction sections, though this does not mean that the revised version totally ignores this rhetorical tool.

Move 1: Establishing a territory (citation required) via
Topic generalization of increasing specificity

Move 2: Establishing a niche (citations possible) via
Step1A: Indicating a gap or
Step1B: Adding to what is known
Step 2: (optional) Presenting positive justification

Move 3: Presenting the present work (citation possible) via
Step 1: (obligatory) Announcing present research descriptively and/or purposively
Step 2: (optional) Presenting research questions (RQs) or hypotheses
Step 3: (optional) Definitional clarifications
Step 4: (optional) Summarizing methods
Step 5: (Probable in Some Fields) Announcing principal outcomes
Step 6: (PISF) Stating the value of the present research
Step 7: (PISF) Outlining the structure of the paper

Lindeberg (2004) argues that Swales' CARS model is based on the rhetorical claiming of territory and niche. For her, the notion of niche itself is rooted in marketing. Furthermore, Berkenkotter and Huckin (1995) note that the rhetorical structure of this model is essentially promotional. Swales himself appears to highlight the promotional aspect of 'claiming centrality' while other moves and steps are also somehow associated with promotion (Lindeberg, 2004), though it should be noted that the CARS model is not meant for the specific investigation of promotion.

In another part of her study, Lindeberg (2004) investigated promotion in other parts of the CARS model as well. She showed that in Move 1, the research topic is promoted through highlighting its importance (claiming centrality); in Move 2, the gap is promoted by presenting the inadequacy of prior research so as to justify the conduction of further research (indicating gaps), and in Move 3, the research is promoted on the basis of the possible contributions it can offer to the discipline (announcing principal findings). She considered claims of centrality as a direct promotional strategy and identified six types of appeals writers in the field of economy make to realize it, that is, appeals to authority, economy, practitioner, research, scope, and topicality. However, in other disciplines including Applied Linguistics claiming centrality had not been elaborated until very recently.

In an in-depth analysis, Wang and Yang (2015) investigated claiming centrality as a promotional strategy in the introduction section of Applied Linguistics RAs. They analyzed 51 RA introductions from three top tier journals in the field, namely, TESOL Quarterly, Modern Language Journal, and Applied Linguistics both qualitatively and quantitatively. Although they used CARS model as the starting point, they did not confine themselves to the first move of the model. Noting that centrality claims can appear in other moves as well, they searched for its realization throughout the introduction section. First, based on the kind of value expressed in the text, they identified four types of appeals, namely, appeals to salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity. Then, they identified two types of entities to which the appeals can be ascribed. As these are the categories of analysis for the present study, we shall discuss them in detail below in the methods section.

After completing the qualitative part, Wang and Yang (2015) also conducted a quantitative analysis to investigate the prevalence of each type of appeals and their orientation. They found that claiming centrality through appeal to magnitude had the highest prevalence. With a minor difference, appeal to salience was the second in terms of the frequency of occurrence. The appeal to problematicity was the third most frequent strategy, which was just slightly more prevalent than appeal to topicality, which had the lowest occurrence in the introduction section of Applied Linguistics RAs. As regards the orientation of the claims, their results showed that centrality is claimed making reference to both research and real worlds, though reference to the former was found to be slightly more frequent (51.3% vs 48.7%, respectively).

Objective reporting of research findings is the socially recognized purpose of RAs (e.g. Barrass, 2002; Zobel, 2004). On the other hand, it is argued that academic writing carries a representation of the writer (Hyland, 2002; Ivanic, 1998), is interactional in nature (Hyland, 2004) and has been permeated with promotion (Mautner, 2010). Bearing these in mind, it seems that gaining the ability to observe all these disciplinary and generic conventions requires much more effort and awareness. This becomes even more difficult when one writes in a language other than his/her mother tongue where interference from their first language can add to the complexity of the issue. Thus, more studies are needed to raise writers' awareness about these aspects of RAs.

From among the aspects of RAs mentioned above, promotion has received less attention, especially when it comes to the specific strategies serving that. Claiming centrality, as one of the promotional strategies, has been investigated by Lindeberg (2004) in a study which dealt with promotion in the three disciplines of Financing, Organization and Management, and Marketing, some of the findings of which were reported above. Another study in this regard was conducted by Wang and Yang (2015), who analyzed claiming centrality in the discipline of Applied Linguistics, which was also reported above. To the best of our knowledge, no study has investigated intercultural differences in the ways through which academic writers claim centrality. Thus, in the present study, we aim to explore the introduction section of RAs written by native English speakers (L1 RAs) and those written by Iranian non-native writers (L2 RAs) in order to highlight their possible differences and/or similarities in promoting their research through the strategies of claiming centrality.

intros.text:
In contemporary academic discourse, the landscape of scholarly communication has undergone a profound transformation, driven by the pervasive influence of marketization across public spheres. As Fairclough (1993) argues, the adoption of market structures and practices by public institutions, including higher education, has fundamentally altered the nature of academic discourse. Universities are increasingly required to operate as businesses, selling their intellectual products to consumers in a competitive global marketplace. This shift has given rise to what Mautner (2010, 2015) terms a 'market society,' where conventions and practices typical of market-based relationships have permeated sectors traditionally governed by public or academic values. In this context, academic discourse has not remained immune to these changes; rather, it has been deeply influenced by a 'promotional culture' (Wernick, 1991), a phenomenon where the rhetoric of marketing and promotion becomes integral to the production and dissemination of knowledge.

The impact of this promotional culture is particularly evident in the realm of scientific publication. The publication of Research Articles (RAs) has become a determinant factor in scholars' professional advancement, career progression, and institutional ranking. Consequently, the degree of competitiveness in publishing papers in top-tier journals continues to grow, creating a high-stakes environment for researchers (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010). In such a condition, scholars must employ appropriate structural and rhetorical tools to demonstrate the value of their work and gain acceptance among the gatekeepers of the disciplinary community (Martin & Perez, 2014). It is within this competitive landscape that the concept of 'promotion' in academic writing has gained significant traction. Through the use of discoursal and rhetorical elements that function to enhance the perceived value of one's research, writers actively promote their work to their peers and potential readers (Bhatia, 2005). As Bekenkotter and Huckin (1995) observe, today's scientists seem to be promoting their work to a degree never seen before, suggesting that the current promotional culture is changing discoursal practices and creating hybrid genres where the boundaries between objective reporting and strategic persuasion are increasingly blurred.

Promotion in academic writing can be expressed in various forms, realized by means of linguistic choices that seek to change or affect the opinions or behaviors of an audience in terms of positively assessing the research contribution (Martin & Perez, 2014). This discourse feature has been studied through multiple lenses, including evaluation (Hunston & Thomson, 2000), metadiscourse (Hyland, 2005), and lexicogrammatical features such as self-reference and self-citation (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2000, 2005). Furthermore, other strategies have been identified as functioning as promotional elements, such as explicitly highlighting the novel contributions of the study to the discipline or commenting briefly on the findings in the introduction section (Martin & Perez, 2014). Among the various sections of a research article, the introduction has emerged as a major focus of attention for scholars investigating promotion. This section is generally regarded as entailing a great deal of complexity in terms of rhetorical options, among them the possibility of including promotional elements (Martin & Perez, 2014). It serves as the primary interface between the researcher and the reader, where the initial case for the study's importance is made.

To understand the rhetorical organization of research article introductions (RAIs), Swales' (1990) seminal work on genre analysis provides a foundational framework. His Create a Research Space (CARS) model has been revolutionary in the analysis and teaching of academic writing, serving as the basis for numerous subsequent studies (e.g., Bhatia, 1993; Burgess, 2002; Fredrickson & Swales, 1994; Loi, 2010; Nwugo, 1991). The CARS model assumes that writers, in an attempt to develop an effective introduction, follow a general organizational pattern comprising three main actions referred to as 'Moves'. Move 1, 'Establishing a territory,' sets the ground for introducing the research topic. This move typically involves claiming centrality (Step 1), making topic generalizations (Step 2), and/or reviewing items of previous research (Step 3). Move 2, 'Establishing a niche,' involves persuading readers that the research is important and valuable by indicating a gap, counter-claiming, raising a question, or continuing a tradition. Finally, Move 3, 'Occupying the niche,' involves outlining the purpose, announcing the present research, announcing principal findings, and indicating the structure of the article. 

Of particular relevance to the current discussion of promotion is Step 1 of Move 1: Claiming Centrality. Swales (1990) defines this step as appeals through which authors argue that their research is 'part of a lively, significant or well established research area' (p. 144). Lindeberg (2004) argues that the CARS model is fundamentally based on the rhetorical claiming of territory and niche, noting that the notion of niche itself is rooted in marketing. Furthermore, Berkenkotter and Huckin (1995) suggest that the rhetorical structure of this model is essentially promotional. While Swales himself highlights the promotional aspect of 'claiming centrality,' it is important to note that the CARS model was not originally designed for the specific investigation of promotion. However, Lindeberg (2004) extended this analysis, investigating promotion across all three moves. She demonstrated that in Move 1, the research topic is promoted through highlighting its importance (claiming centrality); in Move 2, the gap is promoted by presenting the inadequacy of prior research; and in Move 3, the research is promoted based on its potential contributions. Lindeberg (2004) identified six types of appeals writers in the field of economy make to realize claiming centrality: appeals to authority, economy, practitioner, research, scope, and topicality. Despite this foundational work, the specific realization of claiming centrality in other disciplines, particularly Applied Linguistics, had not been elaborated until very recently.

In an in-depth analysis, Wang and Yang (2015) investigated claiming centrality as a promotional strategy specifically within the introduction sections of Applied Linguistics Research Articles. They analyzed 51 RA introductions from three top-tier journals in the field, namely *TESOL Quarterly*, *Modern Language Journal*, and *Applied Linguistics*, employing both qualitative and quantitative methods. Although they utilized the CARS model as a starting point, they did not confine themselves to Move 1, noting that centrality claims can appear in other moves as well. Their analysis identified four types of appeals based on the kind of value expressed in the text: appeals to salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity. Additionally, they identified two types of entities to which these appeals can be ascribed: entities in the real world and entities in the research world. Their quantitative analysis revealed that appeals to magnitude had the highest prevalence, followed by appeals to salience. Appeals to problematicity were the third most frequent, while appeals to topicality had the lowest occurrence. Regarding orientation, their results showed that centrality is claimed by making reference to both research and real worlds, with a slight preference for the former.

While the existing literature has provided valuable insights into the nature of promotion and claiming centrality in academic discourse, significant gaps remain. Most studies related to promotion have investigated the introduction sections of RAs in general or have focused on specific disciplines such as economics or general science (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Berkenkotter & Huckin, 1995; Bhatia, 2004; Lindeberg, 2004). Although Wang and Yang (2015) made a significant contribution by focusing on Applied Linguistics, their study did not distinguish between native and non-native writers. This distinction is crucial, as academic writing is interactional in nature (Hyland, 2004) and carries a representation of the writer (Hyland, 2002; Ivanic, 1998). Gaining the ability to observe all these disciplinary and generic conventions requires much effort and awareness. This becomes even more difficult when one writes in a language other than their mother tongue, where interference from their first language can add to the complexity of the issue. Furthermore, the increasing competitiveness of academic publication (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010) necessitates a deeper understanding of how different groups of writers navigate these rhetorical demands.

To the best of our knowledge, no study has investigated intercultural differences in the ways through which academic writers claim centrality. The existing literature has largely treated writers as a homogeneous group, overlooking the potential variations in rhetorical strategies employed by native English speakers (L1) versus non-native English speakers (L2). Understanding these differences is vital for several reasons. First, it contributes to the theoretical understanding of genre variation across linguistic and cultural boundaries. Second, it has significant pedagogical implications for instructors of writing courses in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) and English for Specific Purposes (ESP). As noted by Hyland (2005), raising writers' awareness about these aspects of RAs is essential for their successful integration into the global academic community. Without such awareness, L2 writers may struggle to position themselves effectively within the relevant disciplinary community and gain credit for their research.

Therefore, the present study aims to explore the introduction sections of Research Articles written by native English speakers (L1 RAs) and those written by Iranian non-native writers (L2 RAs) in the field of Applied Linguistics. Specifically, this study seeks to highlight the possible differences and/or similarities in promoting their research through the strategies of claiming centrality. By utilizing the framework established by Wang and Yang (2015), this research will analyze the frequency, types, and orientations of centrality claims in a corpus of 50 RA introductions. The findings of this study are expected to provide a clear picture of how centrality claims are realized by different groups of writers. This knowledge can be used by instructors of writing courses to address promotion better, as well as by article authors to report their research findings more convincingly. Ultimately, this research contributes to the broader understanding of how marketization and promotional culture influence the rhetorical practices of academic writing in a globalized context, offering insights into the specific challenges and strategies faced by non-native writers in the competitive arena of international publication.

intros.text:
Academic writing is often described as a vehicle for the objective reporting of research findings, and research articles are conventionally expected to present knowledge claims in a cautious, impersonal and evidence-based manner (Barrass, 1978; Zobel, 2004). Yet research articles are also persuasive texts. They are written for particular disciplinary audiences, evaluated by reviewers and editors, and positioned within competitive systems of academic recognition. Writers therefore need not only to report what they have done but also to convince readers that the work is timely, relevant and worth reading. This persuasive dimension has become increasingly visible in contemporary academic discourse, where scholars compete for publication space, citations, institutional rewards and professional advancement. In this context, the ability to promote one’s research appropriately has become an important part of successful participation in disciplinary communities.

The growing prominence of promotional discourse in academia is closely related to wider processes of marketization. Fairclough (1993) argues that public institutions, including universities, have increasingly adopted the values, structures and discursive practices of the market. Mautner (2010, 2015) similarly observes that market principles have extended beyond commercial settings into public domains such as education, government and health care, giving rise to discourses in which visibility, competition and self-presentation play central roles. In higher education, this shift is reflected in the pressure on universities and individual academics to demonstrate productivity, impact and excellence. Publication in prestigious journals has become a key measure of academic value, and the competition for journal space has intensified, particularly for scholars seeking to publish in English-medium international outlets (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2013). Under these conditions, research writing is shaped not only by epistemic norms of accuracy and objectivity but also by the need to present research as significant and valuable.

Promotion in academic discourse does not normally take the form of overt advertising. Rather, it is embedded in the rhetorical and linguistic choices through which writers construct the relevance of their topics, identify gaps in previous knowledge, foreground their contributions and align their work with disciplinary expectations. Bhatia (2005) notes that promotional discourse is realized through generic patterns that enhance the perceived value of a product, service or activity; in academic writing, the “product” is the research itself. Berkenkotter and Huckin (1994) also argue that genre knowledge is inseparable from disciplinary practice and that academic genres evolve in response to changing institutional and professional conditions. In contemporary research articles, promotion can therefore be understood as a legitimate rhetorical activity through which writers seek recognition for their work while conforming to the norms of scholarly communication.

A considerable body of research has examined the interpersonal and evaluative resources through which academic writers negotiate this promotional task. Studies of evaluation have shown that writers use linguistic resources to express judgements of importance, novelty, limitation and contribution (Hunston & Thompson, 2001). Research on metadiscourse has demonstrated that academic texts are interactional, involving writers in the management of relationships with readers through stance, engagement and textual guidance (Hyland, 2001, 2005). Other studies have focused on self-mention, self-citation and authorial presence, showing that writers strategically balance authority and modesty when presenting their claims (Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2002). These lines of work have challenged the view of research writing as purely impersonal and have emphasized that successful academic writing depends on the writer’s ability to anticipate readers’ expectations, establish credibility and construct a persuasive authorial identity (Ivanič, 1998; Hyland, 2004).

Within the research article, the introduction section is especially important for understanding promotion. Research article introductions are the point at which writers first engage readers, locate their work within an existing field and justify the need for the present study. They are rhetorically complex because they must establish a topic, review relevant research, identify a problem or gap and announce the contribution of the current paper, often within a limited space. For this reason, introductions have been central to genre-based research in English for Academic Purposes and English for Specific Purposes. Swales’ (1990) Create a Research Space (CARS) model has been particularly influential in describing the rhetorical organization of research article introductions. In this model, writers typically establish a territory, establish a niche and then occupy that niche. The first move introduces the research area and may include claiming centrality, making topic generalizations and reviewing previous research. The second move creates a space for the new study by indicating a gap, raising questions, counter-claiming or continuing a tradition. The third move presents the current research by stating its purpose, announcing the study and, in some cases, summarizing findings or outlining the structure of the article.

The CARS model has provided a productive framework for analysing research article introductions across disciplines and languages (Bhatia, 2004; Loi, 2010; Nwogu, 1991; Swales, 2004). It has also been useful pedagogically, helping novice and second-language writers understand how introductions are conventionally organized. However, the model is not only a description of textual structure; it also points to the persuasive work that introductions perform. Lindeberg (2006) notes that the concepts of “territory” and “niche” have affinities with marketing, since writers must claim a space for their work in a crowded intellectual environment. Berkenkotter and Huckin (1994) similarly view research article introductions as strongly promotional, because they require writers to demonstrate that the research area is important, that something remains to be done and that the present study is capable of addressing that need. Thus, while academic introductions are not promotional in the same way as advertisements, they are sites where writers subtly enhance the value of their research.

One key promotional strategy in research article introductions is claiming centrality. In Swales’ (1990) original CARS model, claiming centrality is identified as a step in Move 1, through which writers assert that their research topic belongs to a significant, active or well-established area. A centrality claim may state that a topic is important, widely studied, increasingly relevant, controversial or problematic. Such claims help writers justify why readers should care about the topic before the particular niche of the study is introduced. Although Swales’ (2004) revised model no longer treats claiming centrality in exactly the same way, the rhetorical function remains important: writers still need to persuade readers that the territory in which their research is situated deserves attention. Claiming centrality can therefore be regarded as a direct means of promotion because it foregrounds the value of the topic and prepares the ground for the value of the study.

Despite its importance, claiming centrality has received less focused attention than other aspects of academic promotion. Lindeberg’s work on promotion in economics-related disciplines showed that centrality claims can be realized through different types of appeals, such as appeals to authority, economy, practitioners, research, scope and topicality. More recently, Wang and Yang (2015) offered a detailed account of claiming centrality in applied linguistics research article introductions. They argued that centrality claims are not restricted to the first move of the introduction but can occur throughout the section wherever writers foreground the value of the research topic. Their analysis identified four main types of appeal: salience, magnitude, topicality and problematicity. Appeals to salience explicitly state the importance, usefulness or significance of a topic or key construct. Appeals to magnitude imply importance by referring to the prevalence, popularity or extensive investigation of a topic. Appeals to topicality highlight newness, recency or timeliness. Appeals to problematicity foreground difficulties, challenges, controversies or unresolved issues associated with the topic. Wang and Yang (2015) also distinguished between claims oriented to the research world, such as references to scholarly attention or gaps in research, and claims oriented to the real world, such as references to social, educational or practical phenomena.

This typology is particularly relevant to applied linguistics because the field is both research-oriented and practice-oriented. Applied linguistics research often addresses issues that matter to teachers, learners, testers, curriculum designers and policy makers, while also contributing to theoretical and empirical debates. Writers in the field can therefore claim centrality by referring either to developments in scholarship or to practical concerns in language education and communication. For example, a writer may promote a topic by stating that it has attracted considerable research attention, that it affects large numbers of language learners, that it has recently become prominent in educational policy, or that it remains a persistent challenge for classroom practice. These options provide writers with a repertoire of promotional strategies, but they also require rhetorical judgement. Different writers may prefer different appeals depending on their linguistic resources, disciplinary experience, publication context and cultural background.

The question of how first-language and second-language writers use promotional strategies is especially important in the present global academic environment. English has become the dominant language of international research publication, and many scholars must write for English-medium journals in a language that is not their first language. This can impose additional burdens on L2 writers, who may face difficulties not only with grammar and vocabulary but also with genre conventions, rhetorical expectations and interpersonal positioning (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2013). Writing a research article introduction requires sensitivity to what can be claimed, how strongly it can be claimed and how the value of a study can be made visible without appearing exaggerated. Such sensitivity may be particularly demanding for scholars who are negotiating between local academic traditions and international English-language publication norms.

Previous contrastive genre studies have shown that research article introductions may vary across languages and academic cultures. Loi (2010), for instance, found differences in the rhetorical organization of Chinese and English research article introductions in educational psychology, even though both sets of texts broadly reflected the CARS pattern. Such findings suggest that writers’ rhetorical choices are shaped by cultural and institutional expectations as well as disciplinary conventions. However, while there is now substantial research on move structure, metadiscourse and authorial stance in L1 and L2 academic writing, relatively little is known about whether L1 and L2 writers differ in the specific strategies they use to claim centrality. This is a notable gap because centrality claims are among the earliest and most direct ways in which writers promote their research topic and invite readers to accept its significance.

The present study addresses this gap by examining centrality claims in English research article introductions written by two groups of applied linguistics scholars: native English-speaking writers and Iranian non-native English writers. The focus on Iranian L2 writers is significant because Iranian applied linguists, like many scholars working in expanding-circle contexts, are increasingly expected to publish in English and to participate in international academic networks. At the same time, they may draw on rhetorical preferences and writing practices shaped by local educational and academic traditions. Comparing their use of centrality claims with that of L1 English writers can therefore provide insight into both shared disciplinary conventions and possible areas of rhetorical difference.

Using Wang and Yang’s (2015) framework, this study investigates not only how frequently L1 and L2 writers claim centrality but also which types of appeal they use and whether these appeals are oriented toward the research world or the real world. The study is guided by the following broad questions: To what extent do L1 and L2 English research article introductions in applied linguistics employ centrality claims? What types of appeals are used to realize these claims? And how are these claims oriented in relation to research-world and real-world entities? By answering these questions, the study aims to contribute to research on academic promotion, genre analysis and L2 scholarly writing. It also has pedagogical relevance for EAP and ESP instruction, where raising writers’ awareness of promotional strategies can help them construct more persuasive introductions and present their research more effectively to disciplinary audiences.

Swales’ (1990) Create a Research Space (CARS) model has been particularly influential in describing the rhetorical organization of research article introductions. In this model, writers typically establish a territory, establish a niche and then occupy that niche. The first move introduces the research area and may include claiming centrality, making topic generalizations and reviewing previous research. The second move creates a space for the new study by indicating a gap, raising questions, counter-claiming or continuing a tradition. The third move presents the current research by stating its purpose, announcing the study and, in some cases, summarizing findings or outlining the structure of the article.

The CARS model has provided a productive framework for analysing research article introductions across disciplines and languages (Bhatia, 2004; Loi, 2010; Nwogu, 1991; Swales, 2004). It has also been useful pedagogically, helping novice and second-language writers understand how introductions are conventionally organized.

intros.text:
The research article has long been regarded as a principal means through which scholars report findings, contribute to disciplinary knowledge, and participate in the collective construction of academic understanding. Yet contemporary academic writing is not merely a neutral vehicle for presenting information. In increasingly competitive publication contexts, research writers are also expected to persuade editors, reviewers, and readers that their work is timely, relevant, and worthy of attention. This persuasive dimension has become particularly salient as higher education and research have been influenced by broader processes of marketization, through which public institutions adopt values and practices associated with the marketplace (Fairclough, 1993; Mautner, 2010, 2015). In such an environment, academic texts often need to display not only methodological rigour and disciplinary relevance but also the value and attractiveness of the research being reported.

The marketization of academic discourse has been closely associated with what Wernick (1991) terms promotional culture. Universities, journals, and individual researchers operate within systems where visibility, productivity, and publication in high-status outlets are increasingly consequential. Publication in international journals has become a major index of scholarly achievement, while competition for acceptance in such journals continues to intensify (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010). These pressures have made promotional discourse an important aspect of academic communication. Promotion in research writing can be understood as the use of rhetorical and linguistic resources that encourage readers to positively evaluate a study, its topic, its methods, or its contribution (Bhatia, 2005; Martín Martín & León Pérez, 2013). Although research articles are conventionally associated with objectivity and impersonal reporting (Barrass, 1978; Zobel, 2004), they also involve interactional choices through which writers construct authority, negotiate community expectations, and represent themselves as credible contributors (Hyland, 2001, 2002, 2004; Ivanič, 1998).

Research article introductions are especially important sites for such rhetorical work. The introduction is the section in which writers typically establish the relevance of the topic, position the study in relation to prior research, identify a research space, and present the contribution of the current work. Because readers’ first evaluations of a study are often shaped by this section, introductions provide opportunities for writers to make strategic claims about the significance and necessity of their research. Genre-based studies have therefore paid considerable attention to the rhetorical organization of research article introductions, especially following Swales’ (1990) Create a Research Space (CARS) model. In this model, writers are seen as moving from establishing a territory, to establishing a niche, and then occupying that niche. The model, later revised by Swales (2004), has served as a central framework for analysing introductions across disciplines and languages (Bhatia, 1993; Loi, 2010; Nwogu, 1991).

One of the most explicit promotional resources in research article introductions is claiming centrality. In Swales’ (1990) original model, claiming centrality appears as a step in Move 1, where writers seek to convince readers that the research area is important, active, or well established. A centrality claim may foreground the importance of a topic, the prevalence of a phenomenon, the amount of research interest it has attracted, its recent emergence, or the challenges it poses. Although this rhetorical act may appear to be a relatively small component of the introduction, it performs a crucial persuasive function: it helps justify why the topic deserves scholarly attention before the writer turns to a specific gap or contribution. In this sense, claiming centrality contributes to the broader promotional work of the introduction by making the research territory itself appear valuable.

Previous research has examined promotion in academic writing through several related perspectives. Studies of evaluation have shown how writers encode attitudes, values, and judgements in texts (Hunston & Thompson, 2001). Research on metadiscourse has demonstrated how authors guide readers, signal stance, and build relationships with their audience (Hyland, 2005). Other studies have investigated specific lexicogrammatical resources such as self-mention, self-citation, and explicit statements of novelty or contribution (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2000, 2005). Together, this body of work indicates that academic writing is not simply informational but also interpersonal and persuasive. Writers must present their work in ways that conform to disciplinary expectations while also distinguishing it from existing research.

Within this line of inquiry, several scholars have argued that the rhetorical structure of research article introductions is inherently promotional. Berkenkotter and Huckin (1995) suggest that contemporary scientific writing increasingly involves the promotion of one’s work, reflecting changes in disciplinary communication and academic reward systems. Lindeberg (2004) similarly argues that the CARS model is grounded in the rhetorical claiming of territory and niche, and that its moves are closely connected to promotional purposes. Establishing a territory promotes the topic by presenting it as important or active; establishing a niche promotes the research problem by showing that prior work is incomplete or insufficient; and occupying the niche promotes the present study by emphasizing its aims, findings, or contribution. Claiming centrality is therefore one of the most direct strategies through which writers promote the importance of their research area.

Lindeberg’s (2004) analysis of promotion in business-related disciplines identified several types of appeals through which writers claimed centrality, including appeals to authority, economy, practitioners, research, scope, and topicality. Her work demonstrated that centrality claims are not uniform but are realized through different value bases depending on disciplinary and rhetorical context. More recently, Wang and Yang (2015) provided a detailed account of claiming centrality in applied linguistics research article introductions. Their study showed that centrality claims may occur not only in the first move of the introduction but throughout the section, and they identified four main types of appeals: salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity. Appeals to salience directly state the importance, usefulness, or significance of a topic or construct; appeals to magnitude emphasize prevalence, frequency, or extensive research interest; appeals to topicality highlight newness or recency; and appeals to problematicity foreground difficulties, challenges, controversies, or conflicts related to the topic. Wang and Yang also distinguished between appeals oriented to entities in the research world, such as research areas, studies, and researchers, and those oriented to entities in the real world, such as learners, teachers, institutions, or social phenomena.

Applied linguistics is a particularly suitable field for examining such promotional strategies. It is an internationally active and highly interdisciplinary area whose research often addresses both theoretical concerns and practical issues in language teaching, learning, assessment, and use. Research article introductions in applied linguistics therefore frequently need to connect academic debates with real-world educational concerns. Writers may claim centrality by pointing to the importance of a pedagogical issue, the number of learners affected by a phenomenon, the growth of scholarly interest in a construct, or the problems faced by teachers and students. These different appeals may reflect not only individual rhetorical preferences but also broader disciplinary conventions and cultural writing practices.

For scholars writing in English as an additional language, the ability to use such strategies effectively is especially consequential. English remains the dominant language of international academic publishing, and many non-native English-speaking scholars are required to publish in English to gain professional recognition. However, writing research articles in a second language imposes additional burdens related to linguistic proficiency, rhetorical expectations, and access to disciplinary conventions (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010). L2 writers may be fully competent researchers yet still face challenges in aligning their texts with the persuasive norms expected by international journals. These challenges are not limited to grammar or vocabulary; they also include the ability to manage stance, construct authorial identity, and promote research claims appropriately.

Cross-cultural and contrastive genre studies have shown that writers from different linguistic and academic backgrounds may organize research article introductions differently. For example, Loi (2010) found differences between Chinese and English research article introductions in educational psychology, including variation in the use of moves and steps associated with Swales’ CARS model. Such findings suggest that rhetorical practices are shaped by disciplinary, cultural, and institutional contexts. If claiming centrality is an important promotional resource, then it is reasonable to expect that L1 and L2 writers may differ not only in how often they make centrality claims but also in the kinds of appeals they prefer and the entities to which they attach value.

Despite the growing interest in academic promotion, relatively little attention has been paid to claiming centrality as a specific rhetorical strategy, and even less is known about how it may vary across L1 and L2 English research writing. Existing studies have provided valuable descriptions of promotional discourse in research articles (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Bhatia, 2005; Martín Martín & León Pérez, 2013) and of centrality claims in particular disciplinary contexts (Lindeberg, 2004; Wang & Yang, 2015). However, intercultural differences in the realization of claiming centrality remain underexplored, especially in applied linguistics research article introductions written by native English-speaking authors and by Iranian non-native English-speaking authors. This gap is important because centrality claims are among the first rhetorical resources through which writers invite readers to view their topic and study as significant. Differences in their use may influence how convincingly writers position their work within the discipline.

The present study addresses this gap by examining strategies for claiming centrality in English research article introductions in applied linguistics written by two groups of authors: native English-speaking writers and Iranian non-native English-speaking writers. Drawing on Wang and Yang’s (2015) framework, the study analyses the types of appeals used to claim centrality—salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity—as well as the orientation of these appeals to real-world or research-world entities. The analysis is based on a corpus of 50 empirical research article introductions, comprising 25 L1 English articles published in international applied linguistics journals and 25 L2 English articles written by Iranian authors and published in respected national journals in the field.

By comparing these two sub-corpora, the study aims to determine whether L1 and L2 writers differ in the overall frequency of centrality claims and, more importantly, in the specific rhetorical strategies through which such claims are realized. It also seeks to identify whether the two groups differ in their tendency to ground centrality in real-world phenomena or in research-world activity. In doing so, the study contributes to research on academic discourse, genre analysis, and English for Academic Purposes by providing a more fine-grained account of a promotional strategy that is central to the persuasive work of research article introductions.

The findings have potential pedagogical and practical significance. For EAP and ESP instructors, a clearer understanding of how centrality claims are constructed can inform the teaching of research writing beyond general move structures, helping novice scholars attend to the specific evaluative and promotional choices through which research topics are made persuasive. For L2 writers, especially those seeking publication in English-medium journals, awareness of the range of centrality-claiming strategies may support more effective positioning of their work within disciplinary conversations. More broadly, examining claiming centrality in L1 and L2 writing can illuminate how academic promotion operates at the intersection of language, culture, disciplinary practice, and the contemporary marketized conditions of scholarly communication.

segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the importance phrase “a major index of scholarly achievement” claims the centrality of international journal publication.

segments.text: These pressures have made promotional discourse an important aspect of academic communication.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit importance marker “an important aspect” claims the centrality of promotional discourse in academic communication.

segments.text: Promotion in research writing can be understood as the use of rhetorical and linguistic resources that encourage readers to positively evaluate a study, its topic, its methods, or its contribution (Bhatia, 2005; Martín Martín & León Pérez, 2013).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the cited definition of promotion in research writing reviews prior conceptual work by Bhatia and Martín Martín and León Pérez.

segments.text: Although research articles are conventionally associated with objectivity and impersonal reporting (Barrass, 1978; Zobel, 2004), they also involve interactional choices through which writers construct authority, negotiate community expectations, and represent themselves as credible contributors (Hyland, 2001, 2002, 2004; Ivanič, 1998).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the multiple citations synthesize prior research on objectivity, interactional choices, authority, and authorial credibility in research articles.

segments.text: Research article introductions are especially important sites for such rhetorical work.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit centrality marker “especially important sites” claims the importance of research article introductions.

segments.text: The introduction is the section in which writers typically establish the relevance of the topic, position the study in relation to prior research, identify a research space, and present the contribution of the current work. Because readers’ first evaluations of a study are often shaped by this section, introductions provide opportunities for writers to make strategic claims about the significance and necessity of their research.
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the uncited explanatory description of what introductions do and why they shape readers’ evaluations makes topic generalizations.

segments.text: Genre-based studies have therefore paid considerable attention to the rhetorical organization of research article introductions, especially following Swales’ (1990) Create a Research Space (CARS) model. In this model, writers are seen as moving from establishing a territory, to establishing a niche, and then occupying that niche. The model, later revised by Swales (2004), has served as a central framework for analysing introductions across disciplines and languages (Bhatia, 1993; Loi, 2010; Nwogu, 1991).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews prior genre-based research and the CARS model through citations to Swales, Bhatia, Loi, and Nwogu.

segments.text: One of the most explicit promotional resources in research article introductions is claiming centrality.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the importance marker “one of the most explicit promotional resources” claims the centrality of claiming centrality.

segments.text: In Swales’ (1990) original model, claiming centrality appears as a step in Move 1, where writers seek to convince readers that the research area is important, active, or well established. A centrality claim may foreground the importance of a topic, the prevalence of a phenomenon, the amount of research interest it has attracted, its recent emergence, or the challenges it poses.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews Swales’ model and describes how prior genre theory characterizes centrality claims.

segments.text: Although this rhetorical act may appear to be a relatively small component of the introduction, it performs a crucial persuasive function: it helps justify why the topic deserves scholarly attention before the writer turns to a specific gap or contribution. In this sense, claiming centrality contributes to the broader promotional work of the introduction by making the research territory itself appear valuable.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit importance phrase “performs a crucial persuasive function” claims the centrality of claiming centrality in introductions.

segments.text: Previous research has examined promotion in academic writing through several related perspectives. Studies of evaluation have shown how writers encode attitudes, values, and judgements in texts (Hunston & Thompson, 2001). Research on metadiscourse has demonstrated how authors guide readers, signal stance, and build relationships with their audience (Hyland, 2005). Other studies have investigated specific lexicogrammatical resources such as self-mention, self-citation, and explicit statements of novelty or contribution (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Harwood, 2005a, 2005b; Hyland, 2000, 2005). Together, this body of work indicates that academic writing is not simply informational but also interpersonal and persuasive.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews and synthesizes prior studies on evaluation, metadiscourse, and promotional lexicogrammatical resources.

segments.text: Writers must present their work in ways that conform to disciplinary expectations while also distinguishing it from existing research.
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the uncited broad statement generalizes about writers’ need to conform to and distinguish themselves within disciplinary expectations.

segments.text: Within this line of inquiry, several scholars have argued that the rhetorical structure of research article introductions is inherently promotional. Berkenkotter and Huckin (1995) suggest that contemporary scientific writing increasingly involves the promotion of one’s work, reflecting changes in disciplinary communication and academic reward systems. Lindeberg (2004) similarly argues that the CARS model is grounded in the rhetorical claiming of territory and niche, and that its moves are closely connected to promotional purposes. Establishing a territory promotes the topic by presenting it as important or active; establishing a niche promotes the research problem by showing that prior work is incomplete or insufficient; and occupying the niche promotes the present study by emphasizing its aims, findings, or contribution.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews prior arguments by Berkenkotter and Huckin and Lindeberg about the promotional nature of research article introductions.

segments.text: Claiming centrality is therefore one of the most direct strategies through which writers promote the importance of their research area.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit importance phrase “one of the most direct strategies” claims the centrality of claiming centrality as a promotional resource.

segments.text: Lindeberg’s (2004) analysis of promotion in business-related disciplines identified several types of appeals through which writers claimed centrality, including appeals to authority, economy, practitioners, research, scope, and topicality. Her work demonstrated that centrality claims are not uniform but are realized through different value bases depending on disciplinary and rhetorical context. More recently, Wang and Yang (2015) provided a detailed account of claiming centrality in applied linguistics research article introductions. Their study showed that centrality claims may occur not only in the first move of the introduction but throughout the section, and they identified four main types of appeals: salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity. Appeals to salience directly state the importance, usefulness, or significance of a topic or construct; appeals to magnitude emphasize prevalence, frequency, or extensive research interest; appeals to topicality highlight newness or recency; and appeals to problematicity foreground difficulties, challenges, controversies, or conflicts related to the topic. Wang and Yang also distinguished between appeals oriented to entities in the research world, such as research areas, studies, and researchers, and those oriented to entities in the real world, such as learners, teachers, institutions, or social phenomena.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews specific prior studies by Lindeberg and Wang and Yang and summarizes their findings about centrality-claiming appeals.

segments.text: Applied linguistics is a particularly suitable field for examining such promotional strategies.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the value marker “particularly suitable” claims the relevance and importance of applied linguistics for examining promotional strategies.

segments.text: It is an internationally active and highly interdisciplinary area whose research often addresses both theoretical concerns and practical issues in language teaching, learning, assessment, and use. Research article introductions in applied linguistics therefore frequently need to connect academic debates with real-world educational concerns. Writers may claim centrality by pointing to the importance of a pedagogical issue, the number of learners affected by a phenomenon, the growth of scholarly interest in a construct, or the problems faced by teachers and students. These different appeals may reflect not only individual rhetorical preferences but also broader disciplinary conventions and cultural writing practices.
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the uncited description of applied linguistics and its rhetorical practices makes topic generalizations about the field.

segments.text: For scholars writing in English as an additional language, the ability to use such strategies effectively is especially consequential.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit importance marker “especially consequential” claims the centrality of centrality-claiming strategies for additional-language scholars.

segments.text: English remains the dominant language of international academic publishing, and many non-native English-speaking scholars are required to publish in English to gain professional recognition.
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the uncited broad statement generalizes about English dominance and publication requirements in international academic publishing.

segments.text: However, writing research articles in a second language imposes additional burdens related to linguistic proficiency, rhetorical expectations, and access to disciplinary conventions (Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Lillis & Curry, 2010).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews cited prior research on the burdens faced by second-language research article writers.

segments.text: L2 writers may be fully competent researchers yet still face challenges in aligning their texts with the persuasive norms expected by international journals. These challenges are not limited to grammar or vocabulary; they also include the ability to manage stance, construct authorial identity, and promote research claims appropriately.
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the uncited broad statements generalize about challenges faced by L2 writers in meeting persuasive journal norms.

segments.text: Cross-cultural and contrastive genre studies have shown that writers from different linguistic and academic backgrounds may organize research article introductions differently. For example, Loi (2010) found differences between Chinese and English research article introductions in educational psychology, including variation in the use of moves and steps associated with Swales’ CARS model. Such findings suggest that rhetorical practices are shaped by disciplinary, cultural, and institutional contexts.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews prior contrastive genre research, especially Loi’s findings, and synthesizes their implications.

segments.text: If claiming centrality is an important promotional resource, then it is reasonable to expect that L1 and L2 writers may differ not only in how often they make centrality claims but also in the kinds of appeals they prefer and the entities to which they attach value.
segments.label: move_2__question_raising
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the conditional inference “it is reasonable to expect” raises a question about possible L1/L2 differences in centrality claims.

segments.text: Despite the growing interest in academic promotion, relatively little attention has been paid to claiming centrality as a specific rhetorical strategy, and even less is known about how it may vary across L1 and L2 English research writing.
segments.label: move_2__indicating_a_gap
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the phrases “relatively little attention” and “even less is known” explicitly indicate a gap in existing research.

segments.text: Existing studies have provided valuable descriptions of promotional discourse in research articles (Afros & Schryer, 2009; Bhatia, 2005; Martín Martín & León Pérez, 2013) and of centrality claims in particular disciplinary contexts (Lindeberg, 2004; Wang & Yang, 2015).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews existing studies and their contributions to descriptions of promotional discourse and centrality claims.

segments.text: However, intercultural differences in the realization of claiming centrality remain underexplored, especially in applied linguistics research article introductions written by native English-speaking authors and by Iranian non-native English-speaking authors.
segments.label: move_2__indicating_a_gap
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the explicit absence marker “remain underexplored” indicates the specific research gap.

segments.text: This gap is important because centrality claims are among the first rhetorical resources through which writers invite readers to view their topic and study as significant. Differences in their use may influence how convincingly writers position their work within the discipline.
segments.label: move_2__indicating_a_gap
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the phrase “This gap is important because” develops the significance of the identified gap rather than reviewing prior work.

segments.text: The present study addresses this gap by examining strategies for claiming centrality in English research article introductions in applied linguistics written by two groups of authors: native English-speaking writers and Iranian non-native English-speaking writers.
segments.label: move_3__outlining_purpose
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the phrase “The present study addresses this gap by examining” explicitly outlines the study’s purpose.

segments.text: Drawing on Wang and Yang’s (2015) framework, the study analyses the types of appeals used to claim centrality—salience, magnitude, topicality, and problematicity—as well as the orientation of these appeals to real-world or research-world entities. The analysis is based on a corpus of 50 empirical research article introductions, comprising 25 L1 English articles published in international applied linguistics journals and 25 L2 English articles written by Iranian authors and published in respected national journals in the field.
segments.label: move_3__announcing_present_research
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the methodological signals “Drawing on Wang and Yang’s framework,” “analyses,” and “based on a corpus of 50” announce the present research design and data.

segments.text: By comparing these two sub-corpora, the study aims to determine whether L1 and L2 writers differ in the overall frequency of centrality claims and, more importantly, in the specific rhetorical strategies through which such claims are realized. It also seeks to identify whether the two groups differ in their tendency to ground centrality in real-world phenomena or in research-world activity.
segments.label: move_3__outlining_purpose
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the aim signals “aims to determine” and “seeks to identify” outline the study’s purposes.

segments.text: In doing so, the study contributes to research on academic discourse, genre analysis, and English for Academic Purposes by providing a more fine-grained account of a promotional strategy that is central to the persuasive work of research article introductions.
segments.label: move_3__announcing_principal_findings
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the contribution signal “the study contributes” announces the intended principal contribution of the research.

segments.text: The findings have potential pedagogical and practical significance. For EAP and ESP instructors, a clearer understanding of how centrality claims are constructed can inform the teaching of research writing beyond general move structures, helping novice scholars attend to the specific evaluative and promotional choices through which research topics are made persuasive. For L2 writers, especially those seeking publication in English-medium journals, awareness of the range of centrality-claiming strategies may support more effective positioning of their work within disciplinary conversations. More broadly, examining claiming centrality in L1 and L2 writing can illuminate how academic promotion operates at the intersection of language, culture, disciplinary practice, and the contemporary marketized conditions of scholarly communication.
segments.label: move_3__announcing_principal_findings
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the implication cues “potential pedagogical and practical significance,” “can inform,” “may support,” and “can illuminate” announce the study’s anticipated significance and implications.

intros.text: Larsen-Freeman (2006) understands language as a complex, dynamic system and language  use/acquisition as dynamic adaptedness to a specific context. This, in her own words (2006:  590) “proves a useful way of understanding change in progress, such as that which occurs  with a developing L2 system”. As Larsen-Freeman states, because language is complex,  progress cannot be totally accounted for by performance in any subsystem. She refers to van  Geert and Steenbeek (2005) to explain that linguistic subsystems, dimensions of language proficiency (accuracy, fluency, and complexity), and even individual elements of language interact in ways that could be both supportive and competitive. This perspective sees “linguistic signs not as autonomous objects of any kind, either social or psychological, but  as contextualised products of the integration of various activities by [particular] individuals  in particular communicative situations” (Larsen-Freeman, 2006: 594). Written competence is a subset of learners’ language competence, with an emphasis on  writing-specific abilities such as the production of a variety of genres and rhetorical features,  but also including language-specific abilities like the use of a range of vocabulary and  syntactic structures (Wolfe-Quintero, Inagaki & Kim, 1998: 2). Written competence as a  subset of language competence is also complex and can only be explained by the interaction  of different dimensions of language proficiency. Moreover, fluctuations in one component,  such as fluency or complexity, might be associated with various fluctuations in another  (Skehan, 1998, 2009).  As our framework for the present study, the notions of complexity, accuracy, and  fluency which make up the Common Assessment Framework (CAF) are regarded as the  principal constructs to capture the multidimensionality of L2 written performance.  Within  this framework we intend to examine two dimensions of written language proficiency,  namely, grammatical complexity and accuracy, considering the relationships and interactions  between them. Moreover, the aim is to study and analyse the errors in the written English of  EFL learners as an indicator of their developmental stage in morphology, syntax and lexis.  This study examines learners at two levels of proficiency, upper intermediate (B2) and  advanced (C1) users according to the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001).

intros.text:
The development of second language (L2) writing has long occupied a central place in applied linguistics and English language teaching research, in part because written production offers a tangible window into the state of a learner's interlanguage. Among the constructs used to describe and measure such production, complexity, accuracy and fluency (CAF) have become well established as the principal dimensions of L2 performance (Skehan, 2009; Wolfe-Quintero, Inagaki & Kim, 1998). Foster and Skehan (1996) conceptualised accuracy as the relative absence of errors and grammatical complexity as the use of progressively more elaborate language and a greater variety of syntactic patterning, associating complexity with growth and change in the interlanguage system and accuracy with control at a given developmental point. Investigating how these dimensions behave as proficiency increases has therefore become a fruitful, though far from settled, line of enquiry.

Despite a substantial body of work, findings on L2 writing development remain notably inconclusive. Some studies report gradual improvement in holistic scores and in accuracy and complexity as proficiency rises (e.g. Larsen-Freeman, 2006), whereas others fail to detect such gains, observing improvement only in fluency or holistic ratings. Equally, the pattern of error development is contested: while certain studies suggest a broadly linear reduction of errors, others describe non-linear trajectories characterised by stabilisation and even regression. These divergent results indicate that the relationship between proficiency and written accuracy and complexity is more intricate than a simple linear model would predict.

A parallel strand of research has examined specific error categories, including grammatical morphemes, prepositions, articles, connectors, collocations, spelling and punctuation, with several of these features proving persistently resistant to improvement even among advanced learners. Following early insights that learner errors constitute valuable evidence of the developmental stages learners have reached (Brown & Fraser, 1964; Corder, 1967), we take error analysis as a means of tracing developmental trajectories.

The present study addresses these gaps by comparing the compositions of Spanish EFL undergraduates at two levels of proficiency—upper intermediate (B2) and advanced (C1) as defined by the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe, 2001)—two levels that have received comparatively little attention. Using measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity, and a detailed analysis of morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling and punctuation errors, the study seeks both to determine whether written competence differs significantly across these levels and to describe how errors evolve as proficiency increases.
