intros.text:
The development of writing competence has long occupied a central place in second language acquisition research, since writing constitutes one of the most demanding productive skills for learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL). Within this field, a substantial body of work has approached the assessment of written performance through the interrelated dimensions of complexity, accuracy and fluency, which are widely regarded as robust indicators of learners' interlanguage development (Skehan, 2009; Wolfe-Quintero et al., 1998). Following Foster and Skehan (1996), accuracy is generally understood as freedom from errors, while grammatical complexity refers to the use of progressively more elaborate language and a greater variety of syntactic patterning. Together, these constructs offer a valuable lens through which to trace how learners advance as their proficiency increases.

A considerable number of studies have used these measures to examine writing development over time and across proficiency levels. Some of them report significant gains in holistic scores as well as in accuracy and complexity as learners progress (e.g. Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Tedick, 1990). However, other investigations have failed to find comparable improvement, observing gains only in fluency while accuracy and complexity remain unchanged (e.g. Knoch et al., 2014, 2015; Nicolás-Conesa et al., 2014). Contrasting results have likewise been obtained regarding the evolution of errors: whereas some studies point to a broadly linear development, others describe non-linear trajectories in which progress, stabilisation and even regression coexist (Thewissen, 2013).

In view of these conflicting findings, two questions remain unresolved: whether and how written competence, as captured by accuracy and grammatical complexity, develops as proficiency increases, and what pattern the evolution of specific error types follows. Moreover, upper-intermediate and advanced learners, the very levels at which such questions are most pressing, have received comparatively little attention, and error types such as spelling and punctuation have rarely been examined developmentally.

The present study addresses these gaps by examining and comparing the compositions of Spanish EFL undergraduates at two proficiency levels (B2 and C1 as per the CEFR), using measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity. It further describes the evolution of the morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling and punctuation errors committed by both groups. In doing so, the study seeks to clarify contradictory prior findings and to identify weak developmental points that may inform L2 writing pedagogy at these under-researched competence levels (Ortega & Byrnes, 2008).

intros.text:
The study of second language (L2) writing development often centers on the interplay between accuracy, complexity, and fluency—three dimensions that provide a comprehensive window into a learner's interlanguage system. Accuracy is generally defined as the degree of freedom from errors, while grammatical complexity refers to the use of progressively more elaborate language and a wider variety of syntactic patterns (Foster & Skehan, 1996). In the field of applied linguistics, these constructs are frequently used to quantify proficiency and track the developmental trajectories of learners (Broussard et al., 2001). Theoretical frameworks, such as those proposed by Skehan (2009), explore how these dimensions interact under different task conditions, often discussing potential trade-offs between the cognitive demands of producing complex structures and the ability to maintain linguistic control.

Despite extensive research, findings regarding the development of written competence remain conflicting. Some studies report a linear progression where holistic scores, accuracy, and complexity improve consistently as proficiency increases (e.g., Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Tedick, 1990). Conversely, other research suggests that gains in accuracy or complexity may stagnate even after significant periods of university-level study (e.g., Knoch et al., 2014, 2015; Nicolás-Conesa et al., 2014). Similarly, the evolution of errors is not always linear; while some learners show steady improvement, others experience periods of stabilisation or even regression as they attempt to employ more sophisticated linguistic features (Thewissen, 2013).

Much of the existing literature has focused on beginner to intermediate learners, leaving a gap in our understanding of the transition between upper-intermediate and advanced levels. This is particularly relevant when aligning learner performance with the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001), as the distinction between B2 and C1 levels involves nuanced shifts in linguistic control. Furthermore, while morphological and syntactic errors are well-documented, surface-level errors such as spelling and punctuation have received less attention in developmental studies.

Accordingly, the present study aims to compare the writing products of EFL university students at the upper-intermediate and advanced levels. Specifically, it seeks to examine whether significant differences exist in their writing across measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity, and to describe the evolutionary patterns of morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling, and punctuation errors. By doing so, this research intends to clarify the developmental trajectories of high-proficiency learners.

intros.text:
The assessment of writing proficiency in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) has long been a central concern in applied linguistics, as writing represents a complex manifestation of a learner's overall communicative competence. Central to this evaluation are the constructs of accuracy and grammatical complexity. Accuracy is generally defined as the freedom from errors or the absence of deviations from a linguistic norm, while grammatical complexity refers to the use of progressively more elaborate language and a wider variety of syntactic patterning (Foster & Skehan, 1996). The interplay between these dimensions, often analyzed alongside fluency, provides critical insight into the developmental trajectories of second language (L2) learners (Broussard et al., 2001; Skehan, 2009). 

Previous research has attempted to correlate these linguistic measures with proficiency levels, yet the findings remain inconsistent. Some studies report a linear improvement in accuracy and complexity as proficiency increases (Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Tedick, 1990), while others fail to observe significant gains in these areas even over extended periods of university study (Knoch et al., 2014, 2015; Nicolás-Conesa et al., 2014). Similarly, evidence regarding error development is conflicting; while some researchers observe a steady decline in errors, others suggest non-linear patterns characterized by stabilization or regression (Thewissen, 2013). Furthermore, while much attention has been paid to syntactic and morphological errors, surface-level features such as spelling and punctuation have received comparatively little developmental attention.

Given these contradictions, there is a need to further investigate how written competence evolves at the higher end of the proficiency spectrum. The present study addresses this gap by comparing the writing products of EFL university students at the upper-intermediate (B2) and advanced (C1) levels, as defined by the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001). The primary objective is twofold: first, to examine whether significant differences exist between these two levels in terms of accuracy and grammatical complexity; and second, to describe the evolution of specific morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling, and punctuation errors. By analyzing these patterns, the study aims to provide a clearer account of the developmental trajectories of advanced L2 writers and offer pedagogical implications for EFL instruction.

intros.text:
The development of second language (L2) writing proficiency is a central concern in applied linguistics, particularly regarding how learners progress in accuracy and complexity. While early SLA research established errors as valuable evidence of developmental stages (Brown & Fraser, 1964; Corder, 1967), contemporary frameworks often analyze writing performance through the interplay of complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF). Skehan (2009) and Larsen-Freeman (2006) have highlighted that these dimensions do not always develop linearly; instead, they may fluctuate, stabilize, or regress as learners attempt more sophisticated linguistic structures. The Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe, 2001) further underscores the need to assess these dimensions across proficiency levels, yet the trajectory of development at upper-intermediate and advanced stages remains under-researched.

Existing literature presents conflicting evidence regarding L2 writing development. Some longitudinal studies suggest gradual improvement in holistic scores and specific linguistic measures (Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Tedick, 1990). Conversely, other research indicates that while fluency may increase, accuracy and complexity often remain static or show minimal gains even after years of instruction (Knoch et al., 2014, 2015; Nicolás-Conesa et al., 2014). Furthermore, error analysis studies reveal varying patterns: some report linear development (Bardovi-Harlig & Bofman, 1989), while others identify non-linear trends where certain errors persist or regress despite increasing proficiency (Thewissen, 2013). Specifically, the development of morphological, syntactic, and lexical accuracy at higher proficiency levels (B2–C1) requires further investigation, as these levels have received limited attention compared to beginner or intermediate stages.

This study aims to address these gaps by examining the writing products of EFL university students at upper-intermediate (B2) and advanced (C1) levels. The primary objectives are twofold: (a) to compare writing competence using measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity, and (b) to analyze the evolution of specific error categories, including morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling, and punctuation errors. By focusing on these higher proficiency levels, the study seeks to clarify whether significant developmental differences exist between groups and to identify which error types persist despite increased proficiency. Drawing on the CAF framework and error analysis traditions, this research contributes to a nuanced understanding of L2 writing development, offering implications for pedagogy and assessment in advanced EFL contexts.

intros.text:
The assessment of second language (L2) writing development has long been a central concern in applied linguistics, particularly regarding the interplay between accuracy and grammatical complexity. As learners progress through proficiency levels, researchers have sought to determine whether these dimensions develop linearly or exhibit more complex, dynamic patterns. The Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe, 2001) provides a standardized metric for such progression, yet empirical evidence regarding the specific trajectories of writing competence at upper-intermediate and advanced levels remains mixed.

Early research into L2 writing often focused on holistic measures or single dimensions of performance. However, contemporary scholarship increasingly adopts a multidimensional approach, examining complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF) simultaneously. Skehan (2009) and Larsen-Freeman (2006) argue that these dimensions do not always develop in tandem; rather, they may fluctuate, stabilize, or even regress as learners negotiate the demands of production. For instance, Larsen-Freeman (2006) demonstrated that while group performance might show linear improvement, individual trajectories often display non-linear evolution, characterized by periods of rapid growth interspersed with stability. Similarly, Broussard et al. (2001) highlighted the challenges in correlating linguistic measures with proficiency, noting the variability in indicators used across studies.

Despite the breadth of existing literature, conflicting findings persist regarding the developmental patterns of specific error types and grammatical structures. While some studies suggest a gradual reduction in errors as proficiency increases (e.g., Tedick, 1990), others indicate that certain morphological and syntactic features remain resistant to improvement even at advanced stages. Furthermore, research has predominantly focused on lower proficiency levels or general trends, leaving a gap in our understanding of the specific error development patterns between upper-intermediate (B2) and advanced (C1) learners. This is a critical area, as the transition from B2 to C1 represents a pivotal shift from functional communication to academic precision.

To address these gaps, the present study investigates the writing products of Spanish EFL university students at upper-intermediate and advanced levels. Specifically, it aims to compare the groups using measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity, and to examine the evolution of morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling, and punctuation errors. By analyzing these dimensions, the study seeks to clarify whether significant differences exist between proficiency levels and to identify which error categories show developmental progress. The findings aim to contribute to the ongoing debate on L2 writing development and offer implications for pedagogy targeting advanced learners.

intros.text:
Writing is a central component of foreign language proficiency and an important indicator of learners’ ability to mobilise linguistic resources for academic and communicative purposes. In university EFL contexts, written production is especially relevant because students are expected not only to convey meanings coherently, but also to demonstrate control over grammar, lexis, spelling and punctuation in line with higher levels of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (Council of Europe, 2001). Yet describing how such control develops remains a complex task, particularly at upper-intermediate and advanced levels, where progress may be less visible and where persistent errors can coexist with increasingly elaborate language use.

Research on second language writing has commonly examined development through the constructs of complexity, accuracy and fluency, which provide complementary perspectives on learner performance (Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Skehan, 2009; Wolfe-Quintero et al., 1998). Accuracy is usually understood as the degree to which learners’ production is free from error, whereas grammatical complexity refers to the use of more varied and elaborated syntactic structures. These constructs are particularly useful because development in one dimension does not necessarily imply parallel gains in another. From a dynamic perspective, second language development may be nonlinear, variable and sensitive to interactions among subsystems (Van Geert & Steenbeek, 2005). Thus, learners may become more syntactically ambitious while still showing instability in morphology, lexical choice or mechanics.

Previous studies have produced mixed findings regarding the extent to which L2 writing improves with proficiency. Some research has reported gains in accuracy and complexity across levels or over time, while other studies have found limited change, particularly among more proficient learners. Similarly, error-analysis studies have shown that some error types decrease steadily, whereas others stabilise or remain resistant to instruction and increased exposure. Reviews of writing development measures have also pointed to the need for more precise analyses of specific linguistic domains rather than reliance on global scores alone (Broussard et al., 2001). Despite this growing body of work, upper-intermediate and advanced EFL undergraduates remain comparatively underexplored, especially with respect to the combined analysis of grammatical complexity, accuracy and detailed error categories.

The present study addresses this gap by comparing the written production of Spanish university EFL learners at upper-intermediate and advanced levels. It examines whether the two proficiency groups differ in measures of grammatical complexity and accuracy, and it analyses the distribution and development of morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling and punctuation errors in their compositions. In doing so, the study seeks to contribute to a more fine-grained understanding of advanced-level EFL writing development and to identify areas that may require sustained pedagogical attention.

intros.text:
Writing is a central component of foreign language proficiency and a particularly demanding skill for university students who must express complex meanings with control, coherence and linguistic precision. Within the Common European Framework of Reference, written production is treated as part of communicative competence and is described in relation to progressively more effective control of linguistic resources across proficiency levels (Council of Europe, 2001). For learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), however, development in writing is not limited to producing longer texts or more ideas; it also involves increasing accuracy and grammatical complexity, two dimensions that offer useful evidence of learners’ interlanguage development.

Research on second language writing has frequently examined development through the triad of complexity, accuracy and fluency. Accuracy is commonly understood as freedom from error, whereas grammatical complexity refers to the use of more elaborate and varied syntactic patterns. These dimensions are important because they may develop at different rates and may even compete for learners’ attentional resources during performance (Skehan, 2009). From a dynamic perspective, second language development is also expected to be variable rather than strictly linear, with periods of progress, stabilisation and possible regression (Larsen-Freeman, 2006; Van Geert & Steenbeek, 2005). Consequently, the analysis of written competence requires measures that can capture both global differences between proficiency groups and more fine-grained patterns in specific error categories.

Previous studies have used a range of measures to assess L2 written development, including error-free units, ratios of errors to production units, syntactic complexity indices and analyses of particular error types. Reviews of research on fluency, accuracy and complexity have shown that these measures can provide valuable but sometimes inconsistent evidence of writing development (Broussard et al., 2001). Some studies report improvement in accuracy and complexity as proficiency increases, whereas others find limited or no development in these areas. Similarly, error-based studies have shown that some linguistic features decline with increasing proficiency, while others remain resistant even at advanced levels. Such findings suggest that the relationship between proficiency and written accuracy is still not fully understood, especially at the upper-intermediate and advanced levels.

The present study addresses this issue by comparing the written compositions of Spanish EFL university students at two proficiency levels, upper intermediate and advanced. It aims to determine whether the two groups differ in measures of accuracy and grammatical complexity and to describe the development of morphological, syntactic, lexical, spelling and punctuation errors in their writing. By focusing on university learners at relatively high levels of competence, the study seeks to clarify which aspects of written performance show progress and which continue to pose difficulties as proficiency increases.

intros.text: The (complex) nominal group1 is commonly found in scientific discourse (Halliday, 1993).  This is a distinct feature of technical English (which is also referred to as English for  Specific Purposes, ESP)2 because it allows the ‗packing‘ of lexical items as a syntactic unit  into a clause. However, this results in higher lexical density and it gives rise to syntactic  ambiguity.  Moreover, it is important to distinguish the term syntactic ambiguity from the  term syntactic polysemy, the latter being ―the immediate realisation of more than one  categorial meaning within the head element of a language structure‖ (Kozerenko, 2004: 2).  Hence, polysemous structures ―display variable manifestation of their categorical features depending on the functional role in the sentence‖ (Kozerenko, 2004: 2)  Meanwhile, an  ambiguous syntactic structure ―presupposes alternative ways of interpretation‖ (Kozerenko,  2004: 2) and, in order to understand and correctly interpret such ambiguous structures (e.g.  the new control system updated continuously displayed robust performance), a broader  context is deemed necessary.  In this paper, we use the term syntactic ambiguity since we deal  with nominal groups of complex structures that are difficult to process and which can easily  be misunderstood or interpreted alternatively.  Nominal groups constitute ―a substantial majority of all technical vocabulary‖  (Justeson & Katz, 1995: 9) and are distinguished from other types of nominal groups. Biber,  Stig, Leech, Conrad and Finegan (1999: 578) have shown that ―in all registers, noun phrases  with premodifiers are somewhat more common than those with postmodifiers.‖ In addition,  the ability of the English language to form complex nominal groups is ―an efficient means by  which dense information content can be packed into as few words as possible‖ (cf. Zhoulin,  2016: 76), which allows more information to be communicated at once. Furthermore,  Halliday (1993) holds that written language is more lexically dense than spoken language  and ―in much scientific writing, almost all the lexical items in any clause occur inside just  one or two nominal groups‖ (Halliday, 1993: 84). Hence, nominal groups create most  difficulty in processing because ―they consist of strings of lexical words without any  grammatical words in between‖ (ibid.) (e.g. piston outlet lubrication oil temperature ‗the  temperature of the lubrication oil that is used to cool the piston and which is measured at the  outlet‘).  Although the extralinguistic context helps us to understand complex nominal groups  (cf. Kereković, 2016), very specific technical knowledge is required to do so and nonspecialists of the field (e.g. ESP teachers) generally do not possess this knowledge.  Hence,  this paper aims to find an efficient method of processing and analysing complex nominal  groups in technical English, specifically those that consist of three or more elements and  which exhibit one of the following structures: N1 + N2 + N3 + NN; Adj+ N1 + N2 + NN.  This paper is laid out as follows: Section 2 outlines the theoretical framework that is  adopted (i.e. Systemic Functional Grammar) and the key concepts pertaining to the analysis.  In Section 3, the methodology is explained. Section 4 presents the analysis and discussion.  Finally, Section 5 draws the conclusions and outlines the implications for further research.

intros.text:
Technical English, as a variety of English for Specific Purposes (ESP), is characterised by a high degree of lexical density that allows a great deal of information to be packed into a single clause. One of the primary means through which this compactness is achieved is the (complex) nominal group, in which several lexical items are combined to modify a single head. Halliday (1989) demonstrated that the grammar of scientific English, and in particular its heavy reliance on nominalisation and elaborate premodification, constitutes a genuine learning problem for those being introduced to a specialised discipline. While such structures serve the ideational economy of scientific and technical discourse, they simultaneously give rise to syntactic ambiguity, since the meaning relations holding between the constituent items are frequently left implicit and must be recovered by the reader.

The difficulty is compounded by the fact that technical terminology tends to cluster in noun-phrase form. As Justeson and Katz (1995) have shown, technical terms consist overwhelmingly of noun phrases containing adjectives, nouns and, occasionally, prepositions, rarely involving verbs or conjunctions. Consequently, the identification and interpretation of a term hinges on the analyst's ability to determine which items function as head and which as modifiers, and how the modifiers relate to one another. Comprehensive descriptive grammars of English (Quirk, Greenbaum, Leech & Svartvik, 1985; Biber et al., 1999) offer general accounts of premodifier ordering, but these are not always sufficient to resolve ambiguity in dense multi-word technical strings, where several nouns may premodify a single head.

Such ambiguity is not merely a theoretical curiosity; it has immediate consequences for language pedagogy. The ESP teacher, unlike the domain specialist or even the advanced student of the discipline, typically lacks the extralinguistic and terminological knowledge that native experts draw on to disambiguate complex nominal groups almost automatically. Where the expert can rely on shared knowledge and contextual plausibility, the ESP teacher must fall back on linguistic evidence. This gap raises the central question motivating the present study: can the linguistic structure of the nominal group itself—and, more specifically, the position and type of its modifiers—help the ESP teacher to recover the extralinguistic content and thereby to process, understand and successfully teach these structures?

To address this question, we adopt the framework of Systemic Functional Grammar (Halliday & Matthiessen, 2004), which provides an efficient means of analysing the experiential and logical structure of the nominal group and of distinguishing epithets from classifiers according to their relative permanence and specifying potential. Building on functional, corpus-based analyses of complex nominal groups in specialised registers such as written business discourse (Ruan, 2016), and on studies of ambiguity in languages for specific purposes (Kerekoć, 2016), we argue that the ordering of modifiers around the head, together with the distinction between linear (stacked) and non-linear (submodifying) modification, plays a decisive role in disambiguation. We illustrate this with a corpus of marine engineering texts, from which complex terms were extracted and analysed to determine whether the position a nominal group occupies within a larger group can be linked to its frequency and structure. The paper thus contributes primarily to ESP teacher education, offering non-specialist teachers a principled, linguistically grounded strategy for making sense of the complex nominal groups that pervade technical English.

intros.text:
Technical English, as a variety of English for Specific Purposes (ESP), is characterised by a high degree of lexical density which distinguishes it markedly from everyday language. One of the most conspicuous features of scientific and technical registers is the frequent use of complex nominal groups, in which several lexical items are packed together into compact syntactic units (Halliday, 1989). This packaging is functionally motivated: nominal modification allows writers to convey a great deal of specialised content economically, achieving the compactness that technical communication demands (Varantola, 1993). It is precisely for this reason that complex nominal structures have long been recognised as a defining property of technical terminology, since technical terms consist for the most part of noun phrases containing adjectives, nouns and occasionally prepositions (Justeson & Katz, 1995).

Grammatical descriptions of English have devoted considerable attention to the internal organisation of the noun phrase and to the ordering of premodifiers (Broussard et al., 2000; Quirk, Greenbaum, Leech & Svartvik, 1985). Within Systemic Functional Grammar, the nominal group has been analysed in terms of its experiential and logical structures, and this framework has proved productive for describing how epithets, classifiers and heads combine in specialised discourse. Corpus-based functional analyses have shown, for instance, that classification is the dominant experiential function in complex nominal groups and that submodification serves to specify the head referent further (Ruan, 2016). Such work confirms that the position of modifiers within a nominal group is far from arbitrary and that it encodes systematic meaning relations (Pastor Gómez, 2010).

However, the very compactness that makes nominal groups so useful is achieved at the expense of explicitness, and this trade-off is a well-documented source of syntactic ambiguity in the language of specialised fields (Kereković, 2016). When a head noun is preceded by two or more nominal or adjectival modifiers, the meaning relations between the constituents may support more than one interpretation. Skilled readers typically resolve such ambiguity by drawing on context and on the extralinguistic, domain-specific knowledge that they share with other specialists. Yet this shared knowledge, which motivates the reduction in explicitness in the first place, is precisely what the ESP teacher tends to lack, since he or she is generally not a specialist in the technical field being taught. While studies of disambiguation have been undertaken in computational and translation contexts (Cheung & Fung, 2004), comparatively little attention has been paid to how the internal grammar of the nominal group itself can assist a non-expert reader, such as the ESP teacher, in recovering the intended meaning of complex technical terms.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines (complex) nominal groups in the technical English of marine engineering. We propose that, alongside context and extralinguistic knowledge, the structure of the nominal group—and in particular the position of modifiers and the type of modification, whether linear or non-linear—plays a decisive role in resolving syntactic ambiguity. Adopting a Systemic Functional approach and a corpus-based methodology, we ask whether the linguistic structure of the nominal group can help the ESP teacher access the extralinguistic content. In doing so, the paper aims to contribute to ESP teacher education by providing linguistic tools that enable teachers who are not specialists in (marine) engineering to process, understand and successfully teach complex nominal groups.

intros.text:
Complex nominal groups are a hallmark of technical English, particularly within the realm of English for Specific Purposes (ESP). These structures allow for a high degree of lexical density by tightly packing multiple lexical items into a single clause, which facilitates the concise communication of sophisticated concepts. However, as Justeson and Katz (1995) observe, technical terminology predominantly consists of noun phrases containing adjectives and nouns, a structural preference that often leads to significant syntactic ambiguity. While the compactness of N + N and N + N + N structures is efficient for specialists, it often comes at the expense of explicitness, potentially obscuring the meaning relations between elements in a nominal group.

In scientific and technical discourse, the resolution of such ambiguity typically relies on context and extralinguistic knowledge—the shared technical background between interlocutors. As Halliday (1989) notes, the grammatical peculiarities of scientific English can create substantial learning problems for students and non-specialists. This challenge is particularly acute for ESP teachers who, while proficient in English, are rarely experts in the specific technical domain they are teaching, such as marine engineering. When the necessary shared knowledge is absent, the teacher must rely on linguistic means to disambiguate complex nominal groups. While various approaches to disambiguation exist in computational linguistics and translation (Cheung & Fung, 2004), the pedagogical need for a systematic linguistic framework to help teachers process these structures remains pressing. Recent studies in other professional registers, such as business discourse, have highlighted the importance of analyzing the internal functional and logical structures of complex nominal groups to understand how sub-modification specifies head referents (Ruan, 2016). Similarly, the problem of ambiguity in specialized language is a recognized issue across different domains and languages (Kereković, 2016).

This paper proposes that the internal structure of the nominal group—specifically the position of modifiers relative to the head—plays a critical role in resolving syntactic ambiguity. Drawing on traditional descriptions of English syntax (Broussard et al., 2000) and functional models, we argue that the sequence of modifiers is not arbitrary but is governed by the specifying potential of each element. We suggest that modifiers positioned farthest from the head are generally less specific, while those closest to the head further restrict the meaning of the entire group.

By employing a corpus-based approach and the theoretical framework of Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG), this study analyzes (complex) nominal groups within the field of marine engineering. The primary objective is to determine whether the linguistic structure of the nominal group can provide sufficient clues to help an ESP teacher understand extralinguistic content without possessing deep domain expertise. The main contribution of this research is to provide ESP teachers with a structural methodology for interpreting complex nominal groups, thereby enabling them to teach technical English more successfully. The central research question, therefore, asks: to what extent can the linguistic structure of the nominal group be helpful in understanding the extralinguistic content of specialized technical texts?

intros.text:
In the field of English for Specific Purposes (ESP), the analysis of technical discourse is of paramount importance due to the specialized nature of the language used in scientific and engineering domains. A defining characteristic of technical English is the prevalence of complex nominal groups, which allow for a high degree of lexical density by packing multiple items of information into a single clause. As noted by Justeson and Katz (1995), technical terms predominantly consist of noun phrases containing adjectives and nouns, a structural preference that facilitates the concise transmission of complex concepts. However, while this compactness is an asset for efficiency, it often comes at the expense of explicitness. Halliday (1989) highlighted that the grammatical structures of scientific English can create significant learning obstacles for students and non-specialists, often leading to difficulties in processing and comprehension.

The primary challenge associated with these complex structures is syntactic ambiguity. When multiple premodifiers are stacked before a head noun, the relationship between the elements can become unclear, leaving the reader to struggle with the correct interpretation of the nominal group. While research has explored the functional analysis of such structures in other domains—for instance, Ruan (2016) investigated the logical relationships and premodification patterns in business discourse—there remains a need for further empirical investigation into how these structures operate within the specific context of marine engineering. Furthermore, most disambiguation strategies rely heavily on context or extralinguistic knowledge (Cheung & Fung, 2004). For the ESP teacher, who is typically a language expert rather than a subject-matter specialist, the lack of shared technical background can make the disambiguation of these complex groups nearly impossible using traditional grammatical intuition alone.

This study aims to address this gap by examining whether the linguistic structure of the nominal group itself, rather than relying solely on extralinguistic knowledge, can serve as a reliable tool for disambiguation. Specifically, we explore the role of modifier position and the distinction between linear and non-linear modification in resolving syntactic ambiguity. By applying the framework of Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG), we hypothesize that the position of modifiers relative to the head reveals a hierarchy of specifying potential that can guide the reader toward the correct meaning.

To test this, the current research employs a corpus-based methodology, utilizing specialized corpora of marine engineering articles and books to analyze the distribution and structure of complex nominal groups. The paper first establishes the theoretical underpinnings of the nominal group within SFG and then presents a corpus-driven analysis of frequent technical terms. The findings suggest that the type of modification (linear vs. non-linear) provides critical support for disambiguation, offering a practical pedagogical resource for ESP teachers. The remainder of the article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides the theoretical background on SFG; Section 3 details the corpus compilation and methodology; Section 4 presents the results and discussion; and Section 5 offers the final conclusions and implications for teacher education.

intros.text:
Technical English, often referred to as English for Specific Purposes (ESP), is characterised by a high lexical density and the frequent use of complex nominal groups. These structures allow lexical items to be tightly packed into a clause, facilitating the efficient communication of complex technical concepts. However, this compactness often leads to syntactic ambiguity, posing significant challenges for learners and teachers alike, particularly when the extralinguistic knowledge required to disambiguate meaning is absent. As Halliday (1989) notes, scientific English constitutes specific learning problems for students being introduced to science, necessitating a deeper understanding of the grammatical structures that generate these difficulties.

The linguistic properties of technical terminology have been extensively discussed in the literature. Justeson and Katz (1995) identify that technical terms consist mostly of noun phrases containing adjectives and nouns, rarely incorporating verbs or adverbs. This preference for nominalisation contributes to the density and complexity found in technical registers. Furthermore, the Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English (Broussard et al., 2000) provides a comprehensive description of the syntactic phenomena of English, highlighting the structural intricacies of noun phrases. In the context of business English, Ruan (2016) has similarly demonstrated that complex nominal groups possess distinctive functional and logical structures, where classification is the main function of the experiential structure and sub-modification is used for further specifying the head referent. These findings suggest that the internal structure of nominal groups is not random but follows specific patterns that can be analysed and understood.

Despite the abundance of research on technical terminology, the role of syntactic structure in resolving ambiguity remains a critical area of investigation. Kereković (2016) highlights the issues of polysemy and terminologisation in medical language, illustrating how a lack of familiarity with specific terminology can hinder understanding even for specialists. Similarly, Cheung and Fung (2004) discuss the complexities of disambiguation in mixed language queries, emphasising the importance of context and seed-words in resolving meaning. In the context of ESP teaching, the challenge is often exacerbated by the fact that the teacher may not possess the specialised knowledge of the field. Consequently, the ESP teacher must rely on linguistic means to interpret and teach these complex structures effectively.

This paper analyses complex nominal groups in technical English, specifically within the domain of marine engineering. We propose that, in addition to context and extralinguistic knowledge, the structure of the nominal group itself plays a crucial role in the resolution of syntactic ambiguity. Specifically, the position of modifiers within the group and the type of modification (linear or non-linear) are key factors in disambiguating meaning. Our study aims to bridge the gap between linguistic theory and ESP pedagogy by demonstrating how Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG) can be utilised to process and understand complex nominal groups. By focusing on the logical structure of these groups, we seek to provide ESP teachers with tools to successfully teach technical English without requiring them to be specialists in the field. The following sections will outline the theoretical background, methodology, and results of our corpus-based analysis, ultimately contributing to the field of ESP teacher education.

intros.text:
Technical English, a prominent variety of English for Specific Purposes (ESP), is characterized by a high lexical density and the frequent use of complex nominal groups. These structures allow for the compact packing of information, a necessity in specialized discourse where precision and conciseness are paramount (Halliday, 1989). However, this efficiency often comes at the cost of syntactic ambiguity, creating significant challenges for learners and, crucially, for ESP teachers who may lack the domain-specific knowledge required to resolve these ambiguities. While previous research has extensively documented the linguistic properties of technical terminology, such as the prevalence of noun phrases and patterns of repetition (Justeson & Katz, 1995), there remains a gap in understanding how the internal syntactic structure of these groups aids in disambiguation without reliance on extralinguistic knowledge.

Theoretical frameworks like Systemic Functional Grammar (SFG) offer robust tools for analyzing these phenomena. Halliday (1989) noted that scientific English constitutes specific learning problems, particularly regarding the interpretation of complex textual structures. More recent corpus-based studies, such as Ruan (2016), have explored the functional and logical structures of complex nominal groups in business discourse, highlighting the role of classification and sub-modification. Similarly, Biber et al. (2000) provide a comprehensive description of syntactic phenomena in English, yet their focus remains broad rather than specialized. In the context of translation and machine processing, Cheung and Fung (2004) proposed methods for disambiguation based on context seed-words, while Kereković (2016) examined terminologization strategies in medical language. Despite these contributions, the specific interplay between modifier position, logical structure, and the disambiguation of complex nominal groups in technical English—particularly from the perspective of the non-specialist teacher—remains underexplored.

A critical issue arises when ESP teachers, who are often linguists rather than subject matter experts, encounter dense nominal compounds. As Pastor Gómez (2010) argues, shared knowledge between interlocutors reduces explicitness, but this shared knowledge is absent for the teacher. Consequently, teachers must rely on linguistic means to interpret the structure. While frequency and keyness scores are often used to identify terms (Justeson & Katz, 1995), our preliminary observations suggest that corpus frequency alone may not suffice to resolve syntactic ambiguity. The position of modifiers within the group—specifically whether the modification is linear or non-linear—appears to be a decisive factor in determining meaning. For instance, in the phrase *steam reciprocating engine* versus *reciprocating steam engine*, the position of the participle significantly alters the semantic interpretation. However, the extent to which this structural analysis can support the disambiguation process for non-specialists has not been empirically investigated.

To address this gap, the present study analyzes complex nominal groups in technical English, specifically within the domain of marine engineering. We propose that the structure of the nominal group, particularly the position of modifiers and the type of modification (linear or non-linear), plays a pivotal role in resolving syntactic ambiguity. This research aims to determine if linguistic structure can compensate for a lack of extralinguistic knowledge. By employing a corpus-based approach and applying SFG analysis, this paper seeks to provide ESP teachers with a methodological framework for processing and teaching complex nominal groups effectively. The findings offer implications for ESP teacher education, suggesting that a deeper understanding of syntactic structure can enhance the teaching of technical English without requiring the teacher to be a specialist in the field.

intros.text:
Technical English is characterised by a high concentration of information in relatively compact grammatical structures. One of the most important resources for achieving such compactness is the nominal group, especially when several nouns, adjectives or participles occur before the head. In scientific and technical registers, these structures contribute to lexical density and terminological precision, but they also create problems of processing and interpretation (Halliday, 1989). A sequence such as fuel oil pump or cylinder head temperature may appear transparent to specialists because the relevant technical object or process is already known to them. For language teachers and learners, however, the same sequence may be ambiguous: it is not always immediately clear which element functions as head, which elements form a unit, and how the modifying relations should be interpreted.

The problem is particularly relevant in English for Specific Purposes (ESP). ESP teachers are normally trained as language specialists rather than as engineers, physicians or business professionals. They are therefore expected to teach the linguistic form of specialised discourse without necessarily sharing the full extralinguistic knowledge of the professional community. Since technical terms are very often realised as complex noun phrases or nominal groups, the teacher’s ability to analyse their internal structure becomes central to classroom explanation, reading comprehension and terminology work. Previous research has shown that technical terminology has recurrent linguistic properties and that many terms consist of noun phrases containing nouns and adjectives rather than verbs or adverbs (Justeson & Katz, 1995). Corpus-based grammars have likewise demonstrated that nominal premodification is strongly associated with informational and specialist registers (Broussard et al., 2000). However, frequency and recurrence do not by themselves explain how meaning relations inside complex nominal groups are to be recovered.

Ambiguity in specialised discourse has often been discussed in relation to lexical meaning, translation, terminology and context (Cheung & Fung, 2004; Kereković, 2016). In technical English, however, ambiguity is also syntactic. The same sequence of words may permit more than one structural interpretation, particularly where two- or three-word terms are embedded inside longer nominal groups. For instance, a complex term may function as the head of a larger nominal group in one context and as a premodifier in another. Moreover, modification may be linear, with each modifier successively narrowing the head, or non-linear, where two elements form a lower-rank unit that behaves as a single lexical item. Such structures are common in technical language because shared professional knowledge allows writers to omit more explicit clausal or prepositional formulations. The resulting compactness is efficient for specialists but can be opaque for non-specialists.

Systemic Functional Grammar offers a useful framework for addressing this problem because it treats the nominal group not only as a syntactic unit but also as a configuration of meanings. Halliday’s distinction between experiential and logical structures makes it possible to examine how epithets, classifiers and heads are ordered and how their position contributes to meaning (Halliday, 1989). Recent corpus-based functional work on complex nominal groups in specialised discourse has shown that classification and submodification play an important role in written business English (Ruan, 2016), suggesting that similar mechanisms may operate in other ESP domains. Marine engineering English provides a particularly suitable field for such analysis because it contains numerous multiword terms denoting components, systems and processes.

This study investigates syntactic ambiguity in complex nominal groups in technical English, with special reference to marine engineering discourse. It asks whether the internal structure of the nominal group, and especially the position and type of modifiers, can help disambiguate meaning when extralinguistic knowledge is limited. Using corpus data and automatic term extraction, the paper analyses frequent marine engineering terms embedded in larger nominal groups and examines whether they function as heads or premodifiers, whether their modification is linear or non-linear, and whether frequency alone can guide interpretation. The broader aim is pedagogical: to provide ESP teachers with linguistically grounded strategies for understanding and teaching complex nominal groups in domains where they may not be subject specialists.

intros.text:
Technical English is characterised by a high degree of lexical density, much of which is achieved through the frequent use of complex nominal groups. Such structures allow specialised information to be compressed into compact grammatical units, a feature that is particularly useful in scientific and technical communication but also potentially problematic for readers who do not share the specialist knowledge of the discourse community. In English for Specific Purposes (ESP), this issue is especially important because teachers are often language specialists rather than subject specialists, yet they are expected to help learners interpret and produce domain-specific texts accurately.

The difficulty of scientific and technical English has long been associated not only with unfamiliar vocabulary but also with grammar. Halliday (1989) showed that scientific English creates learning problems through patterns such as nominalisation, dense noun modification and the condensation of processes and relations into nominal structures. Similarly, corpus-based descriptions of English grammar have confirmed that written informational registers make extensive use of phrasal complexity, especially noun phrases with multiple premodifiers (Biber et al., 1999; Broussard et al., 2000). In technical discourse, many of these nominal groups are also terms. Justeson and Katz (1995) note that technical terminology is predominantly realised by noun phrases containing nouns and adjectives, and that repeated multi-word noun phrases constitute a substantial part of technical vocabulary.

Complex nominal groups, however, do not merely present lexical difficulty. Their internal structure may be syntactically ambiguous because the relations among their components are often not overtly marked. A sequence such as N + N + N or Adj + N + N can be interpreted in more than one way unless the reader can determine which elements form a unit, which element functions as the head, and whether the modification proceeds linearly or involves submodification. In specialised communication, ambiguity may be resolved by shared professional knowledge; once the referent is known, the intended interpretation becomes relatively transparent. Yet this condition cannot be assumed in ESP teaching contexts. Kereković (2016), for example, demonstrates that ambiguity and terminological opacity in languages for specific purposes can create comprehension difficulties even when users possess general language competence. The problem is therefore not simply whether an ESP teacher knows individual terms, but whether linguistic evidence can help compensate for limited extralinguistic knowledge.

Previous research has offered useful ways of approaching complex nominal groups in specialised registers. Systemic Functional Grammar provides a functional account of the nominal group in terms of experiential and logical structure, distinguishing roles such as epithet, classifier and Thing, and explaining why more permanent or classifying attributes tend to occur closer to the head. Corpus-based functional work has also shown that complex nominal groups display register-specific patterns. Ruan (2016), for instance, found that written business discourse makes extensive use of classification and submodification in complex nominal groups, with clear pedagogical implications for business English learners. Nevertheless, less attention has been given to how the structural position of multi-word technical terms inside larger nominal groups may assist disambiguation in technical English, particularly from the perspective of ESP teachers working outside their own subject expertise.

The present study addresses this issue by analysing complex nominal groups in marine engineering English. It investigates whether the linguistic structure of a nominal group—especially the position of modifiers and the distinction between linear and non-linear modification—can help resolve syntactic ambiguity when contextual or specialist knowledge is insufficient. Using a corpus-based approach and drawing on Systemic Functional Grammar, the study examines selected high-frequency marine engineering terms and their occurrence as heads or premodifiers within larger nominal groups. By doing so, it aims to show how complex terms behave as lexicalised units and how their internal and external modification patterns can guide interpretation. The study contributes to ESP teacher education by offering linguistically grounded strategies for processing, explaining and teaching complex nominal groups in technical English.

segments.text: Previous research has offered useful ways of approaching complex nominal groups in specialised registers. Systemic Functional Grammar provides a functional account of the nominal group in terms of experiential and logical structure, distinguishing roles such as epithet, classifier and Thing, and explaining why more permanent or classifying attributes tend to occur closer to the head. Corpus-based functional work has also shown that complex nominal groups display register-specific patterns. Ruan (2016), for instance, found that written business discourse makes extensive use of classification and submodification in complex nominal groups, with clear pedagogical implications for business English learners.

intros.text: Educational assessment is an important part of the process of teaching and learning.  According to Stiggins and Conklin (1992), regularly teachers spend up to half of their time in the classroom,assessing and analyzing the learning of students. Scholars' and practitioners’ interest in evaluation has always been very strong, and in recent years, evaluation has been one of the key objectives of educational research. As a consequence, the way students are assessed in the classroom has undergone numerous worldwide adjustments  The assessment tools used in the classroom in the 21st century go beyond traditional quizzes with paper and pencil.  It has many more tasks and is used for various uses such as diagnosis, monitoring, grading, feedback, instructional improvement, motivation, and other (MacMillan, 2014). Formative assessment (MacMillan, 2014) is one of the forms of classroom evaluation aimed at "gathering evidence of student learning and providing feedback to teachers and modifying educational approaches to improve achievement" (p. 93)  Formative assessment, a commonly promoted practice in teacher education, is defined as a process for examining one’s own teaching.  The utilization of formative assessment, whether it is continuous or occasional, is meant to tell and improve teachers’ understanding while developing their own teaching practice (Yorke, 2003).  Traditionally, formative assessment is supported through the processes of reflection and/or self-assessment.  Both of these approaches are widely utilized in education as a way for guiding preservice teachers looking inward to further develop their understanding of pedagogy and pedagogical content knowledge (Van Zee & Roberts, 2001).  Formative assessment plays an important role in the improvement of student learning and achievement.  As Heritage (2007) asserts, effective use of FA can provide sufficient information to move learning forward. The utilization of FA improves students’ knowledge and skills (Bennett, 2011). Nevertheless, there is a limited understanding and application of FA in the context of upper education (Duckor, 2014), despite the pressure on universities to reinforce their teaching and; therefore, improve the quality of student learning assessment (Hattie, 2009).      Popham (2014) stresses the term "process" in his concept of FA, stating that it is a calculated process rather than a test. FA is a structured mechanism in which instructors use test-related proof of student status to change their current instructional practices or students to modify their learning strategies (Popham, 2014). Therefore, a pupil is regarded as an active participant responsible for their learning in FA. It offers students the opportunity to prepare their further acts on the suggestions of the teacher. Nevertheless, Shavelson (2006) made a somewhat contradictory statement about the efficacy of FA based on his experience of introducing and researching its effects:   After five years of work, our euphoria has become a fact that FA, like so many other changes in education, has a long way to go before a majority of teachers can learn it. In other words, producing positive outcomes in the application of FA is a very long and complicated process and its success does not occur automatically (p. 65).   Other researchers have shown that teachers in general are not familiar with different modes of assessment (Watmani, Assadollahfam, & Behin, 2020).  School assessments are of two types of formative and summative and both play important roles in education.  One major challenge for teachers is to balance formative and summative assessments in their teaching. Since the most important purpose of assessment in education is to support learning (Black & Wiliam, 2006), the value of formative assessment becomes clear. In some countries, like Hong Kong, the educational system has made some changes in the assessment modes of teachers with more emphasis on the formative assessment by making it an inherent part of teaching (Yan & Cheng, 2015). However, pressure from the top of the hierarchal system cannot be effective if those who have to implement formative assessment, i.e., teachers, do not want to employ it in their classes (Rink & Mitchell, 2002). Teachers’ unwillingness for conducting formative assessment can be due to their lack of knowledge or negative beliefs about the subject (Brown, Hui, Yu, & Kennedy, 2011).  Therefore, it is clear that successful implementation of formative assessment in schools depends on teachers' understanding, participation, and support as teachers' views have a significant impact on any change in educational systems (Hallinger, 2011)  Therefore, it is essential to gain an understanding of teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment.  There have not been many studies on the factors which influence teachers’ intentions concerning formative assessment and the impact of attitudinal factors on their formative assessment practices.  Formative assessment identifies learners’ strengths and weaknesses, enhances their motivation and metacognition, and provides feedback to inform both teaching and learning (Black & Wiliam, 1998). Empirical studies have shown that integration of formative assessment into teaching has a clear and notable impact on students’ achievement and learning (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Hattie, 2009; Wiliam, Lee, Harrison, & Black, 2004)  Although, these benefits of formative assessment are well-accepted among educators, conducting it is a very difficult task and it cannot be added to the teaching practices quickly.  Teaching is a very personal task and teachers have their own teaching philosophies and thus their attitudes and beliefs about formative assessment greatly impact their practices (Harrison, 2013).       The theory of planned behavior (TPB) proposed by Ajzen (1985, 1991) is a theoretical framework which attempts to predict behavior based on individuals’ attitudes, emotions, and intentions. According to TPB, three factors including attitude towards the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control affect behavior through intentions. This means that those who approve a behavior, have positive subjective norms (social pressure from others), and enjoy a high level of perceived behavioral control (one's perception of the difficulty of and control over performing the behavior) are more likely to perform the behavioor  This study employed TPB to identify the contribution of significant factors (affective, subjective norms, control, etc.) to the behavior of performing formative assessment in Iraqi teachers.  Most of the studies published on the FA concentrated on the advantages and influences that may affect classroom engagement and the effect of the FA on student learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017).  There has not been any in-depth study conducted to describe in detail the understanding of FA by teachers and how their perspective affects their ways of doing follow-up actions. The perception of the teachers' in FA certainly affects the kinds of input they provide as well as the actions they take to follow up.  Therefore, the current study aims to investigate the attitudes, intentions, and practices in conducting FA in Iraqi EFL classrooms. Also, the study intends to highlight the applicability of FA in EFL classrooms in terms of the use of the correct FA strategy to match the objective or the purpose of the assessment. The study aims to pinpoint the pedagogical implications of using FA  To the best knowledge of this researcher, no study was applied with reference to the contributions of attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding FA to student learning improvement in Iraqi universities and schools.  2.1. Research Questions 1. What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards FA?  2. How frequent do Iraqi EFL teachers use FA? 3. To what extent are different components of attitudes to FA related to the application of FA? 4. Do Iraqi teachers’ attitudes to FA differ in terms of sex and level of education?

segments.text: Since the most important purpose of assessment in education is to support learning (Black & Wiliam, 2006), the value of formative assessment becomes clear. In some countries, like Hong Kong, the educational system has made some changes in the assessment modes of teachers with more emphasis on the formative assessment by making it an inherent part of teaching (Yan & Cheng, 2015). However, pressure from the top of the hierarchal system cannot be effective if those who have to implement formative assessment, i.e., teachers, do not want to employ it in their classes (Rink & Mitchell, 2002). Teachers’ unwillingness for conducting formative assessment can be due to their lack of knowledge or negative beliefs about the subject (Brown, Hui, Yu, & Kennedy, 2011). intros.text:
Assessment lies at the heart of teaching and learning, serving not only to certify what students have achieved but also to guide and shape the learning process itself. Within the broad landscape of educational assessment, a fundamental distinction is commonly drawn between summative assessment, which measures learning at the end of an instructional period, and formative assessment (FA), which is embedded in ongoing instruction and used to inform and improve teaching and learning while they are still taking place (Black & Wiliam, 1998; Bennett, 2011). Over the past three decades, formative assessment has attracted sustained international attention as an instructional approach with considerable potential to raise the quality of learning. In their seminal review, Black and Wiliam (1998) marshalled substantial evidence to argue that strengthening classroom formative assessment yields significant learning gains, particularly for lower-achieving students. Subsequent intervention studies, such as those reported by Wiliam et al. (2004), reinforced these claims, demonstrating measurable improvements in student achievement when teachers were supported in developing formative assessment strategies over time.

Formative assessment is best understood not as a single technique but as a cyclical, interactive process in which teachers and students elicit, gather, and interpret information about learning, and then use that information through feedback to close the gap between where learners are and where they need to be (Heritage, 2007; Bennett, 2011). This process involves practices such as effective questioning, the provision of high-quality feedback, self- and peer-assessment, and the adjustment of instruction to meet identified learning needs (Duckor, 2014; Yorke, 2003). Heritage (2007) has emphasised that successfully enacting these practices requires teachers to possess specific knowledge and skills, including domain knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, knowledge of students' prior learning, and knowledge of assessment itself. Shavelson (2006) similarly argued for the integration of formative assessment into the fabric of teaching rather than treating it as an activity separate from instruction. Despite the strong theoretical and empirical case for formative assessment, however, its widespread adoption in classrooms has proven difficult, and researchers have repeatedly observed a gap between the enthusiasm expressed for formative assessment in principle and its actual implementation in practice (Stiggins et al., 1992; Yan & Cheng, 2015).

One influential explanation for this gap points to the central role of teachers' beliefs and conceptions of assessment. What teachers believe about the nature and purposes of assessment shapes the practices they adopt in their classrooms, and these beliefs are themselves embedded in wider cultural and societal contexts (Brown et al., 2011). In many educational systems, assessment continues to be associated primarily with high-stakes testing and accountability, and teachers may consequently view it as something that competes with, rather than supports, teaching (Rink & Mitchell, 2002; Heritage, 2007). Harrison (2013) has documented the complex interplay between teachers' beliefs and their formative feedback practices, showing that even teachers who value formative approaches may enact them inconsistently as a result of contextual constraints, limited professional development, and differing assumptions about their students. Such findings underscore the importance of examining not only whether teachers hold favourable attitudes towards formative assessment, but also the extent to which those attitudes translate into classroom behaviour.

To capture the relationship between attitudes and behaviour in a systematic way, researchers have increasingly turned to the theory of planned behaviour (TPB). According to Ajzen (1985, 1991), an individual's intention to perform a given behaviour is shaped by three key determinants: attitudes towards the behaviour, subjective norms (perceived social pressure from significant others), and perceived behavioural control, which encompasses beliefs about one's capability and control over the behaviour. Intention, in turn, is proposed to be the most proximal predictor of the behaviour itself. The TPB provides a coherent framework for understanding why teachers who hold positive views of formative assessment may nonetheless fail to implement it, since intentions and their translation into action may be constrained by factors such as self-efficacy, perceived control over assessment decisions, and the influence of educational authorities and colleagues. Building on this framework, Yan and Cheng (2015) developed and validated the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ), which operationalises attitudes towards formative assessment through affective and instrumental attitude components, alongside subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, intention, and actual behaviour. Their study of primary teachers revealed that while affective attitude, subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, and intention were interrelated, they were only weakly associated with teachers' reported formative assessment practices, suggesting that positive dispositions do not automatically produce corresponding classroom action.

Much of the existing research on formative assessment has concentrated on documenting its benefits and its effects on student engagement and learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017; Hattie, 2009; Hattie & Zierer, 2017). Comparatively less attention has been devoted to understanding, in detail, how teachers themselves conceive of formative assessment and how their conceptions relate to their practices. Yet teachers' understanding of formative assessment is decisive, because it shapes the kind of feedback they offer and the follow-up actions they take in response to assessment information (Harrison, 2013). This concern is especially pressing in contexts where formative assessment is a relatively recent or unevenly established practice. In many parts of the world, and particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) settings, examination-oriented and summative traditions remain dominant, and teachers may have limited access to training, resources, and models of good practice in formative assessment. Understanding teachers' attitudes and practices in such contexts is therefore an important step towards designing effective professional development and towards making meaningful use of formative assessment to enhance language learning.

The Iraqi EFL context represents one such under-researched setting. English occupies an important place in the Iraqi educational system, being taught from primary school through to university level, yet relatively little is known about how Iraqi English teachers understand and enact formative assessment. Assessment cultures are notoriously difficult to change, and simply investing resources in reform is unlikely to succeed unless teachers' underlying conceptions of assessment are also addressed (Yan & Cheng, 2015). Examining the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment can thus illuminate both the current state of practice and the factors most likely to encourage greater and more effective use of formative approaches in Iraqi classrooms.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment using an Arabic-language adaptation of the TCPFAQ (Yan & Cheng, 2015). Drawing on the theory of planned behaviour as its guiding framework, the study seeks to describe teachers' conceptions of formative assessment, to determine how frequently they actually use it, to examine which components of their attitudes are most strongly associated with its application, and to explore whether attitudes vary according to teachers' sex and level of education. To the best knowledge of the researcher, no previous study has examined the contribution of teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment to the improvement of student learning in Iraqi universities and schools. In doing so, the study also considers the pedagogical implications of matching appropriate formative assessment strategies to the purposes of assessment. Accordingly, the study is guided by four research questions: (1) What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards formative assessment? (2) How frequently do Iraqi EFL teachers use formative assessment? (3) To what extent are the different components of attitudes to formative assessment related to its application? and (4) Do Iraqi teachers' attitudes to formative assessment differ in terms of sex and level of education? By answering these questions, the study aims to contribute both to the theoretical understanding of the attitude–behaviour relationship in assessment and to the practical enterprise of improving English language teaching in Iraq.
