intros.text:
Assessment lies at the heart of the teaching and learning process, and over the past three decades the role of assessment in shaping classroom learning has attracted growing international attention. Assessment plays a crucial role in any educational milieu (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017), and the recognition that it can be a resource for learning rather than merely a means of measuring it has given rise to a large body of scholarship on formative assessment (FA). Formative assessment is an instructional approach that has received considerable international attention because of its potential to improve teaching and learning. Although a single definition has not emerged among researchers and practitioners, common elements recur across the literature: formative assessment is understood as a cyclical process involving interactions between teachers and students, in which information about learning is elicited, interpreted, and used to provide feedback that helps students confirm or improve their understanding (Bennett, 2011). In contrast to summative assessment, which summarises and ranks what students have learned, formative assessment is embedded in instruction and used to diagnose learning needs and adjust teaching accordingly.

The influence of formative assessment on learning outcomes has been documented in a number of seminal studies. Black and Wiliam (1998) reviewed a large volume of evidence and concluded that strengthening the practice of formative assessment produces significant learning gains, particularly for lower-achieving students. Subsequent research reinforced these claims: Wiliam, Lee, Harrison, and Black (2004) reported a mean effect size of 0.32 in favour of classrooms in which teachers developed formative assessment strategies, and Hattie (2009) placed feedback and assessment-related practices among the more powerful influences on achievement in his synthesis of hundreds of meta-analyses. Building on these findings, scholars have described the knowledge and skills that teachers require in order to enact formative assessment effectively, including domain knowledge, pedagogical content knowledge, knowledge of students' prior learning, and knowledge of assessment itself (Heritage, 2007), as well as concrete classroom moves such as posing good questions, probing responses, and involving students in assessing their own and others' learning (Duckor, 2014). Formative assessment has also been examined at the level of higher education, where it has been theorised as a driver of pedagogic enhancement (Yorke, 2003), and within teacher education, where its integration into instruction has been proposed as a route to more coherent teaching and learning (Shavelson, 2006).

Much of this scholarship, however, has concentrated on the benefits and effects of formative assessment on student engagement and learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017). A parallel strand of research has begun to stress that whether and how these benefits are realised depends heavily on teachers themselves. The beliefs teachers hold about assessment influence their classroom practices and reflect broader cultural and societal differences (Brown, Hui, Yu, & Kennedy, 2011). Teachers' conceptions of formative feedback and their assumptions about their students shape the input they provide and the follow-up actions they take, and these conceptions are further mediated by contextual factors such as professional development opportunities, collegial support, and the pressures of high-stakes testing (Harrison, 2013; Rink & Mitchell, 2002). Investigating classroom assessment practices, then, requires attention not only to what formative assessment can achieve, but also to teachers' attitudes, intentions, and self-reported behaviour (Stiggins, Conklin, & National Education Association, 1992).

One fruitful framework for connecting attitudes and intentions to behaviour is Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen, 1985, 1991), which holds that behaviour is predicted by intention, which in turn is shaped by attitudes, subjective norms, and perceived behavioural control. Drawing on this framework, Yan and Cheng (2015) developed the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ) and used it to examine primary teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices, operationalising the constructs through subscales measuring affective attitude, instrumental attitude, subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, intention, and behaviour. Their study, and related work applying planned-behaviour models to teacher assessment (Yan, 2014), revealed an intriguing disjuncture: although teachers generally reported positive attitudes and strong intentions towards formative assessment, these did not translate consistently into frequent classroom use, with the behaviour subscale correlating only weakly with the other measures. This tension between what teachers believe about formative assessment and what they actually do has been observed repeatedly across contexts (Black & Wiliam, 1998), and it points to the importance of understanding teachers' conceptions in detail rather than assuming that favourable attitudes will automatically produce widespread practice.

Despite the wealth of research on formative assessment and its impact on learning, there has been little in-depth study describing teachers' own understandings of formative assessment and how their perspectives shape their follow-up actions. The gap is particularly acute outside the English-speaking and East Asian contexts in which most of the existing instruments and models have been developed and validated. In many EFL settings, teachers work within examination-driven cultures and with limited resources, and it cannot be assumed that findings from primary science classrooms in Singapore or Hong Kong will generalise to their circumstances. In the Iraqi context specifically, the study of English language teaching and assessment literacy remains underdeveloped, and to the best knowledge of the present researcher no study has investigated the contributions of teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment to student learning in Iraqi universities and schools. Given the growing emphasis on language assessment literacy as a component of teacher professionalism (Atmani et al., 2021), and the recognition that changing assessment cultures requires attention to teachers' beliefs rather than resources alone, there is a clear need to describe how Iraqi EFL teachers conceive of and enact formative assessment.

The present study addresses this gap by exploring the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment. Grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior, it seeks to investigate not only whether these teachers value formative assessment but also the extent to which the various components of their attitudes are related to their actual application of it, and whether such attitudes vary by gender and level of education. The study also aims to highlight the applicability of formative assessment in EFL classrooms, particularly the alignment of appropriate strategies with assessment purposes, and to identify pedagogical implications for teacher education in Iraq. To this end, four research questions guide the investigation: (1) What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards formative assessment? (2) How frequently do Iraqi EFL teachers use formative assessment? (3) To what extent are the different components of attitudes to formative assessment related to its application? and (4) Do Iraqi teachers' attitudes to formative assessment differ in terms of sex and level of education?

To answer these questions, the study administered an Arabic version of the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (Yan & Cheng, 2015) to 102 EFL teachers working across primary schools, high schools, private institutes, and universities in Iraq. The instrument was translated and back-translated, and its validity was examined through confirmatory factor analysis before descriptive and inferential statistics were computed to characterise teachers' conceptions and to test relationships among the constructs. By providing the first empirical account of Iraqi EFL teachers' formative assessment attitudes and practices, the study may inform the design of professional development programmes and contribute to a fuller understanding of the conditions under which positive assessment beliefs are, or are not, converted into classroom practice.

intros.text:
Assessment is a cornerstone of the educational process, serving not only as a means of evaluating student achievement but also as a powerful tool for driving instructional improvement. Within the broad spectrum of educational evaluation, formative assessment (FA)—often referred to as assessment for learning—has gained significant international attention as an instructional approach with the potential to transform teaching and learning (Bennett, 2011). Unlike summative assessment, which aims to summarize what students have learned at the end of a unit for the purpose of ranking or grading, formative assessment is a cyclical, interactive process occurring during instruction. It involves eliciting evidence of student learning, providing timely feedback, and adjusting teaching strategies to bridge the gap between a student's current status and the desired learning goal (Heritage, 2007; Bennett, 2011). The seminal work of Black and Wiliam (1998) highlighted the substantial positive impact of formative assessment on student achievement, sparking a global shift toward its integration in classrooms. Subsequent research has continued to emphasize that when teachers effectively employ FA strategies, student engagement and learning outcomes improve significantly (Wiliam et al., 2004; Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017).

Despite the theoretical consensus on the benefits of FA, its practical implementation remains a complex challenge. Many teachers continue to view assessment as something in competition with teaching rather than an integral part of it (Heritage, 2007). In many educational contexts, the pressure of high-stakes standardized testing and accountability frameworks creates a tension where teachers feel compelled to 'teach to the test,' thereby marginalizing formative practices in favor of summative results (Wiliam et al., 2004; Rink & Mitchell, 2002). This tension is particularly evident in various Asian contexts, where cultural traditions of accountability and the use of examinations to drive quality often overshadow the iterative nature of formative feedback (Brown et al., 2011). Consequently, there is often a noticeable discrepancy between teachers' stated beliefs about the value of FA and their actual classroom behaviors (Yorke, 2003).

To understand why this gap between conception and practice persists, researchers have turned to psychological frameworks that explain human behavior. One of the most influential is the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), developed by Ajzen (1985, 1991). According to TPB, an individual's intention to perform a specific behavior is the most immediate predictor of that behavior. This intention is, in turn, influenced by three primary factors: attitudes toward the behavior (the degree to which a person has a favorable or unfavorable evaluation of the behavior), subjective norms (the perceived social pressure to perform or not perform the behavior), and perceived behavioral control (the perceived ease or difficulty of performing the behavior, often linked to self-efficacy) (Ajzen, 1991). In the context of formative assessment, this suggests that a teacher's decision to implement FA is not merely a matter of knowing its benefits, but is a result of their affective and instrumental attitudes, the perceived expectations of school leadership and colleagues, and their confidence in their own skills and resources to execute these strategies (Yan & Cheng, 2015).

In the field of English Language Teaching (ELT), the implementation of FA is particularly critical given the communicative nature of language acquisition. For EFL teachers, the ability to diagnose learner difficulties in real-time and provide tailored feedback is essential for fostering fluency and accuracy. However, the application of these principles is often mediated by the teacher's assessment literacy—their knowledge and skills regarding the design and use of assessments (atmani et al., 2021). When teachers lack sufficient training or supporting materials, their self-efficacy decreases, which can hinder their intention to move away from traditional, teacher-centered assessment methods toward more student-involved formative practices (Heritage, 2007; Dixon & Haigh, 2009).

While much research has explored the general advantages of FA or its impact on specific skills like listening comprehension (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017), there remains a scarcity of in-depth studies that specifically examine the interplay between teachers' internal conceptions and their external practices in specific regional contexts. In Iraq, the EFL classroom is subject to unique socio-educational pressures and systemic challenges. To date, there has been limited empirical investigation into how Iraqi EFL teachers perceive formative assessment and the extent to which these perceptions translate into actual classroom practice. Understanding the attitudes and intentions of these teachers is vital, as their personal beliefs regarding the utility of FA directly influence the types of input they provide to students and the follow-up actions they take to enhance learning.

Furthermore, it is essential to investigate whether demographic factors, such as gender or the level of education (from primary school to university), play a role in how FA is perceived and implemented. Previous studies have suggested that teacher beliefs are not monolithic and can be influenced by professional experience, institutional environment, and individual dispositions (Harrison, 2013; Brown et al., 2011). By examining these variables, researchers can better identify the specific barriers—whether they be psychological, such as low self-efficacy, or contextual, such as lack of resources—that prevent the widespread adoption of FA in Iraqi schools and universities.

Given this gap in the literature, the present investigation seeks to explore the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment. By employing the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ), this study aims to provide a detailed analysis of how various components of attitude—including affective and instrumental dimensions, subjective norms, controllability, and self-efficacy—predict the intention and actual behavior of teachers. Specifically, the study seeks to answer whether a positive belief in the utility of FA is sufficient to drive its application, or if external pressures and perceived control are more dominant factors in the Iraqi context. By pinpointing these dynamics, the study hopes to offer pedagogical implications for teacher professional development in Iraq, suggesting ways to move FA from a theoretical ideal to a consistent classroom reality. The ultimate goal is to foster a shift in assessment culture where FA is viewed not as an added burden or an 'extra' component of the curriculum, but as an integrated, essential part of regular instruction that promotes deeper student learning.

intros.text:
Assessment plays a fundamental role in any educational environment, serving as the primary mechanism through which student progress is monitored and instructional effectiveness is evaluated. Within the broad spectrum of educational evaluation, formative assessment (FA)—often referred to as assessment for learning—has gained significant international attention as an instructional approach with immense potential to enhance both teaching and learning (Bennett, 2011). Unlike summative assessment, which focuses on ranking students or summarizing achievement at the end of a unit, formative assessment is conceptualized as a cyclical, interactive process. It involves the elicitation of information about student thinking, the analysis of that evidence by both teacher and learner, and the provision of targeted feedback to bridge the gap between current performance and desired learning goals (Bennett, 2011; Heritage, 2007). 

The importance of FA is well-documented in pedagogical literature. Seminal research by Black and Wiliam (1998, 2006) has emphasized that the systematic use of formative strategies leads to higher quality learning and significant gains in student achievement. Similarly, Wiliam et al. (2004) demonstrated that when teachers are supported in developing FA strategies, there is a measurable positive impact on student performance. Beyond achievement, FA is seen as a tool for fostering student self-regulation and autonomy (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017). For these reasons, many educational systems worldwide have attempted to shift their assessment cultures away from a reliance on high-stakes standardized testing—which often puts assessment in competition with instruction (Heritage, 2007; Rink & Mitchell, 2002)—toward a more integrated model where assessment informs daily teaching practices (Shavelson, 2006).

Despite the theoretical consensus on the benefits of FA, its successful implementation depends heavily on the teachers who enact it. Research suggests that teachers' conceptions, beliefs, and attitudes regarding assessment are primary drivers of their classroom behavior (Brown et al., 2011). As Harrison (2013) observed, there is often a complex interplay between what teachers believe to be effective feedback and how they actually implement those strategies in the classroom. This discrepancy is frequently influenced by contextual factors, such as institutional pressure, available resources, and the teacher's own professional development history (Harrison, 2013; Yan & Cheng, 2015). Because the perception of FA determines the types of input a teacher provides and the subsequent follow-up actions they take, understanding the psychological and cognitive drivers behind these practices is essential for any meaningful educational reform.

To analyze these drivers, researchers have frequently turned to psychological frameworks such as the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB). Proposed by Ajzen (1985, 1991), TPB posits that an individual's behavior is determined by their intention to perform that behavior, which is in turn influenced by three main factors: attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms (perceived social pressure), and perceived behavioral control (including self-efficacy). In the context of education, this implies that a teacher's decision to employ formative assessment is not merely a result of knowing that FA is beneficial, but is a product of their emotional response to the practice, the expectations of their colleagues and supervisors, and their confidence in their own ability to execute the tasks required (Ajzen, 1991).

While the general advantages of FA and its impact on student achievement have been extensively researched (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017; Wiliam et al., 2004), there remains a significant gap in the literature regarding the specific internal and external factors that translate teachers' beliefs into actual classroom practice. Many studies have focused on the outcome of FA rather than the process of teacher adoption. Specifically, there has been a lack of in-depth investigation into how teachers' detailed understandings and perspectives on FA influence their follow-up actions. Furthermore, the discrepancy between positive attitudes and actual usage remains a puzzling phenomenon; as Yan and Cheng (2015) noted, teachers may value FA in theory but fail to integrate it into regular instruction, often viewing it as an additional burden rather than a core component of teaching.

This gap is particularly evident in the context of Iraq. To the best of the researcher's knowledge, no empirical study has been conducted to examine the contributions of attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment among EFL teachers in Iraqi schools and universities. Given the unique educational landscape in Iraq, it is crucial to determine whether the global trends in FA adoption are mirrored in this region and to what extent local contextual factors—such as administrative pressure or resource availability—influence teacher behavior.

Therefore, the present study aims to explore the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding the implementation of formative assessment. By utilizing the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ), this research seeks to provide a nuanced account of how affective and instrumental attitudes, subjective norms, and self-efficacy predict the intention to use FA and, more importantly, the actual frequency of its application in the classroom. Additionally, the study intends to highlight the applicability of FA in Iraqi EFL contexts and pinpoint the pedagogical implications of these findings to inform future teacher professional development.

To achieve these objectives, the study is guided by the following research questions:
1. What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards FA?
2. How frequent do Iraqi EFL teachers use FA?
3. To what extent are different components of attitudes to FA related to the application of FA?
4. Do Iraqi teachers' attitudes to FA differ in terms of sex and level of education?

By addressing these questions, the study hopes to offer insights into why certain factors may or may not lead to the actual employment of FA in Iraqi classrooms. The results may provide an evidence-based foundation for redesigning teacher training programs, shifting the focus from theoretical knowledge to the development of practical self-efficacy and the belief in the instrumental value of FA for student learning. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: the next section describes the methodology, including the participants and the instrumentation used; the following section presents the descriptive and inferential results of the data analysis; and the final section discusses the findings and their implications for English language teaching in Iraq.

intros.text:
Formative assessment (FA), often referred to as assessment for learning, has garnered significant international attention as an instructional approach with the potential to substantially improve teaching and learning outcomes. Unlike summative assessment, which serves to certify learning at the end of an instructional period, formative assessment is a cyclical process involving interactions between teachers and students designed to elicit evidence of learning and provide feedback that can be used to adjust instruction and support student progress (Bennett, 2011). Seminal research by Black and Wiliam (1998) demonstrated that effective implementation of formative assessment strategies could lead to significant gains in student achievement, with effect sizes that are among the highest reported in educational research. This evidence has led to widespread policy initiatives and professional development programs aimed at integrating FA into classroom practices globally. However, despite the compelling evidence regarding its benefits, the translation of formative assessment policies into actual classroom practice remains a complex and often challenging endeavor.

The gap between the theoretical promise of formative assessment and its practical implementation is well-documented in the literature. Researchers have noted that while teachers may acknowledge the value of FA, their actual practices often do not align with their conceptions or intentions (Harrison, 2013). This discrepancy suggests that a teacher's decision to implement formative assessment is influenced by a complex interplay of factors beyond mere knowledge of its benefits. Understanding these factors is crucial for educators and policymakers who aim to foster assessment cultures that genuinely support student learning. In this context, the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) has emerged as a useful theoretical framework for investigating the determinants of teachers' assessment practices. Developed by Ajzen (1985, 1991), the TPB posits that behavior is directly determined by behavioral intention, which is in turn influenced by three key factors: attitude toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. In the context of teaching, this framework suggests that a teacher's intention to use formative assessment is shaped by their personal beliefs about the utility of FA (attitude), the perceived social pressure from colleagues and administrators to use it (subjective norms), and their confidence in their ability to implement it effectively (perceived behavioral control or self-efficacy).

Several studies have applied the TPB to understand teachers' assessment practices. For instance, Yan and Cheng (2015) utilized this framework to examine primary teachers' attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment in Singapore. Their findings highlighted that while teachers generally held positive attitudes toward FA, the correlation between these attitudes and actual classroom behavior was often weak. They suggested that external and contextual factors, such as the pressure of high-stakes examinations, might mediate the relationship between intention and practice. Similarly, Brown et al. (2011) explored teachers' conceptions of assessment in Chinese contexts, identifying a tripartite model of accountability, improvement, and irrelevance. Their work underscores how cultural and societal differences shape teachers' beliefs about the purpose of assessment, which in turn influences their classroom practices. In the context of language teaching, the importance of assessment literacy has been emphasized by researchers such as Heritage (2007) and Atmani et al. (2021), who argue that teachers need specific knowledge and skills to effectively integrate assessment into their instruction. Without adequate training and support, teachers may view assessment as an added burden rather than an integral part of the teaching and learning process.

Despite the growing body of research on formative assessment, there is a notable scarcity of studies focusing on the Iraqi EFL context. Iraq presents a unique educational landscape characterized by specific cultural, political, and institutional challenges that may influence how formative assessment is perceived and practiced. Following years of conflict and educational disruption, the Iraqi education system has undergone various reforms, yet the implementation of modern pedagogical approaches remains inconsistent. While some studies have investigated the impact of formative assessment on student learning in other contexts (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017), there has been limited in-depth research describing the understanding of FA by Iraqi EFL teachers and how their perspectives affect their follow-up actions. The perception of teachers regarding FA certainly affects the kinds of input they provide as well as the actions they take to support student learning. Therefore, investigating the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers is essential for understanding the current state of assessment in the region and for identifying the barriers to effective implementation.

Furthermore, the applicability of formative assessment in EFL classrooms in Iraq requires careful examination in terms of the use of correct FA strategies to match specific objectives or purposes. The pedagogical implications of using FA in a context where traditional, summative-oriented assessment practices may still dominate are significant. To the best of the researcher's knowledge, no study has been applied with reference to the contributions of attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding FA to student learning improvement in Iraqi universities and schools. This gap in the literature is particularly concerning given the potential of FA to enhance language learning outcomes, which are critical for students' future academic and professional success in a globalized world. Understanding the specific factors that drive or hinder the adoption of FA in Iraq can inform the design of more effective teacher training programs and policy interventions.

The present investigation aims to address these gaps by exploring the attitudes, intentions, and practices of Iraqi EFL teachers regarding formative assessment. Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following research questions: (1) What are Iraqi EFL teachers' attitudes towards FA? (2) How frequently do Iraqi EFL teachers use FA? (3) To what extent are different components of attitudes to FA related to the application of FA? (4) Do Iraqi teachers' attitudes to FA differ in terms of sex and level of education? By employing the Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ) developed by Yan and Cheng (2015), this study utilizes a validated instrument to measure the key constructs of the Theory of Planned Behavior within the Iraqi context. The questionnaire, translated and validated for this study, allows for a nuanced examination of affective and instrumental attitudes, subjective norms, controllability, self-efficacy, intentions, and actual behaviors related to formative assessment.

The significance of this study lies in its potential to contribute to the broader understanding of how theoretical models of behavior apply to assessment practices in non-Western, resource-constrained educational settings. By identifying the specific predictors of formative assessment use among Iraqi EFL teachers, the findings can guide the development of targeted professional development initiatives. If, for instance, self-efficacy is found to be a primary driver of intention, then training programs should focus on building teachers' confidence and skills. Conversely, if subjective norms are more influential, efforts might be directed at changing the institutional culture and administrative support for FA. Moreover, by examining differences based on gender and educational level, the study can uncover demographic factors that may influence assessment practices, offering insights for more inclusive and effective policy-making. Ultimately, this research aims to bridge the gap between the theoretical benefits of formative assessment and its practical application in Iraqi EFL classrooms, thereby contributing to the improvement of English language teaching and learning in the region. As noted by Wiliam et al. (2004) and Hattie (2009), the successful integration of formative assessment requires not only a shift in policy but also a fundamental change in teacher beliefs and practices, a process that this study seeks to illuminate.

intros.text:
Formative assessment (FA), often conceptualized as assessment for learning, has emerged as a critical component in contemporary educational discourse, garnering significant attention from policymakers, researchers, and practitioners globally. The centrality of FA lies in its potential to transform classroom practices by shifting the focus from merely evaluating student performance to actively enhancing the learning process itself. Unlike summative assessment, which serves to certify learning at the end of an instructional period, formative assessment is characterized by its cyclical nature, involving the elicitation of evidence of learning, the interpretation of that evidence, and the provision of feedback to inform subsequent teaching and learning decisions (Bennett, 2011). This pedagogical approach is predicated on the understanding that assessment should not be an isolated event but rather an integral, ongoing part of instruction that empowers students to take ownership of their learning journey.

The theoretical underpinnings of FA are robust, with seminal work by Black and Wiliam (1998) demonstrating that systematic implementation of formative assessment strategies can lead to substantial improvements in student achievement. Their meta-analysis revealed that such practices could produce effect sizes ranging from 0.4 to 0.7, significantly higher than most other educational interventions. This finding has been corroborated by subsequent research, including Hattie’s (2009) Visible Learning synthesis, which aggregated over 800 meta-analyses and identified feedback and formative evaluation as among the most influential factors affecting student outcomes. Consequently, FA has been adopted as a cornerstone of educational reform in numerous jurisdictions, with the expectation that its integration into daily classroom routines will foster deeper learning and improved academic performance.

However, despite the overwhelming evidence supporting the efficacy of formative assessment and its widespread endorsement in educational policy, the translation of these ideals into actual classroom practice remains a complex and often elusive endeavor. A growing body of literature suggests a persistent gap between teachers’ conceptions of assessment and their enacted practices. While many educators acknowledge the theoretical value of FA, the reality of its implementation is frequently hindered by a myriad of contextual, institutional, and psychological factors. For instance, Harrison (2013) highlights that teachers’ beliefs about assessment significantly influence their classroom practices, yet these beliefs are often shaped by broader cultural and societal expectations that prioritize accountability and high-stakes testing over formative improvement. Similarly, Brown et al. (2011) developed a tripartite model of assessment conceptions in Chinese contexts, revealing that while teachers may associate assessment with improvement, they often view it primarily through the lens of accountability, which can constrain the adoption of formative strategies.

The disconnect between positive attitudes towards FA and its actual frequency of use has been a recurring theme in international research. Yan and Cheng (2015) conducted a pivotal study examining primary teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment, utilizing the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) as a theoretical framework. Their findings indicated that while teachers generally held positive attitudes and strong intentions to use FA, these psychological factors did not strongly predict actual behavior. Instead, the study suggested that external constraints and the perception of FA as an additional burden rather than an integrated component of instruction played a significant role in limiting its practice. This aligns with Heritage’s (2007) observation that in many accountability-driven environments, assessment is viewed as a tool for ranking and summarizing rather than a source of information to guide instruction, leading to a dissonance between what teachers believe and what they do.

The Theory of Planned Behavior, proposed by Ajzen (1985, 1991), provides a valuable lens for understanding the factors that influence teachers’ assessment practices. According to this model, human action is guided by three kinds of considerations: beliefs about the likely outcomes of the behavior (attitudes), beliefs about the normative expectations of others (subjective norms), and beliefs about the presence of factors that may facilitate or impede performance (perceived behavioral control). These factors collectively shape an individual’s intention to perform a behavior, which in turn is the immediate antecedent of actual behavior. Applying this framework to the context of formative assessment allows researchers to disentangle the complex interplay between teachers’ internal motivations and external pressures. For example, Dixon and Haigh (2009) found that self-efficacy—a key component of perceived behavioral control—was a strong predictor of teachers’ willingness to try new assessment initiatives. However, the extent to which these psychological constructs translate into sustained classroom practice varies significantly across different educational contexts.

In the specific context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education in Iraq, the landscape of assessment practices is shaped by unique cultural, linguistic, and institutional dynamics. While the global discourse on formative assessment has permeated many educational systems, the extent to which these concepts have been adopted and adapted in Iraqi EFL classrooms remains underexplored. Most existing studies on FA have concentrated on the advantages and influences that may affect classroom engagement and the effect of FA on student learning achievement (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017), often focusing on Western or East Asian contexts. There has not been any in-depth study conducted to describe in detail the understanding of FA by teachers in the Iraqi context and how their perspective affects their ways of doing follow-up actions. The perception of teachers regarding FA certainly affects the kinds of input they provide as well as the actions they take to follow up, yet the specific nature of these perceptions among Iraqi EFL teachers remains largely undocumented.

Furthermore, the applicability of FA in EFL classrooms in Iraq raises questions regarding the use of correct FA strategies to match specific instructional objectives. To date, no study has been applied with reference to the contributions of attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding FA to student learning improvement in Iraqi universities and schools. This represents a significant gap in the literature, as understanding the specific barriers and facilitators within the Iraqi educational context is essential for designing effective professional development programs and policy interventions. The lack of empirical data on this specific population limits the ability of stakeholders to tailor assessment reforms to the local needs and realities of Iraqi educators.

Therefore, the current study aims to investigate the attitudes, intentions, and practices in conducting FA in Iraqi EFL classrooms. It seeks to explore the extent to which the constructs of the Theory of Planned Behavior—specifically affective attitude, instrumental attitude, subjective norm, controllability, and self-efficacy—predict teachers’ intentions to use formative assessment and their actual classroom behaviors. Additionally, the study intends to highlight the applicability of FA in EFL classrooms in terms of the use of the correct FA strategy to match the objective or the purpose of the assessment. By pinpointing the pedagogical implications of using FA, this research aims to contribute to the broader understanding of how assessment cultures can be transformed in non-Western, EFL contexts.

intros.text:
Assessment is a central component of language education because it shapes what teachers teach, how learners study, and how classroom success is interpreted. In many educational systems, however, assessment is still commonly associated with tests, grades, certification, and accountability rather than with the ongoing improvement of learning. This summative orientation is particularly visible in contexts where examinations carry high stakes for students, teachers, and institutions. Although such assessments may provide useful information about achievement at the end of a course or unit, they are less able to support learning while it is taking place. In contrast, formative assessment (FA), often referred to as assessment for learning, is designed to generate evidence of learners’ current understanding and to use that evidence to adapt teaching and learning activities. In English as a foreign language (EFL) classrooms, where learners require frequent opportunities to notice gaps, receive feedback, revise output, and develop self-regulation, formative assessment can be especially important.

Formative assessment has been widely discussed as a powerful means of improving classroom learning. Black and Wiliam’s (1998) influential review argued that assessment practices embedded in instruction can produce substantial gains in student achievement, particularly when teachers use evidence of learning to provide feedback and adjust instruction. Subsequent work has continued to emphasize that FA is not simply a set of classroom techniques, but a cyclical process involving the elicitation, interpretation, and use of evidence about learning (Bennett, 2011). In this process, teachers clarify learning goals, identify the gap between current and desired performance, provide feedback, involve learners in self- and peer-assessment, and make instructional decisions based on the evidence collected (Heritage, 2007). Research has also shown that when teachers are supported in developing assessment-for-learning strategies, student achievement can improve even in school systems where external testing remains influential (Wiliam et al., 2004).

In language teaching, formative assessment is closely connected to feedback, interaction, and learner autonomy. EFL teachers can use questioning, observation, short tasks, diagnostic quizzes, peer review, portfolios, and oral or written feedback to identify learners’ strengths and weaknesses and to guide subsequent instruction. Such practices can help students understand learning goals, monitor their own progress, and regulate their learning strategies. For example, diagnostic formative assessment has been found to enhance listening comprehension and self-regulation among language learners (Ghazizadeh & Motallebzadeh, 2017). Similarly, classroom questioning and feedback moves can create opportunities for students to make their thinking visible and for teachers to respond to emerging learning needs (Duckor, 2014). These features make FA particularly relevant to communicative language teaching, where assessment should not merely measure linguistic knowledge but should support learners in developing the ability to use language effectively.

Despite its recognized potential, formative assessment is difficult to implement consistently. One reason is that FA requires teachers to possess specific forms of assessment literacy, including knowledge of learning goals, subject matter, students’ prior knowledge, assessment methods, and feedback strategies (Heritage, 2007). Teachers also need the practical skill to integrate assessment into daily instruction rather than treating it as an additional activity separate from teaching. Shavelson (2006) argued that integrating formative assessment into teaching and learning has important implications for teacher education because teachers must learn to interpret classroom evidence and respond pedagogically. Similarly, Black and Wiliam (2006) emphasized that teacher learning is central to classroom assessment reform. If teachers do not understand how FA works, or if they lack confidence in designing and using formative tasks, the practice may remain superficial or irregular.

Teachers’ conceptions and beliefs are therefore crucial. Assessment practices are not determined only by policy, curriculum, or available techniques; they are also shaped by what teachers believe assessment is for. Brown et al. (2011) showed that teachers’ conceptions of assessment may include ideas about improvement, accountability, and irrelevance, and that these conceptions are influenced by educational and cultural contexts. Stiggins et al. (1992) also drew attention to the importance of classroom assessment practices being in teachers’ hands, highlighting the role of teachers as decision-makers in everyday assessment. When teachers view assessment mainly as a tool for grading or accountability, they may be less likely to use it formatively. Conversely, when they believe that assessment can improve learning, they may be more willing to integrate feedback, questioning, and instructional adjustment into their lessons.

The gap between teachers’ positive views of formative assessment and their actual classroom practices has become a recurring concern. Many teachers may express support for FA in principle but still use it infrequently or narrowly in practice. This discrepancy may occur because teachers perceive FA as time-consuming, because they face pressure to prepare students for summative examinations, or because they lack resources and professional support. Heritage (2007) noted that teachers often see assessment as competing with teaching rather than as an integral part of instruction. Bennett (2011) similarly observed that although international interest in FA has grown, questions remain about how it is conceptualized, implemented, and supported in real classrooms. Harrison (2013) further demonstrated that teachers’ beliefs, contextual constraints, professional development experiences, and assumptions about learners all influence the enactment of formative feedback.

Understanding teachers’ attitudes and intentions is therefore essential for explaining whether and how formative assessment is adopted. One useful framework for this purpose is Ajzen’s theory of planned behavior (TPB), which proposes that behavior is predicted by behavioral intention, and that intention is shaped by attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control (Ajzen, 1985, 1991). In the context of FA, teachers may be more likely to intend to use formative practices if they believe these practices are valuable, if important others such as school leaders and educational authorities expect them to use them, and if they believe they have the ability and autonomy to do so. However, the relationship between intention and actual practice is not always straightforward. Contextual barriers, institutional expectations, workload, lack of materials, or examination pressures may prevent teachers from translating positive intentions into classroom behavior.

Yan and Cheng (2015) applied this perspective to examine primary teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment and developed the Teachers’ Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire (TCPFAQ). Their framework distinguishes affective attitude, instrumental attitude, subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, intention, and behavior. This multidimensional view is useful because it recognizes that teachers may like FA, believe it is beneficial, feel social pressure to use it, perceive control over its use, and feel capable of implementing it, yet still differ in the extent to which they actually practice it. Such an approach allows researchers to move beyond general claims that teachers are “positive” or “negative” toward FA and to identify which components of attitude are most closely related to classroom application.

The Iraqi EFL context provides an important setting for investigating these issues. English is taught across different levels of education in Iraq, from primary school to university, and teachers work within diverse institutional conditions. As in many EFL contexts, assessment often plays a strong role in determining learners’ progression and success, while classroom time, resources, and professional development opportunities may vary considerably. If formative assessment is to contribute meaningfully to English language learning in Iraq, it is necessary to understand not only whether teachers value FA but also whether they intend to use it and how frequently they report using it in practice. Such information can inform teacher education, professional development, and assessment reform by identifying the beliefs and contextual factors that support or hinder the integration of FA into classroom instruction.

Although the international literature on formative assessment is extensive, relatively little empirical work has examined Iraqi EFL teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices using a validated theoretical instrument. Much previous research has focused on the effects of FA on student achievement, motivation, engagement, or self-regulation, while fewer studies have investigated teachers’ perspectives and the relationship between those perspectives and reported classroom behavior. This gap is important because teachers are the agents through whom assessment reform is enacted. Without understanding their conceptions, perceived control, self-efficacy, and institutional pressures, attempts to promote FA may remain policy aspirations rather than classroom realities.

Accordingly, the present study investigates Iraqi EFL teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment across different educational levels and institutions. Using the Arabic version of Yan and Cheng’s (2015) Teachers’ Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire, the study examines teachers’ affective and instrumental attitudes toward FA, perceived subjective norms, controllability, self-efficacy, intentions, and reported behavior. It also explores the relationships among these dimensions and considers whether attitudes and practices differ according to gender and institutional level. By focusing on Iraqi EFL teachers, the study seeks to contribute to the growing literature on formative assessment in language education and to provide evidence that may guide teacher professional development and the more effective integration of assessment for learning in Iraqi English classrooms.

intros.text:
Assessment is a central component of language education because it shapes what teachers teach, what learners attend to, and how educational systems define achievement. In EFL contexts, where classroom time is limited and learners often depend heavily on school instruction for exposure to English, assessment practices can either support ongoing language development or reduce learning to the preparation for tests. Traditionally, assessment has often been associated with summative examinations, grades, and accountability. However, a growing body of research has emphasized the instructional value of formative assessment (FA), commonly understood as assessment procedures used during learning to elicit evidence of students’ understanding, provide feedback, and adapt teaching and learning activities accordingly.

Formative assessment has attracted sustained attention in educational research because of its potential to improve learning outcomes and classroom interaction. Black and Wiliam’s (1998) influential review argued that assessment becomes formative when evidence about student learning is used to modify teaching and learning, and subsequent work has continued to associate assessment for learning with gains in achievement and learner engagement. Wiliam et al. (2004), for example, reported positive effects when teachers were supported in developing formative assessment strategies in secondary classrooms. Similarly, Hattie (2009) and Hattie and Zierer (2017) highlighted the importance of feedback and visible evidence of learning as key influences on achievement. In language learning, diagnostic and formative assessment can help teachers identify learners’ strengths and weaknesses, provide timely feedback, and encourage self-regulation; Ghazizadeh and Motallebzadeh (2017), for instance, found that diagnostic formative assessment improved EFL learners’ listening comprehension and self-regulation.

Despite this broad agreement about the value of FA, its classroom implementation is complex. Bennett (2011) noted that formative assessment does not have a single universally accepted definition, but that most accounts include a cyclical process of eliciting evidence, interpreting it, providing feedback, and using that information to improve learning. Heritage (2007) similarly argued that teachers need specific knowledge and skills to conduct formative assessment effectively, including knowledge of learning goals, students’ prior understanding, feedback processes, and ways of adjusting instruction. Thus, FA is not merely a set of assessment techniques; it requires teachers to integrate assessment with pedagogy, curriculum objectives, classroom discourse, and learner participation. Duckor (2014), for example, showed how questioning techniques can become formative when teachers use them to probe thinking and generate evidence of learning rather than simply check answers.

Teachers are therefore crucial agents in the success or failure of formative assessment. Research on teachers’ assessment conceptions has shown that what teachers believe about assessment influences how they use it in classrooms. Stiggins et al. (1992) drew attention to classroom assessment as a practice largely “in teachers’ hands,” while Brown et al. (2011) demonstrated that teachers’ conceptions of assessment may include beliefs about improvement, accountability, and irrelevance, and that these conceptions vary across cultural and educational contexts. Harrison (2013) also showed that teachers’ beliefs about formative feedback affect how feedback is enacted, and that contextual factors such as professional development, institutional support, and classroom conditions mediate the relationship between belief and practice. These findings suggest that understanding teachers’ attitudes toward FA is necessary for any attempt to promote assessment reform.

The distinction between positive attitudes and actual classroom practice is particularly important. Teachers may value formative assessment in principle yet use it only occasionally if they lack time, resources, confidence, institutional encouragement, or assessment literacy. Heritage (2007) observed that assessment is often viewed as competing with teaching rather than as part of teaching, especially in systems dominated by high-stakes examinations. Rink and Mitchell (2002) similarly noted that accountability and high-stakes assessment can shape reform efforts in ways that do not necessarily lead to meaningful classroom change. Shavelson (2006) emphasized the need to integrate formative assessment into teaching and teacher education, while Black and Wiliam (2006) linked classroom assessment reform to teacher learning. These perspectives indicate that FA implementation depends not only on whether teachers like or endorse it, but also on whether they feel capable of using it and whether their educational environment supports such use.

One useful framework for investigating the relationship between attitudes, intentions, and behavior is the theory of planned behavior. Ajzen (1985, 1991) proposed that human behavior is predicted by intention, and that intention is shaped by attitudes toward the behavior, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. In educational assessment research, this framework makes it possible to examine not only whether teachers have favorable views of FA, but also whether they perceive social pressure to use it, whether they believe they have control over its implementation, whether they feel efficacious, and whether these factors translate into actual practice. This distinction is important because teachers’ reported willingness to use FA may not correspond closely to their classroom behavior.

Yan and Cheng (2015) applied this perspective in their study of primary teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and practices regarding formative assessment. Their work showed that teachers generally held positive attitudes toward FA and intended to use it, but that attitudes and intentions were only weakly associated with reported classroom practice. This finding raises a significant issue for assessment reform: teachers may believe that FA is valuable and may express willingness to implement it, yet may still not use it frequently or systematically. The gap between belief and practice has also been noted in studies of teacher learning and classroom assessment (Black & Wiliam, 2006; Harrison, 2013), suggesting that contextual and professional factors must be considered alongside individual attitudes.

In EFL contexts, this issue is especially relevant because language assessment practices are often influenced by examinations, curriculum requirements, institutional expectations, and teachers’ own language assessment literacy. Language teachers need to assess not only factual knowledge but also communicative competence, receptive and productive skills, vocabulary, grammar, interaction, and learner strategies. Consequently, formative assessment in EFL classrooms may include questioning, observation, peer and self-assessment, feedback on written or spoken production, diagnostic tasks, portfolios, and instructional adjustment. However, teachers may not always have sufficient training in selecting appropriate formative procedures or in using assessment evidence to support language learning. Recent discussions of language assessment literacy emphasize the need for language teachers to understand assessment principles and to connect assessment with pedagogy (Atmani et al., 2021). Without such knowledge, FA may be treated as an additional requirement rather than an integrated part of instruction.

Although international research has examined formative assessment from multiple perspectives, relatively little is known about Iraqi EFL teachers’ conceptions, intentions, and practices. Iraq provides an important educational context for such inquiry because English is taught across school and university levels, yet assessment practices are often shaped by institutional routines, examination demands, and uneven access to professional development and teaching resources. Understanding how Iraqi EFL teachers perceive FA, how frequently they report using it, and what factors predict their use of it can contribute to both local teacher education and the broader literature on formative assessment in under-researched EFL settings.

Existing studies have tended to focus more on the effects of formative assessment on student achievement and engagement than on teachers’ psychological and contextual readiness to implement it. While research such as Ghazizadeh and Motallebzadeh (2017) has demonstrated the benefits of formative assessment for language learners, fewer studies have examined how teachers’ affective attitudes, instrumental beliefs, subjective norms, perceived controllability, self-efficacy, and intentions relate to actual FA practices. Moreover, to the best of the researcher’s knowledge, no empirical study has investigated these relationships among Iraqi EFL teachers across primary schools, high schools, private institutes, and universities. This gap limits the ability of teacher educators, school leaders, and policy makers to design professional development that responds to teachers’ actual beliefs and classroom realities.

The present study addresses this gap by examining Iraqi EFL teachers’ attitudes, intentions, and self-reported practices regarding formative assessment. Drawing on the Teachers’ Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Questionnaire developed by Yan and Cheng (2015) and informed by the theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991), the study investigates seven dimensions: affective attitude, instrumental attitude, subjective norm, controllability, self-efficacy, intention, and behavior. The Arabic version of the questionnaire was administered to 102 Iraqi EFL teachers working in primary schools, high schools, private institutes, and universities. In addition to describing teachers’ attitudes and frequency of FA use, the study examines the relationships among the questionnaire dimensions and explores whether attitudes differ by gender and institutional level.

Specifically, the study seeks to answer four questions: What are Iraqi EFL teachers’ attitudes toward formative assessment? How frequently do Iraqi EFL teachers use formative assessment? To what extent are different components of attitudes toward FA related to its application? Do Iraqi teachers’ attitudes toward FA differ according to sex and level of education? By answering these questions, the study aims to clarify whether positive perceptions of FA are reflected in reported classroom practice and to identify which attitudinal factors are most strongly associated with implementation. The findings may inform EFL teacher education in Iraq by indicating whether professional development should focus primarily on raising awareness of FA benefits, strengthening teachers’ assessment literacy and self-efficacy, addressing contextual constraints, or changing how teachers conceptualize the relationship between assessment and instruction.

intros.text: The internet, nowadays, has prepared the ground for interaction in many modalities. The higher  and richer the form of communication, the more limitations are placed upon individuality.  Roughly all forms of mediated educational interaction are now strengthened, and if one  ameliorates the utilization of the web to increase classroom-based education, the internet  supports them all  The online interaction learning model, developed by Benbunan-Fich, Hiltz,  and Harasim (2005) was based on constructivist learning theory. In preparing a model of online  learning, Benbunan-Fich et al. (2005) coalesced Fosnot and Perry’s (2005) opinions and built  a model that encompassed inputs, processes, and outputs. The inputs were the characteristics  of courses, instructors, EFL learners, and technology. Interaction has been a significant and critical component of the educational process and  context (Anderson, Rourke, Garrison, & Archer, 2001). Yet, the term itself is utilized in numerous ways to describe various types of interactions between different actors and objects  related to teaching and learning. It has been demonstrated that online courses with high levels  of student-to-student interaction have a tremendously positive effect on learning. As a case in  point, it is believed that student-to-student interaction is pivotal to building community in an  online setting, which promotes creative and nourishing learning, and assists students to develop  problem-solving and critical thinking skills (Kolloff, 2019). In one study it was depicted that students who had high levels of interaction with other  peers stated high levels of fulfillment and learning (Swan, 2020). Students in an online course  with a plethora of interactions attained far higher scores than students in the same online course  with only no interaction (Beaudoin, 2020). Interaction has an influence on student  accomplishment and satisfaction, as mirrored by test performance and scores (Roblyer &  Ekhaml, 2019). The online interaction learning model, developed by Benbunan-Fich et al.  (2005) was founded on constructivist learning theory. “Principally, constructivism means that  as people experience something novel, they compare this experience to internalized knowledge  constructs based on previous experiences, and then amend their constructs accordingly”  (Benbunan-Fich et al. 2005. p.21). Vygotsky was a pioneer in social constructivism and his  work has been invigorated in online learning theories as scholars consider learning processes  that comprise social contexts such as collaborative learning (Alavi & Dufner, 2005). Vygotsky well defined the zone of proximal development; when a child could be  directed to learn through interactions that pushed the child to just beyond his boundaries of  knowledge and then aid the child to construct knowledge through interacting with a teacher,  with other children, and with the content. Alavi (1994) used collaborative learning to online  learning experiences based on the theory that cognitive developments and learning were social  activities. Benbunan-Fich et al. (2005) believed that constructivism was the best educational  elucidation to online learning due to the fact that how well it reinforced the collaborative  learning format. Fosnot and Perry (2005) described constructivism as being applicable to  education by postulating some distinctive practices. They believe that in constructivism, the  learning outcome is not the result of development, but it is development. Also, they maintained  that disequilibrium, which is a component of constructivism, facilitates learning and reflective  abstraction is the driving force of learning. The last typical practice proposed by Fosnot and  Perry (2005) is that dialogue within a community engenders further thinking (p. 34). In building a model of online learning, Benbunan-Fich et al. (2005) incorporated Fosnot  and Perry’s (2005) ideas and created a model that was made up of inputs, processes, and  outputs. The inputs were the features of courses, instructors, EFL learners, and technology. The  processes encompassed both individual and collaborative learning and unified interactivity and  perceived social presence, sense of community, and media richness.  As shown in Figure 1, the variables in this model are interconnected and no variable  comprehensively or excessively influences the whole scheme.  The learning processes might  influence all outcome variables contingent on the instructional design, pedagogies utilized by  teachers, student features, the technology used, and the content being studied

intros.text:
The rapid expansion of online and distance education has transformed the ways in which learning occurs, placing interaction at the centre of contemporary pedagogical debate. Interaction has long been recognised as a defining feature of meaningful learning, particularly within constructivist perspectives that emphasise the social genesis of knowledge and the value of engaging with the perspectives of others (Bosnot et al., 2006). From this vantage point, learning is not the passive transmission of fixed bodies of information but an active process in which learners construct knowledge through reciprocal exchanges with content, instructors, and peers. Such an understanding has become increasingly urgent as institutions of higher education move instruction online and seek to preserve, and even enhance, the interactive dimensions of the classroom (Swan, 2002).

A substantial body of scholarship has examined the role of interaction in technology-mediated environments. Alavi (1994) demonstrated that computer-supported collaborative learning can produce higher levels of perceived skill development, self-reported learning, and even improved test performance compared with non-supported collaborative approaches. Subsequent work has continued to elaborate the social and interpersonal dynamics that underpin online learning (Alavi & Dufner, 2004), while Anderson et al. (2019) developed instruments to assess teaching presence within computer-conferencing contexts, drawing on the influential model of critical thinking and practical inquiry proposed by Garrison, Anderson, and Archer. Swan (2002) further underscored that building learning communities online depends fundamentally on carefully designed interaction, and Kolloff (2019) articulated concrete strategies for fostering effective student-to-student interaction in online courses. Collectively, these studies confirm that interaction is not a peripheral feature of online education but a core determinant of its quality and effectiveness.

Among the theoretical accounts that seek to integrate these insights, the Online Interaction Learning Model offers a comprehensive framework grounded in constructivist learning theory. Conceived as an input-process-output model, it treats a range of moderating variables—the characteristics of courses, instructors, learners, and technology—as inputs that shape the interactive processes through which learning outcomes are generated (Benbunan-Fich et al., 2004). This model provides a structured means of understanding how the various components of an online learning environment combine to influence learners' experiences and achievement. Prior research has identified several categories that appear indispensable to any online interaction model. Endres, Chowdhury, and Frye (2009), for instance, isolated course materials, instructor performance, and access to technology as central elements, while other work has drawn attention to the importance of learning practices and student-to-student interaction (Kolloff, 2019). Building on this cumulative body of evidence, the present study conceptualises the Online Interaction Learning Model as comprising five constructs: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology.

Despite the theoretical maturity of the Online Interaction Learning Model and its adoption by numerous researchers, a notable gap persists in the literature. Feedback and assessment have long been regarded as powerful tools for improving teaching and learning (Mandouit, 2018), yet there exists no validated and reliable instrument specifically designed to measure the Online Interaction Learning Model as an integrated whole. While tools have been developed to capture particular aspects of online learning, such as teaching presence (Anderson et al., 2019) or the broader Community of Inquiry framework (Garrison, Anderson & Archer, 2000), the multidimensional model that combines course-, instructor-, learner-, and technology-related factors has not been operationalised through a psychometrically sound questionnaire. This absence is particularly significant in the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction, where online interaction plays a decisive role in learners' engagement and achievement, yet where such measurement instruments remain scarce.

The present study addresses this gap by designing and validating a comprehensive questionnaire to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model among Iranian university and higher education EFL learners. Employing exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses together with reliability estimates, the study seeks to establish whether the newly developed 35-item instrument constitutes a valid and reliable measure of the five hypothesised constructs. In addition, it examines the relationships between the model and its components and learners' academic achievement, as reflected in their grade point average, and explores whether scores on the model differ by gender. By providing a rigorously validated instrument, this research aims to offer a practical and theoretically grounded tool for future investigators and educators concerned with enhancing interaction in online EFL learning environments.

intros.text:
The rapid expansion of online and distance education has repositioned interaction as one of the most critical determinants of the quality of teaching and learning. In an era when learning is increasingly mediated by technology, understanding how learners engage with course content, instructors, peers, and the digital environment is central to designing effective educational experiences. Interaction has long been recognised as the essence of formal education, and the growing reliance on internet-based delivery has only intensified interest in how meaningful, learner-centred engagement can be fostered online (Swan, 2002; Anderson et al., 2019). Consequently, both practitioners and researchers have devoted considerable attention to modelling and measuring the interactive dimensions of online learning.

Interaction in educational settings has been conceptualised in a variety of ways. Early distance-education theorists emphasised the reciprocal relationship between learner and instructor, while later scholars broadened the notion to include interactions among learners, between learners and content, and between learners and the learning interface. The most influential taxonomies distinguish student–student, student–teacher, and student–content interaction, later extended to teacher–teacher, teacher–content, and content–content forms. Underpinning much of this work is constructivist learning theory, which holds that knowledge is actively constructed by learners through social and cognitive engagement, and that the perspective of another person—typically obtained through interaction—is a crucial constituent of learning. Building on these foundations, technology-mediated and computer-supported collaborative learning has been shown to enhance perceived skill development, self-reported learning, and academic performance (Alavi, 1994; Alavi & Dufner, 2004). A sense of community and social presence has likewise been widely accepted as a factor in improving both the quality of learning and learners' motivation to study.

Within this tradition, the Online Interaction Learning Model offers an integrated theoretical framework for learning networks, conceptualised as an input–process–output model in which moderating variables—the characteristics of the courses, the instructors, the learners, and the technology—shape learning outcomes (Benbunan-Fich et al., 2004). Numerous studies have sought to identify the essential components of such models. Endres, Chowdhury, and Frye (2009), for example, isolated course materials, instructor performance, and access to technology as key categories, while other researchers have highlighted the importance of learning practices and student-to-student interaction (Kolloff, 2019). Drawing these strands together suggests that five constructs—course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology—constitute the core of the Online Interaction Learning Model.

Despite the theoretical maturity of this model and its adoption by a large number of researchers, empirical work grounded in it remains surprisingly scarce. Much of the existing scholarship has been descriptive or conceptual, and although related instruments such as the Community of Inquiry survey exist (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 2000), no validated measurement tool has been developed specifically to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model as an integrated set of constructs. This is a notable shortcoming, because without a reliable and valid instrument it is difficult to examine the model systematically or to establish the degree to which its dimensions relate to other variables such as learners' academic achievement. To date, no study to the researcher's knowledge has designed and validated such an instrument, particularly within the field of English as a foreign language (EFL). This absence leaves both researchers and practitioners without a dependable means of capturing the interactive quality of online EFL courses.

The present study addresses this gap by designing and validating a comprehensive questionnaire to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model. Founded on constructivist learning theory and informed by prior frameworks, the newly developed instrument comprises 35 items measuring the five constructs identified above. Two hundred fifty-nine Iranian university and higher education EFL learners completed the questionnaire, and its psychometric properties were examined through exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and reliability estimation. In addition, the study investigates the relationship between the model and its components and learners' academic achievement (GPA), as well as possible differences between male and female learners. By providing a validated and reliable instrument, this study aims to offer a practical tool for future researchers working on online interaction, and to contribute empirical evidence to a field that has, until now, remained largely theoretical.
