intros.text:
The integration of technology into higher education has fundamentally reshaped the pedagogical landscape, shifting the focus from traditional instructional modes toward more collaborative, computer-supported approaches. As noted by Alavi (1994), traditional classroom methods often struggle to foster the critical thinking and problem-solving skills necessary in a rapidly evolving information economy. Consequently, there has been a significant move toward technology-mediated collaborative learning, which views the social genesis of learning as a process rooted in interpersonal interactions (Alavi & ufner, 2004). In the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), the ability to facilitate meaningful interaction is not merely a technical requirement but a pedagogical imperative to ensure that students move beyond passive reception to active knowledge construction.

Central to this shift is the constructivist learning theory, which posits that learning is an active process of creating meaning through social negotiation and interaction. This perspective is further developed in the concept of communal constructivism, which emphasizes the role of the learning community in e-learning environments (Cosnot et al., 2006). Within these digital spaces, the quality of interaction—whether between students and instructors, students and peers, or students and content—becomes the primary determinant of educational success. For instance, the development of online learning communities relies heavily on the ability of designers to weave together the self, the subject, and the students to create a cohesive social and cognitive presence (Swan, 2002). Furthermore, the efficacy of teaching presence in computer-conferencing contexts suggests that the design and organization of discourse are critical for fostering a productive online environment (Anderson et al., 2019).

To conceptualize these dynamics, the Online Interaction Learning Model was developed as an integrated theoretical framework for learning networks (Endrebunan-Fich et al., 2004). This model operates as an input-process-output system, where various moderating variables—including course characteristics, instructor performance, learner attributes, and technological affordances—interact to produce learning outcomes. Despite the theoretical robustness of this model, the practical application of its constructs often remains fragmented. While some researchers have focused on specific strategies for enhancing student-student interaction (Kolloff, 2019), and others have emphasized the role of student feedback as a tool for improving teaching practices (Mandouit, 2018), there is a lack of a holistic approach to measuring how these diverse components collectively influence academic achievement (Roblyer et al., 2019).

In the specific domain of EFL, the need for a validated instrument to assess these interactions is acute. Interaction serves multiple functions, including facilitating program adaptation and encouraging learner control, yet educators often lack the tools to empirically measure the extent to which their online environments are truly interactive. While the Online Interaction Learning Model identifies key pillars such as course materials, instructor performance, and access to technology, there has been a notable scarcity of empirical studies dedicated to validating a comprehensive tool that captures all these dimensions simultaneously. Without a reliable measurement instrument, it remains difficult for practitioners to determine which specific components of the online interaction model are most strongly correlated with student success or how these factors might vary across different learner demographics.

Therefore, the present study aims to fill this critical gap in the literature by designing and validating a comprehensive questionnaire based on the Online Interaction Learning Model. By employing both exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), this research seeks to establish a reliable and valid instrument that measures five core constructs: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. Beyond the validation of the tool, the study further explores the relationship between these interaction components and the academic achievement (GPA) of Iranian university EFL learners, as well as potential gender-based differences in their perceptions of online interaction. It is hoped that this instrument will provide future researchers and educators with a rigorous means of evaluating and optimizing online interaction to enhance language learning outcomes.

intros.text:
The integration of technology into educational settings has fundamentally reshaped the pedagogical landscape, making online interactivity a cornerstone of contemporary teaching and learning. In the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), online interactivity is viewed as a multifaceted form of communication between students, their peers, and their instructors, mediated by various technological tools to facilitate knowledge acquisition (Famularsih, 2020). The importance of this interaction is rooted in constructivist learning theory, which posits that learning is a social process where the exchange of diverse viewpoints is essential for developing mindfulness and achieving meaningful learning outcomes (Shank, 1993; Visser, 2000). Consequently, creating a robust sense of community and social presence in virtual environments has been widely recognized as a critical factor in enhancing both student motivation and the overall quality of the educational experience (Haythornthwaite & Andrews, 2011; Swan, 2002).

Historically, the role of interaction in distance education has been extensively documented. Early scholars emphasized the necessity of individualized interaction between the student and the instructor (Holmberg, 1981), while subsequent models expanded this view to include a tripartite relationship between the learner, the teacher, and the content (Garrison & Shale, 1990; Laurillard, 1997). In the modern digital era, the internet has provided an unprecedented platform for these interactions to occur across multiple modalities. Research has identified various layers of interaction, ranging from the learner's internal reflection to the interaction with human and non-human resources, and finally to the meta-level interaction with the e-learning strategy itself (Hirumi, 2002). To manage these complexities, theoretical frameworks such as the Online Interaction Learning Model have been proposed to integrate key concepts and relationships within learning networks (Endrebunan-Fich et al., 2004). Previous research into the components of such models has highlighted several essential categories, most notably course materials, instructor performance, and access to technology (Endres, Chowdhury, & Frye, 2009).

Despite the theoretical acknowledgment of the pivotal role that interaction plays in online learning, there remains a significant gap in the empirical literature regarding how to accurately measure these dynamics. While various studies have explored the benefits of collaborative learning and the impact of teaching presence (Alavi, 1994; Anderson et al., 2019), there is a dearth of validated instruments specifically designed to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model as a comprehensive construct. Most existing evaluations rely on general student feedback or fragmented surveys that do not encapsulate the holistic input-process-output nature of the interaction model. Without a reliable and validated tool, educators and researchers lack the means to empirically determine the effectiveness of online interaction strategies or to understand how specific components of the model correlate with student success.

Addressing this void, the present study aims to design and validate a comprehensive questionnaire specifically tailored to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model. The primary objective is to develop a reliable instrument that measures five key constructs: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. By employing both exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), this research seeks to establish the psychometric validity and reliability of the new scale. Furthermore, the study investigates the relationship between these interaction components and the academic achievement of EFL learners, as measured by their Grade Point Average (GPA), while also examining potential gender-based differences in perceived online interaction. It is anticipated that this instrument will provide a beneficial resource for future researchers and practitioners striving to optimize interactive learning environments in the field of EFL.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed review of the literature on educational interaction and the theoretical underpinnings of the Online Interaction Learning Model. Section 3 describes the methodology, including the participant profile and the instrument design process. Section 4 presents the results of the factor analyses and correlation tests, followed by a discussion of the findings. Finally, Section 5 offers conclusions and suggestions for future research.

intros.text:
The rapid proliferation of digital technologies in higher education has fundamentally transformed the landscape of language learning, necessitating a re-evaluation of pedagogical frameworks that govern online instruction. Within this context, interaction has emerged as a cornerstone of effective learning environments, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) settings where communicative competence is paramount. The Online Interaction Learning Model, grounded in constructivist learning theory, posits that learning is an active process of knowledge construction facilitated through reciprocal events between learners, instructors, content, and technology (Wagner, 2001). Despite the theoretical robustness of this model, empirical research regarding its measurement remains scarce. While various scholars have explored the dimensions of interaction, there is a notable absence of a comprehensive, validated instrument specifically designed to assess the multifaceted nature of the Online Interaction Learning Model. This gap limits the ability of researchers and practitioners to systematically evaluate the efficacy of online learning environments and their impact on student achievement.

Interaction in educational contexts serves multiple critical functions, including permitting learner control, facilitating program adaptation based on learner input, and fostering meaningful learning communities (Sims, 1999). Constructivist theories emphasize the value of diverse viewpoints obtained through interaction as a crucial constituent of learning (Shank, 1993). In distance education, the dominance of individualized interaction between student and instructor has long been recognized (Holmberg, 1981), yet the digital age has expanded these possibilities. Garrison and Shale (1990) describe all forms of education, including distance learning, as fundamentally interactions between content, learners, and teachers. Laurillard (1997) further argues that interaction is the major module of the educational process, enabling learners to transform passive information into personal knowledge. Consequently, the internet provides a ground for interaction in many modalities, reinforcing the need for tools that can capture these complex dynamics.

Theoretical frameworks have attempted to categorize these interactions. Christenson and Menzel (1998) identified three common types: student-student, student-teacher, and student-content. Anderson et al. (2001) extended this to include teacher-teacher, teacher-content, and content-content interactions, suggesting that adequate levels of profound learning can be developed provided that one of these forms is at a high level. However, identifying the specific components that constitute a comprehensive model for online interaction remains a challenge. Endres, Chowdhury, and Frye (2009) identified course materials, instructors' performance, and access to technology as main categories. Similarly, Enbunan-Fich et al. (2004) proposed an integrated theoretical framework for learning networks, highlighting the need for a structured approach to understanding these variables. Despite these contributions, the literature lacks a unified instrument that operationalizes these components into a measurable scale for EFL contexts.

Existing studies have often relied on fragmented measures or adapted tools from general distance education contexts, which may not fully capture the nuances of EFL online learning. For instance, while the Community of Inquiry Survey (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 2000) assesses teaching, social, and cognitive presence, it does not specifically target the broader constructs of the Online Interaction Learning Model, such as learning practices or specific technological access variables. Furthermore, the relationship between these interaction components and academic achievement, such as Grade Point Average (GPA), requires precise measurement to establish causal or correlational links. Alavi (1994) and Alavi & Ufner (2004) have highlighted the importance of computer-mediated collaborative learning, yet their empirical evaluations did not focus on a holistic interaction model tailored for language learners. The need for a validated instrument is further underscored by the findings of Famularsih (2020), who asserts that online interactivity must follow a precise model to yield fruitful results for both students and instructors.

Moreover, demographic variables such as gender may influence how learners engage with online interaction models. Previous research suggests that male and female learners may exhibit different patterns of interaction and engagement in digital environments, yet few studies have systematically investigated these differences within the framework of the Online Interaction Learning Model. Understanding these variations is essential for designing inclusive and effective online learning environments. Therefore, the present study aims to address these gaps by designing and validating a comprehensive questionnaire to assess the Online Interaction Learning Model among Iranian university EFL learners. By employing exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, this research seeks to establish the psychometric properties of a new instrument that measures five key constructs: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. This instrument will provide a reliable tool for future researchers to investigate the impact of online interaction on academic achievement and to explore the nuanced ways in which learners engage with digital educational environments.

The rapid proliferation of online learning environments in higher education has fundamentally transformed how English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners engage with content, instructors, and peers. As institutions increasingly adopt digital platforms to facilitate instruction, the quality of interaction within these virtual spaces has emerged as a critical determinant of academic success. Interaction, broadly defined as reciprocal events where objects and actions mutually impact one another (Wagner, 2001), serves as the cornerstone of constructivist learning theories, which posit that knowledge is actively constructed through social engagement (Shank, 1993). In the context of distance and online education, interaction is not merely a supplementary feature but a vital mechanism for fostering learner control, facilitating program adaptation, and supporting meaningful learning outcomes (Sims, 1999). Consequently, understanding the dynamics of online interaction is essential for educators and researchers aiming to optimize educational effectiveness in digital contexts.

The theoretical underpinnings of online interaction have been extensively explored, with scholars identifying various dimensions that contribute to a robust learning environment. Christenson and Menzel (1998) initially categorized these interactions into three primary types: student-student, student-teacher, and student-content. This framework was later expanded by Anderson et al. (2001) to include teacher-teacher, teacher-content, and content-content interactions, acknowledging the complexity of mediated educational exchanges. Building on these foundations, the Online Interaction Learning Model (OILM) was developed as an integrated theoretical framework to explain how these diverse interactions function within a cohesive system (Endres-Fich et al., 2004). Grounded in constructivist principles, the OILM conceptualizes learning as an input-process-output model influenced by moderating variables such as course characteristics, instructor attributes, learner profiles, and technological affordances. Despite the model's theoretical promise, empirical validation remains limited, particularly regarding the psychometric properties of instruments designed to measure its constructs.

While numerous studies have investigated the efficacy of specific interaction types, such as the role of teaching presence in computer conferencing (Anderson et al., 2019) or the importance of student feedback in improving instructional practices (Mandouit, 2018), there is a notable scarcity of research focused on the comprehensive assessment of the Online Interaction Learning Model as a unified construct. Existing literature often isolates individual components—such as course materials, instructor performance, or access to technology (Endres, Chowdhury, & Frye, 2009)—without examining their interrelationships within a validated measurement framework. Furthermore, although the Community of Inquiry Survey (Garrison, Anderson, & Archer, 2000) provides a reliable tool for assessing specific dimensions of online learning, it does not fully capture the multifaceted nature of the OILM, which includes unique constructs such as learning practices and student-to-student interaction specific to the EFL context. This gap in the literature underscores the need for a dedicated instrument that can accurately measure the five core components of the OILM: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology.

The absence of a validated questionnaire to assess the OILM presents a significant barrier to advancing research in this domain. Without a reliable measurement tool, it is difficult to empirically examine how online interaction influences key educational outcomes, such as academic achievement or learner retention. Alavi (1994) emphasized the importance of developing computer-supported pedagogical approaches that enhance student learning, yet few instruments exist to evaluate the specific interaction patterns that drive these improvements in online EFL settings. Consequently, educators and researchers lack the necessary data to inform instructional design and policy decisions regarding online learning environments. To address this deficiency, the present study aims to design and validate a comprehensive questionnaire for assessing the Online Interaction Learning Model among Iranian university EFL learners. By employing exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, this research seeks to establish the psychometric validity and reliability of the new instrument, thereby providing a robust tool for future investigations into the impact of online interaction on academic performance and learner engagement.

intros.text:
Online learning has become an increasingly important mode of higher education, particularly in contexts where learners require flexible access to instructional resources, instructors, and peers. In English as a foreign language (EFL) education, online environments offer opportunities for exposure to language input, collaborative practice, feedback, and learner autonomy beyond the limits of the traditional classroom. However, the effectiveness of such environments depends not merely on the availability of digital platforms but on the quality of interaction that they support. Online learning is therefore best understood as a pedagogical system in which technology, course design, instructor performance, learner practices, and peer communication jointly shape learning experiences and outcomes.

The theoretical importance of interaction in learning is well established. Constructivist perspectives view knowledge as actively constructed through engagement with content, tasks, and social discourse rather than passively transmitted from teacher to learner. From this standpoint, interaction enables learners to test ideas, negotiate meaning, receive feedback, and connect new information with prior knowledge. In technology-mediated learning, these processes may be supported through discussion forums, conferencing tools, collaborative tasks, online materials, and instructor facilitation. Early empirical work on computer-mediated collaborative learning showed that technology-supported interaction could enhance learners’ perceived skill development, learning, evaluation of classroom experience, and achievement (Alavi, 1994). Similarly, research on technology-mediated collaborative learning has emphasized the social and cooperative dimensions of learning in digital environments (Alavi & Dufner, 2004).

Within the field of online education, interaction has been conceptualized in multiple but complementary ways. A central distinction is commonly made among learner-content, learner-instructor, and learner-learner interaction, each of which contributes differently to learning quality. Learner-content interaction supports engagement with instructional materials; learner-instructor interaction provides guidance, feedback, organization, and direct instruction; and learner-learner interaction promotes collaboration, social presence, and community building. Swan (2002) argued that interaction is central to building learning communities in online courses, while Kolloff (2019) highlighted the need for deliberate strategies to foster effective student-student interaction. In addition, the Community of Inquiry framework has drawn attention to teaching presence, cognitive presence, and social presence as interrelated dimensions of successful online learning. Anderson et al. (2019), for example, presented a tool for assessing teaching presence in computer conferencing contexts, identifying design and organization, facilitation of discourse, and direct instruction as key indicators of instructor contribution.

The Online Interaction Learning Model provides an integrated way of approaching these dimensions. Developed as a theoretical framework for learning networks, the model is grounded in constructivist learning theory and organized around an input-process-output logic (Benbunan-Fich et al., 2004). Its inputs include characteristics of the course, instructor, learners, and technology; its processes involve interaction and learning practices; and its outputs may include satisfaction, perceived learning, and academic achievement. Such a model is particularly relevant to EFL education because language learning requires sustained engagement with materials, meaningful communication, feedback, practice, and opportunities for interaction with other users of the language. If online EFL instruction is to be evaluated meaningfully, researchers and practitioners require instruments that capture the multiple components of interaction rather than focusing on a single dimension such as technology access or instructor behavior.

Despite the growing body of research on online learning, several measurement challenges remain. Existing instruments often assess specific aspects of online education, such as teaching presence, student feedback, satisfaction, or collaborative learning, but do not comprehensively operationalize the Online Interaction Learning Model as a multidimensional construct. Student feedback can provide valuable information for improving teaching practice (Mandouit, 2018), and established frameworks such as the Community of Inquiry have contributed important tools for examining online discourse and presence. Nevertheless, there remains a need for a concise, psychometrically validated questionnaire that measures the major components of online interaction learning in EFL contexts. Such an instrument would allow researchers to examine how learners perceive online course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, peer interaction, and access to technology, and how these dimensions relate to academic outcomes.

The present study addresses this gap by designing and validating a questionnaire for assessing the Online Interaction Learning Model among Iranian EFL learners. Drawing on constructivist theory, prior work on technology-mediated collaborative learning, online learning communities, teaching presence, and the Online Interaction Learning Model, the study conceptualizes online interaction learning through five components: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. The study further examines the psychometric properties of the instrument through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses and reliability estimation. In addition, it investigates the relationship between learners’ scores on the questionnaire and their academic achievement, as measured by grade point average, and explores possible gender differences in perceptions of online interaction learning. By developing and validating this instrument, the study aims to contribute a practical research tool for evaluating online EFL learning environments and for supporting future inquiry into the role of interaction in technology-mediated language education.

intros.text:
Online learning has become an increasingly central mode of instruction in higher education, particularly in contexts where learners require flexible access to language learning opportunities. In English as a foreign language (EFL) education, online environments are not merely channels for delivering course content; they are social and pedagogical spaces in which learners interact with instructors, peers, materials, and technological systems. Because language learning depends heavily on meaningful communication, feedback, participation, and negotiation of meaning, the quality of interaction in online courses is a crucial concern for teachers, course designers, institutions, and researchers.

Interaction is widely regarded as a core element of effective learning in technology-mediated environments. From a constructivist perspective, learners build knowledge through active engagement with content and through social exchange with others. Communal and social constructivist accounts of e-learning emphasize that knowledge construction is strengthened when learners participate in communities, share perspectives, and reflect on experience (Fosnot et al., 2006). Similarly, research on computer-mediated collaborative learning has shown that technology-supported collaboration can improve learners’ perceived skill development, self-reported learning, evaluation of the learning experience, and academic performance (Alavi, 1994). Such findings suggest that online learning should be understood not only in terms of access to digital materials, but also in terms of the forms and quality of interaction that learners experience.

The Online Interaction Learning Model provides a useful framework for conceptualizing these relationships. Benbunan-Fich et al. (2004) proposed the model as an integrated theoretical framework for learning networks, bringing together the input, process, and output dimensions of online learning. Within this perspective, learning outcomes are shaped by a combination of course-related, instructor-related, learner-related, and technology-related variables. Course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology can therefore be viewed as interrelated components that contribute to learners’ experiences in online settings. These components are especially relevant in EFL contexts, where learners often rely on instructors for scaffolding, on peers for communicative practice, on materials for linguistic input, and on technology for sustained access to learning opportunities.

Previous research has examined several dimensions of online interaction and has highlighted their contribution to learning. Teaching presence, for example, has been described in terms of course design and organization, facilitation of discourse, and direct instruction, all of which help structure online learning and support learners’ cognitive engagement (Anderson et al., 2019). Student feedback has also been shown to provide valuable information about teaching effectiveness and areas for pedagogical improvement (Mandouit, 2018). In addition, student-to-student interaction has been emphasized as a key condition for building learning communities in online courses (Swan, 2002), and practical strategies have been proposed to strengthen peer interaction in virtual learning environments (Kolloff, 2019). Together, these studies indicate that online interaction is multidimensional and that successful online learning depends on the alignment of instructional design, teacher support, peer communication, learner activity, and technological access.

Despite this growing body of work, measurement remains a significant challenge. Studies of online learning have often focused on specific constructs, such as teaching presence, collaborative learning, student feedback, or peer interaction, rather than on a comprehensive assessment of the Online Interaction Learning Model as an integrated construct. Although existing instruments have contributed to the evaluation of particular aspects of online education, there is still limited evidence concerning a valid and reliable questionnaire that measures the major components of the Online Interaction Learning Model together. This gap is important because, without an empirically validated instrument, researchers and practitioners may find it difficult to diagnose the strengths and weaknesses of online EFL courses, compare learners’ perceptions across contexts, or examine the relationship between online interaction and academic achievement.

The need for such an instrument is particularly pressing in EFL higher education contexts, where online learning may vary considerably in terms of instructional quality, learner participation, technological resources, and opportunities for communication. It also remains unclear how learners’ perceptions of online interaction are associated with indicators of academic success, such as grade point average, and whether these perceptions differ according to demographic variables such as gender. Addressing these issues can provide a more systematic basis for evaluating online courses and for designing learning environments that support interaction-rich language learning.

Accordingly, the present study aimed to design and validate a comprehensive questionnaire for assessing the Online Interaction Learning Model among Iranian university and higher education institute EFL learners. Drawing on the theoretical and empirical literature on online interaction, the study developed a 35-item instrument covering five components: course materials, instructor performance, learning practices, student-to-student interaction, and access to technology. The study examined the factorial validity of the questionnaire through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, estimated its reliability, and investigated the relationships between the model components and learners’ academic achievement. It also explored whether male and female EFL learners differed in their scores on the Online Interaction Learning Model. By providing evidence for the validity and reliability of the instrument, the study seeks to offer researchers and practitioners a practical tool for assessing interaction in online EFL learning environments.

intros.text: Standardized high-stakes exams have been widely used in China to assess learners’ English proficiency and play as the key gatekeeper for their academic development. The National Higher Education Entrance Examination, known as Gaokao in Chinese, is taken annually by millions of high school graduates across China. As the major gatekeeper, Gaokao is the most visible and important exam in China which predominately determines whether a high school graduate is able to continue his/her higher education in a prestige university (Qi, 2007). For most provinces in China, the current structure of Gaokao can be described as “3+X.” The 3 refers to the three compulsory subjects that each testee needs to take, namely Chinese, Mathematics, and English. The X differs according to the testee’s disciplinary choice. For testees pursuing the Humanities stream, the subjects in the X are History, Politics, and Geography; whereas for the Sciences stream, the subjects in the X are Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. In sum, most testees need to take six subject exams in Gaokao in total. Regarding the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), as one of the three compulsory exams in Gaokao, it plays a considerable role in influencing one’s Gaokao final result. Although some provinces implement different exam structures depending on the local educational circumstances, the major content of the NMET is uniformly prescribed by China’s Ministry of Education.  The National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA), operating directly under the Ministry of Education, issues a guideline for the NMET each year, which provides an essential guide about the exam for testees’ preparation as well as authorities of individual provinces in designing their own exams (Cheng & Qi, 2006; Farley & Yang, 2020). Throughout the years, the NMET has been gradually reformed toward the direction of examining learners’ communicative skills. For instance, listening has been added as an essential component since 1999 (Cheng & Qi, 2006). In addition, despite a relatively low share of the total score, speaking has been adopted as a separate section beyond the written sections in different cities and provinces (Cheng, 2008). By reforming and diversifying the content of the NMET, the intention of the test constructors is to improve Chinese English learners’ languageuse ability rather than mere linguistic knowledge of English (Ministry of Education, 2017; Qi, 2007); nevertheless, as Gaokao has been remaining as the predominant gatekeeper for most students to pursue higher education and testing grammatical knowledge on paper-based exams continues to take up the major weighting in the NMET, the reality of teaching and learning to the test and focusing on rote memorization stays in the practice of English education in China (Qi, 2005; Yan, 2015).  Despite various reforms of the NMET, reading comprehension has always been an essential component of the exam, which takes approximately 25 – 30% of the total points. According to the general guideline from the National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA, 2019a), designing the exams in Gaokao should be based on specific requirements from different universities and the national curriculum standards. The major objectives suggested in the general guideline include being able to understand common topics like announcement, instruction, and advertisement in books, newspapers, and magazines. The testees are expected to obtain useful information from the passage to understand the main ideas and specific details, grasp the major structure, comprehend the author’s purpose, attitude, and opinions, and infer meanings of specific vocabulary and phrases (NEEA, 2019b). Regarding the General High School English Curriculum Standards, the 2003 and 2017 editions both confirm these objectives (Ministry of Education, 2003, 2017).  Although the NMET has been acting as the baton of English teaching and learning in China and understanding the longitudinal test development may greatly influence pedagogical practices, few empirical studies have investigated the development of the reading comprehension passages included in the exam from a longitudinal perspective. In particular, to the best of the researcher’s knowledge, no study has used natural language processing tools to analyze the changes of the text complexity of the passages via a systematic and comprehensive manner, including longitudinal analyses at lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels.  Therefore, employing corpus-based analyzing methods, the current study aims to provide a comprehensive picture of how the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages in the NMET has changed throughout the past 25 years, from 1996 to 2020.  The results of the study are expected to fill the gap in relevant research fields and offer insights for test designing and pedagogical activities.  The following research questions led to the investigation of the study:  1. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the lexical level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)? 2. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the syntactic level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)? 3. How has the text complexity of the reading comprehension passages at the discourse level changed over the past 25 years (i.e., 1996-2020)?

intros.text:
In China, English language testing occupies a uniquely prominent position within the educational system. With a testing tradition that can be traced back nearly two thousand years to the imperial examination system, contemporary China administers standardized English tests to billions of learners, for whom success on these assessments frequently determines academic advancement and broader life prospects (Cheng, 2008). Among these high-stakes examinations, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), a compulsory component of the National College Entrance Examination (commonly known as the Gaokao), is arguably the most consequential. Taken annually by millions of high school graduates seeking admission to higher education institutions, the NMET functions as a unified national placement test that distinguishes learners across the full spectrum of English proficiency (Cheng & Qi, 2006). Unlike more comprehensive admissions systems used in Western contexts, where standardized test scores are weighed alongside extracurricular records and personal statements, the Gaokao relies on a single set of examination questions to determine eligibility, a design intended to safeguard fairness and equity across a vast and socioeconomically diverse population (Farley & Yang, 2019).

Beyond its selection function, the NMET has also been explicitly designed to serve as an agent for pedagogical change, aiming to promote reform in English language teaching and learning in schools (Qi, 2005, 2007). However, research on the washback of the NMET has consistently demonstrated that these dual purposes are frequently in tension. Qi (2005, 2007) found that the selection function and the intended reform function of the NMET often conflict with one another, rendering the test a powerful trigger for teaching to the test but an ineffective vehicle for the classroom changes envisioned by its designers and policymakers. Similarly, Yan (2015) documented a persistent implementation gap between the goals of curriculum reform and teachers' classroom practices, attributing this gap in large part to the pervasive backwash effect of the examination-oriented culture that dominates Chinese schooling. These studies collectively suggest that the characteristics of the NMET itself exert a profound influence over what and how students learn, making the systematic examination of the test's content a matter of considerable practical and theoretical importance.

Given this influence, the reading comprehension component of the NMET warrants particular attention. Reading comprehension accounts for a substantial proportion of the total score, and the texts that students are required to process constitute a central determinant of the demands the test places on learners. According to widely accepted models of reading comprehension, the features of a text—its vocabulary load, linguistic structure, discourse organization, and genre—directly shape the representations readers construct and thereby influence comprehension outcomes (Snow, 2002; Alderson, 2000). For second language readers in particular, textual characteristics such as rhetoric, genre, and text complexity play a critical role in shaping understanding, especially among intermediate-level learners (Hornof, 2008; Guthrie, Klauda, & Ho, 2013). Text complexity, understood as the set of measurable linguistic properties of a text that can be analyzed independently of any particular reader (Mesmer, Cunningham, & Hiebert, 2012), therefore provides an especially informative lens through which to interrogate the changing demands of a high-stakes reading assessment. If the complexity of NMET reading passages has shifted over time, such shifts would carry direct implications for the expectations placed on learners, the alignment between the test and national curriculum policy, and the equity considerations that underpin the Gaokao's design.

Despite the extensive scholarship on the washback and policy dimensions of the NMET, comparatively little research has systematically examined the linguistic properties of its reading passages, and even fewer studies have tracked how these properties have developed over an extended period. Recent advances in corpus linguistics and natural language processing now make it possible to measure text complexity at multiple linguistic levels with far greater precision, reliability, and comprehensiveness than traditional readability formulas or manual analysis allow (Benjamin, 2012; Crossley, Greenfield, & McNamara, 2008). A suite of freely available automated tools—including those designed to analyze lexical sophistication, lexical diversity and density, syntactic complexity, and textual cohesion—enables fine-grained, batch-processed analyses of large text collections across lexical, syntactic, and discourse dimensions. These developments open the possibility of a rigorous, longitudinal investigation into whether and how the reading demands of the NMET have evolved.

The present study addresses this gap by examining the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the national version of the NMET over the past 25 years, from 1996 to 2020. Drawing on a corpus of 206 reading passages, the study measures text complexity at the lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels using established natural language processing tools and compares these measures longitudinally across the years. Specifically, the study asks how lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level text complexity have changed over this period, and it further evaluates the observed patterns against the relevant national curriculum standards and examination guidelines. By tracing the trajectory of text complexity and situating the findings within the policy context, this study aims to contribute empirical evidence to inform test design, curriculum alignment, and pedagogical practice for reading comprehension in the Chinese EFL context and beyond.

intros.text:
In China, English is a compulsory subject in schools and one of the three core components of the National College Entrance Examination, commonly known as the Gaokao. The English testing tradition in China, though relatively recent compared to the country's imperial examination history, now involves millions of learners for whom examination performance is inextricably linked to academic and life opportunities (Cheng, 2008). Among these tests, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET) occupies a uniquely powerful position. As a high-stakes placement instrument administered directly under the Ministry of Education through the National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA), the NMET not only selects candidates for higher education but also exerts a profound influence on English language teaching and learning across secondary schools (Cheng & Qi, 2006). Given that the Gaokao provides all students with a single, standardized set of questions in the name of educational equity (Farley & Yang, 2019), the design and difficulty of its components have far-reaching consequences for a vast and diverse population of test-takers.

Because of its enormous stakes, the NMET has attracted considerable research attention, particularly with respect to its washback effects on classroom practice. A recurring finding is that the test's dual functions of selection and pedagogical reform are frequently in tension, so that instead of promoting the intended communicative changes in English language teaching, the exam encourages teaching to the test (Qi, 2005, 2007). Similarly, studies of curriculum reform in China have shown that teachers often perceive an implementation gap between the goals of the national curriculum and their classroom realities, driven largely by the backwash of the prevailing examination culture (Yan, 2015). These lines of inquiry share an underlying premise: what the NMET actually measures and demands has powerful downstream effects on what and how learners are taught. Yet, while stakeholders' perceptions and the washback of writing tasks have been examined in detail, comparatively little attention has been directed at the linguistic properties of the reading materials that constitute a substantial portion of the exam.

Reading comprehension is central to the NMET, typically accounting for a quarter to nearly a third of the total score. Theoretical models of reading comprehension emphasize that the text itself—its vocabulary load, syntactic structure, discourse organization, and genre—directly shapes comprehension outcomes, alongside reader and task characteristics embedded in a sociocultural context (Snow, 2002; Alderson, 2000). For second language readers in particular, the complexity of the text plays a critical role in influencing understanding, especially at intermediate levels of proficiency (Hornof, 2008; Guthrie, Klauda, & Ho, 2013). A robust body of empirical work has demonstrated that lexical features, syntactic structures, and discourse-level cohesion all bear a strong relationship to reading difficulty (Wright & Cervetti, 2017; Shiotsu & Weir, 2007; Graesser, McNamara, & Louwerse, 2003). Consequently, understanding the text complexity of high-stakes reading passages is essential to evaluating what the exam demands of learners and whether those demands align with stated policy expectations.

Advances in corpus linguistics and natural language processing have made it possible to move beyond traditional readability formulas, which relied largely on surface-level counts such as word and sentence length, toward more fine-grained and theoretically grounded measures of text complexity (Benjamin, 2012). Tools such as TAALES (Kyle & Crossley, 2015), TAALED (Kyle, Crossley, & Jarvis, 2020), TAASSC (Kyle, 2016), and TAACO (Crossley, Kyle, & McNamara, 2016) now allow researchers to assess lexical sophistication, diversity, and density, syntactic complexity and sophistication, and multiple dimensions of cohesion with greater reliability and validity than earlier approaches. Despite the availability of these instruments, no study to date has systematically applied them to trace the longitudinal development of text complexity in a major Chinese high-stakes reading test. While there is evidence of rising vocabulary demands in provincial entrance examinations over shorter time spans, the extent to which the nationwide NMET reading passages have changed across the multiple decades of its existence, and whether such changes cohere with the national curriculum standards, remains largely unexplored. This gap is significant because any drift between the linguistic demands embedded in the exam and the vocabulary and proficiency targets specified in official guidelines could disadvantage students who lack access to supplementary learning resources.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the NMET over the past 25 years, from 1996 to 2020. Drawing on a corpus of 206 reading passages from 46 sets of the national version of the exam, it measures text complexity at the lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels using TAALES, TAALED, TAASSC, and TAACO, and employs ANOVA and MANOVA analyses to compare changes across five-year intervals. Specifically, the study asks how lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level complexity have developed longitudinally, and whether these developments are reflected in the general curriculum standards and exam guidelines. In doing so, the study aims to reveal whether the linguistic demands of the NMET reading passages have shifted over time and to what extent these demands correspond to policy expectations. The findings are intended to offer evidence-based insights for test designers and to inform pedagogical practices, thereby contributing to a fuller understanding of a test whose consequences reach far into the lives of Chinese learners of English.

intros.text:
In the landscape of English language education in China, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), commonly known as part of the Gaokao, stands as one of the most consequential high-stakes examinations in the world. As Cheng (2008) notes, the history of English language testing in China has evolved rapidly, with tests becoming the primary determinant of academic success and future life trajectories for millions of learners. Because the NMET serves as the critical gateway for admission into higher education institutions, it exerts a profound influence on the teaching and learning of English across the country. The weight of this examination often creates a significant washback effect, where the nature of the test dictates classroom priorities and pedagogical strategies (Qi, 2005; Qi, 2007). Consequently, any shift in the linguistic requirements of the NMET can trigger widespread changes in how English is taught in high schools, often leading to a 'teaching to the test' phenomenon that may conflict with broader curricular goals (Qi, 2005; Yan, 2015).

Central to the NMET's ability to assess proficiency is the reading comprehension section, which typically constitutes 25% to 30% of the total score. The effectiveness of these reading tasks depends heavily on the complexity of the texts selected. In applied linguistics, text complexity is understood as a multifaceted construct encompassing lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level features that independently and collectively influence a reader's ability to construct mental models of the text. While the National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA, 2019a) provides guidelines and word lists to standardize the exam, there is often a perceived gap between these official standards and the actual linguistic demands of the test papers. As Yan (2015) suggests, teachers often feel unable to implement curriculum reforms unless the examinations themselves change, highlighting the need for an objective analysis of how the NMET has evolved over time.

Historically, the analysis of text difficulty relied on human judgment or traditional readability formulas based on surface-level measures such as sentence and word length. However, recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and corpus linguistics have allowed for a more nuanced understanding of text complexity. Modern computational tools can now measure lexical sophistication (the use of low-frequency and academic vocabulary), lexical diversity (the range of vocabulary used), and syntactic sophistication (the complexity of clausal and phrasal structures) with high reliability. Furthermore, discourse-level analysis, particularly regarding cohesion, provides insight into how the connectivity of ideas facilitates or hinders comprehension. Despite the availability of these tools, there has been a lack of longitudinal research examining the developmental trajectory of text complexity within the NMET over a sustained period.

Understanding the longitudinal development of the NMET is crucial for several reasons. First, it allows researchers and policymakers to determine whether the exam has remained aligned with the General High School English Curriculum Standards. If the complexity of the reading passages has increased significantly beyond the prescribed vocabulary and grammatical thresholds, it may create an equity issue, as students with access to external private tutoring may be better equipped to handle the increasing difficulty than those relying solely on classroom instruction (Farley & Yang, 2019). Second, by identifying the specific dimensions—lexical, syntactic, or discourse—that have seen the most growth, educators can better tailor their instructional materials to bridge the gap between textbook content and exam reality.

While some studies have looked at specific provinces or shorter timeframes, a comprehensive, multi-decade analysis of the national version of the NMET is currently missing. There is a pressing need to investigate whether the reading passages have become more demanding and, if so, in what specific linguistic dimensions. Such an investigation would provide empirical evidence to either support or challenge the adequacy of current curriculum guidelines and offer a data-driven foundation for future test design.

Therefore, the present study aims to examine the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the NMET over a 25-year period, from 1996 to 2020. By employing a suite of advanced NLP tools—including TAALES for lexical sophistication, TAALED for diversity and density, TAASSC for syntactic complexity, and TAACO for cohesion—this research seeks to quantify the changes across three primary levels of linguistic analysis. Specifically, the study addresses three research questions: (1) How has lexical complexity evolved in the NMET reading passages over the past 25 years? (2) To what extent has syntactic complexity changed during this period? (3) Has there been a significant shift in discourse-level cohesion within these texts? By comparing these findings against national curriculum standards and NEEA guidelines, the study intends to shed light on the alignment between policy and practice in Chinese high school English education.

intros.text:
In the landscape of English language education in China, high-stakes examinations exert a profound influence on both pedagogical practices and learner priorities. Among these, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), commonly known as part of the Gaokao, stands as the most critical gateway for students seeking admission to institutions of higher education (Cheng, 2008). Because performance on this unified national standardized test largely determines a student's academic future and subsequent life opportunities, it carries immense weight within the Chinese sociocultural context (Farley & Yang, 2019). Consequently, the NMET is not merely a tool for assessment but also a powerful driver of the "washback effect," where the nature of the test dictates the focus of classroom instruction (Qi, 2005, 2007). Indeed, many secondary teachers have noted that significant shifts in curriculum implementation are often impossible unless the exams themselves change (Yan, 2015).

Reading comprehension is a central component of the NMET, typically accounting for 25% to 30% of the total score. The effectiveness of these reading assessments depends heavily on the nature of the texts selected, as the linguistic properties of a passage—its complexity—directly impact a reader's ability to construct mental models and achieve comprehension (Snow, 2002). Text complexity is a multidimensional construct encompassing lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level features. At the lexical level, the load of low-frequency words and the density of content words can either facilitate or hinder understanding (Wright & Cervetti, 2017). Syntactically, the length of sentences and the sophistication of clausal structures influence the ease with which a reader can parse a text (Kyle, 2016). Furthermore, at the discourse level, the degree of cohesion—the linguistic links that bind a text together—is essential for maintaining coherence and reducing cognitive load (Graesser et al., 2003).

Given the high stakes associated with the NMET, there is a critical need to ensure that the reading passages are aligned with national curriculum standards and guidelines. The National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA, 2019a) and the Ministry of Education provide frameworks for the expected vocabulary size and language proficiency of high school graduates. However, while the NMET is designed to distinguish students of varying proficiency levels (Cheng & Qi, 2006), the actual linguistic demands of the test passages may evolve independently of these official guidelines. If the complexity of the test materials increases without a corresponding shift in curriculum standards, a mismatch occurs, potentially placing an undue burden on students and exacerbating educational inequality based on access to external resources.

Despite the importance of the NMET, most research on this examination has focused on its washback effects, the perceptions of stakeholders, or the impact of specific test reforms (Qi, 2005; Yan, 2015). To date, there has been a lack of longitudinal, empirical research utilizing modern natural language processing (NLP) tools to analyze how the actual text complexity of the reading passages has developed over several decades. While some regional studies have noted trends in vocabulary requirements, a comprehensive nationwide analysis covering a significant timespan is missing. Understanding the longitudinal trajectory of text complexity is essential not only for test designers to maintain validity and fairness but also for educators to adapt their instructional materials to the reality of the examination.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the NMET over a 25-year period, from 1996 to 2020. By employing a corpus of 206 passages, the study utilizes advanced NLP tools—including TAALES for lexical sophistication, TAALED for lexical diversity and density, TAASSC for syntactic complexity, and TAACO for discourse cohesion—to provide a fine-grained analysis of linguistic changes. The main objective is to determine whether there has been a steady increase in lexical, syntactic, or discourse complexity and to analyze whether these changes align with the general curriculum standards and official guidelines.

Specifically, this research seeks to answer the following questions: (1) How has the lexical complexity of NMET reading passages evolved from 1996 to 2020? (2) What changes have occurred in the syntactic complexity of these texts over the same period? (3) To what extent has discourse-level cohesion fluctuated across the years? By answering these questions, the study aims to shed light on the evolving demands of high-stakes reading assessments in China and provide evidence-based suggestions for both test design and pedagogical practices.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a detailed review of the literature regarding text complexity, readability, and corpus-based measurements. Section 3 describes the corpus and the methodology used for data analysis. Section 4 presents the results of the lexical, syntactic, and discourse analyses. Finally, Section 5 discusses the findings in relation to national curriculum standards, explores the pedagogical implications, and outlines the limitations of the study.

intros.text:
In China, the National Matriculation English Test (NMET), commonly known as the Gaokao English section, stands as the most significant high-stakes examination in the English language education landscape. As a unified national standardized test, a student’s eligibility to enroll in higher education is largely determined by their performance on this exam (Farley & Hong Yang, 2019). Given its pivotal role in academic and career trajectories, the NMET exerts a profound influence on English language teaching and learning practices across the country. Cheng (2008) notes that for billions of learners in China, success in these English tests is often the key to their academic and life success. Consequently, the design and characteristics of the NMET, particularly its reading comprehension component, warrant close scrutiny to understand its impact on learners and the alignment with educational policies.

The NMET was designed not only to select candidates for higher education but also to promote changes in English Language Teaching (ELT) in schools (Qi, 2005). However, research has indicated that the test has struggled to achieve its intended washback effects due to conflicting aims between its selection function and its function as an agent for pedagogical change (Qi, 2005; Qi, 2007). This tension often results in a culture of 'teaching to the test,' where classroom practices are driven by exam requirements rather than broader educational goals (Yan, 2015). The reading comprehension section, which typically accounts for 25-30% of the total score, is a critical component of the NMET. As students' ability to comprehend texts is central to their overall language proficiency, the complexity of the reading passages used in the exam plays a crucial role in determining the difficulty of the test and the skills it assesses.

Text complexity is a multifaceted construct that encompasses various linguistic features, including lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level characteristics. According to the RAND Reading Study Group model, text features such as vocabulary load, linguistic structure, and discourse style directly impact readers' comprehension outcomes (Snow, 2002). In the context of L2 reading, text complexity is particularly critical as it influences how learners process and construct meaning from the text (Hornof, 2008; Guthrie, Klauda, & Ho, 2013). Traditional readability formulas have long been used to assess text difficulty, often relying on surface-level measures like sentence length and word frequency. However, contemporary approaches emphasize the need for more comprehensive analyses that incorporate cognitive and psycholinguistic features to better capture the nuances of text complexity (Benjamin, 2012; Crossley, Greenfield, & McNamara, 2008).

Despite the importance of text complexity in reading comprehension, there is a paucity of longitudinal research examining the development of text complexity in the NMET over an extended period. While some studies have investigated specific aspects of the NMET or compared it with other examinations, few have systematically analyzed the linguistic features of reading passages across multiple decades. Understanding the historical trajectory of text complexity in the NMET is essential for evaluating whether the exam has evolved in line with national curriculum standards and guidelines. The National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA, 2019a) provides guidelines for the exam, and the Ministry of Education has issued curriculum standards that specify vocabulary requirements for high school graduates (Ministry of Education, 2003, 2017). However, it remains unclear whether the actual text complexity of the reading passages aligns with these policy documents.

This study aims to address this gap by examining the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the NMET from 1996 to 2020. Over the past 25 years, China's English education landscape has undergone significant changes, influenced by curriculum reforms and shifts in educational policy. By analyzing 206 reading passages across lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels, this study seeks to uncover trends in text complexity and evaluate their implications for test design and pedagogical practice. The study employs natural language processing tools, including TAALES, TAALED, TAASSC, and TAACO, to conduct a comprehensive corpus-based analysis of the linguistic features of the passages. This approach allows for a fine-grained examination of lexical sophistication, diversity, and density, as well as syntactic complexity and discourse cohesion.

The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights for test designers, policymakers, and educators. By revealing the longitudinal development of text complexity, the study can inform decisions regarding the alignment of the NMET with national curriculum standards and help identify potential mismatches between exam requirements and students' preparedness. Furthermore, the results can guide pedagogical practices by highlighting the specific linguistic challenges students may face in the reading comprehension section. As the NMET continues to shape English language education in China, understanding the evolution of its text complexity is crucial for ensuring that the exam remains a valid and reliable measure of students' reading abilities while supporting their overall language development.

intros.text:
The National Matriculation English Test (NMET) in China, commonly known as the Gaokao English subtest, stands as the most significant high-stakes examination in the country's English language education landscape. Administered by the National Education Examinations Authority (NEEA), the NMET serves as the primary gateway for students seeking admission to higher education institutions. Given its immense impact on students' academic trajectories and social mobility, the test exerts a powerful influence on English language teaching and learning practices across secondary schools (Cheng, 2008; Qi, 2005). As a high-stakes test, the NMET is not merely a selection tool but is also intended to function as an agent of pedagogical change, promoting reforms in English language teaching (ELT) (Qi, 2007). However, the alignment between the test's design, the national curriculum standards, and actual classroom practices remains a critical area of inquiry. Understanding the characteristics of the test items, particularly reading comprehension passages, is essential for evaluating the validity of the test and its washback effects on instruction (Yan, 2015).

Reading comprehension is a central component of the NMET, accounting for a substantial proportion of the total score. Theoretical models of reading comprehension, such as the RAND Reading Study Group model, posit that reading is a complex interaction between the reader, the text, and the task (Snow, 2002). Within this framework, text complexity is a crucial independent variable that directly influences comprehension outcomes. Text complexity encompasses various linguistic features, including lexical sophistication, syntactic structures, and discourse cohesion. While traditional readability formulas have long relied on surface-level metrics like sentence length and word frequency, contemporary research advocates for a more multidimensional approach. Recent advancements in corpus linguistics and natural language processing (NLP) have enabled researchers to analyze text complexity with greater precision, incorporating measures of lexical density, diversity, and semantic cohesion (Benjamin, 2012; Crossley et al., 2008). These sophisticated tools allow for a granular examination of how linguistic features evolve over time and how they may affect learners' processing of texts.

Despite the growing recognition of the importance of text complexity in L2 reading, longitudinal studies examining the development of text complexity in high-stakes standardized tests within the Chinese context remain limited. Previous research has extensively documented the washback effects of the NMET on teaching practices and the conflicts between its selection function and its intended role in promoting pedagogical reform (Qi, 2005; Yan, 2015). Studies have also explored the general characteristics of the NMET and its evolution over specific periods (Cheng & Qi, 2006). However, few studies have employed quantitative, corpus-based methods to systematically analyze the linguistic features of reading passages across a long time span. Specifically, there is a lack of empirical evidence regarding how lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level complexity in NMET reading passages has changed over the past two decades. It remains unclear whether the increasing difficulty of the test aligns with the vocabulary requirements specified in the national curriculum standards or if it creates a mismatch that disadvantages certain student groups.

Furthermore, while the general trend of increasing difficulty in high-stakes exams is often assumed, the specific nature of this increase—whether it is driven by lexical sophistication, syntactic elaboration, or discourse cohesion—has not been rigorously investigated using modern NLP tools. Existing readability research often focuses on general educational texts rather than the specific genre of standardized test passages. Consequently, the extent to which the NMET reading passages have become more linguistically complex, and the implications of these changes for test validity and pedagogical practice, constitute a significant gap in the literature. This study addresses these gaps by examining the longitudinal development of text complexity in NMET reading comprehension passages from 1996 to 2020.

The primary objective of this study is to analyze the changes in text complexity at lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels over a 25-year period. By utilizing advanced natural language processing tools, including TAALES, TAALED, TAASSC, and TAACO, this research aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven account of the linguistic evolution of the NMET. The study seeks to answer the following research questions: (1) How has lexical complexity (sophistication, diversity, and density) in NMET reading passages changed from 1996 to 2020? (2) What are the trends in syntactic complexity (length and structural complexity) over the same period? (3) How has discourse-level cohesion evolved in these passages? By comparing the empirical findings with the vocabulary requirements outlined in the National High School English Curriculum Standards, this study also aims to evaluate the alignment between the test and the curriculum. The results of this investigation are expected to offer valuable insights for test designers, policymakers, and language teachers, highlighting potential mismatches between exam demands and educational guidelines, and suggesting directions for future test design and pedagogical adaptation.

intros.text:
High-stakes examinations exert a powerful influence on educational opportunities, classroom practices, and public perceptions of learning outcomes. In China, the National College Entrance Examination, or Gaokao, is one of the most consequential selection mechanisms for access to higher education, and its English component—the National Matriculation English Test (NMET)—has long been central to senior secondary English education. Although English language testing in China has a relatively short history compared with the country’s examination tradition, large-scale English tests have become decisive for millions of learners’ academic progression and, in many cases, future life chances (Cheng, 2008). The NMET is therefore not merely an assessment instrument; it is also a policy-related mechanism that shapes what is taught, what is learned, and how English proficiency is valued in schools.

The NMET has been designed to serve multiple purposes. Its primary function is selection: it must differentiate among candidates for university admission. At the same time, it has also been expected to encourage desirable changes in English language teaching and learning, in line with national curriculum reforms and broader communicative goals (Cheng & Qi, 2006; Qi, 2005, 2007). These dual purposes may create tension. When an examination must both rank students reliably and promote pedagogical reform, the need for discrimination can conflict with curriculum alignment and classroom feasibility. Previous research on washback has shown that the NMET strongly influences teaching and learning, but not always in the ways intended by test designers or policymakers (Qi, 2005, 2007). Teachers may support curriculum reform in principle while continuing to prioritize examination preparation because of institutional accountability, parental expectations, student resistance, and the broader examination culture (Yan, 2015). Consequently, careful empirical scrutiny of NMET materials is needed to understand how the test has developed and whether its demands correspond to curriculum expectations.

Among the components of the NMET, reading comprehension occupies a particularly important position. Reading passages and associated multiple-choice items usually account for a substantial proportion of the total English score, and performance on this section is likely to be affected not only by readers’ abilities and test-taking strategies but also by the linguistic properties of the texts themselves. In models of reading comprehension, the interaction among reader, text, activity, and sociocultural context is central (Snow, 2002). For second language readers, textual features such as vocabulary load, syntactic structure, cohesion, genre, and organization can place considerable processing demands on comprehension. In a high-stakes context, the complexity of reading passages therefore has implications for construct representation, fairness, curriculum alignment, and classroom preparation.

Text complexity is especially relevant in the Chinese senior secondary context because national curriculum standards and examination outlines specify expectations for English learning, including vocabulary knowledge and reading ability. The General High School English Curriculum Standards identify target vocabulary ranges and emphasize the ability to understand and use words in context, while the NMET examination outline provides guidance for test preparation (Ministry of Education, 2003, 2017; National Education Examinations Authority, 2019a). If the linguistic demands of examination passages substantially exceed these expectations, students may need learning resources beyond regular classroom instruction. Such a mismatch could intensify inequalities associated with access to tutoring, extensive reading materials, and other forms of educational support. Conversely, if the texts remain below the intended curriculum level, the exam may fail to promote higher-level reading development. Thus, tracking the development of text complexity in the NMET can provide evidence for evaluating the relationship between assessment practice and curriculum policy.

Previous discussions of the NMET have focused mainly on test design, washback, reform, and stakeholders’ perceptions (Cheng, 2008; Cheng & Qi, 2006; Qi, 2005, 2007; Yan, 2015). These studies have demonstrated the social and pedagogical significance of the examination and have highlighted the difficulties of using high-stakes tests as agents of educational change. However, less attention has been given to the longitudinal linguistic characteristics of the reading passages themselves. In particular, there is a need for systematic corpus-based research that examines whether the texts used in the NMET have become more complex over time, and if so, at which linguistic levels. Such evidence is important because changes in reading passage difficulty may occur gradually and may not be transparent to teachers, students, or policymakers without quantitative analysis.

Recent advances in corpus linguistics and natural language processing make it possible to examine text complexity more comprehensively than traditional readability formulas allow. Earlier readability measures often relied on surface-level indicators such as sentence length and word length, whereas contemporary approaches can capture multiple dimensions of lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level complexity. Lexical complexity may include vocabulary frequency, range, academic word use, lexical diversity, and lexical density. Syntactic complexity may involve sentence length, subordination, coordination, clausal elaboration, and phrasal complexity. Discourse-level complexity may be reflected in cohesion, including lexical overlap, semantic overlap, connectives, and givenness. Together, these dimensions offer a richer account of the linguistic demands imposed by reading passages.

The present study therefore investigates the development of text complexity in NMET reading comprehension passages over a 25-year period, from 1996 to 2020. Using a corpus of 206 passages from national versions of the NMET, the study applies a set of automated analysis tools to measure lexical sophistication, lexical diversity, lexical density, syntactic complexity, syntactic sophistication, and cohesion. It then compares these measures across years and five-year intervals to identify longitudinal patterns. In addition, the findings are interpreted in relation to national curriculum standards and examination guidelines in order to consider whether the linguistic demands of the reading passages are aligned with official expectations for senior secondary English learning.

Specifically, the study addresses three research questions: (1) How has lexical-level text complexity in NMET reading comprehension passages changed from 1996 to 2020? (2) How has syntactic-level text complexity changed over the same period? (3) How has discourse-level text complexity, particularly cohesion, changed over time? By answering these questions, the study aims to contribute to research on high-stakes language testing, corpus-based text analysis, and EFL reading assessment in China. It also seeks to provide practical implications for test designers, curriculum policymakers, and classroom teachers who must respond to the evolving demands of the NMET.
