intros.text:
The National Matriculation English Test (NMET), as the English component of the Gaokao, is one of the most consequential English language tests in China. Performance on this high-stakes examination plays a direct role in university admission and, consequently, in students’ future educational opportunities. English testing in China has therefore attracted sustained attention not only because of the large number of test takers involved, but also because of the powerful influence such tests exert on secondary English teaching and learning (Cheng, 2008; Cheng & Qi, 2006). As a national selection mechanism, the NMET is expected to distinguish among candidates with different levels of English proficiency; as an educational instrument, it is also expected to reflect curriculum goals and to promote desirable washback in classroom practice. These dual roles make the linguistic demands of the test an important issue for test developers, teachers, learners, and policymakers.

Previous research on the NMET and related high-stakes English examinations in China has shown that tests can strongly shape pedagogical priorities. Qi (2005, 2007), for example, argued that the NMET’s selection function and its intended reform-oriented washback may conflict with each other, often leading teachers and students to focus narrowly on examination preparation rather than broader language development. Yan (2015) similarly reported that secondary English teachers’ implementation of curriculum reform was constrained by the examination culture surrounding the Gaokao, with teachers frequently feeling that substantial classroom change would be difficult unless the examination itself changed. These findings suggest that the content and design of the NMET are not merely technical testing issues; rather, they are closely connected to what is taught, how it is taught, and what forms of English competence are valued in school contexts.

Reading comprehension is a central component of English language proficiency assessment, and in the NMET it constitutes a substantial proportion of the total score. Reading test performance is influenced by the interaction among readers, tasks, and texts. Among these factors, the linguistic features of texts are especially important because they determine, to a considerable extent, the lexical, syntactic, and discourse processing demands placed on test takers. Text complexity refers to measurable properties of a text that may affect comprehension, including vocabulary load, lexical sophistication, lexical diversity, sentence and grammatical complexity, and cohesion. Unlike test difficulty, which is partly dependent on readers’ performance and task demands, text complexity can be examined independently through linguistic analysis. For high-stakes reading assessment, understanding text complexity is essential because uncontrolled or unexamined changes in passage difficulty may affect score interpretation, fairness, curriculum alignment, and preparation practices.

The development of corpus-based and computational tools has made it possible to analyze text complexity more comprehensively than traditional readability formulas allow. Early readability measures typically relied on surface features such as sentence length and word length, but more recent approaches incorporate a wider range of lexical, syntactic, and discourse-level indices. Tools such as the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Lexical Sophistication (TAALES), the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Lexical Diversity (TAALED), the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Syntactic Sophistication and Complexity (TAASSC), and the Tool for the Automatic Analysis of Cohesion (TAACO) enable researchers to examine large numbers of texts across multiple linguistic dimensions. Such tools are particularly useful for longitudinal studies of examination passages, where subtle changes across years may not be visible through manual inspection or simple readability scores.

Despite the importance of the NMET, relatively little is known about how the linguistic complexity of its reading comprehension passages has developed over an extended period of time. Existing studies of English language testing in China have provided valuable accounts of the history, functions, washback, and policy implications of the NMET (Cheng, 2008; Cheng & Qi, 2006; Qi, 2005, 2007). Comparative discussions of the Gaokao have also highlighted its role in educational selection and equity (Farley & Yang, 2019). However, less attention has been given to the textual characteristics of the reading passages themselves, particularly from a longitudinal, corpus-based perspective. If the passages have become increasingly complex over time, such a development may indicate changing expectations for high school graduates’ English reading ability. It may also reveal potential mismatches between the actual demands of the examination and the vocabulary and reading requirements specified in national curriculum standards and examination guidelines.

This issue is especially important in the Chinese secondary education context because curriculum standards and national examination outlines provide official guidance on the expected level of English proficiency. The National Education Examinations Authority (2019a) publishes examination outlines for the Gaokao, and the national English curriculum standards specify vocabulary and reading requirements for high school learners. If the lexical or syntactic demands of NMET reading passages substantially exceed these stated expectations, students may need to rely on extensive extracurricular resources to meet examination demands. Such a situation could intensify inequalities among students with different levels of access to supplementary instruction, authentic materials, and test preparation resources. Conversely, if the passages remain stable or align closely with curriculum requirements, this would support the validity and fairness of the examination as a measure of expected high school English achievement.

To address this gap, the present study investigates the development of text complexity in the reading comprehension passages of the national version of the NMET over a 25-year period, from 1996 to 2020. Specifically, it analyzes 206 reading passages at lexical, syntactic, and discourse levels using a set of natural language processing tools. Lexical complexity is examined through frequency bands, lexical sophistication, lexical diversity, and lexical density; syntactic complexity is examined through traditional and fine-grained syntactic indices; and discourse-level complexity is examined through cohesion measures. The study further compares the observed changes with curriculum standards and examination guidelines in order to consider whether the linguistic demands of the NMET reading passages are consistent with official expectations for high school English learners.

By providing a longitudinal, multi-dimensional account of NMET reading passage complexity, this study contributes to research on high-stakes language testing, corpus-based text analysis, and EFL reading assessment in China. The findings may help test designers monitor the linguistic demands of reading passages more systematically, assist teachers in understanding the changing nature of examination reading texts, and inform discussions of alignment between curriculum policy and assessment practice.

intros.text: In the domain of second language testing, testing language proficiency has always been a major issue regardless of any specific set of instructional materials, examinees educational and linguistic background.  Testing specialists have always tested and tried various approaches to invent new procedures for testing language proficiency because they are not satisfied with the existing instruments testing language proficiency.  Spolsky (1973) stated that: “In searching for a test of overall proficiency, then, we must try to find some way to get beyond the limitations of testing a sample of surface features and seek rather tap underplaying linguistics competence” (p. 175). To this end, Spolsky has offered two options: The first one is an interview which has been used continuously as a valid measure of language proficiency. But difficulties in administration and establishing the reliability of scoring limited its implementation. The second one is the reduced redundancy principle (RRP). The second option has been well-received by many professionals who have been trying to operationalize this principle through a variety of testing procedures: dictation, the noise test, partial dictation, cloze test, cloze elide, multiplechoice cloze, rational dictation cloze, and the C-Test (Klein-Braley, 1997).  Naturally, languages are redundant. Based on RRP native speakers of languages can fix the missing parts of broken sentences, or they have the capability of understanding the meaning of a sentence without having whole information.  This characteristic of the human verbal communication system decreases the possibility of making errors and permits communication where there is some interference in the communication channel (Spolsky, 1973). According to Hughes (2003), native speakers of a language can cope well when this redundancy is reduced. For example, they can understand what someone is saying although there are noises in the environment that prevent them from hearing every sound that is made. Likewise, they can infer the meaning of the text of a newspaper that has been left outside in the rain, causing the print to become blurred. Because non-native speakers generally find it more difficult to cope with reduced redundancy, the deliberate reduction of redundancy has been used as a means of estimating foreign language ability. Learners' overall ability has been estimated by measuring how well they can restore a reduced text to its original form  Tests that are constructed under the basis of the reduced redundancy principle (RRP) use authentic materials. Authentic materials are those which are not written for learning purposes. These authentic materials are damaged in some way and then examinees are asked to restore the materials.  On the other hand, Klien-Barley (1985) believes that no language test is authentic, if what we mean by authentic is normal language in everyday use: normal language is not produced to be assessed. Therefore, the question of test authenticity cannot be solved directly.  A large number of test developers and researchers (Baghaei, 2008a, 2008b, 2010, 2011, 2014; Eckes, 2006, 2011; Eckes & Baghaei, 2015; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006; Forthmann, Grotjahn, Doebler, & Baghaei, 2020; Raatz, 1984, 1985) in the field of language testing confirmed that C-Test is a valid, reliable, economical, and easy to construct, but in the Afghan context of education, the utility, application, validity, and reliability of C-Test have not been researched so far.  The purpose of this study is to build validity evidence for the C-Test as a measure of general language proficiency among Afghan students of English  English language proficiency tests used in Afghanistan are made with several components like listening, speaking, reading, writing, vocabulary, and grammar; therefore, they are time-consuming both to the examinees and the examiners. Examinees should spend 120 or 150 minutes doing all the items. And finally, it is difficult to score because it consists of a large number of questions. intros.text:
Language testing occupies a central position in second and foreign language education, serving purposes as varied as placement, selection, diagnosis, and the measurement of overall proficiency. Yet the design and administration of comprehensive proficiency tests that tap all four language skills is a demanding, time-consuming, and often costly enterprise. Established international examinations such as the TOEFL and IELTS are widely accepted as valid and reliable measures of general English language proficiency, but their expense, the logistical resources they require, and the length of time needed to administer and score them place them beyond the reach of many educational contexts. This is particularly the case in developing and conflict-affected settings, where institutional resources are limited and where large numbers of language teachers have received little or no training in the principles of test development (Coniam, 2009). In such settings, there is a clear and practical need for an economical, quick, and psychometrically sound instrument capable of yielding an accurate estimate of a learner's overall language ability.

The C-Test, developed by Raatz and Klein-Braley (1982), is one instrument that appears to meet this need. The C-Test belongs to the family of reduced redundancy tests, which rest on the assumption articulated by Spolsky (1968) that knowing a language entails the ability to function even when the redundancy of natural language is reduced through distortion or the masking of portions of text. In a C-Test, several short authentic passages are presented in which the second half of every second word is deleted; test-takers are required to restore the mutilated words by drawing on their knowledge of the language and their sensitivity to contextual constraints. Because a C-Test typically comprises four to six passages with twenty to twenty-five deletions each, it samples a wide range of vocabulary, structure, and text types, thereby reducing the likelihood that a particular examinee will be advantaged by prior familiarity with the content of a single passage, as can occur in a traditional cloze test (Baghaei & Grotjahn, 2014a). Well-constructed C-Tests are also highly reliable, with reliability coefficients frequently exceeding 0.85 for shorter versions and 0.90 for longer ones. These qualities have led numerous researchers to advocate and use the C-Test as a general indicator of foreign language competence (Baghaei, 2011; Klein-Braley, 1997).

Despite this accumulated evidence, the question of what the C-Test actually measures has long been debated. Because the C-Test does not engage learners in oral or aural performance, some scholars have questioned whether its scores can legitimately be interpreted as indices of general language proficiency rather than as more restricted measures of reading and writing ability (Alderson, 2002; Shohamy, 1982). Concurrent validation studies have produced mixed findings in this regard. A number of investigations report only modest correlations between the C-Test and measures of listening and speaking, with speaking generally correlating more weakly than listening (Chapelle & Abraham, 1990; Dörnyei & Katona, 1992; Grotjahn, 1992), whereas other studies report substantially higher correlations (Coleman, 1994; Arras, Eckes, & Grotjahn, 2002). Using Rasch measurement modelling and confirmatory factor analysis, Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) provided strong evidence that a German C-Test constituted a highly reliable, unidimensional instrument that measured the same general dimension as the reading, listening, writing, and speaking sections of the TestDaF, while also demonstrating that proficiency could be further divided into more specific components. Subsequent work employing more advanced psychometric techniques has continued to interrogate the dimensionality, local dependence, and construct validity of the C-Test (Eckes & Baghaei, 2015; Forthmann et al., 2019; Grotjahn, 2016), and the instrument has even been proposed as an integrative measure of crystallized intelligence (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015). Earlier factorial studies likewise supported the convergent and factorial validity of the C-Test as a marker of the general factor in a battery of language measures (Raatz, 1984, 1985). Taken together, this body of research indicates that, while the debate has not been fully resolved, there is considerable support for treating the C-Test as a valid and economical measure of general language proficiency.

An important limitation of this literature, however, is that the validation of the C-Test has been carried out predominantly in European, North American, and East Asian contexts, and to a lesser extent among learners in the Middle East. The extent to which findings on the reliability and validity of the C-Test generalise to other learner populations remains an empirical question, since validity is not a fixed property of a test but must be established for each new use and each new group of examinees. To date, no published study has examined the psychometric qualities of the C-Test among Afghan learners of English as a foreign language. This is a notable gap given the acute practical need in Afghanistan for economical assessment tools and the limited access of many Afghan teachers to training in test construction. Establishing whether the C-Test functions as a reliable and valid measure of general English proficiency in this context could therefore have direct pedagogical value, offering teachers and institutions an accessible instrument for placement and proficiency assessment.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the validity and reliability of the C-Test among Afghan EFL learners. One hundred advanced English majors were administered a C-Test composed of four authentic passages together with a Preliminary English Test (PET) proficiency measure covering listening, reading, and writing. Drawing on descriptive statistics, reliability estimation, correlational analysis, and factor analysis, the study asks whether the C-Test is a reliable instrument in this population, whether it correlates with independent measures of listening, reading, writing, and a composite proficiency score, and whether it loads on the same underlying dimension as these criterion measures. In doing so, the study seeks to determine whether the C-Test can serve as an economical, quick, and dependable alternative to more resource-intensive proficiency tests for Afghan students of English as a foreign language, thereby extending the cross-linguistic and cross-cultural evidence base for the C-Test as a measure of general language ability.

intros.text:
Language testing occupies a central position in foreign language education, since the decisions made about learners' placement, progress, and achievement depend heavily on the quality of the instruments used to measure their abilities. As the demand for efficient, dependable, and economical assessment of general language proficiency has grown, so too has the interest of researchers in developing test formats that yield accurate information about learners while placing minimal demands on time and resources. Among the various approaches proposed for this purpose, tests grounded in the reduced redundancy principle have attracted sustained attention. The underlying assumption is that knowledge of a language necessarily entails the ability to function even when redundancy is reduced, so that learners with greater command of the language can more successfully exploit the redundancy of natural discourse to reconstruct a mutilated text (Spolsky, 1968; Klein-Braley, 1997).

The C-Test, first proposed by Raatz and Klein-Braley in the early 1980s, is the most prominent representative of this family of reduced redundancy tests. A C-Test typically consists of several short authentic passages in which the second half of every second word is deleted, and test-takers are asked to restore the missing parts by drawing on all they know of and about the language. Because a single C-Test comprises a number of independent texts rather than one passage, it samples a wide range of linguistic knowledge and is less vulnerable to the influence of a test-taker's familiarity with a particular topic than a conventional cloze test (Baghaei & Grotjahn, 2014a; Baghaei & Grotjahn, 2014b). Over the past four decades, numerous scholars have advocated the use of the C-Test as an economical, realistic, quick, accurate, and reliable indicator of overall competence in a second or foreign language (see the extensive body of work reviewed in Baghaei, 2011). The reported reliability coefficients of well-constructed C-Tests are impressive, frequently exceeding 0.85 for shorter versions and 0.90 for longer ones, which makes the format especially attractive for practical assessment purposes.

The question of what the C-Test actually measures, however, has generated considerable debate. The strongest claim made on its behalf is that it is a measure of general language proficiency, so that examinees' scores can be interpreted as reflecting their overall foreign language ability. A number of construct validation studies employing Rasch modeling and confirmatory factor analysis have supported this claim, demonstrating that C-Tests tend to be highly reliable and unidimensional instruments that tap the same general dimension as tests of reading, listening, writing, and speaking (Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006; Grotjahn, 2016; Eckes & Baghaei, 2015). Baghaei's (2008a, 2008b, 2010, 2011) programme of work likewise provides evidence, through Rasch analysis, for the coherence of the C-Test construct, while investigations into the factorial validity of the format have consistently reported results favourable to the general proficiency interpretation (Raatz, 1984; Raatz, 1985). More recently, the C-Test has even been proposed as an integrative measure of crystallized intelligence, extending its potential range of application well beyond conventional language assessment (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015).

Nevertheless, this interpretation has not gone unchallenged. Because the C-Test does not directly engage learners in oral or aural skills, some scholars have argued that its scores are better understood as measures of reading and writing ability than of listening or speaking proficiency (Alderson, 2002; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006). The correlational evidence bearing on this issue is decidedly mixed: studies have reported coefficients ranging from as low as 0.24 between a French C-Test and self-ratings of speaking to as high as 0.76 for listening comprehension, with correlations for speaking generally lower than those for listening. These inconsistent findings indicate that the extent to which the C-Test can legitimately be interpreted as a general proficiency measure remains an open empirical question, one whose answer may well depend on the particular population, language, and version of the test involved.

Despite the wealth of validation research accumulated in European, and to a lesser degree Middle Eastern, contexts, the great majority of these studies have been conducted with German, English, and Iranian learners. To date, there appears to be no published research examining the psychometric qualities of the C-Test among Afghan students of English as a foreign language. This is a notable gap given the distinctive circumstances of English language education in Afghanistan, where a large number of teachers have neither received training in test development nor acquired the expertise needed to construct sound assessment instruments (cf. Coniam, 2009). In such a setting, a test that is both easy to construct and economical to administer, yet capable of delivering reliable information about learners' general proficiency, would be of considerable practical value. Whether the encouraging validity evidence obtained elsewhere generalises to Afghan EFL learners cannot simply be assumed and needs to be established empirically.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the reliability and validity of the C-Test as a measure of overall English language proficiency among Afghan EFL learners. To this end, one hundred advanced English majors were administered a C-Test composed of four authentic passages, three drawn from written discourse and one from spoken discourse, alongside a criterion measure consisting of the listening, reading, and writing sections of a standard English proficiency test. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha reliability estimates, Pearson correlation coefficients, and factor analysis were employed to examine the concurrent and construct validity of the C-Test against these criterion measures. It is anticipated that establishing the C-Test as a reliable and valid indicator of general proficiency in this context would offer practical benefits for teachers, test administrators, and students in Afghanistan, providing an efficient alternative to lengthier and costlier proficiency tests for placement and general assessment purposes, and would extend the international body of C-Test validation research to a hitherto unexamined population.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics, the development and validation of effective language assessment tools are paramount for ensuring that educational outcomes are measured accurately and fairly. For educators and researchers, the challenge lies in creating instruments that are not only psychometrically sound—possessing high reliability and validity—but also practical in terms of administration and scoring. This is particularly critical in contexts where resources are limited or where teachers may lack specialized training in test development. As Coniam (2009) highlights, many EFL teachers produce tests that do not provide usable or accurate information about student abilities due to a lack of expertise in test specification and item analysis. Consequently, there is a pressing need for assessment tools that balance technical rigor with ease of construction and implementation.

One such tool that has gained prominence in second language research is the C-Test. A member of the 'reduced redundancy' family of tests, the C-Test is based on the theoretical premise that language is inherently redundant. According to Spolsky (1968), knowing a language involves the ability to function even when the communication channel is distorted or when parts of the message are missing. Reduced redundancy tests, such as the C-Test and cloze tests, operationalize this principle by deleting segments of a text and requiring the test-taker to restore the original meaning using their overall linguistic competence. As the learner's control of the language increases, they become more adept at utilizing the remaining redundancy to reconstruct the text, thus achieving higher scores.

Compared to traditional cloze tests, the C-Test offers several distinct advantages. It typically employs multiple short passages, which reduces the likelihood that a student's score will be artificially inflated by prior familiarity with a single text. Furthermore, the C-Test is widely regarded as an economical, quick, and reliable measure of language skills. Research has consistently advocated for its use as a general indicator of competence in various second language contexts (Baghaei, 2011). Its psychometric properties have been extensively studied; for instance, Eckes and Baghaei (2015) utilized testlet response theory to examine local dependence, confirming that the C-Test is a robust instrument for placement and screening. Similarly, Klein-Braley (1997) found that the C-Test emerged as the most economical and reliable procedure among several reduced redundancy tests, exhibiting high empirical validity.

Despite these strengths, the exact construct measured by the C-Test remains a subject of academic debate. Specifically, there is ongoing discussion regarding whether the C-Test truly measures general language proficiency—which encompasses listening, speaking, reading, and writing—or if it is primarily a measure of reading and writing skills. Some scholars argue that because the C-Test does not directly elicit oral or aural production, it cannot fully capture a learner's communicative competence. However, other research suggests a stronger link. Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) provided evidence through confirmatory factor analysis that the C-Test measures the same general dimension as integrated proficiency tests that include listening and speaking. Furthermore, some researchers have expanded the conceptual scope of the C-Test, suggesting it may serve as an integrative measure of crystallized intelligence, as it taps into the linguistic component of general cognitive ability (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015).

While the C-Test has been validated in various European and Asian contexts, there is a dearth of empirical research concerning its validity and reliability among Afghan EFL learners. In Afghanistan, the English language teaching environment faces unique challenges. Many language trainers and instructors lack formal training in the principles of assessment and the technical skills required to develop standardized tests. In such a setting, a test that is easy to construct yet psychometrically valid could significantly improve the quality of placement and proficiency testing in classrooms. Given that the C-Test requires only authentic texts and a simple deletion rule to be implemented, it represents a viable solution for the Afghan educational context.

Therefore, the primary objective of the present study is to validate the C-Test as a measure of overall English language proficiency among Afghan EFL students. To achieve this, the study employs a concurrent validation design, correlating C-Test scores with a comprehensive proficiency test that assesses listening, reading, and writing. By examining the correlations between the C-Test and these specific skill-based measures, the study seeks to determine if the C-Test can serve as a reliable proxy for general language ability. Additionally, the study utilizes factor analysis to explore the unidimensionality of the construct, testing whether the C-Test and the various components of the proficiency test load onto a single underlying factor of language competence.

By providing empirical evidence of the C-Test's validity within the Afghan EFL population, this research aims to offer practical implications for test administrators and teachers. If validated, the C-Test could provide a fast, economical, and accurate alternative to more cumbersome and expensive standardized tests, empowering local educators to implement more scientific assessment practices in their institutions.

intros.text:
Language testing and assessment represent pivotal components of applied linguistics and English language education, maintaining an inextricable relationship with broader social changes and technological progress (Shively, 2004). In the pursuit of measuring a learner's linguistic competence, the development of instruments that are both psychometrically sound and practically viable remains a primary concern for educators and researchers alike. Within this field, the concept of reduced redundancy has proven to be a particularly fruitful approach. The theoretical underpinning of this approach suggests that knowing a language involves the ability to function even when the communicative signal is distorted or incomplete, as the inherent redundancy of natural language allows a proficient user to restore missing information (Spolsky, 1968). Consequently, tests based on this principle assume that as a learner's control of a language increases, they can more effectively utilize the remaining linguistic cues to reconstruct the original meaning.

Among the various types of reduced redundancy tests—including classical cloze, cloze-elide, and multiple-choice cloze—the C-Test has emerged as a highly regarded instrument (Klein-Braley, 1997). The C-Test typically involves several short passages where the second half of every second word is deleted, requiring the test-taker to restore the mutilated segments. Because it relies on authentic materials and requires the integration of various linguistic resources, it is categorized as a pragmatic language test. Over the past few decades, a wide array of scholars has advocated for the C-Test as an economic, accurate, and reliable indicator of general language proficiency in second language acquisition (see Chapelle, 1994; Coleman, 1994a, 1994b; Singleton, 1999). Its popularity stems largely from its efficiency; unlike comprehensive batteries that require extensive time and resources, the C-Test provides a quick yet robust measure of overall competence.

Recent research has further expanded the utility of the C-Test beyond mere proficiency screening. For instance, Baghaei and Tabatabaee (2015) have argued that the C-Test can serve as an integrative measure of crystallized intelligence, suggesting that the construct underlying the test closely matches the abilities associated with the language component of general intelligence. Furthermore, advanced psychometric modeling has been used to refine the instrument. Eckes and Baghaei (2015) employed Testlet Response Theory to examine local dependence in C-Tests, finding that while reliability might be slightly overestimated if dependence is ignored, the instrument remains highly stable. Similarly, Grotjahn (2016) and Forthmann et al. (2019) have explored the validity of C-Tests in measuring academic and everyday language proficiency, with the latter comparing different Item Response Theory models to improve the diagnostic accuracy of speeded C-Tests. From a construct perspective, Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) provided evidence that the C-Test is a unidimensional instrument that measures the same general dimension as traditional multi-skill tests encompassing reading, listening, writing, and speaking.

Despite these strengths, the C-Test is not without its critics. A recurring point of contention is whether a text-based completion task can truly represent general language proficiency, given that it does not directly elicit oral or aural production. Some scholars argue that C-Test scores may be more accurate reflections of reading and writing skills than of listening or speaking abilities (Shohamy, 1982). Indeed, several concurrent validation studies have reported inconsistent correlation coefficients between C-Tests and oral-aural measures, with low correlations appearing more frequently than high ones (Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006). This ongoing debate suggests that while the C-Test is widely accepted, its validity may vary depending on the target population and the specific linguistic context being measured.

In the context of Afghanistan, the need for reliable and accessible assessment tools is particularly acute. Many English language teachers in Afghanistan lack formal training in test development and the expertise required to construct high-quality, validated instruments (Coniam, 2009). This often results in the use of teacher-made tests that may not provide accurate information about students' actual abilities. Given that the C-Test is relatively easy and economical to construct, it presents a promising alternative for placement and proficiency testing in the Afghan EFL environment. However, to date, there has been a dearth of empirical research specifically validating the C-Test among Afghan learners of English. While the instrument has been validated in various European and Asian contexts, it remains unclear whether the same psychometric properties—specifically reliability and concurrent validity—hold true for students in the Afghan educational system.

Therefore, the present study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the validity and reliability of the C-Test as a measure of overall English language proficiency among Afghan EFL learners. Specifically, the research aims to determine the extent to which C-Test scores correlate with a criterion measure consisting of listening, reading, and writing components. By analyzing these correlations and employing factor analysis to examine the unidimensionality of the construct, the study intends to provide empirical evidence regarding the suitability of the C-Test for the Afghan context. It is hypothesized that the C-Test will demonstrate high reliability and a significant positive correlation with general proficiency scores, thereby justifying its use as a practical assessment tool in Afghan classrooms.

The findings of this research may offer important implications for test administrators and practitioners in Afghanistan, potentially providing a validated, low-cost alternative to time-consuming proficiency exams. The remainder of the article is organized as follows: the second section provides a detailed review of the literature on reduced redundancy testing and the C-Test; the third section describes the participants and the methodology used for validation; the fourth section presents the results of the reliability and correlational analyses; and the final section discusses the findings and their pedagogical implications.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics and language testing, the development of valid and reliable instruments for assessing foreign language proficiency remains a paramount concern for educators, researchers, and policymakers. Among the various methodologies employed to measure language competence, reduced redundancy tests have garnered significant attention due to their efficiency and psychometric properties. Specifically, the C-Test, a derivative of the traditional cloze procedure, has been widely advocated as a pragmatic, economic, and accurate measure of general language proficiency. Originally proposed by Raatz and Klein-Braley (1982), the C-Test is grounded in the principle that language knowledge involves the ability to function effectively even when redundancy is reduced. As Spolsky (1979) argued, true knowledge of a language necessitates the ability to process sequences of linguistic elements under conditions of reduced redundancy, a concept that forms the theoretical backbone of the C-Test. Unlike the standard cloze test, which typically deletes every nth word, the C-Test deletes the second half of every second word, requiring test-takers to reconstruct the missing segments based on contextual clues and linguistic competence.

The theoretical underpinnings of the C-Test suggest that it measures a general language proficiency factor rather than specific isolated skills. Oller (1979) posited that pragmatic language tests require learners to process sequences of elements that conform to normal contextual constraints, relating linguistic elements to extralinguistic contexts through pragmatic mappings. This aligns with the design of the C-Test, which utilizes authentic materials and requires learners to infer meaning from both immediate and long-range contextual constraints. Consequently, C-Tests are often interpreted as measures of overall foreign language skill, encompassing reading, writing, listening, and speaking abilities, despite the fact that the test format itself is primarily written. However, this interpretation has been subject to debate. While some scholars argue that C-Tests are valid indicators of general proficiency, others contend that they may primarily measure reading and writing skills, with weaker correlations to oral-aural abilities. For instance, Alderson (2002) noted that the C-Test might not be an appropriate measure of general language proficiency because it does not directly tap into oral-aural abilities. Empirical studies have yielded mixed results regarding this issue; while some research reports low correlations between C-Test scores and listening or speaking tests (e.g., Chapelle & Abraham, 1990; Dörnyei & Katona, 1992), others have found moderate to high correlations (e.g., Coleman, 1994; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006).

Despite the extensive validation of the C-Test in various linguistic contexts, particularly in European settings where it is used for German as a Foreign Language (DaF), there is a paucity of research examining its validity among non-Western populations, specifically in the context of Afghan English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. The majority of validation studies have been conducted in contexts with different educational backgrounds, cultural norms, and linguistic interference patterns. For example, Baghaei (2011) utilized Rasch modeling to validate the C-Test construct, while Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) employed confirmatory factor analysis to demonstrate the unidimensionality of the test in a German context. Similarly, Klein-Braley (1997) compared the C-Test with other reduced redundancy tests, concluding that it was the most economical and reliable procedure. More recent studies have explored the C-Test as a measure of crystallized intelligence (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015) and have investigated its psychometric properties using Item Response Theory (Eckes & Baghaei, 2015; Forthmann et al., 2019). However, these studies predominantly focus on European or Asian contexts, leaving a significant gap in the literature regarding the applicability of the C-Test in the Afghan educational landscape.

In Afghanistan, the assessment of English language proficiency is critical given the country's increasing engagement with international education and employment sectors. However, the development of high-quality language tests poses a significant challenge. Many teachers in Afghanistan lack the necessary training and expertise in test development, often relying on ad-hoc assessments that may not be psychometrically sound. Coniam (2009) highlighted the importance of training teachers in test development principles to ensure that classroom tests accurately report test-takers' abilities. In this context, the C-Test offers a promising alternative due to its ease of construction, cost-effectiveness, and high reliability. The construction of a C-Test follows specific rules, such as leaving the first and last sentences intact and deleting the second half of every second word, which makes it relatively straightforward for educators to implement compared to more complex proficiency tests like the TOEFL or IELTS. Furthermore, the C-Test's reliance on reduced redundancy makes it a robust tool for measuring the underlying linguistic competence of learners, even in resource-constrained environments.

Given the lack of empirical evidence regarding the validity of the C-Test among Afghan EFL learners, this study aims to address this gap in the literature. Specifically, the research seeks to validate the C-Test as a measure of overall language proficiency for advanced Afghan students of English as a foreign language. To achieve this, the study administered a C-Test composed of four different texts alongside a comprehensive language proficiency test that included listening, reading, and writing components. By analyzing the correlations between the C-Test scores and the criterion measures, as well as examining the reliability and factor structure of the test, this study provides empirical evidence on the psychometric properties of the C-Test in the Afghan context. The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the broader understanding of reduced redundancy testing and offer practical implications for language testing and assessment in Afghanistan, where the need for valid, reliable, and economical assessment tools is acute. Ultimately, establishing the validity of the C-Test in this context could empower local educators to adopt a more standardized and scientifically grounded approach to language assessment, thereby improving the quality of English language education in the region.

intros.text:
The assessment of foreign language proficiency remains a central concern in the field of applied linguistics and language education, particularly in contexts where English is taught as a foreign language (EFL). Accurate measurement of language ability is vital for educational placement, curriculum design, and the evaluation of learner progress. Among the various instruments available for this purpose, reduced redundancy tests have gained significant attention due to their efficiency and psychometric properties. Specifically, the C-Test, a variant of the cloze procedure, has been widely advocated as a pragmatic, economic, and reliable measure of general language proficiency. However, the validity of the C-Test as a comprehensive indicator of overall language ability, encompassing both receptive and productive skills, continues to be a subject of debate within the scholarly community.

The theoretical underpinnings of the C-Test are rooted in the concept of redundancy in language. Spolsky (1968) argued that knowledge of a language necessitates the ability to function even when redundancy is reduced, a principle that forms the basis of the C-Test design. Unlike the traditional cloze test, where every nth word is deleted, the C-Test deletes the second half of every second word in a text, requiring test-takers to reconstruct the missing segments based on contextual clues and linguistic competence. This procedure assumes that as a learner's control of the language increases, they will be able to make more successful use of the redundancy provided by natural language, thereby achieving higher scores (Klein-Braley, 1985). Consequently, the C-Test has been positioned as a unidimensional measure of general proficiency, capable of capturing the underlying construct of language ability across different skills.

Empirical research has extensively investigated the psychometric qualities of the C-Test. Early studies by Raatz and Klein-Braley (1982) established the C-Test as an economic, realistic, quick, accurate, and reliable measure of language skills. Subsequent research has supported these findings, with numerous studies advocating for the C-Test as a general indicator of competence in second language acquisition (e.g., Chapelle, 1994; Coleman, 1994a, 1994b; Djiwandono, 1998; Eckes & Grotjahn, 2006; Singleton, 1990, 1999). For instance, Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) utilized Rasch measurement modelling and confirmatory factor analysis to demonstrate that the C-Test is a highly reliable, unidimensional instrument that measures the same general dimension as comprehensive proficiency tests covering reading, listening, writing, and speaking. Similarly, Baghaei (2011) employed Rasch modeling to validate the construct of the C-Test, further reinforcing its status as a robust assessment tool.

Despite the substantial body of evidence supporting the C-Test, questions regarding its construct validity persist, particularly concerning its ability to measure oral and aural skills. Alderson (2002) has argued that the C-Test is not an appropriate measure of general language proficiency because it does not directly tap into oral-aural abilities. This critique is supported by concurrent validation studies that have reported mixed results. For example, Chapelle and Abraham (1990) reported a correlation coefficient of 0.47 between an English C-Test and the listening section of the Iowa State English Placement Test, while Dörnyei and Katona (1992) found correlations of 0.33 and 0.51 between an English C-Test and listening components of other proficiency tests. Conversely, other studies have found stronger relationships. Coleman (1994) reported a correlation coefficient of 0.76 for listening comprehension, and Arras, Eckes, and Grotjahn (2002) found a correlation of 0.64 between a German C-Test and TestDaF speaking and listening subtests. These contradictory findings suggest that the relationship between C-Test performance and specific language skills may vary depending on the context, the language being tested, and the specific instruments used for validation.

Furthermore, the application of the C-Test in diverse EFL contexts remains underexplored. While the instrument has been validated in European and Asian contexts, there is a paucity of research examining its validity among Afghan EFL learners. The unique linguistic and educational landscape of Afghanistan, characterized by specific challenges in test development and administration, necessitates local validation studies. Coniam (2009) highlighted that the quality of teacher-produced tests in EFL contexts often varies, and that training in test development principles is crucial for ensuring accurate reporting of test-takers' abilities. In Afghanistan, where many language teachers lack expertise in test construction, the C-Test offers a promising alternative due to its ease of construction and administration (Baghaei & Tabatabaee, 2015). However, without empirical validation, the assumption that the C-Test functions equivalently in this specific context remains unverified.

The present study aims to address this gap by validating the C-Test among Afghan students of English as a foreign language. Specifically, this research seeks to examine the reliability and concurrent validity of the C-Test by correlating its scores with a comprehensive language proficiency test that includes listening, reading, and writing components. By employing a sample of 100 advanced English majors, this study utilizes multiple statistical analyses, including Pearson correlation and factor analysis, to determine whether the C-Test serves as a valid and reliable measure of general language proficiency in this specific population. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to the broader understanding of the C-Test's applicability in diverse EFL settings and provide practical implications for test administrators and educators in Afghanistan. Ultimately, this research seeks to establish whether the C-Test can be effectively utilized as a placement and proficiency tool, offering an economical and efficient alternative to more time-consuming traditional assessments.

intros.text:
Assessment is a central concern in English as a foreign language (EFL) education because decisions about placement, achievement, certification, and instructional planning depend on the quality of the instruments used to measure learners’ abilities. A useful language test should provide dependable information about test takers’ proficiency while remaining practical for teachers and institutions to administer and score. In many EFL contexts, however, comprehensive proficiency tests that include several skills are time-consuming, costly, and difficult to develop locally. This problem is particularly important in settings where teachers may have limited training in test construction and validation. Research on teacher-produced EFL tests has shown that classroom tests do not always yield accurate information about learners’ abilities unless teachers are supported in test specification, moderation, item analysis, and test refinement (Coniam, 2009). Therefore, economical and psychometrically sound alternatives to lengthy proficiency batteries are of considerable pedagogical and institutional value.

One such alternative is the C-Test, a reduced redundancy procedure introduced by Raatz and Klein-Braley as a development of earlier cloze-based and pragmatic approaches to language testing. The theoretical basis of reduced redundancy testing is the assumption that language users draw on their linguistic knowledge to reconstruct incomplete or distorted messages. Spolsky (1968) argued that knowing a language involves the ability to understand language even when part of the signal is masked or made noisy, because natural language contains redundancy and because linguistic competence enables users to infer missing information. In the same tradition, C-Tests require examinees to restore systematically deleted parts of words in short authentic texts. Typically, the first sentence is left intact to establish context, and from the second sentence onward the second half of every second word is deleted. Test takers must reconstruct the missing word parts by using lexical, grammatical, semantic, and discourse-level cues. Because successful performance requires the integration of several aspects of language knowledge, the C-Test has often been regarded as an integrative measure of general language proficiency.

The C-Test has attracted considerable attention in applied linguistics and language testing because it combines practicality with strong psychometric potential. Compared with many conventional proficiency tests, it is relatively easy to construct, brief to administer, and objective to score. It also reduces the risk that performance will be unduly influenced by familiarity with one topic, since a complete C-Test normally consists of several short passages rather than one long text. Klein-Braley (1997), in comparing C-Tests with other reduced redundancy formats such as classical cloze, cloze-elide, and multiple-choice cloze, found the C-Test to be an economical and reliable representative of the general language factor. Subsequent research has also supported the usefulness of C-Tests for placement, screening, and feedback in language learning contexts (Eckes & Baghaei, 2015; Forthmann et al., 2019). These qualities make the C-Test especially attractive for EFL programs that need rapid but defensible estimates of learners’ proficiency.

Despite its practical appeal, the construct validity of the C-Test has been a persistent issue. The main question is what C-Test scores actually represent. If the test is claimed to measure overall language proficiency, it should demonstrate meaningful relationships with established measures of language ability and should exhibit an interpretable internal structure. Early investigations into the factorial validity and dimensionality of C-Tests provided evidence that they were closely related to language proficiency, although such studies also raised methodological questions about how dimensionality should be examined (Raatz, 1984, 1985). More recent work using modern measurement models has further explored the C-Test construct. Baghaei (2008a, 2008b, 2010, 2011), for example, investigated C-Test performance through Rasch modeling and examined issues such as model fit, item and person invariance, and the effect of rhetorical organization on the construct. Eckes and Grotjahn (2006), using Rasch measurement and confirmatory factor analysis, found that a German C-Test was highly reliable and largely unidimensional and that it measured a general dimension shared with the reading, listening, writing, and speaking sections of TestDaF. At the same time, they noted that language proficiency is multicomponential and that C-Test performance may vary according to proficiency level. Grotjahn (2016) similarly emphasized the need to examine the validity of C-Tests as measures of academic and everyday language proficiency through multidimensional modeling.

Another important debate concerns whether a written reconstruction task can legitimately represent oral and aural aspects of proficiency. Since C-Tests are text-based and do not directly require speaking or listening, some researchers have questioned their status as general proficiency measures. If C-Test performance depends mainly on reading and writing ability, its use as a substitute for a broader proficiency battery would be limited. However, empirical findings have been mixed. Some studies have reported modest correlations between C-Tests and listening or speaking measures, while others have found stronger associations. The issue is therefore context-sensitive and requires further validation in different languages, educational settings, and learner populations. Evidence that a C-Test correlates not only with reading and writing but also with listening would strengthen the argument that it taps a broader underlying language ability rather than a narrow written skill.

The need for local validation is especially pressing in Afghanistan. English is widely taught in universities, private language institutes, and educational centers, yet the assessment resources available to teachers and institutions are often limited. International proficiency tests such as TOEFL and IELTS are well established, but they are expensive and impractical for routine classroom placement or progress monitoring. Locally produced tests may be more accessible, but their reliability and validity are not always empirically examined. In such a context, a C-Test could provide a fast and economical tool for estimating English proficiency, provided that it functions reliably and validly for Afghan EFL learners. Although a substantial body of research has investigated C-Tests in European, Asian, and other EFL/ESL contexts, little empirical evidence is available regarding their use with Afghan students. Because test validity is not an inherent property of an instrument but depends on the interpretation and use of scores for a particular population and purpose, findings from other contexts cannot simply be assumed to apply to Afghan learners.

The present study addresses this gap by validating a C-Test among Afghan students of English as a foreign language. It examines whether a four-text English C-Test can serve as a reliable and valid measure of general English proficiency for advanced Afghan EFL learners. To do so, the study compares C-Test scores with criterion measures of listening, reading, and writing drawn from a proficiency test and investigates the internal consistency and factorial structure of the measures. Specifically, the study seeks to determine whether the C-Test demonstrates acceptable reliability, whether it correlates significantly with separate language-skill measures and with a composite proficiency score, and whether C-Test passages and proficiency components load on a common factor. By providing empirical evidence from the Afghan EFL context, the study aims to inform teachers, test administrators, and language programs about the potential use of the C-Test as a practical alternative or supplement to more extensive proficiency testing.

intros.text:
Valid and reliable assessment is central to English language teaching because decisions about placement, achievement, certification, and instruction depend on the quality of the instruments used to measure learners’ language ability. In EFL contexts, where learners may have limited opportunities to use English outside the classroom, teachers and institutions often need tests that can provide dependable information about general proficiency while remaining practical, economical, and easy to administer. Conventional proficiency tests that include separate measures of listening, reading, writing, and speaking can yield useful profiles of learners’ abilities, but they also require considerable time, expertise, scoring procedures, and resources. For many language programmes, especially those operating with limited testing infrastructure, there is therefore a continuing need for brief and psychometrically sound measures of overall language proficiency.

One testing format that has received sustained attention in applied linguistics is the C-Test. Developed from the principle of reduced redundancy, the C-Test typically consists of several short authentic texts in which the second half of every second word is deleted after an initial intact sentence. Test takers are required to reconstruct the missing word parts by drawing on their linguistic knowledge, contextual understanding, and ability to process discourse. The theoretical rationale for such tests is that knowledge of a language involves the ability to understand and restore messages even when part of the linguistic signal is missing. Spolsky (1968) argued that language is inherently redundant and that a person’s ability to function under conditions of reduced redundancy is an important indication of language competence. In this sense, C-Tests are integrative tests: successful performance depends not only on vocabulary or grammar in isolation but also on the interaction of lexical, morphosyntactic, semantic, and discourse-level knowledge.

Previous research has frequently described the C-Test as a practical and efficient measure of general language proficiency. Klein-Braley (1997), comparing C-Tests with other reduced redundancy formats such as cloze, cloze-elide, and multiple-choice cloze tests, reported that the C-Test was economical, reliable, and empirically valid as a representative of a general language factor. Early validation studies also examined the dimensionality and factorial validity of C-Tests, suggesting that they are strongly related to language proficiency constructs (Raatz, 1984, 1985). More recent work has continued to support the usefulness of the C-Test while applying increasingly sophisticated psychometric methods. Baghaei (2008a, 2010, 2011), for example, investigated C-Test data through Rasch modelling and considered issues such as item fit, measurement invariance, and construct validation. Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) provided evidence that C-Tests can be highly reliable and unidimensional, while also showing that the construct may relate to more specific components of language ability depending on proficiency level. Further studies have addressed methodological questions such as local dependence among C-Test passages (Eckes & Baghaei, 2015), multidimensional modelling of academic and everyday proficiency (Grotjahn, 2016), and the scaling of speeded C-Tests (Forthmann et al., 2019).

Despite this considerable body of work, the exact construct measured by C-Tests has remained a topic of discussion. Because the format is based on written passages and requires written reconstruction of deleted word parts, some scholars have questioned whether C-Test scores can be interpreted as measures of overall language proficiency, particularly when oral and aural skills are not directly elicited. Eckes and Grotjahn (2006) noted that C-Test performance is related to a general language dimension but may also show multicomponentiality. Baghaei and Tabatabaee (2015) further argued that the C-Test may tap abilities associated with crystallized intelligence, especially verbal knowledge, which broadens the interpretation of what C-Test performance may represent. These discussions indicate that the validity of C-Test score interpretations should not be assumed universally; rather, they require empirical examination in particular populations and assessment contexts.

Context is especially important in language testing. Test validity is not a property of an instrument alone but of the interpretations and uses made from test scores in a specific setting. A C-Test that functions well in one educational or linguistic environment may not necessarily show the same degree of reliability, dimensionality, or relationship with criterion measures in another. Text familiarity, learners’ educational background, first language, exposure to English, and the quality of test construction can all influence test performance. In addition, the practical value of C-Tests is particularly relevant in contexts where teachers may not have extensive training in test development. Coniam (2009) showed that teacher-produced EFL tests can vary substantially in quality and argued for greater attention to assessment training and support. In Afghanistan, many English teachers and institutions face similar practical challenges: they need efficient instruments for placement and proficiency estimation, yet the development and administration of comprehensive proficiency tests may be difficult.

Although C-Tests have been widely studied in European and other EFL/ESL settings, little empirical evidence is available on their validity for Afghan learners of English as a foreign language. This absence is noteworthy because English education in Afghanistan has expanded through universities, private language institutes, and international educational programmes, creating a need for accessible tools for evaluating learners’ proficiency. If a C-Test can provide valid and reliable information about Afghan EFL learners’ general English ability, it could serve as a useful alternative or supplement to longer proficiency tests, especially for classroom placement and diagnostic purposes. However, without local validation, such use would be premature. The relationship between C-Test scores and performance on criterion measures of listening, reading, and writing among Afghan students remains unclear.

The present study addresses this gap by examining the validity and reliability of a C-Test administered to Afghan EFL learners. Specifically, it investigates whether C-Test scores correlate significantly with scores on a general English proficiency measure composed of listening, reading, and writing sections, and whether the C-Test demonstrates acceptable internal consistency and construct validity. One hundred undergraduate and institute-based Afghan learners of English completed a four-passage C-Test and a Preliminary English Test-based proficiency measure. Reliability analysis, Pearson correlations, and factor analysis were used to evaluate the psychometric properties of the C-Test and its relationship with criterion measures.

By validating the C-Test in the Afghan EFL context, this study contributes to the broader literature on reduced redundancy testing and to local assessment practice. The findings may help teachers, test administrators, and language programmes determine whether the C-Test can be used as an economical, rapid, and dependable measure of general English proficiency. More broadly, the study adds contextual evidence to ongoing debates about what C-Tests measure and how far their scores can support interpretations of overall language ability across different learner populations.

intros.text: Academic writing is an integral part of tertiary education in Malaysia (Rahman &  Rahim, 2016). At this level, undergraduates are expected to have the necessary  linguistic skills to be able to produce writing that adheres to different genres and  disciplines.  However, among English as a second language (ESL) students, academic  writing is often described as challenging, complex and often linked to writing  anxiety.  In particular, the comments made about Malaysian L2 writers are often  bleak, imbued with issues that range from plagiarism (Habali & Fong, 2016), low selfefficacy (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015) to writing anxiety (Maringe & Jenkins,  2015). As a result, such factors have been reported to act as barriers for students’  engagement and overall academic performance in the academic writing class (Badiozaman, 2015).  Evidently, academic writing is not an easy skill to master especially in a second language (L2). Particularly with ESL or English as a F foreign language(EFL) students, research has attributed this to linguistics difficulties (Zhang, 2013) and the tacit nature of academic writing (Elton, 2010). Furthermore, since academic writing  “serves different purposes in different units and requires students to assume different social roles ” (Zhu, 2004, p. 30), this has implications for the academic writing class in Malaysian universities, where students may be studying in different  disciplines and have little to no academic writing experience  For this reason, many  higher learning institutions in Malaysia make it compulsory for students to undertake units such as Academic Reading and Writing, and Technical Report  Writing. These units aim to equip students with the necessary language skills and the ability to read and write for academic purposes so that they can function effectively  within an academic environment.  Nonetheless, despite the fact that such units are ubiquitous in higher  learning institutions in Malaysia, little is known about its effectiveness.  The limited  research on the improvements made by L2 learners in their academic writing in a L2  setting provided the impetus for this study.  The focus on academic writing in this  study is also due to the role of writing in tertiary education (Othman & Mohamad,  2009).  Students’ achievements at tertiary level are evaluated mainly on written  assessments, be it in the form of large extended writing (e.g. projects, proposal and  reports) or short-response essays (e.g. examinations and quizzes).  As the demand and participation in English-medium higher education  increase, so is the expectation for students to have academic literacy skills. Hence, it  is necessary to understand academic writing improvements that are made in  academic literacy classes.  Furthermore, factors involved in the development of  academic writing such as organisation of ideas, identifying audience for various  genres and synthesising from multiple sources are scarce.  Therefore, this study aims  to address this gap. In particular, it first seeks to explore how much impact the  Academic Writing1 unit (AW hereafter) has upon the writing development of our ESL  undergraduate students. Secondly, it will examine the transferability of skills to  other academic units.

intros.text:
Academic writing is widely regarded as an integral part of tertiary education, functioning as the principal means through which students demonstrate knowledge, establish membership within academic discourse communities, and are assessed on their scholarly abilities (Rahman & Rahim, 2016; Zhu, 2004). Undergraduates are expected to advance their own ideas within a framework of discipline knowledge, integrate sources appropriately, and engage the reader in an academic discourse. Yet the acquisition of these skills is demanding, particularly for second language (L2) writers, who must not only navigate the linguistic requirements of English but also internalise the often tacit conventions and expectations of the academic writing genre (Elton, 2010). For many students transitioning from secondary school to university, this shift represents a significant challenge, one that is heightened when learning takes place in an English-medium environment such as an international branch campus.

In Malaysia, the proliferation of foreign university branch campuses has been accompanied by an increasing reliance on academic literacy units, such as Reading for Academic Purposes and Academic Writing, to equip students with the reading and writing skills required for undergraduate study. Such units are frequently made compulsory, particularly for students who do not meet the institution's English language entry requirements. Despite their ubiquity, however, remarkably little is known about the effectiveness of these units or the extent to which the skills they claim to develop are genuinely acquired and transferred to other areas of study.

The difficulties L2 students encounter in academic writing are well documented. Many have a general grasp of grammatical rules yet struggle to write academically at the expected level, owing to limited experience with formal writing in prior educational settings (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015) and inadequacies in academic English proficiency. International and L2 students may further experience apprehension, stigma, and tension as they negotiate unfamiliar academic writing conventions (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). Compounding these challenges are the cognitive and metacognitive demands of writing, and the reality that students' self-concept as writers, shaped by both internal and external factors, influences their engagement and receptiveness to learning (Adi Badiozaman, 2015). Studies examining whether English for Academic Purposes or Academic Writing courses actually produce measurable writing development have yielded mixed results, with some reporting clear gains through explicit and synthesis-oriented instruction (Zhang, 2013) and others finding little evidence of improvement.

Given these mixed findings and the scarcity of research on L2 learners' academic writing improvements in English-medium contexts, there is a pressing need to examine what students actually gain from academic literacy units and whether those gains transfer across disciplines (Rahman & Rahim, 2016). This longitudinal, mixed methods study addresses this gap by investigating the academic writing developments of undergraduate students at a foreign branch campus in Malaysia. Reporting on the first phase of the study, this paper explores students' self-concept in academic writing, the perceived impact of a compulsory Academic Writing (AW) unit on their writing development, and the transferability of the skills acquired to other academic units. In doing so, it seeks to inform a more evidence-based approach to the pedagogy of academic writing in L2 settings.

intros.text:
Academic writing is widely acknowledged as one of the most important and enduring means of communicating knowledge within the academic community. It is a central concern in higher education, where the quality of students' written work not only demonstrates the acquisition of new knowledge but also determines their standing and identity within discipline-specific discourse communities (Zhu, 2004; Rahman & Rahim, 2016). As students progress through university, the communicative expectations placed upon them shift, requiring them to move from general academic tasks to more specialised, discipline-specific writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012). This trajectory is particularly demanding for Malaysian students transitioning from secondary school to higher learning institutions, many of whom study at international branch campuses where English is the medium of instruction.

The acquisition of academic writing skills is a challenging endeavour, especially for second language (L2) writers. Academic writing is an elaborated and grammatically complex form of discourse, produced under carefully planned and edited conditions (Staples, Egbert, Biber, & Gray, 2016), and it requires students to advance their own ideas within a framework of disciplinary knowledge (Hyland, 2002). For ESL students, difficulties stem not only from inadequate English language proficiency but also from a lack of experience with formal writing and an incomplete understanding of academic writing conventions and expectations (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015; Zhu, 2004). International students, in particular, have been shown to negotiate new academic writing conventions with considerable tension and apprehension (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). These challenges are compounded by cognitive and metacognitive demands, as well as by the affective dimensions of self-concept and confidence that shape learners' engagement with writing (Adi Badiozaman, 2015).

In response to such challenges, many foreign university branch campuses in Malaysia make it compulsory for students to undertake academic literacy units, such as Reading for Academic Purposes or Academic Writing (AW), in order to equip them with the language, reading and writing skills required for tertiary study. Despite the ubiquitousness of these units, surprisingly little is known about their actual effectiveness. Studies investigating the development of academic writing have yielded mixed findings; while some report gains following explicit strategy instruction (Zhang, 2013), others have found no significant improvement despite students completing English for Academic Purposes or writing-intensive courses. Research examining the improvements L2 learners make in their academic writing within an L2 medium setting remains few and far between, and this scarcity provides the impetus for the present study.

This longitudinal, mixed methods study aims to address this gap by exploring the effectiveness of an AW unit at an international branch campus of an Australian university in Malaysia. Specifically, it seeks to investigate (i) students' self-concept in academic writing, (ii) the perceived impact of the AW unit on their writing development, and (iii) the transferability of the skills acquired to other academic units. This paper reports on the first, quantitative phase of the study, drawing on questionnaire data gathered from undergraduates who had completed one semester of the unit. In doing so, the study aims to disclose the challenges these students face and to inform a more objective and grounded approach to the pedagogy of academic writing in L2 settings.

intros.text:
Academic writing is widely recognized as a cornerstone of tertiary education, serving as the primary vehicle through which students communicate knowledge and demonstrate their scholarship (Rahman & Rahim, 2016). For undergraduate students, particularly those in second language (L2) settings, the transition to university-level writing is often fraught with difficulty. This challenge is not merely a matter of linguistic proficiency but involves navigating complex rhetorical conventions, internalizing discipline-specific genres, and managing the high cognitive and metacognitive demands of the writing process. In the context of international branch campuses in Malaysia, students often face the dual pressure of adapting to a foreign academic culture while striving to meet rigorous English language standards.

Research indicates that international students frequently experience significant apprehension and tension as they negotiate these new conventions, often positioning themselves as vulnerable outsiders in an environment where their native linguistic identities may be marginalized (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). Furthermore, the self-concept of L2 learners in academic writing is complex and multifaceted, shaped by a combination of internal beliefs and external institutional factors (Badiozaman, 2015). Many ESL students enter higher education with a lack of experience in formal writing or inadequate academic English proficiency, which can hinder their ability to produce the sophisticated, evidence-based discourse required at the university level (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015).

To mitigate these challenges, many foreign branch campuses in Malaysia mandate academic literacy units, such as Academic Writing (AW), to equip students with essential skills in reading, synthesis, and report writing. While the importance of such interventions is acknowledged, there remains a debate regarding the most effective instructional approach. Some perspectives suggest that general writing skills are transferable across disciplines, while others argue that academic writing requires a nuanced understanding of the unique communication processes inherent to specific fields (Zhu, 2004). Moreover, while some studies suggest that explicit instruction in synthesis and discourse can significantly improve L2 writing abilities (Zhang, 2013), other evidence suggests that improvements in linguistic accuracy and complexity are slower to materialize (Storch, 2009).

Despite the ubiquity of academic writing units, there is a paucity of longitudinal research exploring their actual effectiveness and the extent to which the skills acquired in these units transfer to other core academic modules. Understanding this transferability is crucial, as the ultimate goal of EAP instruction is to facilitate successful integration into the broader academic community. Therefore, the present study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the developments of undergraduate students at a foreign branch campus in Malaysia. Specifically, this research aims to: (i) explore students' self-concept in academic writing; (ii) examine the perceived impact of a compulsory Academic Writing unit on their writing development; and (iii) evaluate the transferability of the acquired skills to other academic units. By doing so, the study intends to provide empirical insights into the pedagogy of academic writing in L2 settings and the support mechanisms necessary for first-year student success.
