intros.text:
The development of academic writing skills is widely recognized as a central concern in tertiary education, as the ability to communicate knowledge effectively remains the primary method of scholarship within the academic community. For undergraduate students, this transition involves moving from general writing tasks to specialized, discipline-specific discourse (Nesi & Gardner, 2012). In the context of English-medium higher education, particularly for second language (L2) learners, this process is often fraught with difficulty. International students frequently experience significant tensions and apprehensions as they negotiate unfamiliar rhetorical conventions, often positioning themselves as vulnerable outsiders in a high-stakes linguistic environment (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). 

Existing research highlights that academic writing is a complex, recursive process involving significant cognitive and metacognitive demands (Hyland, 2002). For Malaysian ESL students, these challenges are often exacerbated by a lack of formal writing experience in secondary education (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015). Consequently, many foreign university branch campuses in Malaysia have implemented compulsory academic literacy units to equip students with necessary reading and writing skills. While some studies have demonstrated the positive effects of explicit instruction on specific skills, such as discourse synthesis (Zhang, 2013), others have found no significant improvement despite the provision of English for Academic Purposes (EAP) courses (A. Green, 2005; Terraschke & Wahid, 2011). Furthermore, the internal psychological state of the learner, specifically their self-concept as a writer, is known to be multifaceted and influenced by both internal and external factors (Badiozaman, 2015).

Despite the ubiquitous nature of academic writing units in Malaysian branch campuses, there remains a paucity of longitudinal empirical evidence regarding their actual effectiveness and the extent to which the skills acquired in these units transfer to other academic disciplines. While faculty views vary on whether academic writing consists of general transferable skills or discipline-specific processes (Zhu, 2004), little is known about how students perceive this transfer in practice. There is a clear need for research that explores not only the linguistic gains but also the development of student self-efficacy and the perceived utility of these courses across the curriculum.

Addressing this gap, the present study employs a sequential mixed-methods design to investigate the academic writing developments of undergraduate students at a foreign branch campus in Malaysia. Specifically, the research aims to: (i) explore the extent of the impact that a dedicated Academic Writing (AW) unit has on the writing development of ESL undergraduates, and (ii) examine the transferability of these acquired skills to other academic units. By focusing on both students' self-concept and their perceived skill acquisition, this study seeks to provide a more objective and tactile approach to the pedagogy of teaching academic writing in an L2 setting. The following sections detail the methodology used in the first phase of this study, present the quantitative findings from student questionnaires, and discuss the implications for first-year academic support.

intros.text:
In the contemporary landscape of higher education, the acquisition of academic writing skills is widely recognised as a critical determinant of student success, particularly within the context of international branch campuses. As students transition from secondary education to university-level study, they are required to navigate a complex shift from general writing tasks to specialised, discipline-specific discourse (Nesi & Gardner, 2012). This transition is particularly challenging for English as a Second Language (ESL) learners, who must not only master the linguistic complexities of academic English but also internalise the rhetorical and genre conventions of their academic communities. In Malaysia, where foreign university branch campuses have proliferated, academic literacy units—such as Reading for Academic Purposes and Technical Report Writing—are often made compulsory to equip students with the necessary language skills and academic competencies. Despite the ubiquitousness of such units in Malaysian higher learning institutions, little is known about their actual effectiveness in fostering writing development and facilitating the transfer of skills to other academic domains.

The acquisition of academic writing is reported to be challenging for myriad reasons. Advanced academic writing is an elaborated form of discourse that is grammatically complex, requiring students to carefully plan, edit, and produce detailed, specific content (Staples, Egbert, Biber, & Gray, 2016). Furthermore, writing in academic contexts demands that students advance their own ideas within a framework of discipline knowledge and engage the reader in an academic discourse (Hyland, 2002). While English language proficiency is critical to academic performance, it is not the sole factor in determining writing success. Researchers have acknowledged that students often encounter difficulties in internalising the requirements of the academic writing genre, which vary across disciplines and specific registers (Leki, 2011). Consequently, students' struggles in adjusting to academic writing in higher learning could stem from an inadequate understanding of academic writing standards and the expectations of lecturers and institutions (D. Green, 2010).

Moreover, the psychological dimensions of writing cannot be overlooked. International students often experience stigma, tensions, and apprehension regarding their ability to negotiate new academic writing conventions, positioning themselves as vulnerable outsiders in an ill-defined but highly valued language environment (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). This anxiety is compounded by the cognitive and metacognitive demands of the writing process, which involves recursive sub-processes such as pre-writing, translating, reviewing, planning, and revising (Barkaoui, 2007). For L2 learners, the interrelated influence of internal and external factors significantly shapes their self-concept in academic writing, which in turn influences their engagement and performance (Badiozaman, 2015). Despite the recognition of these challenges, empirical evidence regarding the developmental trajectory of L2 academic writers in branch campus settings remains limited. While some studies have noted no significant improvement despite EAP courses (A. Green, 2005; Terraschke & Wahid, 2011), others suggest that explicit instruction in writing processes can yield positive changes in students' planning and reviewing strategies (Kolb, Longest, & Jensen, 2013).

This longitudinal study aims to address this gap by investigating the impact of a semester-long Academic Writing (AW) unit on undergraduate students in a foreign branch campus in Malaysia. Specifically, this paper reports on data collected from the first phase of a mixed methods study that seeks to explore (i) students' self-concept in academic writing, (ii) the perceived impact of the AW unit on writing development, and (iii) the transferability of skills to other academic units. By examining these dimensions, the study seeks to provide insights into the effectiveness of academic literacy units in preparing L2 learners for the demands of tertiary education and to inform pedagogical practices in this context.

intros.text:
The development of academic writing skills is widely recognised as a major educational concern, particularly at the university level. As students progress through their academic years, they are asked to move from more general academic writing tasks to more specialised, discipline-specific writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012). This is particularly true for Malaysian students transitioning from secondary schools to higher learning institutions, studying in an international branch university. The acquisition of academic writing skills is reported to be challenging for many reasons. For example, advanced academic writing is widely recognised as an elaborated form of discourse that is grammatically complex. Staples, Egbert, Biber, and Gray (2016) maintain that 'academic writing is produced in circumstances where language is carefully planned and edited, detailed and specific, and produced in a concise format' (p. 151). Writing in academic contexts also requires students to advance their own ideas within a framework of discipline knowledge and engage the reader in an academic discourse (Hyland, 2002). Furthermore, there is a lack of consensus with regard to which writing approach meets all students' needs (Biber & Gray, 2010). This is further complicated by the fact that writing involves many processes, namely pre-writing, translating, reviewing, planning and revising (Hyland, 2002). Compositional literature has also ascertained that writers move back and forth among these sub-processes (Barkaoui, 2007) in a recursive process. Writing, thus, poses great cognitive and metacognitive demands.

While English language proficiency is critical to academic performance, it is not the sole factor in determining academic writing performance. As evidenced from the literature review, students not only encounter difficulties in English language proficiency, but also in internalising the requirements of the academic writing genre. Note that researchers acknowledged there were important differences within academic writing, showing that the use of complexity features varies across parameters like academic discipline and specific register/genres of academic writing (Leki, 2011). Thus, students' difficulties in adjusting to academic writing in higher learning could also stem from inadequate understanding of academic writing standards and expectations from the lecturers and the institution (D. Green, 2010). Many foreign university branch campuses in Malaysia make it compulsory for students to undertake academic literacy units (i.e. Reading for Academic Purposes, Technical Report Writing) in order to equip them with language skills as well as reading and writing for academic purposes. Despite the ubiquitousness of such units in universities, little is known about their effectiveness.

Studies investigating the development of academic writing often have varying results. There are studies which noted no significant writing improvement, despite students taking English for Academic Purposes (EAP) or Academic Writing courses (i.e. A. Green, 2005; Terraschke & Wahid, 2011). This could be attributed to various contextual and individual factors, and what actual development is being investigated. Nevertheless, a study by Kolb, Longest, and Jensen (2013) which investigated the effectiveness of a writing-intensive first-year seminar revealed changes in students' writing process. The data collected via pre -test and post-test interview of 34 students noted that the first year students became better planners and reviewers after receiving explicit instructions. The seminar reported in this study was designed based on the underlying premise; 'a better (writing) process yields a better product' (Kolb et al., 2013, p.20). For this reason, the students were 'taught to change their writing strategies and practices' (Kolb et al., 2013, p. 23), and writing activities were designed into discrete tasks that culminate into broader final product-paced evenly throughout the term (Kolb et al., 2013, p. 21). Similarly, Wischgoll's (2016) experimental study also revealed that cognitive and metacognitive strategy training improved the university's academic writing skills significantly. Thus, it is likely that writing classes which reflect the most realistic writing processes will likely improve students' writing skills.

The capacity to write well academically at tertiary level is a plausible expectation of university students. Interestingly, studies on the development of learners' language skills have been few and far between. The limited research on the improvements made by L2 learners in their academic writing in an L2 setting provided the impetus for this study. The study sought to investigate what features of academic writing, if any, develop as a result of studying in academic literacy unit, such as the 'Academic Writing (AW)' unit in an L2 medium university after one semester (12 weeks). In doing so, not only will the study help disclose the potential challenges that are bound to be faced by the students; it will also facilitate a more objective and tactile approach towards the pedagogy of teaching academic writing in an L2 setting. Thus, the current study has the following two main aims: (i) to explore the extent of impact the AW unit has upon the writing development of our ESL undergraduate students; and (ii) to examine the transferability of skills to other academic units that AW units often claim to do.

intros.text:
The capacity to write effectively in academic contexts is central to students’ participation and success in higher education. At university, writing is not merely a vehicle for displaying knowledge; it is also a means through which students learn disciplinary content, demonstrate critical engagement, construct arguments, and enter academic discourse communities. Yet the conventions that govern academic writing are often tacit, institutionally situated, and unevenly communicated to novice writers (Elton, 2010). For undergraduate students studying in English as a second language, these demands are intensified by the need to manage linguistic accuracy, genre expectations, source use, argumentation, and disciplinary ways of meaning-making simultaneously.

These issues are particularly salient in transnational higher education contexts such as foreign university branch campuses in Malaysia. Students in such institutions are commonly required to undertake their degrees through English-medium instruction while adapting to the assessment practices of an overseas university system. Although many Malaysian undergraduates have had substantial exposure to English, prior schooling may not have prepared them for the forms of extended, evidence-based, and discipline-related writing expected at university. Research in Malaysian and other ESL contexts has shown that students frequently report difficulties in formal academic writing, including vocabulary, sentence structure, organisation, synthesis, citation, and confidence (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015). In addition, academic writing needs may vary across disciplines, raising questions about whether general academic literacy provision can adequately support students from diverse programmes (Zhu, 2004; Rahman & Rahim, 2016).

In response to these challenges, many universities provide English for Academic Purposes or academic literacy units intended to equip students with transferable reading, writing, and research skills. Such units typically claim to support students not only in the writing class itself but also in their broader academic studies. Empirical work suggests that explicit instruction can improve particular academic writing abilities, including source-based synthesis (Zhang, 2013), planning, revision, and awareness of genre expectations. However, findings on the effectiveness of EAP and academic writing interventions remain mixed, partly because writing development is gradual, multidimensional, and shaped by contextual and learner-related factors. It is therefore important to examine not only whether students improve in measurable linguistic terms, but also how they perceive their development, confidence, and ability to apply writing-related skills across academic settings.

Learners’ self-concept is especially relevant in this regard. Academic writing can be experienced as a site of apprehension, vulnerability, and stigma, particularly for students whose linguistic and rhetorical backgrounds differ from those privileged by the institution (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). In Malaysia, self-concept in academic writing has been shown to be complex and influenced by interrelated internal and external factors, including English proficiency, prior experience, classroom support, and institutional expectations (Badiozaman, 2015). Understanding students’ perceptions of their own writing competence and of the usefulness of academic writing instruction can therefore provide insight into how they engage with writing tasks and negotiate the transition into university study.

Despite the widespread provision of compulsory academic writing units in international branch campuses, relatively little is known about their perceived effectiveness for Malaysian ESL undergraduates or about the extent to which students transfer the skills taught in such units to other academic modules. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates undergraduate students’ self-concept in academic writing after completing a 12-week Academic Writing unit at a foreign branch campus in Malaysia. It further examines students’ perceptions of the unit’s impact on their writing development and the transferability of acquired skills to their disciplinary studies. By focusing on students’ reported experiences in the first phase of a longitudinal mixed methods project, the study contributes to ongoing discussions about academic literacy support, first-year transition, and the teaching of writing in English-medium higher education.

intros.text:
Academic writing is central to participation and success in higher education. In English-medium universities, students are expected not only to display content knowledge but also to organise arguments, integrate sources, adopt appropriate disciplinary conventions, and communicate with clarity and authority. These expectations are especially consequential for second language (L2) undergraduates, for whom academic writing often becomes both a means of learning and a high-stakes form of assessment. As writing functions as evidence of students’ readiness to enter academic discourse communities, difficulties with it may affect performance across the curriculum rather than in language-related units alone.

The challenge is intensified in international and transnational higher education settings, including foreign branch campuses in Malaysia, where students may enter degree programmes with varied prior experiences of formal academic writing in English. Academic writing is not simply a set of surface-level language skills; it also involves tacit knowledge about institutional expectations, argumentation, reader positioning, and acceptable ways of using evidence (Elton, 2010). Faculty perspectives further suggest that academic writing may be understood either as a transferable set of general skills or as a set of discipline-specific practices requiring collaboration between writing specialists and disciplinary lecturers (Zhu, 2004). For undergraduates who are still negotiating new academic norms, such expectations may remain implicit and difficult to interpret.

Previous research has shown that L2 writers often experience academic writing as demanding, affectively charged, and closely connected to identity and confidence. International students have been reported to feel apprehension and marginalisation when adapting to unfamiliar academic writing conventions (Maringe & Jenkins, 2015). In the Malaysian context, learners’ self-concept in academic writing has been found to be complex and shaped by interrelated internal and external factors, including self-concept in English, prior learning experiences, and classroom support (Badiozaman, 2015). Studies of ESL writing development after language programmes also indicate that learners may perceive improvement while continuing to experience difficulties in lexis, grammar, and syntax (Shammodin & Nimehchisalem, 2015). These findings point to the importance of understanding not only students’ written products but also their perceptions of development, confidence, and need for support.

In response to these challenges, many universities offer academic literacy or English for Academic Purposes units designed to prepare students for tertiary writing demands. Such units commonly include instruction in reading academic texts, paraphrasing, summarising, synthesising sources, referencing, and producing extended written assignments. There is evidence that targeted instruction can improve particular academic writing abilities, including synthesis writing (Zhang, 2013), and recent work has emphasised the need to attend to undergraduates’ academic writing needs across disciplines (Rahman & Rahim, 2016). However, the effectiveness of compulsory academic writing units cannot be assumed. In particular, relatively little is known about how students in foreign branch campus contexts perceive the impact of such units on their academic writing development, or whether they regard the skills learned as transferable to other disciplinary units.

This study addresses this gap by investigating an Academic Writing (AW) unit offered at an international branch campus of an Australian university in Malaysia. Specifically, it explores undergraduate ESL students’ self-concept in academic writing, their perceptions of the impact of a 12-week AW unit on their writing development, and the extent to which they perceive the skills acquired in the unit as transferable to other academic units. The paper reports the first, questionnaire-based phase of a larger sequential mixed methods study. By focusing on students’ reported experiences after completing the AW unit, the study offers insight into the role of early academic literacy support in helping L2 undergraduates negotiate the transition into English-medium university study.

intros.text:
The English article system is widely recognised as one of the most challenging aspects of English for second language learners to master, particularly for those whose first language lacks a comparable system (Master, 1997; Hewson, 2017). The system comprises the definite article 'the', the indefinite article 'a/an', and the zero article Ø, and the correct choice among them depends on interrelated features such as countability, number, definiteness, and specificity. Because these distinctions are grammaticalised differently across languages, learners frequently transfer patterns from their first language, resulting in systematic errors (Hasbún, 2012). Research on EFL learners has repeatedly shown that overuse of articles, especially the definite article 'the', is a common feature of learner production and is at least partly attributable to first language interference (Hasbún, 2009).

Pashto, a widely spoken language in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province of Pakistan, has no article system as such. Definiteness and indefiniteness are instead conveyed, to some extent, through demonstratives and indefinite numerals such as /yaw/ (one). This mismatch between Pashto and English raises questions about how adult Pashto speakers acquire and use English articles. Although the acquisition of English articles has been extensively studied among speakers of many languages, very little research has examined Pashto learners specifically. The present study addresses this gap by investigating the types, nature, and loci of the errors that adult Pashto learners make when using English articles, examining these errors from the perspectives of both noun types and noun phrase environments, and considering the role of first language transfer.

intros.text:
The English article system is widely recognised as one of the most challenging areas for second language learners, particularly for those whose first language lacks an equivalent system. Articles carry subtle semantic and pragmatic distinctions of definiteness, specificity and countability that do not map neatly across languages, and this makes their acquisition a persistent source of difficulty in EFL contexts (Hewson, 2017; Master, 1997). Considerable research has examined how non-native speakers acquire and use English articles, drawing on frameworks of noun classification (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999; Master, 1990), noun phrase environments (Bickerton, 1981; Huebner, 1983; Ionin, Ko, & Wexler, 2004), and first language transfer (Bataineh, 2005; Crompton, 2011). Studies of learners from various language backgrounds have repeatedly reported patterns such as overuse and omission of articles, often attributed to interference from the mother tongue (Hasbún, 2012).

Despite this substantial body of work, very little research has addressed the acquisition and use of English articles by Pashto (L1) learners of English. Pashto has no article system; definiteness and indefiniteness are conveyed instead through demonstratives and indefinite numerals, creating a considerable mismatch with English. It remains unclear how such learners cope with English article choice across different noun types and noun phrase environments. The present study addresses this gap by investigating what, where and why adult Pashto learners of English make errors when using articles. It is anticipated that the findings will offer a fuller account of the actual difficulties Pashto learners and comparable EFL learners face in article use.

intros.text:
The acquisition of the English article system—comprising the definite article 'the', the indefinite 'a/an', and the zero article (Φ)—represents one of the most challenging aspects of English language learning, particularly for students whose first language (L1) lacks a corresponding article system. Research has consistently shown that EFL learners struggle with the complex interplay between noun classification and the semantic environment of the noun phrase (NP). Previous studies have highlighted these difficulties across various linguistic backgrounds; for instance, Hasbún (2012) noted a prevalence of article overuse among EFL learners, often attributed to L1 interference, while Master (1997) found the zero article to be particularly problematic for Thai learners. 

For adult Pashto learners, the challenge is compounded by the absence of a formal article system in Pashto, where definiteness and indefiniteness are instead conveyed through demonstratives or indefinite numerals. This structural mismatch often leads to errors driven by L1 transfer and overgeneralization. While extensive research exists on article acquisition globally, there is a paucity of data specifically targeting Pashto speakers. Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the difficulties adult Pashto learners encounter in the acquisition and use of English articles. By analyzing errors through the lenses of noun types and NP environments, this research seeks to answer what, where, and why these learners make errors, providing insight into the loci of difficulty for this specific population.

intros.text:
The acquisition of English articles represents one of the most challenging aspects of second language learning, particularly for students whose first language lacks a corresponding article system. Previous research has highlighted that the complexity of choosing between the definite article 'the', the indefinite 'a/an', and the zero article Φ often leads to significant errors in EFL contexts (Hasbún, 2012). Scholars have approached this phenomenon through various lenses, including noun classification (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999; Master, 1990), noun phrase environments (Bickerton, 1981; Huebner, 1983), and the influence of L1 transfer (Bataineh, 2005; Crompton, 2011). Master (1997) further emphasized that learners' metalinguistic knowledge often diverges from linguistic theory, frequently resulting in the overuse of specific articles based on limited structural cues.

Despite the abundance of research on article acquisition, very few studies have specifically investigated the difficulties faced by native Pashto speakers. While Pashto utilizes demonstratives and numerals to convey definiteness and indefiniteness, it possesses no formal article system, creating a linguistic mismatch that may impede L2 acquisition. This study aims to address this gap by identifying the types and loci of errors made by adult Pashto learners of English. Specifically, the research asks: what, where, and why do these learners make errors within the contexts of noun types and noun phrase environments? By analyzing gap-fill task data, this study seeks to provide a comprehensive account of the role of L1 transfer and noun categorization in article choice.

intros.text:
The acquisition of the English article system remains one of the most formidable challenges for second language learners, particularly those whose first language (L1) lacks an article system entirely. English articles—definite 'the', indefinite 'a/an', and the zero article (Ø)—function to signal definiteness, specificity, and noun classification (Master, 1997). For learners from article-less backgrounds, such as Pashto speakers, the mapping of these semantic features onto English grammar often results in systematic errors. While extensive research has explored article acquisition among various L1 groups, studies focusing specifically on adult Pashto learners of English remain scarce. Pashto, though lacking a formal article system, conveys definiteness through demonstratives and numerals, creating a complex transfer scenario (Raverty, 1860).

Previous studies indicate that L1 transfer significantly influences article choice, often leading to overgeneralization or omission errors (Hasbún, 2012; Hewson, 2017). Furthermore, the interaction between noun types (count, non-count, proper) and noun phrase environments (generic, referential) complicates acquisition (Huebner, 1983). Despite these known difficulties, there is limited empirical data regarding the specific loci of errors made by Pashto speakers in these contexts. This study addresses this gap by investigating the difficulties in the acquisition and use of English articles among adult Pashto learners. Utilizing a gap-fill task, the research examines error patterns across different noun types and noun phrase environments. The primary aim is to identify the specific nature of these errors and determine whether they stem from L1 transfer, noun classification confusion, or environmental factors. By analyzing these patterns, this study seeks to provide pedagogical insights for teaching English articles to learners from article-less linguistic backgrounds.

intros.text:
The acquisition of the English article system presents one of the most persistent challenges for second language learners, particularly those whose first languages lack such a grammatical category. The English system comprises the definite article 'the', the indefinite articles 'a/an', and the zero article (Ø), all of which are governed by complex semantic and syntactic rules regarding definiteness, countability, and noun phrase environments. For learners from article-less backgrounds, mastering these distinctions requires navigating significant cross-linguistic interference.

Previous research has extensively documented these difficulties across diverse learner populations. Master (1997) highlighted that Thai learners often struggle with metalinguistic knowledge, particularly regarding the zero article, while Hasbún (2012) found that EFL learners frequently overuse articles due to L1 interference. Similarly, studies by Hewson (2017) emphasize the intricate relationship between noun classification and article choice. Despite this growing body of literature, very limited research has focused on the specific acquisition patterns of adult Pashto learners. Although Pashto conveys definiteness through demonstratives and numerals, it lacks a dedicated article system, creating a unique learning gap.

This study addresses this niche by investigating the specific difficulties adult Pashto learners face in acquiring and using English articles. Drawing on theoretical frameworks of noun classification and noun phrase environments, the research aims to identify the types, loci, and causes of errors in article usage. Specifically, it examines whether errors stem from noun type identification, noun phrase contexts, or language transfer. The findings offer critical insights into the interplay between L1 transfer and article acquisition, providing pedagogical implications for EFL instruction in Pashto-speaking contexts.

intros.text:
The English article system is a persistent source of difficulty for learners of English as a foreign or second language. Although articles are short and frequent, their use depends on an interaction of definiteness, specificity, countability, number, and discourse context. English requires learners to distinguish among the definite article the, the indefinite article a/an, and the zero article, each of which signals different semantic and pragmatic relations between the speaker, the hearer, and the noun phrase. As Hewson (2017) and Master (1997) note, article choice is closely tied to the relationship between article and noun, making the system complex even for advanced learners.

These difficulties are especially acute for learners whose first language does not have an article system comparable to that of English. Previous research has shown that EFL learners often omit, overuse, or confuse English articles, and that such errors may be influenced by first-language transfer, instructional input, and incomplete knowledge of noun phrase reference (Master, 1997; Hasbún, 2012). Learners may also experience particular problems with zero article contexts, generic reference, abstract and non-count nouns, and idiomatic expressions, where article use is less transparent and less easily captured by simple classroom rules.

Pashto presents an important context for investigating these issues because it lacks an English-like article system, although definiteness and indefiniteness may be expressed through demonstratives and the numeral meaning “one”. This mismatch may lead Pashto learners to rely on partial equivalents, overgeneralized rules, or transfer from Pashto noun classification. The present study therefore examines the acquisition and use of English articles by adult Pashto learners, focusing on the types of errors they make and the noun types and noun phrase environments in which these errors occur.

intros.text:
The English article system is a central but persistently difficult area of grammar for learners of English as a foreign or second language. Although the system appears small, consisting of the definite article the, the indefinite article a/an, and the zero article Ø, its use depends on several interacting semantic and grammatical factors, including definiteness, specificity, countability, number, and the discourse status of the noun phrase. Consequently, learners must not only select an article form but also identify the type of noun and the referential environment in which the noun phrase occurs.

Previous research has shown that article acquisition is especially problematic for learners whose first languages do not possess an article system comparable to English (Master, 1997; Hasbún, 2012). Studies of English articles have commonly examined learners’ choices through noun classification and noun phrase environments, drawing on accounts of article function and reference such as those proposed by Hewson (2017) and Master (1997). However, while article use has been investigated in a range of EFL contexts, relatively little is known about how adult Pashto-speaking learners acquire and use English articles. This gap is important because Pashto has no article system equivalent to English, although definiteness and indefiniteness may be expressed through demonstratives and the numeral yaw ‘one’.

The present study investigates the difficulties adult Pashto learners face in choosing English articles. It identifies the types and locations of their errors in relation to noun types and noun phrase environments, using a gap-fill task administered to 75 learners. The study asks what errors these learners make, where they occur, and why they arise, with particular attention to noun classification, referential context, and L1 transfer.

intros.text: The concept of self-mention is described by Hyland (2005) as the use of the firstperson pronouns and possessive adjectives to provide interpersonal information. The rules governing the personal pronouns are easy to learn, but the rules that regulate their use appear to be challenging for non-native speakers of English  (Natsukari, 2012). Exploring self-mention in relation to the proficiency levels has  received little attention (Choung & Oh, 2017; Lee & Oh, 2018; McCrostie, 2008; Oh &  Kang, 2013). This issue has been reported by several scholars that written texts by  non-native speakers have been characterized by having greater subjectivity (Gilquin  & Paquot, 2008; Herriman & Aronsson, 2009; Hinkel, 1999; Ishikawa, 2008; Luzon,  2009; Natsukari, 2012; Petch-Tyson, 1998). The use of the first-personal pronouns  makes academic writing less formal, and objective (Biber, Johansson, Leech, Conrad & Finnegan, 1999; Chafe, 1982; Fowler & Aaron, 2010; Korhonen & Kusch, 1989;  Kuo, 1999; Smith, 1986)  As Milton (1999) states, personal pronouns used by nonnative English speakers are associated with conversation. While there has been research into the use of the first-person pronouns in academic writing, few studies  have been reported in L2 writing, particularly the essays produced by learners with  lower proficiency levels (Chang, 2015; McCrostie, 2008).  Therefore, the aim of this  study is to contribute to the research on the learners’ use of the first-person pronouns used by Yemeni EFL learners of Arabic cultural background through  comparing the occurrences and distribution of these features across three  proficiency levels (i.e. low, intermediate, advanced). This comparison attempts to  provide an insight into how Yemeni EFL learners of English project their voice in their  argumentative writing

intros.text:
In academic writing, writers do not merely convey information but also project themselves into their texts, negotiating a relationship with their readers and establishing their credibility. One of the most salient means of achieving this is through self-mention, defined as the use of first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives by which writers refer to themselves (Hyland, 2005). Through the appropriate use of self-mention, writers can build a positive self-representation, assert their authorial identity, and strengthen the writer-reader relationship (Kuo, 1999). However, the use of these features is far from straightforward. It has long been observed that self-mention can be challenging for native speakers and even more so for non-native writers, who often struggle to balance the demands of objectivity and formality with the need to project a convincing voice.

A recurring finding in learner corpus research is that EFL writers tend to overuse first-person pronouns, drawing on features more typical of speech than academic prose (Gilquin & Paquot, 2008; Petch-Tyson, 1998). Studies have further shown that this tendency is linked to proficiency, with less proficient learners relying more heavily on self-mention than their more advanced counterparts (Choung & Oh, 2017; Lee & Oh, 2018; McCrostie, 2008). The overuse of formulaic expressions such as 'I think' has also been widely reported (Natsukari, 2012).

Despite this body of research, most investigations of self-mention have been conducted within Western contexts, and studies focusing on learners of Arabic cultural background remain scarce (Chang, 2015). This gap is significant given that cultural orientation may shape how writers position themselves in their texts. The present study therefore aims to explore and compare the use of first-person pronouns across three proficiency levels in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni EFL undergraduate students.

intros.text:
In academic writing, the ways writers project themselves into their texts have attracted considerable interest, since these choices shape how writers construct their authorial identity and manage their relationship with readers. One of the key resources for achieving this is self-mention, defined as the use of first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives through which writers make their presence explicit (Hyland, 2005). By deploying such features appropriately, writers establish a positive self-representation, build a strong writer-reader relationship, and gain credibility (Kuo, 1999). Yet self-mention is frequently regarded as being at odds with the objectivity and formality valued in academic prose, and its overuse can render a text less scholarly. For non-native learners of English, managing this feature is a particularly demanding task.

Over the last two decades, self-mention has been widely investigated in second and foreign language writing, especially in research articles across disciplines and in learner argumentative essays (Chang, 2015; Lee & Oh, 2018; Natsukari, 2012; Petch-Tyson, 1998). Studies also suggest that proficiency shapes writers' reliance on first-person pronouns, with less proficient learners tending to overuse them (Choung & Oh, 2017; McCrostie, 2008). However, much of this research has been conducted within Western contexts, and, as several scholars note, self-mention produced by non-native writers remains understudied and incomplete (Hyland & Jiang, 2017). In particular, learners of Arabic cultural background have received little attention, and how self-mention varies across proficiency levels in such contexts is still unclear.

To address this gap, the present study explores and compares the use of first-person pronouns across three proficiency levels in argumentative paragraphs written by 80 third-year Yemeni undergraduate students. The findings may inform writing pedagogy by highlighting how learners project their voice and how instruction might help them do so more appropriately.

intros.text:
In academic writing, the projection of the writer's voice is a critical component of discourse, allowing authors to establish credibility and shape the relationship between the writer and the reader (Hyland, 2005). One of the primary linguistic resources for achieving this interaction is 'self-mention,' typically manifested through the use of first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives. While traditional views often suggested that self-mention contradicts the requirements of objectivity and formality (Hinkel, 1999), contemporary research recognizes its role in establishing authorial presence and stance. However, mastering the appropriate use of these features remains a challenging task for both native and non-native speakers.

Within the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), learners often struggle with register variation, sometimes employing features more typical of spoken language than academic prose (Gilquin & Paquot, 2008). In argumentative writing—a genre central to university education—this struggle is particularly evident. Previous studies have indicated that EFL learners frequently overuse first-person pronouns, often relying on formulaic expressions such as "I think" to convey opinions (Natsukari, 2012; Lee & Oh, 2018). Furthermore, research suggests that this tendency is often linked to proficiency levels, with lower-proficiency learners typically exhibiting higher frequencies of self-mention (Choung & Oh, 2017).

Despite these insights, much of the existing literature has focused on Western contexts or East Asian learners, leaving the writing patterns of learners from Arabic cultural backgrounds largely overlooked (Chang, 2015). Given that cultural orientation can significantly influence authorial identity, there is a need to explore how Yemeni EFL students navigate self-mention. Therefore, this study aims to explore and compare the use of first-person pronouns in argumentative paragraphs across three proficiency levels among Yemeni university students.

intros.text:
In academic discourse, the projection of the writer's voice is a vital component of interaction, allowing authors to establish credibility and shape their relationship with the reader (Hyland, 2005). A primary mechanism for this is self-mention, which refers to the use of first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives. While traditionally viewed as a threat to the objectivity and formality required in academic writing, appropriate self-mention is now recognized as a means for writers to portray themselves as reliable members of a scholarly community. However, achieving this balance remains a challenging task for non-native speakers, who often struggle with register variation and may use features more typical of speech than of formal prose (Gilquin & Paquot, 2008).

Extensive research has investigated self-mention across various disciplines, often highlighting how L2 writers differ from native speakers. For instance, studies on Korean learners have indicated an overuse of first-person pronouns in argumentative writing, with frequency typically decreasing as proficiency increases (Chang, 2015; Lee & Oh, 2018). Similarly, Japanese EFL learners have been found to excessively rely on the pronoun 'I' and formulaic expressions like 'I think' (Natsukari, 2012). Despite these insights, the majority of such research has been situated within Western or East Asian contexts, leaving the practices of learners from Arabic cultural backgrounds largely overlooked.

Therefore, the present study aims to explore and compare the use of first-person pronouns across three proficiency levels in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni EFL undergraduate students. By analyzing these patterns, the research seeks to determine how proficiency affects authorial presence and whether cultural background influences the choice of pronouns. The findings may provide pedagogical insights into how L2 writers can more effectively project their voice in academic texts.

intros.text:
The use of self-mention, defined as the employment of first-person pronouns and possessive adjectives, is a critical feature in academic writing that allows writers to project their voice and establish credibility (Hyland, 2001). While traditionally viewed as contrary to objectivity and formality (MacIntyre, 2017), contemporary research suggests that appropriate self-mention facilitates a positive self-representation and strengthens the writer-reader relationship (Mur Duenas, 2007). Despite its significance, the use of self-mention remains a challenging task for non-native speakers (Atkinson, 2004), particularly within the context of argumentative writing where persuasion is paramount (Intraprawat, 2000). 

Previous studies have extensively investigated self-mention in Western contexts and research articles, often revealing that low-proficiency learners tend to overuse first-person pronouns compared to their higher-proficiency counterparts (Choung & Oh, 2017; Lee & Deakin, 2016; Natsukari, 2012). For instance, Chang (2015) found that Korean learners used the pronoun 'I' more frequently than native speakers in argumentative texts. However, research into the actual use of self-mention by EFL learners of Arabic cultural background remains largely overlooked (Hyland & Jiang, 2017). This gap is significant, as cultural factors, such as collectivism, may influence the preference for plural versus singular pronouns (Naj & Choi, 2009). 

Furthermore, while the relationship between proficiency and self-mention has been explored in various disciplines, few studies have focused specifically on the argumentative genre within an Arabic EFL context. Consequently, this study aims to explore and compare the use of first-person pronouns across three proficiency levels in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni undergraduate students. By examining these patterns, the research seeks to contribute to the understanding of how EFL learners from non-Western backgrounds navigate the complex requirements of academic voice and writer visibility.

intros.text:
The use of self-mention in academic writing has long been a subject of significant debate within applied linguistics. Traditionally, the inclusion of first-person pronouns was often viewed as contrary to the conventions of objectivity and formality required in scholarly discourse (MacIntyre, 2017). However, contemporary research suggests that self-mention serves a vital function in establishing the writer's stance and building a credible relationship with the reader (Hyland, 2001; Mur Duenas, 2007). Despite this shift in understanding, the appropriate use of self-mention remains a challenging task for non-native speakers, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts (Atkinson, 2004).

Existing literature on self-mention has predominantly focused on Western cultural contexts and research articles written by native speakers or advanced learners (Chávez Muñoz, 2013; Luzón, 2009). While studies such as those by Chang (2015) and Lee and Deakin (2016) have investigated the use of the first-person pronoun 'I' in argumentative writing among Korean learners, there is a notable scarcity of research concerning EFL learners from Arabic cultural backgrounds. Hyland and Jiang (2017) note that research into self-mention by non-native speakers remains incomplete, with little attention paid to how cultural factors and proficiency levels influence these linguistic choices. Furthermore, while some studies indicate that lower-proficiency learners tend to overuse self-mention compared to their more advanced counterparts (Choung & Oh, 2017; McCrostie, 2008), the specific patterns of this usage in Yemeni EFL contexts remain unexplored.

This study aims to address this gap by exploring and comparing the use of first-person pronouns across three proficiency levels in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni undergraduate students. By analyzing the frequency and distribution of self-mention features among low, intermediate, and high-proficiency learners, this research seeks to illuminate how proficiency and cultural background intersect to shape writer identity in EFL argumentative writing.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not a purely impersonal presentation of information; it is also an interactional activity through which writers signal stance, guide readers, and construct an authorial identity. One important resource for this interaction is self-mention, commonly realised through first-person pronouns and possessive forms such as I, we, my, and our (Hyland, 2005). Although traditional academic writing instruction has often associated first-person reference with informality and reduced objectivity, research has shown that self-mention can contribute to credibility, clarity of argument, and writer-reader negotiation when it is used appropriately (Kuo, 1999; Hyland, 2005). For EFL learners, however, the use of self-mention is particularly difficult because it requires sensitivity to genre, register, audience expectations, and the degree of personal involvement permitted in academic discourse.

Previous studies have reported that learner writing often displays a relatively high degree of writer visibility and involvement compared with more conventional academic prose (Petch-Tyson, 1998; Gilquin & Paquot, 2008). In argumentative writing, where students are expected to take a position and persuade readers, first-person pronouns may be especially salient. Studies of EFL argumentative essays have shown that learners frequently rely on I and formulaic expressions such as I think to present opinions, and that such use varies according to proficiency level (Natsukari, 2012; Chang, 2015; Lee & Oh, 2018). Research on proficiency has further suggested that lower-level learners may depend more heavily on personal pronouns and a narrower range of stance resources, whereas more proficient writers tend to employ less direct and more varied means of expressing position (Oh & Kang, 2013; Choung & Oh, 2017).

Despite this growing body of work, self-mention in EFL writing has been investigated mainly in East Asian and Western learner contexts, with limited attention to learners from Arabic-speaking backgrounds. Yemeni EFL students’ use of first-person pronouns in academic argumentation therefore remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study examines the frequency of self-mention in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni undergraduate EFL learners across low, intermediate, and advanced proficiency levels.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not an impersonal presentation of facts only; it is also an interactional act through which writers position themselves, evaluate propositions, and negotiate relationships with readers. One important resource for such positioning is self-mention, commonly realised through first-person pronouns and possessive forms. Although academic conventions have often associated the explicit presence of the writer with informality and reduced objectivity, recent work has shown that controlled self-mention can help writers construct stance, credibility, and reader engagement (Hyland, 2005; Kuo, 1999). For EFL learners, however, deciding when and how to make the self visible in writing is particularly demanding because it requires sensitivity to genre, register, audience expectations, and disciplinary or cultural norms.

This issue is especially relevant in argumentative writing, a genre in which writers are expected to advance claims, express viewpoints, and persuade readers while maintaining an appropriately academic style. Previous learner-corpus studies have reported that EFL writers often rely heavily on visible writer/reader references and speech-like features, which may make their academic prose appear overly conversational (Petch-Tyson, 1998; Gilquin & Paquot, 2008). Studies of first-person pronouns in argumentative essays have similarly found frequent use of I and formulaic expressions such as I think among Japanese and Korean learners (Natsukari, 2012; Chang, 2015; Lee & Oh, 2018). Proficiency also appears to shape such choices: higher-level learners generally use fewer and more varied interpersonal resources than lower-level learners (Choung & Oh, 2017; Oh & Kang, 2013).

Despite this growing interest, self-mention in EFL writing has been investigated mainly in Western or East Asian contexts, while learners from Arabic cultural backgrounds remain under-researched. Little is known about how Yemeni university students deploy first-person pronouns in English argumentative writing, or whether their use varies across proficiency levels. To address this gap, the present study explores and compares self-mention in argumentative paragraphs written by Yemeni EFL undergraduates at low, intermediate, and advanced proficiency levels. intros.text: On one hand, since the emergence of communicative approach to teaching and  learning a second language (L2), communicative activities have come into  prominence to enhance learners’ fluency (Renou, 2001). Communicative language  teaching, where the emphasis is on meaning as opposed to form or grammar, has enabled language learners to use the modern foreign language but de-emphasised accuracy and metalanguage (Alderson & Steel, 1994). Therefore, explicit L2  instruction has been glossed over (Gutierrez, 2013)  In this sense, it is essential to  consider the differences between learning one’s mother tongue and learning a  second language  For one, it is known that we learn our mother tongue without an  awareness or knowledge about grammar (Renou, 2001). However, in learning a  second language, linguistic accuracy is interrupted unless emphasis is placed on  language form (Renou, 2001). Additionally, certain types of knowledge and skills in a  second language may be difficult to obtain through untutored learning and thus  require instruction (Gutierrez, 2013). Consequently, communicative language  teaching has been criticised recently for neglecting attention to forms of language,  and SLA research has begun to underscore the developmental value of “enhanced  noticing” and “consciousness raising” in L2, paving the way for the language  awareness movement to develop (Carter, 2003). Language awareness, also known  as “knowledge about language”, refers to “the consciousness of and sensitivity to  the forms and functions of language” (Carter, 2003, p. 64).  On the other hand, language education in monolingual countries, such as  Turkey, generally relies on formal teaching and learning of the target language, as  these countries are acquisition-poor environments, in which foreign language  learners cannot find many opportunities to hear and speak the foreign language  (Yeşilyurt, 2005). In addition, learners’ inabilities to be proficient listeners and  speakers of the foreign language may be associated with this acquisition-poor  environment.  As a result, language awareness and explicit knowledge of language,  and thus the metalinguistic knowledge about the foreign language being learned,  emerges as particularly important.  Regarding the relationship between metalinguistic knowledge and foreign  language proficiency, it is necessary to indicate that many researchers have stressed  the importance of this issue even though some have not found clear evidence that  metalinguistic knowledge contributes to the use of language in actual settings  Berry  (2005), for example, points out that knowledge and use of metalanguage is likely to  make the development of an L2 learner’s metalinguistic awareness, which in turn is  likely to foster second language development. Additionally, Zipke (2007) states that  bilinguals’ better ability to understand an unknown language compared to  monolinguals may be attributed mostly to their greater metalinguistic awareness.  Moreover, studies investigating learner strategies and good language learners reveal  the benefits of metalinguistic skills such as treating language as a system and paying  attention to form.  Furthermore, some SLA researchers note usefulness of explicit L2  knowledge (Ellis, 1994; 2009). To exemplify, explicit L2 knowledge may make  learners’ establishment of links between form and meaning faster and thus  facilitates L2 acquisition. It may also provide saliency for certain grammar features,  which is likely to enable learners to notice them. In addition to this, explicit L2  knowledge may contribute to linguistic problem-solving where implicit knowledge is  insufficient. It may help L2 learners to produce the target language consciously as  well, which may turn into implicit learning through practice.  Although initial research in language awareness has shown findings on its  behalf, some factors have been densely researched, such as “the role of metalanguage in learners’ responses and whether metalinguistic knowledge can  enhance or hinder language development” (Carter, 2003, p. 65)  Of these limited  number of studies, some found weak or no correlation between metalinguistic  knowledge and L2 proficiency, while some others found positive correlations. The  results are inconclusive and thus it is not clear how metalinguistic knowledge  contributes to SLA.  Therefore, further research is needed on the relationship  between metalinguistic knowledge and L2 proficiency in order to gain better insights  into the role of metalinguistic knowledge in SLA development.  The purpose of this study is to find out the nature of metalinguistic  knowledge that intermediate-level adult Turkish EFL learners have developed, and  to examine the relationship between their metalinguistic knowledge and L2 production, operationalised in writing.  In this study, L2 production has been chosen  instead of overall L2 proficiency because it is assumed to represent learners’ implicit  knowledge of the foreign language, which is commonly referred to as procedural  knowledge due to the processes engaged in the development and use of non-declarative knowledge stores.  In other words, the main concern of the present study  is whether EFL learners are able to transfer their explicit knowledge (metalinguistic  knowledge) to implicit knowledge or procedural knowledge (L2 production). L2  production is operationalised in writing (opinion essays) because it is believed to be  easier to measure compared to oral production.

intros.text:
The role of grammar and explicit knowledge about language in second language (L2) learning has long been a matter of debate within the field of Second Language Acquisition (SLA). With the ascendency of communicative language teaching, the explicit teaching of grammatical rules and the cultivation of learners' conscious knowledge about the target language fell out of favour for a considerable period. In recent years, however, the notion of metalinguistic knowledge has been regaining scholarly attention, prompting renewed interest in whether, and to what extent, learners' conscious knowledge of the formal properties of a language contributes to their ability to use that language (Carter, 2003; Berry, 2005). This renewed interest is particularly pertinent in foreign language (EFL) contexts, where learners typically receive substantial explicit grammar instruction and yet have limited opportunities for authentic communicative interaction with the target language.

Before examining the empirical questions at the heart of the present study, it is important to clarify the conceptual terrain, which is characterised by considerable terminological variation. A useful starting point is the distinction between explicit and implicit L2 knowledge. Whereas implicit knowledge is intuitive, procedural and readily accessed in fluent, spontaneous language use, explicit knowledge is conscious, declarative and available for controlled processing (Ellis, 1994). Metalinguistic knowledge is generally understood as a form of explicit knowledge, and it has been operationalised in the literature as learners' ability to correct, describe and explain L2 errors (Roehr, 2007). A further distinction, however, has been drawn between metalinguistic knowledge, understood as the explicit knowledge of the language itself, and metalingual knowledge, understood as the knowledge of the technical terminology, or metalanguage, used to talk about the language (Berry, 2005; Gutierrez, 2013). This distinction is analytically significant because learners may be able to explain why a sentence is grammatically incorrect without necessarily commanding the technical vocabulary conventionally associated with such explanations. Metalinguistic awareness, in turn, has been described as the conscious awareness of the formal, and especially the grammatical, aspects of a language, an awareness that enables speakers to reflect upon and manipulate that language deliberately (Renou, 2001; Andrews, 2005).

The empirical relationship between metalinguistic knowledge or awareness and L2 proficiency remains contested. Early work by Alderson, Clapham and Steel (1997) found only weak associations between metalinguistic knowledge and French proficiency among university learners, leading the authors to conclude that metalinguistic knowledge and language proficiency constitute two largely separate factors of linguistic ability. A number of subsequent studies, however, have reported more encouraging findings. Renou (2001), for instance, found a moderate significant correlation between grammaticality judgement performance and French proficiency, a relationship that strengthened for learners exposed to explicit grammar instruction. Elder and Manwaring (2004) similarly reported that metalinguistic knowledge was more strongly related to L2 performance among late-starting learners, while Roehr (2007) documented a strong positive correlation between metalinguistic knowledge and L2 proficiency among advanced learners of German. More recently, Gutierrez (2013) has shown that analysed knowledge and knowledge of metalanguage differ in the strength of their associations with various proficiency measures, and Wistner (2014) demonstrated that metalinguistic knowledge statistically predicted L2 writing performance in terms of complexity, accuracy and fluency. Taken together, this body of research suggests that metalinguistic knowledge may play a facilitative, though possibly variable, role in L2 development, particularly for learners who have been exposed to explicit grammar instruction.

Despite this growing interest, several gaps remain. First, much of the existing research operationalises L2 proficiency through discrete-point or multiple-choice measures rather than through actual language production, which limits what can be inferred about how metalinguistic knowledge relates to learners' capacity to deploy the target language. intros.text:
The role of explicit knowledge about language has long occupied a central place in debates within Second Language Acquisition (SLA) and foreign language pedagogy. Language learners are frequently required to demonstrate not only that they can use a target language accurately and fluently, but also that they can reflect upon, describe, and analyse its structures. This capacity to reason about language, commonly referred to as metalinguistic knowledge, has attracted renewed scholarly attention in recent years after having been overshadowed for decades by the dominance of communicative language teaching. As the demand for effective grammar-focused instruction persists in many foreign language settings, understanding the nature of learners' metalinguistic knowledge and its relationship to actual language production has become an increasingly pressing concern for teachers, researchers, and curriculum designers alike.

Before examining this relationship, it is important to situate metalinguistic knowledge within the broader distinction between implicit and explicit knowledge. Implicit knowledge is intuitive, procedural knowledge of a language that is accessed automatically during fluent performance and held without conscious awareness, whereas explicit knowledge is conscious, analysed knowledge about a language that learners can access with controlled effort and articulate when needed (Ellis, 1994). Metalinguistic knowledge is generally treated as a component of, or synonymous with, explicit knowledge, and has been operationalised as the ability to correct, describe, and explain second language (L2) errors. A related but distinct construct, metalingual knowledge, concerns learners' command of the technical terminology or metalanguage used to talk about language (Berry, 2005; Gutiérrez, 2013). Researchers have argued that metalinguistic awareness, understood as conscious knowledge of the formal properties of a language, may enhance learners' comprehension of input, support their performance on the many form-focused examinations they encounter, and contribute to the development of learner autonomy (Berry, 2005; Carter, 2003). The importance of such awareness is further underscored by evidence that its absence can hinder learners' ability to comprehend and manipulate the structure of a language.

Despite the intuitive appeal of the claim that knowing about a language helps one to use it, the empirical evidence bearing on this question remains strikingly inconsistent. Early large-scale work by Alderson, Clapham, and Steel (1997) found only a weak relationship between metalinguistic knowledge and language proficiency among university learners of French, concluding that metalinguistic knowledge and proficiency constitute two separate factors of linguistic ability and that there was no justification for teaching metalinguistic knowledge as a means of improving proficiency. In contrast, a considerable body of subsequent research has reported significant, if moderate, associations between the two. Renou (2001), for instance, found a positive relationship between grammaticality judgement performance and French proficiency for her whole sample, though this relationship held only for learners exposed to grammar-based instruction and disappeared for those taught communicatively. Comparable positive findings have emerged across a range of learner populations and first-language backgrounds, including studies of foreign language learners in East Asian and Middle Eastern contexts, where metalinguistic knowledge has been shown to correlate with, and in some cases predict, various aspects of proficiency and even writing performance. More recently, researchers have begun to disaggregate explicit knowledge into analysed knowledge and knowledge of metalanguage, reporting that the former relates to a wider range of proficiency components than the latter (Gutiérrez, 2013).

Taken together, these studies reveal genuine controversy: while many findings underscore the value of metalinguistic knowledge for L2 development, particularly among learners who have received explicit grammar instruction, others find little or no such benefit. This inconsistency is compounded by considerable variation in how metalinguistic knowledge and proficiency have been operationalised, and by the fact that the available evidence is distributed unevenly across different first-language and target-language combinations. In the Turkish EFL context specifically, the picture is especially limited; earlier work, such as Yeşilyurt (2005), reported no significant role for metalinguistic knowledge in foreign language proficiency, but that study measured proficiency largely through multiple-choice tests and elicited very little extended learner production. Consequently, relatively little is known about how the metalinguistic knowledge of Turkish EFL learners relates to their actual L2 production, and in particular to their writing, where declarative knowledge must be transformed into language use. Given that writing is a tangible embodiment of L2 production that can be measured more objectively than speech, and that few studies have examined its complexity, accuracy, and fluency in relation to metalinguistic knowledge, further investigation in this context is clearly warranted.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating, first, the nature of the metalinguistic knowledge that intermediate-level adult Turkish EFL learners have developed, and second, the relationship between that knowledge and the complexity, accuracy, and fluency of their L2 writing. To this end, seventy-eight learners completed a placement test and both productive and receptive measures of metalinguistic knowledge, and a smaller subgroup produced opinion essays that were analysed for complexity, accuracy, and fluency. In doing so, the study seeks to contribute contextualised evidence to an ongoing debate and to inform pedagogical decisions about the place of explicit, form-focused instruction in EFL classrooms.

intros.text:
The role of metalinguistic knowledge in second language acquisition (SLA) has long been a subject of scholarly debate, particularly regarding how conscious knowledge about a language translates into actual linguistic performance. At the core of this discussion is the distinction between explicit and implicit knowledge. While implicit knowledge refers to the intuitive 'knowledge of language' that is accessed automatically during fluent performance, explicit knowledge is 'knowledge about the language,' often involving a conscious awareness of rules and the ability to verbalize them (Han & Ellis, 1998). Within the realm of explicit knowledge, researchers often distinguish between metalinguistic knowledge—the ability to identify, correct, and explain linguistic features—and metalingual knowledge, which refers specifically to the mastery of the technical terminology or metalanguage used to describe those features (Berry, 2005; Gutierrez, 2013).

Understanding the relationship between these constructs is vital for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pedagogy. Metalinguistic awareness allows learners to think about and use language consciously, potentially enhancing their ability to process input and monitor their own output (Andrews, 2005; Kuile & Weldhuis, 2010). However, the extent to which this explicit knowledge contributes to overall L2 proficiency remains controversial. Early research, such as the study by Alderson et al. (1994), suggested that metalinguistic knowledge and language proficiency constitute two separate factors, finding only a weak relationship between the two and concluding that higher levels of metalinguistic knowledge did not necessarily result in better linguistic performance. Similarly, Yeåilyurt (2005) found no significant evidence for the role of metalinguistic knowledge in foreign language proficiency within the Turkish context.

Conversely, other studies have indicated that metalinguistic awareness can indeed facilitate L2 development. Renou (2001) found a positive correlation between metalinguistic awareness and proficiency, particularly among learners exposed to explicit grammar instruction. This suggests that for certain learners, the ability to consciously analyze language serves as a bridge to higher proficiency. More recent evidence has further supported this link; for instance, Gutierrez (2013) found that metalinguistic and metalingual knowledge correlated with written measures of L2 proficiency. Furthermore, Wistner (2014) demonstrated that metalinguistic knowledge could statistically predict L2 procedural knowledge in writing, specifically in terms of complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF).

Despite these insights, there is still a lack of consensus, and research often varies significantly depending on the L1-L2 language combination and the specific measures of proficiency employed. Writing, in particular, provides a rich medium for investigating this relationship because it allows for a more objective and stable measurement of a learner's ability to transform declarative knowledge into procedural performance than oral production does. In the Turkish EFL context, where learners are frequently exposed to explicit grammar instruction from a young age, it is particularly pertinent to investigate whether this accumulated metalinguistic knowledge actually informs their writing production. While some Turkish studies have suggested a negligible impact, others point to the potential for explicit knowledge to refine the accuracy of written output.

There remains a gap in the literature regarding the specific nature of metalinguistic knowledge among intermediate-level adult Turkish learners—specifically, the difference between their ability to explain rules (metalinguistic) versus their ability to use technical terms (metalingual)—and how these distinct facets relate to the CAF dimensions of their writing. Most studies treat metalinguistic knowledge as a monolithic construct, but as Gutierrez (2013) and Berry (2005) suggest, the ability to recognize a rule and the ability to name it using formal metalanguage may operate differently in the learner's mind.

Therefore, the present study aims to fill this gap by investigating two primary objectives. First, it seeks to examine the nature of metalinguistic knowledge among intermediate-level adult Turkish EFL learners, distinguishing between productive and receptive knowledge, as well as between rule explanation and the use of technical language. Second, it explores the relationship between this metalinguistic knowledge and L2 writing performance, specifically focusing on the dimensions of complexity, accuracy, and fluency. By doing so, this study hopes to provide a clearer understanding of whether explicit linguistic awareness serves as a predictor for written accuracy and to offer pedagogical implications for the integration of form-focused instruction in the EFL classroom.
