intros.text:
Learners of a foreign language often need to communicate before they have fully mastered the linguistic resources required for accurate expression. In such situations, they may draw on communication strategies: conscious or semi-conscious attempts to overcome gaps in lexical, grammatical, phonological or orthographic knowledge while maintaining the communicative goal. Research on communication strategies has shown that learners do not simply abandon messages when difficulty arises; rather, they may approximate, restructure, borrow, code-switch, appeal for help, or use other compensatory devices to make meaning negotiable (Dörnyei & Scott, 1997; Faérch & Kasper, 1984; Yule & Tarone, 1987). These strategies are particularly important in beginner foreign language classrooms, where learners’ desire to express meanings frequently exceeds their available proficiency.

Mandarin Chinese presents distinctive challenges for learners whose first languages are alphabetic or non-tonal. Unlike alphabetic writing systems, Chinese characters do not consistently encode pronunciation in a transparent sound–symbol relationship. Although hanyu pinyin provides a Romanised representation of Mandarin sounds, learners must still master unfamiliar phonemic contrasts, syllable structures and tones while also learning characters. From a contrastive perspective, language learning difficulties are partly shaped by the distance between the target language and the learner’s existing linguistic system (Lado, 1957). For Malaysian learners whose dominant linguistic backgrounds are Malay, English or other local languages, several Mandarin sounds—such as retroflex and alveolar affricates and fricatives, aspirated and unaspirated plosives, and certain finals—may not have direct equivalents in their prior phonological repertoire. Consequently, learners may perceive and reproduce these sounds imprecisely, especially at beginning levels.

Previous studies on the learning of Chinese as a foreign language have paid considerable attention to character recognition, character production and character-learning strategies. Learners have been reported to use rote copying, repeated writing, component analysis, phonetic or semantic cues, and idiosyncratic memory techniques when learning Chinese characters (Ke, 1998; McGinnis, 1999; Sung, 2012). Other studies have examined the relationship between pronunciation, character identification and meaning recognition, suggesting that phonological knowledge may support the acquisition of Chinese orthography (Everson, 1998; Yang, 2000). However, less attention has been given to how learners strategically manipulate similar sounds in writing when they cannot retrieve or produce the exact Mandarin word or character. Such written attempts are important because they leave visible evidence of learners’ phonological awareness, uncertainty and problem-solving behaviour.

One strategy that emerges in this context is the use of similar sounding words. Instead of omitting an intended word or switching to another language, learners may write a pinyin form, a near-spelling, or a Chinese character that approximates the pronunciation of the target item. Although such forms are inaccurate, they may still provide enough phonetic information for the reader to infer the intended meaning. This strategy is intralingual in nature because it operates within Mandarin, yet it is also shaped by the learner’s developing perception of Mandarin sounds and by transfer from previously acquired languages.

The present study investigates the use of similar sounding words as a written communication strategy among Malaysian university students learning Mandarin as a foreign language. Specifically, it identifies the forms of similar sounding words produced in written tasks and examines the phonological or orthographic patterns underlying their use. By focusing on learners’ written approximations, the study aims to show not only the difficulties encountered in Mandarin phonetics and pinyin spelling, but also the constructive strategies learners employ to keep communication going despite limited proficiency.

intros.text:
Learners of a foreign language frequently need to communicate with linguistic resources that are still developing. In classroom settings, this need is especially visible when learners attempt to express meanings for which they have not yet fully mastered the relevant vocabulary, pronunciation, or writing system. Communication strategies therefore occupy an important place in second and foreign language learning because they reveal how learners manage gaps between communicative intention and available linguistic knowledge. Rather than simply indicating failure, such strategies can show active problem solving and learners’ willingness to sustain communication.

Communication strategies have been widely discussed in second language research. Dörnyei and Scott (1997) review how these strategies have been defined and classified, highlighting their problem-oriented and often conscious nature. Earlier taxonomies distinguish between strategies that reduce the intended message and those that help learners achieve it despite limited competence. In achievement-oriented strategies, learners may borrow from another language, translate literally, switch codes, approximate a target item, coin words, restructure an utterance, or appeal for assistance. Such strategies are particularly relevant when learners face lexical retrieval problems or uncertainty about the target form.

For learners of Mandarin as a foreign language, communication problems may be intensified by the distance between Mandarin and the learners’ familiar language systems. The contrastive view of language learning has long suggested that differences between languages may influence areas of difficulty for learners (Trager & Lado, 1957). Mandarin presents challenges not only at the lexical level but also in its phonological and orthographic systems. Its writing system does not operate like alphabetic scripts, and the relationship between Chinese characters and pronunciation is less transparent than the sound-symbol correspondence familiar to learners from alphabetic backgrounds. At the same time, Mandarin contains phonetic contrasts that may not exist in learners’ first languages, including distinctions among retroflex, alveolar and alveolo-palatal sounds, as well as aspirated and unaspirated consonants.

Previous research on Chinese as a foreign language has paid considerable attention to character recognition, character production, and character-learning strategies. Studies have examined how learners use repetition, character components, semantic and phonetic information, and other memory-based strategies in learning Chinese characters. This line of work has contributed to understanding how learners recognise and produce written Chinese. However, less attention has been given to how learners use written forms strategically when they cannot retrieve or produce the accurate Mandarin word. In particular, the use of similar sounding words as a written communication strategy remains insufficiently explored, although it may provide important evidence of learners’ phonological awareness, uncertainty and attempts to keep communication going.

This study investigates the use of similar sounding words by Malaysian learners of Mandarin as a foreign language. It focuses on written data produced by second- and third-year university students and examines how learners manipulate hanyu pinyin and Chinese characters when they are unsure of the accurate form. Specifically, the study identifies the types of similar sounding words used and the phonetic or orthographic features involved. By analysing these forms, the study aims to show how learners draw on partial knowledge of Mandarin sounds and writing to convey meaning, and how such strategies can inform the teaching of Mandarin pronunciation and writing to foreign language learners.

intros.text: Writing	may	be	the	most	challenging	activity	in	EFL	classroom.  Nepomuceno	(2011)	stated	that	writing	appears	to	be	the	most	difficult	among	the	four	language	skills.	Not	only	do	students	need	to	have	an	adequate	vocabulary	to	convey	their	thoughts	or	ideas	in	written	English,	but	they	need	to	pay	attention	to	grammar,	spelling,	and	punctuation.	Moreover,	they	should	be	able	to	make	their	composition	cohesive	and	coherent	to	make	it	meaningful	and	understandable.	Consequently,	many	English	as	a	Foreign	Language	(EFL)	students	are	hardly	able	to	produce	good	writing	due	to	the	language	limitation	and	poor	writing	skill.				That	English	is	a	foreign	language	makes	it	reasonable	to	consider	it	as	the	condition	underlying	the	students’	language	limitation.  Students	rarely	use	English	for	daily	communication	and	may	only	use	it	when	learning	it	at	school.	Students’	exposure	to	English	as	the	target	language	then	should	be	adequate	to	mitigate	this	issue.	Internet	technologies	ease	people	to	find	a	way	to	get	in	touch	with	English	in	a	virtual	world.	When	it	is	hard	to	find	a	way	to	communicate	in	English	in	the	physical	world,	students	can	make	it	possible	by	involving	themselves	in	virtual	societies	offering	such	possibility.	Blogging,	for	example,	can	be	utilised	to	support	English	teaching	and	learning  Nadzrah	and	Ismail	(2011)	emphasised	that	the	language	teaching	and	learning	should	not	be	secluded	from	society	to	enlarge	the	scope	of	language	that	students	can	learn.  The	application	of	blogs	in	teaching	and	learning	has	received	significant	attention,	including	in	writing.  Zhang	(2009)	claimed	that	the	potentials	of	blogs	used	for	EFL	writing	class	are	huge.	However,	Ozdemir	and	Aydin	(2015)	found	that	blogging	“is	not	superior	to	traditional	pen-paper	regarding	writing	achievement”	(p.	378).	The	schema	of	blog	use	in	teaching	and	learning	is	by	creating	personal	blogs	in	some	blogging	platforms,	such	as	WordPress.org	and	Blogger.com	(Ozdemir	&	Aydin,	2015;	Abu	Bakar	&	Ismail,	2011;	Zhang,	2009).  Such	a	mode	may	have	some	drawbacks,	such	as	the	audience	limited	to	the	students	of	the	classroom	when	no	attempts	are	made	to	attract	other	readers.  Thus,	the	way	the	blogging	activity	carried	out	in	this	study	was	not	through	personal	blogs	but	through	a	social	network	website,	MyEnglishClub,	whose	members	come	from	many	countries.	It	allows	its	members	to	upload	blog	posts	on	the	website	which	means	that	they	can	reach	a	wider	audience.  The	research	questions	addressed	in	this	study	were	if	incorporating	blogging	activity	into	an	EFL	writing	course	improved	EFL	students’	writing	skill,	and	how	student’s	perceptions	towards	blogging	were.

intros.text:
Writing is widely regarded as one of the most demanding skills for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL). It requires learners not only to master linguistic knowledge such as grammar, vocabulary, and mechanics, but also to organise ideas coherently and to communicate them effectively to an audience. In many EFL contexts, however, the limited hours allocated to writing instruction and the scarcity of opportunities for authentic writing practice beyond the classroom make it difficult for students to develop this skill. This challenge is even more pronounced in courses where English is taught for specific purposes and where writing competes with other language skills for classroom time. Consequently, teachers have increasingly sought ways to extend writing practice outside the classroom while at the same time engaging students in meaningful, authentic communication.

The rapid development of Internet technologies has opened new avenues for language teaching and learning. Among these technologies, blogs have attracted considerable attention as tools for teaching writing because they combine writing activity with virtual social interaction and easy web publishing (Abu Bakar & Ismail, 2011; Nepomuceno, 2011). Blogging enables students to write for a real and often global audience, to receive feedback from peers, teachers, and other readers, and to respond to comments on their own posts. In this way, writing becomes an interactive and social process rather than a solitary task performed only for the teacher. Blogs also expose learners to authentic reading texts, allowing them to observe the conventions of writing as they engage with the language as it is used beyond the classroom (Nepomuceno, 2011).

A growing body of research has examined the potential of blogging to support EFL and ESL writing. Zhang (2009) argued that blogs are effective tools for improving English writing and for engaging students in reflective learning. Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) reported that blogging encouraged students to go beyond the classroom and to write more constructively in English. Other studies, however, have shown that blogging alone does not guarantee better writing achievement, and that the writing instruction accompanying the activity plays a decisive role in learners' progress (Özdemir & Aydin, 2015). This suggests that blogging is likely to be most beneficial when it is integrated with a sound pedagogical approach to teaching writing rather than treated as an isolated technological add-on.

Against this background, the present study set out to improve the writing skill of EFL nursing students by incorporating a blogging activity, carried out on a social network website, into a writing course taught through the process-genre approach. Employing action research with mixed methods over two cycles, the study sought to determine whether such integration could enhance students' writing performance and to explore students' perceptions of the blogging activity.

intros.text:
Writing is widely acknowledged as one of the most demanding skills for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL) to master. Unlike speaking, which is more spontaneous, writing requires learners to attend simultaneously to content, organisation, vocabulary, grammar, and mechanics, and this complexity often makes it a challenging area both to teach and to learn. In recent years, the rapid development of Internet technologies has opened up new possibilities for supporting the teaching and learning of writing, and blogging in particular has attracted considerable attention as a tool that combines writing practice with authentic social interaction beyond the classroom.

A blog, or weblog, can be understood as a website that enables writers to publish running commentaries, thoughts, and stories publicly, while allowing readers to interact with the writers by giving comments (Abu Bakar & Ismail, 2011; Nepomuceno, 2011). The popularity of blogging stems partly from the ability of the Internet to connect people around the world and let them share ideas with one another (Nepomuceno, 2011). Assigning students to write online outside of classroom hours therefore allows them to learn in authentic social contexts and to be exposed to authentic learning materials, which supports the process of knowledge co-construction consistent with a social constructivist view of learning. Several studies have explored the pedagogical potential of blogs for writing, reporting that blogging encourages students to go beyond the classroom and interact with people (Abu Bakar & Ismail, 2011), that it can serve as an effective tool for improving English writing (Zhang, 2009), and that it can function as a viable alternative writing activity in tertiary ESL classes (Nepomuceno, 2011).

Despite this growing interest, the evidence on the effects of blogging on writing is not entirely consistent. Özdemir and Aydin (2015), for example, found that blogging itself did not guarantee better writing achievement among Turkish EFL learners, and that it was the process-based writing instruction, rather than the blog environment alone, that positively affected achievement. Relatively few studies have examined how blogging can be integrated with a principled writing approach within a specific EFL context, and little is known about how such integration works with ESP learners such as nursing students whose exposure to academic writing is limited. There remains a need to explore, in a real classroom, how incorporating blogging alongside an appropriate instructional approach might improve students' writing and how students perceive the activity.

The present study addresses this need by incorporating a blogging activity, carried out on a social network website that provides a blog section, into an EFL writing course taught through the process-genre approach. Using action research with mixed methods over two cycles, it aims to improve undergraduate nursing students' writing skill and to investigate their perceptions towards blogging.

intros.text:
The integration of advanced Internet technologies into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) pedagogy has transformed the way writing is taught and acquired. Among these technologies, blogging—the act of maintaining a weblog to publicly convey thoughts, stories, and opinions—has emerged as a powerful tool for language development. By transitioning writing activities from the traditional classroom to a virtual social environment, educators can provide students with opportunities to engage in authentic social contexts and expose them to genuine learning materials (Nepomuceno, 2011). Unlike traditional classroom assignments, blogging allows learners to interact with a global audience, fostering a sense of community and providing a platform for meaningful communication.

Research has increasingly highlighted the pedagogical potential of weblogs in the ESL/EFL context. Zhang (2009) suggests that blog exchanges are effective for improving English writing and encouraging reflective learning. Similarly, Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) found that blogging provides students with the freedom to express their thoughts while allowing them to connect and engage with peers online, thereby encouraging them to extend their learning beyond the physical boundaries of the classroom. However, the mere adoption of technology does not guarantee success. Özdemir and Aydın (2015) argue that blogging alone may not significantly enhance writing achievement; rather, it is the implementation of structured writing instruction, such as a process-based approach, that drives improvement. This suggests that for blogging to be effective, it must be integrated into a coherent instructional framework that emphasizes drafting, revising, and feedback.

From a theoretical perspective, blogging aligns closely with social constructivism, which posits that knowledge is co-constructed through social interaction and collaborative activity. When students post their work online, they receive feedback from peers, teachers, and native speakers, which helps them reconstruct their understanding of linguistic conventions. Furthermore, the ability to read and analyze authentic texts written by others enhances their awareness of grammar, coherence, and genre-specific patterns (Nepomuceno, 2011).

Despite these benefits, many EFL learners, particularly those in specialized fields like nursing, struggle with writing proficiency due to limited exposure to academic English and the complexities of English grammar. There is a need to explore how the synthesis of a process-genre approach and blogging can specifically address these challenges. Therefore, this study employs an action research design to investigate the impact of incorporating blogging into an EFL writing course for undergraduate nursing students. The aim is to determine whether this integration can improve students' writing skills and to explore their perceptions of using a social network website as a virtual writing platform.

intros.text:
The integration of advanced Internet technologies and virtual social interaction into English language teaching has gained considerable attention in recent years, particularly within the domain of writing instruction. Among these technologies, blogging has emerged as a popular tool for enhancing linguistic competence. By assigning students to write online outside of classroom hours, educators can provide learners with exposure to authentic learning materials and opportunities to engage in genuine communication within social contexts. 

Previous research has highlighted the pedagogical potential of weblogs in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) and English as a Second Language (ESL) classrooms. Zhang (2009) noted that blogs are effective tools for improving English writing and fostering reflective learning. Similarly, Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) found that blogging encourages students to extend their learning beyond the classroom, offering them a viable platform to express thoughts and connect with peers. Furthermore, Nepomuceno (2011) argued that blogs provide authentic reading texts that make learners more aware of writing conventions such as grammar and coherence. Despite these benefits, the impact of blogging on writing achievement is not always uniform. For instance, Özdemir and Aydın (2015) observed that blogging alone may not guarantee better writing performance unless it is paired with structured process-based writing instruction.

While the general benefits of blogging are documented, there remains a need for further empirical evidence on how blogging can be effectively integrated into specific EFL contexts—such as English for Specific Purposes (ESP)—and how it interacts with synthesized instructional frameworks like the process-genre approach. Most existing studies focus on general English proficiency, leaving a gap in understanding how blogging supports learners in professional contexts, such as nursing, where specific descriptive genres are required. Moreover, more research is needed to explore how a cyclical action research design can refine the implementation of blogging to address the diverse proficiency levels of adult learners.

Therefore, the purpose of the present study is to improve the writing skills of undergraduate nursing students by incorporating blogging activities into an EFL writing course. Specifically, this research employs an action research design consisting of two cycles to evaluate the effectiveness of combining blogging with a process-genre based approach. By utilizing a social network website to facilitate peer feedback and authentic interaction, this study aims to demonstrate how online writing can enhance students' linguistic accuracy and confidence. The results are expected to provide practical insights for EFL practitioners on leveraging social technologies to foster autonomous learning. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: the literature review discusses the theoretical foundations of social constructivism and the process-genre approach; the methodology describes the subjects and the action research cycles; the results section presents the quantitative and qualitative findings; and the discussion concludes with the pedagogical implications of the study.

intros.text:
The integration of technology into English language teaching has transformed traditional pedagogical approaches, particularly in the realm of writing instruction. Among various digital tools, blogs have gained considerable attention for their potential to enhance language learning through authentic social interaction. As defined by Martindale and Wiley (2004), blogs reduce technical barriers to web publishing, while Armstrong and Retterer (2008) describe them as running logs of commentaries and multimedia. In the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), blogging offers a platform where learners can engage in writing activities outside classroom hours, exposing them to authentic learning materials and social contexts (Nepomuceno, 2011). 

The theoretical underpinning for utilizing blogs in language education is Social Constructivism, a theory developed by Lev Vygotsky that emphasizes the collaborative nature of learning within cultural and social contexts (Jennings, Surgenor, & McMahon, 2013). According to this perspective, knowledge is co-constructed through interaction. Blogging facilitates this process by enabling social interaction between students, teachers, and a wider online audience. Through peer feedback and teacher guidance, students can reconstruct their understanding of language use, effectively operating within their Zone of Proximal Development (Vygotsky, 1978). Furthermore, blogs provide authentic texts that result from genuine communication rather than materials written specifically for language teaching (Nunan, 1999). These authentic texts allow learners to observe and analyze writing conventions such as grammar, mechanics, and coherence, thereby bridging the gap between classroom learning and real-world language use (Kilickaya, 2004).

Despite the growing popularity of blogging in language education, its specific impact on writing achievement remains a subject of investigation. Özdemir and Aydın (2015) found that while blogging itself does not guarantee better performance, a process-based writing instruction positively affects achievement in blog environments. Similarly, Zhang (2009) highlighted the effectiveness of blog exchanges for improving English writing and fostering reflective learning. In the ESL context, Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) noted that students view blogging as a viable platform that encourages constructive writing and interaction. However, many studies focus on general EFL contexts or specific regions, leaving a gap regarding the application of blogging within specific vocational courses, such as nursing, in the Indonesian context.

To address this gap, this study investigates the incorporation of blogging into an EFL writing course for nursing students. The research aims to improve students' writing skills by integrating blogging activities into a process-genre approach. This approach synthesizes product, process, and genre perspectives, ensuring that students practice writing skills while learning text structures and conventions (Badger & White, 2000). By utilizing a social network website, MyEnglishClub, the study explores whether blogging can enhance writing proficiency and foster positive perceptions among adult learners. Through an action research design involving two cycles of planning, acting, observing, and reflecting, this study seeks to provide empirical evidence on the efficacy of blogging as a pedagogical tool for developing autonomous and competent EFL writers.

intros.text:
The application of blogs in English teaching and learning, particularly in writing instruction, has gained considerable attention in recent years. As a digital tool that combines learning activities with advanced Internet technologies and virtual social interaction, blogging offers a promising avenue for enhancing language acquisition. Assigning students to write online outside classroom hours enables them to learn in authentic social contexts and exposes them to genuine learning materials, moving beyond the traditional confines of the classroom (Nepomuceno, 2011). This shift aligns with the growing recognition of the importance of integrating technology into language pedagogy to foster autonomous and communicative learners.

The theoretical underpinning for using blogs in education is often rooted in Social Constructivism, developed by Vygotsky (1978). This theory emphasizes the collaborative nature of learning and the importance of cultural and social context, positing that knowledge is co-constructed through interaction. In the context of blogging, students engage in social interaction with teachers and peers, receiving feedback that helps them construct knowledge and reconstruct their understanding. This process facilitates the 'zone of proximal development,' where learners can achieve more with guidance from more capable peers or adults (Jennings, Surgenor, & McMahon, 2013). Furthermore, blogs provide authentic texts for learners to observe and analyze, making them aware of writing conventions such as grammar, mechanics, and coherence (Nepomuceno, 2011). Unlike texts written specifically for language teaching, these authentic texts result from genuine communication, allowing learners to experience language as it is used in real-world contexts (Nunan, 1999).

Despite the potential benefits, the integration of blogging into EFL writing courses requires careful pedagogical design. Previous research has yielded mixed results regarding the direct impact of blogging on writing achievement. For instance, Özdemir and Aydın (2015) found that blogging itself does not guarantee better writing performance; rather, it is the process-based writing instruction within the blog environment that positively affects achievement. Similarly, while Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) noted that students viewed blogging as a viable platform for improving writing skills, they also highlighted challenges such as accessibility and the need for structured guidance. These findings suggest that the mere presence of a blog is insufficient; the pedagogical approach matters significantly.

In the realm of writing pedagogy, the process-genre approach has emerged as a synthesized model that combines the strengths of product, process, and genre-based approaches (Badger & White, 2000). This approach emphasizes both the linguistic knowledge required for specific text types and the cognitive processes of prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing (Brown, 2001). Incorporating blogging activities into a writing course supports this approach by allowing students to practice writing skills through iterative drafting and revision while receiving feedback from a diverse audience.

However, there remains a gap in the literature regarding the specific application of blogging within an action research framework in the Indonesian EFL context, particularly for nursing students. While studies have explored blogging in various settings, few have investigated its effectiveness when combined with the process-genre approach in a cyclical action research design. This study aims to address this gap by investigating the improvement of students' writing skills through the incorporation of blogging activities into an EFL writing course. Specifically, it seeks to determine the extent to which this intervention enhances writing proficiency and to explore students' perceptions of the blogging experience. By utilizing a mixed-methods approach, this research integrates quantitative data from writing tests with qualitative insights from observations and interviews to provide a comprehensive understanding of the intervention's impact.

intros.text:
Writing is a central skill in English as a foreign language (EFL) learning because it enables learners to communicate ideas, demonstrate linguistic knowledge, and participate in academic and professional communities. Yet for many EFL learners, writing remains difficult. They need to generate ideas, organize them coherently, choose appropriate vocabulary, use grammatical structures accurately, and observe mechanics such as spelling and punctuation. These demands are even more challenging for students whose main discipline is not English, such as nursing students, because English writing receives limited classroom time while still being relevant to their academic and professional needs.

The rapid development of Internet technologies has created new possibilities for addressing such challenges. One online medium that has attracted attention in language teaching is the blog. Blogs allow learners to publish texts, read other writers’ posts, and exchange comments with a real or wider audience. In this sense, blogging can extend writing practice beyond the classroom and transform writing from an individual classroom task into a more interactive social activity. Zhang (2009) argues that blogs can support English writing by encouraging reflection and providing opportunities for written exchange. Similarly, Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) report that blogging encourages ESL students to write constructively in English and to interact beyond classroom boundaries. Nepomuceno (2011) also suggests that blogs can function as alternative writing activities in tertiary ESL classes because they combine writing, reading, sharing, and responding to others’ texts.

However, the use of blogs does not automatically lead to better writing. Özdemir and Aydın (2015), for example, found that blogging alone did not produce higher EFL writing achievement, whereas process-based writing instruction contributed positively in both traditional and blog-based environments. This suggests that technology needs to be integrated with an appropriate pedagogical approach. A writing course that incorporates blogging should therefore include systematic guidance in planning, drafting, revising, editing, and publishing, as well as attention to genre, audience, language form, and feedback. From a social constructivist perspective, blogging is potentially valuable because learners can construct knowledge through interaction with teachers, peers, and other online participants. Feedback and discussion may help learners notice errors, compare language use, and revise their writing more meaningfully.

Despite increasing interest in blogging for language learning, classroom-based studies are still needed to show how blogging can be implemented in specific EFL contexts, particularly with adult learners and students from non-English majors. The present action research was conducted in an EFL writing course for undergraduate nursing students in South Kalimantan, Indonesia. It aimed to improve students’ writing skill by incorporating blogging activities through an English learning social network website, where students posted their writing, read others’ texts, received comments, and revised their work. The study also sought to explore students’ perceptions of blogging as part of the writing course.

intros.text:
Writing is one of the central skills in English language learning, yet it is often one of the most difficult for EFL learners to develop. Unlike oral communication, writing requires learners to control ideas, organization, vocabulary, grammar, and mechanics while also considering purpose and audience. In EFL contexts, where opportunities to use English outside the classroom may be limited, students frequently need additional spaces in which they can practise writing, receive responses, and revise their texts meaningfully. The rapid development of Internet technologies has created such spaces by enabling learners to publish texts, interact with readers, and access authentic language use beyond classroom boundaries.

Among the available online tools, blogs have attracted increasing attention in English teaching and learning. A blog provides a web-based environment in which users can post written texts, multimedia, and links, and readers can respond through comments. In language learning, this feature turns writing from a private classroom task into a social activity involving real or potential audiences. Abu Bakar and Ismail (2011) argue that blogs can encourage ESL students to write constructively because they provide opportunities for expression and interaction. Similarly, Zhang (2009) describes blogs as useful tools for English writing because they allow students to practise, exchange ideas, and reflect on their own writing. Nepomuceno (2011) also notes that blogging can function as an alternative writing activity in tertiary ESL classes, as it involves not only composing texts but also reading, sharing experiences, and responding to others.

The pedagogical value of blogging is closely related to social constructivist views of learning. From this perspective, knowledge is constructed through interaction with others and through participation in meaningful social contexts. When students write blog posts, read other texts, receive comments, and revise their writing, they engage in a process of co-constructing knowledge with peers, teachers, and wider online communities. Blogs may also expose learners to authentic texts and genuine communication, which are important for helping students observe how language is used outside instructional materials.

Nevertheless, the use of blogs does not automatically lead to better writing. Özdemir and Aydın (2015), for example, found that blogging by itself did not guarantee higher EFL writing achievement; rather, improvement was associated with process-based writing instruction in both traditional and blog environments. This suggests that blogging needs to be integrated with an appropriate pedagogical approach, such as a process-genre approach, in which students receive input on text organization and language features while also moving through planning, drafting, revising, and publishing stages. More classroom-based studies are therefore needed to examine how blogging can be incorporated into particular EFL writing courses and how students respond to such integration.

Responding to this need, the present action research investigated the incorporation of blogging into an EFL writing course for undergraduate nursing students in South Kalimantan, Indonesia. The study aimed to improve students’ writing skill through blogging activities conducted on an English learning social network website. Using mixed methods within two cycles of action research, the study examined students’ writing progress through test scores and explored classroom processes and student perceptions through observations and interviews.

intros.text: In teaching English as a Foreign Language, one of the ultimate goals is to develop interculturally competent citizens capable of interacting in multicultural environments (Byram 2020, 2008). Since language and culture are inseparable, culture must play a central role in the classroom. Textbooks, as institutionally sanctioned artefacts, are among the main carriers of cultural information, and learners tend to treat them as carriers of truth. For this reason, special attention should be paid to their cultural content, particularly at a time when English functions increasingly as a medium of international communication (McKay 2003; Baker 2011). Scholars have long argued that the acquisition of a particular culture should not be the only aim; rather, learners should develop the attitudes, skills and knowledge that allow them to negotiate cultural difference (Larrea Espinar 2015; Méndez García 2005). This article compares the cultural content of six B2-level EFL textbooks used in Spain, published between 1992 and 2013 by well-known publishing houses. Drawing on Lee's (2009) culture learning model, the study designs a three-fold cultural checklist to determine whether cultural content—general, big 'C' and small 'c'—has been incorporated into newer editions to answer globalised needs, and which skill is preferably used to do so.

intros.text: In teaching and learning English as a Foreign Language, developing interculturally competent citizens has become a central goal, and culture, therefore, plays a major role in the classroom (Byram 1997; Baker 2011). Since textbooks are institutionally sanctioned artefacts and carriers of cultural information, the cultural content they convey deserves close attention. A renewed interest in how culture is represented in EFL materials has produced numerous analyses, including studies by Lee (2009), Yuen (2011) and, in the Spanish context, Méndez-García (2005) and Larrea-Espinar (2015). These works consistently suggest that the invisible, small 'c' aspects of culture, crucial for understanding a society's values and ways of thinking, tend to be neglected in favour of visible, big 'C' facts. However, little is known about whether newer editions have incorporated broader cultural dimensions to answer to globalised needs, and even less about how the four language skills are distributed across cultural learning. To address these gaps, the present study compares the cultural content of six B2-level textbooks published in Spain between 1992 and 2013. Adopting Lee's (2009) culture learning model and content analysis methodology (Krippendorff 2004), it examines whether general, big 'C' and small 'c' content has evolved, and which skill is preferably used to convey it.

intros.text:
In the field of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), the primary objective has evolved beyond linguistic proficiency toward the development of interculturally competent citizens. Given that language and culture are inextricably linked, the role of cultural content in the classroom is paramount. Textbooks, as institutionally sanctioned artifacts, serve as the principal carriers of this cultural information, making their analysis essential for understanding how intercultural competence is fostered (Weninger & Kiss, 2015). Previous research in Spain has examined sociocultural content in high school materials (Méndez-García, 2005) and B1-level adult textbooks (Larrea-Espinar, 2015), often noting a neglect of the 'invisible' aspects of culture. However, there remains a need for a synchronic analysis that evaluates how these materials have evolved to meet the demands of a globalized world and how different communicative skills are utilized to transmit this content.

This study compares six B2-level textbooks published between 1992 and 2013 to identify the extent to which general culture, big 'C' (visible), and small 'c' (invisible) dimensions have been incorporated. Specifically, it seeks to determine if newer editions better address globalized needs and which linguistic skills—reading, listening, speaking, or writing—are predominantly used to deliver this cultural learning.

intros.text:
In the teaching and learning of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), a primary goal is to develop interculturally competent citizens. Consequently, culture must play a major role in the curriculum. As textbooks are the primary carriers of cultural information in the classroom, special attention must be paid to their cultural content. This article compares the cultural content of six B2-level EFL textbooks used in Spain, published between 1992 and 2013. The study aims to identify whether cultural content—specifically general culture, big 'C' culture, and small 'c' culture—has been incorporated into newer editions to address globalised needs. Furthermore, it seeks to determine which language skills are preferably used to transmit this content. 

While scholars like Byram (1997, 2008) have emphasised the importance of intercultural communicative competence (ICC) and intercultural citizenship, previous research suggests textbooks often focus on superficial, visible cultural aspects (Kramsch, 1993). Recent studies by Larrea-Espinar (2015) and Méndez-García (2005) in the Spanish context highlight a neglect of invisible cultural dimensions. Adopting a culture learning model developed by Lee (2009) and utilising content analysis methodology (Krippendorff, 2004), this study quantifies qualitative data to assess the evolution of cultural representation. The findings will inform whether publishing houses are effectively responding to the demands of a globalised world or merely decorating texts with anecdotal facts.

intros.text: In English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts, developing intercultural competence is widely acknowledged as a primary goal of language education. As textbooks serve as the primary carriers of cultural information in the classroom, their content requires critical scrutiny to ensure they align with these pedagogical aims. Theoretical frameworks, such as Byram's (2020) Intercultural Communicative Competence, emphasize the need to move beyond superficial knowledge of 'big C' culture—facts, festivals, and folklore—towards an understanding of 'small c' culture, encompassing values, beliefs, and worldviews. However, despite this theoretical shift, empirical evidence suggests a persistent gap between intended curriculum and textbook reality. Previous studies in the Spanish context, including Méndez García (2005) and Larrea Espinar (2015), have highlighted the neglect of invisible cultural aspects in EFL materials. Yet, few investigations have examined the evolution of cultural content across decades of publication or analyzed how specific language skills are utilized to transmit different cultural dimensions. This study addresses these gaps by conducting a content analysis of six B2-level textbooks published between 1992 and 2013. Specifically, it investigates whether newer editions incorporate general and small 'c' cultural content to meet globalized needs and determines which language skills are preferentially used for cultural transmission. The findings aim to inform textbook design and pedagogy, advocating for materials that foster genuine intercultural awareness rather than mere cultural tourism.

intros.text: Culture has become a central concern in English as a Foreign Language teaching because learning a language also entails learning how meanings, identities and social practices are negotiated across communities. In a context where English increasingly functions as an international language, learners cannot be prepared only to imitate native-speaker norms or accumulate facts about English-speaking countries; rather, they need intercultural awareness and the ability to interpret, compare and mediate among diverse cultural perspectives (McKay, 2003; Baker, 2011; Byram, 2020). This shift has important implications for classroom materials, since textbooks remain one of the main sources through which learners encounter cultural representations and tasks. Previous research has shown that EFL textbooks often privilege visible, factual or touristic aspects of culture, while giving less attention to values, beliefs, interactional norms and reflective intercultural learning (Méndez García, 2005; Larrea Espinar, 2015). In Spain, where commercial textbooks are widely used in language centres and higher education contexts, examining how culture is embedded in such materials is therefore especially relevant. This study analyses six B2-level EFL textbooks published between 1992 and 2013 in order to determine whether more recent materials incorporate broader dimensions of cultural learning—general culture, big ‘C’ culture and small ‘c’ culture—and to identify which language skills are most commonly used to mediate this content.

intros.text:
The inseparability of language and culture has long been recognised in English language teaching, but its pedagogical significance has become more pressing as English is increasingly used for international and intercultural communication. In this context, EFL education is expected not merely to transmit linguistic forms or factual information about English-speaking countries, but to help learners develop intercultural communicative competence and intercultural citizenship (Byram, 2008, 2020). Such aims require attention to both visible cultural products and practices, often described as big “C” culture, and less visible values, beliefs and interactional norms, or small “c” culture, as well as more general abilities to interpret, compare and negotiate cultural meanings (Baker, 2011).

Textbooks are central mediators of this process because they organise much of what learners encounter in institutional EFL classrooms. Previous research has shown that cultural representation in ELT materials is often uneven, stereotypical or excessively focused on target-language national cultures (Méndez García, 2005; Larrea Espinar, 2015; McKay, 2003). However, further evidence is needed on whether more recent textbooks reflect the intercultural turn and on how cultural content is linked to language skills. This study analyses six B2-level EFL textbooks used in Spain, published between 1992 and 2013, to determine the presence of general, big “C” and small “c” cultural content and the skills through which such content is presented.

intros.text: The  popularity  of  Content  and  Language  Integrated  Learning  (CLIL)  across  Europe has escalated in recent decades (Marsh 2013).  The rationale behind CLIL is that it is both possible and desirable to expand learners’ linguistic competence in one or more additional language(s) through their use as vehicular language(s) in the teaching of selected content subjects (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010; Mehisto, Marsh and Frigols 2008). In  spite  of  this  predominantly  positive  view,  some  critical  voices  have  been  raised  against  the  ‘CLIL  frenzy’.  Bonnet  (2012:  66)  states  that  the  “added  value  of  CLIL”  needs  to  be  questioned.  In  fact,  in  some  contexts  research  confirms  the  negative  effect  of  CLIL  on  learners’  knowledge  of  content  subjects  and  on  their  command of the language of instruction, partly attributed to the inappropriate input they receive from their teachers (Costa and D’Angelo 2011). For some, it is possible that  the  purported  benefits  of  CLIL  stem  from  external  factors,  such  as  the  socio-educational background of CLIL students, rather than to CLIL tuition itself (Bonnet 2012; Bruton 2011, 2013; Costa and D’Angelo 2011). Even the consideration of CLIL as an umbrella term, encompassing “any learning activity where language is used as a tool to develop new learning from a subject area or theme” (Coyle, Holmes and King 2009: 6), has led others (Cenoz, Genesee and Gorter 2013, Cenoz 2015) to wonder whether  there  is  any  teaching  or  learning  activity  that  does  not  fall  within  CLIL.  On  the  other  hand,  the  outcomes  of  this  approach  have  been  covered  extensively. CLIL allows the construction of content and language knowledge on the  basis  of  semantic  scaffolding  (Lorenzo  et  al.  2009;  Marsh  2009;  Meyer  2010).  Besides, CLIL learners are credited with a better mastery of oral registers (Berton 2008;  Marsh  2007;  Frigols  2008),  particularly  speaking  (Coyle  2013;  Lasagabaster  2008; Ruiz de Zarobe 2008, 2011), lexico-grammatical competence and pragmatic efficiency  (Jexenflicker  and  Dalton-Puffer  2010;  Lo  and  Murphy  2010;  Lorenzo  et  al.  2009;  Madrid  2011).  Learners  experience  greater  involvement  in  a  more  enjoyable  environment  (Coyle  2013)  and,  as  a  result,  they  are  more  motivated  towards learning an additional language (Arnold 2011; Coonan 2012; Frigols 2008; Merisuo-Storm 2007; D’Angelo and García 2012; Ruiz de Zarobe 2013). CLIL is also said to contribute to broader educational objectives, such as critical thinking and intercultural learning (Méndez García 2013). In  terms  of  professional  growth,  CLIL  creates  an  egalitarian  atmosphere  in  which  both  teachers  and  students  become  co-experts  in  the  additional  language  and cooperate to co-construct language learning and classroom interaction “while the  technical  content  expertise  remains  with  the  teacher”  (Hüttner,  Dalton-Puffer  and  Smit  2013:  276).  CLIL  also  boosts  teachers’  self-esteem  and  motivation  by  triggering “rethinking of their teaching vision” (D’Angelo and García 2012: 76). In this  context,  teachers’  perceptions  of  their  actual  performance  may  significantly  affect their understanding of the challenges that CLIL entails (Halbach 2009; Ramos Ordóñez and Pavón 2015), how to construct teacher collaboration (Meyer 2010), and  how  to  scrutinise  teachers’  profile  and  competences  (D’Angelo  and  García,  2012;  Hylliard  2001;  Pavón  and  Ellison  2013).  A  lot  of  attention  then  has  been  given to reviewing teachers’ opinions of their role in CLIL and a number of studies have  specifically  investigated  teachers’  perceptions  of  CLIL  in  different  European  contexts (Hüttner et al. 2013 [Austria]; Infante, Benvenuto and Lastrucci 2009 [Italy]; Moliner 2013; Pena and Porto 2008; Travé 2013 [Spain]; Viebrock 2012 [Germany])  This paper sets out to look into teachers’ views of professional coordination. Coordination has been reported to produce positive results in English as a Second Language  (ESL)  and  content-based  instruction  contexts  (Creese  2010;  Davison  2006; Tan 2011)  In particular, this paper investigates teachers’ opinions about the difficulties and benefits arising from collaboration between content and language teachers,  and  on  the  roles  they  take  while  establishing  this  coordinated  work;  it  also  analyses  CLIL  in  their  professional  careers  and,  more  specifically,  how  it  influences their own academic and professional development.

intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has emerged over the past two decades as one of the most dynamic educational trends in Europe, offering an approach in which academic content and an additional language are taught simultaneously (Coyle, Hood & Marsh 2010; Marsh 2013). While CLIL and content-based instruction share their essential properties (Cenoz 2015), the widespread adoption of CLIL programmes has generated considerable interest in identifying the factors that determine their success. A substantial body of research has explored learners' language gains (Ruiz de Zarobe 2008; Lasagabaster 2008; Dalton-Puffer et al. 2010), the development of literacy and vocabulary (Merisuo-Storm 2007; Lo & Murphy 2010), and learners' motivation and perceptions of successful learning (Coonan 2012; Coyle 2013). Yet, alongside these learner-oriented enquiries, growing attention has been paid to the conditions under which effective integration of content and language actually takes place, and, in particular, to the coordination and collaboration between the professionals who plan, implement and assess CLIL provision (Davison 2006; Lorenzo, Trujillo & Vez 2011; Viebrock 2012).

A decisive, though frequently underexplored, factor in this respect is the teacher. Teachers' perceptions of their own professional identity, their pedagogical standpoints and their sense of the roles they take are known to exert a considerable influence on how educational innovations are enacted in the classroom (Tan 2011; Viebrock 2012). Research on teacher cognition has long acknowledged that beliefs, though not directly observable, are 'a guide to thought and behaviour' (Borg 2001) and that, without addressing teachers' pre-existing beliefs, changes 'cannot successfully be implemented in teacher attitudes or behaviour' (Hüttner et al. 2013). In CLIL settings specifically, teachers' lay theories have been shown to shape the very construction of what counts as success (Hüttner et al. 2013), while their attitudes, expectations of support and perceived achievements condition their willingness to engage in collegial participation (Pena & Porto 2008; Méndez García & Pavón 2012). Understanding teachers' professed views is therefore essential if the drivers of effective CLIL are to be more fully grasped.

Central to these views is the question of coordination. The literature converges on the idea that partnership between language and content teachers is a prerequisite of quality integrated teaching, requiring shared conceptualisation of planning, common curricula, agreed roles and joint assessment procedures (Davison 2006). However, such collaboration is far from unproblematic: it demands time, incentives and relationship building, and it may be met with anxiety, resistance and clashes over control (Hargreaves 1994; Musanti & Pence 2010). Moreover, pedagogies valued by language professionals are often perceived as less important than content teachers' own practices (Creese 2010), which complicates the negotiation of a shared methodological foundation. Beyond the language–content interface, coordination among content teachers and among the various language teachers present in the curriculum has received comparatively little attention, despite indications that it may foster the assimilation of academic material and the transfer of communication strategies across languages (Méndez García & Pavón 2012; Ramos Ordóñez & Pavón 2015).

This study addresses these concerns in the context of Andalusia, a monolingual Spanish region where the Plan to Promote Plurilingualism has driven the large-scale introduction of partial-immersion CLIL programmes across primary and secondary schools (Junta de Andalucía 2005; Méndez García 2013). Drawing on qualitative data gathered from 42 primary and secondary teachers of both content and language subjects, the aim is to investigate how CLIL shapes teachers' perceptions of the roles they take and of their own professional development, as well as their understanding of the importance of establishing coordination processes. The study explicitly examines professed rather than enacted beliefs, exploring how teachers perceive the impact of CLIL on their practice and how they conceive of interdisciplinary coordination at three distinct levels: between foreign language and content teachers, among content teachers themselves, and among foreign language and first language teachers. In doing so, it seeks to give voice to practitioners actively engaged in CLIL and to illuminate the perceived benefits, roles and obstacles associated with building a structure of collaboration — dimensions that ultimately bear upon the quality and sustainability of CLIL provision (Mehisto 2009; Marsh & Meyer 2012).

intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has emerged since the turn of the millennium as one of the most dynamic pedagogical trends in European education, gaining considerable momentum and being progressively incorporated into academic programmes across the continent (Coyle, Hood & Marsh 2010; Ruiz de Zarobe 2013). In monolingual regions such as the southern Spanish Autonomous Community of Andalusia, the introduction of bilingual programmes has arguably produced one of the most significant turning points in the country's recent educational history (Méndez García 2013). This expansion has been accompanied by a growing body of research seeking to understand which factors underpin the effectiveness of CLIL and what conditions must be met for it to yield the benefits attributed to it. Given the sheer variety and complexity of the variables involved, however, there is broad consensus that no single, standardised CLIL model exists (Cenoz, Genesee & Gorter 2013; Marsh 2013).

Among the many drivers of successful CLIL implementation, considerable attention has been paid to the significance of coordination and collaboration between all the stakeholders involved (Lorenzo, Casal & Moore 2009; Viebrock 2012). Particularly decisive are the exchanges between language teachers and content teachers, since it is through the integration of content and language that the approach is expected to work. Davison (2006) has set out the foundations of content and language teaching co-operation as a process requiring shared conceptualisation of tasks, a common curriculum, agreed goals and assessment, and clearly defined roles and responsibilities. Yet collaboration is far from unproblematic: it calls for external support and incentives, internal resources, time, and relationship-building, and may generate anxiety, resistance and personality clashes (Hargreaves 1994; Musanti & Pence 2010).

Parallel to this line of enquiry, research on teacher cognition has repeatedly stressed the importance of teachers' beliefs and perceptions of their own professional identity, pedagogical standpoints and classroom performance, since these constitute a decisive factor in teaching and in teachers' willingness to embrace change (Borg 2006; Tan 2011). The way teachers view educational practices exerts an enormous influence on their actions in the classroom, and without addressing their pre-existing beliefs, changes cannot be successfully implemented (Hüttner, Dalton-Puffer & Smit 2013). Investigating teachers' perceptions therefore offers valuable insight not only into their own classroom behaviour and professional development, but also into how they conceive of and engage in the collaborative processes that CLIL demands (Pena & Porto 2008; Méndez García & Pavón Vázquez 2012).

Despite this growing interest, several aspects of teacher coordination in CLIL remain insufficiently explored. Much of the existing research on collaboration has focused on classroom methods and techniques or on the linguistic demands of content areas, with comparatively little attention devoted to the process of co-planning and co-teaching itself (Davison 2006; Creese 2010). Moreover, while coordination between language and content teachers has attracted sustained interest, coordination among content teachers and, above all, coordination between teachers of the different languages present in the curriculum has received far less attention. There is thus a need to examine how teachers themselves perceive and structure these various levels of interdisciplinary coordination, and how participation in CLIL shapes their views of their own professional development.

The present study aims to address this gap by investigating teachers' perceptions of how CLIL influences content and language teachers' understanding of the roles they take and of their own professional development, as well as their opinions on the importance of establishing coordination processes. It should be noted that the study looks into professed rather than enacted beliefs. More specifically, it explores coordination between language and content teachers, between content teachers, and between teachers of the different languages in the curriculum, guided by four research questions concerning the impact of CLIL on professional development and the ways in which teachers perceive and structure these three types of coordination. To this end, qualitative data were gathered through an open-ended questionnaire administered to forty-two primary and secondary teachers involved in the Andalusian Plan to Promote Plurilingualism, and analysed following an inductive, grounded-theory approach. The findings are expected to shed light on how teachers conceive of coordination and collaboration, and to offer implications for schools and educational administrations seeking to foster effective CLIL practice.

intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has emerged as a dominant trend in European education, offering a pedagogical framework where an additional language is used as the medium for teaching academic content (Coyle et al., 2010). By integrating the study of a foreign language with non-linguistic disciplines, CLIL aims to enhance both linguistic proficiency and cognitive development (Bruton, 2011). While various models of integration exist, and research has highlighted significant gains in lexico-grammar and vocabulary among students (Bruton, 2011; Lo & Murphy, 2010), the successful implementation of these programmes is often complex and varies according to local contexts (Marsh, 2013). In Spanish monolingual areas, specifically in Andalusia, the introduction of such programmes has represented a major turning point in educational history, focusing not only on language competence but also on the development of intercultural communicative competence (Méndez García, 2013).

A critical driver for the success of any CLIL programme is the human element, specifically the teachers' cognition and their professional identity. Literature on teacher cognition emphasizes that beliefs—defined as propositions consciously or unconsciously held—serve as a guide to thought and behaviour (Borg, 2001). Because changes in educational practice cannot be successfully implemented without addressing pre-existing beliefs (Hüttner et al., 2013), understanding how teachers perceive their roles is essential. Teachers' perceptions of their own identity and pedagogical standpoints act as decisive factors in how they embrace innovation (Tan, 2011). In the CLIL context, these perceptions are often intertwined with the affective domain, including motivation and the stress associated with the demanding nature of teaching in a second language (Arnold, 2011; Coonan, 2012).

Central to the operational efficacy of CLIL is the necessity for stakeholders to coordinate and collaborate (Viebrock, 2012). The integration of content and language is not an automatic outcome of using a vehicular language; rather, it requires a structured process of co-planning and co-teaching (Davison, 2006). Effective coordination between foreign language (FL) teachers and content teachers is often viewed as a sine qua non for success, as it allows for the alignment of linguistic support with academic demands. However, this collaboration is frequently hindered by systemic issues such as incompatible schedules and a lack of institutional resources (Davison, 2006; Tan, 2011). Furthermore, there is often a tension between the pedagogical practices of language specialists and those of content teachers, which can lead to resistance or personality clashes (Creese, 2010).

While much research has focused on the coordination between language and content specialists, other dimensions of interdisciplinary collaboration remain under-explored. This includes the coordination among content teachers themselves to ensure thematic cohesion, as well as the synergy between teachers of the mother tongue (L1) and the additional language (FL) to promote metalinguistic reflection and positive transference (Méndez García & Pavón, 2012). Establishing a comprehensive structure of connection across these three levels is thought to be crucial for the achievement of sustainable educational outputs (Baetens-Beardsmore, 2009).

Given this backdrop, the present study aims to investigate how CLIL influences the professional development and self-perceptions of teachers in Andalusia. Specifically, it seeks to explore how content and language teachers perceive and structure their roles within a framework of cross-curricular coordination. By examining professed beliefs regarding the collaboration between FL and content teachers, among content teachers, and between FL and L1 teachers, this research endeavours to gain insight into the perceived benefits and challenges of establishing a truly integrated curriculum. In doing so, the study hopes to contribute to the evidence base for CLIL, highlighting the professional shifts required to move from isolated teaching practices toward a collaborative, interdisciplinary model.

intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has emerged since the millennium as a major trend in European education (Coyle, Hood & Marsh, 2010). By using an additional language as the medium of instruction for non-linguistic subjects, CLIL aims to foster both academic content mastery and linguistic competence simultaneously. Given its innovative nature, the approach has gained significant traction across various educational levels and contexts, often viewed as a catalyst for enhancing learners' motivation and cognitive development (Coonan, 2012; Bruton, 2011). However, the successful implementation of CLIL is a complex endeavour, as there is no single standardised model that fits all contexts (Marsh, 2013). Instead, its effectiveness depends on a variety of intersecting factors, including curricular organisation, pedagogical choices, and the roles assumed by the educators involved (Cenoz et al., 2013).

Central to the success of any CLIL programme is the human element—specifically, the teachers. Research in teacher cognition highlights that teachers' beliefs and perceptions are not merely background variables but are decisive factors in how they embrace educational change and perform in the classroom (Tan, 2011; Méndez García & Pavón, 2012). In CLIL environments, these beliefs often revolve around professional identity and the perceived challenge of balancing subject expertise with linguistic demands (Hüttner et al., 2013). Because beliefs act as a guide to behaviour, understanding how teachers perceive their roles is essential for ensuring that the theoretical goals of CLIL are translated into effective classroom practice.

Furthermore, because CLIL inherently blends two distinct domains of expertise, cross-curricular coordination is widely regarded as a sine qua non for the approach's success (Lorenzo, Trujillo & Vez, 2011). Effective integration requires a high degree of collaboration between foreign language (FL) teachers, who provide the linguistic scaffolding, and content teachers, who ensure academic rigour (Davison, 2006). Ideally, this coordination involves co-planning, shared assessment criteria, and a unified pedagogical foundation (Coyle et al., 2009). Despite these recognized benefits, establishing such partnerships is often fraught with difficulties, ranging from scheduling conflicts and bureaucratic burdens to resistance to pedagogical shifts (Davison, 2006; Creese, 2010). While much research has focused on the linguistic outcomes for students or the general methodology of CLIL, there remains a need for deeper insight into how teachers themselves perceive these coordination processes and how such collaboration influences their own professional growth.

To date, while the necessity of collaboration has been established, fewer studies have empirically explored the nuanced perceptions of teachers regarding the different levels of coordination—not only between language and content specialists but also among content teachers themselves and between various language teachers (L1 and FL). Understanding these perspectives is crucial for developing support structures that move beyond intuition and toward evidence-based professional development.

Therefore, the main objective of the present qualitative study is to investigate teachers' perceptions regarding the impact of CLIL on their professional development and their understanding of the roles they assume within a coordinated framework. Specifically, the study seeks to answer: (a) In what way does CLIL affect teachers' perception of their professional development? (b) How do content and foreign language teachers perceive and structure interdisciplinary coordination? (c) How do content teachers perceive and structure their own interdisciplinary coordination? and (d) How do foreign language and first language teachers perceive and structure their own interdisciplinary coordination?

By exploring these questions, the study aims to offer a contextualised account of how collaboration facilitates the assimilation of academic content and improves language proficiency. The findings may provide valuable insights for school administrators and policymakers in designing schedules and incentives that foster genuine teacher collaboration. The remainder of this article is organised as follows: Section 2 reviews the literature on teacher beliefs and perceptions; Section 3 discusses the theoretical framework of cross-curricular coordination; Section 4 details the research design and methodology; Section 5 presents the results; and Section 6 provides a discussion and concluding remarks.

intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has emerged as a prominent educational approach across Europe, driven by the desire to enhance both content knowledge and foreign language proficiency simultaneously. While the theoretical underpinnings of CLIL are well-documented, the practical implementation of such programmes relies heavily on the human element: the teachers. Success in CLIL is not merely a function of curriculum design or policy mandates but is significantly influenced by the perceptions, beliefs, and professional identities of the educators involved. As Hüttner et al. (2013) argue, the strength of teachers' beliefs and their lay theories regarding language learning and CLIL success play a central role in how these programmes are enacted in the classroom. Without addressing these pre-existing beliefs, changes in teacher attitudes or behaviour cannot be successfully implemented. Consequently, understanding how teachers perceive their own roles and professional development within a CLIL context is a critical area of research.

A decisive factor in the effectiveness of CLIL is the coordination and collaboration between language teachers and content teachers. In traditional educational settings, these two groups often operate in isolation, with distinct curricula and pedagogical approaches. However, CLIL necessitates a shift towards a more integrated model where the boundaries between language and content are blurred. Davison (2006) highlights that effective collaboration requires teachers to conceptualise tasks together, adopt a common curriculum, and agree on roles and responsibilities. This process is not without its challenges; it demands external support, internal resources, and the development of trust, which can take time to establish. Furthermore, Creese (2010) notes that pedagogies perceived as highly effective by language professionals are sometimes viewed as less important by content teachers, creating potential friction in collaborative efforts. Despite these difficulties, co-operation constitutes a *sine qua non* of the teaching profession in CLIL environments, as it is only through peer exchanges that isolation is overcome and knowledge is co-constructed.

Research on teacher cognition acknowledges that beliefs are closely related to constructs such as assumptions and knowledge, often referred to as BAK (Woods 1996). These beliefs guide thought and behaviour, influencing how teachers respond to educational innovations (Borg 2001). In the context of CLIL, teachers' perceptions of their practice and their willingness to engage in collegial participation are influenced by factors such as their expectations of support, their attitude towards CLIL, and the effort they perceive is required (Coonan 2007; Moliner 2013). Moreover, the implementation of CLIL in monolingual regions, such as Andalusia in Spain, presents unique challenges. As Méndez García (2013) suggests, the introduction of CLIL in such areas represents a significant turning point in educational history, potentially fostering intercultural competence but also requiring a radical redefinition of teacher roles.

While previous studies have examined the effects of CLIL on student outcomes (e.g., Cenoz et al. 2013; Lorenzo et al. 2009) or focused on specific aspects of language development (e.g., Bruton 2011), fewer studies have delved deeply into the teachers' own perceptions of their professional development and the structural coordination required to make the programme work. Tan (2011) found that teachers' beliefs about their respective roles as content or language teachers can limit students' language learning opportunities, highlighting the need for sustained professional development. Similarly, Coonan (2012) points out that while CLIL can promote interest and enthusiasm, the added difficulties of the learning environment can lead to negative reactions if not managed well. Therefore, it is essential to investigate how teachers themselves view the impact of CLIL on their professional profiles and their understanding of the importance of establishing coordination processes.

The aim of this study is to investigate how CLIL influences content and language teachers' perceptions regarding the roles they take and their own professional development. Specifically, it endeavours to gain insight into CLIL teachers' opinions on the importance of establishing coordination processes between foreign language teachers and content teachers, as well as among teachers of the same subject area. By focusing on the Andalusian context, where the Plan to Promote Plurilingualism has been in operation for several years, this research seeks to provide a nuanced understanding of the collaborative dynamics in a partial-immersion programme. The study addresses the gap in literature regarding the 'professed' beliefs of teachers concerning cross-curricular coordination, a factor that is often cited as fundamental to the success of CLIL but remains under-explored from the perspective of the practitioners themselves. Through this inquiry, the study hopes to contribute to the broader discourse on how teacher collaboration can be effectively structured to support the dual goals of content and language learning.
