intros.text:
Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) has become one of the most influential educational initiatives for promoting multilingualism in Europe. By teaching curricular content through an additional language, CLIL is expected to increase learners’ exposure to the foreign language while preserving the learning of subject matter. In Spain, where foreign language competence has traditionally been a major educational concern, bilingual programmes have expanded rapidly across autonomous communities and have become a central component of language education policy. This expansion has been particularly visible in monolingual regions, where the school often constitutes the main setting in which students can encounter and use English for meaningful purposes.

The growth of CLIL has been accompanied by an increasingly substantial body of research. Early and subsequent reviews have underlined its potential to foster language learning, motivation, and methodological innovation, while also pointing to the complexity of its implementation in real school contexts (Pérez Cañado, 2011; Dalton-Puffer et al., 2010; Llinares, 2011). Research has also shown that CLIL cannot be understood as a single, uniform model: it is shaped by local policies, available resources, teacher profiles, school cultures, and the beliefs of the actors who implement it (Dalton-Puffer & Smit, 2013). Thus, the effectiveness of bilingual education depends not only on the formal design of programmes, but also on how teachers, students, families, management teams, and educational authorities interpret and enact them.

At the same time, the enthusiastic spread of CLIL has generated debate. Some authors have warned against presenting CLIL as an unquestioned educational solution or panacea, especially when empirical evidence is uneven or when programmes rely on student selection, high levels of investment, or exceptional teacher commitment (Bruton, 2011; Paran, 2013). In response, other scholars have called for more balanced research agendas that acknowledge both the documented benefits and the unresolved difficulties of CLIL implementation (Pérez Cañado, 2016). Such a balanced perspective is particularly necessary in contexts where bilingual programmes have moved from small-scale innovation to system-wide policy. Once programmes are no longer experimental, research needs to examine not only outcomes, but also the conditions that allow schools to sustain quality.

Stakeholder perceptions are especially relevant in this regard. The way participants understand CLIL influences their expectations, classroom practices, willingness to collaborate, and evaluation of success. Hüttner et al. (2013) argue that beliefs and lay theories form part of extended language policy, because they mediate the relationship between official regulations and local practice. Their work shows that teachers and learners may construct notions of CLIL success that differ from those assumed by policy-makers or researchers. Similarly, studies which give voice to learners reveal that students’ accounts can illuminate dimensions of classroom learning that are not always visible through achievement measures alone (Coyle, 2013). Perception studies therefore provide valuable evidence for identifying what schools experience as strengths, tensions, and needs.

Previous research has explored the views of different groups involved in bilingual programmes. At tertiary level, Dafouz et al. (2007) examined teachers’ and students’ reactions to CLIL implementation, while Fernández-Costales (2015) analysed teacher satisfaction in bilingual programmes. In school contexts, Pladevall-Ballester (2014) investigated students’, teachers’, and parents’ opinions in Catalan primary schools and found generally positive attitudes alongside concerns about materials, support, and teacher preparation. Martínez and Llavador (2016), in their assessment of bilingual sections in Castile and León, reported high teacher satisfaction but also highlighted continuing needs for professional development and international links. In Colombia, McDougald (2015) showed that teachers tended to value CLIL positively but also felt uncertain about methodology and content-language integration. These studies suggest that favourable attitudes often coexist with practical constraints, and that perception research can help locate the gap between policy aspirations and everyday implementation.

In Spain, research on CLIL has also examined affective factors, language competences, and additional learning benefits. Lasagabaster and Doiz (2015) considered the impact of CLIL on affective variables, while Navarro Pablo (2018) analysed motivation and its relationship with language attainment. Nieto Moreno de Diezmas (2016) reported evidence on the contribution of CLIL to English competences in primary education, and later work explored possible effects on cross-curricular competences such as digital competence (Nieto Moreno de Diezmas, 2018). These studies have contributed to the discussion of CLIL outcomes, but they also reinforce the need to understand the institutional and human factors that make such outcomes possible.

One of the most frequently mentioned factors is coordination. Since CLIL involves the integration of language and content, it requires collaboration between content teachers, language teachers, coordinators, and school leadership. Pavón Vázquez and Méndez García (2017) stress that cross-curricular coordination is fundamental for effective CLIL practice and for redefining teachers’ professional roles. However, coordination is not merely a methodological recommendation; it is also an organizational demand which depends on timetables, workload, recognition, and shared responsibility. Where these conditions are weak, language teachers may remain peripheral to bilingual programmes, content teachers may feel overburdened, and programme coordinators may lack sufficient authority or time.

Another recurring issue concerns resources and teacher support. Effective CLIL programmes require suitable materials, methodological training, linguistic competence, reduced ratios in some contexts, and opportunities for internationalization. Teacher education has therefore been identified as a key dimension of sustainable CLIL (Banegas et al., 2011; Navés, 2009). The role of native language assistants has also attracted attention, particularly in Spanish bilingual schools, where assistants are often viewed as valuable linguistic and cultural resources (Tobin & Abello-Contesse, 2013). Yet the value attributed to native speakers may also reveal underlying beliefs about language learning, pronunciation, authenticity, and legitimate models of English, as shown in ethnographic research on bilingualism in Castilla-La Mancha (Relaño-Pastor, 2018). Exploring how stakeholders talk about native assistants can therefore uncover broader assumptions about bilingual education.

Despite the relevance of these issues, more localised research is still needed. Dalton-Puffer and Smit (2013) explicitly call for investigations into policy issues and stakeholder perceptions in situated CLIL realities. In many studies, the views of one or two groups are considered, most commonly students and teachers, but the full range of school actors involved in implementation is less often represented. In particular, management teams and CLIL programme coordinators play a decisive role in interpreting regulations, organizing resources, supporting staff, and sustaining a bilingual culture at school, yet their perspectives are not always integrated with those of CLIL teachers, English teachers, and students. Doiz and Lasagabaster (2017) show the importance of comparing beliefs held by management teams and teaching staff, but further research is required to understand whether these groups share priorities, where tensions emerge, and how institutional responsibilities are distributed.

The case of Castilla-La Mancha is especially relevant for such an inquiry. As a largely monolingual region with limited everyday contact with foreign language speakers, it has relied heavily on schooling to increase students’ competence in English and other European languages. Since the first bilingual initiatives linked to the Ministry of Education and the British Council, the region has progressively expanded its own bilingual programmes. This expansion has been accompanied by successive regulatory changes, including the transformation of European or Bilingual Sections into Linguistic Programmes and, more recently, into Bilingual and Multilingual Projects. These policy shifts reflect both the ambition to extend bilingual education and concerns about maintaining programme quality in a context of limited resources.

Against this background, the present study explores the shared beliefs and perceptions of the main actors involved in CLIL programmes in two state secondary schools in Castilla-La Mancha. Unlike studies which focus on a single stakeholder group, this research includes students, CLIL teachers, English teachers, CLIL programme coordinators, and members of management teams. Its purpose is to identify common perceptions of the strengths of bilingual programmes, areas in need of improvement, and points of tension among the groups responsible for their implementation. To this end, the study draws on Likert-type questionnaires supplemented with open-ended questions and interviews, allowing both quantitative tendencies and qualitative explanations to be considered.

By bringing together the voices of learners, teachers with different professional roles, coordinators, and school leaders, this article aims to contribute to a more nuanced understanding of CLIL as it is experienced in everyday school life. It also seeks to inform reflection on programme coordination, teacher support, resource allocation, and the lay theories about bilingualism that may shape expectations and practices. In doing so, the study responds to calls for balanced, context-sensitive research capable of taking stock of CLIL after more than a decade of implementation and of identifying the conditions required for effective and sustainable bilingual education.

intros.text: The development of the notion of communicative competence in the language testing and evaluation field has had a great impact on theories of second language (L2) learning in the past decades.  This  concept not only refers to individuals’ underlying knowledge of grammatical and structural forms of  language (Chomsky, 1965), but also to their capacity in using this insight in real conversations (Hymes,  1972). This move from mastery of mechanical aspects of language to the mastery of functionally or pragmatically appropriate language use, greatly influenced the development of theories and models of  communicative proficiency in the field of language learning and assessment (e.g. Bachman, 1990;  Bachman and Palmer, 1996, 2010; Canale, 1983; Canale & Swain, 1980; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995).  Within various frameworks of communicative language ability, pragmatic capacity is a core ability that learners of a new language require to acquire.  Pragmatic capacity is mainly about how meaning is  created and understood in a specific context (Bachman & Palmer, 2010). In fact, it is the study of actions  performed intentionally by individuals for some purposes, and it encompasses individuals’ beliefs,  opinions, intentions, and actions (Thomas, 1995). That is, it is not the words, speakers, or even hearers  that are responsible for creating or conveying meanings, per se; rather meaning is constantly negotiated,  in a dynamic interaction, between speakers, hearers, and the context of interaction.  In pragmatics, the  focus is on meaning, particularly, on the functional aspect of language whereby language use is  described as a form of social behavior that people exhibit through their utterances.  Due to the significance of pragmatic knowledge in the flourishing of interactive language ability of  language learners, many research studies have been centered upon speech acts comprehension and  production (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Felix-Brasdefer, 2007;  Matsumura, 2001, 2003; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). Equally important in the realm of pragmatics is  the investigation of implicit meaning or implicature  Despite this importance, a few researchers have  examined L2 comprehension of conversational implicatures (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999;  Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007).  Implicature as a notion refers the functional aspect of language; it identifies how individuals  comprehend meanings that are not stated in an explicit way in their speech (Archer et al., 2012;  Levinson, 1983; Verschueren, 1999). In fact, implicature is produced as a result of interlocutors'  interpretations and it conveys meanings beyond the surface structure of the utterances (Archer et al.,  2012). Identifying the gap between surface and deep meaning, when comprehending implied meanings,  creates a major difficulty for learners of a second or foreign language. This is due to the fact that factors  such as cultural background, L2 exposure, implicature type, and general L2 proficiency influence learners’ comprehension (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978;  Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013).  Studies on implicature comprehension (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999;  Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2010; Tagouchi 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013) have largely contributed  to the field of second language learning.  However their approach to the notion of conversational  implicature has not been adequate and comprehensive enough, particularly, with regard to matters such  as the type of the instruments used, the construct, and its subtypes. Moreover, it has been argued that  face management is one of the major factors responsible for violating the maxim of relevance.  Nevertheless, as far as the available literature shows, no empirical research study has systematically set  out to develop and validate an original instrument that tests conversational implicature taking into  account the insights from relevance maxim and face management theory.  Accordingly, the present study  set out to eliminate this gap through the construction and validation of an authentic measurement that  test the degree to which EFL learners in Iran have developed pragmatic inferential skills in  comprehending conversational implicature used in every day spoken English

intros.text:
The ability to use and interpret language appropriately in social contexts has long been acknowledged as a central dimension of communicative competence. Since Chomsky's (1965) distinction between competence and performance, applied linguists have sought to broaden the notion of what it means to know a language. Hymes (1972) introduced the concept of communicative competence, arguing that linguistic knowledge alone is insufficient for successful communication and that learners must also acquire knowledge of when, where, and to whom particular utterances are appropriate. Subsequent models expanded this idea. Canale and Swain (1980) and Canale (1983) proposed frameworks encompassing grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse, and strategic competencies, while Celce-Murcia, Dörnyei, and Thürrell (1995) later refined the construct to include actional and sociocultural components. Across these formulations, pragmatic competence—the ability to convey and comprehend meaning in context—emerges as an indispensable element of second and foreign language ability (Bachman & Palmer, 1996).

Despite this recognition, pragmatic competence remains one of the least investigated components of communicative language ability. Much of the research in interlanguage pragmatics has concentrated on the production and comprehension of speech acts, particularly requests, apologies, and refusals, often within cross-sectional or study-abroad designs (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). The instruments used in these studies are frequently framed by the speech act paradigm, drawing on discourse completion tasks and related elicitation techniques. In contrast, comparatively little attention has been paid to conversational implicature, the process by which hearers infer meanings that go beyond the literal content of utterances (Grice, 1975; Levinson, 1983; Verschueren, 1999; Archer, Aijmer, & Wichmann, 2012). The comprehension of implied meaning is arguably as crucial to successful communication as the recognition of illocutionary force, yet it has been examined by only a modest body of research (Bouton, 1988, 1994; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Roever, 2006, 2013; Taguchi, 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013).

The available evidence indicates that cultural background, second language exposure, implicature type, and general L2 proficiency all shape learners' ability to interpret implicatures the way native speakers do. Bouton (1988, 1994) demonstrated that non-native speakers from different cultural backgrounds derive divergent meanings from implicatures and that idiosyncratic implicatures are learned slowly when not deliberately taught. Taguchi's (2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013) series of studies established that proficiency and exposure influence the accuracy and speed of implicature comprehension, with more conventional implied meanings proving easier to interpret than nonconventional ones. Roever (2006, 2013) similarly reported that learners' knowledge of implicature increases with proficiency, and he stressed that comprehension depends on learners' recognizing the divergence between surface and intended meaning. A recurring concern in this literature is the need for valid and reliable instruments capable of measuring implicature comprehension, an area where the field lags well behind the assessment of other aspects of L2 competence (Roever, 2006; Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Kane, 2011).

The present study addresses this gap by constructing and validating a test of conversational implicature comprehension for use in the Iranian EFL context. Drawing on Grice's (1975) conversational maxims and Goffman's (1967) insights on face management, and following the model articulated by Holtgraves (1998), the construct of conversational implicature is defined in terms of hearers' inferential responses to violations of the relevance maxim. Face management is treated as a principal motivation for indirectness, since interlocutors employ implicatures to protect their own and others' face (Brown & Levinson, 1987; Thomas, 1995). Within this framework, four subtypes of implicature—indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes—are hypothesized to constitute the underlying structure of the construct. Two lines of evidence are pursued to establish construct validity: confirmatory factor analysis through structural equation modeling, testing whether a four-factor model fits the data, and a differential group study, examining whether learners of differing proficiency levels differ significantly in their comprehension. By developing a validated listening-based instrument and applying rigorous statistical procedures, this study aims to extend the scope of second and foreign language pragmatic research and to offer a practical tool for assessing an under-researched dimension of EFL learners' communicative ability.

intros.text:
Communicative language ability has long been recognised as a multifaceted construct that extends well beyond grammatical knowledge. Following the influential distinction between linguistic competence and communicative competence (Chomsky, 1964; Hymes, 1972), scholars have refined and elaborated frameworks that place pragmatic ability at the heart of what it means to know a language (Canale, 1980; Canale & Swain, 1983; Celce-Murcia, Dörnyei, & Thurrell, 1995). Within these models, pragmatic competence – the ability to use and interpret language appropriately in context – is considered one of the principal elements of second and foreign language learners' communicative language ability. Consequently, understanding how learners comprehend and produce meaning that goes beyond the literal has become a central concern in applied linguistics and language testing (Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Levinson, 1983; Verschueren, 1999).

The field of interlanguage pragmatics has generated a substantial body of empirical work on how learners acquire and perform pragmatic functions (Trosborg, 1995; Archer, Aijmer, & Wichmann, 2012). Much of this research has been informed by the speech act framework, with requests, apologies, refusals, offers, and advice-giving receiving particular attention across a range of learning contexts (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001; Rose, 2000). This concentration on speech acts has, understandably, shaped the design of assessment instruments, so that a considerable proportion of the tools developed to measure learners' pragmatic ability are built around production tasks such as discourse completion tests. In relative terms, however, learners' pragmatic competence remains far less researched than other components of communicative language ability, and the instruments available for assessing it are correspondingly narrower in scope.

One dimension of pragmatic ability that has attracted comparatively little attention is the comprehension of conversational implicature – the process by which hearers infer implied, non-literal meaning from utterances that appear to violate conversational expectations (Grice, 1975). Although a small but valuable line of research has examined how learners interpret implicature (Bouton, 1988, 1994a, 1994b, 1999; Keenan, 1978; Holtgraves, 1998, 1999; Roever, 2006, 2013; Taguchi, 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008, 2013), these studies converge in identifying cultural background, L2 exposure, implicature type, and general proficiency as the main factors shaping comprehension, while leaving the measurement of the construct itself relatively underdeveloped. Holtgraves (1998) offered a particularly useful model in which implicature comprehension is grounded in Grice's (1975) conversational logic coupled with Goffman's (1967) insights on face management, distinguishing four types of implicature generated by violations of the relevance maxim. Yet the assessment of conversational implicature has not kept pace with theoretical accounts of it. To our knowledge, no validated listening test of conversational implicature has been developed, and the few existing measures have typically relied on reading rather than listening, thereby departing from the way conversation is ordinarily encountered in real life (Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Roever, 2006). This constitutes a clear gap: while the speech act tradition has yielded a range of validated instruments, the assessment of implicature comprehension – an equally central facet of pragmatic ability – remains under-researched, particularly in EFL settings where learners have little exposure to the target language beyond the classroom.

The present study addresses this gap by expanding the scope of second and foreign language pragmatic research through the construction and validation of a test of conversational implicature comprehension for Iranian EFL learners. Drawing on Grice's (1975) conversational maxims and Goffman's (1967) account of face work, and operationalising Holtgraves' (1998) four-component model – indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes – a hypothesised measurement model was formulated and examined. Content validity was established through expert review and successive pilot testing, and construct validity was investigated using confirmatory factor analysis within a structural equation modelling framework, supplemented by a differential group study. Specifically, it was hypothesised that a four-factor model would emerge to reflect the structure of the construct, and that more proficient learners would score significantly higher than less proficient ones. Administered as a listening test to 385 university students at two proficiency levels, the instrument thus offers a systematically validated tool for tapping the inferential skills of EFL learners, and the findings are expected to contribute both methodological and pedagogical insight into how implicature comprehension can be assessed and better understood.

intros.text:
Pragmatic competence is widely recognized as a cornerstone of a learner's overall communicative language ability (Canale, 1980, 1983). While linguistic competence focuses on the formal properties of language—a tradition rooted in the generative grammar of Chomsky (1964)—communicative competence encompasses the social and functional rules of language use, allowing speakers to convey and interpret meaning effectively within specific contexts (Hymes, 1972). Over the decades, various models have refined this construct, emphasizing the integration of discourse, sociocultural, and strategic competencies to achieve successful interaction (Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Despite its importance, pragmatic competence remains less researched than other components of language ability, and the development of robust assessment tools for this domain is still an ongoing challenge in applied linguistics (Archer et al., 2012; Trosborg, 1995; Verschueren, 1999).

Within the field of interlanguage pragmatics, a substantial body of research has focused on speech act theory, exploring how learners produce and perceive requests, apologies, and compliments (Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Rose, 2000). However, another critical dimension of pragmatic ability—the comprehension of conversational implicature—has received significantly less attention. Conversational implicature refers to the meaning a speaker conveys beyond the literal sense of the utterance, often relying on the listener's ability to recognize the violation of conversational maxims, such as the maxim of relevance (Grice, 1975; Levinson, 1983). Because implicatures are inherently indirect, they are often employed for face management (Goffman, 1967), allowing speakers to protect their own image or that of their interlocutor by avoiding direct, face-threatening acts (Brown & Levinson, 1987; Holtgraves, 1998).

Failure to accurately derive implied meanings can lead to significant communication breakdowns in cross-cultural interactions. Empirical evidence suggests that the ability to interpret implicatures is influenced by several factors, including the learner's cultural background, length of residence in the target country, and overall L2 proficiency (Bouton, 1988, 1994; Taguchi, 2002, 2005). For instance, Bouton (1988) demonstrated that cultural background significantly predicts whether non-native speakers derive the same meanings as native speakers. Similarly, studies by Taguchi (2007, 2008) and Roever (2006) have highlighted that while L2 proficiency strongly correlates with the accuracy of implicature comprehension, the speed of processing and the interpretation of formulaic routines may be more dependent on L2 exposure. Despite these insights, there remains a paucity of validated instruments specifically designed to measure the comprehension of conversational implicatures, particularly in the context of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners in non-Western environments.

Most existing assessments of pragmatics have relied on reading-based tasks or discourse completion tests. However, as conversations are primarily oral events, the use of listening tests is essential to increase the authenticity of the assessment (Bachman & Palmer, 1996), ensuring that the results reflect real-world communicative performance (Kane, 2011). There is a pressing need for a validated tool that can categorize and measure different types of implicatures—such as indirect refusals and topic changes—to provide a more nuanced understanding of learner deficiencies.

To address this gap, the present study aims to construct and validate a listening test designed to assess the comprehension of conversational implicatures among Iranian EFL university students. Drawing upon the theoretical framework proposed by Holtgraves (1998), which integrates Gricean maxims with Goffman's (1967) insights on face management, the study proposes a four-factor model of implicature. The research seeks to provide empirical evidence for the construct validity of this instrument using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Additionally, the study examines whether a significant difference exists in the comprehension of implicatures between learners of varying English proficiency levels, thereby contributing to the broader understanding of pragmatic development in the EFL context.

intros.text:
Pragmatic competence is widely recognized as a fundamental pillar of a second or foreign language learner's overall communicative language ability (Canale, 1980, 1983). While linguistic competence focuses on the formal properties of language, communicative competence encompasses the ability to use language appropriately within specific social and cultural contexts (Hymes, 1972; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Within this framework, pragmatic competence—the knowledge of how to use language to achieve specific goals and the ability to interpret intended meanings—is essential for successful interaction (Archer et al., 2012; Trosborg, 1995). Consequently, the development and assessment of this competence have become central concerns in applied linguistics and English language teaching (Verschueren, 1999).

Much of the existing research in interlanguage pragmatics has focused on the production and comprehension of speech acts, such as requests, apologies, and refusals (Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Rose, 2000). While these studies have provided valuable insights into how learners acquire sociopragmatic norms, they represent only one facet of pragmatic ability. Another critical component is the comprehension of conversational implicature—the process by which a hearer derives a meaning that is not explicitly stated by the speaker. According to Grice (1975), implicatures often arise when a speaker flouts a conversational maxim, prompting the listener to perform an inferential leap to recover the intended message. In real-life communication, this indirectness is frequently employed for face management, as speakers seek to protect their own image or the face of their interlocutors to avoid conflict or embarrassment (Goffman, 1967; Brown & Levinson, 1987).

Despite its importance, the assessment of conversational implicature remains significantly under-researched compared to speech act research. A limited number of empirical studies have explored this area, with researchers investigating the roles of cultural background (Bouton, 1988), L2 exposure (Bouton, 1994; Roever, 2010), and general language proficiency (Taguchi, 2002, 2005) in the interpretation of implied meanings. For instance, Taguchi (2007, 2008) has highlighted the differences in accuracy and speed when learners process indirect refusals versus indirect opinions. However, most of these studies have relied on reading-based tests, which may lack the authenticity of natural spoken interaction, where implicatures are most commonly encountered (Bachman & Palmer, 1996).

Furthermore, there is a notable dearth of validated instruments specifically designed to measure the comprehension of conversational implicature in diverse EFL contexts, particularly in Iran. While the general relationship between proficiency and pragmatic comprehension has been established (Roever, 2006), there is a need for a robust, validated tool that can empirically distinguish between various types of implicatures and provide evidence of construct validity through rigorous statistical modeling. To date, few studies have combined theoretical frameworks of face management and conversational logic with advanced psychometric validation techniques such as confirmatory factor analysis (CFA).

To address this gap, the present study aims to construct and validate a listening test designed to assess EFL learners' comprehension of conversational implicature. Drawing on the theoretical model proposed by Holtgraves (1998), the study examines four specific types of implicatures: indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes. The primary objective is to determine whether a four-factor model provides a statistically sound representation of the construct of conversational implicature. Additionally, the study explores the impact of English proficiency on the comprehension of these implicatures to provide further evidence of the instrument's construct validity. By employing structural equation modeling (SEM) and differential group analysis among Iranian university students, this research seeks to offer a validated tool for assessing inferential skills in the EFL classroom.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a comprehensive review of the literature on conversational implicature, politeness, and face work. Section 3 details the methodology, including the theoretical development of the instrument and the data collection procedures. Section 4 presents the results of the CFA and the findings regarding proficiency levels, followed by a discussion. Finally, Section 5 offers conclusions and suggestions for future research.

intros.text:
Pragmatic competence is widely recognized as a fundamental component of communicative language ability, yet it remains significantly under-researched compared to other linguistic domains such as grammar and vocabulary (Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Within the framework of interlanguage pragmatics, the majority of empirical studies and assessment instruments have focused on speech acts, such as requests, apologies, and complaints (Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). While the acquisition and performance of speech acts have been extensively documented, the assessment of conversational implicature, a critical sub-component of pragmatic ability, has received considerably less attention. Conversational implicature refers to the inferred meaning that arises when a speaker violates a conversational maxim, requiring the listener to derive meaning beyond the literal utterance (Grice, 1975). The ability to comprehend these implied meanings is essential for effective cross-cultural communication, as misinterpretations can lead to significant pragmatic failure (Bouton, 1988).

The theoretical underpinnings of conversational implicature are rooted in Grice's (1975) Cooperative Principle and its associated maxims, alongside Goffman's (1967) insights regarding face management. According to these frameworks, speakers often employ indirectness to protect their own or their interlocutor's face, particularly when conveying negative information or refusals (Holtgraves, 1998). Consequently, understanding implicature involves not only linguistic decoding but also sociocultural inference. Despite the importance of this skill, there is a paucity of validated instruments designed to measure EFL learners' comprehension of conversational implicature. Existing research on implicature comprehension has largely relied on reading-based tasks or unvalidated measures, which may not accurately reflect the real-time processing required in spoken interaction (Taguchi, 2002, 2005, 2008). Furthermore, while studies by Bouton (1988, 1994) and Roever (2006, 2010) have explored the role of culture and proficiency in implicature interpretation, there is a need for robust, psychometrically sound assessment tools that can be utilized in EFL contexts.

The scarcity of validated tests for conversational implicature presents a significant gap in the field of language assessment. As noted by Kane (2011), the development of language assessments requires rigorous evidence to support their validity and reliability. Without such instruments, it is difficult to determine the extent to which learners have acquired the necessary pragmatic skills to navigate complex social interactions. Most previous instruments have focused on speech act performance, often neglecting the inferential processes involved in understanding implied meaning (Roever, 2013). Additionally, the majority of studies have been conducted in ESL contexts or with learners residing in the target culture, leaving the specific challenges faced by EFL learners in non-target language environments largely unexplored (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Matsumura, 2001).

To address these limitations, the present study aims to construct and validate a listening-based test of conversational implicature for Iranian EFL university students. Drawing on Holtgraves' (1998) model, which categorizes implicatures into indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes, this study seeks to develop a multiple-choice instrument that captures the nuances of these pragmatic phenomena. The study is guided by two primary objectives. First, it aims to establish the content and construct validity of the proposed test through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Second, it seeks to investigate the relationship between English proficiency levels and the comprehension of conversational implicatures, hypothesizing that higher proficiency will correlate with better performance. By validating this instrument, the study contributes to the growing body of research on interlanguage pragmatics and provides a practical tool for assessing a crucial aspect of communicative competence in EFL settings.

intros.text:
Pragmatic competence is widely recognized as a fundamental component of communicative language ability, essential for successful interaction in a second or foreign language. As learners navigate social contexts, the ability to interpret implied meanings—conversational implicatures—becomes critical for avoiding misunderstandings and maintaining face. Despite the centrality of pragmatics in language proficiency, research attention has disproportionately focused on speech acts, leaving the assessment of conversational implicature relatively underdeveloped. This imbalance is significant, as implicatures often arise from violations of conversational maxims, requiring complex inferential processing that distinguishes advanced communicative competence from mere grammatical accuracy.

Theoretical frameworks such as Grice’s (1975) Cooperative Principle and Goffman’s (1967) concept of face management provide the foundation for understanding how indirectness functions in communication. According to these models, speakers frequently employ indirect language to protect their own or their interlocutor’s face, particularly when conveying negative information or refusing requests. Consequently, comprehending such implicatures demands that learners recognize the violation of a maxim, such as relevance, and infer the underlying intent. While empirical studies have explored factors influencing this comprehension—such as cultural background, L2 exposure, and proficiency (Bouton, 1988, 1994; Taguchi, 2002, 2005; Roever, 2006, 2010)—the field lacks robust, validated instruments specifically designed to measure these inferential skills in listening contexts. Most existing assessments rely on reading-based tasks or speech act frameworks, which may not fully capture the dynamic nature of spoken implicature comprehension.

Furthermore, while researchers like Bouton (1988) and Roever (2010) have developed measures for implicature interpretation, these instruments have often been limited by their format or scope. For instance, many studies utilize reading-based tests that fail to replicate the authenticity of real-life spoken interactions. Roever (2006) noted that while proficiency correlates with implicature comprehension, the role of L2 exposure varies across implicature types, suggesting a need for more nuanced assessment tools. Additionally, the validation of such instruments often lacks rigorous psychometric evidence, such as confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), to establish construct validity. This gap is particularly pronounced in Iranian EFL contexts, where pragmatic instruction is often implicit, and learners may struggle with the cultural and linguistic subtleties of English implicatures.

To address these limitations, the present study aims to construct and validate a listening-based test of conversational implicature comprehension tailored for Iranian EFL university students. Grounded in Holtgraves’ (1998) model of indirect replies, which integrates Gricean maxims with face management theory, the study proposes a four-factor structure comprising indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes. The primary objective is to empirically validate this hypothesized model through confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM). Additionally, the study seeks to gather evidence for construct validity by comparing performance across proficiency levels, hypothesizing that more proficient learners will demonstrate significantly higher comprehension scores. By developing a reliable and valid instrument, this research contributes to the growing body of interlanguage pragmatics assessment, offering a tool that reflects the complexities of real-world spoken communication and supports more targeted pragmatic instruction.

intros.text:
The ability to communicate successfully in a second or foreign language involves more than mastery of grammar and vocabulary. Since Hymes’ (1972) critique of purely formal accounts of linguistic competence, communicative competence has been understood as encompassing the knowledge needed to use language appropriately in social interaction. Subsequent models of communicative language ability have similarly foregrounded pragmatic, sociolinguistic, discourse, and strategic dimensions alongside linguistic knowledge (Canale, 1980, 1983; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Within language testing, this broader view has important implications: if language assessments are to support valid interpretations of learners’ communicative ability, they should include constructs that reflect how language is actually understood and used in context (Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Kane, 2011). Pragmatic competence is therefore a central, rather than peripheral, component of second and foreign language ability.

Pragmatics is concerned with meaning in interaction: how speakers use contextual, social, and linguistic resources to convey intentions, and how hearers infer meanings that are not always explicitly encoded in utterances (Levinson, 1983; Thomas, 2014; Verschueren, 1999). For second/foreign language learners, this dimension of communication can be particularly challenging because pragmatic interpretation depends not only on linguistic decoding but also on culturally and contextually situated expectations about what counts as appropriate, polite, relevant, or indirect. Research in interlanguage pragmatics has shown that learners may differ from native or more proficient users in their production and comprehension of requests, apologies, advice, email requests, and other speech acts, and that pragmatic development is shaped by instruction, proficiency, exposure, and learning context (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). Nevertheless, compared with grammatical, lexical, and reading/listening skills, pragmatic competence remains relatively underrepresented in assessment research.

One especially important but less frequently assessed area of pragmatic competence is the comprehension of conversational implicature. Conversational implicature refers to meanings that speakers imply rather than state directly and that hearers infer on the basis of contextual assumptions and principles of cooperative communication. Grice’s (1975) account of the cooperative principle and conversational maxims provides a foundational explanation of how such meanings arise: when an utterance appears to violate a maxim, hearers search for an intended meaning that makes the contribution communicatively sensible. For example, a speaker may respond indirectly to a request, offer an opinion without explicitly criticizing, avoid disclosing embarrassing information, or shift topic in a way that signals an unstated message. Because implicatures depend on inference, they can easily become sites of misunderstanding in intercultural and foreign language communication.

Empirical work has demonstrated that the comprehension of implicature is affected by culture, proficiency, exposure, and implicature type. Bouton’s (1988) cross-cultural study showed that learners from different linguistic and cultural backgrounds did not always derive the same meanings from English implicatures as native English speakers, and that cultural background remained influential even when English proficiency was controlled. Later work suggested that implicature comprehension can improve gradually with residence in the target-language environment and can also benefit from explicit instruction, especially for more formulaic implicatures (Bouton, 1994; Bouton, 1994b; Bouton, 1999). Taguchi’s studies further showed that L2 learners’ accuracy in interpreting implied meaning is related to proficiency, exposure, and interaction, while comprehension speed and accuracy may develop differently (Taguchi, 2002, 2005, 2007, 2008). Similar findings have been reported in other target languages, including L2 Chinese, where proficiency and learner background influenced comprehension of conventional and non-conventional implicatures (Taguchi et al., 2013). Roever (2006) also found that implicature knowledge increased with proficiency in a web-based test of ESL pragmalinguistics, although different pragmatic subcomponents displayed distinct developmental patterns.

A further theoretical issue concerns why speakers choose indirectness. Holtgraves (1998) argued that indirect replies can be interpreted through a model combining Gricean conversational logic with Goffman’s (1967) notion of face. From this perspective, hearers who encounter an apparently irrelevant reply infer a nonliteral meaning by considering why the speaker might have violated the maxim of relevance. Face management is a major motivation: speakers may use indirectness to avoid threatening their own or another person’s social image. Politeness theory likewise treats indirectness as a resource for managing face-threatening acts (Brown & Levinson, 1987). Holtgraves’ model identifies several relevance-based indirect replies, including indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes, which provide a useful theoretical basis for operationalizing conversational implicature as an assessable construct.

Despite these advances, validated instruments for assessing learners’ comprehension of conversational implicature remain limited, particularly in EFL contexts where learners may have restricted access to naturalistic English interaction. Much previous research has relied on reading-based or mixed-format measures, while implicatures in everyday communication are typically encountered through listening. In the Iranian EFL context, there is a need for empirically validated tools that can capture learners’ ability to infer implied meanings in spoken conversational exchanges. The present study addresses this need by developing and validating a multiple-choice listening test of conversational implicature for Iranian university EFL learners. Drawing on Grice’s theory of implicature and Holtgraves’ face-management model, the study proposes a four-factor structure comprising indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes. It further examines whether learners at different English proficiency levels differ in their comprehension of these implicature types, thereby providing additional evidence for the construct validity of the measure.

intros.text:
The ability to communicate successfully in a second or foreign language involves more than the mastery of grammar and vocabulary. Since the emergence of communicative approaches to language teaching and testing, language ability has been conceptualized as a multidimensional construct that includes not only linguistic knowledge but also the capacity to use language appropriately in social interaction. Hymes (1972) challenged a purely formal view of competence, and later models of communicative competence incorporated sociolinguistic, discourse, strategic, and pragmatic dimensions (Canale, 1980, 1983; Celce-Murcia et al., 1995). Within this broader view, pragmatic competence has become a central component of communicative language ability because it enables learners to understand speakers’ intentions, manage interpersonal meanings, and select contextually appropriate forms in interaction.

Pragmatics is concerned with meaning in use, particularly with how interlocutors interpret utterances in relation to context, shared assumptions, social relationships, and communicative goals (Levinson, 1983; Thomas, 2014; Verschueren, 1999). For EFL learners, pragmatic competence is especially important because failure to understand intended meanings may lead to misunderstanding even when the linguistic form of an utterance is familiar. Such difficulty is particularly evident in indirect communication, where speakers often mean more, or something different, from what they explicitly say. Conversational implicature is one of the key pragmatic phenomena through which such indirect meanings are conveyed. Based on Grice’s (1975) cooperative principle and conversational maxims, implicature refers to the process by which hearers infer a speaker’s intended meaning when an utterance appears to violate expectations of informativeness, truthfulness, relevance, or manner.

Research in interlanguage pragmatics has shown that learners’ pragmatic development does not necessarily parallel their grammatical development. Studies on requests, apologies, advice, and other speech acts have demonstrated that learners may experience difficulty in selecting pragmatically appropriate forms or interpreting social meanings, even after considerable formal study of the target language (Biesenbach-Lucas, 2007; Byon, 2004; Cohen & Shively, 2007; Félix-Brasdefer, 2007; Matsumura, 2001; Rose, 2000; Trosborg, 1995). Compared with speech act production and comprehension, however, the comprehension of conversational implicature has received more limited attention. This is problematic because implicatures are common in everyday conversation and are often used to maintain politeness, avoid directness, or protect the speaker’s or hearer’s face.

The interpretation of indirect replies has been closely linked to face management. Goffman (1967) argued that participants in interaction are concerned with maintaining face, or the socially valued image of self presented in communication. Brown and Levinson’s (1987) politeness theory further emphasized that indirectness can serve as a strategy for reducing face threat. Holtgraves (1998) integrated Gricean conversational logic with Goffman’s notion of face, proposing that hearers interpret violations of the maxim of relevance by considering why a speaker might avoid a direct response. In this view, indirect replies may convey meanings such as refusal, negative opinion, embarrassing disclosure, or topic change, particularly when direct expression would threaten face. This theoretical account provides a useful basis for examining how learners comprehend implied meanings in spoken interaction.

Empirical studies have indicated that the comprehension of implicature is affected by several factors, including cultural background, length and type of exposure to the target language, implicature type, and general L2 proficiency. Bouton (1988) found that learners from different cultural backgrounds differed in their ability to interpret English implicatures in native-like ways. His later work suggested that some implicatures may be acquired gradually through exposure, whereas others may benefit from explicit instruction (Bouton, 1994; Bouton, 1999). Taguchi (2005, 2007, 2008) showed that proficiency is related to accuracy in pragmatic comprehension, although speed and accuracy may develop differently. Taguchi et al. (2013) also reported differences in the comprehension of conventional and non-conventional implicatures in L2 Chinese. Similarly, Roever (2006, 2013) emphasized the importance of assessing implicature as one component of pragmalinguistic knowledge and found that learners’ knowledge of implicature generally increased with proficiency.

Despite these contributions, the assessment of conversational implicature remains underdeveloped in comparison with the assessment of other areas of pragmatic competence. Much of the available testing research in interlanguage pragmatics has focused on speech acts, routines, or broader pragmalinguistic ability, and relatively few studies have developed instruments specifically designed to measure learners’ comprehension of implicature. Moreover, in many EFL contexts, including Iran, there is a need for validated measures that can provide reliable evidence about learners’ ability to interpret implied meanings in spoken English. Because validity is not a property of a test alone but of the interpretations and uses of test scores, test development requires systematic evidence regarding content, construct representation, reliability, and relationships with relevant learner characteristics (Bachman & Palmer, 1996; Kane, 2011).

The present study addresses this need by developing and validating a test of conversational implicature for Iranian EFL university students. Drawing on Grice’s (1975) theory of conversational implicature and Holtgraves’ (1998) model of indirect replies, the study conceptualizes implicature comprehension as comprising four related but distinct subtypes: indirect refusals, negative opinions, disclosures, and topic changes. The study aims to examine whether a test based on these four categories provides evidence of construct validity and whether learners at different levels of English proficiency differ in their comprehension of conversational implicatures. To this end, a multiple-choice listening test was developed, reviewed, piloted, and administered to EFL learners, and its factorial structure was investigated through confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. In addition, differential group performance was examined as further validity evidence. By offering a validated measure of implicature comprehension, the study seeks to contribute to the assessment of pragmatic competence and to the understanding of EFL learners’ ability to interpret indirect meanings in English conversation.

intros.text: Contemporary instructed language learning approaches emphasize on encouraging learners to actively take part in communicative tasks (Ellis, 2014). However, despite efforts made by teachers to provide such opportunities, it is very common for them to face learners who are reluctant to engage in verbal communication; which is due to various reasons (Zulkepli, Othman, & Khaja, 2013). The issue of reticence occurs not only among less proficient learners, but also the proficient ones such as preservice ESL teachers (Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016; Yousef, Jamil, & Razak, 2013; Zulkepli, Tajuddin, AlBakri, Atan, & Bakar, 2019). Empirical studies have long proven the strong link between speaking and learning a target language (Goh, 2014; Long, 2015; Swain, 2000).  This has triggered interest among scholars in the area of willingness to communicate (WTC); resulting in numerous empirical studies that set to investigate the variables that affect this psychological construct (Pawlak, Mystkowska-Wiertelak, & Bielak, 2016; Shirvan, Khajavy, MacIntyre, & Taherian, 2019; Zhang, Beckman, & Beckman, 2018).  However, studies done on this area predominantly focus on in-class WTC where learners normally engage in interaction with “familiar interlocutors, such as teachers and peers, in relatively predictable L2 scenarios” (Lee & Hsieh, 2019, p. 64)  To date, there is scanty research on out-of-class WTC where learners will speak with “unfamiliar acquaintances or strangers in somewhat unpredictable situations” (Lee & Hsieh, 2019: 64); which will be more challenging even for motivated and advanced learners.  Thus, the purpose of the study is to identify the link between motivation and WTC among a group of advanced learners i.e., pre-service ESL teachers.

intros.text:
The importance of speaking in second language (L2) learning has long been established. Producing output allows learners to test hypotheses about the target language and to notice gaps in their linguistic knowledge, thereby contributing to acquisition (Swain, 2000; Elbers, 2000). For this reason, developing learners' oracy skills has become a central concern in second language pedagogy (Goh, 2014; Goh & Vandergrift, 2021), and engaging learners in meaningful, communicative interaction is widely regarded as essential to language development (Long, 2015). However, opportunities to speak are of little value if learners are unwilling to take them up. This readiness to initiate communication when free to do so is captured in the construct of willingness to communicate (WTC), which has attracted extensive empirical attention in both classroom and non-classroom contexts (Pawlak et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018; Lee & Hsieh, 2019).

A recurring and somewhat puzzling observation is that WTC is not always high, even among proficient and motivated learners. Studies conducted in Malaysia's multicultural setting have reported that many trainee teachers avoid using English despite their excellent proficiency (Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016; Yousef et al., 2013). Meta-analytic evidence suggests that motivation, alongside self-confidence and anxiety, is among the key correlates of WTC (Shirvan et al., 2019), pointing to the value of examining motivational constructs such as Dörnyei's L2 motivational self-system (L2MSS).

While prior work has explored WTC among Malaysian pre-service teachers (Zulkepli et al., 2019), few studies have investigated how the ideal and ought-to selves predict out-of-class WTC in this population. The present study addresses this gap by examining the relationship between L2MSS components and out-of-class WTC among a group of pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia.

intros.text:
The role of speaking in second language learning has been widely acknowledged, with theorists arguing that learners' own output serves as a crucial input for analysis and acquisition (Elbers, 2000; Swain, 2000; Long, 2015). Given this, the extent to which learners are willing to communicate in the target language becomes central to their eventual success. Willingness to communicate (WTC), defined by MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément and Noels (1998) as 'the probability of engaging in communication when free to choose to do so', has therefore attracted considerable research attention across in-class, out-of-class, and digital contexts (Lee & Hsieh, 2019; Pawlak et al., 2016). Meta-analytic evidence confirms that motivation, perceived competence, and anxiety are consistent correlates of L2 WTC (Shirvan et al., 2019).

Within the Malaysian setting, several studies have examined pre-service ESL teachers' WTC (Yousef et al., 2013; Ahmed Fahim & Mogana Dhamotharan, 2016; Zulkepli et al., 2019). A recurring observation is that even proficient learners often avoid English communication, revealing that high proficiency does not guarantee high WTC. However, much of this work has concentrated on in-class WTC, and comparatively little is known about learners' willingness to communicate outside the classroom, where authentic practice opportunities in multicultural Malaysia are abundant. Furthermore, while Dörnyei's (2005) L2 motivational self-system (L2MSS) has been linked to WTC, few studies have investigated whether the ideal self or the ought-to self more strongly predicts out-of-class WTC among trainee teachers.

Addressing this gap, the present study examines the perceived level of out-of-class WTC among 111 pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia and explores the relationship between their L2MSS components and out-of-class WTC, identifying which self-guide is the stronger predictor.

The development of oral proficiency is fundamental to mastering a second language (L2), as the ability to engage in real-time interaction is a primary indicator of communicative competence (Goh & Vandergrift, 2021). Central to this process is the 'output hypothesis,' which suggests that producing language serves as a critical mechanism for acquisition (Swain, 2000). However, despite possessing high linguistic proficiency, many learners exhibit reticence and avoid speaking opportunities (Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016). This phenomenon is often analyzed through the lens of willingness to communicate (WTC), defined as the probability that a learner will engage in communication when given the choice (MacIntyre et al., 1998). While WTC is influenced by various affective and situational factors (Lee & Hsieh, 2019; Shirvan et al., 2019), it remains a dynamic construct that fluctuates based on the interlocutor and context (Pawlak et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).

One theoretical framework used to explain these individual differences is the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), which emphasizes the role of the 'ideal L2 self' and the 'ought-to L2 self' in driving learner behavior (Dörnyei, 2005). For pre-service ESL teachers, WTC is particularly vital, as their future professional success depends on both pedagogical skill and high target language proficiency (Yousef et al., 2013). Despite the abundance of practice opportunities in multicultural environments like Malaysia, advanced learners may still struggle with out-of-class WTC. Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the relationship between the L2MSS components and the out-of-class WTC of pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia, identifying which self-guide serves as the stronger predictor of their willingness to communicate.

intros.text:
The development of communicative competence is a central goal of second language acquisition, with a particular emphasis on the role of speaking in mastering the target language. Within this domain, willingness to communicate (WTC)—defined as the probability of engaging in speaking when free to do so—has emerged as a pivotal construct for understanding language learners' success (Shirvan et al., 2019). In the Malaysian context, research has highlighted that WTC is a dynamic variable influenced by interlocutors and specific communicative settings (Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016), and it remains a valuable indicator of oral skill among pre-service English teachers (Yousef et al., 2013). 

Despite its importance, high proficiency does not always translate into a high WTC; many advanced learners remain reticent, failing to seize beneficial verbal opportunities outside the classroom (Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016). While studies have explored affective variables like grit and anxiety as predictors of WTC (Lee & Hsieh, 2019), there is a need to further examine the role of the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS)—specifically the ideal and ought-to selves—in predicting out-of-class communication. Although previous research has linked L2MSS to WTC, empirical evidence focusing specifically on the out-of-class behavior of pre-service ESL teachers remains limited.

This study aims to identify the relationship between the L2MSS and out-of-class WTC among 111 pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia. Specifically, it seeks to determine the participants' perceived WTC levels and identify whether the ideal self or the ought-to self serves as the stronger predictor of their willingness to communicate. By addressing this gap, the study provides pedagogical insights into encouraging teacher trainees to engage more frequently in target language use beyond the classroom.

intros.text: Empirical studies have long established the critical link between speaking and second language acquisition. However, despite its importance in determining success in mastering a target language, willingness to communicate (WTC) is not always high, even among motivated and advanced English language learners. This often leads to learners avoiding opportunities to engage in beneficial verbal activities. While WTC has been extensively researched, particularly within classroom contexts, there remains a need to explore its dynamics in out-of-class settings, especially among pre-service teachers. Previous research in Malaysia has highlighted that WTC fluctuates across interlocutors and contexts (Ahmed Fahim & Mogana Dhamotharan, 2016), and that pre-service teachers often display varying levels of willingness depending on their year of study and gender (Yousef et al., 2013). Furthermore, studies indicate that affective variables such as confidence and anxiety significantly predict WTC across different communicative environments (Lee & Hsieh, 2019). Theoretical frameworks such as the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS) offer valuable insights into these motivational dynamics. Dörnyei’s model posits that the ideal self and the ought-to self drive language learning behaviors. While empirical studies have investigated the relationship between L2MSS and WTC, findings suggest that the ideal self is often a stronger predictor than the ought-to self (Öz & Bursali, 2018). However, limited research has specifically examined these predictors among pre-service ESL teachers in out-of-class contexts. This study aims to address this gap by investigating the relationship between the L2MSS components (ideal self and ought-to self) and out-of-class WTC among pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia. By understanding these motivational predictors, educators can better support teacher trainees in developing the communicative confidence necessary for their future professional roles.

intros.text:
Empirical studies have long established the critical link between speaking and second language acquisition. Despite its centrality in determining language mastery, willingness to communicate (WTC) remains a complex construct, as learners often refrain from verbal engagement despite high proficiency. MacIntyre et al. (1998) define WTC as the probability of engaging in communication when free to choose, noting it is not merely a stable personality trait but a situational variable influenced by multiple layers of antecedents. While recent scholarship has extensively explored WTC in classroom settings (Pawlak et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018), less attention has been paid to out-of-class contexts, particularly among advanced learners who possess the necessary linguistic competence. 

Furthermore, while Dörnyei’s (2005) L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS) has been widely adopted to explain individual differences in motivation, the specific relationship between its components—the ideal self and the ought-to self—and out-of-class WTC remains underexplored. Existing studies have primarily focused on in-class dynamics or general motivation (Lee & Hsieh, 2019; Shirvan et al., 2019). Although some research has investigated WTC among pre-service teachers (Ahmed Fahim & Mogana Dhamotharan, 2016; Yousef et al., 2013), there is a lack of quantitative evidence examining how future self-guides specifically predict their willingness to communicate outside the classroom environment. 

This study addresses this gap by investigating the relationship between L2MSS components and out-of-class WTC among pre-service ESL teachers in Malaysia. Specifically, it aims to determine the perceived level of out-of-class WTC, examine the correlations with ideal and ought-to selves, and identify the stronger predictor. Drawing on a quantitative design with 111 participants, the findings indicate that while proficiency is high, out-of-class WTC is only satisfactory. Crucially, the ideal self emerges as a significantly stronger predictor than the ought-to self. These results suggest that personal aspirations, rather than external obligations, drive communicative willingness in out-of-class settings, offering vital implications for teacher education.

intros.text:
Speaking is central to second language development because it provides learners with opportunities to test linguistic hypotheses, receive feedback, and develop communicative competence through meaningful interaction (Swain, 2000; Long, 2015). In English language teaching, this is especially important for learners who are expected not only to know the language but also to use it confidently in real-life situations. Yet successful oral development depends partly on learners’ willingness to take up opportunities to communicate. Willingness to communicate (WTC) refers to the probability that a learner will choose to engage in communication when free to do so (MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément, & Noels, 1998). Research has shown that WTC is dynamic and shaped by contextual, interpersonal, and affective factors rather than proficiency alone (Pawlak et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018). Thus, even advanced learners may avoid using English when opportunities arise, particularly outside formal classroom settings.

In the Malaysian ESL context, this issue is pedagogically significant because English is widely available in many educational and social domains, but learners’ actual use of the language may vary across interlocutors and situations (Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016). For pre-service ESL teachers, WTC is even more consequential: their future professional identity requires high English proficiency and the ability to model communicative language use. Previous studies on Malaysian pre-service teachers have highlighted the relevance of WTC to oral language development and teacher preparation (Yousef et al., 2013; Zulkepli et al., 2019).

One motivational framework that may explain learners’ readiness to communicate is Dörnyei’s L2 motivational self system, particularly the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self (Dörnyei, 2005). Prior research has linked motivation and L2 self-guides to WTC, with the ideal L2 self often emerging as an important predictor (Lee & Hsieh, 2019; Elahi Shirvan et al., 2019). However, less is known about how these self-guides relate specifically to out-of-class WTC among advanced Malaysian pre-service ESL teachers. The present study addresses this gap by examining their perceived out-of-class WTC and determining whether the ideal self or the ought-to self better predicts it.

intros.text:
Developing learners’ ability to communicate orally in English remains a central goal of second language education, particularly in ESL contexts where opportunities for interaction extend beyond classroom instruction. Speaking is not merely an outcome of learning but also a condition for further development, as language production can mediate acquisition through meaningful use and collaborative dialogue (Swain, 2000; Long, 2015). For pre-service ESL teachers, this issue is especially important because professional competence is closely tied to the capacity to model and use English confidently in varied communicative situations.

Yet learners who are linguistically capable do not always choose to speak when opportunities arise. Willingness to communicate (WTC), commonly understood as the probability that a learner will initiate communication when free to do so, has therefore become a key construct in explaining second language use (MacIntyre et al., 1998). Research has shown that WTC is shaped by both individual and contextual factors and may fluctuate across interlocutors, settings, and modes of communication (Pawlak et al., 2016; Ahmed Fahim & Dhamotharan, 2016; Lee & Hsieh, 2019). Studies in Malaysia and other ESL/EFL contexts have further suggested that even trainee teachers may vary considerably in their readiness to communicate in English (Yousef et al., 2013; Zulkepli et al., 2019).

Motivation is one of the affective variables most consistently associated with L2 WTC (Elahi Shirvan et al., 2019). Within Dörnyei’s L2 motivational self system, learners’ imagined future identities are represented through the ideal L2 self and ought-to L2 self, both of which may influence language-related behaviour. Although previous studies have examined links between L2 motivational self-guides and WTC, less is known about how these self-guides predict out-of-class WTC among Malaysian pre-service ESL teachers, a group expected to use English beyond formal learning spaces. Accordingly, the present study investigates their perceived level of out-of-class WTC, examines its relationship with the ideal and ought-to selves, and identifies which self-guide is the stronger predictor.
