intros.text: Culture consists of the moral and material elements valued, shared, and transferred to each other and  future generations by the members of a society (İçli, 2012, p.104). Culture involves all of the knowledge,  beliefs, art, morality, law, traditions, and the talents and habits acquired by the person as a member of  the a society (Tylor, 1871)  While culture determines our behavioural patterns and beliefs, it shapes the  way we learn and teach on the other hand.  Culture takes place in the heart of anything done in the name  of education (Gay, 2014). According to Redfield (1943), an anthropologist, education is the process of  transfer and renewal of culture (Tezcan, 1978, p. 7). The individual is adapted to the society cognitively,  affectively and physically by education (Yücel, 2010, p. 10). Cultural transfer and information acquisition are ensured through language. At this point, language  becomes an indispensable tool not only for communication, but also for the process of learning and  teaching (Pearson, 2007).  According to Atkinson (2013), language is important for social actions, and  language plays a role firstly in adaptation of the person to the social environment.  The person learns  through language how to behave by adapting to the social environment (Atkinson, 2013).  People in  places where different languages are spoken learn a common language beside their native language and  become “bilingual”.  According to Mackey (1982), bilingualism is the use of two or more languages by  a person alternately. Children begin the socialization process in their family, long before starting school. In this process, the  child begins to learn his social roles by joining different groups, which forms part of his personality  development (Tezcan, 1985). Later, the child starts school and joins the school culture. Stolp and Smith  (1995) define school culture as meaning patterns involving the norms, values, beliefs, traditions and  myths transferred by the organization members from the past to the present. According to Deal and  Peterson (1999), school culture comprises the values, rules, behavioural patterns and traditions forming  from establishment of the school. The second culture joined by children at school is the classroom culture. Classroom culture is a broad  concept involving the classroom experiences, the teacher and the students (Shannon, 1995). Therefore,  classroom culture involves the values, attitudes, rules, understandings and activities formed by the  students and the teacher together in a classroom, and all the characteristics held by that classroom. Any  behaviour, attitude, mentality, and the language used in the classroom form the classroom culture.  Classroom culture defines the character of the interaction of the children in the classroom, and involves  several arrangements with a potential to affect the students’ motivation, learning and social performance  (Koca & İlhan, 2017). The third culture faced by children is the peer culture. Corsaro (2012) defines peer culture as the set of  regular routines, works, values and anxieties produced by and shared with each other by children. The  cultural practices in these regular routines, works and values prepare the children for their future life  and shed light on their process of change. Peer culture is strengthened through games, behaviour and  various activities acquired by children as a result of their interaction with their peers (Kantor & Fernie,  2003). Since these interactions can realize through language, it is possible to say that the languages used  by children is also an important component of peer culture. Preschool education is an educational process that offers children rich stimulant environmental  opportunities for their physical, social, emotional, and cognitive and language development, that  develops them in the same direction as their cultural values, and that forms a basis for their future  educational steps (Katrancı, 2016). The existing literature showed that most of the behaviour adopted in  the preschool period form the habits, and moral and value judgements in their adulthood (Koşan, 2015;  Susar Kırmızı et al., 2019). Therefore, the culture formed during preschool is deemed important. When the culture at home and the culture at the educational institution of children are different, teachers  might misinterpret the children’s behaviour and adopt instinctive reactions and a disciplinary style  conflicting with the norms of the society (Delpit, 1991). Besides, when children with a different native  language start school, they have difficulty in understanding the language of education and there occurs  a problem of communication (Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Teachers also have difficulty at schools and  classrooms with children with a native language different from the common language (Akdağ, 2014).  In Turkey, particularly in the rural areas of the Eastern and South-eastern Anatolia regions are children  that begin taking preschool education with no knowledge of Turkish (Kesmez, 2015; Koşan, 2015).  Since these children are also illiterate, the communication that they develop with their teacher is wondered. At the same time, bilingualism is the most important difficulty faced by most of the preschool  teachers who teach in these regions (Çetin & Yalçın Su, 2019; Akdağ, 2014; Yağan Güder, 2019). Previous research shows that bilingualism may have reflections in education on the school environment  (Susar Kırmızı et al., 2019), on the classroom environment (Çabuk Er, Karageyik & Tokgöz, 2018;  Shannon, 1995) and on peer relationships (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018)  However, no research study is  found in literature about what these reflections are. Also, previous studies are not beyond the  measurements of standard scales and they are superficial (Erşan, 2011; Kol, 2006). This approach  silenced the children’s voice and gave secondary information about them  However, descriptive studies,  ethnographic research in particular, provides an opportunity to look through children’s behaviour and  relationships in their natural environments (Yanık & Yaşar, 2018; Corsaro, 2015)  Elimination of the difficulties caused by bilingualism firstly requires the knowledge of what these  difficulties are.  This situation and the other mentioned situations were assessed as a lack in literature  and decided to research by the researcher.  Purpose of this research study is to examine the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education.  Responses were researched to the following questions for this purpose: 1-What are the reflections of bilingualism on school culture in preschool education? 2-What are the reflections of bilingualism on classroom culture in preschool education? 3-What are the reflections of bilingualism on peer culture in preschool education?  Findings to be obtained as a result of this research study are expected to form a basis for studies to be  done to extend preschool education in regions with a different native language by finding the advantages  and disadvantages caused by bilingualism in preschool education

intros.text:
Language is one of the most fundamental carriers of culture and, at the same time, one of the primary tools through which individuals become members of a society. The relationship between culture and education has long been recognised as so intimate that a distinct field, educational anthropology, has developed to examine how cultures are transmitted, reproduced and transformed through educational processes (Tezcan, 1978). Culture, in its broadest anthropological sense, encompasses the values, norms, beliefs, traditions and shared meanings that a group of people constructs and passes on to the next generation (Tylor, 2010). Because education is the deliberate mechanism through which societies socialise their members into these shared meanings, schools inevitably become sites where the cultural life of a community is reflected, negotiated and, at times, contested. When the language spoken within the walls of a school differs from the language spoken in the surrounding community, this reflective relationship becomes especially visible and worthy of close scholarly attention.

Bilingualism, understood as the regular use of two languages by an individual or a community, is a widespread phenomenon in many parts of the world (Mackey, 1982). It is not merely a linguistic condition but a social one, shaped by factors such as the quantity and quality of language input, the relative status of the languages involved, access to literacy, patterns of family language use and the degree of community support that a minority language receives (Pearson, 2007). In Turkey, the Southeastern Anatolia region provides a distinctive context in which large numbers of children grow up speaking Kurdish at home while Turkish serves as the official language of education. Studies conducted in similar settings have shown that bilingual children frequently use their mother tongue in the home and social environment and only encounter the official language of instruction upon entering school (Kesmez, 2015; Koşan, 2015). For these children, the transition into formal education coincides with a transition into a new language, and this coincidence has consequences that extend well beyond vocabulary acquisition.

Preschool education occupies a particularly important place in this discussion. It is the first structured educational environment that most children experience and is widely regarded as a critical period for cognitive, social and emotional development as well as for readiness for later schooling (Katrancı, 2016). For children whose mother tongue differs from the language of instruction, the preschool years may serve as the primary opportunity to acquire the official language before beginning primary school. Research has indicated that early childhood education can positively influence the school readiness and subsequent literacy development of children whose home language is not Turkish (Susar, 2019; Çabuk, 2018). At the same time, the encounter between the child's home language and the school's language can generate difficulties in adaptation, communication and the implementation of educational programmes, difficulties that teachers who do not share their students' mother tongue must find ways to manage (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016).

The school itself can be understood as a cultural organisation with its own values, symbols, rituals and modes of communication. School culture is shaped and directed to a significant degree by the attitudes and behaviours of administrators and teachers, who model and reinforce the shared meanings that make an individual an accepted member of the institution (Deal & Peterson, 1999; Stolp & Smith, 1995). Within the school, the classroom constitutes a distinct cultural space in which the teacher, as the source of authority, plays a central role in shaping the roles, values and expectations that govern daily interaction (Shannon, 1995; Koca & İlhan, 2017). In a classroom composed of bilingual students, the teacher's approach to language, whether it is tolerant, restrictive or adaptive, becomes an important element in the culture that develops, and it can either support or hinder the children's engagement in learning (Delpit, 1991). The way in which language mediates the relationship between the teacher and the student, and between the school and the wider community, therefore deserves careful examination.

A third layer of culture that is especially salient in early childhood settings is peer culture. Drawing on the notion of interpretive reproduction, children are understood not simply to internalise adult culture but to actively create their own peer cultures through play, negotiation and interaction with one another (Corsaro, 2012). Ethnographic studies of preschool classrooms have shown that children construct complex peer cultures through symbols, games and shared routines, and that language use is deeply implicated in the formation and maintenance of these cultures (Yanık, 2018). Language supports socialisation among peers, and in turn peer interaction supports the learning of language (Atkinson, 2013). In bilingual settings, the language a child speaks may influence friendship relations, participation in games and status within the peer group, making bilingualism a potentially powerful organising principle of children's social worlds.

Although there is a substantial body of work in Turkey concerning the problems faced by primary and secondary teachers working with students whose mother tongue is not Turkish, considerably less attention has been devoted to the preschool level, and even less to the ways in which bilingualism is reflected simultaneously across the interconnected domains of school culture, classroom culture and peer culture. Much of the existing research relies on survey or interview data collected from teachers outside the immediate context of practice, and comparatively few studies have entered bilingual preschool classrooms to observe, over an extended period, how bilingualism is lived and enacted by children, teachers and parents together. An ethnographic approach, which seeks to understand and describe the culture of a group from within, is well suited to capturing the layered and situated nature of these reflections. By combining participant observation, interviews, document analysis and a researcher's diary, such an approach can reveal not only what participants say about bilingualism but how it actually operates in the routines, communications and relationships of everyday school life.

Accordingly, the present study was designed as an ethnographic case study to identify the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education in a village setting in the Southeastern Anatolia region of Turkey, where children speak both Kurdish and Turkish. The study seeks answers to three guiding questions: what are the reflections of bilingualism on school culture, what are its reflections on classroom culture, and what are its reflections on peer culture? By examining these three interrelated domains, the study aims to provide an integrated and detailed portrait of how the coexistence of two languages shapes communication among school personnel and parents, the implementation of the preschool educational programme, the experiences and emotions of teachers, and the friendships, groupings and status of children within their peer group. In doing so, it is hoped that the findings will contribute both to the theoretical understanding of the culture–language–education relationship and to the practical support of teachers and children working in bilingual early childhood contexts.

intros.text:
Preschool education constitutes a formative period in which children acquire the linguistic, social and cognitive foundations upon which their later schooling is built. During this stage, play, communication and adaptation to the culture of the school and the classroom are central to development (Katrancı, 2016). It is widely accepted that early childhood education plays a decisive role in preparing children for formal schooling and in supporting their emotional, social and cognitive growth. Because so much of what happens in the preschool classroom depends on communication between teachers and children and among the children themselves, language occupies a particularly important place at this level of education. When children arrive at school already competent in the language of instruction, the socialisation process unfolds relatively smoothly; when they do not, the entire dynamic of teaching, learning and peer interaction is affected in ways that merit careful investigation.

Bilingualism is a common reality in many parts of the world, and Turkey is no exception. In several regions of the country, and especially in the Southeastern Anatolia region, large numbers of children grow up speaking Kurdish at home and encounter Turkish, the official language of education, for the first time when they begin school. Whether a child who has access to two languages actually becomes bilingual, and how far that bilingualism supports or complicates schooling, depends on a range of social factors, including the quantity and quality of input, the relative status of the languages, and the degree of community and family support (Pearson, 2007). Bilingualism is therefore not merely a linguistic phenomenon but a social and cultural one, closely bound up with identity, community belonging and the everyday interactions that take place inside and outside the school.

Education and culture are deeply intertwined, and schools function as sites where the culture of the surrounding community and the institutional culture of formal education meet and interact (Tezcan, 1978). The concept of school culture encompasses the values, norms, rituals, traditions and shared meanings that give an institution its distinctive character (Deal & Peterson, 1999; Stolp & Smith, 1995). Within the school, the classroom develops its own culture, shaped strongly by the teacher, who acts as a source of authority and as a guide to the roles, values and expectations that operate there (Shannon, 1995; Koca & İlhan, 2017). Alongside these adult-directed cultures, children actively construct their own peer cultures. Rather than simply internalising the adult world, children reproduce and transform it through their negotiations with adults and their creative interactions with one another, producing distinctive peer cultures of their own (Corsaro, 2012). Ethnographic studies of Turkish preschool classrooms have shown how children build complex peer cultures through symbols, games and everyday routines, and how they resist and negotiate the influence of their teachers (Yanık, 2018). Language is central to all three of these cultural levels, since it is the principal means through which socialisation and communication occur, and communication in turn supports the learning of language (Atkinson, 2013).

A growing body of research in Turkey has examined the difficulties encountered by children whose mother tongue is not Turkish and by the teachers who work with them. Studies conducted with primary school teachers have documented persistent communication problems, showing that children who cannot express themselves in Turkish struggle to convey their needs and that teachers frequently rely on bilingual peers, sign and body language, and other improvised strategies to bridge the linguistic gap (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Research on the transition to literacy has found that children who do not speak Turkish and who have not attended preschool experience considerable difficulty in the early reading and writing process, encountering problems with adaptation, self-expression and the understanding of instructions (Susar, 2019). Investigations of early childhood education have further suggested that preschool experience can positively affect the school readiness of bilingual children and can help them acquire Turkish before they begin primary school (Koşan, 2015; Çabuk, 2018). Teachers working in bilingual and rural settings, meanwhile, have reported that the demands of these contexts affect their professional practice and their emotional well-being (Yağan Güder, 2019; Akdağ & Haser, 2016).

Despite this valuable work, most existing studies have concentrated on primary and later levels of schooling or have relied primarily on teacher opinions gathered through questionnaires and interviews. Comparatively little attention has been paid to the preschool level itself, and even less to how bilingualism actually plays out in the lived, day-to-day cultural life of the preschool. In particular, while school culture, classroom culture and peer culture have each been studied in their own right, there is little research that examines how bilingualism is reflected simultaneously across all three of these interrelated cultural dimensions in an authentic preschool setting. How bilingual children and their teachers negotiate language choice in the corridors, the teachers' room and the classroom; how bilingualism shapes the implementation of the preschool programme; how it affects teachers' sense of competence and their communication with children and parents; and how children themselves draw on their two languages to form friendships, organise their games and gain status among their peers, all remain insufficiently explored. Understanding these processes from within, as they unfold naturally, requires an approach capable of capturing the cultural texture of everyday classroom life rather than only reported perceptions of it.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education through the lens of school culture, classroom culture and peer culture. Adopting an ethnographic case study design, it seeks to describe and understand, in an integrated and meaningful way, how bilingualism manifests itself in the everyday life of a preschool serving Turkish–Kurdish bilingual children in the Southeastern Anatolia region. The research was conducted with the participation of eight preschool teachers working in different village schools and thirteen preschool students, and data were gathered over an extended period through participant observation, unstructured and semi-structured interviews, document analysis and a researcher's diary, and analysed by means of content analysis. Guided by this design, the study pursues three questions: what are the reflections of bilingualism on school culture, on classroom culture, and on peer culture?

By examining these three levels together within a single naturalistic context, the study is intended to offer a rich, contextualised account of how bilingualism shapes the cultures of the preschool. The findings may deepen understanding of the challenges that bilingual children and their teachers face at this critical educational stage, illuminate both the difficulties and the possible advantages that bilingualism brings to peer relations and socialisation, and inform teacher education, in-service training and classroom practice in linguistically diverse settings. In doing so, it aims to contribute to the wider discussion of how schools can respond to linguistic and cultural diversity in ways that support the development and well-being of all children.

intros.text:
Culture is a multifaceted and comprehensive concept that encompasses the shared values, beliefs, norms, and traditions of a society, profoundly shaping the way individuals perceive and interact with the world. In the field of educational sciences, the intersection of culture and education has given rise to the discipline of educational anthropology, which examines how anthropological concepts and data are applied to educational institutions to understand the processes of socialization and acculturation (Tezcan, 1978). Education is not merely a technical process of knowledge transfer but is deeply embedded within the cultural fabric of the community it serves. As schools and society function as mirrors reflecting one another, the linguistic and cultural characteristics of the local environment inevitably permeate the school gates, influencing every level of the educational experience (Yiğit & Bayrakdar, 2006).

One of the most significant cultural variables in the educational landscape is bilingualism. In regions where multiple languages coexist, students often enter the formal education system possessing a native language that differs from the official language of instruction. This linguistic duality creates a complex dynamic within the school environment. Bilingualism is not simply the ability to speak two languages; it is a social phenomenon influenced by language status, community support, and family language use (Pearson, 2007). In such contexts, the choice of language is rarely arbitrary; it varies according to the interlocutor, the setting, and the subject of the conversation (Cengiz, 2006). When the language spoken at home differs from the language of the classroom, it can lead to significant challenges in communication and adaptation, particularly during the early years of schooling.

Preschool education serves as the first formal step in a child's educational journey and is critical for school readiness. For children who are not native speakers of the official language, this period is especially pivotal. Research suggests that without early childhood educational services, bilingual children may enter primary school without a full command of the language of instruction, which can hinder their academic progress and socialization (Koşan, 2015). The early childhood period is characterized by the primacy of play, which acts as a primary vehicle for learning and social interaction (Katranǁ, 2016). However, when a language barrier exists, the effectiveness of play-based learning can be compromised, affecting the child's ability to express their emotions, follow instructions, and integrate into the peer group.

Within the school ecosystem, the impact of bilingualism manifests across three primary cultural dimensions: school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture. School culture refers to the overarching set of norms and values established by the administration and shared by the staff (Stolp & Smith, 1995). The attitudes of school administrators toward linguistic diversity often determine whether a bilingual environment is viewed as an asset or a hurdle, as they hold the primary authority in shaping the institutional atmosphere (Deal & Peterson, 1999). Classroom culture, on the other hand, is the more immediate social environment where the teacher acts as the central authority and a primary agent of socialization (Shannon, 1995). In a bilingual classroom, the teacher must navigate the tension between maintaining the official curriculum and acknowledging the students' native linguistic identities. Failure to bridge this gap can lead to cultural conflict, where the worldviews of the students are dismissed or viewed as deficient (Delpit, 1991). Effective management of such classrooms requires teachers to be culturally responsive, helping students maintain their differences while providing them with the linguistic tools necessary for success (Major et al., 2004).

Peer culture represents the unique social world created by children themselves, often distinct from the adult-led culture of the school (Corsaro, 2012). In bilingual settings, language becomes a powerful tool for social organization, determining friendship groupings and the hierarchy of popularity (Atkinson, 2013). Students may use their native language as a means of establishing intimacy and identity, while switching to the official language to navigate the expectations of the teacher. This dynamic can lead to the emergence of 'translator' roles, where bilingual students gain social capital by mediating between their peers and the teacher, potentially enhancing their self-confidence and social standing (Çetintaş & Yazıcı, 2016).

Despite the importance of these dynamics, many preschool teachers find themselves ill-equipped to handle the challenges of bilingualism. The inability to communicate with students in their native language can lead to feelings of incapacity, loneliness, and psychological distress for the educator (Yılmaz & şekerci, 2016). Furthermore, the language gap often extends to parent-teacher communication, where parents who do not speak the official language may feel excluded or fearful of prejudice, thereby limiting their involvement in their child's education (Yağan Güder, 2019). This disconnection can result in a fragmented educational experience where the child's home life and school life remain isolated from one another.

Previous studies have highlighted various problems associated with native language differences in the classroom, including difficulties in understanding instructions and a tendency for students to withdraw (Mercan Uzun & Bütün, 2015; Susar Kırmızı et al., 2019). However, there is a need for more in-depth, ethnographic research that examines how bilingualism reflects on the holistic culture of the preschool—incorporating the perspectives of teachers, students, and the broader school environment. While some research has focused on primary school settings (Gözüküç & Kıran, 2018), the specific nuances of the preschool period, where language acquisition is most fluid and social bonds are first formed, require closer scrutiny.

Therefore, the present study aims to identify the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education through an ethnographic lens. By focusing on a specific case in Southeastern Anatolia, this research seeks to explore how bilingualism shapes school culture, classroom dynamics, and peer interactions. The study intends to uncover how teachers adapt to these challenges, how students negotiate their identities between two languages, and how the linguistic environment influences the implementation of the preschool educational programme. Through this exploration, the research hopes to provide insights that can inform teacher training and policy development for more inclusive and culturally sensitive early childhood education.

intros.text:
Education and culture are inextricably linked domains, with the relationship between them forming the foundation of educational anthropology (Tezcan, 1978). In any educational setting, culture is not merely a backdrop but a dynamic force that shapes the interactions, values, and learning outcomes of all participants. Within the school environment, this manifests as school culture—the set of shared beliefs, rituals, and norms that define the institutional identity (Deal & Peterson, 1999). Specifically, the culture of the classroom serves as a critical socialization site where students internalize the roles and expectations of the dominant society (Shannon, 1995). Furthermore, children do not simply absorb adult culture; they actively contribute to its reproduction by creating their own distinct peer cultures through negotiation and creative play (Corsaro, 2012). For young children in the preschool period, these cultural dimensions are particularly vital, as this stage serves as the primary transition from the home environment to formal education, making it a cornerstone for future academic success and social integration (Katrancı, 2016).

In many regions globally, this cultural intersection is further complicated by bilingualism. Bilingualism occurs when individuals possess the ability to use two languages, a phenomenon often driven by the sociolinguistic characteristics of the local community. The process of second language acquisition is fundamentally a sociocognitive one, where learners adapt to their ecosocial environment through continuous interaction (Atkinson, 2013). However, the success of this adaptation is heavily influenced by social factors, including family language use, community support, and the attitudes held by the school system (Pearson, 2007). When the language spoken at home differs from the official language of instruction, a linguistic gap emerges that can significantly impact a child's early educational experience. In the Turkish context, children in certain regions enter preschool speaking Kurdish as their native language while Turkish serves as the official medium of education. This linguistic duality creates a complex dynamic where the school becomes a site of negotiation between the child's primary identity and the requirements of the state educational system.

Previous research has highlighted several challenges associated with this linguistic divide. Studies have shown that children who enter school without a sufficient command of the official language often face significant hurdles in their readiness for literacy and general school adaptation (Koşan, 2015; Susar, 2019). Specifically, language barriers can lead to difficulties in understanding classroom instructions and following school rules, which in turn may hinder the overall implementation of the preschool educational programme (Ağgül et al., 2018). Furthermore, the communication gap between teachers and students can lead to feelings of frustration and social withdrawal among learners, as they may struggle to express their basic needs and emotions in a language they have not yet mastered (Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). These challenges are not limited to the students; teachers often report feeling incapable or psychologically burdened when they cannot communicate effectively with their pupils, leading to an increase in professional stress and a perceived lack of efficacy (Karataş & Kınalıoğlu, 2018).

Despite these documented difficulties, some scholars argue that bilingualism can offer cognitive and social advantages. The ability to navigate two linguistic systems can foster flexibility of thinking, creativity, and a deeper awareness of cultural diversity (Çetintaş & Yazıcı, 2016). When teachers embrace the native languages of their students or attempt to learn them, it can create a more supportive atmosphere, making students feel closer to their educators and more confident in their own identities (Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Thus, the impact of bilingualism in the preschool classroom is not unilaterally negative but is instead mediated by the attitudes of the teachers and the overarching school culture.

While there is a body of literature focusing on the general difficulties of bilingual students in primary education (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018) or the perceived readiness of bilingual preschoolers (Çabuk, 2018), there remains a scarcity of comprehensive ethnographic research that examines how bilingualism reflects across multiple cultural layers simultaneously. Most existing studies employ quantitative measures or focused interviews with teachers, which may overlook the nuanced, everyday interactions that constitute the lived experience of the classroom. There is a particular need to understand how bilingualism manifests not only in the teacher-student dyad but also in the broader school culture—including interactions with parents and administrators—and within the autonomous peer cultures that children develop among themselves. Understanding these multifaceted reflections is essential for developing culturally responsive pedagogical strategies that can bridge the gap between a child's home life and their school experience (Delpit, 1991).

Therefore, the present study aims to identify the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education by examining it through three specific lenses: school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture. By adopting an ethnographic case study design, this research seeks to provide a thick description of how the coexistence of Turkish and Kurdish influences the daily routines, social hierarchies, and instructional processes in a village school in Southeastern Anatolia. Specifically, the study explores how bilingualism affects the exercise of the educational programme, the psychological state of the teachers, and the social dynamics among students during free play and structured activities.

Through this investigation, the study intends to reveal the complex ways in which language functions as both a barrier and a bridge within the educational environment. It is anticipated that the findings will offer valuable insights into the practical challenges faced by teachers in bilingual settings and highlight the role of student translators in shaping peer popularity and confidence. Ultimately, the results of this research may contribute to the development of more inclusive preschool policies and provide a rationale for integrating multilingualism and adaptation training into teacher education programmes. The following sections of the article describe the ethnographic methodology employed, present the findings regarding the three cultural dimensions, and discuss the implications of these results in light of existing literature on bilingualism and school culture.

intros.text:
Preschool education constitutes a critical period in a child's development, laying the foundation for future academic success and socialization. During these early years, children acquire fundamental skills, including language, cognitive abilities, and social interactions, which are essential for their holistic growth (Katrancı, 2016). However, the educational landscape is increasingly diverse, with many children entering preschool settings with linguistic backgrounds that differ from the official language of instruction. This linguistic diversity, particularly in regions where bilingualism is prevalent, presents unique challenges and opportunities for educators and policymakers. In Turkey, for instance, the Southeastern Anatolia region is home to a significant Kurdish-speaking population, where children often grow up bilingual, speaking both Kurdish and Turkish. Understanding the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education is therefore crucial for developing effective educational practices that support these children's learning and development.

Bilingualism, defined as the ability to use two languages, has been a subject of extensive research in applied linguistics and education. While some studies highlight the cognitive and social benefits of bilingualism, others point to the challenges it poses in educational settings, particularly when the child's home language differs from the language of instruction (Pearson, 2007). In the context of preschool education, bilingualism can influence various aspects of the learning environment, including school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture. School culture, encompassing the values, norms, and practices that characterize a school, can be significantly shaped by the linguistic diversity of its community (Deal & Peterson, 1999). Similarly, classroom culture, which refers to the social and academic environment within a specific classroom, is influenced by the interactions between teachers and students, as well as the language policies adopted by educators (Shannon, 1995). Peer culture, on the other hand, involves the social relationships and interactions among children, which can be affected by their linguistic abilities and preferences (Corsaro, 2012).

The impact of bilingualism on preschool education has been explored in various studies, yet there is a need for more in-depth research that examines the specific reflections of bilingualism on school, classroom, and peer cultures. For instance, research by Yılmaz and Şekerci (2016) highlights the communication challenges faced by teachers when working with students whose native language is not Turkish. These challenges can lead to difficulties in understanding instructions, following rules, and participating in classroom activities, ultimately affecting the children's learning outcomes. Similarly, Susar (2019) found that bilingual children who have not received preschool education often struggle with literacy acquisition when they enter primary school, underscoring the importance of early language support.

Furthermore, the role of teachers in navigating bilingual environments is critical. Teachers may face psychological and professional challenges when they lack proficiency in the students' home language, leading to feelings of inadequacy and frustration (Akdağ & Haser, 2016). On the other hand, teachers who are bilingual or who make efforts to learn the students' home language can foster a more inclusive and supportive classroom environment, enhancing students' sense of belonging and engagement (Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). The attitudes of school administrators also play a significant role in shaping the linguistic landscape of the school, as their policies and practices can either support or hinder the integration of bilingual students (Stolp & Smith, 1995).

In addition to the challenges, bilingualism can also offer opportunities for cultural exchange and social development. Children who are bilingual often develop advanced cognitive skills, such as flexibility in thinking and the ability to navigate between different cultural contexts (Çetintaş & Yazıcı, 2016). Moreover, bilingualism can enhance children's social skills, as they learn to communicate effectively with peers from diverse linguistic backgrounds (Atkinson, 2013). However, these benefits are contingent on the educational environment being supportive and responsive to the linguistic needs of bilingual children.

Despite the growing body of research on bilingualism in education, there is a gap in the literature regarding the specific reflections of bilingualism on preschool education in rural and village settings in Turkey. Most studies have focused on urban contexts or have examined bilingualism from a cognitive or linguistic perspective, without considering the broader cultural and social dimensions. This study aims to fill this gap by conducting an ethnographic case study in a village school in the Southeastern Anatolia region of Turkey. The study seeks to identify the reflections of bilingualism on school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture, providing insights into the experiences of teachers and students in a bilingual preschool setting.

The significance of this research lies in its potential to inform educational policies and practices that support bilingual children in preschool education. By understanding the challenges and opportunities associated with bilingualism, educators and policymakers can develop more effective strategies for promoting inclusive and equitable education. Furthermore, the study's findings can contribute to the broader discourse on bilingualism in education, highlighting the importance of culturally responsive teaching practices and the need for teacher training programs that prepare educators to work in multilingual contexts.

In conclusion, this study aims to explore the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education in a village school in Southeastern Anatolia, Turkey. By examining the impacts on school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture, the study seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the linguistic and cultural dynamics at play in bilingual preschool settings. The findings will offer valuable insights for educators, policymakers, and researchers working to support the educational needs of bilingual children in diverse contexts.

intros.text:
Preschool education serves as a foundational pillar in the developmental trajectory of children, shaping their cognitive, social, and linguistic competencies before they enter formal schooling. In an increasingly globalized world, the linguistic diversity within early childhood classrooms has become a defining characteristic of contemporary educational landscapes. Bilingualism, in particular, has garnered significant attention from researchers and practitioners alike, given its profound implications for child development, classroom dynamics, and institutional culture. The intersection of bilingualism and preschool education is not merely a linguistic concern but a complex sociocultural phenomenon that influences how children interact with their peers, engage with teachers, and navigate the norms of the school environment. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for developing pedagogical strategies that support both language acquisition and holistic development in multilingual settings.

The concept of culture in education is central to understanding how bilingualism operates within preschool institutions. Culture, broadly defined, encompasses the shared values, beliefs, and practices that shape human interaction and learning. In the context of schools, culture manifests in various forms, including school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture. School culture refers to the overarching norms and values that permeate the entire institution, often influenced by administrative decisions and community interactions. Classroom culture, on the other hand, is more immediate and specific, reflecting the daily interactions, rules, and pedagogical practices within a particular learning space. Peer culture, as defined by Corsaro (2012), represents the unique social structures and interpretive processes that children create among themselves, often distinct from adult-imposed structures. These three layers of culture are interconnected, and the presence of bilingualism can significantly alter the dynamics within each layer. For instance, the language used in the classroom can dictate the flow of communication, the formation of friendships, and the interpretation of rules.

Previous research has extensively explored the challenges and benefits of bilingualism in educational settings. Studies have highlighted the cognitive advantages of bilingualism, such as enhanced executive function and metalinguistic awareness (Atkinson, 2013). However, the focus has often been on the individual learner, with less attention paid to the broader cultural and institutional contexts in which bilingualism occurs. In the Turkish context, where Kurdish is spoken by a significant minority, the dynamics of bilingualism in preschool education have specific socio-political and cultural dimensions. Research by Yılmaz and Şekerci (2016) indicates that teachers often face significant communication barriers when working with students whose first language is not Turkish. These barriers can lead to misunderstandings, reduced student participation, and feelings of inadequacy among teachers. Similarly, Susar (2019) found that children who do not speak the language of instruction struggle with understanding instructions and following classroom rules, which can hinder their academic progress and social integration.

Despite the growing body of literature on bilingualism in education, there remains a gap in understanding how bilingualism specifically reflects on the various layers of culture within preschool settings. While studies have examined teacher-student communication and language acquisition, fewer have adopted an ethnographic approach to explore the nuanced ways in which bilingualism shapes school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture. For example, the extent to which bilingualism influences the physical structure of the school, the enforcement of rules, and the formation of peer groups remains under-researched. Furthermore, the emotional and psychological impact of bilingualism on teachers, particularly those who do not speak the students' native language, has not been fully explored. The existing literature often focuses on the linguistic outcomes, neglecting the cultural and social dimensions that are equally critical for a comprehensive understanding of the educational experience.

This study aims to address these gaps by investigating the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education through an ethnographic case study. The research seeks to provide a detailed account of how bilingualism influences school culture, classroom culture, and peer culture in a village school in Southeastern Anatolia, Turkey. By focusing on the interactions between teachers, students, and parents, the study aims to uncover the hidden dynamics of bilingualism that are often overlooked in quantitative studies. The research questions guiding this study are: (1) How does bilingualism reflect on school culture? (2) How does bilingualism reflect on classroom culture? and (3) How does bilingualism reflect on peer culture? These questions are designed to explore the multifaceted impact of bilingualism on the educational environment, moving beyond simple linguistic proficiency to examine the cultural and social implications.

The significance of this study lies in its potential to inform educational policies and practices in multilingual contexts. By providing a rich, qualitative account of the lived experiences of bilingual preschoolers and their teachers, the study can offer practical recommendations for educators and policymakers. For instance, understanding the role of peer culture in language acquisition can help teachers design activities that leverage peer interactions to support language learning. Similarly, insights into the challenges faced by teachers can lead to the development of targeted professional development programs that equip educators with the skills needed to navigate multilingual classrooms effectively. Furthermore, the study contributes to the broader discourse on cultural diversity in education by highlighting the importance of recognizing and valuing the linguistic and cultural backgrounds of all students.

In conclusion, while bilingualism is often viewed through a linguistic lens, its impact on the cultural fabric of preschool education is profound and multifaceted. This study seeks to illuminate these cultural dimensions, offering a nuanced perspective that can enhance the quality of education for bilingual children. By examining the interplay between language and culture at the levels of school, classroom, and peer groups, the research aims to fill a critical gap in the literature and provide actionable insights for improving educational outcomes in multilingual settings. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to a more inclusive and culturally responsive approach to early childhood education, ultimately benefiting children, teachers, and the broader educational community.

intros.text:
Language is not only a means of communication but also one of the most visible carriers of culture, identity and social participation. In educational settings, therefore, the language or languages used by children, teachers, families and school staff become part of the social organisation of schooling. Culture has long been understood as the complex whole of knowledge, beliefs, values, customs and habits acquired by individuals as members of society (Tylor, 2010), and education is one of the main processes through which culture is transmitted, transformed and reproduced (Tezcan, 1978). Schools are thus cultural environments as well as instructional institutions. Their routines, rules, rituals, symbols, interpersonal relationships and patterns of communication shape how children become members of the school community (Deal & Peterson, 1999; Stolp & Smith, 1995). When more than one language is actively present in such environments, bilingualism becomes an important dimension of school culture, classroom culture and peer culture.

Bilingualism may be broadly defined as the use of two languages by individuals or communities, although the degree of proficiency, domains of use and social status of each language may vary considerably (Mackey, 1982; Pearson, 2007). In multilingual societies, language choice is shaped by interlocutor, setting, purpose, social identity and perceived language status. Children may use one language at home, another in school, and both languages with peers, depending on the communicative situation. Pearson (2007) emphasises that input, family language practices, community support, literacy opportunities and attitudes toward language all influence whether children develop and maintain two languages. From a sociocognitive perspective, second language development is also inseparable from participation in social environments: learners adapt to and engage with the world through interaction, bodily action and situated communication (Atkinson, 2013). For young children, this means that learning the language of schooling is not merely a cognitive task but a social process embedded in daily routines, play, affective relationships and institutional expectations.

The preschool period is a particularly important stage in this respect. Preschool education supports children’s cognitive, social, emotional, linguistic and motor development and helps them adapt to later schooling (Katrancı, 2016). It is also one of the first institutional contexts in which many children encounter sustained expectations regarding the official language of education. In Turkey, the language of formal education is Turkish; however, many children, especially in some regions, grow up using Kurdish, Zazaki, Arabic or other languages in their homes and communities. For children whose home language differs from Turkish, preschool may be the first systematic environment in which they are expected to understand instructions, follow rules, communicate with teachers and participate in activities in Turkish. Studies on children whose first language is not Turkish indicate that they may experience difficulties in self-expression, communication with teachers, understanding instructions, adaptation to school and early literacy preparation (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Susar, 2019; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). At the same time, preschool education may facilitate school readiness and support the acquisition of Turkish before primary school (Koşan, 2015).

The educational consequences of bilingualism cannot be understood only as individual language proficiency. They are closely related to classroom culture and the ways teachers respond to linguistic diversity. A classroom is a social and cultural space in which norms, roles, values, expectations and relationships are continuously produced. Shannon’s (1995) ethnographic work on an urban bilingual classroom shows that classroom culture socialises children into particular ways of acting, speaking and belonging. Teachers, as central figures of authority, can either create inclusive classroom cultures that recognise children’s linguistic resources or produce conflict when the language and culture of children are treated as obstacles. Delpit (1991) argues that the schooling of children from minority language and cultural groups should both respect children’s own cultural backgrounds and explicitly support access to the dominant linguistic codes of schooling. Similarly, culturally responsive education requires teachers to build bridges between children’s home experiences and school expectations rather than positioning difference as deficiency (Gay, 2014).

Research conducted in Turkey has shown that teachers working with students whose mother tongue is not Turkish often encounter language-related problems and use various strategies to overcome them. These strategies include using bilingual students as translators, benefiting from visual and auditory materials, relying on body language, learning basic words in the children’s language, communicating through parents or school staff, and in some cases restricting the use of the home language in the classroom (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Such practices reflect not only pedagogical decisions but also teachers’ beliefs, emotions and professional preparedness. Beginning early childhood teachers may already experience concerns about classroom management and communication (Akdağ & Haser, 2016); in bilingual contexts these concerns may intensify when teachers cannot understand children’s needs, emotions or peer interactions. Rural teaching contexts may also involve additional challenges related to cultural adaptation, parent communication and professional isolation (Yağan Güder, 2019). Therefore, the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education must be examined in relation to teachers’ experiences as well as children’s learning.

Another key dimension is peer culture. Children are not passive recipients of adult culture; they actively interpret, negotiate and reproduce social life through their interactions with other children (Corsaro, 2012). In preschool classrooms, peer culture emerges through play, routines, secrets, rules, alliances, conflicts and shared meanings. Ethnographic research in a Turkish preschool classroom has shown that children create complex peer cultures through games, symbols and negotiations, and that they sometimes resist or reinterpret adult expectations in spaces such as washrooms, cafeterias and free-play areas (Yanık, 2018). In bilingual classrooms, language choice becomes part of this peer culture. Children may choose one language to build intimacy, another to address the teacher, and may attribute prestige or usefulness to peers who can mediate between languages. Thus, bilingualism can influence friendship relations, participation in play, group formation, popularity, exclusion, leadership and children’s sense of belonging.

Although there is a growing body of research in Turkey on the educational experiences of students whose mother tongue is not Turkish, much of this work has focused on primary school, early literacy, teacher opinions or general communication problems (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Susar, 2019; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Fewer studies have examined bilingualism in preschool settings through sustained observation of daily life. Yet preschool classrooms are rich environments in which the effects of bilingualism can be seen not only in formal learning activities but also in arrival routines, crying and separation from parents, free play, breakfast, rule-following, peer translation, teacher-child communication and school-parent relations. Moreover, bilingualism in school is not confined to the classroom. It is also reflected in school culture through administrators’ language attitudes, staff communication, parent interactions and the symbolic presence or absence of languages in the physical environment.

For these reasons, an ethnographic perspective is especially valuable. Ethnography allows researchers to understand the meanings, practices and relationships that constitute the culture of a group from within its everyday context. Rather than treating bilingualism only as a variable affecting achievement, ethnographic inquiry makes it possible to observe how language is used, negotiated, restricted, valued and transformed in natural settings. This approach is consistent with the view that language learning and socialisation are embedded in interaction and participation (Atkinson, 2013), and with sociological approaches that regard children as active contributors to classroom and peer cultures (Corsaro, 2012; Yanık, 2018).

In this context, the present study aims to identify the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education in a village school in Southeastern Anatolia, Turkey, where children use both Kurdish and Turkish. The study focuses on three interrelated cultural domains: school culture, classroom culture and peer culture. Specifically, it seeks to reveal how bilingualism is reflected in communication among school personnel, parents and children; how it affects classroom routines, rules, activities, teacher experiences and implementation of the preschool education programme; and how it shapes children’s peer relations, play, language preferences and social positioning. By examining these processes through observation, interviews, document analysis and researcher diary, the study aims to contribute an in-depth account of bilingualism as a lived cultural reality in preschool education.

intros.text:
Language is one of the most visible carriers of culture and one of the primary means through which children participate in social life, schooling and learning. In multilingual communities, children enter educational settings with linguistic resources shaped by family, neighbourhood and peer interaction, while schools often operate through an official or dominant language. This creates a particularly important pedagogical and cultural context in early childhood education, where communication, play, routines and social relations are central to learning. Preschool education is not only a preparation for later schooling but also a period in which children develop cognitive, social, emotional and linguistic skills through interaction with adults and peers. For this reason, understanding how bilingualism is reflected in preschool settings is important for teachers, school administrators and policy makers who seek to provide equitable and developmentally appropriate education.

Bilingualism may be broadly understood as the use of two languages by individuals or communities, although the degree of proficiency, the domains of use and the social value attached to each language may vary considerably. Children’s bilingual development is influenced by the amount and quality of input they receive, the language practices of their families, the status of the languages in the community and school support for language use (Pearson, 2007). From a sociocognitive perspective, language learning is not an isolated mental process but an adaptation to social environments through embodied interaction with people, objects and routines (Atkinson, 2013). Thus, the languages children use at home, in the playground and in the classroom are not simply communication tools; they are also part of the social worlds through which children make meaning, negotiate identities and participate in learning.

The relationship between culture and education has long been emphasised in educational sociology and anthropology. Culture includes values, norms, language, customs, symbols and practices that are produced and reproduced in social life (Tylor, 2019; Tezcan, 1978). Schools are cultural settings in which institutional rules, leadership practices, rituals, communication patterns and community expectations come together. School culture influences the experiences of teachers and students, and educational reforms or programmes cannot be understood apart from the particular cultures of schools (Deal & Peterson, 1999; Stolp & Smith, 1995). In multilingual regions, language becomes an especially salient component of school culture because it shapes who communicates with whom, how parents and teachers interact, which language is associated with authority, and how children understand school rules and expectations.

Classrooms also have their own cultures. Classroom culture is formed through the teacher’s expectations, routines, management practices, values and interactions, but children are not passive recipients of these arrangements. They interpret, resist, reproduce and transform the cultural patterns around them. In bilingual classrooms, the classroom culture may be shaped by the official language of instruction, the children’s home language, the teacher’s language knowledge and the strategies used to bridge communication gaps. Shannon’s (1995) ethnographic work on an urban bilingual classroom showed that language and culture are central to children’s socialisation into classroom roles and expectations. Delpit (1991) similarly argued that cultural and linguistic differences can lead to misrecognition when schools treat the dominant group’s language and norms as universal. These perspectives indicate that bilingualism in classrooms should be examined not only as a language proficiency issue but also as a cultural and relational phenomenon.

Peer culture is another crucial dimension of preschool life. Children produce peer cultures through play, routines, shared meanings and negotiations with one another (Corsaro, 2012). In preschool classrooms, children create games, rules, group memberships, jokes and forms of resistance that may differ from adult expectations. Ethnographic research in Turkish preschool settings has shown that young children construct complex peer cultures through symbols, games and shared spaces, and that these cultures are central to everyday classroom life (Yanık, 2018). In bilingual settings, language choice may organise peer relations by affecting who can join a game, who can translate for others, who becomes popular and who remains silent or excluded. Therefore, the study of bilingualism in preschool education requires attention not only to teacher-child communication but also to children’s interactions with peers.

In Turkey, the official language of education is Turkish; however, many children grow up in homes and communities where another language, such as Kurdish, is used extensively. When these children begin school without sufficient Turkish proficiency, they may experience difficulties in understanding instructions, expressing needs, participating in activities and adapting to school routines. Previous studies have reported that teachers working with students whose first language is not Turkish encounter communication problems, especially in the early years of schooling (Gözüküçük & Kıran, 2018; Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Teachers have also reported using strategies such as translator students, gestures, visual materials and attempts to learn children’s home language in order to maintain communication (Yılmaz & Şekerci, 2016). Research on preschool education suggests that early childhood education can support the school readiness and literacy preparation of children whose mother tongue is not Turkish (Koşan, 2015; Susar, 2019), yet the same context may also reveal difficulties in implementing the preschool curriculum when children do not understand the language of instruction.

Although bilingualism in education has been discussed in relation to communication problems, literacy readiness, teacher experiences and school adaptation, there remains a need for studies that examine how bilingualism is lived in the everyday culture of preschool institutions. Much of the existing research in Turkey has focused on primary school students or has relied mainly on teacher views. Less is known about how bilingualism is reflected simultaneously in school culture, classroom culture and peer culture in preschool village schools where Turkish and Kurdish coexist in daily life. It is also unclear how children’s language choices affect routines, activities, friendships, play and status among peers, and how teachers experience bilingualism in the process of implementing the preschool education programme.

Addressing this gap, the present study aims to identify the reflections of bilingualism on preschool education. More specifically, it examines how bilingualism is reflected in school culture, classroom culture and peer culture in a village preschool classroom in Southeastern Anatolia, Turkey. To obtain an in-depth and contextualised understanding of these reflections, the study adopts an ethnographic case study design. Data were collected through participant observation, interviews with preschool teachers and children, document analysis and a researcher diary during the 2019–2020 academic year. By focusing on the everyday practices of bilingual children, their teachers, school personnel and parents, the study seeks to illuminate bilingualism as a cultural, pedagogical and social phenomenon rather than merely as a linguistic variable.

The findings of this study may contribute to discussions on culturally and linguistically responsive preschool education. They may also provide insights for teacher education, in-service training and curriculum implementation in regions where children begin school with a home language different from the official language of instruction. Understanding how bilingualism shapes school, classroom and peer cultures can help educators design more inclusive practices that support both children’s participation in Turkish-medium schooling and their existing linguistic and cultural resources.

intros.text: Any human being may have similarities with others or may have some differences from others.  Psychology as an academic field strives to probe these similarities and differences to make generalizable  facts about human beings  Human beings can act differently even though they have similarities in age,  gender, and so on. The reason for this could be associated with the uniqueness of the human mind. This  uniqueness particularly is the matter of Individual Differences (IDs) studies within psychology  (Dewaele, 2009).  IDs in Second Language Acquisition (SLA) accordingly endeavor to anatomize the  differences in language learning process, such as different language learning rates, choice of learning  styles, and so forth  Within this research agenda, motivation has a vital role as it is both intriguing and  closely related to other aspects of language learning process. Language learning is an easy process for  some people; however, the same situation is not valid for others. Therefore, it is a kind of problematic  matter. At this point, if one has motivation at a satisfactory level, he or she may be successful in the end.Therefore, the notion of motivation has attracted so many scholars’ attention, and the research into  motivation has led to other constructs to emerge such as Willingness to Communicate (WTC). Even  though WTC has emerged within first language (L1) studies, it is unquestionably related with second or  foreign language (L2) as it is remarkably proper for L2 learning process and its fundamental point is to  make people communicate with each other in L2 (MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément, & Noels, 1998). The early studies on L2 motivation and L2 WTC have emphasized the role of integrative motivation  on L2 WTC  However, the motivational research paradigm is progressively focusing on the micro level  analysis rather than macro level analysis with the emphasis on the individual. intros.text:
Motivation has long been recognised as one of the most influential individual difference factors affecting success in learning a second or foreign language (L2) (Dewaele, 2009; Dörnyei, 2005). Over the past three decades, the study of motivation has undergone considerable transformation, both theoretically and methodologically. Perhaps the most significant of these developments has been the emergence of Dörnyei's (2005, 2009) L2 Motivational Self System (L2 MSS), which has become one of the most influential contemporary frameworks in the field. Building on earlier socio-psychological approaches, most notably Gardner and Lambert's Socio-Educational Model and its notion of integrativeness, the L2 MSS reconceptualises motivation around learners' future self-images. It comprises three components: the ideal L2 self, which represents the attributes one ideally wishes to possess as an L2 user; the ought-to L2 self, which reflects the attributes one believes one ought to possess to meet external expectations and avoid negative outcomes; and the L2 learning experience, which concerns situated aspects of the immediate learning environment (Dörnyei, 2009). This shift towards the self is particularly valuable in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts, where learners' opportunities for direct contact with the target language community are limited and the classical notion of integrative motivation becomes difficult to apply.

A related line of inquiry has focused on learners' willingness to communicate (WTC), which MacIntyre, Dörnyei, Clément, and Noels (1998) defined as the readiness to enter into discourse at a particular time with a specific person or persons using an L2. Rather than a stable personality trait, L2 WTC is now understood as the product of psychological, situational, and linguistic variables, and it has been proposed as the ultimate goal of language instruction. Because communication is central to language learning, understanding what makes learners willing to speak in the L2 has important pedagogical implications.

Given that both constructs are grounded in motivational research, it is reasonable to expect a link between the L2 MSS and L2 WTC. A growing, though still limited, body of research has begun to examine this connection, generally reporting that the ideal L2 self predicts L2 WTC, while the relationship between the ought-to L2 self and L2 WTC tends to be indirect or non-significant (Bursalı & Öz, 2017; Khajavy & Ghonsooly, 2017; Öz, 2016; Yashima, 2009). However, findings vary considerably across contexts, and comparatively little research has been conducted in the Turkish EFL setting. The present study therefore seeks to contribute to this emerging literature by investigating the relationship between the two dimensions of the L2 MSS — the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self — and L2 WTC among university preparatory-programme students in Turkey. Specifically, the study explores the participants' perceived levels of motivation and willingness to communicate, and examines whether these self-guides are significantly related to L2 WTC inside the classroom.

intros.text:
Over the past three decades, research into the motivation to learn a second or foreign language (L2) has witnessed remarkable theoretical and methodological innovation. Motivation has consistently been regarded as one of the most influential individual difference factors accounting for success in L2 learning (Dörnyei, 2005; Dewaele, 2009). Among the most recent and widely adopted frameworks, Dörnyei's (2005, 2009) L2 Motivational Self System (L2 MSS) has become an influential theory that reoriented the field from the socio-educational tradition of integrativeness towards a self-based, micro-level understanding of learner motivation. The L2 MSS comprises three components: the ideal L2 self, which represents a learner's future self-image as a competent L2 user; the ought-to L2 self, shaped by external expectations and social pressures; and the L2 learning experience, which relates to the immediate learning environment. This reconceptualization has proven especially valuable in English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts, where opportunities for direct contact with the target community are limited.

Parallel to these developments, willingness to communicate (WTC) has attracted growing scholarly attention. Originally emerging within L1 communication studies, WTC in the L2 has come to be understood not as a stable personality trait but as the integration of psychological, situational, and linguistic variables that predisposes learners to initiate communication when the opportunity arises (MacIntyre et al., 1998). Because sustained and spontaneous use of the L2 is regarded as a central goal of language instruction, understanding what drives learners to communicate is of considerable pedagogical importance.

Given that both constructs are grounded in the psychology of the learner, a natural question concerns how motivation, as conceptualized within the L2 MSS, relates to L2 WTC. A body of research has established links between the ideal L2 self and WTC, with several studies reporting the ideal L2 self as a significant predictor (Bursalı & Öz, 2017; Munezane, 2013, 2016; Öz, 2016; Yashima, 2009). The role of the ought-to L2 self, by contrast, appears far less consistent, with its relationship to WTC often reported as indirect, mediated by anxiety, or statistically non-significant (Khajavy & Ghonsooly, 2017; Papi, 2010). Despite this interest, studies explicitly examining the association between the L2 MSS and L2 WTC remain relatively few, and their findings vary across contexts and populations, suggesting that cultural and contextual factors warrant closer scrutiny. Moreover, much of the existing evidence derives from English majors rather than general preparatory learners in Turkish EFL settings.

To address this gap, the present study investigates the possible relationship between the L2 MSS and L2 WTC among preparatory program students at a private university in Turkey. Specifically, it examines learners' perceived levels of motivation and WTC, the associations between L2 WTC and both the ideal and ought-to L2 selves, and whether the relationship between the ideal L2 self and L2 WTC persists when the ought-to L2 self is controlled.

intros.text:
Understanding the individual differences that influence second language acquisition is central to the field of applied linguistics, as these factors significantly impact the effectiveness of the learning process (Dörnyei, 2005; Dewaele, 2009). Among these variables, motivation has long been recognized as a primary driver of success. For decades, the Socio-Educational Model prevailed, emphasizing integrative motivation as the desire to identify with the target language community. However, in many English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts, limited opportunities for direct interaction with native speakers have rendered this traditional view insufficient, prompting a shift toward more psychologically grounded frameworks.

To address these limitations, Dörnyei (2005, 2009) proposed the L2 Motivational Self System (L2 MSS). This framework shifts the focus from macro-level social integration to micro-level individual psychology, comprising three components: the Ideal L2 Self (the desired future version of oneself as a proficient speaker), the Ought-to L2 Self (the attributes one believes one ought to possess to meet external expectations), and the L2 Learning Experience. While the Ideal L2 Self is driven by internal desires, the Ought-to L2 Self is shaped by external pressures from family and society. These constructs provide a more nuanced understanding of how learners envision their future linguistic competence and how these images motivate their current efforts.

Parallel to these developments in motivation is the construct of L2 Willingness to Communicate (L2 WTC). Moving beyond the view of communication as a stable personality trait, MacIntyre et al. (1998) conceptualized L2 WTC as a situational, volitional act—the readiness to enter into a conversation at a particular moment. Because L2 WTC is seen as the ultimate goal of language instruction, researchers have sought to identify the predictors that trigger this readiness, ranging from linguistic competence to psychological factors like anxiety and motivation (Yashima, 2012).

Recent research has begun to explore the intersection of the L2 MSS and L2 WTC. Several studies have indicated that the Ideal L2 Self serves as a significant predictor of a learner's willingness to communicate (Bursalı & Öz, 2017; Öz, 2016; Yashima, 2009). In contrast, the role of the Ought-to L2 Self remains more ambiguous; some evidence suggests it may have an indirect relationship with WTC, often mediated by anxiety (Khajavy & Ghonsooly, 2017). Despite these insights, empirical studies linking these two frameworks remain relatively scarce, particularly within the Turkish EFL context.

Therefore, the present study seeks to investigate the relationship between L2 MSS and L2 WTC among university students in a preparatory English program in Turkey. Specifically, the study aims to determine the perceived levels of motivation and WTC, examine the correlation between these constructs (focusing on the Ideal and Ought-to L2 selves), and explore whether the relationship between the Ideal L2 Self and WTC persists when the Ought-to L2 Self is controlled.
