intros.text:
Idioms constitute a pervasive yet notoriously challenging feature of English for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL). Native speakers of English draw on idiomatic expressions with striking frequency; Polio, Barlow, Fine, and Polio (1977) estimated that an English native speaker produces an average of four idioms per minute of speech. For EFL learners, however, idioms present inherent difficulties because the meanings of the constituent words do not straightforwardly combine to yield the meaning of the whole expression. Compounding this difficulty is the fact that speakers of different languages tend to conceptualise experience differently, so that the figurative logic underlying an English idiom is often opaque to learners whose first language encodes the same domains of experience in other ways. Traditional pedagogical practice has commonly treated idioms as arbitrary, unanalysable chunks to be committed to memory through rote-learning. Such an approach, as Cho (2010) observes, fails to establish associations between new input and learners' prior knowledge and therefore does little to support the formation of durable cognitive structures.

Cognitive linguistics (CL) offers an alternative account of idiomatic language that has attracted growing attention in English language teaching. Grounded in cognitive, social, and communicative theories, CL holds that language reflects the ways in which humans encode their embodied interactions with the physical and social world (Evans & Green 2006; Langacker 2008). Within this framework, most idioms are not arbitrary but semantically motivated: they are examples of conceptual metaphors through which meaning is mapped from concrete, spatial domains onto more abstract ones (Lakoff & Johnson 1980; Lakoff 1993). The recognition that expressions such as 'love is a journey' rest on systematic cross-domain mappings suggests that learners who become aware of the conceptual metaphors underlying idioms may be better able to comprehend and retain them. This meaning-motivated view resonates with theories of meaningful learning, which propose that language items processed in relation to existing knowledge are more likely to be organised, retained, and transferred than items learned in isolation (Ausubel 2000; Hung 2019).

The pedagogical implications of CL also align with broader debates in second language teaching between interventionist and non-interventionist positions. Explicit, teacher-led instruction has been argued to foster explicit knowledge that, under appropriate conditions and with opportunities for use, can facilitate language production and even feed into implicit knowledge (Ellis 2005; Ellis 2015). This is especially relevant in EFL contexts, where learners have limited daily exposure to the target language and therefore depend on classroom input as a principal source of learning (Harmer 2015; Ur 2012). A CL-informed pedagogy, delivered explicitly and followed by controlled drills and communicative tasks, thus appears well suited to adult EFL learners.

A number of CL-motivated experiments have provided empirical support for teaching idioms and other figurative language through awareness-raising of conceptual metaphors. Boers (2000) found that grouping idioms into metaphorical themes aided retention among Dutch EFL learners, while Csabi (2004) and Condon (2008) reported that learners who engaged with the conceptual motivation of idioms outperformed those who learned them as arbitrary units. Comparable advantages for CL-based instruction have been documented for prepositions (Hung 2017; Hung & Vien 2018), tense and aspect (Bielak & Pawlak 2013), and modal verbs (Tyler et al. 2010). Despite these encouraging findings, several gaps remain. Much of the existing research has been conducted in European contexts, and previous studies have called for replication elsewhere. Vietnamese EFL learners have received little attention, idioms in business and financial discourse have rarely been targeted, and, notably, most prior treatments have relied on instruction and translation drills without incorporating productive, communicative tasks.

The present study addresses these gaps by applying basic concepts in cognitive linguistics to the teaching of twelve English idioms about finance to Vietnamese first-year EFL college students. Using a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest between-group design, it compares a CL-based treatment that raises learners' awareness of the conceptual metaphors of MONEY with a treatment for rote-learning and a no-treatment control group. Distinctively, both experimental treatments incorporate a productive speaking task following instruction. The study asks whether CL-based treatment yields superior receptive and productive knowledge of the target idioms, both immediately after instruction and after a delay, thereby contributing new evidence on the effectiveness of CL for teaching idioms in an under-researched context.

intros.text:
Idioms are pervasive in natural language and constitute a fundamental component of communicative competence for learners of English as a foreign language (EFL). Studies of native speaker production have shown that idiomatic expressions occur with remarkable frequency in everyday discourse, with Polio, Barlow, Fine, and Polio (1977) estimating that a native speaker uses an average of four idioms per minute of spoken language. Despite their centrality, idioms pose particular difficulties for EFL learners because the meaning of an idiom cannot be derived from the literal meanings of its constituent words. Compounding this challenge is the fact that speakers of different languages tend to conceptualise experience in different ways, so that the semantic motivation underlying an English idiom is frequently opaque to a learner whose first language encodes the world differently.

Traditionally, idioms have been treated pedagogically as arbitrary, unanalysable strings whose meanings must be memorised. This rote-learning approach, however, does not help learners build a cognitive structure, since new input is not connected to previously learned items or existing knowledge (Cho, 2010). Theories in second language acquisition and educational psychology suggest that learning which is not meaningful fails to promote retention, because learners need to organise and systematically classify target items for cognitive processing to take place (Ausubel, 2000; Hung, 2019). This concern has motivated a search for pedagogical alternatives grounded in principled accounts of how idioms mean.

Cognitive linguistics (CL) offers such an account. Grounded in cognitive, social, and communicative theories, CL holds that language reflects how humans encode their embodied experiences of interacting with the physical world (Evans & Green, 2006; Langacker, 2008). A key insight is that many idioms are not arbitrary but semantically motivated: they are examples of conceptual metaphors in which meaning is transferred from a concrete, spatial domain to an abstract one (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980; Lakoff, 1993). On this view, raising learners' awareness of the conceptual metaphors underlying idioms should scaffold comprehension and support long-term retention, an implication that aligns closely with the interventionist position in English language teaching that explicit instruction, followed by drills and opportunities for productive use, is a valuable input in EFL contexts where daily exposure to the target language is scarce (Ellis, 2005; Thornbury, 2002).

A growing body of CL-motivated research has begun to test these implications empirically. Boers (2000) found that grouping idioms into conceptual-metaphor themes helped Dutch EFL learners retain target items, while Csábi (2004) and Condon (2008) reported that semantic explanation of the conceptualisation behind idioms produced superior learning compared with treatments that ignored it. Similar advantages for CL-based instruction have been documented for prepositions and for tense and aspect, with treated groups outperforming those relying on rule-based or rote-learning approaches in both immediate and delayed posttests (Tyler et al., 2010; Hung & Vien, 2018; Hung, 2017). Studies such as Bielak and Pawlak (2013) further incorporated productive tasks after explicit instruction.

Despite these encouraging findings, several gaps remain. Most CL-based experiments on idioms have relied on instruction and translation drills, with relatively little attention to productive, communicative tasks such as speaking. Almost all of this work has been conducted in European contexts, and researchers have repeatedly called for the applications to be replicated in other settings; to our knowledge, no such experiment has involved Vietnamese learners. Moreover, there has been little interest in teaching idioms drawn from business and financial discourse, despite their practical relevance for learners. Langacker (2008) has also stressed that the hypotheses of cognitive linguistics require further empirical testing.

The present study addresses these gaps by applying basic concepts in cognitive linguistics to the teaching of English financial idioms to Vietnamese EFL learners. Twelve idioms expressing conceptual metaphors of MONEY were taught to 50 first-year college students, who were assigned to a cognitive group receiving CL-based treatment, a traditional group receiving rote-learning treatment, and a control group. Using a quasi-experimental pretest–posttest between-group design, the study compares the two treatments in terms of learners' receptive and productive knowledge on immediate and delayed posttests, thereby seeking to determine whether awareness of conceptual metaphors enhances both learning and long-term retention of idioms in this under-researched context.

intros.text:
Idioms are an integral component of natural language proficiency, yet they present significant challenges for learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL). Because the meaning of an idiomatic expression is not typically a literal summation of its parts, these phrases are often perceived as arbitrary and opaque. Traditional pedagogical approaches have largely treated idioms as fixed blocks of language to be acquired through rote-learning, a method that often fails to provide learners with a cognitive framework to associate new input with existing knowledge (Cho, 2010). Consequently, EFL learners often struggle not only with the initial acquisition of idioms but also with their long-term retention and productive use.

In the field of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), the debate between interventionist and non-interventionist approaches highlights the role of explicit instruction in language development. Interventionists argue that explicit input is crucial for the formation of explicit knowledge, which can subsequently facilitate language use (Ellis, 2005). This is particularly pertinent for adult learners in EFL contexts where naturalistic exposure to the target language is limited. Meaningful learning, which involves the logical organization of knowledge and the linking of new information to a learner's prior cognitive structure, is essential for ensuring that language is not merely memorized but retained in long-term memory (Ausubel, 2000; Hung, 2019). Without such cognitive engagement, learners often find 'language chunks' difficult to master, regardless of their overall proficiency level.

Cognitive Linguistics (CL) offers a promising alternative to traditional rote-learning by positing that language is a reflection of how humans encode their physical and social experiences. Central to this approach is the theory of conceptual metaphor, which suggests that many idioms are not arbitrary but are 'semantically motivated.' According to Lakoff and Johnson (1980), metaphors are grounded in everyday experience, allowing humans to map concepts from a concrete spatial domain to an abstract one. For example, the conceptualization of LOVE as a JOURNEY allows speakers to use spatial terms like 'crossroads' to describe relational decisions. From this perspective, idioms are viewed as examples of conceptual metaphors rather than random linguistic accidents.

Recent empirical evidence suggests that applying CL principles to the classroom can significantly enhance the learning of complex linguistic items. Studies have shown that CL-based instruction is effective in teaching English prepositions (Hung, 2017; Hung & Truong Vien, 2018) and modal verbs (Tyler et al., 2010), often outperforming traditional rule-based or picture-based methods. In the specific domain of idioms, research has indicated that awareness-raising instruction focused on the underlying conceptual metaphors helps learners form more durable memory traces and improve both receptive and productive knowledge. However, much of this research has been conducted in European or East Asian contexts, such as with Dutch or Japanese learners, leaving a gap in the literature regarding the application of these methods in Southeast Asia.

Furthermore, there has been limited research focusing on the acquisition of idioms within specialized domains, such as business or finance, which are critical for college-level EFL students entering professional fields. While some studies have combined CL instruction with translation drills, there is a need to investigate the integration of productive tasks, such as speaking activities, to facilitate the transfer of explicit knowledge into communicative competence.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the effectiveness of a Cognitive Linguistic approach compared to traditional rote-learning in teaching English idioms related to finance to first-year Vietnamese EFL college students. By employing a quasi-experimental design with a control group, this research seeks to determine whether an awareness of conceptual metaphors enhances both the immediate acquisition and the long-term retention of idiomatic expressions. Specifically, the study examines the impact of CL-based treatment on both the receptive and productive knowledge of the learners, contributing to the broader discourse on meaning-motivated instruction in the Vietnamese EFL context.

intros.text:
In the field of English Language Teaching (ELT), the debate between interventionist and non-interventionist approaches continues to shape pedagogical practice. Interventionists emphasize the necessity of explicit teacher instruction to provide the input required for language development, arguing that conscious learning facilitates the formation of explicit knowledge, which can subsequently be transferred to implicit use (Ellis, 2005). Conversely, non-interventionists advocate for naturalistic exposure and implicit acquisition (Krashen, 1985). In many EFL contexts, however, the lack of daily exposure to the target language makes explicit instruction a vital tool for learners. Consequently, there is a growing consensus that integrating these approaches—providing concise, explicit input followed by productive practice—is the most effective way to foster language proficiency (Harmer, 2015).

One framework that aligns with the need for meaningful, explicit instruction is Cognitive Linguistics (CL). CL posits that language is not an arbitrary set of rules but a reflection of how humans encode their physical and social experiences into linguistic forms (Evans & Green, 2006). Central to this approach is the concept of meaningful learning, which suggests that retention is enhanced when new input is logically organized and associated with the learner's existing cognitive structures (Ausubel, 2000). By focusing on the semantic motivation behind linguistic forms, CL-based instruction aims to move beyond rote memorization, allowing learners to build a more durable cognitive map of the language (Hung, 2019).

This approach is particularly relevant for the teaching of English idioms. Idioms have traditionally been viewed as figurative expressions whose meanings are arbitrary and opaque, making them notoriously difficult for EFL learners to acquire. Conventional pedagogical techniques often rely on rote-learning—treating idioms as 'language chunks' to be memorized in isolation—which frequently fails to create long-term memory because it lacks cognitive association (Cho, 2010). However, cognitive linguists argue that most idioms are not arbitrary but are examples of conceptual metaphors (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980). By understanding the mapping from a concrete domain (e.g., a physical journey) to an abstract domain (e.g., a romantic relationship), learners can perceive the semantic motivation behind an expression, thereby facilitating easier acquisition and recall.

Several studies have already demonstrated the efficacy of CL-based instruction in ELT. For instance, research on English prepositions has shown that students receiving CL-based treatment outperformed those receiving traditional instructions in both spatial and metaphorical understanding (Hung & Truong, 2018; Hung, 2017). Similarly, studies on English modals have suggested that CL provides a more effective basis for grammar instruction than traditional speech-act perspectives (Tyler et al., 2010). Regarding idioms specifically, experimental evidence has indicated that awareness-raising instruction based on conceptual metaphors helps learners form longer-term memories compared to traditional methods (Boers, 2000).

Despite these promising results, there remains a significant gap in the literature. First, the majority of these experiments have been conducted in European or East Asian contexts, with a notable lack of empirical research involving Vietnamese EFL students. Second, there has been limited focus on the application of CL to idioms within specific professional discourses, such as business or finance. Finally, while many studies focus on receptive knowledge, there is a need for further investigation into how CL-based instruction supports the productive use of idioms in communicative tasks.

Addressing these gaps, the present study aims to investigate the effects of a Cognitive Linguistic approach on the acquisition of English idioms related to finance among Vietnamese first-year college students. Specifically, the study compares the effectiveness of CL-based instruction against traditional rote-learning in terms of both receptive and productive knowledge, measuring gains in both immediate and delayed posttests. By incorporating a productive speaking task into the treatment, this research seeks to offer a more comprehensive account of how conceptual metaphor awareness facilitates the long-term retention and use of idiomatic expressions in an EFL context.

intros.text:
English idioms present a persistent challenge for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners, often due to the arbitrary nature of their meanings which do not align with the literal definitions of their constituent words. Traditional pedagogical approaches frequently treat idioms as isolated lexical items to be memorized through rote learning, a method that often fails to foster long-term retention or deep understanding (Cho et al., 2010). In contrast, Cognitive Linguistics (CL) posits that language is grounded in human cognition and embodied experience, suggesting that many idioms are not arbitrary but are motivated by conceptual metaphors. This theoretical perspective offers a promising avenue for enhancing the teaching and learning of figurative language in EFL contexts. 

The theoretical foundation of this study rests on the premise that language learning is most effective when it facilitates meaningful connections between new input and existing knowledge structures. Ausubel (2000) argues that meaningful learning, which involves associating new information with relevant concepts in the learner's cognitive structure, is superior to rote memorization for retention and transfer. In the context of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), Ellis (2005) highlights the dynamic interface between explicit and implicit knowledge, suggesting that explicit instruction can facilitate the initial acquisition of patterns which are subsequently internalized through use. This aligns with the interventionist approach to language teaching, which emphasizes the crucial role of explicit teacher input in EFL settings where naturalistic exposure is limited (Condon & Kelly, 2002). 

Recent scholarship has increasingly explored the application of CL principles to English Language Teaching (ELT). Studies have demonstrated that raising learners' awareness of the conceptual metaphors underlying grammatical structures and lexical items can significantly improve learning outcomes. For instance, Tyler et al. (2010) found that a CL-based approach to teaching English modals was more effective than traditional speech-act approaches. Similarly, Hung (2017) and Hung & Vien (2018) conducted quasi-experimental studies with Vietnamese students, showing that CL-based instruction on English prepositions outperformed traditional methods in both spatial and metaphorical meanings. These studies suggest that explaining the semantic motivation behind language items helps learners organize knowledge hierarchically, thereby enhancing memory retention (Hung, 2019). 

Despite these advancements, there remains a gap in the literature regarding the application of CL to the teaching of idioms, particularly within the Vietnamese EFL context. While previous research has focused on prepositions and modals, idioms—often categorized as 'dead metaphors' or conceptual metaphors (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980)—have received less attention in experimental studies involving Vietnamese learners. Furthermore, many existing studies have focused primarily on European contexts or different linguistic domains. The specific challenges faced by Vietnamese learners, who may have limited exposure to English outside the classroom, necessitate further investigation into pedagogical strategies that maximize the efficiency of classroom instruction. 

This study aims to address this gap by applying basic concepts of cognitive linguistics to the teaching of English idioms to Vietnamese first-year EFL college students. Specifically, it investigates the effectiveness of a CL-based treatment, which raises awareness of conceptual metaphors, compared to a traditional rote-learning approach. The study focuses on a set of idioms related to finance, categorized under conceptual metaphors such as MONEY AS A CREATURE and MONEY AS A SUBSTANCE. By employing a quasi-experimental design with pretest, immediate posttest, and delayed posttest measures, this research seeks to determine whether CL-based instruction facilitates superior retention of both receptive and productive knowledge of idioms over time. The findings of this study contribute to the growing body of empirical evidence supporting the integration of cognitive linguistic theories into EFL pedagogy, offering practical implications for teachers seeking to enhance students' figurative language competence.

intros.text:
In the realm of English language teaching (ELT), the acquisition of idiomatic expressions remains a persistent challenge for learners, particularly in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts. Idioms are often described as figurative expressions where the meaning of the whole cannot be deduced from the literal meanings of the constituent words. Because idioms are deeply rooted in the conceptualization of the target culture, they frequently expose inherent difficulties to learners whose first language (L1) conceptualizes the world differently. As noted by Polio et al. (1977), native speakers use an average of four idioms per minute, yet EFL learners often struggle to interpret unfamiliar ones due to pedagogical techniques that treat idioms as arbitrary matters. Consequently, traditional approaches, often characterized by rote-learning, fail to establish the cognitive structures necessary for long-term retention (Cho et al., 2010). This limitation underscores the importance of exploring alternative pedagogical frameworks that can bridge the gap between literal and conceptual semantics.

Cognitive Linguistics (CL) has emerged as a promising theoretical framework for addressing these challenges. Grounded in cognitive, social, and communicative theories, CL posits that language is not merely a formal system but a reflection of how humans encode their experiences of the physical and social world (Evans & Green, 2006; Langacker, 2008). Within this framework, idioms are viewed not as arbitrary units but as examples of conceptual metaphors. Lakoff and Johnson (1980) argued that metaphor is not just a literary device but is grounded in everyday experience, allowing information to be projected from a concrete source domain to an abstract target domain. For instance, the conceptual metaphor LOVE IS A JOURNEY helps explain idioms such as 'we are at a crossroads' or 'the marriage is on the rocks.' By understanding these underlying conceptual mappings, learners can make sense of the semantic motivation behind idioms, potentially facilitating deeper processing and better retention.

The application of CL to ELT has gained traction in recent years, with researchers investigating its efficacy in teaching various linguistic components. Previous studies have demonstrated that CL-based instruction can be effective for teaching prepositions (Hung, 2017; Hung & Truong Vien, 2018) and modal verbs (Tyler et al., 2010). For example, Tyler et al. (2010) found that a CL treatment group significantly outperformed a speech-acts treatment group in learning English modals. Similarly, Boers (2000) and Condon (2008) reported that raising learners' awareness of conceptual metaphors in idioms helped them retain target items longer than those who learned through traditional methods. These studies suggest that meaningful learning, which connects new input to existing knowledge, is crucial for forming long-term memory (Ausubel, 2000). However, while these findings are encouraging, they have primarily focused on European contexts or specific linguistic categories such as prepositions and modals.

Despite the growing body of research supporting CL-based instruction, a significant gap remains regarding its application to Vietnamese EFL students, particularly in the domain of business or finance-related idioms. Most existing studies have been conducted in Europe or with learners of different L1 backgrounds, leaving the specific cognitive processing of Vietnamese learners underexplored. Furthermore, while previous research has often relied on translation drills or controlled exercises, there is a need to investigate the impact of productive tasks, such as speaking activities, within a CL framework. The current study aims to address these gaps by examining the effectiveness of a CL-based approach compared to traditional rote-learning methods in teaching English idioms about finance to Vietnamese first-year EFL college students. Specifically, this research investigates whether raising awareness of conceptual metaphors enhances both immediate and delayed retention of idiomatic knowledge. By employing a quasi-experimental design with a control group, this study seeks to provide empirical evidence on the pedagogical value of CL in an EFL context where exposure to English is limited, thereby contributing to the ongoing discourse on meaningful learning in language education.

intros.text:
Idiomatic expressions are a pervasive feature of everyday English and an important component of communicative competence. For learners of English as a foreign language (EFL), however, idioms are also among the most difficult lexical items to acquire because their meanings cannot usually be inferred from the literal meanings of their constituent words. When learners encounter expressions such as funds are drying up or taxes are eating me alive, word-by-word decoding is unlikely to lead to an adequate interpretation. This difficulty is intensified in EFL contexts, where learners have limited opportunities for incidental exposure to figurative language and where instruction often treats idioms as fixed, arbitrary expressions to be memorised. Such rote-learning may support short-term recognition, but it gives learners little basis for organising idioms meaningfully or retaining them over time.

A growing body of work in second language acquisition suggests that explicit attention to form–meaning relationships can assist adult language learning, especially in instructional settings where naturalistic input is limited. Explicit knowledge and implicit language use are not identical, but they can interact dynamically: conscious noticing and analysis may help learners register patterns that are later strengthened through practice and use (Ellis, 2005). From a cognitive perspective, meaningful learning is more likely to promote retention than isolated memorisation because new input is linked to existing knowledge structures (Ausubel, 2000). In language education, this implies that learners need opportunities not only to encounter target expressions but also to understand how they are motivated, organise them systematically, and use them in meaningful tasks (Hung, 2019).

Cognitive linguistics (CL) offers a particularly relevant framework for idiom instruction. Rather than viewing linguistic meaning as an autonomous system of rules, CL regards language as grounded in embodied experience, conceptualisation, and usage. Usage-based accounts hold that linguistic knowledge develops from recurring form–meaning pairings in communicative experience (Diessel, 2015; Lieven et al., 2008). In this view, many idioms are not wholly arbitrary; they are semantically motivated by broader conceptual patterns. One of the central insights of CL is that metaphor is not merely a literary device but a basic mechanism of thought through which abstract domains are understood in terms of more concrete experience. Thus, idioms can often be interpreted as expressions of conceptual metaphors. Financial idioms, for example, may conceptualise money as a liquid, substance, or living creature. Recognising these mappings can help learners see systematicity among expressions that might otherwise appear unrelated.

Pedagogical research inspired by CL has shown promising results in several areas of English language teaching. Studies on prepositions have demonstrated that presenting polysemous meanings through networks, prototypes, and motivated semantic relations can improve learners’ understanding and retention more effectively than traditional explanation alone (Cho et al., 2010; Hung, 2017; Hung & Vien, 2018). CL-based instruction has also been applied to grammar, including tense, aspect, and modals, with evidence that motivated semantic explanations can outperform more conventional pedagogical descriptions (Tyler et al., 2010). These findings are consistent with broader arguments that grammar and vocabulary instruction should help learners notice meaningful patterns rather than simply memorise isolated rules or forms (Thornbury, 2002).

The application of CL to idiom teaching is especially compelling because idioms are often presented to learners as lexical chunks without internal logic. If learners are guided to identify the conceptual metaphors underlying idiomatic expressions, they may be able to group idioms into meaningful categories, infer figurative meanings more effectively, and retain them for longer. At the same time, instruction needs to be embedded in classroom procedures that include practice and communicative use. Recent work in EFL pedagogy has emphasised the value of tasks and learner engagement, including technology-mediated and task-based approaches, for creating purposeful language use (Chen & Lin, 2018). Although the present study is not technology-based, it draws on the same pedagogical principle that explicit input should be followed by opportunities for meaningful practice.

Despite increasing interest in CL-informed pedagogy, further empirical evidence is still needed, particularly in under-researched EFL contexts and with specialised idiomatic domains. Much previous experimental work has examined European or other Asian learner populations, and relatively little attention has been paid to Vietnamese EFL students’ learning of English idioms. In addition, business and finance idioms are pedagogically important for college learners but have received limited experimental investigation. The present study therefore examines whether a cognitive linguistic approach can enhance Vietnamese first-year EFL students’ acquisition and retention of English finance-related idioms. Specifically, it compares a CL-based treatment, in which learners are introduced to conceptual metaphors and asked to classify and paraphrase idioms, with a traditional rote-learning treatment and a no-treatment control condition. The study investigates the effects of these treatments on learners’ receptive and productive knowledge immediately after instruction and after a delay, thereby addressing both short-term learning and longer-term retention.

intros.text:
Idiomatic competence is an important component of communicative competence in English because idioms occur frequently in everyday, academic, and professional discourse and often carry meanings that cannot be inferred through word-by-word decoding. For learners of English as a foreign language (EFL), idioms are particularly challenging: the lexical items that compose an idiom usually contribute to an overall figurative meaning rather than to a transparent literal interpretation. In business and finance discourse, expressions such as funds are drying up, taxes are eating me alive, or the company poured money into education require learners not only to know the words but also to understand the conceptual patterns through which abstract financial events are represented. When idioms are treated as arbitrary expressions to be memorized, learners may acquire short-term recognition of forms and translations, but they often have difficulty retaining and using them productively.

A cognitive linguistic perspective offers a principled explanation for why many idioms are learnable rather than wholly arbitrary. Cognitive linguistics views language as grounded in human experience, conceptualization, and usage, and it assumes that linguistic meaning reflects the ways in which speakers structure and encode their interactions with the physical and social world. From this view, figurative language is not peripheral to language but central to meaning construction. Lakoff and Johnson’s account of conceptual metaphor has been especially influential in showing that abstract domains are commonly understood through more concrete domains; for example, relationships may be conceptualized as journeys, and money may be conceptualized as a substance, liquid, or living entity. Such mappings help explain why many idioms are semantically motivated even when their meanings are not literally compositional.

This theoretical position has clear pedagogical relevance for EFL instruction. Meaningful learning depends on learners’ ability to relate new input to existing cognitive structures rather than store isolated items mechanically (Ausubel, 2000). Similarly, work on the relationship between explicit and implicit knowledge suggests that conscious attention to form–meaning relationships can support language learning and later use, particularly in instructed second language contexts where learners may have limited exposure to naturally occurring input (Ellis, 2005). In EFL classrooms, explicit instruction, practice, and opportunities for meaningful production may therefore work together: instruction can raise awareness of semantic patterns, drills can consolidate form–meaning associations, and communicative tasks can encourage learners to retrieve and use the target items.

Previous research has provided growing support for applying cognitive linguistics to language teaching. Studies on prepositions, modals, tense and aspect, and other difficult areas of English have shown that cognitively motivated explanations can help learners understand systematic semantic networks more effectively than traditional rule-based or translation-based instruction (Cho et al., 2010; Tyler et al., 2010; Hung, 2017; Hung & Vien, 2018). In relation to idioms, research has also suggested that learners benefit from identifying the conceptual metaphors underlying figurative expressions and from classifying idioms according to motivated semantic themes. Such findings are consistent with the broader claim that cognitive linguistic instruction can make opaque language items more meaningful and memorable by linking them to embodied experience and conceptual organization.

However, several issues remain insufficiently explored. Much of the existing experimental work on cognitive linguistic instruction has been conducted in contexts outside Vietnam, and relatively little is known about how Vietnamese EFL college students respond to conceptual-metaphor-based instruction for English idioms. In addition, idioms in business and finance discourse have received less pedagogical attention than idioms expressing emotions or general everyday experience, despite their usefulness for learners in higher education and professional settings. Finally, many studies of idiom instruction have relied heavily on explanation, classification, and translation, while fewer have incorporated productive speaking tasks after explicit conceptual instruction. It therefore remains necessary to examine whether a cognitive linguistic treatment that combines awareness raising, controlled practice, and productive use can improve both immediate learning and longer-term retention of finance-related idioms in an EFL context.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the effects of a cognitive linguistic approach to teaching English idioms about finance to Vietnamese first-year college EFL students. Specifically, it compares a conceptual-metaphor-based treatment with a traditional rote-learning treatment and a no-treatment control condition. The target idioms are organized around conceptual metaphors of money, including MONEY AS A CREATURE, MONEY AS A SUBSTANCE, and MONEY AS A LIQUID. The study asks whether students receiving cognitive linguistic instruction outperform those receiving traditional instruction in their receptive and productive knowledge of the instructed idioms, and whether any advantage is maintained in delayed testing. By providing experimental evidence from a Vietnamese EFL setting, the study contributes to research on cognitive linguistics in instructed language learning and offers pedagogical implications for teaching idiomatic expressions as semantically motivated rather than arbitrary language chunks.

intros.text: Motivation is defined as "the learner's attitude, desire, interest and willingness to invest effort in learning a second language" (Richards, 2015, p. 149). Motivation plays an important role in foreign or second language (L2) learning as it acts as an incentive drive for a long-term and tiresome learning process (Dörnyei, 2005)  Also, motivation can explain why people think and act accordingly, so it has the potential to determine success or failure in any learning situation. To be successful, L2 learners need to be enthusiastic, committed and persistent. Strongly argued, the smartest learners may not be able to master the L2 if they lack adequate motivation to sustain the effort in a lengthy L2 learning process  In other words, learners lacking motivation to learn are more likely to fail than the motivated ones (Dörnyei, 2002; 2005). Supported by Richards (2015), motivation increases the amount of invested time and effort of the learners who need to be committed to the L2 learning, which only some learners can do so due to their robust interest in learning the L2. Based on early works on learning motivation pioneered by Gardner and Lambert (1959), motivation is divided into two main types, that is, integrative and instrumental motivation (Richards, 2015). Integrative motivation concerns "a positive attitude toward the target language and culture, and a desire to interact with it and assume some of its values" (Richards, 2015, p. 150). It represents the wish to become a target language community member, which is an internal motivation (Gardner & Lambert, 1972). In the L2, learners who wish to integrate themselves into the target language culture community (Harmer, 2015) or learn L2 for their own self-perceived needs and goals (Brown, 2014) possess integrative motivation. In contrast, instrumental motivation reflects a primarily practical reason for learning a language (Richards, 2015). Instrumental learners may perform a task for rewards such as money, prizes and grades, or positive feedback (Brown, 2014). To be successful in learning, integrative motivation is encouraged. Subsequently, due to globalisation and the role of English as a world lingua franca, the traditional concept of motivation has been reconceptualised to focus on self and identity rather than integration into the target language community (Dörnyei, 2009; Ushioda, 2011). Ushioda (2011) points out three reasons. First, it is because more curricula treat English as an essential basic educational skill. Second, there is no clear definition of the target language community for English learners to integrate into. Third, the Internet and online communication networks connect language users around the world and flatten geographical boundaries separating the language users' community.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been recognised as one of the most influential individual difference factors affecting success in second and foreign language learning (Gardner & Lambert, 1959; Gardner, 2006). For decades, the concepts of integrativeness and integrative motivation dominated the field, emphasising a learner's disposition towards the target language community and its culture. However, as English has increasingly acquired the status of a global lingua franca and a "must-have" basic educational skill without a clearly defined target community, traditional constructs such as integrativeness have lost much of their explanatory power (Ushioda, 2011). In response, Dornyei (2009) reconceptualised L2 motivation and proposed the L2 motivational self system (L2MSS), which reoriented attention from the external domain of the language community to the internal domain of the learner's self and identity. Drawing on the theory of possible selves and self-discrepancy theory, the L2MSS comprises three components: the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self, and the L2 learning experience.

This framework has particular relevance in foreign language contexts where no English-speaking community exists, since motivation to reduce the gap between one's current and desired ideal selves can drive sustained learning effort (Winke, 2007). As Dornyei (2001) argues, motivating learners for long-term development is the responsibility of every teacher, and effective classroom conditions are central to maintaining such motivation (Richards, 2015; Harmer, 2015). Understanding how learners construct their motivational selves is therefore essential for planning appropriate pedagogy and for fostering the self-regulated, autonomous learning behaviours that are associated with higher language proficiency (Brown, 2014).

Despite growing interest in the L2MSS across Asian settings, most studies have been conducted with university students, and findings regarding which component exerts the strongest influence remain inconclusive. In the Thai context in particular, research adopting the full three-component L2MSS framework is scarce. Even recent large-scale studies with Thai high school students have relied on pre-reconceptualisation notions of motivation, and several existing studies have omitted the L2 learning experience construct altogether. Yet findings from the undergraduate context cannot be generalised to school learners, and the secondary school years have been described as among the most suitable for instructed language learning. High school students with a strong ideal L2 self also tend to employ deep learning strategies that positively affect achievement, making the school stage a critical site for motivational research.

Given these gaps, and the limited attention paid to the motivational lives of Thai high school learners, the present study aims to explore the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of the L2MSS among Thai EFL senior high school students. The findings are expected to offer insight into the motivational self system of young learners, to inform more effective and appropriate pedagogy, and to provide further evidence concerning the self aspects of the L2MSS framework.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been regarded as one of the most influential factors in second and foreign language learning, since without it even talented learners struggle to sustain the effort required to attain long-term goals (Dörnyei, 2001; Gardner & Lambert, 1959). For decades, the field was dominated by Gardner and Lambert's (1959) socio-educational model and its notion of integrativeness, which emphasised learners' attitudes towards the target language community and its culture. However, as English has increasingly become a global lingua franca and a "must-have" educational skill rather than the language of a clearly defined community, traditional concepts such as integrative motivation have lost much of their explanatory power (Ushioda, 2011). This is particularly evident in foreign language contexts where no English-speaking community is readily available for learners to identify with (Gardner, 2006).

In response to this discontent, Dörnyei (2009) reconceptualised L2 motivation and proposed the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), which redirects attention from external relationships to the internal domain of self and identity. Drawing on the theory of possible selves and self-discrepancy theory, the framework comprises three constructs: the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self, and the L2 learning experience (Dörnyei, 2009; Ushioda, 2011). This theoretical shift towards learners' visions of who they want to become as language users carries important implications for how teachers engage students' motivation, interests, and identities (Ushioda, 2011; Richards, 2015). Since its introduction, the L2MSS has generated considerable research interest across Asian contexts, linking the three constructs to variables such as language proficiency, learning strategies, and self-regulated learning (Brown, 2014).

Despite this growing body of work, several gaps remain. Most L2MSS studies have been conducted with university students, and findings regarding which component most strongly influences learning have been inconsistent. In the Thai context in particular, research addressing all three components is scarce, and even the most recent large-scale study of Thai high school learners adopted the concept of motivation prior to Dörnyei's reconceptualisation. Moreover, several existing studies omitted the L2 learning experience construct altogether. Crucially, findings from undergraduate contexts cannot be readily generalised to high school learners, whose motivational profiles may differ and whose developmental stage has been described as particularly suitable for language learning within instructional settings. There is therefore a pressing need to understand how basic-education students construct their L2 motivational selves.

Addressing this gap, the present study aims to explore the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of the L2MSS among Thai EFL senior high school students. Employing an explanatory mixed-methods design combining a questionnaire and semi-structured interviews, it seeks to offer insight into the motivational self system of young learners and its role in their language learning. The findings are expected to inform English language pedagogy and pave the way for further L2MSS research in the Thai context.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been recognized as a critical determinant of success in second language acquisition. For decades, the field was dominated by the socio-educational model proposed by Gardner and Lambert (1959), which emphasized integrative motivation—the desire to identify with and integrate into the community of the target language (Gardner, 2006). However, in the era of globalization, where English has become a global lingua franca and a "must-have" basic educational skill, the traditional concept of integrativeness has lost much of its explanatory power, particularly in foreign language contexts where no immediate target language community exists (Ushioda, 2011).

In response to these limitations, Dörnyei (2009) reconceptualized motivation by developing the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS). Shifting the focus from external social domains to the internal domain of self and identity, the L2MSS consists of three components: the Ideal L2 Self (the person the learner wishes to become), the Ought-to L2 Self (the attributes the learner believes they should possess to meet expectations or avoid negative outcomes), and the L2 Learning Experience (situation-specific motives related to the immediate learning environment). This framework suggests that the discrepancy between a learner's actual state and their ideal self-image serves as a powerful catalyst for motivation and self-regulated learning (Dörnyei, 2009; Winke, 2007).

Despite the theoretical appeal of the L2MSS, empirical research has predominantly focused on university students, leaving a gap in our understanding of younger learners. In the Thai EFL context, research on the L2MSS remains scarce, particularly at the basic education level. While some studies have explored university students in Thailand, findings from higher education cannot be generalized to high school students, for whom the secondary school age is considered one of the most suitable periods for language learning within instructional contexts (Boo, Dörnyei & Ryan, 2015). Furthermore, many existing studies in Thailand have neglected the L2 Learning Experience construct, focusing only on the self-image components.

Given that strong ideal L2 self-images are linked to deeper learning strategies and higher achievement, it is essential to understand how Thai high school students construct their motivational self-systems. Understanding these dynamics allows teachers to create more effective classroom conditions to maintain motivation (Richards, 2015) and fulfill their responsibility to support learners' long-term development (Dörnyei, 2002). Therefore, the objective of this study is to explore the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. The findings aim to provide pedagogical insights into the motivational drivers of young learners and pave the way for further research within the Thai educational context.

intros.text:
Motivation is widely recognized as a central driver of success in second language acquisition (SLA). For decades, the field was dominated by the socio-educational model, which emphasized integrative motivation—the desire to identify with and integrate into the community of the target language (Gardner & Lambert, 1959; Gardner, 2006). However, as English has evolved into a global lingua franca, the traditional concept of integrativeness has lost much of its explanatory power, particularly in foreign language contexts where no immediate target-language community exists (Ushioda, 2011). In response to this shift, Dörnyei (2009) reconceptualized motivation through the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), moving the focus from external social domains to the internal domain of the self. This framework comprises three components: the Ideal L2 Self (the desired future version of oneself as a proficient user), the Ought-to L2 Self (the attributes one believes they should possess to meet expectations or avoid negative outcomes), and the L2 Learning Experience (situation-specific motives related to the immediate learning environment).

Despite the theoretical robustness of the L2MSS, empirical research has predominantly focused on university students, leaving a gap in our understanding of younger learners. In the Thai context, research on the L2MSS remains scarce at the basic education level. While some studies have addressed high school students, many have either relied on outdated motivational concepts (Imsa-ard, 2020) or omitted the L2 Learning Experience construct entirely (Malirum, 2018; Nguyen, 2019). This is a significant omission, as the secondary school years are considered the most suitable period for language learning within instructional contexts (Boo, Dörnyei & Ryan, 2015). Furthermore, findings from tertiary education cannot be simply generalized to high schoolers, whose motivational drivers and learning strategies may differ significantly (Imsa-ard, 2020).

Therefore, the present study aims to explore the Ideal L2 Self, Ought-to L2 Self, and L2 Learning Experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. By employing an explanatory mixed-methods design, this research seeks to provide a nuanced understanding of how these three constructs manifest among young learners in Thailand. It is expected that these findings will offer insightful information for educators to better engage students' interests and identities (Ushioda, 2011) and help teachers develop more effective strategies for maintaining long-term motivation (Dörnyei, 2001; Richards, 2015). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: the literature review examines the theoretical underpinnings of L2MSS, followed by the methodology, the results of the quantitative and qualitative analyses, and finally, a discussion of the pedagogical implications.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been recognised as a critical factor in second language acquisition, with traditional models such as Gardner and Lambert's (1959) integrative and instrumental orientation dominating the field for decades. However, as English has evolved from a target language to a global lingua franca, the relevance of integrative motivation—rooted in the desire to identify with a specific target language community—has been questioned, particularly in contexts where no such community exists (Ushioda, 2011). This shift necessitates a reconceptualisation of motivation that aligns with contemporary theories of self and identity. Addressing this need, Dörnyei (2009) proposed the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), a framework grounded in the theories of possible selves and self-discrepancy. The L2MSS comprises three core components: the ideal L2 self (the attributes an individual wishes to possess), the ought-to L2 self (attributes one believes they ought to possess to meet external expectations), and the L2 learning experience (situation-specific motives related to the immediate learning environment). Unlike earlier models, this framework emphasises the internal domain of motivation, focusing on how learners envision their future selves and the discrepancy between their current and ideal states.

While the L2MSS has gained substantial traction in applied linguistics, the majority of empirical research has been conducted within tertiary education contexts, often overlooking secondary school students. This is a significant gap, as the secondary school age is considered particularly suitable for language learning within an instructional context (Boo, Dörnyei & Ryan, 2015). Furthermore, existing studies frequently omit the L2 learning experience component or fail to account for the specific cultural and educational nuances of non-Western contexts. In the Thai context, research on motivation has historically relied on pre-reconceptualisation frameworks, and large-scale studies specific to high school students remain scarce (Imsa-ard, 2020). Although recent work has begun to explore motivation among Thai undergraduates (Darling & Chanyoo, 2018), there is a paucity of literature investigating the L2MSS constructs among senior high school students, who face unique academic pressures and developmental stages.

Understanding the motivational profiles of Thai EFL senior high school students is essential, as motivation is a prerequisite for long-term goal achievement (Dörnyei, 2005). Without adequate motivation, even capable learners may struggle to sustain the effort required for proficiency. Moreover, the interplay between the three L2MSS components and their impact on learning strategies and achievement in the Thai context remains under-explored. For instance, while some studies suggest that a strong ideal L2 self correlates with deep learning strategies (Irgatoğlu, 2021), it is unclear if this holds true for Thai adolescents. Additionally, the role of external factors, such as parental influence and the immediate learning environment, in shaping these self-guides requires further investigation. As Richards (2015) notes, maintaining learning motivation is contingent upon effective classroom conditions, making the L2 learning experience a vital area of inquiry.

Therefore, this study aims to explore the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. By employing an explanatory mixed-methods design, this research seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of how these motivational constructs manifest in the Thai context. The findings are expected to offer insights into the motivational self-system of young learners, paving the way for pedagogical interventions that enhance motivation and, consequently, language learning achievement. Ultimately, this study contributes to the broader discourse on L2 motivation by addressing the gap in secondary education research and validating the applicability of the L2MSS framework within the Thai EFL context.

intros.text:
In the realm of English Language Teaching (ELT), learner motivation has long been recognized as a pivotal factor influencing second language acquisition. Traditional perspectives, notably those of Gardner and Lambert (1959) and Gardner (2006), emphasized integrative motivation, suggesting that a desire to identify with the target language community drives learning success. However, in the contemporary globalized context, particularly within English as a Foreign Language (EFL) settings where a distinct target language community is often absent, the explanatory power of integrativeness has been questioned (Ushioda, 2011). Consequently, the field has witnessed a paradigm shift towards internal psychological constructs, specifically the self-system, to better understand the motivational dynamics of modern learners.

Addressing this theoretical evolution, Dörnyei (2009) reconceptualized motivation through the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS). This framework posits that motivation is driven by the discrepancy between a learner's current self and their possible future selves. The L2MSS comprises three core components: the ideal L2 self (the attributes one wishes to possess), the ought-to L2 self (attributes one believes one ought to possess to meet external expectations), and the L2 learning experience (situation-specific motives related to the immediate environment). While this model has garnered significant attention, the majority of empirical research has focused on university students in tertiary contexts. For instance, Darling and Chanyoo (2018) explored these constructs among Thai undergraduates, and Subekti (2018) examined their impact on Indonesian university students. Furthermore, studies often isolate specific components; for example, research in the Thai context by Malirum (2018) investigated high school students but omitted the L2 learning experience construct, leaving a gap in understanding the holistic motivational profile of younger learners.

This limitation is critical because the secondary school age is considered a crucial period for language learning within an instructional context (Boo, Dörnyei & Ryan, 2015). Findings from undergraduate populations cannot be automatically generalized to high school students, whose motivational drivers may differ significantly due to developmental stages and educational pressures. Additionally, the interaction between the L2 learning experience and future self-guides remains less clearly theorized (Ushioda, 2011), necessitating further investigation into how immediate learning environments shape long-term motivational goals in EFL settings. Without adequate motivation, even capable learners may fail to achieve long-term goals (Dörnyei, 2005), making it imperative to identify the specific motivational constructs that impact this demographic.

Therefore, this study aims to explore the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. By employing an explanatory mixed-methods design, this research seeks to fill the existing gap regarding the L2MSS in basic education. It is expected that the findings will offer insightful information about the motivational self-system of young learners and its roles in their language learning. Ultimately, understanding these dynamics will pave the way for pedagogical strategies that effectively enhance student motivation and support their long-term development as autonomous language users.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been regarded as one of the most influential individual difference variables in second and foreign language learning. Even learners with adequate aptitude and access to instruction may fail to sustain the effort required for long-term language development if they lack sufficient motivation (Dörnyei, 2001; Winke, 2007). In English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts, where opportunities to use English outside the classroom may be limited, understanding what energises learners’ engagement is particularly important for teachers, curriculum planners, and researchers. Motivation is also closely connected with learners’ capacity to regulate their own learning; studies in Asian EFL settings, for example, have shown links between self-regulated learning strategies and language proficiency (Brown, 2014). Thus, investigating learners’ motivational orientations can provide useful insight into how English learning may be supported more effectively.

Early work on second language motivation was strongly shaped by Gardner and Lambert’s socio-educational perspective, especially the concepts of integrative and instrumental motivation (Gardner & Lambert, 1959; Gardner, 2006). However, the global spread of English has raised questions about the explanatory power of integrativeness, particularly in contexts where English is learned not to join a specific target-language community but as a global resource for education, work, technology, and communication. In response to this theoretical shift, Dörnyei (2009) proposed the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), which reconceptualises motivation through learners’ self-images and learning experiences. The model consists of three components: the ideal L2 self, referring to the learner’s desired future image as a competent L2 user; the ought-to L2 self, referring to attributes learners believe they should possess because of duties, expectations, or avoidance of negative outcomes; and the L2 learning experience, referring to motives arising from the immediate learning environment, including teachers, peers, curriculum, and classroom experience.

The L2MSS is especially relevant in contemporary English learning because it places self, identity, and future vision at the centre of motivation. Ushioda (2011) argues that globalisation and the status of English as a basic educational and communicative resource require motivation research to account for learners’ identities, aspirations, and digitally mediated worlds. In practical terms, this perspective also suggests that teachers can foster motivation by creating meaningful classroom conditions and by connecting English learning with learners’ personal goals and imagined futures (Richards, 2015). For Thai senior high school students, such issues are significant because they are at a stage where future study and career choices become increasingly salient, while English instruction may still be strongly shaped by school-based curricula and examinations.

Although the L2MSS has generated considerable research interest, much of the existing work has focused on university learners. Findings from tertiary contexts cannot necessarily be generalised to secondary school students, whose learning goals, classroom experiences, parental influences, and examination pressures may differ. In Thailand, research on high school students’ English learning motivation remains limited, and some studies have not examined all three L2MSS components, particularly the L2 learning experience. This gap is important because classroom experience may be a key source of motivation in EFL environments where learners have relatively few opportunities for authentic communication outside school.

To address this gap, the present study explores the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. By combining questionnaire data with interview evidence, the study aims to provide a richer understanding of how these learners imagine their English-using futures, how external expectations shape their motivation, and how their school learning context contributes to or constrains their engagement with English.

intros.text:
Motivation has long been recognised as a crucial individual difference in second and foreign language learning. Learners may possess adequate aptitude, access to instruction, and opportunities for practice, yet sustained progress is unlikely without the desire and effort to engage in learning over time. In EFL contexts, where English is often learned primarily through classroom instruction rather than daily interaction with an English-speaking community, understanding what energises learners’ effort is especially important for teachers and curriculum planners. Motivation is also closely connected with self-regulated learning and proficiency, as learners who can direct and sustain their own learning tend to achieve better language outcomes (Brown, 2014).

Early work on second language motivation was strongly influenced by Gardner and Lambert’s socio-educational perspective, particularly the role of attitudes, integrative motivation, and learners’ orientation toward the target language community (Gardner & Lambert, 1959; Gardner, 2006). However, the global spread of English has challenged the explanatory power of integrativeness, especially in settings where learners do not necessarily aspire to join a specific English-speaking community. In response to these theoretical and contextual changes, Dörnyei (2009) proposed the L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), which reconceptualises motivation through three dimensions: the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self, and the L2 learning experience. The ideal L2 self refers to learners’ desired future image as competent L2 users, whereas the ought-to L2 self concerns attributes learners feel they should possess because of duties, expectations, or avoidance of negative consequences. The L2 learning experience captures situated motives arising from the immediate learning environment, including teachers, peers, materials, and classroom experiences.

This self-based perspective is particularly relevant to contemporary English language education because learners’ imagined futures, identities, and experiences with English increasingly extend beyond the classroom through digital media, entertainment, international mobility, and career aspirations. Ushioda (2011) argues that the shift toward self and identity has important implications for how teachers engage learners’ interests and future visions. Similarly, Dörnyei’s work on motivational teaching practice stresses that classroom conditions and teacher strategies can help generate and maintain learner motivation (Dörnyei, 2001), while Richards (2015) highlights the importance of effective learning conditions in sustaining motivation.

Although the L2MSS has generated considerable research interest, much existing work has focused on university learners. Findings also vary regarding which component most strongly supports language learning, and the L2 learning experience has not always been included in studies of learners’ motivational self systems. In Thailand, research on English motivation among high school students remains limited, and findings from tertiary contexts cannot simply be generalised to basic education. This is a significant omission because senior high school is a formative period for developing future self-images, learning habits, and attitudes toward English as a tool for further study, communication, and work.

To address this gap, the present study explores the ideal L2 self, ought-to L2 self, and L2 learning experience of Thai EFL senior high school students. Using an explanatory mixed-methods design, it combines questionnaire data with semi-structured interviews in order to describe students’ motivational profiles and explain how these motivational dimensions are constructed in their learning context. The findings are expected to provide insights into the motivational self system of Thai adolescent EFL learners and to inform pedagogical efforts to enhance and sustain their English learning motivation.

intros.text: The theoretical notion of “English as a Lingua Franca” (henceforth ELF) emerged in the second half of the 1990s.  ELF is the form of English used as a contact language by people from varying lingua-cultural backgrounds (Firth 1996). Researchers using the ELF approach distinguish the form of ELF from English as a native language (ENL) and the pedagogic subject English as a foreign language (EFL). Traditionally, the study of English by nonnative speakers is largely based on ENL norms, with the goal of communicating effectively with native speakers; differences from ENL norms in all aspects are regarded as errors that result from learners’ incomplete acquisition and when this takes place, teachers’ correction and remediation are very much needed (Jenkins 2006). However, the aim of English study for an ELF speaker is to communicate with other non-native speakers, so technically, ENL norms should not be applied to set the linguistic agenda of ELF (Jenkins 2012). Instead, the norms of ELF are negotiated by its users for specific purposes by relying on their linguacultural resources and are derived from interactions involving efforts and adjustments from all parties (Jenkins 2009, Cogo 2010). Based on this tenet of the theory, differences from ENL norms are not always signs of language incompetence, but can be indicative of emerging or potential features of ELF (Jenkins et al. 2011). That is, ELF speakers are viewed as language users in their own right who make use of English for their own purposes. According to Cogo and Dewey (2006) and Jenkins (2006), there are three criteria for determining whether features are emerging trends. First, they must be systematic in nature. Secondly, they must occur frequently and are produced by numerous speakers. Finally, they should not cause a breakdown in communication. Modifications that meet these criteria are regarded as “deviations” or “variants”, which are a natural part of language contact and language change, and not as “errors”, which are a result of the incomplete knowledge of English.  Despite the focus on linguistic form, there are fewer ELF studies on morphosyntax, compared to phonology and pragmatics.  In fact, research at this level is also crucial to the understanding of ELF communication.  Many morphosyntactic features are redundant and serve communal, not communicative, purposes, resulting in speakers avoiding them and deviating from ENL norms (Seidlhofer 2008).  Furthermore, many studies have analysed ELF forms in Europe (such as France and Italy) and the outer circle of Asian countries (such as Singapore and India); however, studies on the expanding circle of Asian countries (such as Japan and Thailand) are far less common (Bolton 2008).  In addition, ELF research has predominantly dealt with spoken interactions (Dewey 2014).  Although there has been recent interest in written language, not many implications have been drawn (Jenkins et al. 2011).  Thailand is classified as an Asian country in the expanding circle firstly because it does not have a history of British colonisation and secondly, because English is used mainly for inter-cultural communication.  There are just a few studies on Thai ELF learners and they mostly focus on socio-cultural aspects, not on the linguistic form of the language.  To deal with this limitation and the other limitations of the previous literature as stated above, this study examines ELF’s morphosyntactic system in the academic writing of Thai learners. Given that deviations in tenses and aspects are often found in L2 research (e.g., Ranta 2006, Stapa & Izahar 2010), the target features of the current study include the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive aspect -ing. intros.text:
Over the past few decades, English has become the world's foremost contact language, used more often between speakers who do not share a first language than between native speakers themselves. This demographic shift, driven by globalisation and the deepening interconnectedness of contemporary social life, has fundamentally transformed the way English is used and conceptualised (Dewey 2007). Where speakers of different linguistic and cultural backgrounds meet, English functions as a lingua franca (ELF), and this use has grown from a minority interest within applied linguistics into a major field of study in its own right (Jenkins 2012). Central to the ELF perspective is the recognition that English used in lingua franca interactions is not a deficient version of native English (ENL) but a legitimate form of communication occupying its own space, one that is neither English as a foreign language nor failed native English (Jenkins 2006).

Since the pioneering work of Firth (1996), ELF scholars have sought to describe the phenomenon empirically, arguing that ELF must be well grounded in systematic description in order to gain acceptance as a legitimate variety (Jenkins 2009). Research has revealed patterns of change and linguistic fluidity emerging across all levels of language, including phonology, pragmatics, and morphosyntax (Jenkins et al. 2011, Cogo 2010). One of the most significant insights to emerge from this body of work is that many of the deviations from ENL norms observed among ELF users are not errors resulting from inadequate knowledge, but principled adjustments motivated by the pragmatic demands of communication. Cogo and Dewey (2006), for instance, demonstrated how pragmatic or functional motives such as efficiency, added prominence, and the exploitation of redundancy can lead to lexico-grammatical innovation, revealing an intimate interrelationship between pragmatics and morphosyntax. Similarly, Ranta (2006) showed that ELF speakers extend the use of the progressive aspect for expressive purposes, drawing on the 'attractiveness' of its form and meaning rather than misapplying a rule.

Within Asia, where the numbers of English users have grown exponentially and where distinct varieties continue to develop, questions of proficiency and norm have become especially pressing (Bolton 2008). Thailand offers a productive site for such inquiry. Although the country has no official second language and its population is overwhelmingly Thai-speaking, English serves as the de facto second language and is used across a wide range of domains including business, tourism, and higher education. As a member of ASEAN, which has adopted English as its official working language, Thailand relies on English as a lingua franca linking it culturally, intellectually, and commercially with its neighbours and the wider world. Given this status, it is reasonable to expect that identifiable features of ELF used by Thai speakers will emerge, and a study of this group promises to reveal both features particular to Thai users and broader characteristics of the nature of ELF communication.

Despite the growing interest in the morphosyntax of ELF, relatively little attention has been paid to how proficient Thai users handle specific grammatical systems, and even less to why they deviate from ENL norms when they do. Verbal inflectional suffixes provide a revealing test case because they carry information that is frequently redundant, being recoverable through other means, yet they remain heavily emphasised in traditional L2 pedagogy, which treats grammatical accuracy as central to success (Dewey 2014). Following the principle that ELF description should be drawn from communication between proficient users so that systematic patterns can be identified (Cogo & Dewey 2006, Jenkins 2009), the present study examines the academic writing of advanced and upper-intermediate Thai English-major students. It focuses on three suffixes: the third person singular present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing. The study addresses two questions: in what ways do Thai ELF learners deviate from ENL norms in their use of these three suffixes, and what linguistic and functional causes underlie these deviations? By analysing the circumstances in which learners omit the tense suffixes and extend the meaning of the progressive, this study aims to determine whether such deviations constitute emerging ELF features, to clarify the relationship between morphosyntax and pragmatics, and to draw out implications for the teaching of English in international settings, where distinguishing core features from unproblematic variants is of considerable pedagogical value (Seidlhofer 2005).
