intros.text:
The spread of English across the globe has profoundly reshaped who uses the language and how it is used. As people from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds interconnect for a wide range of purposes, English has increasingly come to function as a world-wide contact language, spoken far more often among non-native speakers than between native speakers. This demographic shift is now widely acknowledged in applied linguistics, and it has given rise to a rapidly growing field of inquiry into English as a Lingua Franca (ELF), that is, English used among speakers who do not share a first language (Cogo, 2010; Jenkins, 2009; Jenkins et al., 2011). What distinguishes ELF is that it draws on forms shared with English as a Native Language (ENL) as well as forms that differ from ENL and that emerge through contact across geographical, linguistic, and cultural boundaries (Jenkins, 2009).

Since the 1990s, ELF scholars have been particularly interested in describing the linguistic forms that characterise lingua franca communication, in the belief that ELF needs to be well-grounded in empirical description in order to be recognised as a legitimate manifestation of English rather than a deficient version of it. Studies have shown patterns of change and linguistic fluidity emerging at all levels of the language, including phonology, pragmatics, and morphosyntax (Cogo & Dewey, 2006; Firth, 1996; Jenkins, 2006; Jenkins et al., 2011). Importantly, this line of research has argued that deviations from ENL norms among proficient ELF users should not be treated as errors caused by inadequate knowledge, but rather as systematic and functionally motivated features. Cogo and Dewey (2006), for instance, demonstrated the interrelationship between pragmatics and morphosyntax by showing how pragmatic motives such as the efficiency of communication and the exploitation of redundancy can drive lexico-grammatical innovation. Similarly, Ranta (2006) found that ELF speakers extend the use of the progressive aspect for reasons of expressivity and explicitness, exploiting the 'attractiveness' of the -ing form rather than misusing it.

Much of this descriptive work, however, has been based on European corpora and on ELF speakers of various first-language backgrounds, and it has often focused on spoken rather than written data. In Asia, where the numbers of English users have grown exponentially and where distinct varieties continue to emerge (Bolton, 2008), the systematic morphosyntactic features of particular speaker groups remain comparatively underexplored. Thailand is a case in point. Although Thailand has no official second language, English functions as the de facto second language: it is a compulsory subject throughout schooling and higher education and is used across business, tourism, the internet, and scientific and technological domains (Baker, 2012; Foley, 2005). As a member of ASEAN, which has adopted English as its official working language, Thailand relies on English as a lingua franca that links it culturally, intellectually, and commercially with the rest of the world. Given this status, it is reasonable to expect that recognisable ELF features are developing among Thai users, yet little is known about the specific morphosyntactic patterns that characterise this group. A close examination of Thai ELF learners would therefore not only reveal features particularly associated with these speakers but would also shed further light on the nature of ELF communication more generally.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the use of three English verbal inflectional suffixes, the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing, in the academic writing of advanced and upper-intermediate Thai ELF learners. Following the principle that ELF description should be drawn from proficient users so that systematic emerging patterns can be identified (Cogo & Dewey, 2006; Jenkins, 2009), it examines how these learners' usage deviates from ENL norms and analyses the linguistic and functional causes underlying such deviations. Specifically, the study asks under what circumstances these learners omit the tense suffixes or extend the progressive aspect, and whether syntactic complexity and pragmatic motives account for these choices. In doing so, it seeks to establish whether such deviations constitute emerging ELF features rather than errors, and to consider what implications the findings hold for teaching English in intercultural settings, where a distinction can usefully be drawn between features crucial for intelligibility and those that are unproblematic for communication (Seidlhofer, 2005, 2008).

intros.text:
The global spread of English has fundamentally transformed the language from the property of a few native-speaking nations into a global contact language. This process of globalisation has fostered a worldwide interconnectedness that necessitates a medium for communication between speakers of diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Consequently, the phenomenon of English as a Lingua Franca (ELF)—English used as a means of communication among speakers who do not share a native language—has gained significant prominence in applied linguistics (Cogo, 2010; Dewey, 2014). Unlike traditional Second Language Acquisition (SLA) perspectives, which often view deviations from native-speaker norms as errors or signs of inadequate proficiency, the ELF paradigm conceptualises such forms as legitimate linguistic innovations (Jenkins, 2006). As ELF users adapt the language to meet their communicative needs, they often create a 'third space' that is distinct from both English as a Native Language (ENL) and traditional English as a Foreign Language (EFL) (Jenkins, 2006).

Recent research into ELF has shifted from a purely descriptive account of linguistic forms to an exploration of the interrelationship between pragmatics and morphosyntax. Scholars have noted that the linguistic fluidity observed in ELF interactions is often driven by pragmatic motives, such as the desire for communicative efficiency, increased explicitness, and the exploitation of redundancy (Cogo & Dewey, 2006; Jenkins et al., 2011). For instance, certain grammatical features may be omitted or modified if they are deemed redundant and do not hinder mutual intelligibility. Moreover, some ELF speakers have been found to extend the use of specific grammatical structures to gain expressivity, a phenomenon exemplified by the 'attractive' use of the progressive aspect to add prominence to an utterance (Ranta, 2006).

In the context of Asia, the role of English is particularly salient. As noted by Bolton (2008), the emergence of Asian Englishes reflects the region's growing economic and political influence. Thailand, in particular, views English as a de facto second language and a vital link for intellectual and commercial exchange within the ASEAN community. Given the high prevalence of English in Thai higher education and business, it is likely that Thai speakers have developed their own characteristic patterns of ELF use. While many Thai learners are schooled to conform to ENL norms, their actual usage in demanding contexts—such as academic writing—may reveal emerging patterns that prioritise communicative effectiveness over strict grammatical adherence.

Despite the growing body of ELF research, there is still a need for empirical studies that specifically examine the morphosyntactic deviations of proficient learners in academic settings. Academic writing is a particularly fruitful domain for such research because it requires the management of complex ideas and varied structures, which can expose the tension between formal grammatical rules and functional communicative goals. While some studies have looked at agreement strategies in other Asian contexts (e.g., Stapa et al., 2010), there is a dearth of research focusing on the specific inflectional patterns used by advanced Thai ELF learners.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the patterns and causes of deviations in three specific English verbal inflectional suffixes: the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing. By analysing the academic writing of proficient Thai English majors, this study seeks to determine under what circumstances these learners deviate from ENL norms and whether these deviations are the result of linguistic complexity or functional, pragmatic motives. By doing so, the research intends to contribute to the broader understanding of ELF's morphosyntactic evolution and provide insights into how the drive for communicative efficiency shapes the way English is used by non-native speakers in a globalised academic context.

intros.text:
The phenomenon of globalization has fundamentally reshaped contemporary social life, fostering an unprecedented level of worldwide interconnectedness (Held et al., 1999). This shift has had a profound impact on language, specifically accelerating the spread of English as a global contact language used by speakers from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Within this context, English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) has emerged as a distinct field of study, focusing on English used among speakers who do not share a first language (Cogo, 2010). Because ELF operates in multicultural contexts, it is characterized by a degree of linguistic fluidity and innovation, often resulting in forms that deviate from English Native Speaker (ENL) norms across phonological, pragmatic, and morphosyntactic levels (Jenkins et al., 2011).

Historically, ELF research has transitioned from a narrow focus on linguistic forms to a broader exploration of various domains, including business and higher education (Cogo, 2010; Dewey, 2014). A central tenet of the ELF approach is the belief that the language must be grounded in empirical description to be recognized as a legitimate version of English rather than a failed attempt at native-like proficiency (Jenkins, 2006). Scholars have noted that in ELF interactions, the primary objective is often successful communication and mutual intelligibility rather than strict adherence to L1 norms (Jenkins et al., 2011). Furthermore, there is an increasing recognition of the interrelationship between pragmatics and morphosyntax, where pragmatic motives—such as the need for efficiency or added prominence—can lead to systematic lexico-grammatical innovations (Cogo & Dewey, 2006).

In the Southeast Asian region, English plays a vital role in linking nations culturally and commercially (Bolton, 2008). In Thailand, specifically, English serves as the de facto second language, remaining a compulsory subject in education and a primary tool for international communication within the ASEAN framework. Given its status, the development of specific ELF forms among Thai speakers is highly probable. While general ELF research has highlighted various emerging patterns, there is a need for more localized empirical data to understand how these patterns manifest in specific learner populations. In particular, while some studies have touched upon the 'extended' use of certain aspects like the progressive (Ranta, 2006), there remains a gap in the research regarding the systematic patterns and underlying causes of deviations in verbal inflectional suffixes among proficient Thai ELF learners.

To address this gap, the present study investigates the use of three specific verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—among advanced and upper-intermediate Thai ELF learners. The primary objective is to identify how these learners deviate from ENL norms and to analyze the linguistic and functional causes responsible for these deviations. By examining these patterns, the study aims to determine whether such deviations are mere errors or representative of emerging ELF features prioritized for communicative efficiency.

This research employs a qualitative approach, analyzing data collected from the academic writing of 116 English-major students at a university in Bangkok. Academic writing was selected as the data source because its demanding nature often reflects the highest point of L2 attainment and can reveal emerging linguistic standards. The study expects to demonstrate that deviations in tense and aspect are not the result of ignorance of ENL rules, but are driven by syntactic complexity and pragmatic motives, such as the exploitation of redundancy and the desire for expressivity. These findings may provide important implications for ELT pedagogy, suggesting a shift in focus from 'unproblematic' grammatical variants to communicative strategies that enhance intelligibility.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows: the next section provides a detailed review of the ELF approach and its role in Thailand. The methodology section describes the participants and the data collection process. Subsequently, the results are presented for each of the three inflectional suffixes, followed by a comprehensive analysis of the causes of deviation. Finally, the discussion and conclusion summarize the findings and offer pedagogical implications.

intros.text:
The globalisation of English has fundamentally transformed the landscape of language learning and teaching, shifting the focus from native-speaker norms to the communicative realities of English as a Lingua Franca (ELF). As English has spread geographically and across domains, the backgrounds of its users have been integrated into the characteristic features of ELF interactions (Jenkins, 2009). This shift has necessitated a re-evaluation of linguistic norms, particularly in the morphosyntactic system, where deviations from English as a Native Language (ENL) standards are increasingly viewed not as errors, but as emerging features of a legitimate variety. While early research into ELF concentrated on phonology and pragmatics, recent scholarship has turned attention to lexico-grammatical features, investigating how pragmatic motives lead to changes in linguistic forms (Cogo & Dewey, 2006; Jenkins et al., 2011). Within this context, the study of verbal inflectional suffixes among non-native speakers offers critical insights into the fluid nature of ELF communication.

In the context of Asia, the role of English is particularly significant. The region hosts a vast number of English learners, and the emergence of distinct Asian Englishes has played an important part in the global story of English (Bolton, 2008). Thailand, specifically, serves as a pertinent case study. Although Thai is the dominant language, English functions as the de facto second language and the official working language of ASEAN (Baker, 2012). Consequently, English in Thailand is used extensively in business, tourism, and higher education, linking the country culturally and commercially with the rest of the world. Given this status, the forms of ELF used by Thai speakers are likely to develop distinct characteristics that reflect their specific sociolinguistic context. Understanding these features is essential for shedding light on the nature of ELF communication in the region.

Despite the growing body of ELF research, there remains a need for empirical studies that focus on specific morphosyntactic features within Asian contexts. Previous studies have identified various patterns of deviation in ELF, such as the omission of the third person singular -s suffix and the extended use of the progressive aspect (Ranta, 2006; Stapa et al., 2010). However, these studies have often been based on European or other non-Asian contexts, and less is known about the specific patterns and causes of deviations among Thai learners. Furthermore, traditional Second Language Acquisition (SLA) research has often viewed such deviations as interlanguage errors or fossilization, failing to recognise their potential communicative value in ELF contexts (Jenkins, 2006). This perspective is increasingly challenged by ELF scholars who argue that efficiency of communication and pragmatic motives often drive linguistic innovations (Cogo & Dewey, 2006).

The present study investigates the use of three verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—among Thai ELF learners. It examines how advanced and upper-intermediate Thai learners deviate from ENL norms in their academic writing and analyses the causes of these deviations. The study is grounded in the premise that ELF interactions are characterised by linguistic fluidity and that deviations from standard norms are often functional rather than deficient (Jenkins et al., 2011). By focusing on proficient users, this research aims to identify systematic emerging patterns that reflect the unique characteristics of Thai ELF. Specifically, it explores whether syntactic complexity and pragmatic motives, such as the efficiency of communication and the exploitation of redundancy, influence the omission of tense suffixes. Additionally, it investigates whether the 'attractive' form and meaning of the progressive aspect lead Thai learners to extend its use to contexts such as general truths or habits, thereby gaining expressivity and explicitness (Ranta, 2006).

This research addresses a gap in the literature by providing a detailed analysis of verbal inflectional suffixes in the academic writing of Thai ELF learners. Unlike previous studies that may have focused on spoken interaction or lower proficiency levels, this study targets advanced learners who have received formal instruction in English. The findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the ownership of English and the legitimacy of non-native norms (Seidlhofer, 2008). By distinguishing between features that are crucial for intelligibility and those that are redundant, the study offers implications for English language teaching in intercultural contexts. Ultimately, it seeks to demonstrate that deviations in the use of verbal inflectional suffixes among Thai learners are not merely errors, but strategic adjustments that prioritise successful communication over strict adherence to ENL norms.

intros.text:
The global spread of English has fundamentally altered the landscape of language teaching and research, shifting the focus from native speaker norms to the realities of English as a Lingua Franca (ELF). As noted by Jenkins et al. (2011), the demographic shift in English usage means that L2 speakers now outnumber L1 speakers, necessitating a re-evaluation of how English is described and taught. This shift is particularly evident in Asia, where the visibility and importance of English have grown exponentially, leading to the emergence of distinct varieties and the development of ELF as a legitimate mode of communication (Kingsley Bolton, 2008). Consequently, understanding the linguistic features of ELF is vital for developing pedagogical approaches that align with the communicative needs of international users.

Research into ELF has expanded significantly over the past few decades, moving from a focus on phonology to a broader examination of lexicogrammar, pragmatics, and morphosyntax (Cogo, 2010; Jenkins et al., 2011). Scholars such as Cogo and Dewey (2006) have highlighted the interrelationship between pragmatic motives and lexicogrammatical innovations, arguing that functional efficiency often drives changes in linguistic form. Similarly, Seidlhofer (2008) has suggested that many grammatical features in English are redundant and can be omitted without hindering intelligibility. Despite these advances, the specific patterns of morphosyntactic deviation among Thai ELF learners remain underexplored. While studies have examined agreement strategies in other contexts, such as among Malaysian Chinese speakers (Stapa et al., 2010), there is a lack of empirical data regarding how Thai learners negotiate verbal inflectional suffixes in academic writing.

Specifically, the use of verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—has received limited attention in the context of Thai ELF. Traditional Second Language Acquisition (SLA) research often views deviations from native norms as errors resulting from fossilization or L1 interference (Jenkins, 2006). However, ELF research challenges this perspective, suggesting that such deviations may be systematic innovations driven by communicative efficiency and expressivity. For instance, Ranta (2006) investigated the 'attractive' use of the progressive aspect in ELF, proposing that learners extend its use to gain prominence and explicitness. Yet, it remains unclear whether similar functional causes underlie deviations in tense suffixes among Thai learners, particularly in written academic contexts where formal norms are expected.

Furthermore, while the role of ELF in Thailand is increasingly recognized due to its status as a lingua franca in ASEAN and its widespread use in education and business (Baker, 2012), the linguistic characteristics of Thai ELF are not well-documented. Given that Thai learners are often trained to conform to ENL norms, their deviations in academic writing may reveal important insights into the tension between standardization and functional communication. It is therefore necessary to investigate not only the patterns of these deviations but also the linguistic and functional causes that drive them.

This study addresses this gap by examining the use of three verbal inflectional suffixes among advanced and upper-intermediate Thai ELF learners. It aims to identify the specific contexts in which deviations from ENL norms occur and to analyze the underlying causes. The research questions are: (1) How do Thai ELF learners deviate from ENL norms in the use of the present tense -s, past tense -ed, and progressive -ing suffixes in academic writing? (2) What linguistic and functional causes explain these deviations? By analyzing the academic writing of 116 English-major students in Bangkok, this study contributes to the growing body of ELF research by providing empirical evidence of morphosyntactic fluidity. The findings suggest that deviations are not merely errors but strategic choices influenced by syntactic complexity and pragmatic motives such as efficiency and expressivity, offering implications for ELF-oriented pedagogy.

intros.text:
The global spread of English has altered the sociolinguistic conditions under which the language is learned, used, and evaluated. In many contemporary contexts, English functions less as a foreign language used primarily for communication with native speakers than as a lingua franca among speakers from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds. This shift is especially visible in Asia, where the number of English-knowing and English-using populations has expanded rapidly and where distinct local and regional practices of English have become increasingly salient (Bolton, 2008). As a result, English is no longer adequately described only through reference to English as a native language (ENL) norms. Rather, it is also necessary to examine the forms and functions that emerge when multilingual users employ English for intercultural communication.

Research on English as a lingua franca (ELF) has therefore argued that deviations from ENL norms should not automatically be interpreted as errors, fossilised interlanguage forms, or evidence of deficient competence. ELF users are often competent multilingual communicators who draw on available linguistic resources in flexible and strategic ways to achieve intelligibility and communicative effectiveness (Firth, 1996; Jenkins, 2006, 2009). From this perspective, variation in ELF may reveal systematic tendencies shaped by interactional purposes, processing demands, and the multilingual repertoires of speakers. Empirical ELF research has consequently moved beyond a concern with native-speaker correctness to investigate how phonological, pragmatic, lexical, and morphosyntactic forms are used in actual lingua franca communication (Cogo, 2010; Jenkins et al., 2011).

Morphosyntax is a particularly important area for ELF inquiry because it is often the domain in which language teaching and assessment most strongly preserve native-speaker standards. Yet previous studies suggest that some grammatical features traditionally treated as obligatory in ENL may be communicatively redundant in ELF. Cogo and Dewey (2006), for example, show that pragmatic motives such as efficiency, explicitness, and prominence can lead to lexico-grammatical innovation. Seidlhofer (2008) similarly argues that certain grammatical markings are maintained more for communal or normative reasons than for communicative necessity. Such claims are especially relevant to English verbal inflection, where suffixes such as third person singular present tense -s and past tense -ed encode information that may also be recoverable from subjects, adverbials, discourse context, or temporal sequencing. At the same time, not all deviations involve omission. Ranta (2006) demonstrates that ELF speakers may extend the use of the progressive -ing form, not because of communicative failure, but because the form is perceived as salient, expressive, and useful for making meaning more explicit.

Thailand provides a significant setting for examining these issues. Although Thai is the dominant national language, English has a strong presence in education, business, tourism, technology, media, and international communication. Thailand’s membership in ASEAN, where English is the official working language, has further strengthened the role of English as a regional and global lingua franca. Thai users of English therefore increasingly need the language for communication with other non-native speakers as well as with native speakers. However, English teaching in Thailand, as in many expanding-circle contexts, has traditionally emphasised conformity to Standard British or American norms. This creates a tension between pedagogical expectations of grammatical accuracy and the communicative realities of ELF use.

Despite the growing body of ELF research, relatively little empirical work has focused on the morphosyntactic patterns of Thai ELF learners, particularly in academic writing. Academic writing is a demanding context in which learners are expected to express complex ideas through formal and accurate language. It therefore provides a useful site for investigating whether deviations from ENL verbal inflectional norms occur among relatively proficient users and, if they do, whether such deviations are random errors or patterned responses to linguistic and communicative pressures. The verbal inflectional suffixes -s, -ed, and -ing are especially relevant because they are central in English grammar instruction, frequent in written production, and differently related to communicative meaning: the first two primarily mark tense and agreement, while the progressive form contributes aspectual meaning and discourse salience.

This study investigates the use of three English verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—among Thai ELF learners. Drawing on academic essays written by advanced and upper-intermediate English-major students at a university in Bangkok, it examines the patterns in which these learners’ use of the suffixes deviates from ENL norms and analyses the possible linguistic and functional causes of such deviations. By focusing on proficient Thai learners, the study aims to contribute to the empirical description of ELF morphosyntax and to a more nuanced understanding of how grammatical forms are negotiated in lingua franca communication. It also seeks to offer implications for English language teaching in contexts where learners are likely to use English primarily as an international means of communication rather than exclusively as a native-speaker-oriented target language.

intros.text:
The unprecedented spread of English has made it a principal medium of intercultural communication in many parts of the world, particularly in Asia, where the number of English-knowing and English-using speakers has expanded rapidly in recent decades (Bolton, 2008). In this context, English is no longer used mainly in interactions involving native speakers, but increasingly among speakers from different first-language backgrounds. This sociolinguistic reality has led to the development of English as a lingua franca (ELF), a field of inquiry concerned with how English is used, adapted, and negotiated for communication across linguistic and cultural boundaries (Firth, 1996; Jenkins, 2009; Jenkins et al., 2011). Rather than treating all departures from English as a native language (ENL) norms as errors, ELF research examines whether such forms are systematic, communicatively motivated, and intelligible in lingua franca contexts.

A central concern in ELF studies has therefore been the description of linguistic features that emerge in actual use. Early work focused strongly on phonology, but subsequent research has increasingly addressed pragmatics, lexis, and morphosyntax (Cogo, 2010; Jenkins et al., 2011). This shift is important because ELF communication is characterised by flexibility and adaptation: speakers draw on available linguistic resources to achieve mutual understanding, and in doing so they may regularise, simplify, extend, or otherwise reshape established forms. Cogo and Dewey (2006), for example, show that pragmatic motives such as efficiency, explicitness, prominence, and the exploitation of redundancy can give rise to lexico-grammatical innovations. Such findings suggest that morphosyntactic forms in ELF should be investigated not only in terms of their conformity to ENL norms, but also in relation to the communicative functions they serve.

Verbal inflection is a particularly relevant area for such investigation. In standard ENL descriptions, the third person singular present tense suffix -s, the past tense suffix -ed, and the progressive suffix -ing are central elements of the English tense-aspect system. In second language learning, absence or extension of these forms has often been interpreted as evidence of incomplete acquisition. From an ELF perspective, however, the status of such deviations is less straightforward. Some inflections may carry information that is recoverable elsewhere in the clause or discourse, while others may be exploited because their form or meaning is communicatively salient. Ranta’s (2006) study of the progressive in academic ELF, for instance, argues that the -ing form can be “attractive” because it makes verbs more prominent and expressive, and that its extended use does not necessarily disrupt communication. Similarly, the omission of verbal agreement or tense marking may reflect the relative redundancy of these forms in contexts where subject reference or temporal meaning is otherwise clear (Seidlhofer, 2008).

Despite the growth of ELF research, more empirical work is needed on how particular groups of English users employ specific morphosyntactic resources. Much existing research has drawn on multilingual corpora or spoken interaction, while less attention has been paid to written production by proficient users in particular national contexts. Thailand is a significant site for such inquiry. Although Thai is the dominant language of the country, English functions as a de facto second language in education, tourism, business, the internet, and regional communication. Thailand’s membership in ASEAN, where English serves as the working language, further strengthens the role of English as a lingua franca. Thai users of English are therefore increasingly likely to use the language not simply as learners aiming at native-speaker norms, but as participants in international and regional communication.

However, relatively little is known about the specific morphosyntactic patterns that characterise Thai ELF learners’ use of verbal inflectional suffixes, or about the causes of their deviations from ENL norms. It remains necessary to ask whether such deviations indicate lack of grammatical knowledge, whether they occur in identifiable linguistic environments, and whether they can be explained by communicative motives associated with ELF use. Addressing these questions can contribute both to the empirical description of ELF and to pedagogical debates about which forms require sustained instructional attention in contexts where intelligibility and effective communication are central goals (Jenkins, 2006, 2012).

This study investigates the use of three English verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—among Thai ELF learners. It examines how advanced and upper-intermediate Thai English-major students use these suffixes in academic writing, identifies patterns of deviation from ENL norms, and analyses the linguistic and functional causes of those deviations. By focusing on written data from 116 university students in Bangkok, the study seeks to determine whether deviations in Thai ELF learners’ verbal inflection are random errors or systematic features shaped by syntactic complexity, redundancy, prominence, and the communicative priorities of ELF.

segments.text: In standard ENL descriptions, the third person singular present tense suffix -s, the past tense suffix -ed, and the progressive suffix -ing are central elements of the English tense-aspect system. In second language learning, absence or extension of these forms has often been interpreted as evidence of incomplete acquisition. From an ELF perspective, however, the status of such deviations is less straightforward. Some inflections may carry information that is recoverable elsewhere in the clause or discourse, while others may be exploited because their form or meaning is communicatively salient.

Similarly, the omission of verbal agreement or tense marking may reflect the relative redundancy of these forms in contexts where subject reference or temporal meaning is otherwise clear (Seidlhofer, 2008).

segments.text: Thailand is a significant site for such inquiry. Although Thai is the dominant language of the country, English functions as a de facto second language in education, tourism, business, the internet, and regional communication. Thailand’s membership in ASEAN, where English serves as the working language, further strengthens the role of English as a lingua franca. Thai users of English are therefore increasingly likely to use the language not simply as learners aiming at native-speaker norms, but as participants in international and regional communication.

segments.text: This study investigates the use of three English verbal inflectional suffixes—the present tense -s, the past tense -ed, and the progressive -ing—among Thai ELF learners. It examines how advanced and upper-intermediate Thai English-major students use these suffixes in academic writing, identifies patterns of deviation from ENL norms, and analyses the linguistic and functional causes of those deviations. intros.text: As authorised by the National Education Act (2002-2016) expressing the need for becoming autonomous and lifelong learners, the question of how Thai students can develop a more dynamic and responsible role in their own language learning is part of many teachers’ concerns (OECD/UNESCO, 2016). For this reason, learning reform through the learnercentred approach has been implemented widely, particularly the reform of curricula and learning processes.  This research was initiated by the author’s concern about the reform movement in English language teaching (ELT) in the Thai university context and the interest in the Thai adult learners’ self-evaluation of their writing practice.  Curriculum and syllabus goals in the Thai educational system encourage students to work more independently and take responsibility for their own learning, particularly the students in higher education (OECD/UNESCO, 2016). A review of the literature on evaluation (e.g., Nicol & MacfarlaneDick 2006, Rust et al. 2003, Sambell et al. 2013) also raises the researcher’s awareness of the importance of understanding the students’ own evaluation of their EFL writing performance as well as for the elaboration of evaluation procedures.  Nevertheless, in Thailand, both students and teachers seem to have little previous experience of evaluation procedures in the language classroom as the evaluation has traditionally been the teachers’ exclusive privilege and obligation. Besides, there has been no research carried out on the conditions that govern adult learners’ participation in evaluation.  Much of the previous research on formative evaluation and summative evaluation in language learning has focused on young learners learning a foreign language (Brown & Harris 2013, Lee 2017). According to Brown and Harris (2016), self-evaluation practices need to be explored in order to support the implementation of adult learners’ lifelong learning skill which is important for their language learning process.  The focus on writing in the teaching of English as a foreign language was chosen because English is the language most Thai students learn, and writing has become more important in foreign language teaching at higher education level. Accordingly, as the role of writing in English as foreign language learning increases, the students’ ability to self-evaluate their writing skills is also important because selfevaluation could help reflect individual students’ understanding and possibility of improvement.  This study will provide valuable insights into Thai adult learners’ selfevaluation in their English writing practice with regard to various aspects. As such, the research findings could, in turn, help improve the evaluation practice and bring about benefits to English language teaching and learning in this context. Moreover, it is expected that other useful implications can be formulated and would be applicable for the teaching and learning of other courses in university settings in Thailand.  This research, therefore, aims to contribute to an understanding of whether the use of self-evaluation in the writing course of English as a foreign language in university can help develop lifelong language learning skills and further development of broader and fairer evaluation practices. The study centres on how the adult learners (or “students” hereafter in this study) self-evaluate their writing ability in general and their writing performance task based on the grading criteria of English writing compared with the evaluation of their teacher. The ultimate aim is to find out what the students and the teacher have experienced from the self-evaluation practice in the writing class. The results could be useful for further developing the students’ English writing ability.  Three main research questions are developed based on the objectives of the study: 1) How do the students self-evaluate their English writing performance compared with the evaluation of their teacher? 2) Based on the evaluation criteria, how do the students’ self-evaluate their English writing performance compared with the evaluation of their teacher? 3) What do the students and the teacher experience from the use of students’ selfevaluation of English writing performance to further develop the students’ writing ability?

intros.text:
Evaluation lies at the heart of language teaching and learning, yet the ways in which learners are assessed have long been dominated by teacher-centred and product-oriented practices. In recent decades, however, scholars in applied linguistics and education have called for alternative and critical approaches to evaluation that recognise learners as active participants in judging their own progress (Pennycook, 2001; Brown, 2016). Within this broader shift, self-evaluation has emerged as a practice with the potential not only to measure achievement but also to empower learners, foster reflection, and cultivate the self-regulating capacities essential for lifelong learning (Taras, 2002; Brown & Harris, 2013). Understanding how learners evaluate their own performance, and how such evaluation relates to that of the teacher, is therefore central to developing more responsive and learner-oriented pedagogies.

The teaching and evaluation of writing present a particularly fertile ground for exploring self-evaluation. Writing is a complex, recursive skill that requires learners to attend simultaneously to content, organisation, linguistic accuracy, and style, and its development benefits from the kind of sustained reflection that self-evaluation encourages (Icy Lee, 2017). When learners are invited to appraise their own texts, they gain opportunities to internalise assessment criteria, to identify where they stand in relation to expected standards, and to take responsibility for their own improvement. Research suggests that developing students' understanding of assessment criteria and processes can significantly enhance learning and that these gains may be durable and transferable across contexts (Rust et al., 2003). Self-evaluation, in this sense, functions both as a means of assessment and as a tool for learning, bridging the path towards greater learner autonomy.

Despite this promise, the relationship between students' self-evaluation and teachers' evaluation remains contested. Learners frequently overestimate or underestimate their abilities, and their appraisals may diverge from those of their teachers in ways that raise questions about what is actually being evaluated and how criteria are understood on each side. Existing studies indicate that self-evaluation is most beneficial when it is accompanied by teacher feedback, when grades are withheld until learners have first exercised their own judgement, and when learners are given repeated opportunities to work with explicit criteria (Taras, 2002; Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006). Yet relatively little research has examined students' self-evaluation of task-based writing performance, and even less has explored how both learners and teachers experience the practice, particularly in adult and postgraduate contexts.

The present study addresses this gap within the setting of Thai higher education. As Thailand continues to reform its education system in response to national and international policy priorities (ECD/UNESCO, 2016), there is growing interest in pedagogies that promote independent, reflective, and lifelong learning. English writing occupies a strategic position in graduate study, where students are expected to communicate complex ideas accurately and appropriately in academic genres. Adult learners at this level bring considerable experience and motivation to their studies, yet they are often accustomed to teacher-dominated evaluation and may have had few opportunities to appraise their own writing systematically. Examining how such learners evaluate their writing, and how these evaluations correspond to those of an experienced teacher, offers valuable insight into the feasibility and value of self-evaluation as a formative practice in the Thai EFL context.

Against this background, the present research investigates the self-evaluation of Thai adult learners in English writing practice. It seeks to understand, first, how these learners evaluate their own writing performance in relation to the teacher's evaluation across two different writing tasks, and second, what the students and the teacher experience through engaging in the self-evaluation process. Drawing on students' and the teacher's evaluation forms, learners' writing tasks, and individual interviews, the study combines quantitative and qualitative evidence to build a comprehensive picture of the practice and its pedagogical implications. In doing so, it contributes to the wider body of scholarship concerned with learner-centred assessment and the cultivation of learner autonomy (Sambell et al., 2013). More broadly, the study aims to demonstrate that students' self-evaluation can serve as a genuine and valid source of information for developing the teaching of EFL writing, while supporting learners in becoming more reflective, self-regulating, and lifelong learners of English.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics and English language teaching, evaluation constitutes an integral component of effective teaching and learning. Traditionally, the responsibility for evaluating language performance has rested primarily with the teacher, who assigns grades, provides feedback, and determines whether learners have achieved the goals set out in a course. Increasingly, however, scholars have recognised that involving learners themselves in the evaluation of their own performance can transform the way learning takes place. Self-evaluation, as an alternative form of assessment grounded in the critical applied linguistics perspective, has attracted considerable attention as a means of empowering learners rather than suppressing them, of encouraging them to think and learn more, and of underpinning their development as autonomous and lifelong learners. Within English as a foreign language (EFL) writing in particular, self-evaluation offers a promising route through which students can identify where they stand in their writing development and take greater responsibility for their own learning.

A substantial body of research has emphasised the value of engaging students in assessment processes. Rust et al. (2003) demonstrated that student learning can be improved significantly, and durably, when students are helped to understand assessment criteria and the assessment process through structured intervention. Brown and Harris (2013) similarly highlighted the importance of self-assessment in empowering students to identify their strengths and areas for growth, while later work (Brown, 2016) situated self-assessment within a broader consideration of the human and social conditions that shape how assessment is experienced. In the context of second language writing specifically, Lee (2017) has examined how classroom writing assessment and feedback can be reconceived to support learners more effectively. Together, these studies suggest that self-evaluation may function not merely as a measurement device but as a genuine learning tool, particularly when it operates alongside teacher feedback and a clear understanding of evaluation criteria (Sambell et al., 2013).

Despite this growing interest, there has been comparatively little empirical research on students' self-evaluation of task-based writing performance, and fewer studies still that examine how self-evaluation aligns with teacher evaluation in authentic classroom settings. Much of the existing work has been conducted in Western higher education or in nursing and general education contexts, and questions remain about how self-evaluation operates among adult EFL learners in Asian contexts. In Thailand, where English-medium graduate study places substantial demands on students' academic writing (OECD/UNESCO, 2016), it is unclear whether adult learners are able to evaluate their own writing performance in ways that correspond meaningfully with a teacher's judgement, or how both learners and teachers experience the practice of self-evaluation within a writing course. If students are able to evaluate their own performance more or less in accordance with the teacher's evaluation, important questions arise concerning what is actually being evaluated and how the criteria for assessing writing are understood on both sides. These gaps warrant closer investigation, especially given the potential of self-evaluation to foster the autonomy and lifelong learning that graduate-level EFL programmes increasingly aim to cultivate.

This study therefore sets out to investigate how Thai adult learners self-evaluate their English writing performance in relation to their teacher's evaluation, and what both the students and the teacher experience from the self-evaluation practice. Specifically, the research addresses three questions: how closely students' self-evaluations of their writing tasks correspond with the teacher's evaluation; how self-evaluation relates to students' satisfaction with particular writing skills; and what views and experiences students and their teacher hold regarding the use of self-evaluation to develop writing ability. To pursue these questions, the study draws on data from 32 Thai graduate students and one experienced Thai EFL writing teacher, collected through students' self-evaluation and teacher's evaluation forms, two writing tasks, and individual interviews, with qualitative and quantitative data considered together to gain a comprehensive picture of the issue under investigation.

In addressing these aims, the study offers insight into the extent to which adult EFL learners can serve as a valid source of information about their own writing achievement. Its findings are expected to highlight the importance of students' self-evaluation for developing the teaching of EFL writing and for promoting learners' autonomy, while drawing implications for the design of independent learning goals within graduate writing courses and pointing to directions for future research.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics, the evaluation of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing is an essential component of the teaching and learning process. Effective writing evaluation does not merely serve as a means of assigning grades but acts as a dynamic tool that helps students identify their current developmental stage and understand the specific supports required to enhance their proficiency. Central to this process is the concept of self-evaluation, which shifts the evaluative focus from a purely teacher-led approach to one that empowers the learner. By engaging in self-evaluation, students are encouraged to think critically about their own performance, promoting a transition toward autonomy and lifelong learning.

Within the Thai educational context, the drive toward improving English proficiency is a national priority, as highlighted in reviews of national education policies (ECD/UNESCO, 2016). For adult learners, particularly those at the graduate level, the ability to self-regulate their learning is crucial for academic success and professional advancement. However, the effectiveness of self-evaluation often depends on the students' understanding of the assessment criteria and the processes involved. As Rust et al. (2003) argue, student learning can be significantly improved when there is a structured effort to develop their understanding of assessment criteria, making the evaluation process transparent and transferable across different contexts. When students are well-versed in what constitutes quality writing, they can more accurately bridge the gap between their current performance and the desired learning outcomes.

Despite the theoretical benefits of self-assessment—such as empowering students to identify strengths and growth areas (Brown & Harris, 2013)—there remains a need for empirical research on how these practices manifest in specific EFL writing contexts. In many traditional classrooms, evaluation is viewed as a summative event rather than a formative process. This often leads to a disconnect between a teacher's judgment and a student's perception of their own ability. While some scholars emphasize the role of technology in modernizing L2 writing assessment and feedback (Lee, 2017), the fundamental human interaction between the teacher's feedback and the student's self-reflection remains the core of linguistic development. Furthermore, challenges in higher education assessment, as seen in various international contexts (Sambell et al., 2013), suggest that aligning student self-perceptions with institutional standards is a complex task that requires careful pedagogical intervention.

To ensure that evaluation is fair and functional, it must account for the human and social conditions under which assessment occurs (Brown, 2016). This is particularly relevant for adult learners who may possess different motivations and levels of self-confidence compared to younger students. If learners are not trained in self-criticality, they risk either overestimating their abilities—thereby ignoring critical gaps in their knowledge—or underestimating their competence, which may hinder their willingness to take linguistic risks. Therefore, it is imperative to investigate the degree of congruence between student self-evaluations and teacher evaluations to determine if self-evaluation serves as a valid source of information for both the learner and the instructor.

This research aims to investigate how Thai adult learners in a graduate EFL writing course self-evaluate their writing performance in relation to their teacher's evaluation. Specifically, the study seeks to explore the experiences of both the students and the teacher during the evaluation process. By analyzing the alignment between self-ratings and teacher-ratings, and by eliciting qualitative reflections through interviews, this study intends to highlight the importance of student involvement in the evaluative process. Ultimately, the findings aim to provide implications for promoting learner autonomy and refining the delivery of feedback in EFL writing instruction, contributing to the broader goal of developing self-sufficient, lifelong learners.

intros.text:
In the field of applied linguistics, the evaluation of language learning is a fundamental concern, particularly within English as a Foreign Language (EFL) contexts. Effective evaluation is not merely a tool for grading but is integral to the teaching and learning process, allowing students to identify their current developmental stage and understand the support required to progress (Herrington & Curtis, 2003). Within this framework, self-evaluation has emerged as a critical alternative approach, grounded in critical applied linguistics, which shifts the focus from passive reception of grades to an active engagement with one's own learning process (Pennycook, 2001). By encouraging learners to reflect on their performance, self-evaluation empowers them, fostering a sense of agency and encouraging a deeper level of cognitive engagement (Taras, 2002).

Writing, in particular, is a complex skill where the evaluation process can serve a dual purpose: as a summative measure of achievement and as a formative tool for growth. The integration of self-evaluation in EFL writing is widely regarded as vital for bridging the gap toward independent learning. When students are permitted to develop their own judgments before receiving teacher feedback, they are better positioned to recognize their strengths and weaknesses, thereby promoting autonomy and lifelong learning (Taras, 2002). Previous research has demonstrated that when students understand assessment criteria and the processes behind them, their overall learning outcomes can improve significantly (Rust et al., 2003). Furthermore, the use of self-assessment tools has been shown in other professional educational contexts to empower students to identify specific areas for growth, aiding their transition to real-world application (Brown & Harris, 2013).

Despite these recognized benefits, the practical application of self-evaluation in EFL writing remains an area requiring further investigation. While some studies have explored the reliability of self-evaluation through specific tasks like text annotation (Brown & Harris, 2014), there remains a lack of comprehensive research on how adult learners in specific regional contexts, such as Thailand, perceive and execute this process. In Thailand, where national education policies continue to evolve to meet global standards (ECD/UNESCO, 2016), there is a growing need to understand how graduate-level learners engage with autonomous learning strategies. Moreover, it remains unclear to what extent student self-evaluations align with teacher evaluations and how this discrepancy—or lack thereof—influences the learning experience for both the educator and the student.

Addressing this gap, the present study investigates how Thai adult learners self-evaluate their English writing performance in relation to their teacher's evaluations. Specifically, the research seeks to determine the degree of agreement between student and teacher ratings and to explore the qualitative experiences of both parties during the evaluation process. By focusing on graduate students, who are often high achievers with distinct motivational drivers, this study aims to highlight the validity of self-evaluation as a source of information for developing EFL writing pedagogy. It is hypothesized that involving students in the evaluation process not only provides the teacher with deeper insights into student achievement but also cultivates the students' capacity for self-regulation.

To achieve these objectives, the study employs a mixed-methods approach, utilizing self-evaluation and teacher-evaluation forms, analysis of writing tasks, and semi-structured interviews with 32 Thai graduate students and one experienced EFL teacher. The findings provide insights into the accuracy of adult learners' self-perceptions and the implications of these practices for promoting lifelong learning. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: the literature review explores theories of self-evaluation and EFL writing assessment; the methodology section details the participants and instruments used; the results present the quantitative and qualitative findings; and the discussion concludes by examining the implications for autonomous language learning.

intros.text:
In the realm of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, the evaluation of student performance remains a critical component of the teaching and learning process. Traditionally, assessment has been viewed as a summative activity conducted primarily by instructors to measure student achievement against established standards. However, contemporary pedagogical approaches increasingly advocate for the integration of formative assessment strategies that actively involve learners in the evaluation process. Among these strategies, self-evaluation has emerged as a powerful tool for fostering learner autonomy, promoting critical reflection, and enhancing writing proficiency. By engaging students in the assessment of their own work, educators aim to shift the focus from passive reception of grades to active participation in learning, thereby encouraging the development of lifelong learning skills.

The importance of self-evaluation in language learning is well-documented in applied linguistics literature. It is often conceptualized not merely as a method of grading but as a pedagogical intervention that empowers learners to take responsibility for their progress. Brown & Harris (2013) highlight that self-assessment allows students to identify their strengths and areas for growth, facilitating a transition toward greater independence in real-world contexts. Similarly, Rust et al. (2003) argue that developing students' understanding of assessment criteria and processes significantly improves their learning outcomes, suggesting that clarity regarding expectations is a prerequisite for effective self-evaluation. When learners can articulate the standards by which their work is judged, they are better equipped to monitor their own performance and align their efforts with learning goals.

Despite the recognized benefits, the implementation of self-evaluation in EFL contexts, particularly within writing instruction, presents specific challenges. Writing is a complex cognitive and linguistic process that requires not only grammatical accuracy but also coherence, organization, and rhetorical appropriateness. In many EFL settings, students may lack the metacognitive skills necessary to critically evaluate their own writing or may struggle to interpret assessment rubrics accurately. This discrepancy can lead to significant variations between student self-ratings and teacher evaluations. For instance, students may overestimate their proficiency due to a lack of awareness regarding specific linguistic errors, or conversely, underestimate their abilities due to anxiety or low self-efficacy. Understanding the alignment—or misalignment—between student and teacher perspectives is crucial for optimizing the feedback loop and ensuring that self-evaluation serves its intended formative purpose.

Furthermore, the context of adult learners introduces additional dimensions to this dynamic. Adult learners, particularly those at the graduate level, are often characterized by a higher degree of autonomy and a clearer understanding of their learning objectives compared to younger cohorts. However, their self-evaluation practices may still be influenced by prior educational experiences, cultural attitudes toward authority, and the specific demands of academic writing. In the Thai educational context, where traditional teacher-centered approaches have historically dominated, the introduction of self-evaluation represents a significant shift in classroom dynamics. ECD/UNESCO (2016) notes the ongoing reforms in Thai education policy, which increasingly emphasize learner-centered methodologies and the development of critical thinking skills. Yet, the practical application of these policies in EFL writing courses requires empirical investigation to determine their efficacy and the extent to which adult learners can successfully internalize evaluation criteria.

While previous studies have explored self-evaluation in various educational domains, there is a need for more focused research on how Thai adult learners perceive and utilize self-evaluation in the specific context of EFL writing. Brown G.T.L. (2016) and Lee (2017) have touched upon the broader conditions of assessment and the role of technology in feedback, but the interpersonal and reflective aspects of self-evaluation in face-to-face writing instruction remain underexplored. intros.text:
In the landscape of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education, the evaluation of writing performance remains a critical yet complex component of the pedagogical process. For adult learners, particularly those pursuing graduate degrees, the ability to assess one's own linguistic output is not merely an administrative task but a vital mechanism for fostering autonomous and lifelong learning. As the demand for English proficiency in higher education intensifies, so too does the necessity for learners to develop self-regulatory skills that extend beyond the classroom. This shift towards learner autonomy necessitates a re-evaluation of traditional assessment practices, moving from teacher-centric grading to a more collaborative model where students actively participate in the evaluation of their own writing. 

Self-evaluation, grounded in critical applied linguistics, has been increasingly recognized as a powerful tool for empowering learners. Scholars such as Pennycook (2001) and McGroarty (1998) have argued that alternative evaluation methods can challenge standard indicators of learning, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of individual language ability. Taras (2002) further posits that self-evaluation encourages learners to think critically about their performance, thereby transforming assessment from a summative judgment into a formative learning experience. However, the efficacy of self-evaluation is contingent upon the learners' ability to align their self-perceptions with objective criteria. While Brown and Harris (2014) demonstrated that annotated texts can help students reliably self-evaluate specific language skills, the extent to which adult EFL learners can accurately judge their writing performance in relation to teacher evaluations remains a subject of inquiry. 

Despite the theoretical benefits, there is a notable gap in the literature regarding the practical application of self-evaluation in Thai adult EFL contexts. Much of the existing research focuses on Western educational settings or younger learners, leaving the specific dynamics of Thai graduate students underexplored. Furthermore, while studies like Rust et al. (2003) emphasize the importance of students understanding assessment criteria to improve learning, there is limited empirical evidence on how this understanding translates into accurate self-judgment when compared with teacher assessments in a Thai university setting. The interplay between student self-perception and teacher evaluation is crucial; as Falchikov (2005) noted in a meta-analysis, discrepancies between the two can hinder learning if not addressed. Therefore, it is essential to investigate not only the accuracy of these self-evaluations but also the experiences of both students and teachers in implementing such practices. 

This study aims to address these gaps by investigating how Thai adult learners self-evaluate their English writing performance in relation to teacher evaluations and to explore the experiences of both parties within this evaluation practice. Specifically, the research seeks to answer three primary questions: (1) How accurately do Thai adult learners self-evaluate their writing performance compared to teacher evaluations? (2) What are the students' and teacher's experiences regarding the use of self-evaluation in an EFL writing course? and (3) How does the self-evaluation practice influence the development of students' writing ability and autonomy? 

To address these questions, the study employs a mixed-methods approach, collecting data from 32 Thai graduate students and one EFL writing instructor through self-evaluation forms, teacher evaluation forms, writing tasks, and semi-structured interviews. By triangulating quantitative data on evaluation scores with qualitative insights from interviews, the research provides a comprehensive picture of the evaluation process. The findings of this study suggest that adult learners are capable of self-evaluating their writing with reasonable accuracy, particularly when supported by clear criteria and teacher feedback. Furthermore, the results highlight the potential of self-evaluation to enhance teacher insight into student achievement and to promote learner autonomy. These insights contribute to the broader discourse on formative assessment and offer practical implications for developing independent learning goals in EFL writing contexts. The following sections will detail the methodology, present the findings, and discuss the implications for teaching and future research.

intros.text:
English writing remains a central but challenging component of English as a foreign language (EFL) learning, particularly in higher education contexts where students are expected to use written English for academic study, professional communication, and future knowledge development. In Thailand, English has continued to occupy an important position in national educational policy and graduate-level learning, yet many learners still experience difficulty producing accurate, coherent, and rhetorically appropriate written texts (ECD/UNESCO, 2016). For adult learners, these challenges are especially significant because they are often required not only to perform successfully in formal coursework, but also to develop the capacity to continue improving their English independently beyond the classroom. In this respect, writing instruction cannot be limited to teacher correction and grading; it should also help learners understand the quality of their own work and make informed decisions about how to improve it.

Assessment is therefore not merely a mechanism for measuring achievement, but a pedagogical process that can shape how students learn. In writing classrooms, assessment and feedback can direct learners’ attention to content, organisation, language accuracy, style, and audience awareness. However, when assessment is controlled only by the teacher, students may remain dependent on external judgement and may not fully understand the standards by which their writing is evaluated. Research in higher education has shown that students’ learning can be improved when they develop clearer understandings of assessment criteria and assessment processes (Rust et al., 2003). Such understanding is particularly important in writing, where quality is multidimensional and where improvement depends on learners’ ability to notice problems, interpret feedback, revise effectively, and transfer what they have learned to later tasks.

Student self-evaluation has consequently attracted increasing attention as an alternative and complementary assessment practice. Broadly, self-evaluation involves learners making judgements about the quality of their own performance in relation to explicit goals or criteria. It has been associated with learner empowerment, self-regulation, autonomy, and lifelong learning (Brown & Harris, 2013; Brown, 2016). Rather than positioning students as passive recipients of grades, self-evaluation invites them to reflect on what they have done well, what they still need to develop, and how they might move closer to expected standards. In language learning, this reflective dimension is particularly valuable because learners must gradually assume responsibility for monitoring their own communicative effectiveness and linguistic accuracy. When self-evaluation is integrated with teacher feedback, it may also create a more dialogic form of assessment in which both teacher and learner contribute information about learning progress.

Nevertheless, the usefulness of self-evaluation in EFL writing cannot be taken for granted. Learners may overestimate or underestimate their ability, misunderstand criteria, or focus narrowly on surface-level language errors while overlooking broader rhetorical concerns. Teachers may also be uncertain about how far students’ self-evaluations can be trusted as evidence of writing achievement. These concerns are important because the value of self-evaluation depends partly on whether learners can make judgements that are reasonably aligned with informed external assessment. At the same time, perfect agreement with teacher evaluation should not be the only criterion of value. Even when students’ judgements differ from the teacher’s, the process may reveal how they understand writing, which aspects of performance they prioritise, and what kinds of support they need. In this sense, self-evaluation can provide teachers with diagnostic information that conventional grading alone may not supply.

In adult EFL contexts, the relationship between self-evaluation and teacher evaluation is especially worth examining. Adult learners often bring substantial prior learning experience, clearer academic or professional goals, and a potentially stronger sense of responsibility for their own progress. These characteristics may make them suitable candidates for self-evaluation practices. However, empirical evidence is still needed to understand how accurately adult Thai learners evaluate their English writing, how their judgements compare with those of the teacher, and how both students and teacher experience the use of self-evaluation in an actual writing course. Such evidence is also relevant to classroom writing assessment and feedback, including the design of criteria-based tasks and formative procedures that encourage students to revise and improve (Lee, 2017; Sambell et al., 2013).

The present study addresses these issues by investigating self-evaluation in a graduate-level EFL writing course at a Thai public university. It examines Thai adult learners’ self-evaluations of two English writing tasks in relation to the teacher’s evaluations and explores the experiences of both students and teacher in using self-evaluation as part of writing practice. By focusing on students’ judgements, teacher feedback, and participants’ reflections, the study seeks to clarify whether self-evaluation can function as a valid and pedagogically useful source of information for developing EFL writing and promoting autonomous, lifelong language learning.

intros.text:
In contemporary higher education, assessment is increasingly understood not only as a mechanism for measuring achievement but also as a pedagogical practice that can shape learning, autonomy, and learners’ capacity to regulate their own development. This shift is particularly important in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, where students are expected to develop complex abilities involving idea generation, organisation, argumentation, linguistic accuracy, and awareness of audience and purpose. For adult learners at graduate level, writing in English is closely connected with academic success, professional advancement, and participation in wider scholarly and occupational communities. In Thailand, where English continues to occupy an important role in higher education and national development, graduate students are often required to demonstrate increasingly sophisticated academic literacy while learning in an EFL environment (ECD/UNESCO, 2016).

Writing assessment in EFL classrooms has traditionally been associated with teacher judgement, grades, and corrective feedback. However, current views of classroom assessment emphasise that learners should be active participants in assessment processes rather than passive recipients of scores. Self-evaluation, or student self-assessment, invites learners to judge the quality of their own work in relation to explicit goals, criteria, and standards. It can help students identify strengths and weaknesses, monitor progress, and make decisions about future learning. Brown and Harris (2013) argue that self-assessment can empower students by helping them recognise areas for growth, while broader assessment research has highlighted the social and human dimensions of assessment practices and their influence on learning behaviour (Brown, 2016). In writing classrooms, these dimensions are especially salient because feedback and evaluation affect not only students’ texts but also their confidence, motivation, and sense of control over learning.

A growing body of research suggests that students’ understanding of assessment criteria is central to effective learning. Rust et al. (2003), for example, showed that students’ learning can improve when they are supported in understanding assessment criteria and assessment processes through structured interventions. Such work indicates that self-evaluation is unlikely to be effective if learners are merely asked to assign themselves marks; rather, they need opportunities to interpret criteria, compare their work with expected standards, and use feedback to revise their performance. In L2 writing contexts, assessment and feedback are also affected by classroom practices, task design, and available tools, including technological support for writing assessment and response (Lee, 2017). These developments point to the need for assessment practices that are formative, transparent, and integrated into writing instruction.

Despite this interest, the role of self-evaluation in EFL writing remains underexplored in some instructional contexts, particularly with adult learners in Thai higher education. Much of the discussion of student self-assessment has focused on general education or on contexts outside EFL writing, and relatively little is known about how Thai adult learners evaluate their own writing performance when their judgements are compared with those of their teacher. It also remains unclear how learners and teachers experience the use of self-evaluation as part of classroom writing practice: whether students perceive it as useful, whether teachers find it informative, and how both groups understand its relationship to feedback, criteria, and writing development. These questions are important because self-evaluation may support learner autonomy only when it is meaningful to students and credible to teachers.

This study addresses these issues by investigating the self-evaluation of English writing performance among Thai adult learners in a graduate EFL writing course. Specifically, it examines the extent to which students’ self-evaluations correspond with the teacher’s evaluations across two writing tasks, and explores the experiences of both students and the teacher in using self-evaluation to support writing development. The study involves 32 Thai graduate students and one Thai EFL writing teacher at a public university. Data were collected through students’ self-evaluation forms, the teacher’s evaluation forms, students’ writing tasks, open-ended responses, and individual interviews. By combining quantitative comparison of ratings with qualitative accounts of classroom experience, the study seeks to provide a more complete understanding of self-evaluation as both an assessment practice and a learning process.

The study contributes to EFL writing assessment by offering evidence from a Thai graduate context in which adult learners are encouraged to participate in evaluating their own performance. It also highlights the pedagogical value of linking self-evaluation with explicit criteria and teacher feedback. The findings may inform writing teachers who wish to promote learner autonomy, strengthen formative assessment, and help students become more reflective and lifelong learners of English.
