intros.text: SECOND LANGUAGE (L2) SPEECH FLUENCY has been widely studied from various angles, including the connections between fluency measurements and judgments of fluency (utterance fluency and perceived fluency, respectively, Segalowitz, 2010; e.g., Baker–Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2013), fluency development (notably during study abroad; e.g., Lennon, 1990; Mora & Valls–Ferrer, 2012; Towell & Dewaele, 2005; Towell, Hawkins, & Bazergui, 1996), and the differences between learners at different proficiency levels (e.g., Hilton, 2014; Kormos & Dénes, 2004).  Native speakers, representing a relatively homogenous group of ‘ideally’ fluent speakers, have traditionally been the implicit or explicit points of comparison for learners in L2 fluency studies.  Yet studies examining the temporal aspects of L1 speech have shown that individuals vary in their fluency (e.g., Goldman–Eisler, 1968). Furthermore, fluency studies including a native speaker control group have also demonstrated variation in fluency not only among L2 speakers, but also among L1 speakers (e.g., Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014). These findings have significant implications for L2 fluency research, assessment, and teaching: If individuals vary in how they speak their native language, the factors influencing their L1 speech fluency are likely to influence L2 speech as well. In other words, temporal measures, which have been used as indicators of L2 oral proficiency in L2 speech fluency research, can, at least to some extent, also reflect L1 fluency.  Empirical research on the connections between L1 and L2 speech fluency has, nevertheless, been scarce, as L2 speech fluency studies have usually not incorporated data from the same speakers in their L1 and L2 (but see early exploratory studies, e.g., Lehtonen, 1979; Möhle, 1984; Raupach, 1980).  However, in recent years, the effects of L1 speech patterns on L2 speech fluency have attracted more interest, and the studies suggest that at least some of the variance in L2 speech fluency can be explained by the learners’ L1 speech patterns (De Jong et al., 2015; Derwing et al., 2009; Huensch & Tracy–Ventura, 2017).  Examining the connections between L1 and L2 speech fluency can thus help in pinpointing aspects of L2 fluency that are prone to L1 speaking style effects and aspects that are more clearly linked to L2 (oral) proficiency. Therefore, this line of research not only contributes to increasing the reliability of measuring L2 speech fluency, but also has implications for the development of reliable and valid L2 fluency assessment practices, which would ideally emphasize proficiency-related aspects of L2 fluency and focus less on aspects influenced by L1 fluency (see also Segalowitz, 2010, pp. 35, 40–41).  In the present study, 42 Finnish learners of English from two school levels, ninth grade (i.e., the final year of compulsory education) and the second year of upper secondary school, were examined for their L1 and L2 fluency. Compared to previous, mainly quantitative studies, the present study employed a mixed methods approach including both group level (quantitative) and individual level (qualitative) analysis to achieve a holistic picture of the connections between L1 and L2 fluency. First, in the quantitative analysis, correlations between L1 and L2 fluency measures were studied, followed by regression analyses exploring the predictive power of L1 fluency measures in explaining L2 fluency measures. Second, the complementary qualitative analysis involved examining individual differences in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency by focusing on six subjects’ productions with high frequencies of so-called stalling mechanisms (e.g., repetitions and filled pauses, FPs; see Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998).  As previous studies have shown stalling mechanisms to be potentially multifunctional and prone to individual variation (e.g., Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014), examining these features from individuallearners’ productions with a qualitative analysis along with group level tendencies is particularly important; individual differences in L1 and L2 patterns regarding stalling mechanisms may be more prominent than group level patterns.  Seeking to uncover individual patterns in fluency-related features across L1 and L2, the qualitative component of the present study thus provides a new angle to the study of connections between L1 and L2 fluency.

intros.text:
Second language (L2) speech fluency has long been recognized as an important indicator of L2 proficiency, capturing the smoothness and effortlessness with which learners produce speech (Chambers, 1997; Lennon, 1990). Within the Complexity–Accuracy–Fluency framework (Housen, Kuiken, & Vedder, 2012), fluency in its 'narrow sense' is typically operationalized through temporal features of speech such as speaking rate and pausing, distinguishing it from the broader, nontechnical understanding of fluency as general oral proficiency (Lennon, 1990). These objective and measurable features of utterance fluency are generally regarded as reflecting a speaker's underlying cognitive fluency (Segalowitz, 2010). Contemporary research commonly organizes fluency measures into three dimensions—speed, breakdown (pausing), and repair (false starts, repetitions, and reformulations)—each of which has been widely used to characterize learner performance and to relate it to overall proficiency (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012; Kormos & Dénes, 2004).

While numerous factors influencing L2 fluency have been examined, the influence of first language (L1) fluency on L2 fluency remains comparatively poorly understood. Early theorists noted that even L1 speakers vary considerably in their fluency (Goldman-Eisler, 1968; Lennon, 1990), a finding that has been repeatedly confirmed empirically. If individual differences shape L1 fluency, they are likely to be reflected in L2 fluency measures as well (De Jong et al., 2015; Huensch & Tracy-Ventura, 2017). Indeed, several studies have reported large standard deviations in the use of filled pauses and repetitions in both native and nonnative speech (Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014), suggesting that at least these aspects of fluency are subject to substantial individual variation. It has further been proposed that pause length may reflect individual speaking style more than L2 proficiency, and that temporal features such as speech rate and pausing carry over from a speaker's L1 speaking style into L2 production (Raupach, 1980; Segalowitz, 2010; Towell et al., 2005).

A small but growing body of work has addressed the L1–L2 fluency relationship more directly. Derwing et al. Such phenomena are multifunctional and idiosyncratic, and their connections between L1 and L2 may be obscured when examined only through aggregate statistics. The present study addresses this gap by adopting a mixed methods approach that combines quantitative analyses (rank-order correlations and regression) with a complementary qualitative examination of selected learners' L1 and L2 productions. Speech samples were collected from 42 Finnish learners of English at two school levels, allowing the role of proficiency in the L1–L2 fluency relationship to be considered while also introducing a previously understudied language pair.

Guided by this approach, the study addresses three research questions: (RQ1) which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency; (RQ2) to what extent measures of L2 fluency can be predicted from L1 fluency measures; and (RQ3) what kinds of individual differences can be identified in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency through a qualitative analysis of learners' productions with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms.

intros.text:
Second language (L2) speech fluency is widely regarded as a key indicator of L2 oral proficiency, and considerable research effort has been devoted to understanding the factors that shape it (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012; Segalowitz, 2010). Within the influential Complexity-Accuracy-Fluency framework, fluency is typically approached in its 'narrow sense' (Lennon, 1990): the smoothness and effortlessness of speech as captured by measurable temporal features such as speed and pausing, alongside repair and stalling phenomena (Skehan, 2003; Tavakoli & Skehan, 2005). These objective, measurable aspects of utterance fluency are generally viewed as reflecting a speaker's underlying cognitive fluency (Segalowitz, 2010). Much of this body of work has established which temporal measures reliably distinguish more fluent from less fluent learners, and which best predict perceptions of proficiency (Bosker et al., 2012; Kormos & Dénes, 2004).

Despite this accumulated knowledge, one important factor has received comparatively little attention: the influence of a speaker's first language (L1) fluency on their L2 fluency. It has long been recognised that even native speakers vary considerably in their fluency (Fillmore, 1979; Goldman-Eisler, 1968; Lennon, 1990), and it seems plausible that individual differences shaping L1 speech, such as speaking style, working memory, and personality, are also reflected in L2 fluency measures (De Jong et al., 2015; Huensch & Tracy-Ventura, 2017). Indeed, several aspects of fluency, particularly pause length and the use of filled pauses and repetitions, have been argued to relate more to individual speaking style than to L2 proficiency (Cucchiarini et al., 2002; Götz, 2013). If this is so, then treating L2 fluency measures as pure indicators of proficiency, without accounting for L1 behaviour, risks conflating proficiency with individual and cross-linguistic characteristics carried over from the L1.

A small but growing number of studies have addressed the L1–L2 fluency relationship more directly. Derwing et al. (2009) provided the first systematic longitudinal comparison of L1 and L2 productions, finding correlations that shifted over time and that varied according to typological distance between the languages, leading them to question whether fluency is best conceived as 'traitlike' or 'statelike'. De Jong et al. (2015) subsequently demonstrated statistically significant correlations between all their L1 and L2 fluency measures and showed that L1 fluency explained substantial variance in L2 measures, most notably in silent pause duration. Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2017) added a longitudinal, study-abroad perspective, revealing that the contributions of L1 fluency and cross-linguistic differences shift with developing proficiency. Beyond the L2 fluency field, large-scale work by Bradlow et al. (2017) has shown that L2 speech rate can be predicted from L1 speech rate across ten different L1s, even when proficiency is controlled for. Together, these studies converge on the conclusion that L1 speaking style influences several aspects of L2 fluency.

However, this literature shares two important limitations. First, previous studies have relied almost exclusively on quantitative, group-level analyses, which capture overall tendencies but obscure the individual and often idiosyncratic patterns that characterise phenomena such as filled pauses, fillers, and repetitions. Because these stalling mechanisms are known to vary considerably across speakers (Götz, 2013; Kahng, 2014), group-level correlations may fail to reveal connections that exist at the level of individual speakers, or may mask the fact that learners use different features to serve the same communicative function. Second, the language pairs studied to date have not included typologically distinct combinations such as Finnish and English, leaving open questions about how findings generalise. Addressing these gaps, the present study adopts a mixed methods approach, combining quantitative correlational and regression analyses with a complementary qualitative examination of selected learners' use of stalling mechanisms in both languages. Speech samples in L1 Finnish and L2 English were collected from 42 learners at two school levels, allowing proficiency to be considered as well.

Accordingly, the study addresses three research questions: (RQ1) Which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency? (RQ2) To what extent can measures of L2 fluency be predicted from L1 fluency measures? (RQ3) What kinds of individual differences can be found in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency in learners' productions with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms?

intros.text:
Second language (L2) speech fluency is widely regarded as a primary indicator of oral proficiency, reflecting the smoothness and effortlessness of a speaker's production (Chambers, 1997). In the field of applied linguistics, researchers often distinguish between the 'broad sense' of fluency as general oral proficiency (Lennon, 1990) and a 'narrow sense' focusing on objective, measurable temporal aspects of speech, such as speaking rate and pausing. These utterance fluency measures are generally seen as surface manifestations of a speaker's underlying cognitive fluency (Segalowitz, 2010). Most contemporary research categorizes these measures into three dimensions: speed, breakdown (pausing), and repair fluency (Skehan, 2009; Tavakoli & Skehan, 2005). Because of their reliability, these temporal variables are frequently employed in language testing to estimate proficiency levels (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012).

While the majority of L2 fluency research has focused on group-level differences and the relationship between fluency and proficiency, there is growing recognition of the role of individual variation. Even native speakers exhibit significant diversity in their speaking styles (Goldman-Eisler, 1968; Lennon, 1990), and it has been suggested that such individual differences in first language (L1) fluency may be mirrored in L2 production (De Jong et al., 2015). This raises a critical question: to what extent is L2 fluency a reflection of L2-specific linguistic proficiency, and to what extent is it influenced by a speaker's general L1 speaking style? If fluency is a 'traitlike' characteristic, one would expect a stable relationship between L1 and L2 temporal patterns across different stages of development (Derwing et al., 2009).

Empirical evidence regarding this connection has been mixed but generally supportive of a cross-linguistic link. Derwing et al. (2009) found significant correlations between L1 and L2 fluency in the early stages of acquisition, though these patterns varied by language group. More recently, De Jong et al. (2015) demonstrated that L1 fluency measures could explain a substantial portion of the variance in L2 fluency, suggesting that correcting L2 measures for L1 behavior can provide a more accurate assessment of L2-specific proficiency. Similarly, Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2017) observed that the influence of L1 fluency and cross-linguistic differences becomes more prominent as learners develop, particularly after periods of immersion. Other studies have further corroborated that speech rate and pause patterns are frequently affected by L1 speaking style (Bradlow et al., 2017; Hincks, 2008).

Despite these findings, the relationship between L1 and L2 fluency remains relatively under-explored, particularly regarding the use of stalling mechanisms—such as filled pauses, drawls, fillers, and repetitions—which speakers use to manage processing time pressure (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998). While quantitative studies have provided broad correlations, they often overlook the idiosyncratic nature of how individual speakers transfer their L1 coping strategies to the L2. There is a need for research that combines quantitative breadth with qualitative depth to capture both the general trends and the individual variations in fluency behavior.

The present study addresses this gap by employing a mixed methods approach to examine the connections between L1 and L2 fluency among Finnish learners of English at two different school levels (9th grade and upper secondary school). By analyzing both temporal measures and stalling mechanisms, this study seeks to determine the predictive power of L1 fluency on L2 performance and to identify idiosyncratic patterns through a detailed qualitative analysis. Specifically, the study is guided by the following research questions:

RQ1. Which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency?
RQ2. To what extent can measures of L2 fluency be predicted from L1 fluency measures?
RQ3. What kinds of individual differences can be found in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency with a qualitative analysis of learners' productions with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms?

Most research in this domain focuses on three primary dimensions: speed, breakdown, and repair fluency (Skehan, 2003, 2009; Tavakoli & Skehan, 2005). Because these measures are sensitive to processing efficiency, they are frequently employed in both academic research and language testing to estimate proficiency levels (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012).

While much of the existing literature has focused on group-level quantitative differences, researchers have long acknowledged that significant individual variation exists even among native speakers (Fillmore, 1979; Lennon, 1990; Riggenbach, 1991). This internal variation is often attributed to a combination of cognitive factors, personality traits—such as extraversion (Dewaele & Furnham, 2000)—and a speaker's general speaking style. Consequently, it has been proposed that a speaker's first language (L1) fluency behavior may act as a template or influence their second language (L2) production, suggesting that some aspects of fluency may be 'traitlike' rather than solely a reflection of L2 proficiency (Derwing et al., 2009).

(2009) found initial correlations between L1 and L2 fluency among Slavic and Mandarin speakers, though these relationships shifted over time. More recently, De Jong et al. Similarly, Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2017) observed moderate to strong positive correlations between L1 and L2 speed and breakdown measures, noting that the influence of L1 fluency became more prominent as learners developed. Further evidence from outside the L2 field suggests that speech rate and pause patterns are consistently affected by L1 speaking style (Bradlow et al., 2017; Kolly et al., 2015).

Despite these advancements, the effects of L1 fluency on L2 speech fluency remain relatively poorly understood, particularly regarding the nuanced use of stalling mechanisms—such as filled pauses, drawls, and repetitions—which speakers use to manage processing time pressure (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998). To date, research has been predominantly quantitative and focused on group averages, leaving a gap in our understanding of how individual, idiosyncratic patterns in the L1 are mirrored or modified in the L2. There is a clear need for research that combines broad statistical trends with detailed individual analyses to capture the complexity of these cross-linguistic links.

Addressing this gap, the present study employs a mixed methods approach to examine the connections between L1 and L2 fluency among Finnish learners of English. By integrating quantitative rank-order correlations and regression analyses with a qualitative examination of selected participants' productions, this research aims to provide a more holistic account of how L1 speaking styles influence L2 performance. Specifically, the study addresses three research questions: (1) Which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency? (2) To what extent can measures of L2 fluency be predicted from L1 fluency measures? and (3) What kinds of individual differences can be found in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency through a qualitative analysis of learners with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms?

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. The theoretical framework is presented first, followed by the methodology used for data collection and analysis. The results of the quantitative and qualitative analyses are then detailed, and the findings are discussed in relation to existing literature. Finally, the article concludes with the implications of the results for L2 research, assessment, and pedagogy.

intros.text:
Second language (L2) speech fluency is widely recognized as a key indicator of L2 proficiency, often examined alongside accuracy and complexity within the Complexity-Accuracy-Fluency (CAF) framework (Housen, Kuiken, & Vedder, 2012). Fluency is generally understood as the smoothness and effortlessness of speech, frequently operationalized through temporal measures such as speaking rate, pausing, and repair mechanisms (Lennon, 1990; Segalowitz, 2010). While a substantial body of research has investigated the factors influencing L2 fluency, the extent to which first language (L1) fluency influences L2 production remains less understood. Early research suggested that even L1 speakers vary significantly in their fluency (Fillmore, 1979; Goldman-Eisler, 1968), implying that individual speaking styles may transfer to L2 performance. However, the question of whether fluency is a 'traitlike' characteristic, stable across languages, or a 'statelike' feature, dependent on L2 proficiency, has yet to be fully resolved.

Several studies have begun to address the relationship between L1 and L2 fluency. Derwing et al. (2009) conducted a longitudinal study comparing Slavic and Mandarin learners of English, finding significant correlations between L1 and L2 fluency measures in the early stages of L2 exposure, particularly for the Slavic group. They concluded that while a relationship exists, it may change over time, challenging the notion of fluency as a purely traitlike feature. More recently, De Jong et al. (2015) examined Dutch learners with English and Turkish L1s, demonstrating that L1 fluency measures could explain a significant portion of the variance in L2 fluency measures. Their findings suggested that correcting L2 fluency measures for L1 behavior might yield more valid indicators of L2 proficiency, particularly for measures such as syllable duration. Similarly, Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2017) found that L1 fluency, cross-linguistic differences, and proficiency differentially contributed to L2 fluency development, with the influence of L1 fluency becoming more pronounced after study abroad experiences. These studies collectively suggest that L1 speaking style is a significant factor in L2 fluency, though the strength of this relationship may vary based on proficiency and language pair.

Despite these insights, the existing literature has predominantly relied on quantitative, group-level analyses. While such approaches are valuable for establishing general trends, they may obscure individual variations in how L1 fluency manifests in L2 production. For instance, while temporal measures like speech rate and pause duration often show group-level correlations, the use of stalling mechanisms such as filled pauses, drawls, and repetitions may be more idiosyncratic (Brand & Götz, 2011; Kahng, 2014). Furthermore, most studies have focused on adult learners or have not systematically compared different proficiency levels within the same L1 group. Understanding how L1 fluency influences L2 fluency across different developmental stages is crucial for refining fluency assessment and pedagogical practices.

The present study aims to address these gaps by adopting a mixed methods approach to explore the connections between L1 and L2 fluency among Finnish learners of English. By combining quantitative analyses of temporal fluency measures with a qualitative examination of stalling mechanisms, this study seeks to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the L1-L2 fluency relationship. Specifically, the study addresses three research questions: (1) Which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with measures of L2 fluency? (2) To what extent can measures of L2 fluency be predicted from L1 fluency measures? (3) What kinds of individual differences can be found in the connections between L1 and L2 fluency through a qualitative analysis of learners' productions with high frequencies of stalling mechanisms?

This mixed methods approach allows for a nuanced investigation of both group-level trends and individual variations. By examining learners at two school levels, the study also considers the role of proficiency in moderating the L1-L2 fluency relationship. The findings have implications for L2 fluency research, assessment, and teaching, highlighting the importance of acknowledging L1 fluency as a factor in explaining L2 performance.

intros.text:
Second language (L2) speech fluency is a central component of oral proficiency and a key focus in applied linguistics research. It is commonly conceptualized within the Complexity-Accuracy-Fluency (CAF) framework, where fluency relates to the smoothness and effortlessness of speech production (Housen, Kuiken, & Vedder, 2012). While accuracy and complexity have received substantial attention, fluency remains a critical yet complex construct, often operationalized through temporal measures such as speech rate, pausing, and repair mechanisms (Skehan, 2003). These objective measures are widely used in both research and assessment contexts to evaluate L2 proficiency, as they are believed to reflect underlying cognitive processing capacities (Segalowitz, 2010). However, the validity of these measures as indicators of L2 proficiency specifically, rather than general speaking style, has been a subject of ongoing debate.

A significant body of literature has investigated the factors influencing L2 fluency, with a predominant focus on L2-specific variables such as proficiency level, task type, and cross-linguistic differences. For instance, Baker-Smemoe et al. (2014) examined the relationship between utterance fluency and overall L2 proficiency across five languages, finding that while some fluency measures correlate with proficiency, the strength of these relationships varies. Similarly, Bosker et al. (2012) demonstrated that listeners weigh different acoustic aspects of fluency, such as pauses and speed, differently when making global judgments. Despite this extensive research, the role of the first language (L1) in shaping L2 fluency has received comparatively less systematic attention, particularly regarding the extent to which L1 speaking styles transfer to L2 production.

The question of whether L2 fluency reflects a 'trait' (a stable individual characteristic) or a 'state' (dependent on L2 proficiency) is central to this debate. Derwing et al. (2009) conducted a longitudinal study comparing L1 and L2 fluency in Slavic and Mandarin learners of English, finding correlations that suggested a trait-like component, although this relationship was not consistent over time or across language groups. More recently, De Jong et al. (2015) argued that L1 fluency measures significantly predict L2 fluency, suggesting that correcting L2 measures for L1 behavior could yield more accurate indicators of L2 proficiency. Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2016) further expanded on this by examining how L1 fluency, cross-linguistic differences, and proficiency interact over time, highlighting the shifting importance of these factors during development.

However, several gaps remain in the current literature. First, most studies examining the L1-L2 fluency connection have relied exclusively on quantitative methods, focusing on group-level differences and correlations. While these studies provide valuable statistical evidence, they often overlook individual variation and the nuanced ways in which learners manage processing pressure. For example, Kahng (2014) and Hilton (2014) have noted the importance of combining quantitative measures with qualitative insights to understand the cognitive underpinnings of fluency. Second, there is a lack of research specifically addressing the Finnish-English language pair, which presents unique typological features, such as stress patterns and morphological complexity, that may influence fluency development (Lehtonen, 1979). Third, the role of stalling mechanisms—such as filled pauses, drawls, and repetitions—has been examined primarily in isolation, without a holistic view of how learners deploy these mechanisms across L1 and L2 to cope with similar communicative challenges (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998).

To address these gaps, the present study adopts a mixed methods approach to explore the connections between L1 and L2 fluency among Finnish learners of English. By combining quantitative analyses of temporal measures with a qualitative examination of stalling mechanisms, this research aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how L1 fluency influences L2 performance. Specifically, the study investigates which L1 fluency measures correlate most strongly with L2 measures, to what extent L2 fluency can be predicted from L1 fluency, and what individual differences emerge in the use of stalling mechanisms. This approach not only contributes to the theoretical debate on the trait-like versus state-like nature of fluency but also offers practical implications for L2 assessment and pedagogy, emphasizing the need to consider L1 speaking styles when evaluating L2 proficiency.

intros.text:
Fluency is a central dimension of second language (L2) speaking ability and a salient criterion in both research and assessment. In applied linguistics, it is commonly distinguished from accuracy and complexity and treated as one component of oral proficiency, rather than as a synonym for proficiency as a whole (Lennon, 1990; Segalowitz, 2010). In its narrower, utterance-based sense, fluency refers to the temporal smoothness of speech and is typically operationalized through measures of speed, pausing, and repair phenomena, such as speech rate, articulation rate, length of runs, silent pauses, filled pauses, repetitions, and reformulations (Kormos & Dénes, 2004; Bosker et al., 2012; Götz, 2013). These measures have proved useful because they capture observable features of spoken performance that listeners often associate with fluent speech, although not all measures contribute equally to perceived fluency or to estimates of overall proficiency (Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014; Bosker et al., 2012).

A substantial body of research has shown that L2 fluency develops with increased proficiency, experience, and exposure. Longitudinal and study-abroad studies, for example, have reported gains in speech rate, mean length of runs, and reduced pausing as learners gain communicative experience in the target language (Lennon, 1990; Towell et al., 1996; Mora & Valls-Ferrer, 2012). At the same time, fluency is not determined by L2 knowledge alone. Speech production is shaped by processing demands, task conditions, communicative strategies, affective factors, and individual speaking styles (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998; Hilton, 2014; Segalowitz, 2010). Speakers may use hesitation devices, repetitions, fillers, and other stalling mechanisms to cope with processing time pressure while maintaining the flow of speech (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998). Such phenomena are therefore not merely signs of deficiency; they may also reflect strategic management of limited planning time.

One increasingly important question is whether L2 fluency measures reflect L2-specific proficiency or more general, speaker-specific patterns of oral production. Individual differences in fluency are evident even among first language (L1) speakers, whose speech rates, pause patterns, and hesitation profiles vary considerably (Goldman-Eisler, 1968). If a learner is generally a fast or slow speaker, or tends to pause frequently in the L1, similar tendencies may appear in the L2. This possibility has important consequences for interpreting fluency measures in proficiency assessment: an L2 speaker’s pauses or speech rate may partly index stable personal speaking style rather than only L2 processing difficulty. Segalowitz (2010) therefore argued that observable utterance fluency should be considered in relation to the cognitive and individual factors that underlie it, and De Jong et al. (2015) proposed that L2 fluency measures may sometimes need to be corrected for L1 speaking behavior.

Empirical work directly comparing L1 and L2 fluency has begun to clarify this issue. Derwing et al. (2009), in a longitudinal study of Slavic- and Mandarin-speaking learners of English, found relationships between L1 and L2 temporal characteristics, although these relationships differed across language groups and over time. De Jong et al. (2015) reported significant correlations between L1 and L2 fluency measures among learners of Dutch, and showed that L1 behavior explained substantial variance in L2 fluency. Their findings suggested that some measures, particularly aspects of speed, may become stronger indicators of L2 proficiency when L1 speaking style is taken into account. Similarly, Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2016) demonstrated that L1 fluency behavior, cross-linguistic differences, and proficiency contributed differently to L2 fluency before and after residence abroad. Other studies have also suggested links between L1 and L2 temporal behavior, including speech rate and pausing (Raupach, 1980; Möhle, 1984; Towell et al., 2005). For Finnish speakers of English, earlier work has noted the relevance of speech rate and pausing patterns in English production (Lehtonen, 1979), but the relationship between Finnish L1 fluency and English L2 fluency remains underexplored.

Despite these advances, two limitations remain. First, most research on L1–L2 fluency relationships has been predominantly quantitative and group-oriented. Correlations and regressions are indispensable for identifying broad patterns, but they may obscure idiosyncratic ways in which individual learners manage fluency across languages. Second, relatively little attention has been paid to stalling mechanisms as functionally related resources. Filled pauses, drawls, fillers, and repetitions may differ formally across languages, yet serve similar purposes in buying planning time. A lack of direct statistical correspondence between a specific L1 and L2 feature may therefore conceal more complex cross-linguistic connections in speakers’ fluency profiles.

The present study addresses these gaps by examining connections between L1 Finnish and L2 English speech fluency among Finnish learners of English at two school levels. Using a mixed methods design, it combines quantitative analyses of temporal fluency and stalling mechanisms with qualitative analyses of selected learners’ productions. The study asks which L1 fluency measures are most strongly associated with L2 fluency, to what extent L2 fluency can be predicted from L1 behavior, and what individual patterns emerge when learners’ use of stalling mechanisms is examined in detail.

intros.text:
Oral fluency is a central dimension of second language (L2) performance and a salient criterion in language teaching, learning, and assessment. Within the complexity–accuracy–fluency framework, fluency is typically treated as a component of proficiency that concerns the smoothness, speed, and effortlessness of speech production. In L2 fluency research, a distinction is commonly made between fluency in the broad sense, referring to general oral proficiency, and fluency in the narrow sense, referring to measurable temporal characteristics of speech such as speed, pausing, and repair phenomena (Lennon, 1990; Segalowitz, 2010). These utterance fluency measures are widely used because they provide relatively objective indices of spoken performance and have been shown to relate to perceived fluency and proficiency ratings (Bosker et al., 2012; Kormos & Dénes, 2004; Baker-Smemoe et al., 2014).

Much of the empirical work on L2 fluency has therefore examined how learners differ in temporal fluency, how fluency develops over time, and which measures best capture proficiency-related change. Studies have shown, for example, that speech rate, length of run, and pausing patterns are important correlates of perceived fluency (Kormos & Dénes, 2004; Bosker et al., 2012), and that fluency can develop in response to increased exposure or study abroad experience (Towell et al., 1996; Mora & Valls-Ferrer, 2012). Research has also increasingly recognized that fluency is multidimensional, involving speed, breakdown, and repair aspects, and that speakers use a range of devices, including filled pauses, drawls, fillers, and repetitions, to manage processing time pressure during speech production (Dörnyei & Kormos, 1998; Götz, 2013; Hilton, 2014).

At the same time, fluency is not solely a reflection of L2 linguistic knowledge. Speakers vary in how fast they speak, how often they pause, and how they manage hesitation even in their first language (L1). Early and more recent work on spontaneous speech has demonstrated substantial individual variation in L1 temporal patterns (Goldman-Eisler, 1968), and L2 fluency researchers have long noted that such variation may carry over into L2 performance (Lennon, 1990; Segalowitz, 2010). If a learner is characteristically slow, pause-prone, or reliant on particular hesitation devices in the L1, similar patterns may influence their L2 speech independently of L2 proficiency. This possibility is especially important for assessment, because measures intended to index L2-specific ability may partly reflect stable speaking style or cross-linguistic speech habits.

A small but growing body of research has directly investigated the relationship between L1 and L2 fluency. Derwing et al. (2009), in a longitudinal study of Slavic and Mandarin speakers learning English, found that several L1 temporal measures were related to L2 fluency, although the strength of the relationship varied over time and between language groups. De Jong et al. (2015) further showed that L1 fluency measures explained variance in L2 Dutch fluency among English and Turkish L1 speakers, and that correcting some L2 measures for L1 behavior could improve their relationship with L2 proficiency. Huensch and Tracy-Ventura (2016) likewise demonstrated that L1 fluency behavior, cross-linguistic differences, and proficiency contributed differently to L2 Spanish and French fluency before and after study abroad. Related studies outside the immediate L2 fluency tradition have also suggested that speech rate and pausing patterns in the L2 may be influenced by L1 speaking style and language background (Raupach, 1980; Möhle, 1984; Lehtonen, 1979).

Despite these advances, the role of L1 fluency in L2 performance remains insufficiently understood. Existing studies have been predominantly quantitative and have mainly focused on group-level relationships between comparable temporal measures. Less attention has been paid to how individual speakers’ L1 and L2 fluency profiles may correspond in more idiosyncratic ways, particularly in the use of stalling mechanisms such as filled pauses, fillers, drawls, and repetitions. Such features may be infrequent, multifunctional, and unevenly distributed across speakers, making them difficult to interpret through correlations alone. Consequently, a lack of statistical association at group level may obscure meaningful individual connections between L1 and L2 speech behavior.

The present study addresses this gap by adopting a mixed methods approach to the relationship between L1 and L2 fluency. It examines monologue speech samples produced in L1 Finnish and L2 English by Finnish learners of English at two school levels. Quantitatively, the study investigates correlations between L1 and L2 fluency measures and the extent to which L2 fluency can be predicted from L1 fluency. Qualitatively, it explores selected learners’ use of stalling mechanisms in both languages in order to identify individual patterns that may not be visible in group-level analyses. The study is guided by three research questions: which L1 fluency measures are most strongly correlated with L2 fluency, to what extent L2 fluency measures can be predicted from L1 measures, and what individual differences emerge in the L1–L2 relationship when learners with frequent use of stalling mechanisms are examined in detail. By combining quantitative and qualitative evidence, the study aims to clarify the extent to which L2 fluency reflects L1 speaking style and to contribute to more nuanced approaches to L2 fluency research, assessment, and pedagogy.

intros.text: Speaking is an essential tool for communicating Bahadorfar and Omidvar (2014) and (Maharani, 2016). Living in the era of globalization, being able to speak English becomes a necessity (Gani et al., 2015; Muslem, 2015) in order to be able to build social relationships (Al-Auwal, 2017) and to create good communications (Puspitasari & Hanur, 2016) with other people who come from different countries (Efrizal, 2012). So improving the ability to speak English is very important for Indonesian students who know that the ability to speak English well will make a big contribution to their communication skills.  Nevertheless, learning to speak English is not an easy task (Alharbi, 2015; Gani et al., 2015). It needs a lot of practice and strong will-power to keep practicing (Ghiabi, 2014; Halimah et al., 2018). In line with this, Leong and Ahmadi (2017) and Akhyak and Indramawan (2013) have said that to speak English is not easy because skills like pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary, plus fluency, and comprehension need to be mastered by the speakers.  Based on previous studies, speaking is considered the most difficult of the four skills, accordingly there are some problems that are encountered both by the teacher and the students during teaching-learning speaking English in the classroom. These problems can result in the students having low ability in speaking English.  A study by Tuan and Mai (2015) found that low ability was due to inhibition, lack of topical knowledge, low or uneven participation and use of the L1, mother-tongue. Cook (2001), Denizer (2017) and Pathan et al. (2014) also found the same problems in getting students to talk in the classroom. Furthermore, Subandowo (2017) and Gani et al. (2015) found that students had problems with proper pronunciation, while Melendez et al. (2014) and Gani et al. (2015) found that many students lacked an adequate vocabulary and had poor skills with grammar. Next, Savaşçı (2014), Machmud and Abdulah (2017),Yalçın and İnceçay (2014), Kayaoğlu and Sağlamel (2013), and Machmud and Abdulah (2018) said that many students tend to be passive during class because they are too frightened to speak because of speaking anxiety. Lastly, Dewi et al. (2017) listed four speaking problems of EFL students: 1) Fear of making mistakes and fear of being laughed at by their friends or classmates as they are not sure of the correct pronunciation and grammar for what they want to say, 2) EFL students are not confident enough to express their ideas and feelings and are hesitant to speak due to their lack of vocabulary; 3) They feel bored when learning English because the teaching-learning activities are provided in a conventional way. 4) They also cannot speak based on their willingness or lack of it. Based on a number of findings, it can be concluded that there are eight factors causing the low speaking ability of EFL students, namely: a) lack of knowledge about the topic of conversation, b) lack of mastery of speaking aspects, c) students tend to use their mother tongue when learning speaking, d) fear of making mistakes, being humiliated, laughed at, and general lack of confidence, e) lecturers lack of preparation for teaching-learning, f) lecturers lack good material, g) lecturers not very competent in using English during teaching-learning processes, h) and boring methods used for teaching-learning speaking. These problems with teaching-learning speaking EFL happened with students that the researcher was teaching in the second semester of teaching EFL in the English Department at Universitas Suryakancana in the academic year 2016/2017, who became the subject of this research study. At the start, the speaking ability of these EFL students was low. Based on the observations above there were two factors that were mainly the causes of their low scores, namely: 1) problems related to the students’ ability to learn Speaking EFL, and 2) problems related to the lecturer’s ability to teach Speaking EFL. This was supported by research done by Arifin (2017), who said that the two main factors that cause the emergence of problems in speaking EFL are factors to do with the lecturer and factors to do with the students. Meanwhile, Alharbi (2015) found three main factors causing the emergence of problems in teaching-learning speaking, namely: (i) the ability of the lecturers in teaching, (ii) the methods used, and (iii) the students don’t get enough or make enough opportunities to practice speaking English EFL both inside the classroom and out of it. From these findings on the results and factors causing the low ability to speak in English, it appears that new methods need to be used to crack these difficulties in speaking and to enable the students to improve their ESL speaking ability. One such method that can be used is the Community Language Learning (CLL) method. This is in line with Fatemi and Adel (2014), who found that CLL is the most effective learning method that can be applied to learn a foreign language at the university level. CLL can be used by lecturers to explain foreign words, pronunciation and/or grammar terms in the class (Cook, 2001). Meanwhile, Anderson and Chung (2011), Chimombo (1993) and Abdullah (2017) found that CLL increased interest, creativity, and student participation in the learning processes for speaking ESL. Nurhasanah (2015) found that CLL was effective to increase the participation and motivation of students in their EFL speaking class and that, as a result their speaking ability improved.  Based on the studies above, this research was done to find out whether the CLL method could improve the EFL speaking skills of 27 students in their second semester studying English, ESL, in the English Department of a private university in West Java in the 2016/2017 academic year.  The researcher used the CLL method for teaching speaking ESL to find out if it could improve the EFL speaking ability of these students.

intros.text:
Speaking is arguably the most visible measure of a person's competence in a foreign language. When we say that someone "knows" a language, we often mean that the person is able to understand and to speak that language for the purposes of everyday communication. Speaking, in this sense, has been defined as one of the ways in which a person reveals what is in his or her mind orally (Gani et al., 2015; Efrizal, 2012), an ability to produce oral language by comprehending, expressing, and sharing ideas, opinions, or feelings in accordance with the context, participants, experience, environment, and purpose of the interaction (Maharani, 2016), and a process of building and sharing meaning through verbal and non-verbal signals in different contexts (Juhana, 2012). Whichever definition one adopts, the common thread is that speaking is fundamentally a communicative act by which a speaker expresses, shares, and negotiates meaning with others. For students in an English Education Study Program, who are being prepared to become teachers and users of English, the ability to speak the language confidently and accurately is not merely desirable but essential.

Despite its importance, speaking is widely regarded as the most difficult of the four language skills to acquire and to teach. A considerable body of research has reported that learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) find speaking more challenging than reading, writing, or listening (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Melendez et al., 2014; Tuan & Mai, 2015). The difficulties learners face have been attributed to two broad categories of factors. The first concerns psychological factors such as low motivation, anxiety, shyness, fearfulness, and a lack of confidence. A number of studies have demonstrated that anxiety in particular exerts a strong negative influence on the mastery of a second or foreign language and on learners' willingness to speak (Ariyanti, 2016; Kayaoğlu & Sağlamel, 2013; Tuan & Mai, 2015; Yalçın & İncecay, 2014; Arifin, 2017). Students who are anxious or who lack self-esteem often hesitate to speak in front of their teachers and peers because they are afraid of making mistakes and of being judged negatively (Machmud & Abdulah, 2017, 2018). The second category concerns linguistic factors, including limited vocabulary, poor pronunciation, weak grammar, and difficulties with fluency and accuracy, as well as interference from the learners' mother tongue (Gani et al., 2015; Leong & Ahmadi, 2017; Subandowo, 2017). Taken together, these two sets of factors help to explain why so many EFL learners remain reluctant and hesitant speakers even after several years of formal instruction.

These problems were clearly visible among the second-semester students in the English Education Study Program at a private university in West Java, where the present study was conducted. In a preliminary observation, the students appeared confused, hesitant, and anxious when asked to speak. They struggled to express their ideas, had difficulty pronouncing new vocabulary, and showed low motivation during speaking lessons. A preliminary speaking test confirmed the seriousness of the situation: the mean score was only 61, and just six out of twenty-seven students, or 22 percent, reached the minimum passing criterion of 70. Such results indicated an urgent need for a teaching approach that could address both the psychological and the linguistic obstacles hindering the students' oral development.

A range of strategies and techniques has been proposed to help learners overcome these difficulties, including communicative games (Dewi et al., 2016), the use of technology and mobile devices (Bahadorfar & Omidvar, 2014; Machmud & Abdulah, 2017, 2018), story-retelling and story-completion tasks (Ghiabi, 2014), and various media such as puppets (Maharani, 2016). Among the humanistic methods that place learners and their affective needs at the centre of instruction, Community Language Learning (CLL) stands out as a promising option for the speaking classroom. Developed by Charles A. Curran (1976) and his associates under the framework of Counseling-Learning Theory, CLL casts the teacher in the role of a counselor and the students in the role of clients who work together within a supportive community to develop the language they wish to learn (Chimombo, 1993). The method emphasises the wholeness and uniqueness of the learner and the integration of the learner's personality into the educational process, and it envisages learning as progressing through five developmental stages in which the learner gradually moves from complete dependence on the counselor towards independence and mastery. In practice, CLL typically involves recording the students' speech, transcribing it, reflecting on the learning experience, reflective listening, self-correction, and small-group tasks (Nagaraj, 2009). Because it explicitly seeks to lower anxiety, build confidence, and foster collaboration, and because it allows a controlled and supportive use of the first language to convey meaning where necessary (Cook, 2001), CLL appears well suited to the twin challenge posed by the psychological and linguistic barriers to speaking.

Previous studies have offered encouraging evidence for the effectiveness of CLL. Nurhasanah (2015), for instance, found that the method increased students' participation in classroom conversation as well as their motivation to learn, while more recent work has explored the combination of CLL with technological tools such as speaking applications to help learners reduce their fear of speaking and improve their pronunciation, intonation, and fluency (Halimah et al., 2022). Nevertheless, empirical accounts of how the full cycle of CLL activities can be systematically implemented to boost the speaking ability of tertiary-level EFL learners in the Indonesian context remain relatively scarce, and there is a continuing need for classroom-based research that documents both the process and the outcomes of using this method.

Against this background, the present study set out to investigate the effect of using the Community Language Learning method on the teaching and learning of English speaking among second-semester students in the English Education Study Program at a private university in West Java, with the specific aim of improving their speaking ability. Adopting a classroom action research design, the study sought not only to measure any improvement in the students' speaking scores across successive cycles but also to explore the students' difficulties, their responses to the method, and the strengths and weaknesses of its implementation. In doing so, it aims to contribute practical insight into how a humanistic, learner-centred method can be harnessed to build the confidence, motivation, and communicative competence that EFL speakers so often lack, and to inform teachers and lecturers seeking effective ways to enhance their students' spoken English.

intros.text:
Language, in its most natural form, is realised through speech. To understand a living language is commonly taken to mean the ability both to comprehend and to speak it, and speaking is the skill through which people carry out daily communication. Speaking may be described as the ability to reveal orally what is in one's mind, or, more fully, as the ability to produce speech by comprehending, expressing, and sharing ideas, opinions, or feelings, depending on the context, the participants, the experience, the environment, and the purpose (Gani et al., 2015; Maharani, 2016; Juhana, 2012). Understood in this way, speaking is a process of building and sharing meaning through verbal and non-verbal signals in a variety of contexts, and its ultimate purpose is to communicate, whether transactionally or interactionally, in order to convey a message. As English continues to serve as the principal tool of international communication, the capacity to use it fluently in spoken form has become a necessity for learners generally, and for students of English departments in particular, for whom oral competence is central to both their studies and their future professional lives.

Despite its centrality, speaking is widely acknowledged to be the most challenging of the four language skills. A considerable body of research reports that learners find speaking more difficult than reading, writing, and listening (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Melendez et al., 2014; Tuan & Mai, 2015). The factors that account for this difficulty have been examined from a number of angles. One strand of research foregrounds psychological factors, showing how anxiety, shyness, fearfulness, low self-esteem, and a lack of confidence undermine learners' willingness and ability to speak in a foreign language (Arifin, 2017; Kayaogğlu & Sağlamel, 2013; Tuan & Mai, 2015; Yalçın & İnceçay, 2014). A second strand emphasises linguistic factors, including limited vocabulary, weak pronunciation, insufficient grammatical control, and problems of fluency and accuracy, as well as the interference of the learners' mother tongue (Gani et al., 2015; Leong & Ahmadi, 2017; Subandowo, 2017; Cook, 2001). Taken together, these studies suggest that psychological and linguistic factors are the two principal forces that shape the learning of speaking in English as a foreign language (EFL), and that any pedagogical response worth pursuing must address both dimensions simultaneously.

In seeking to help learners overcome such barriers, researchers and practitioners have experimented with a range of instructional strategies. Communicative games, learning-strategy training, story-retelling and story-completion tasks, puppets and other creative and arts-based approaches, and, increasingly, technology-assisted techniques involving smartphones, mobile applications, and immersive multimedia have all been reported to raise learners' motivation and to improve their oral performance (Dewi et al., 2016; Ghiabi, 2014; Maharani, 2016; Anderson & Chung, 2011; Machmud & Abdulah, 2017, 2018; Asnawi, 2015; Bahadorfar & Omidvar, 2014). Several of these studies note, in particular, that techniques able to lower anxiety and to create a supportive classroom atmosphere tend to produce the most encouraging gains, because they allow learners to speak more freely and with greater confidence. Among the approaches that place learner affect at the centre of instruction, the Community Language Learning (CLL) Method stands out as an explicitly humanistic methodology. First developed by Curran (1976) within his Counseling-Learning framework, CLL casts the teacher as a counsellor and the learners as clients, emphasising the wholeness of the person and the integration of the learner's personality into the educational process (Chimombo, 1993). Its recommended procedures—recording learners' speech, transcribing it, reflecting on the learning experience, reflective listening, self-correction, and small-group work (Nagaraj, 2009)—are designed to build confidence and reduce the fear that so often silences EFL speakers.

Given this rationale, CLL appears especially well suited to the twin problems of psychology and language that the literature identifies as obstacles to speaking. Yet, although CLL has long been recognised as a viable option for foreign-language settings, empirical accounts of its use for developing speaking in Indonesian tertiary EFL contexts remain scarce. The relatively few classroom studies that exist have tended to focus on increasing learners' participation in conversation or on combining CLL with digital tools rather than on its direct effect on measured speaking ability (Nurhasanah, 2015; Halimah et al., 2022). Consequently, there is still limited classroom-based evidence documenting how, and to what extent, the systematic application of the CLL Method improves the speaking scores, motivation, and confidence of university students of English education. This is a gap worth addressing, particularly for second-semester students whose speaking competence is often still fragile and whose reluctance to speak, as classroom observation frequently confirms, is bound up with anxiety and a lack of self-assurance.

The present study was undertaken to help fill this gap. Its aim was to find out the effect of using the CLL Method for teaching and learning English speaking among second-semester students in an English Education Study Program at a private university in West Java, in an effort to improve their speaking ability. In pursuing this aim, the study sought both to reveal the difficulties the students faced in developing their speaking and to find solutions to those difficulties through the application of CLL. To this end, a classroom action research design, adapted from the cyclical model of Ferrance (2000), was employed over three cycles, with the lecturer acting as researcher and teacher while a collaborating lecturer served as an independent observer. Data were gathered from classroom observations, a questionnaire, interviews, and a series of speaking tests administered before and after each cycle, so that changes in the learners' performance and attitudes could be traced across the intervention.

It is anticipated that the findings will offer practical evidence of the value of CLL for boosting EFL speaking, showing whether a method grounded in counselling and community can simultaneously raise learners' test scores and enhance their motivation, interest, and confidence. In doing so, the study may contribute to the wider search for classroom techniques that address the psychological and linguistic barriers to speaking, and may inform lecturers and other language practitioners who are looking for humanistic alternatives to more conventional, teacher-centred instruction. The remainder of this article reviews the relevant literature on the nature of speaking, the factors influencing its learning, and the CLL Method; describes the action research method adopted; and then presents and discusses the results obtained from the observations, questionnaire, tests, and interviews before drawing conclusions and offering recommendations for practice.

intros.text:
In the era of globalization, English has established itself as the primary tool for international communication, making the mastery of both written and spoken forms an absolute necessity, particularly for students within English Education Study Programs. Among the four fundamental language skills—reading, writing, listening, and speaking—the ability to speak is often regarded as the most critical for enabling individuals to function effectively in a globalized world (Leong & Ahmadi, 2017). Speaking is fundamentally the process of building and sharing meaning through verbal and non-verbal signals across various contexts, serving the purpose of communicating messages either transactionally or interactionally. It is the primary vehicle through which learners express their ideas, opinions, desires, and feelings to others, depending on the participants, environment, and specific purpose of the interaction.

Despite its importance, a significant body of research indicates that speaking is considered the most challenging skill for many English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students compared to the other three language skills (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Derakhshan et al., 2016; Melendez et al., 2014; Mirhadizadeh, 2016; Tuan & Mai, 2015). This difficulty often stems from a complex interplay of linguistic and psychological factors. Linguistically, students frequently struggle with vocabulary limitations, pronunciation errors, grammar inconsistencies, and a general lack of fluency and accuracy (Gani et al., 2015; Leong & Ahmadi, 2017; Melendez et al., 2014; Subandowo, 2017). Interference from the mother tongue also plays a significant role, often leading to errors in sound production and articulation (Subandowo, 2017).

However, the psychological barriers are often more daunting than the linguistic ones. Many EFL learners experience high levels of anxiety, shyness, and a profound lack of confidence when asked to produce oral language (Ariyanti, 2016; Arnold, 2011; Kayaoğlu & Sağlamel, 2013; Tuan & Mai, 2015). Students often feel a fear of making mistakes, embarrassment, or a sense of being less competent than their peers, which leads to reluctance in participating in classroom conversations (Kayaoğlu & Sağlamel, 2013; Leong & Ahmadi, 2017). Such psychological distress can manifest as speech anxiety and low self-esteem, which not only hinders the student's performance but can also affect the teacher's ability to manage the classroom optimally (Arifin, 2017). Consequently, many students prefer to remain silent during discussion sessions, further impeding their progress in speaking proficiency (Tuan et al., 2015).

To address these challenges, educators have explored various pedagogical interventions. Some have turned to technology, utilizing smartphones, vlogging, or interactive e-modules to reduce anxiety and increase motivation (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Akhyak & Indramawan, 2013; Machmud & Abdulah, 2017, 2018). Others have employed literature-based activities, such as debates and role-playing, or the use of communicative games to create an enjoyable learning atmosphere that reduces stress and boosts enthusiasm (Alharbi, 2015; Dewi et al., 2016). While these methods show promise, there is a growing need for humanistic approaches that prioritize the learner's psychological well-being and integrate their personality into the educational process.

One such humanistic methodology is Community Language Learning (CLL). Developed by Charles A. Curran, CLL is based on the 'Counseling-Learning Theory,' where the traditional roles of teacher and student are reimagined as 'counselor' and 'client.' Unlike traditional methods that may shun the use of the first language (L1), CLL recognizes the L1 as a valuable classroom resource that can be used to convey meaning and organize learning (Cook, 2001). By focusing on the uniqueness and wholeness of the person, CLL aims to reduce the threat often associated with foreign language production. It creates a supportive community where students work together, thereby fostering a sense of security and confidence (Nurhasanah, 2015). The process typically involves recording student speech, transcribing it, and engaging in reflective listening and self-correction, which allows learners to take ownership of their linguistic development.

Previous research suggests that the implementation of CLL can significantly increase student participation and motivation in speaking classes (Nurhasanah, 2015). Furthermore, when combined with modern tools like the Orai application, the CLL method has been shown to help students alleviate the fear of speaking and improve specific aspects of their oral production, such as intonation and speed (Halimah et al., 2022). By reducing the teacher-centered nature of the classroom and increasing student-centered activity, CLL allows learners to develop the social skills and self-esteem necessary for successful communication.

In the context of a private university in West Java, preliminary observations indicated that second-semester students in the English Education Study Program struggled significantly with their speaking abilities. A large majority of these students failed to meet the minimum passing criterion, reflecting a lack of confidence and a struggle to express ideas orally. This situation underscores the urgent need for a teaching intervention that can simultaneously address the linguistic gaps and the psychological barriers hindering these students.

Therefore, the present study was conducted to investigate the effect of the Community Language Learning (CLL) method on boosting the speaking ability of these students. By employing a Classroom Action Research (CAR) design, the study aims to reveal the specific difficulties students face and provide a systematic solution through the iterative cycles of the CLL method. It is hypothesized that by shifting the classroom dynamic toward a counselor-client relationship and utilizing a community-based learning approach, students will exhibit improved mean scores in speaking tests and demonstrate increased confidence and motivation in their EFL learning journey.

intros.text:
In the era of global communication, mastering the English language in both written and spoken forms has become an absolute necessity, particularly for students enrolled in English education programs. Speaking, in particular, is fundamentally defined as the ability to produce oral language by comprehending, expressing, and sharing ideas, opinions, or feelings based on the specific context, participants, and purpose of the interaction. It serves as a vital tool for building and sharing meaning through verbal and non-verbal signals, allowing individuals to communicate either transactionally or interactionally to convey specific messages. Because the primary goal of language acquisition is often the ability to communicate effectively in real-world settings, the development of speaking proficiency is central to the success of any English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learner.

Despite its importance, a significant body of research suggests that speaking is often regarded as the most challenging of the four language skills, surpassing reading, writing, and listening in terms of difficulty (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Derakhshan et al., 2016; Melendez et al., 2014; Mirhadizadeh, 2016; Tuan & Mai, 2015). This difficulty stems from a complex interplay of linguistic and psychological factors. From a linguistic perspective, learners often struggle with vocabulary limitations, poor pronunciation, grammatical inaccuracies, and a general lack of fluency (Gani et al., 2015; Leong & Ahmadi, 2017; Melendez et al., 2014; Subandowo, 2017). Furthermore, the role of the mother tongue often complicates this process, as language interference can lead to persistent errors in sound production and articulation (Subandowo, 2017).

Beyond linguistic hurdles, psychological barriers play a critical role in hindering speaking performance. Numerous studies have highlighted that anxiety, shyness, and a lack of confidence significantly impede the mastery of a second language (Ariyanti, 2016; Arnold, 2011; Kayaoğlu & Sağlamel, 2013; Tuan & Mai, 2015). Many EFL students experience a profound fear of making mistakes, which leads to low self-esteem and a reluctance to participate in classroom discussions (Tuan et al., 2015). This anxiety is often exacerbated by a fear of negative evaluation from peers or teachers, resulting in a state of silence or a heavy reliance on the first language (L1) to compensate for their perceived inadequacies. As noted by Arifin (2017), these psychological problems affect not only the students but can also impact the teacher's ability to manage the classroom optimally, thereby creating an ineffective learning environment.

To address these challenges, educators have explored various instructional strategies. Some have integrated technology, such as the use of smartphones or interactive e-modules, to reduce peer pressure and increase motivation (Ahmed & Alamin, 2014; Machmud & Abdulah, 2017, 2018). Others have employed arts-based creativity, vlogging, or communicative games to create more engaging and less stressful atmospheres (Anderson & Chung, 2011; Akhyak & Indramawan, 2013; Dewi et al., 2016). While these methods have shown promise in increasing student activity, there remains a need for a more holistic, humanistic approach that specifically addresses the psychological security of the learner while simultaneously building their linguistic competence.

One such approach is the Community Language Learning (CLL) method. Developed by Charles A. Curran, CLL is characterized as a 'Counseling-Learning' theory where the teacher functions as a counselor and the students act as clients. Unlike traditional teacher-centered models, CLL emphasizes the wholeness of the person and integrates the learner's personality into the educational process. It recognizes the utility of the first language as a classroom resource to help students bridge the gap between their native tongue and the target language (Cook, 2001). By focusing on the social and emotional needs of the learners, CLL aims to reduce anxiety and build a supportive community where students feel safe to experiment with the language. Previous applications of CLL have indicated its potential to increase student participation and motivation in speaking classes (Nurhasanah, 2015), and recent integrations with specialized applications have further helped students alleviate the fear of speaking (Halimah et al., 2022).

However, while the theoretical benefits of CLL are well-documented, there is still a need for empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in specific academic contexts, particularly among university students in the Indonesian EFL setting who face high levels of speaking anxiety. Many students in West Java, for instance, continue to struggle with confidence and fluency despite their academic training. Therefore, it is important to conduct further research to determine how a structured implementation of CLL—including recording, transcription, and reflection—can systematically boost the speaking abilities of these students.

The primary objective of this study is to investigate the effect of using the Community Language Learning (CLL) method on the speaking ability of second-semester students in the English Education Study Program at a private university in West Java. Specifically, the research seeks to identify the students' speaking difficulties and determine the extent to which the CLL method can improve their mean speaking scores and overall confidence. To achieve this, the study employs a Classroom Action Research (CAR) design, involving three cycles of planning, acting, observing, and reflecting. Data are gathered through a combination of pre-tests, post-tests, observations, questionnaires, and interviews to provide a comprehensive view of the students' progress.

It is expected that the results of this study will demonstrate a significant improvement in students' speaking proficiency and a reduction in their psychological barriers. By shifting the classroom dynamic from a teacher-led environment to a learner-centered community, this research aims to offer practical implications for EFL practitioners seeking to foster a more supportive and effective speaking classroom. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed review of the literature regarding the nature of speaking, influencing factors, and the CLL method; Section 3 describes the methodology and the CAR cycles implemented; Section 4 presents the findings from observations, questionnaires, and tests; and Section 5 offers conclusions and recommendations for future research.
