intros.text:
English has become an important medium for education, employment, international communication, and social mobility in many multilingual societies. In Malaysia, where English functions as a second language and is widely associated with academic and professional advancement, university students are expected to develop sufficient competence to participate in higher education and the global labour market. Yet successful second language acquisition is not determined by exposure and instruction alone. Learners differ considerably in the effort they invest, the goals they set, and the persistence they show when facing linguistic difficulty. Among the individual difference variables that shape second language learning, motivation has consistently been regarded as one of the most influential factors (Gardner et al., 1983; Dörnyei, 2000). Without adequate motivation, learners may avoid practice, experience anxiety, or fail to sustain engagement over the long period required to acquire a second language.

Second language acquisition is affected by a range of linguistic, psychological, and social factors, including vocabulary knowledge, grammatical competence, first-language interference, self-efficacy, and motivation (Adwani & Shrivastava, 2017). However, motivation is distinctive because it energises and directs the learning process. It influences learners’ willingness to participate in classroom activities, communicate in the target language, respond to feedback, and continue learning despite errors or embarrassment. Gardner et al. (1983) conceptualised motivation as the degree to which individuals strive to learn a language because of their desire to do so and the satisfaction they experience through the learning activity. This view highlights both effort and affect, suggesting that motivated learners are not merely aware of the value of English but are also willing to act on that awareness.

Research on language learning motivation has been strongly shaped by Gardner’s socio-educational model, which links motivation, attitudes, cultural beliefs, anxiety, prior achievement, and language proficiency (Gardner et al., 1983). Within this tradition, two major orientations have received particular attention: integrative and instrumental motivation. Integrative motivation refers to learners’ interest in the target language community and their desire to understand, communicate with, or become closer to its members. Instrumental motivation, by contrast, concerns the practical benefits of learning a language, such as passing examinations, obtaining employment, gaining admission to higher education, or improving one’s social and economic prospects. In many English as a second or foreign language contexts, instrumental motivation is especially prominent because English is perceived as a language of opportunity and access rather than as the language of a single local community.

Later developments in motivational theory have broadened this perspective. Dörnyei (2000) argued that motivation should not be treated as a fixed trait but as a dynamic process that changes over time, depending on learners’ goals, classroom experiences, and self-regulatory strategies. His later work on the L2 Motivational Self System further emphasised the role of learners’ future self-images, including the kind of English user they wish to become (Dörnyei, 2009). In addition, intrinsic motivation has been widely discussed in relation to learners’ enjoyment, interest, and satisfaction in the activity of learning itself. Intrinsically motivated learners study English because they find the process meaningful, pleasurable, or personally rewarding. Resultative motivation is also relevant in language learning because achievement can strengthen learners’ motivation: students who perform well may become more confident and more willing to participate, while repeated failure may reduce effort and engagement.

The importance of English learning motivation is particularly evident in Asian educational contexts, where English-in-education policies have expanded in response to globalisation and the demand for internationally competitive graduates (Kam, 2002). In neighbouring contexts such as Indonesia, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Saudi Arabia, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates, studies have shown that learners’ reasons for studying English vary according to educational setting, social expectations, and perceived future benefits. Achmad and Yusuf (2016), for example, found that students in Aceh were motivated by intrinsic, extrinsic, and integrative factors, with integrative motivation emerging as a notable reason for learning English. Ulfa and Bania (2019) reported that EFL students’ motivation was influenced by both internal goals and external factors such as teachers, parents, and the learning environment. Usman et al. (2016) similarly showed that teacher competence can enhance students’ motivation, demonstrating the role of classroom agents in sustaining learners’ engagement.

Other studies have indicated that instrumental reasons often dominate among tertiary learners. At university level, English is commonly linked to academic success, employability, and mobility. Narayanan et al. (2008) noted that factors affecting English learning at the tertiary level include learner-related and contextual influences, while studies in comparable contexts have found that students often value English for its usefulness in examinations, future careers, and international communication. Such findings are relevant to Malaysia, where undergraduate students are likely to associate English proficiency with graduation requirements, professional opportunities, and participation in global academic or workplace environments. At the same time, learners may also show integrative, intrinsic, or achievement-related forms of motivation, particularly when they view English as a means of wider communication or as a subject they personally enjoy.

Despite the extensive research on motivation in second language acquisition, there remains a need for context-specific studies that identify which types of motivation are most salient among Malaysian university students. Motivation is shaped by local educational policies, institutional expectations, learners’ academic programmes, and the social status of English. Therefore, findings from other countries cannot be assumed to apply directly to Malaysian learners. Moreover, many previous studies have focused mainly on integrative and instrumental motivation, leaving less attention to intrinsic and resultative motivation within the same group of learners. A broader examination of these four motivational types can provide a more complete understanding of why students learn English and how strongly they are motivated.

The present study investigates motivation in learning English as a second language among Bachelor students at a private university in Selangor, Malaysia. Specifically, it examines the types of motivation used by Bachelor of Teaching English as a Second Language (BTESL) students and determines their motivational levels in relation to integrative, instrumental, resultative, and intrinsic motivation. By adapting Gardner and Lambert’s Attitude Motivation Test Battery, the study seeks to identify whether learners are primarily motivated by practical goals, social and communicative interests, personal enjoyment, or achievement-related experiences. The findings are expected to contribute to a clearer understanding of Malaysian university students’ ESL motivation and to offer pedagogical implications for lecturers, syllabus designers, and future researchers concerned with improving English language learning in higher education.

intros.text:
English has become a central resource for education, employment, mobility and international communication. In many Asian contexts, including Malaysia, English is learned not only as a school or university subject but also as a language associated with academic success, professional opportunity and participation in wider global communities. As Kam (2002) notes, the growing demand for English across East Asia has encouraged governments and educational institutions to strengthen English language teaching and to respond to the needs of learners in increasingly globalised settings. For university students in particular, English proficiency is often linked to access to knowledge, employability and social advancement. Consequently, understanding the factors that support or hinder English learning remains an important concern in second language acquisition (SLA) and English as a second language (ESL) education.

Among the many factors that influence SLA, motivation has consistently been regarded as one of the most powerful predictors of learners’ effort, persistence and achievement. Language learning is a long-term process, and learners are required to sustain attention, practise regularly, overcome anxiety and cope with failure. Without sufficient motivation, students may avoid participation, give up easily or view English as merely a compulsory requirement. Adwani and Shrivastava (2017) identify motivation, together with vocabulary, grammar, first-language influence and self-efficacy, as a vital factor affecting second language acquisition. Similarly, Gardner et al. (1983) argue that motivation has a direct relationship with second language proficiency within the socio-educational model of language learning. In this sense, motivation is not a peripheral emotional state but a central psychological condition that shapes how learners approach the target language.

Motivation in language learning has been conceptualised in several ways. Gardner and Lambert’s work on language attitudes and motivation has been especially influential in distinguishing between integrative and instrumental orientations. Integrative motivation refers to the learner’s desire to learn a language in order to communicate with, understand or identify with members of the target language community. Instrumental motivation, by contrast, concerns practical benefits such as passing examinations, obtaining employment, entering higher education or improving one’s social and economic position. Gardner et al. (1983) showed that attitudes, cultural beliefs and motivation are closely connected to language achievement, and this framework has continued to inform research on ESL and EFL learners in different educational settings.

Later developments have expanded the understanding of L2 motivation beyond the integrative–instrumental distinction. Dörnyei (2000) proposed a process-oriented view of motivation, emphasising that student motivation develops and fluctuates over time rather than remaining fixed. This perspective is especially relevant to formal education, where learners may study a language for many years and experience changing goals, classroom conditions and levels of confidence. Dörnyei’s (2009) L2 Motivational Self System further highlights the role of learners’ future self-images, including the kind of English user they wish or feel obliged to become. In addition, intrinsic motivation has been widely discussed as the internal interest, enjoyment or satisfaction that learners experience when engaging in language learning activities. Resultative motivation also draws attention to the relationship between achievement and motivation, suggesting that successful learning experiences may strengthen learners’ desire to continue learning.

Previous studies have shown that learners’ motivation for English varies across contexts. In Aceh, Indonesia, Achmad and Yusuf (2016) found that university students were motivated by intrinsic, extrinsic and integrative factors, with integrative motivation emerging as an important reason for learning English. Ulfa and Bania (2019), also in Aceh, reported that both intrinsic and extrinsic motivation influenced EFL students, with teachers playing a major role in extrinsic motivation and students’ own goals contributing strongly to intrinsic motivation. Usman et al. (2016) similarly found that teachers’ cognitive, affective and psychomotor competences could enhance students’ motivation to learn English. These studies suggest that motivation is shaped not only by learners’ personal goals but also by their educational environment and by the support they receive from teachers.

Research in other tertiary contexts has also highlighted the prominence of instrumental reasons for learning English. Studies of university learners often show that students value English because it helps them succeed academically, obtain better employment and communicate in international settings. Narayanan et al. (2008), for example, examined factors affecting English learning at the tertiary level, while research in neighbouring and comparable contexts has repeatedly linked English learning to academic and occupational aspirations. Such findings are understandable in countries where English functions as a second or foreign language but carries strong institutional and economic value. At the same time, motivation may not be limited to one orientation; learners can simultaneously be instrumentally, integratively, intrinsically and resultatively motivated.

Despite the extensive attention given to L2 motivation, there remains a need for more context-specific evidence from Malaysian higher education. Malaysia is a multilingual country in which English plays an important role in education, professional communication and global engagement. However, university students’ reasons for learning English may differ according to programme, discipline, institutional context and future career expectations. In particular, Bachelor students in Teaching English as a Second Language (BTESL) represent an important group because they are not only learners of English but also prospective English language educators. Their motivation may influence their own language development and, eventually, the ways in which they motivate future learners. Yet relatively little is known about the dominant types and levels of motivation among BTESL students in Malaysian private higher education when several motivational dimensions are considered together.

Addressing this gap, the present study investigates motivation in second language acquisition among Bachelor students at a private university in Selangor, Malaysia. Specifically, it aims to identify the types of motivation used by BTESL students in learning English as a second language and to determine their level of motivation. The study focuses on four types of motivation: integrative, instrumental, resultative and intrinsic. By examining these dimensions together, the study offers a broader picture of students’ motivational profiles than studies that consider only one or two orientations.

To achieve these objectives, the study employed a quantitative survey design. Data were collected from 150 second-year BTESL students using a questionnaire adapted from Gardner and Lambert’s Attitude Motivation Test Battery. The questionnaire was modified to suit the objectives of the study and analysed using SPSS. The findings are expected to contribute to the understanding of ESL motivation in Malaysian higher education and to provide useful implications for lecturers, curriculum designers and future researchers. In particular, identifying the dominant motivational orientations of BTESL students can help educators design classroom environments and learning opportunities that sustain students’ interest, strengthen their goals and support successful English language learning.

intros.text: A piece of book is nothing but a lifeless object but it is obvious that a book can revive a mind. Reading books is the process that enriches one’s mind with different branches of knowledge until one dies. It creates new insight and new wisdom. Reading is one of the oldest habits of human civilization and is regarded as the passion of the greatest personalities of all times. To enrich knowledge, the most important task for everyone is to develop the habit and the culture of reading. One of the first documentary sources for reading was manuscript; however, it was accessible only to the elite class of society. Later, the arrival of the Gutenberg printing press ended such discrimination by making the printed word available to all. But, it is a matter of great regret that reading habits are changing due to technological development over time.  In this modern multimedia society, radio, television, cell-phone, computer and the Internet are consuming a big slice of time and reducing the amount of time spent on reading printed books. Huang et al. (2014, p. 438) state that, “the amount of reading is declining significantly and reading skills are decreasing”.  Nowadays, children, youths and adults alike are inclined to use technology for information, entertainment and pleasure. The emergence of Internet has created an extraordinary change in the reading culture. It has made its existence, fully or partially, in the reading behaviour of the people. Presently, because of the Internet revolution, reading sources have been transformed diversely into web sites, web pages, e-books, ejournals, e-papers, e-mails, chat rooms, instant messaging blogs and other multimedia documents. Nowadays, Internet surfing enables people to navigate a world full of interconnected information, to discover new sites, to get up-to-date information and to download things of interest. Consequently, modern people have accepted Internet browsing as their daily habit and surfing the Internet has become a kind of addiction to the new generation. On the contrary, it is still believed that reading books, not browsing the Internet, is the best way through which one can travel upon the realm of knowledge and pleasure. The present generation, especially the college and university students, are well acquainted with the new technology and its applications in the present virtually networked society. To them, reading books for knowledge and enjoyment is a backdated idea  Roberts and Foehr (2004) observe that the Internet has fixed dead roots in the lives of the net generation students than all other technological innovations. But, according to Holte (1998, p. 80), reading “adds quality to life and provides access to culture and cultural heritage”. He pointed out that reading empowers and emancipates citizens and brings people together  Unfortunately, the habit of reading is declining day by day. The world is becoming smaller because of technological advancement and, at the same time, the hearts of people are also shrinking. As a result, many people, especially the young generation, overlook the fact that reading books is the best way to get information and pleasure. Thus, information and communication technology, especially the Internet, exert adverse effect on reading culture  This study shows that the widespread use of technology imprints damage on mind of present people that cannot be healed and that leads the young generation to a bleak future.  1.1 Research Hypothesis To carry out this study the following hypothesis was postulated: • Students are spending more time on using the Internet and social media than reading printed books.  Reading plays a crucial role in the overall development of an individual and the nation at large. Without reading, one’s thinking ability, personality and intellectuality cannot be expanded and a good nation cannot be built.  This study is significant in the sense that it brings out the impact of the Internet and social media on the reading habit of Bangladeshi college and university students as this type of study was not previously conducted in the context of Bangladesh.  Further, the findings of the study might play a great role in showing the state of today’s human mind. Thus, this study tries to make Bangladeshi people in particular and people of the world in general feel and realize that  now-a-days we have broken up our relationship with our best and unique companion — book.

intros.text:
Reading is universally recognised as one of the most powerful instruments of learning and intellectual development. As one of the four basic language skills, it occupies a central place in academic and professional success and plays an especially crucial role in second and foreign language education (Carrell, 1989; Grabe, 1991). Beyond its instrumental value, reading nurtures the mind, expands imagination, and stimulates critical thinking. For this reason, the cultivation of a strong reading habit has long been regarded as essential for lifelong learning. A society that reads is generally a society that thinks, questions, and grows. Recognising the wider social significance of reading, Van der Ploeg (1998) emphasised, in his address to the international library community, the enduring cultural and educational value of books and reading in shaping informed and enlightened citizens.

However, the world in which today's students read is very different from that of previous generations. The rapid expansion of information and communication technology (ICT), the Internet, and social media has transformed the way young people spend their leisure time, seek information, and entertain themselves. Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, blogs, and similar platforms have become integral to the daily lives of adolescents and young adults, offering instant access to entertainment, communication, and information (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010; Junco, 2012). While these technologies have undeniable benefits, there is growing concern that they are gradually eroding the habit of reading printed books. Every new medium of communication, it has been argued, poses a threat to reading, drawing away the time and interest that young people might otherwise devote to books during their leisure hours (Johnsson-Smaragdi & Jönsson, 2006). Loan (2012) similarly observes that the growing use of television, social media, and the Internet has contributed to a marked decline in the book reading habit among young people.

Evidence from various contexts supports these concerns. Studies of college students in the United States, for instance, have found that young people spend considerably more time online than they devote to either academic or extracurricular reading, with Internet use and socialising emerging as significant factors shaping their reading behaviour (Huang, Capps, Blacklock, & Garza, 2014; Roberts, 2015). Such findings suggest that the tension between screen-based media and printed books is not confined to any single country but reflects a broader, global shift in the habits of the younger generation. Where reading a book once demanded sustained concentration and deep engagement, digital media offer more approachable and immediately gratifying alternatives, often centred on images rather than concepts (Johnsson-Smaragdi & Jönsson, 2006; Birkerts, 1994).

Bangladesh is not immune to these developments. As access to smartphones, affordable Internet connectivity, and social networking platforms continues to expand, students at the higher secondary and tertiary levels are increasingly drawn towards digital forms of entertainment and information. Yet, despite the visible growth of technology use among young people, relatively little empirical research has examined how these changes are affecting the reading habits of students in Bangladesh, particularly outside the major metropolitan centres. The southern region of the country, including districts such as Khulna, offers a valuable context in which to explore this question, as students there are simultaneously exposed to expanding digital opportunities and the traditional expectation that reading remains the primary route to knowledge and academic achievement.

Against this backdrop, the present study seeks to investigate the impact of the Internet and social media on students' habit of reading printed books. Specifically, it aims to explore how students spend their leisure time, how much time they devote to reading books compared with using electronic media, and whether they perceive technology and social media as more pleasurable and rewarding than reading. The study draws on primary data collected through a questionnaire survey administered to ninety-six students from two institutions in Khulna, a southern district of Bangladesh. By examining students' attitudes and practices across sixteen variables, the study attempts to bring to light the extent to which technology may be substituting for, rather than supplementing, the habit of reading books.

The significance of this inquiry lies in its potential to illuminate an issue of growing educational and cultural concern. If reading habits are being displaced by passive and superficial forms of information gathering, the long-term consequences for students' intellectual development and for the quality of graduates produced by the nation's institutions could be considerable. This study therefore aims not only to document the present condition of reading habits among students but also to raise awareness of what appears to be an increasingly vulnerable practice, thereby inviting further, larger-scale investigation into this important field.

intros.text:
Reading is universally regarded as one of the most powerful and indispensable means of learning. As one of the four basic language skills, it plays a decisive role in both academic and professional success and occupies a central place in first, second, and foreign language education alike (Carrell, 1989; Grabe, 1991). Reading stimulates the mind, enriches thinking power, and cultivates intellectual depth that few other activities can replicate. For this reason, the development of a sustained reading habit among learners has long been considered essential for a life-long learning experience. A society that reads is a society that grows, and the cultivation of a reading culture has consistently been treated as a matter of national importance by educators, librarians, and policy makers (van der Ploeg, 1998). Reading extensively, and reading for pleasure, is widely viewed as a foundation upon which the quality of a nation's graduates ultimately rests.

Yet the environment in which contemporary students read has changed dramatically. Every new medium of information and communication technology (ICT) has, in one way or another, competed with the printed book for the attention of readers, and the rapid spread of the Internet and social media has intensified this competition to an unprecedented degree. Johnsson-Smaragdi and Jönsson (2006) note that both visual and ICT media are frequently presented as a threat to books and the reading of literature, accused of drawing time and interest away from children and adolescents by offering more approachable alternatives. Loan (2012) similarly reports that reading habits are declining as an offshoot of technological advancement, with the growing use of television, social media, and the Internet contributing to a fall in the book reading habit. Social media—defined as Internet-based applications that allow the creation and exchange of user-generated content (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010)—has become deeply woven into the daily lives of the young generation, with platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter attracting overwhelming numbers of student users (Junco, 2012; Mastrodicasa & Metellus, 2013).

A growing body of research documents this shifting balance between screen and page. Pivec (1998) found that television and the Internet are the chief rivals for teenagers' interest in reading, while Hastings and Henry (2006) reported that a large majority of children prefer watching television to reading. Studies in the United States indicate that college students devote more hours weekly to the Internet than to either academic or extracurricular reading, and that Internet use and socializing are significant factors shaping how much students read (Huang et al., 2014; Roberts, 2015). Others have observed that students growing up in a digital environment reveal different attitudes toward reading (Ramirez, 2003), and that the discontinuous, non-linear, and visually distracting nature of screen reading may discourage the deep, sustained engagement that print fosters (Birkerts, 1994; Schmar-Dobler, 2003; Chartier, 2004; Cushman, 1986).

While these studies establish that the Internet and social media are reshaping reading behaviour across many societies, the great majority of this evidence has been drawn from Western and technologically advanced contexts. Comparatively little is known about how these global pressures are affecting reading habits in developing countries, and empirical research on the situation in Bangladesh remains scarce. Whether the patterns reported abroad hold true for students in a southern district such as Khulna, where access to technology has expanded rapidly among the young generation, has not been adequately investigated. There is therefore a clear need to examine, in this specific local setting, how far the printed book is being displaced by electronic and social media in students' everyday lives.

The present study addresses this gap by investigating the impact of the Internet and social media on the habit of reading printed books among students in the southern region of Bangladesh. It seeks to explore whether students are becoming less interested in reading books and more inclined to gather information and entertainment through passive sources such as movies, television, and the Internet. To this end, primary data were collected through a questionnaire survey of 96 students from two institutions in Khulna, comprising sixteen variables, and analysed using SPSS. By documenting how students actually distribute their time and preferences between reading and technology, the study aims to bring the present vulnerable condition of the reading habit into light. The findings are expected to raise awareness among educators and stakeholders of the alarming effect of technological dependence on reading culture, and to encourage further large-scale research offering new insight into this field.

intros.text:
Reading is fundamentally one of the most vital language skills and serves as an indispensable vehicle for learning, cognitive development, and academic achievement. In both professional and educational contexts, the ability to engage deeply with texts is often the cornerstone of success, particularly within the realm of second or foreign language acquisition (Carrell, 1989; Grabe, 1991). Historically, the habit of reading printed books was viewed not only as a means of gathering information but as a mark of intellectual maturity and cultural literacy. A decade ago, a lack of familiarity with the works of literary giants such as Tagore or Tolstoy might have led to social devaluation, reflecting a culture that prized the printed word as the primary source of wisdom and reflection (Mishra, 2008).

However, the dawn of the digital age has fundamentally altered the landscape of information consumption. The proliferation of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and the subsequent rise of social media have introduced a paradigm shift in how the younger generation spends its leisure time. While technology offers unprecedented access to data, it is increasingly viewed as a threat to traditional reading habits. Visual and ICT media are often accused of displacing the time and interest that adolescents previously devoted to literature by offering more immediate, approachable, and stimulating alternatives (Johnsson-Smaragdi & Jönsson, 2006). As technological advancements accelerate, the traditional habit of reading printed books appears to be on the decline, replaced by the pervasive use of television, the Internet, and social networking sites (Loan, 2012).

Social media, defined as Internet-based applications that facilitate the creation and exchange of user-generated content (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010), has become a dominant force in the lives of students. Platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, Twitter, and LinkedIn allow users to connect based on shared interests, with Facebook alone seeing nearly universal adoption among college students in recent years (Junco, 2012). This shift is not merely a change in medium but a change in cognitive engagement. The nature of digital reading—characterized by non-linear surfing, interactivity, and fragmented information—differs sharply from the linear, static experience of printed text (Birkerts, 1994). Consequently, there are concerns that the digital environment encourages a superficial level of exploration, eroding the capacity for deep reading and prolonged mental engagement (Birkerts, 1994).

Global trends indicate a worrying preference for screen-based entertainment over the printed page. Research has shown that a vast majority of children prefer watching television to reading (Hastings & Henry, 2006), a sentiment echoed by political leaders who have urged the youth to turn off their screens to reach their full potential (Obama, 2008). Similarly, the tendency to prioritize the Internet for academic tasks over library research is well-documented, with students often turning to the web as the first point of reference for assignments (Bowman, 2002). In the United States, studies have indicated that college students devote significantly more weekly hours to the Internet than to extracurricular reading, highlighting the competitive pressure that digital socialization places on traditional literacy (Huang et al., 2014). Furthermore, the lure of media in developed nations suggests a systemic shift in how youth interact with knowledge (Roberts, 2015).

In the context of Bangladesh, particularly in the southern region, these global trends are manifesting in alarming ways. The tactile experience of a printed book—its smell, feel, and physical presence—is being replaced by the blinking graphics and vivid colors of the screen (Schmar-Dobler, 2003). There is a growing risk that the act of buying books is becoming a matter of social status or home decoration rather than a pursuit of knowledge. As the young generation becomes more accustomed to the rapid, passive consumption of information through movies and social media, the intellectual rigor associated with reading is being lost.

Despite the ubiquity of these trends, there is a need for localized empirical data to understand the extent of this decline in the Bangladeshi context. This study, therefore, seeks to investigate the impact of the Internet and social media on the reading habits of students in the southern region of Bangladesh. By focusing on students from two institutions in Khulna, the research aims to explore whether technology is indeed substituting the habit of reading and to bring the current vulnerable state of literacy and intellectual engagement into light.

intros.text:
Reading is one of the four fundamental language skills and serves as an indispensable tool for learning and intellectual growth. Within the realms of academic and professional success, the ability to read effectively is paramount, playing a critical role in both general literacy and second or foreign language acquisition (Carrell, 1989; Grabe, 1991). Beyond its utility in formal education, reading is vital because it stimulates the mind and enhances critical thinking power, fostering a capacity for lifelong learning. Historically, the act of reading literary classics was a marker of intellectual standing and social prestige; as Mishra (2008) notes, a decade ago, an individual's failure to have read authors like Tagore or Tolstoy was often viewed with disapproval. However, the cultural landscape has shifted dramatically with the advent of the digital age.

In recent years, the proliferation of modern technological equipment and social networking systems has begun to substitute traditional reading habits with more immediate, digitally mediated exposures. Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is increasingly perceived as a threat to the sustained interest in reading. As Johnsson-Smaragdi and Jönsson (2006) argue, visual and ICT media are often seen as competitors for the leisure time of children and adolescents, offering more approachable and stimulating alternatives than the printed word. This shift is further compounded by the rise of social media—defined as Internet-based applications that facilitate the creation and exchange of user-generated content (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010)—and social networking sites that allow users to connect based on shared interests (Mastrodicasa & Metellus, 2013). With platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter becoming ubiquitous, the young generation is increasingly drawn away from the tactile experience of books toward the screen.

Previous research has consistently highlighted the rivalry between traditional reading and electronic media. Pivec (1998) identified television and the Internet as the primary rivals for the attention of teenagers, while Hastings and Henry (2006) reported that a vast majority of children prefer television over reading. Even at the political level, the decline in reading has been noted, with Obama (2008) emphasizing that children cannot achieve their full potential unless they distance themselves from the distractions of television. Furthermore, the nature of reading itself has changed. While print reading is linear and static, Internet surfing is non-linear and interactive (Birkerts, 1994). This digital environment may encourage superficial exploration of many topics at the expense of the deep, prolonged engagement required for complex texts. Studies have also pointed to the physical toll of screen reading, noting higher levels of visual fatigue compared to reading on paper (Cushman, 1986) and the tendency of digital content to distract the reader with blinking graphics and vivid colors (Schmar-Dobler, 2003).

Despite these global trends, there remains a need to investigate how these dynamics manifest in specific regional contexts, particularly in developing nations where the transition from print to digital may have unique implications. While studies have explored reading habits in developed contexts, such as the research by Huang et al. (2014) on American college students which found that Internet use and socializing were significant factors reducing time spent on conventional reading, there is a paucity of empirical data concerning students in the southern region of Bangladesh. Understanding the specific vulnerabilities of reading habits in this region is essential for addressing the quality of graduates produced by local higher education institutions.

Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the influence of the Internet and social media on the habit of reading printed books among students in the southern region of Bangladesh. Specifically, the research seeks to explore whether students are becoming less interested in books and more prone to gathering information through passive sources like movies, television, and the Internet. To achieve this, a questionnaire survey was conducted among a sample of 96 students from two institutions in Khulna, utilizing 16 variables to quantify the time and pleasure derived from various media. By bringing the current state of reading habits into light, this study hopes to provide insights into the alarming effect of technological addiction on intellectual development. The remainder of the article is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews the relevant literature; Section 3 details the methodology; Section 4 presents the results; and Section 5 discusses the findings and their implications.

intros.text:
Reading has long been recognized as a fundamental skill essential for academic achievement and lifelong learning. In the context of language education, it serves as a critical conduit for acquiring knowledge, developing critical thinking, and expanding one's worldview. However, the landscape of reading is undergoing a significant transformation due to the rapid proliferation of digital technologies and social media platforms. As the digital age advances, the traditional habit of reading printed books faces an unprecedented challenge from the allure of electronic media. This shift has raised concerns among educators, librarians, and researchers regarding the potential decline in deep reading practices among the younger generation.

The impact of technology on reading habits has been a subject of considerable debate in recent years. While some argue that digital tools offer new avenues for information access, others contend that they fragment attention and reduce the time spent on sustained reading. Frederick Yan der Ploeg (1998), in his address at the IFLA General Conference, highlighted the evolving role of libraries and reading in the information age, suggesting that the traditional methods of knowledge acquisition are being reshaped by new technologies. This observation underscores the need to understand how modern media consumption patterns influence the reading behaviors of students.

Research conducted in various contexts has provided evidence of this trend. Huang et al. (2014) investigated the reading habits of college students in the United States and found that students spent significantly more time on the Internet (8.95 hours per week) compared to academic reading (7.72 hours) and extracurricular reading (4.24 hours). Their study further revealed that Internet usage and socializing were significant factors negatively correlated with conventional reading activities. Similarly, Roberts (2015), in the report "Kids and Media in America," documented the increasing media consumption among children and adolescents, indicating a shift away from traditional reading materials toward digital entertainment. These findings suggest a global pattern where digital engagement competes with, and often supersedes, the habit of reading printed books.

In the specific context of Bangladesh, the situation appears to be equally concerning. The Southern Region, including districts like Khulna, has witnessed a rapid increase in Internet penetration and social media usage among students. Despite the availability of educational resources and libraries, there is a growing perception that students are less inclined to engage with printed books. This phenomenon is not merely a matter of preference but reflects a broader cultural shift influenced by technological advancements. The question arises: to what extent does the use of the Internet and social media affect the reading habits of students in this region?

The decline in reading habits among students has implications for their intellectual development and academic performance. Reading printed books fosters deep engagement, critical analysis, and sustained attention, qualities that are often compromised by the fragmented nature of digital media. As noted by various scholars, the tactile experience of reading a physical book contributes to a richer cognitive process compared to screen-based reading. However, the convenience and immediacy of digital platforms make them more attractive to the younger generation, who are often accustomed to instant gratification and interactive content.

This study aims to explore the influence of the Internet and social media on the reading habits of students in the Southern Region of Bangladesh. By examining the leisure activities, media consumption patterns, and attitudes toward reading among a sample of students, the research seeks to provide insights into the current state of book reading culture. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for educators and policymakers to develop strategies that promote reading in an increasingly digital world. The findings of this study will contribute to the ongoing discourse on the impact of technology on literacy and offer recommendations for fostering a balanced approach to media consumption and reading practices.

intros.text:
In the contemporary educational landscape, reading is universally acknowledged as a fundamental skill essential for academic achievement, professional success, and lifelong learning. It serves as a primary vehicle for knowledge acquisition, critical thinking, and intellectual development. However, the ubiquity of digital technology and the rapid proliferation of social media platforms have precipitated a significant shift in how individuals, particularly the younger generation, consume information and spend their leisure time. This technological revolution, while offering unprecedented access to information, has simultaneously raised concerns regarding its impact on traditional reading habits. As students increasingly turn to electronic devices for entertainment and information, the practice of reading printed books appears to be diminishing, creating a critical issue that demands scholarly attention.

The importance of reading has long been emphasized in educational discourse. It is not merely a skill but a habit that fosters cognitive growth and cultural awareness. Yet, recent observations suggest that the dominance of visual and interactive media is displacing the quiet engagement required for deep reading. Scholars have noted that the rise of the Internet and social networking sites presents a formidable challenge to book reading. For instance, the shift from linear, static print to non-linear, interactive digital content has altered the very nature of engagement with texts. While some argue that digital reading offers new opportunities, others contend that it encourages superficial engagement, reducing the capacity for sustained concentration and deep comprehension. This tension between the benefits of technology and the potential erosion of reading culture forms the backdrop of the current research landscape.

Previous research has attempted to quantify this shift. Huang et al. (2014) conducted a study on college students in the United States, finding that time spent on the Internet significantly correlated with reduced time for both academic and extracurricular reading. Their findings indicated that socializing and internet usage were significant factors diverting attention from conventional reading. Similarly, Roberts (2015) highlighted the pervasive influence of media on children's daily lives, suggesting that screen time is rapidly replacing book time. Furthermore, Van der Ploeg (1998) addressed the broader implications of these trends at an international level, emphasizing the need to preserve reading culture amidst technological advancements. These studies collectively establish that a correlation exists between technology usage and declining reading habits in various contexts.

However, despite the growing body of literature on this subject, there remains a paucity of empirical research focusing specifically on the Southern region of Bangladesh. Most existing studies have been conducted in Western contexts or focus on general global trends, leaving a gap in understanding how these dynamics play out in developing nations with unique socio-cultural and educational infrastructures. While it is generally accepted that technology impacts reading, the specific extent of this influence on students in Khulna and the surrounding areas remains underexplored. It is unclear whether the decline is merely a reflection of global trends or if local factors exacerbate the situation. Moreover, there is a need to investigate the specific preferences of students in this region regarding leisure activities, library usage, and the perceived value of printed books versus digital media.

This study aims to address these gaps by investigating the impact of the Internet and social media on the reading habits of students in the Southern region of Bangladesh. Specifically, it seeks to determine the extent to which electronic media has replaced printed books in students' daily lives and leisure time. The research is grounded in a quantitative approach, utilizing a questionnaire survey to gather primary data from a sample of students in Khulna. By analyzing variables related to leisure activities, time allocation, and attitudes toward reading, this study intends to provide a nuanced understanding of the current state of reading culture among the youth in this specific geographical context. The findings are expected to highlight the vulnerable condition of reading habits in this region and offer insights that could inform educational policies and interventions aimed at revitalizing the culture of reading.

intros.text:
Reading has long been regarded as one of the most important foundations of education, intellectual development and lifelong learning. Beyond its role as one of the four basic language skills, reading enables learners to acquire knowledge, develop imagination, strengthen critical thinking and participate more fully in academic and social life. For students, especially those at higher secondary and tertiary levels, regular reading of books is closely related to vocabulary growth, language proficiency, academic achievement and the capacity for independent learning. In English as a foreign language contexts, reading is even more significant because it exposes learners to varied structures, ideas and styles that may not be available in everyday communication. A strong reading habit therefore does not only support examination performance; it also helps shape reflective, informed and culturally aware individuals.

However, the reading culture among young people has increasingly been challenged by the rapid spread of electronic media, the Internet and social networking platforms. The expansion of digital technology has changed how students search for information, communicate with friends, entertain themselves and spend their leisure time. In earlier periods, books, newspapers and magazines occupied a central place in learning and recreation. Today, mobile phones, Facebook, YouTube, online games, television, movies and other screen-based media compete for students’ attention. As van der Ploeg (1998) suggested in discussing libraries and access to knowledge, information technologies have created new possibilities for communication and learning; yet these possibilities also require societies to reconsider how traditional reading practices can be sustained. The issue is not simply whether technology is useful, but whether the growing dependence on it reduces the time, patience and motivation required for sustained reading.

Several studies have shown that young people now spend considerable amounts of time with digital media. Roberts (2015), in his discussion of children and media in America, highlights the central role media play in the daily lives of the young. Similarly, Huang et al. (2014), in a study of college students in the United States, found that students spent more weekly time on the Internet than on extracurricular reading, and that Internet use and socializing were important factors related to students’ reading habits. Such findings suggest that the problem is not limited to one country or culture; it is part of a wider transformation in students’ literacy practices. Digital media provide quick access to information and entertainment, but they may also encourage fragmented, discontinuous and superficial engagement with texts. Unlike printed books, which often require concentration and extended attention, online materials are frequently consumed through scanning, clicking and rapid movement from one item to another.

Social media has intensified this transformation. Platforms such as Facebook, YouTube, blogs and other networking sites allow users to create, share and respond to content instantly. They offer pleasure, interaction and a sense of connection, which are particularly attractive to adolescents and young adults. Yet this attraction may come at the cost of book reading, especially non-academic reading. Students may consult online sources to complete assignments, but this does not necessarily mean that they cultivate a habit of deep or voluntary reading. In many cases, information is gathered quickly from the Internet, while books are seen as time-consuming, less entertaining or useful only for passing examinations. As a result, printed books may gradually lose their position as companions for leisure, imagination and self-development.

The situation is especially important in Bangladesh, where educational success is often strongly associated with examination results, but where the broader culture of reading for pleasure and knowledge remains uneven. Students in urban and semi-urban areas increasingly have access to smartphones, mobile Internet, satellite television and social media. These technologies connect them with global cultures and provide immediate entertainment, but they may also reshape their attitudes toward libraries, printed books and non-academic reading. In the southern region of Bangladesh, including Khulna, such changes are visible among college and university students, yet empirical evidence on how Internet and social media use influence their book-reading habits remains limited. Without examining students’ actual preferences and practices, it is difficult to understand whether technology merely supplements reading or is gradually replacing it.

The present study therefore investigates the impact of the Internet and social media on students’ habit of reading printed books in two educational institutions in Khulna, Bangladesh. It focuses on how students spend their leisure time, how frequently they read non-academic books, how much time they devote to the Internet and other electronic media, and how they compare the pleasure and usefulness of technology with that of printed books. By surveying higher secondary and tertiary level students, the study seeks to bring into focus the current condition of reading habits among young learners in this region. The central concern is whether increasing attraction to digital media has reduced students’ engagement with printed books and weakened the culture of reading that is essential for intellectual and academic growth.

intros.text:
Reading has long been regarded as a central means of learning, intellectual development, and participation in academic and social life. For students in particular, the habit of reading books contributes not only to language development but also to critical thinking, imagination, concentration, cultural understanding, and lifelong learning. In English language education, reading is especially important because it supports vocabulary growth, comprehension, writing ability, and access to disciplinary knowledge. A sustained reading habit therefore remains a key concern for teachers, parents, librarians, and educational policy makers who seek to develop informed and reflective learners.

At the same time, the context in which young people read has changed rapidly. The expansion of the Internet, mobile phones, television, and social networking sites has created new channels for information, communication, and entertainment. These technologies provide immediate access to news, academic materials, videos, music, games, and global cultural resources. Social media platforms also allow students to communicate continuously with peers and to participate in online communities. As a result, young people now spend a considerable part of their leisure and study time in digital environments. While such access can support learning, it can also compete with the time, patience, and attention required for reading printed books.

Previous research has frequently drawn attention to the changing reading behaviour of young people in technology-rich societies. Van der Ploeg (1998) emphasised the cultural and educational value of libraries and reading in a modern democratic society, suggesting that reading remains closely connected with knowledge, citizenship, and cultural participation. More recent studies, however, show that students’ reading practices are increasingly shaped by digital media. Huang et al. (2014), in a study of college students in the United States, found that students spent more weekly hours on the Internet than on extracurricular reading, and that Internet use and socializing were significant factors associated with conventional academic and leisure reading. Roberts (2015) similarly highlights the strong presence of media in the everyday lives of children and young people in America, indicating that electronic media have become a major part of youth culture.

A growing body of literature also suggests that screen-based media may affect the nature and depth of reading. Social media, commonly understood as Internet-based applications that enable users to create and exchange user-generated content, has become a dominant communicative space for students (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010). Social networking sites connect users through shared interests, activities, and identities (Mastrodicasa & Metellus, 2013), making them highly attractive to young people. Junco (2012) reported the widespread use of Facebook among college students, illustrating the extent to which social networking has entered university life. Other scholars have argued that television and the Internet often compete with book reading by offering faster and more visually stimulating forms of entertainment (Johnsson-Smaragdi & Jönsson, 2006; Loan, 2012). Birkerts (1994) further argues that digital environments encourage non-linear and often superficial reading, whereas printed books demand prolonged attention and deeper engagement.

These concerns are particularly relevant in educational contexts where students’ academic success depends on regular reading but where access to mobile technology and Internet services is rapidly increasing. In Bangladesh, young people are increasingly exposed to smartphones, social media, satellite television, online entertainment, and other digital resources. These technologies are often attractive because they provide quick information, instant communication, and pleasurable leisure activities. However, they may also reduce students’ interest in printed books, non-academic reading, and library use. If students begin to associate books only with examinations, or if they prefer online sources and entertainment media for knowledge and pleasure, the broader educational and cultural functions of reading may be weakened.

Although international studies have examined reading habits and media use among children and college students, less attention has been given to the specific situation of students in the southern region of Bangladesh. Much of the available discussion remains general, and there is a need for local empirical evidence showing how students in this context actually spend their leisure time, how frequently they read printed books, how often they use the Internet and social media, and how they perceive the relative value of books and technology. It also remains important to understand whether students themselves recognise technology as a factor that reduces their time for book reading.

The present study addresses this issue by investigating the influence of the Internet and social media on students’ habit of reading printed books in Khulna, a southern district of Bangladesh. Focusing on students from Govt. M. M. City College, Khulna and Northern University of Business and Technology Khulna, the study examines patterns of leisure activity, daily reading, Internet browsing, social media use, television viewing, library use, and attitudes toward printed books and new technology. Using questionnaire data from 96 students, the study seeks to identify whether students devote more time and interest to electronic media than to reading books and whether this tendency is associated with a declining habit of reading non-academic printed materials. By presenting evidence from a local educational context, the study aims to bring into focus the vulnerable condition of students’ reading habits and to encourage further discussion on how educational institutions can respond to the growing dominance of digital media.

intros.text: The growth of EFL (English as a Foreign Language) in Indonesia has shaped the way that English is being taught in the country. The first language that many Indonesian students need to master is Bahasa Indonesia, or the Indonesian language. In the context of daily life in Indonesia, students also learn vernacular language(s) or traditional language(s), which may be the same or different from their first language. Some students possess vernacular language(s) or traditional language(s) as their mother tongue.  Within this rich linguistic atmosphere, English is considered as a prominent foreign language, which is familiar to most Indonesian students. As a foreign language, English demands its learners to comprehend this language not only in an academic setting but also in a communicative context.  The use of EFL within the international context demands that students are able to master the four basic language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing to use their English appropriately. Research studies that address issues on how students respond to these four skills in teachinglearning EFL are numerous. However, the foci of those studies deal mainly with classifying students’ learning types  In this study, it is specifically argued that listening and speaking are adjustable essential skills for the students, not only in the academic setting but also in the communicative setting. Meanwhile, reading and writing are essential skills that need to be developed more in an academic setting than in the communicative setting  The question worth asking at this point is how far students link teaching-learning reading and writing skills when they learn English.  Studies that focus on advancing teaching strategies, developing curriculum for teaching-learning EFL, and fostering the assessment processes are abundant.  However, studies that focus on learning about students’ responses to teaching-learning basic reading and basic writing as well as how these two skills are connected in the minds of the students within the idea of English literacy are in short supply.  This study was an initial step to understand the complexity of teaching-learning EFL in Padang, the capital city of West Sumatera Province, Indonesia. As such, the problem of this research is related to how far we, as English instructors, get to know the students better in terms of knowing the connection between basic reading and writing in teaching-learning EFL directly from the perspectives of the students.  1.1 Objectives of the Research This research has the following objectives: 1. Investigating EFL students’ preferences between teaching-learning the skills of reading and writing; 2. Investigating EFL students’ preferences for the types of text they prefer to read for teaching-learning EFL English; 3. Investigating the most difficult aspects that students encounter when they have to read a text in EFL English; 4. Investigating the most difficult aspect that students encounter when they have to write a text in EFL English; 5. Investigating what students will prefer to do when they encounter difficult words in reading a text in EFL English; 6. Investigating what students will prefer to do when they encounter difficult words in writing a text in EFL English.  1.2 Significance of the Research This study will provide a significant contribution to teachers of EFL in Indonesia. Teachers of EFL reading and writing in Indonesia will benefit from the results of this study. From this study, it is believed that the students’ perspectives will be seen as a lot more important than the perspectives that we, as teachers, have had about what the students prefer.

intros.text:
Reading and writing are two of the four fundamental skills that English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners must master, and they occupy a central place in the teaching-learning of English within Indonesian higher education. In a country where English holds the status of a foreign language, students learn it not as a medium of daily communication but as a subject to be studied and, for those enrolled in teacher-education programmes, later to be taught. This dual purpose places a particular demand on students in English Education Study Programs, who are expected not only to acquire competence in English but also to understand its underlying structures well enough to transmit them to future learners. As Mappiasse and Sihes (2014) have argued, improving the quality of prospective EFL teachers requires embedding English more meaningfully in the curriculum. Yet in practice, English is often valued narrowly, chiefly as a requirement for satisfactory TOEFL or IELTS scores at graduation, which raises questions about how students actually experience and respond to the process of learning basic reading and writing.

Motivation is widely recognised as a decisive factor in foreign language learning. Cognitive theory, as discussed by Weiner (1985) in Arends (1998), holds that learners' actions are shaped by their beliefs and attributions about success and failure, while needs theory, associated with Maslow, Deci and McClelland (cited in Arends, 1998), emphasises inner drives toward self-fulfilment, achievement and affiliation. Taken together, these perspectives suggest that Indonesian EFL learners are influenced by both internal and external motivations when they engage with English. Research at the senior secondary level in Indonesia (Muliawati, 2017) has indeed shown that students hold varied like-or-dislike attitudes toward English, attitudes that may carry over into how they approach reading and writing at the tertiary level.

Basic reading in an EFL context is more than decoding; it involves cognitive, psychological and ecological components working together (Joshi & Aaron, 2011), and it depends on effective language knowledge and general comprehension abilities (Grabe, 2004). Positive transfer from a learner's first language may support second language reading, particularly where both languages share the Roman alphabet (Birsch, 2002), and effective teachers integrate language and content objectives to nurture this development (Harper & Jong, 2004). Writing, by contrast, is generally regarded as the more complex skill, demanding control over grammar, syntax, coherence, word choice and mechanics (Ibnian, 2011), together with extensive practice and supportive feedback (Salma, 2015; Zaman & Azad, 2012). Fluency alone does not guarantee success in either skill (Taguchi et al., 2004), and the type of writing students undertake should reflect their age, interests and level (Harmer, 2003). Prior survey research in Indonesia found that EFL students rated reading as the most desirable of the four skills, ahead of listening, speaking and writing (Sukandi & Sani, 2017), hinting at differing levels of motivation across skills.

Despite this growing body of literature, comparatively little research has captured how Indonesian EFL students themselves respond to the experience of learning basic reading and writing: which skill they prefer, what texts they read, which aspects they find most difficult, and what strategies they adopt when they encounter obstacles. Understanding these responses is important because they can inform how instructors design reading and writing courses that respond to students' preferences and needs. The present study addresses this gap by surveying 120 students enrolled in Reading 2 and Writing 1 courses in the English Education Study Program at STKIP PGRI Sumatera Barat. Using a questionnaire, it examines their preferences between reading and writing, the kinds of texts they read, the difficulties they face in grammar, spelling and vocabulary, and the ways they respond to unfamiliar words. In doing so, it seeks to illuminate the varied responses that EFL learners bring to the development of their English literacy.

intros.text:
In the Indonesian educational landscape, English holds the status of a foreign language, learned in classrooms rather than acquired through everyday communicative exchange. This position gives English learning in Indonesia a particular character: students master the language not only as a means of communication but, in the case of prospective teachers, as a subject that must eventually be taught to others. The importance of equipping English Education students with strong literacy skills is therefore considerable, since the quality of future EFL teachers is closely tied to the quality of their own reading and writing competence. As Mappiasse and Sihes (2014) have argued, improving the marketability and readiness of prospective EFL teachers depends on strengthening the role of English within the curriculum. Understanding how these students respond to learning basic reading and writing skills is thus central to improving instruction at the tertiary level.

Reading and writing occupy an intertwined place in the development of English literacy. Reading provides learners with the background knowledge and exposure to varied text types that shape their overall image of themselves as literate users of the language (Kuhn & Rasinski, 2009). Effective reading, however, draws on the interaction of cognitive, psychological and ecological components (Joshi & Aaron, 2011), and requires learners to develop both language knowledge and general comprehension skills (Grabe, 2004). Writing, by contrast, is a more complex undertaking, demanding control of grammar, syntax, coherence and mechanics (Ibnian, 2011), together with sustained practice and feedback (Salma, 2015; Zaman & Azad, 2012). Because the amount of reading a learner does directly influences the quality of their writing, the two skills reinforce one another within the growth of a student's literacy.

A growing body of research has examined how Indonesian and other EFL learners respond to English and its constituent skills. Muliawati (2017) found that senior high school students in Banda Aceh differed markedly in their attitudes toward English depending on their academic stream, suggesting that internal conditions strongly influence learner motivation. Sukandi and Sani (2017) similarly reported that university students prefer some skills over others, with reading emerging as the most desirable skill among learners of academic essay writing. Taguchi et al. (2004) further demonstrated that fluency alone does not guarantee successful reading, underscoring that the development of literacy is a gradual and ongoing process. Together, these studies indicate that EFL learners hold varied and skill-specific preferences that carry implications for classroom instruction.

Despite these contributions, relatively little research has captured, in a single study, how EFL students in Indonesian higher education respond to the specific experience of learning basic reading and basic writing side by side. Much of the existing work addresses either reading or writing in isolation, or focuses on secondary-level learners, leaving the responses of tertiary English Education students to the combined learning of these foundational skills insufficiently documented. What preferences these students hold, which text types they read, which linguistic aspects they find most difficult, and what strategies they adopt when facing difficulties remain questions that merit closer empirical attention in this context.

The present study addresses this gap by surveying the responses of 120 students enrolled in Writing 1 and Reading 2 courses in the English Education Study Program of STKIP PGRI Sumatera Barat. Using a questionnaire administered to the whole population, the research investigates students' skill preferences, their reading material choices, the aspects of reading and writing they find most difficult, and the strategies they use when encountering difficult words. The findings offer a contextualised account of learners' responses that may inform how instructors design and support basic reading and writing instruction, and may encourage stronger motivation and richer literacy development among prospective EFL teachers.

intros.text:
In the context of Indonesian higher education, English is predominantly viewed as a foreign language (EFL). For students pursuing degrees in English Education, mastering the language transcends simple communication; it is a professional necessity, as they must fully understand the linguistic modalities of English to effectively teach it in the future. This academic journey is often driven by a complex interplay of internal and external motivations. Cognitive theory suggests that students' actions are heavily influenced by their beliefs regarding success and failure, while needs theory emphasizes the drive toward self-fulfillment and achievement. Together, these frameworks explain the willingness of Indonesian students to engage with English, despite the challenges posed by a curriculum that frequently prioritizes standardized test scores over communicative fluency.

Among the various language skills, reading and writing form the bedrock of English literacy. Basic reading is essential for accessing information and recognizing the diverse ways authors convey meaning. Successful literacy development is often linked to the volume of reading undertaken and the integration of cognitive, psychological, and ecological components. In Indonesia, the process of learning to read in English can be supported by the positive transfer of skills from the first language (Bahasa Indonesia) to the second language (English), provided that instructors effectively organize language and content objectives. However, the attitude toward English can vary significantly among students, often influenced by their academic backgrounds and previous exposure to private language courses, which in turn affects their motivation in university-level literacy courses.

Writing, conversely, presents a higher level of complexity than reading. It requires not only the ability to express ideas clearly and coherently but also a rigorous grasp of grammar, syntax, and writing mechanics. For EFL learners, achieving proficiency in writing demands extensive practice and consistent feedback from both peers and instructors. Because writing is a productive skill, it requires a higher degree of linguistic precision, making it a more daunting task for many students. While reading provides the background knowledge necessary for writing, the transition from consuming a text to producing one is often a significant hurdle for learners in an EFL environment.

Existing research indicates that students often exhibit disparate responses to the four primary language skills. Some studies have shown a marked preference for reading over writing, suggesting that students may feel more comfortable with receptive skills than with the productive demands of academic writing. Furthermore, the role of supportive tools and corrective feedback is paramount in helping students move from basic fluency to genuine mastery of literacy. Understanding how students perceive these challenges—and what strategies they employ to overcome them—is crucial for educators seeking to design more effective instructional materials.

Despite the known interdependence of reading and writing, there is a need for further empirical data on how Indonesian EFL students specifically respond to the learning of these basic skills at the tertiary level. This study, therefore, seeks to investigate the responses of EFL students at the Teachers Academy in West Sumatra [STKIP PGRI Sumatera Barat] toward learning basic reading and writing. By examining students' preferences, the types of texts they engage with, the difficulties they encounter, and the strategies they use to resolve linguistic problems, this research aims to provide insights into the current state of English literacy acquisition in the Indonesian EFL context.
