intros.text:
Academic writing is not merely a vehicle for reporting facts, methods and results; it is also a site where writers position themselves in relation to their claims, their readers and the wider disciplinary community. Research articles in particular require authors to advance new knowledge while acknowledging the provisional character of findings, the limitations of evidence and the possibility of alternative interpretations. This rhetorical balancing is commonly discussed under the notions of stance, evaluation and metadiscourse, all of which refer to the interpersonal resources through which writers comment on propositions and guide readers towards preferred interpretations (Hyland, 2005; Biber, 2006). Among these resources, hedging has received sustained attention because it enables writers to present claims as plausible rather than categorical, thereby reducing personal commitment, displaying caution and facilitating the negotiation of knowledge within a discourse community (Hyland, 1998).

Hedges are especially important in research article writing because scientific claims typically depend on evidence that is partial, context-bound and open to revision. By marking possibility, probability or inference, writers can protect themselves from potential criticism while also showing respect for readers’ expertise and for the norms of disciplinary argumentation. Previous studies have shown that hedging is not randomly distributed across academic texts but is closely related to rhetorical purpose: it is particularly salient in those parts of research articles where authors justify their work, interpret findings and relate their results to existing knowledge (Hyland, 1998). The linguistic realization of hedging is also varied, ranging from modal auxiliaries and epistemic adverbs to lexical verbs and more complex clausal constructions.

One such construction is the extraposed that-clause, as in It is possible that the results were affected by sample size. In English, this structure combines an anticipatory it-subject with a matrix predicate and a postponed content clause. Corpus-based descriptions of English have shown that extraposition is frequent in academic prose and is strongly associated with the expression of stance (Biber et al., 1999). Its rhetorical value lies partly in the separation of the evaluation from the evaluated proposition: the matrix predicate explicitly frames the status of the claim, while the non-referential it allows the source of the evaluation to remain unspecified. In this way, an assessment that may be personal or disciplinary can be presented in an impersonal and apparently objective form. Hewings and Hewings (2001, 2002) have demonstrated that anticipatory it-constructions perform a range of metadiscoursal functions in academic writing, including hedging, attitude marking, emphasis and attribution. Similarly, Hyland and Tse (2005) show that evaluative that-clauses are an important means of thematizing authorial comment and guiding readers’ interpretation of propositional content.

The relevance of such constructions becomes even clearer in contrastive academic writing. Writers working in different languages may share broad academic goals, but they do not necessarily rely on the same rhetorical or grammatical resources to achieve them. This issue is particularly important in contexts where scholars publish both in a national language and in English, since the conventions of one academic culture may not transfer straightforwardly into another. Croatian academic writing has been described as favouring impersonal and neutral expression, and Croatian grammars identify declarative subject da-clauses controlled by predicates such as moguće je da ‘it is possible that’, smatra se da ‘it is considered that’ and čini se da ‘it seems that’ as structurally and functionally comparable to English extraposed that-clauses (Pranjković, 2001; Silić et al., 2005; Silić, 2008). Yet, unlike English extraposition, these Croatian constructions have received little empirical attention in studies of academic discourse.

This gap is significant for both descriptive and pedagogical reasons. Descriptively, little is known about how frequently Croatian academic writers use declarative subject da-clauses as hedging devices, how these uses compare with English extraposed that-clauses, or whether the same types of matrix predicates are preferred in the two languages. Pedagogically, such knowledge can help Croatian scholars and students develop greater awareness of how hedged stance is conventionally expressed in English-medium research writing, particularly in disciplines where international publication is increasingly important.

The present study therefore investigates the hedging functions of English extraposed that-clauses and Croatian declarative subject da-clauses in comparable corpora of psychology research articles. Focusing on matrix predicates that encode epistemic evaluation, the study compares the overall frequency of the target constructions, their distribution across the IMRAD sections of research articles, and the most frequent predicate types used to convey hedged stance in the two languages.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not merely a vehicle for reporting facts, but a site where writers negotiate claims, calibrate commitment and position themselves in relation to readers and disciplinary knowledge. Among the interpersonal resources through which this negotiation is achieved, stance and evaluation have received sustained attention in applied linguistics and English for Academic Purposes, particularly because they are central to the persuasive work of research articles and to the social accreditation of knowledge claims. Hedging is especially important in this respect: by presenting propositions as plausible, probable or open to alternative interpretation, writers can protect themselves from overstatement, acknowledge the provisional nature of knowledge and invite disciplinary ratification (Hyland, 1998, 2005). Corpus-based studies have shown that stance is pervasive in university and research writing, but also that it varies across registers, disciplines and lexico-grammatical realizations (Biber, 2006).

One prominent grammatical resource for expressing stance in English academic prose is the extraposed that-clause, as in It is possible that the results were affected by sampling bias. In such constructions, the evaluative meaning is carried by the matrix predicate, while the proposition evaluated is placed in the dependent that-clause. This separation of evaluation from evaluated content enables writers to foreground an assessment while construing it in an impersonal form. The Longman Grammar of Spoken and Written English identifies extraposed clauses as particularly characteristic of academic prose and notes their association with stance meanings, including degrees of likelihood, certainty and evidentiality (Biber et al., 1999). Similarly, research on anticipatory it has shown that it-extraposition allows writers to encode metadiscoursal meanings such as hedges, attitude markers, emphatics and attribution, with published academic writing showing a marked preference for hedging functions (Hewings & Hewings, 2001, 2002). Evaluative that more generally has also been described as a powerful construction for thematizing a writer’s attitude and guiding readers towards an interpretation of the proposition that follows (Hyland & Tse, 2005).

In Croatian, a broadly corresponding structure is found in declarative subject da-clauses, for example Moguće je da su rezultati drugačije protumačeni ‘It is possible that the results were interpreted differently’. Croatian grammatical descriptions classify such clauses as complement or subject clauses introduced by da and controlled by matrix predicates denoting mental, verbal, modal or attitudinal meanings (Pranjković, 2001; Silić et al., 2005). Descriptions of Croatian scientific style also emphasize impersonality, neutrality and formulaic phraseology as characteristic features of academic expression (Silić, 2008). These observations suggest that declarative subject da-clauses may serve functions comparable to English extraposed that-clauses, particularly when their matrix predicates encode epistemic possibility, assumption or likelihood.

Despite the considerable body of work on stance and hedging in English research writing, cross-linguistic evidence on structurally comparable complement clauses remains limited. English extraposition has been examined in relation to register, disciplinary variation, student and expert writing, and academic phraseology (Biber et al., 1999; Hewings & Hewings, 2001, 2002; Hyland & Tse, 2005), but less is known about how equivalent constructions operate in smaller academic languages such as Croatian. Conversely, Croatian linguistic literature provides valuable grammatical and stylistic descriptions of da-clauses and scientific style, yet empirical corpus-based accounts of their pragmatic role in academic research articles are scarce. It therefore remains unclear whether Croatian academic writers use declarative subject da-clauses for hedging in ways similar to English writers’ use of extraposed that-clauses, and whether the two languages differ in frequency, distribution across research article sections, or preferred matrix predicates.

Addressing this gap is relevant not only for contrastive academic discourse analysis, but also for academic writing pedagogy in non-native English contexts. Scholars who write for international publication often move between local rhetorical conventions and English-medium expectations. A clearer understanding of how hedged stance is grammatically and pragmatically realized across languages can therefore inform instruction by making visible both shared academic practices and language-specific preferences.

The present study investigates the hedging functions of English extraposed that-clauses and Croatian declarative subject da-clauses in comparable corpora of psychology research articles. Specifically, it examines the frequency of the target constructions in English- and Croatian-medium articles, their distribution across the IMRAD sections, and the matrix predicates through which hedging meanings are expressed. By comparing these patterns, the study aims to contribute to research on stance in academic writing and to provide pedagogically useful insights into cross-cultural rhetorical choices in English and Croatian disciplinary discourse.

intros.text: Academic discourse and academic writing skills have been of crucial importance in all disciplines and  fields of study due to its necessary presence in academic genres such as textbooks, research articles,  essays, lectures, theses, etc. The centrality of academic discourse has its roots in factors ranging from  the desire to be a successful student to meeting the requirements of carrying out an influential research  and publishing it  In the arduous path of academic writing, authors accomplish certain interactions with readers, which appear as meta-discourse, a term originally introduced by the linguist Zelig Harris (1959).  In today’s understanding of the concept, Hyland (2017) states that meta-discourse incorporates how we  use language taking into consideration our interactions with readers depending on how we help them  understand what we are saying in the best way possible. These interactions are actualized through the  systems called stance and engagement (Hyland, 2005), the former of which is on the focus in the present  study. Hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention are meta-discourse markers that can be  categorized as the stance taken by the writer towards the text’s content or towards the reader (Hyland,  2004), while engagement has a function of alignment where writers connect to their readers concerning  the positions developed in the text (Hyland, 2005). Hedges and boosters, which are interpersonal metadiscourse markers, are the subject of this paper. They both reflect a writer’s answer to the possible points  of view that may be brought by the reader (Hyland, 2009)  Correct usage of these meta-discourse  markers may imply a sort of awareness of the writers regarding their own academic literacy and  academic writing skills.  Therefore, investigation of the use of various meta-discourse markers across  cultures, disciplines, different text types or student profiles is important, since it may have implications  on the level of the confidence or awareness writers have on their academic discourse knowledge or their  ability to defend their claims in the most appropriate way possible.  The present research aims to compare  MA theses and PhD dissertations written by the same students in ELT departments in Turkey in terms  of the frequency of using hedges and boosters, two of the interpersonal meta-discourse markers.

intros.text:
Academic writing is far from a neutral act of reporting facts; rather, it is a socially situated practice in which writers continuously negotiate their claims with an anticipated audience. Successful academic authors do not merely transmit information but interact with their readers, projecting a stance towards their propositions and inviting engagement (Hyland, 2005). Among the linguistic resources available for this purpose, meta-discourse markers occupy a central position, allowing writers to organise their texts and, crucially, to position themselves in relation to both their claims and their readers (Hyland, 2017). Two of the most extensively studied of these devices are hedges and boosters, which together enable writers to calibrate the degree of certainty they attach to their assertions.

Hedges permit writers to withhold full commitment to a proposition, presenting statements as opinion rather than incontrovertible fact and thereby leaving space for negotiation and reader dissent. Boosters, by contrast, allow writers to express conviction and to emphasise the force of their claims, projecting confidence and persuasiveness. As Hyland (2005) has argued, both markers are integral to the interactive, evaluative dimension of academic prose, contributing to the way writers construct an appropriate authorial identity within their disciplinary communities. Learning to deploy these devices skilfully is a hallmark of developing academic literacy, and expertise in their use is closely bound up with the socialisation of writers into the conventions of their fields (Hyland, 2004, 2009).

While a considerable body of research has examined the functions of meta-discourse and compared its use across genres, disciplines, cultures and gender, comparatively little attention has been paid to how the same writers' use of hedges and boosters develops as they advance through successive stages of academic training. This is particularly the case for non-native writers of English, whose expression of certainty and doubt may differ from that of native speakers. The present corpus-based study addresses this gap by comparing the discussion sections of ten MA theses and ten PhD dissertations written by the same Turkish EFL students in the field of English Language Teaching. By tracing changes in the frequency and type of hedges and boosters from MA to PhD level, the study seeks to illuminate whether and how these writers reshape their epistemic stance as they gain academic experience, and to consider the pedagogical implications of any such developments for academic writing instruction in Turkish higher education.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not merely a matter of transmitting information; it involves a continuous negotiation between writers and readers through which authors project a stance towards their claims and engage their audience. In this interactive dimension of discourse, meta-discourse markers play a crucial role, allowing writers to shape and reshape their assertions, signal appropriate levels of certainty or caution, and persuade readers of the truth value of what they put forward (Hyland, 2005). Among these markers, hedges and boosters stand out as two devices that are central to establishing epistemic authority. Hedges enable writers to withhold full commitment to a proposition, presenting claims as opinion rather than fact, whereas boosters allow writers to express conviction and involvement with the topic (Hyland, 2005). Together they function as two sides of the same coin, jointly contributing to the persuasiveness of academic argument (Vázquez & Giner, 2009).

Given their importance in academic communication, hedges and boosters have attracted considerable scholarly attention. Researchers have examined the functions of meta-discourse markers more broadly (Crismore, 1984; Hyland, 1999, 2000, 2001), while others have compared their use across genres, disciplines, cultures, and between native and non-native writers (Crismore, Markkanen & Steffensen, 1993; Hyland & Milton, 1997; Takimoto, 2015). Studies within the Turkish context have also explored how postgraduate writers claim knowledge and construct stance in English (Akbas & Hardman, 2018).

Despite this rich body of work, comparatively few studies have focused solely on hedges and boosters while comparing writers at different academic levels—such as MA versus PhD—within a single field of study. Even fewer have tracked the same writers as they progress through their academic careers, which would offer a more precise picture of how epistemic stance develops with experience and expertise. The present corpus-based study seeks to address this gap by investigating changes in the frequency of hedges and boosters from MA to PhD level among the same Turkish EFL students working in the field of English Language Teaching. Drawing on the discussion sections of ten MA theses and ten PhD dissertations written by identical authors, and analysed with the concordance program AntConc using Hyland's (2005) classification, the study asks whether meaningful differences exist between the two levels and, if so, what reasons might account for them. Its findings may illuminate how developing academic experience shapes writers' stance-taking and self-confidence.

intros.text:
In the realm of academic writing, the ability to effectively communicate claims while managing the interaction between the author and the reader is paramount. This interaction is largely mediated through metadiscourse markers, which allow writers to project their epistemic stance toward the material they present (Hyland, 2005). Among these markers, hedges and boosters serve as critical tools for navigating the tension between conviction and caution. Hedges are used to mitigate claims and express uncertainty, thereby protecting the writer from criticism and demonstrating academic politeness, whereas boosters are employed to emphasize certainty and convey the writer's confidence in the truth value of their assertions (Hyland, 2005, 2017).

The use of these devices is not uniform; it varies significantly across different genres, disciplinary discourses, and levels of expertise. Previous research has highlighted that the deployment of hedging and boosting is often influenced by disciplinary norms, with argumentation-driven fields typically exhibiting different patterns than data-driven ones (Hyland, 2004). Furthermore, formulaic sequences and metadiscourse patterns often serve as markers that distinguish novice writers from experts within a given academic community (Hyland, 2009). While extensive research has explored metadiscourse across various cultures and disciplines, there is a relative scarcity of studies that specifically compare the developmental trajectory of these markers as students progress through different stages of postgraduate education within a single field of study.

For learners of English as a Foreign Language (EFL), mastering these nuances is particularly challenging, as it requires not only linguistic knowledge but also socio-pragmatic competence. In the Turkish context, there is a need to understand how the transition from a Master's (MA) to a Doctoral (PhD) level influences the way students project their academic voice. Therefore, the present corpus-based study aims to investigate the changes in the frequency and use of hedges and boosters in the discussion sections of MA theses and PhD dissertations written by the same group of Turkish ELT students. By analyzing the writing of the same individuals across two levels of study, this research seeks to determine whether increased academic experience leads to a shift in epistemic stance and a greater command of the rhetorical strategies necessary for academic success.

intros.text:
In the realm of academic writing, the ability to effectively communicate claims and negotiate meanings with readers is paramount. This interaction is largely mediated through metadiscourse markers, which allow authors to project their epistemic stance and manage the interpersonal relationship between the writer and the audience (Hyland, 2005, 2017). Among these markers, hedges and boosters are particularly critical; while hedges enable writers to express uncertainty, mitigate claims, and avoid overgeneralization, boosters allow them to emphasize certainty and demonstrate confidence in their findings (Hyland, 2009). Mastering the balance between these two devices is essential for gaining credibility and navigating the rhetorical expectations of the academic discourse community.

Extensive research has investigated the use of metadiscourse across various dimensions. Scholars have explored gender differences (Holmes, 1990), cross-cultural variations (Crismore et al., 1993), and disciplinary divergences, noting that hedging patterns often vary between argumentation-driven and data-driven fields (Hyland, 2004). Furthermore, studies on learner corpora have highlighted the challenges non-native speakers face in expressing certainty and doubt compared to native speakers (Hyland & Milton, 1997). Despite this wealth of research on metadiscourse functions (Abdi et al., 2010; Crismore, 1984; Hyland, 1999, 2000, 2001; Longo, 1994), there remains a paucity of research that specifically compares the longitudinal development of hedges and boosters as students progress through different stages of postgraduate study within a single field.

To address this gap, the present corpus-based study examines the changes in the frequency and use of hedges and boosters from the MA to the PhD level among Turkish EFL students specializing in English Language Teaching (ELT). By analyzing the discussion sections of ten MA theses and ten PhD dissertations written by the same individuals, this research seeks to determine whether students' epistemic stances evolve as they gain academic experience and expertise. Specifically, the study addresses whether meaningful differences exist in the number of these markers between the two levels and what the underlying reasons for such shifts might be. The findings aim to provide insights into the development of academic writing competency and the socio-pragmatic awareness of graduate students in the Turkish context.

intros.text:
In academic writing, authors establish a complex relationship with their readers through the strategic use of meta-discourse markers. Among these, hedges and boosters play a pivotal role in allowing writers to negotiate their stance, manage certainty, and interact with their audience. As Hyland (2005) notes, these devices are essential for projecting a writer's position and connecting with readers, facilitating the intersubjective positioning required in academic argumentation. While extensive research has examined the function of meta-discourse markers generally (Abdi, Rizi, & Tavakoli, 2010; Crismore, 1984; Hyland, 1999, 2000, 2001; Longo, 1994), there is a paucity of studies focusing specifically on the comparative use of hedges and boosters across different levels of academic proficiency within a specific discipline.

Hedges and boosters represent two sides of the same coin in terms of persuasiveness (Vázquez & Giner, 2009). Hedges allow writers to express uncertainty, mitigate claims, and demonstrate politeness (Brown & Levinson, 1987), whereas boosters enable writers to assert confidence and emphasize the truth value of their propositions (Hyland, 2005). The appropriate balance between these devices is crucial for academic credibility. However, the usage of these markers often varies based on the writer's experience, disciplinary norms, and native language background. For instance, Hyland (2004) highlights cross-disciplinary variations in hedging, while Akbas and Hardman (2018) observed that non-native speakers may display different tendencies in expressing certainty compared to native speakers.

Despite the breadth of existing literature, few studies have investigated the longitudinal development of these linguistic features by tracking the same writers as they progress from Master's to Doctoral levels. Most comparative studies focus on different cohorts or disciplinary differences (Rashidi & Alihosseini, 2012; Takimoto, 2015), leaving a gap in understanding how individual academic writers evolve their epistemic stance over time. This is particularly relevant for Turkish EFL students in the field of English Language Teaching, who must navigate the specific rhetorical demands of international academic discourse while developing their expertise.

Therefore, the present corpus-based study aims to address this gap by comparing the frequencies of hedges and boosters in the discussion sections of MA theses and PhD dissertations written by the same Turkish ELT students. By analyzing the progression from MA to PhD level, this research seeks to uncover whether increased academic experience correlates with changes in the use of meta-discourse markers, and to what extent students demonstrate awareness of these rhetorical strategies as they advance in their academic journey.

intros.text:
In the landscape of academic writing, authors accomplish specific interactions with their readers through meta-discourse markers such as hedges and boosters. These linguistic devices are crucial for conveying the writer's stance and managing the epistemic modality of their claims. While there have been numerous studies examining the function of meta-discourse markers (Abdi, Rizi, & Tavakoli, 2010; Crismore, 1984; Hyland, 1999, 2000, 2001; Longo, 1994), research focusing solely on the comparative use of hedges and boosters across different academic levels remains limited. Specifically, the comparison of Master's (MA) versus Doctoral (PhD) students within a specific field of study is not as well-documented. This gap is significant, as the progression from MA to PhD represents a critical developmental stage in a scholar's academic journey, potentially influencing their rhetorical strategies and confidence in asserting knowledge.

Hedges and boosters serve distinct yet complementary functions. Hedges allow writers to express uncertainty or tentativeness, protecting them from criticism if their claims are later challenged (Hyland, 1998a, 2005). Conversely, boosters demonstrate strong conviction and certainty, helping to persuade readers of the validity of the arguments presented (Hyland, 2005; Vázquez & Giner, 2009). Although the importance of these markers in academic discourse is widely acknowledged, there is insufficient understanding of how their usage evolves as students gain more experience and expertise. While some studies have explored hedging across disciplines (Hyland, 2004) or cultures (Crismore, Markkanen, & Steffensen, 1993), fewer have tracked the longitudinal development of individual writers.

Therefore, the present corpus-based study investigates the possible reasons for changes in the frequencies of hedges and boosters from MA to PhD level among Turkish EFL students specializing in English Language Teaching. By analyzing the discussion sections of ten MA theses and ten PhD dissertations written by the same students, this research aims to identify shifts in epistemic stance. The study addresses two primary questions: (1) Are there meaningful differences in the number of hedges and boosters between discussion sections of ELT MA theses and PhD dissertations written by the same author? and (2) If differences exist, what might be the underlying reasons? The findings may imply changes in students' self-confidence and academic awareness, offering insights for teaching academic writing and meta-discourse in higher education contexts.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not merely a vehicle for reporting information; it is also a social and rhetorical practice through which writers negotiate claims, construct authorial identities, and position themselves in relation to readers and disciplinary communities. In this sense, successful academic texts depend not only on propositional content but also on writers’ ability to signal degrees of certainty, caution, commitment and openness to alternative interpretations. Metadiscourse provides an important framework for understanding these interpersonal dimensions of academic communication, as it concerns the linguistic resources writers use to organize discourse and engage with readers (Hyland, 2004, 2005, 2017). Among these resources, hedges and boosters are particularly central to the expression of stance.

Hedges allow writers to present propositions as plausible rather than absolute, thereby reducing commitment to claims and creating space for negotiation. Boosters, by contrast, enable writers to mark confidence, emphasize certainty and strengthen the force of their arguments. Both devices are essential in academic persuasion: while hedges help writers avoid overstatement and demonstrate awareness of the provisional nature of knowledge, boosters help them foreground significant findings and establish authority. Hyland’s (2005) model of stance and engagement has been especially influential in showing how such linguistic choices contribute to interaction in academic discourse. Research on academic language has also shown that stance features vary according to discipline, genre, writer expertise and linguistic background (Hyland, 2004, 2009).

For writers using English as a foreign language, the appropriate use of hedges and boosters may pose particular challenges. Advanced student writers must learn not only the grammar and vocabulary of academic English but also the rhetorical conventions that govern how strongly or cautiously claims should be expressed. This issue is especially relevant in postgraduate writing, where students are expected to interpret findings, evaluate previous research and contribute to disciplinary conversations. MA theses and PhD dissertations therefore offer valuable data for examining how developing academics manage epistemic stance at different stages of their scholarly trajectories.

Although previous studies have investigated metadiscourse and stance in academic writing, fewer have focused specifically on changes in the use of hedges and boosters across postgraduate levels within the same disciplinary context. Even fewer have compared texts written by the same individuals at MA and PhD levels. Addressing this gap, the present corpus-based study examines the discussion sections of ELT MA theses and PhD dissertations written in English by Turkish EFL writers. By comparing the frequency and distribution of hedges and boosters in these paired texts, the study seeks to explore how writers’ expression of caution and certainty changes as they move from MA to PhD-level academic writing.

intros.text:
Academic writing is not merely the transmission of propositional information; it is also a social and rhetorical act through which writers position themselves in relation to their claims, their readers, and the expectations of disciplinary communities. In postgraduate writing, this interactional dimension is particularly important because novice and developing scholars are required to present findings, evaluate evidence, and negotiate the degree of certainty attached to their interpretations. Metadiscourse provides a useful lens for examining these interpersonal aspects of academic texts, as it reveals how writers organize discourse, signal attitudes, and engage readers (Hyland, 2004, 2005, 2017).

Among metadiscourse resources, hedges and boosters are central to the expression of stance. Hedges allow writers to withhold full commitment, present claims as open to negotiation, and reduce the risk of overstatement, whereas boosters enable writers to express conviction, emphasize certainty, and guide readers toward accepting a proposition. Together, these devices help writers balance caution and confidence, two qualities that are essential for credible academic argumentation. Hyland’s (2005) model of stance and engagement has been especially influential in showing how such linguistic choices contribute to interaction in academic discourse across disciplines and genres.

Previous research has shown that the use of stance markers varies according to disciplinary conventions, genre, cultural background, and writer expertise. Corpus-based studies have also demonstrated that academic writers rely on recurring lexical and grammatical patterns to construct authority and align with disciplinary norms (Hyland, 2009). For learners and users of English as a foreign language, however, the appropriate use of hedges and boosters may be challenging, since it requires not only linguistic knowledge but also awareness of academic expectations and socio-pragmatic conventions. This challenge is particularly relevant in thesis and dissertation writing, where students must display both disciplinary competence and an emerging scholarly identity.

Although metadiscourse has received considerable attention in applied linguistics, fewer studies have focused specifically on changes in the use of hedges and boosters across postgraduate levels within the same field and by the same writers. Comparisons of MA theses and PhD dissertations can offer insight into how writers’ epistemic stance may develop as they gain academic experience. Addressing this gap, the present corpus-based study investigates the frequency and use of hedges and boosters in the discussion sections of English Language Teaching MA theses and PhD dissertations written by Turkish EFL students. More specifically, it examines whether the same writers differ in their use of these stance markers from MA to PhD level and considers possible reasons for such differences.

intros.text: Reading comprehension in a second/foreign language (L2) is regarded as a highly complex cognitive process in which the meaning is constructed through the interaction of the reader with the text (Zhang, 2012). Successful reading comprehension requires several considerable knowledge sources, including decoding skills (García & Cain, 2014), linguistic resources (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Grabe, 2009; Perfetti, Landi, & Oakhill, 2005), and (meta)cognitive processes (Pearson, 2009) along with the right psychological attitudes (Baghaei, Hohensinn, Kubinger, 2014) . Many researchers have developed different theories to explain reading comprehension performance and specify different facets of reading behavior. The ability to read efficiently in a second/foreign language is thought to play a significant role in the process of learning English and the success of individuals in school and in the workplace (Alderson, 2000)  Consequently, the assessment of reading ability is of critical importance in various educational settings and second language programs.  In the field of second language testing and assessment, reading comprehension tests, which require test takers to comprehend a text, are extensively utilized in standardized language proficiency tests. Large-scale standardized English as a second language (ESL) tests are widely used around the world to measure language proficiency of candidates who wish to work or study in English-speaking environments. One well-known language proficiency test is the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), which is widely used in Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK, and the USA.           IELTS is an international high-stakes test of English language proficiency which is jointly owned by three test batteries: The British Council, University of Cambridge ESOL Examinations, and the International Development Program of Australian Universities and Colleges (IDP), now known as IDP: IELTS Australia. The test consists of two modules: General Training module and Academic module. Each module includes four parts: Listening, Reading, Writing, and Speaking. Test takers can take the same Listening and Speaking modules, whereas they are administered different reading and writing modules depending on whether they choose to take either general or academic versions of the test. There are a variety of tasks and response types within each part which measure all four language skills. The general module of IELTS measures the language proficiency of those test-takers who want to work in English language environments, migrate to English-speaking countries, intend to study at below degree level, or generally undertake nonacademic training activities. The academic module of IELTS, however, measures the degree to which test-takers can study or receive training in English at graduate and undergraduate levels. IELTS provides a score for each module and the test scores of each test component are averaged and rounded to generate an Overall Band Score.             A central part of the IELTS is the reading sub-test. As stated by test specifications of the IELTS (IELTS, 2007), the general reading module, which is the main concern of the current study, measures the ability of test-takers to follow instructions, understand main ideas, skim for general information, understand specific information, identify the relationship between information, and summarize. The reading part consists of three sections with 40 questions and different topics designed to be of general interest. The texts are different in lengths with a total of 2000 to 2750 words and are taken from magazines, books, journals, notices, leaflets, advertisements, newspapers, and instruction manuals. The first section, known as ‘Social Survival’, focuses on texts with detailed factual information. The second section involves texts of more complex language. The third section involves texts with more complex language and with the emphasis on descriptive and instructive texts. Different types of questions or tasks are employed to test candidates’ reading comprehension including short-answer, multiple-choice, identifying information (True/False/Not Given), identifying writers’ view/claims (Yes/No/Not Given), flowchart completion, diagram label, sentence completion, summary completion, note completion, table completion, and matching information/ headings. The candidates are supposed to answer the test in 60 minutes. Test takers must enter their answers on an answer sheet during the 60-min test. No extra time is allowed for transferring answers.           As IELTS is a high-stakes language proficiency test, scores obtained from the test represent test takers’ language proficiency and provide appropriate evidence for further decision-making processes. The inferences and decisions made with the scores from the test have tremendous consequences for all stakeholders. Therefore, test developers and test users mainly concern about the validity of IELTS in general and reading comprehension, in particular. It has been wellestablished that validity is the most important feature of a test.  According to Messick (1989), validity is “an integrated evaluative judgment of the degree to which empirical evidence and theoretical rationales support the adequacy and appropriateness of inferences and actions based on test scores or other modes of assessment” (p. 13, italics in original). This view states that what needs to be validated is the interpretations and uses of test scores, not the test itself. As Kane (1992, 2013) proposed in his argumentative approach to validity, test scores are used to support test interpretations and uses. In this approach, there are two types of arguments: the interpretive argument and the validity argument. In the first step, researchers should determine what claims, inferences, and uses are supposed to make regarding the intended meaning based on test scores, and in the second step, the interpretive argument is evaluated to find out whether the claims should be supported or refuted. Although the argument-based account has been well received by language testing researchers and practitioners, Borsboom, Mellenberg, and van Heerden (2004) argue that validity is a simple concept as was lucidly defined by Kelley (1927), i.e., a test is valid if it measures what it claims to measure. In fact, validity is only the property of tests, not test scores and interpretations. According to Borsboom et al. (2004, p. 1061), a test is valid for measuring a construct if (a) the construct exists and (b) variations in the level of the construct causally produce variations in test scores. For example, in a reading comprehension test, the reading ability should cause variations in test scores, that is, individuals with higher level of reading ability should get higher scores, and individuals with lower level of reading ability should get lower scores. This view toward validity relies on the causal theory of measurement which is in line with the latent trait model (Borsboom, 2005).           Over the past few decades, a great deal of research has been conducted to examine the validity of the reading part of the IELTS (Bax, 2013; Clapham, 1996; Green & Hawkey, 2007; Moore, Morton, Price, 2007; Pearson, 2019; Weir, Hawkey, Green, & Devi, 2009; Weir, Hawkey, Green, Unaldi, & Devi, 2009)  Although these studies provided invaluable information on the validity of the test, they mainly focused on the reading part of the Academic module of IELTS and too little attention has been paid to the General Training module. In addition, the methods used in these studies to establish validity rely heavily on statistical tools which have their roots in classical test theory (CTT). Despite its widespread use in measurement, CTT has received some acknowledged limitations  One problem is the issue of sample-dependent statistics, that is, the person parameters depend on the selection of items and item parameters depend on the sample (Embretson, 1996). Another limitation of CTT is that the data should be continuous and normally distributed. Also, scores derived from CTT are not very informative about the item response patterns, and “any combination of scores on any set of items can give the same score on the latent trait” (Palmgren et al., 2018, p. 3)  With respect to the limitations of CTT, item response theory (IRT) was developed as an alternative method to CTT. IRT was developed based on ordinal and nominal data, and models the encounter of an individual with a given ability with a test item.  One branch of the IRT approach is Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA; Mokken, 1971). As a non-parametric IRT, MSA is a popular method to evaluate the psychometric quality of data obtained from scales and determine scales from a larger set of items. Similar to the principles of IRT, MSA examines the relationship between the construct and a set of items. The model assumes that items of a scale are hierarchically ordered along the latent trait continuum. However, compared to conventional or parametric IRT, MSA includes less restrictive assumptions about the data, requires smaller sample sizes to produce stable estimation, and its fit to data is better than parametric IRT models (Mokken & Lewis, 1982; Sijtsma & Van der Ark, 2017). These properties allow researchers to retain more useful items from a scale  Given the advantages of the Mokken model, this study seeks to use the model to examine the validity of the reading part of the General Training module of IELTS.

intros.text:
Reading comprehension is widely recognized as one of the most important skills for academic and professional success, particularly for those who use English as a second or foreign language. It is a complex cognitive activity that draws on a range of interacting knowledge sources and processes. Interactive and compensatory models of reading emphasize that language processes, literacy processes, and world knowledge do not operate independently or sequentially, but simultaneously, buttressing one another as readers construct meaning from text (Grabe, 2009). A substantial body of research has attempted to identify the components that underlie successful reading. Vocabulary knowledge has repeatedly emerged as a strong predictor of reading ability, often more so than grammatical knowledge (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012), while decoding skills have been shown to be strongly, though not perfectly, related to comprehension (García & Cain, 2014). Because reading is such a multifaceted construct, it presents special challenges for those who wish to measure it validly and reliably in high-stakes settings. Understanding what a reading test actually measures, and whether the items constituting it behave coherently, is therefore an enduring concern in language assessment (Perfetti, Landi, & Oakhill; Pearson, 2014).

Among the many instruments developed to assess English reading proficiency, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) occupies a central position. IELTS is one of the most widely used standardized tests of English in the world, and its scores are relied upon by universities, employers, professional bodies, and immigration authorities to make consequential decisions about individuals (IELTS, 2007). The test comprises two modules, Academic and General Training, and assesses the four skills of listening, reading, writing, and speaking. Given the sheer number of test-takers who sit IELTS each year and the gravity of the decisions made on the basis of their scores, the consequences of the test for the lives of candidates are considerable. Recent research has documented that many test-takers fail to meet the band-score goals set by gatekeeping institutions, and that candidates frequently express doubts about the accuracy and fairness of their results (Pearson, 2019). Such findings underscore how much depends on the quality of the measurement and how important it is for the test to yield interpretable, defensible scores. This, in turn, places a premium on the accumulation of validity evidence for the different components of the exam.

The reading component of IELTS has attracted a good deal of attention in the validation literature, but this attention has been unevenly distributed. Clapham (1996), in her seminal study of the development of the test, investigated the extent to which reading scores could be interpreted as indicators of reading ability alone or whether they were confounded by test-takers' background knowledge of subject matter. Later studies examined the construct validity of the Academic reading test by comparing the reading requirements of test items with the reading demands of university study (Moore, Morton, & Price, 2011), and used eye-tracking to explore the cognitive processing of candidates as they completed reading items, thereby contributing to our understanding of the cognitive validity of the test (Bax, 2013). Alderson (2000), in his influential treatment of reading assessment, drew attention to a distinctive feature of the IELTS reading test, namely that a variety of techniques are used to assess understanding of any single passage. He argued that the use of multiple methods is a strength of good reading tests because, in real-life reading, readers respond to texts in a variety of ways. Yet, from a psychometric standpoint, the use of heterogeneous item formats within a single test can introduce method effects that may threaten the interpretability of the resulting scores.

Despite the popularity of the exam and the critical decisions based upon it, remarkably little empirical work has interrogated the psychometric structure of the reading section of the General Training module in particular. Much of the existing validation research has concentrated on the Academic module, or has approached validity through content analysis and process-based methods rather than through analysis of the empirical response behaviour of the items. This is a notable gap, because validity, in contemporary conceptualizations, is best understood as an argument concerning the plausibility of the interpretations and uses of test scores (Kane, 1992, 2013). On an argument-based approach, more ambitious claims—such as the claim that a set of reading items measures a single underlying reading ability that permits the ordering of test-takers—require correspondingly stronger evidence. A complementary strand of thinking, articulated by Borsboom and colleagues, locates validity in ontology and causality: a test is valid for measuring an attribute if the attribute exists and variations in it causally produce variations in the test scores (Borsboom, 2005; Borsboom, Mellenbergh, & van Heerden, 2004). From this perspective, demonstrating that the items of a reading test share a common cause—ideally the intended reading construct—is a central task of validation (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016). Fitting a latent variable model to item responses is one important way of assembling such evidence.

Modern measurement theory offers a range of tools for this purpose. Classical test theory has been progressively supplemented, and in many respects superseded, by item response theory (IRT), which formulates the relationship between the latent trait and the probability of a particular item response and provides new rules of measurement (Embretson, 1996; Linn, 2010). Most applications of IRT in language testing have relied on parametric models, such as the Rasch model, which impose specific functional forms on the item response functions. An attractive alternative is offered by nonparametric IRT, and in particular by Mokken scale analysis (MSA; Mokken, 1971; Mokken & Lewis, 1982). MSA rests on purely ordinal assumptions about the probability that persons respond positively to items and can be regarded as a natural generalization of both Guttman scaling and classical test theory. Its most basic model, the monotone homogeneity model (MHM), assumes unidimensionality, local independence, and monotonicity; when these hold, the total raw score can be used to order examinees on the latent trait. Because the MHM requires fewer and less restrictive assumptions than parametric models, and because scalability coefficients can be readily obtained and their fit to data straightforwardly examined, MSA provides a parsimonious yet powerful means of investigating whether a set of items forms a coherent scale (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). It also incorporates automated procedures, such as the automated item selection procedure (AISP), for exploring the dimensionality of a set of items and identifying subsets that cluster together.

MSA has been applied fruitfully across a wide range of disciplines, including criminology, health sciences, marketing, political science, psychiatry, psychology, and sociology, as well as in educational measurement more broadly (Palmgren et al., 2018; Wind & Engelhard, 2016). In many of these applications MSA has proved a valuable tool for probing the scalability and dimensional structure of questionnaires and tests, sometimes revealing that instruments assumed to be unidimensional in fact lack strong support for that assumption (Palmgren et al., 2018). Within second and foreign language assessment, however, the method remains greatly underused. Only a handful of studies have applied MSA to language tests. Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) used MSA to examine a 20-item reading comprehension test and reported that the MHM fitted all items adequately and that the test was unidimensional, which they treated as evidence of validity. More recently, Baghaei (2021) analysed the listening section of IELTS with the monotone homogeneity model and, using the AISP, found the section to be broadly unidimensional, although two items formed a second dimension and four items were unscalable. These early studies suggest that MSA is a promising approach for accumulating validity evidence in language testing, but they also make clear that the evidence base is thin and that the behaviour of individual language skills under nonparametric IRT scrutiny is far from settled. In particular, no study appears to have examined the reading section of the General Training module of IELTS from this perspective.

The present study addresses this gap by applying Mokken scale analysis to the reading comprehension section of the General Training module of IELTS. Using the monotone homogeneity model, we examine the scalability of the items through item, item-pair, and overall scalability coefficients, evaluate the monotonicity assumption, and investigate the dimensionality of the section using the automated item selection procedure. We also report several reliability indices for the section. In doing so, the study seeks to contribute validity evidence for a widely used but under-examined component of a high-stakes test, and to extend the still limited application of nonparametric IRT within language testing and assessment. The findings are expected to be of interest to test developers, to researchers concerned with the measurement properties of reading tests, and to the many stakeholders whose decisions depend on the meaningfulness of IELTS reading scores.

intros.text:
Reading comprehension is central to academic and professional success, and it occupies a prominent position in the assessment of second and foreign language proficiency. In an era of increasing international mobility for education, employment, and immigration, the ability to read and understand written texts in English has become an indispensable skill for millions of non-native speakers who must demonstrate their linguistic credentials to gatekeeping institutions around the world (Pearson, 2019). Reading is a complex cognitive and linguistic activity that draws on multiple components of language knowledge and processing. Second language reading has been described as both a language process and a literacy process, in which readers who are already literate in their first language must recruit lexical, grammatical, and strategic resources to construct meaning from text (Grabe, 2009). A considerable body of research has documented the contributions of these underlying components to reading comprehension. Vocabulary and grammatical knowledge, for instance, have repeatedly been shown to predict readers' comprehension ability, with lexical knowledge typically bearing a stronger relationship to comprehension than grammatical knowledge (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). Decoding skills, too, are strongly associated with comprehension, particularly among developing readers (García & Cain, 2014), and the cognitive processes involved in comprehending texts continue to be investigated through methods ranging from meta-analysis to eye-tracking and neuroimaging (Bax, 2013; Perfetti et al., n.d.). Taken together, these lines of inquiry underscore that reading comprehension is a multifaceted construct, and that measuring it validly is a demanding enterprise.

Given the importance of reading, it is unsurprising that reading comprehension forms an integral part of large-scale standardized English proficiency tests. Among these, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) is one of the most widely used instruments worldwide (IELTS, 2007). Test-takers' scores on IELTS are routinely used by universities, employers, and immigration authorities to make high-stakes decisions about admission, hiring, and residency. The IELTS is offered in two modules, the Academic module and the General Training module, each intended for distinct populations and purposes. In the reading section, candidates are required to read passages of varying lengths and answer a range of questions employing a variety of test methods and techniques. Alderson (2000) noted that an interesting feature of the IELTS reading test is that different techniques are used to assess understanding of any one passage, and he argued that employing multiple methods reflects the varied ways in which readers respond to texts in real life. The development of the IELTS reading test and the validity of its score interpretations have been the object of scholarly attention over the years. Clapham (1996), for example, investigated whether scores on subject-specific reading tests could be interpreted as indicators of reading ability alone or whether they were confounded by test-takers' background knowledge of the subject matter. More recently, researchers have examined the construct validity of the IELTS academic reading test by comparing the reading requirements of test items with those encountered in university study (Moore et al., 2011), while others have explored the cognitive processing of candidates as they complete reading items (Bax, 2013).

The concept that unites these efforts is validity, which is widely regarded as the most important property of any test. Social scientists broadly agree that the trustworthiness of substantive research and of the decisions made on the basis of test scores depends on the validity of the instruments used to gather the data (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016). Contemporary theorizing conceives of validity in different ways. In the argument-based tradition, validation is understood as the evaluation of the plausibility of the claims, inferences, and assumptions that link test responses to score-based interpretations and uses (Kane, 1992, 2013). In a more ontologically grounded view, a test is valid for measuring an attribute if the attribute exists and if variations in the attribute causally produce variations in the measurement outcomes (Borsboom, 2005; Borsboom et al., 2004). A common way of accumulating validity evidence in educational and psychological measurement is to demonstrate that item response data conform to a latent trait model such as factor analysis or an item response theory model. When data fit such a model, it can be argued that a common cause underlies the covariation among the items, which is ideally the intended construct (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016). Modern, model-based measurement theories, including item response theory, have introduced new rules of measurement that differ substantially from those of classical test theory, offering more powerful ways to examine item quality and the dimensionality of tests (Embretson, 1996). A key assumption in these frameworks is that as the level of the latent trait increases, the probability of a correct or positive response also increases; establishing that this property holds is a central condition for valid measurement (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016).

One particularly attractive family of methods for evaluating the psychometric quality of tests and questionnaires is Mokken scale analysis (MSA), a set of nonparametric item response theory techniques rooted in the work of Mokken (1971) and Mokken and Lewis (1982). MSA can be seen as a natural generalization of both Guttman scaling and classical test theory, resting on purely ordinal assumptions about the probabilities that respondents answer items positively. It offers a set of statistical tools and item selection algorithms for exploring scalability, monotonicity, and the dimensional structure of item sets, and it distinguishes clearly between the construction and evaluation of a scale and the use of a scale to order and make decisions about persons (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). Because Mokken models make relatively weak assumptions, their fit to data is comparatively easy to investigate, which makes MSA a pragmatic and parsimonious approach to examining test data from an item response theory perspective (Palmgren et al., 2018). Over the past decade, MSA has grown rapidly in popularity and has been applied successfully to evaluate the psychometric quality of scales across a wide range of disciplines, including criminology, educational measurement, the health sciences, marketing, political science, psychiatry, psychology, and sociology.

Despite this breadth of application, remarkably little attention has been devoted to MSA in the field of second and foreign language testing and assessment. A review of the literature reveals only a handful of studies that have employed Mokken models to investigate the properties of language tests. Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) applied MSA to a 20-item reading comprehension test and reported that the monotone homogeneity model had an adequate fit to all items, that the ordering of items was invariant across examinees, and that, according to the automated item selection procedure, the test was unidimensional, which they interpreted as evidence of validity. Baghaei (2021) analyzed the listening part of the IELTS with the monotone homogeneity model and found that, although two items formed a second dimension and four items were unscalable, the listening section was broadly unidimensional and reliable. These studies notwithstanding, there remains a clear paucity of research on the application of MSA in language assessment, and more studies are required to explore the suitability of these methods for evaluating the various language skills. This gap is especially conspicuous in the case of the IELTS. Although the IELTS is a popular standardized test whose scores are used to make critical decisions about test-takers, very few attempts have been made to explore the validity of its various components, and the reading part of the General Training module in particular has received scant empirical scrutiny. The General Training module is used for immigration and vocational purposes and thus affects the lives of large numbers of candidates, yet its psychometric quality has been largely unexamined through the lens of nonparametric item response theory.

In view of this gap, the present study sets out to use Mokken scale analysis to examine the validity of the reading part of the General Training module of the IELTS. Specifically, the study employs the monotone homogeneity model to evaluate the psychometric quality of the reading items by inspecting item, item-pair, and total scalability coefficients, by checking the monotonicity assumption through the restscore method and graphical analyses of item response functions, and by investigating the dimensionality of the test using the automated item selection procedure. To this end, the item responses of 352 undergraduate EFL university students to a version of the General Training IELTS reading test, comprising three passages and 40 items, were analyzed. In addition, several reliability coefficients were computed to assess the consistency of the ordering of test-takers. By applying these nonparametric techniques to a test that carries substantial consequences for its takers, this study aims to contribute to the limited body of validation research on the IELTS and, more broadly, to demonstrate the value of Mokken scale analysis as a tool for interrogating the psychometric properties of language tests. The findings are expected to shed light on whether the reading section constitutes a coherent, unidimensional scale capable of ordering examinees appropriately along the underlying reading ability continuum, and to inform test developers, teachers, and researchers about potential sources of construct-irrelevant variance arising from the use of multiple test methods.

When data fit such a model, it can be argued that a common cause underlies the covariation among the items, which is ideally the intended construct (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016). Modern, model-based measurement theories, including item response theory, have introduced new rules of measurement that differ substantially from those of classical test theory, offering more powerful ways to examine item quality and the dimensionality of tests (Embretson, 1996). A key assumption in these frameworks is that as the level of the latent trait increases, the probability of a correct or positive response also increases; establishing that this property holds is a central condition for valid measurement (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016).

Because Mokken models make relatively weak assumptions, their fit to data is comparatively easy to investigate, which makes MSA a pragmatic and parsimonious approach to examining test data from an item response theory perspective (Palmgren et al., 2018).

intros.text:
Large-scale standardized tests in English as a Second Language (ESL), most notably the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), serve as critical instruments for evaluating language proficiency on a global scale. These assessments are utilized by thousands of gatekeeping institutions—including universities and immigration departments—to make high-stakes decisions regarding the academic and professional futures of candidates (Pearson, 2019). Within the IELTS framework, reading comprehension is a fundamental component, requiring test-takers to synthesize information from complex passages to answer a variety of question types. Given the weight placed on these scores, the psychometric validity of the test items is of paramount importance. Validity, in the broadest sense, refers to the extent to which a test accurately measures the attribute it purports to measure (Borsboom et al., 2004). In the context of psychological and educational measurement, this often involves evaluating whether variations in the measured attribute causally produce variation in the measurement outcomes (Borsboom et al., 2004; Borsboom, 2005). Consequently, providing robust validity evidence is not merely a statistical exercise but a necessity for ensuring that score interpretations are fair and meaningful (Kane, 1992; Kane, 2013).

Reading comprehension in a second language is an intricate cognitive process that interfaces both language and literacy skills (Grabe, 2009). It is generally understood that successful reading depends on an interactive interplay of various competencies, including lexical breadth, grammatical knowledge, and the ability to employ strategic reading processes (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). Furthermore, the cognitive load associated with reading tests can be influenced by the candidates' ability to read expeditiously and their focus on specific aspects of the text (Bax, 2013). Because reading is such a multifaceted construct, the development of a valid reading test requires a careful balance between authentic task design and psychometric rigor. Alderson (2000) has noted that the IELTS reading test specifically employs a diverse array of techniques to assess understanding, reflecting the variety of ways readers interact with texts in real-life scenarios. However, from a measurement perspective, the inclusion of multiple item formats can introduce construct-irrelevance variance, potentially threatening the unidimensionality of the scale and complicating the interpretation of the resulting scores.

To evaluate the internal structure and validity of such tests, researchers often turn to latent variable analysis. The core logic of latent trait modeling is based on the assumption of conditional independence; if a set of items fits a specific model, it suggests that a 'common cause'—the latent trait, such as reading ability—is responsible for the co-variation among the items (Baghaei & Tabatabaee Yazdi, 2016). While Classical Test Theory (CTT) has long been the standard, it is limited by its reliance on sample-dependent statistics (Embretson, 1996). This has led to the widespread adoption of Item Response Theory (IRT) and its various derivatives, which offer more sophisticated ways to analyze the relationship between a person's latent ability and their probability of answering an item correctly.

Among the available IRT-based approaches, Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) offers a particularly powerful non-parametric alternative to parametric models like the Rasch model. Developed by Mokken (1971), MSA is based on the assumption of monotonicity: the probability of a correct response to an item should be a non-decreasing function of the latent trait (Mokken & Lewis, 1982). Unlike parametric IRT, MSA does not require strict assumptions about the distribution of the latent trait or the functional form of the item response curves, making it highly flexible and robust for analyzing real-world data (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). By employing models such as the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM), researchers can determine if a set of items forms a scale, meaning they measure a single underlying dimension, and can subsequently order individuals on an ordinal scale based on their total raw scores (Mokken, 2011).

Despite its utility, MSA has seen extensive application in fields such as psychiatry, health sciences, and political science, while remaining relatively underutilized in the domain of second language (L2) testing. Recent efforts have begun to bridge this gap. For instance, Tabatabaee-Yazdi et al. (2021) applied MSA to a 20-item reading test and found evidence of unidimensionality, suggesting that the items effectively ordered students according to their reading ability. Similarly, Baghaei (2021) explored the listening section of the IELTS using the MHM, discovering that while the section was generally unidimensional, some items formed a secondary dimension or were unscalable. These studies highlight the potential of MSA to provide nuanced insights into the psychometric quality of language tests, yet there remains a significant paucity of research specifically targeting the reading component of the IELTS General Training module.

The General Training module of the IELTS is designed for those who are migrating to English-speaking countries or seeking secondary education, and its reading section differs in content and purpose from the Academic module. While there have been studies on the construct validity of the Academic reading test in relation to university study (Moore et al., 2011), the General Training version has received far less scrutiny. Given that the General Training module is used for critical life decisions, it is essential to verify whether its reading section functions as a unidimensional scale or if the various item formats introduce multidimensionality that could distort the measurement of reading proficiency.

Therefore, the present study aims to fill this gap by using Mokken Scale Analysis to examine the validity and dimensionality of the reading comprehension section of the IELTS General Training module. Specifically, the study seeks to evaluate the scalability coefficients of the items to determine the strength of the scale, test the monotonicity assumption to ensure that the items correctly reflect the latent trait of reading ability, and utilize the Automatic Item Selection Procedure (AISP) to identify the number of dimensions present in the test. By doing so, the research intends to provide empirical evidence regarding the psychometric robustness of the IELTS reading section and determine whether it provides a valid measure of a single underlying construct of reading comprehension.
