intros.text:
Large-scale standardized English as a Second Language (ESL) examinations serve as critical gatekeeping mechanisms in the globalized era, providing the empirical basis for high-stakes decisions regarding academic admission, professional certification, and immigration eligibility. Among these, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) stands as one of the most widely recognized and utilized proficiency tests globally (IELTS, 2007). The test is designed to provide a reliable measure of a candidate's communicative competence across four primary language skills: listening, reading, writing, and speaking. Reading comprehension, in particular, is an integral component of this system, requiring test-takers to engage with a variety of texts and demonstrate their ability to extract meaning, identify specific information, and understand the writer's purpose through a series of structured questions. Given that IELTS scores are used by thousands of institutions to make life-altering decisions for candidates, the psychometric integrity and validity of its sub-tests are of paramount importance to stakeholders, including examiners, educators, and the test-takers themselves (Pearson, 2019).

In the field of educational measurement, validity is widely regarded as the most essential characteristic of any assessment tool. As noted by Borsboom et al. (2004), a test is considered valid if the attribute it claims to measure actually exists and if variations in that attribute causally produce the observed variations in measurement outcomes. This perspective shifts the focus from simple correlation to a more ontological and causal understanding of validity, emphasizing the processes that convey the effect of a latent trait—such as reading ability—onto the test scores. Within the framework of argument-based validity, Kane (1992, 2013) suggests that validation is not about the test itself, but about evaluating the plausibility of the claims made based on the scores. Therefore, ensuring that a reading test truly measures 'reading ability' and not an unrelated construct (construct-irrelevance variance) is a continuous and necessary process in language testing (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016).

Reading comprehension in a second language is a complex, multifaceted process. It is not merely the act of decoding symbols but an interactive process where the reader utilizes lexical knowledge, grammatical competence, and world knowledge simultaneously to construct meaning (Grabe, 2009). Previous research has highlighted the significant role of vocabulary and grammar as predictors of reading success, with vocabulary often showing a stronger correlation with comprehension than grammatical knowledge (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). Furthermore, the cognitive processing involved in reading tests can be highly variable. For instance, eye-tracking research by Bax (2013) has revealed distinct differences in how successful and unsuccessful IELTS candidates process information, suggesting that cognitive validity—the alignment between the intended cognitive operations and the actual processes used by test-takers—is a vital dimension of test quality.

Despite the criticality of the IELTS reading section, the specific psychometric properties of the General Training Module have received relatively limited empirical attention compared to the Academic Module. While some studies have explored the effect of background knowledge on reading scores (Clapham, 1996) or compared reading requirements in IELTS with those of university study (Moore et al., 2011), there is a scarcity of research utilizing advanced latent variable models to examine the dimensional structure of the General Training reading component. Traditionally, researchers have relied on Classical Test Theory (CTT) or parametric Item Response Theory (IRT) models, such as the Rasch model, to provide validity evidence (Baghaei et al., 2014). However, as Embretson (1996) argues, the 'new rules of measurement' associated with IRT provide more nuanced insights into item-person interactions than CTT. Among these, nonparametric approaches offer a flexible alternative for analyzing dichotomous item responses without the strict distributional assumptions required by parametric models (Mokken & Lewis, 1982).

One such powerful nonparametric approach is Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA). MSA provides a set of statistical tools to explore the relationship between test items and a latent trait, allowing researchers to determine if a set of items forms a unidimensional scale (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). The primary strength of MSA lies in its ability to identify whether items are 'scalable'—meaning that as a person's level of the latent trait increases, their probability of answering any given item correctly also increases monotonically (Mokken, 2011). MSA has been successfully applied across a vast array of disciplines, including psychiatry, health sciences, criminology, and political science, to evaluate the psychometric quality of various scales (Palmgren et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2008). For example, in medical education research, MSA has been used to probe the dimensional structure of educational environment measures, providing a pragmatic way to investigate if an instrument is measuring a single underlying construct or multiple dimensions (Palmgren et al., 2018).

Interestingly, while MSA has flourished in other social sciences, its application within the realm of second language (L2) testing remains significantly underdeveloped. Only a handful of studies have attempted to integrate MSA into language assessment. Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) recently employed the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM) of Mokken to analyze a 20-item reading comprehension test, finding that the items were scalable and unidimensional, thereby providing evidence of validity. Similarly, Baghaei (2021) applied MSA to the listening section of the IELTS, concluding that while some items formed secondary dimensions, the overall test remained predominantly unidimensional and reliable. These preliminary forays suggest that MSA can be a valuable tool for L2 researchers to verify if a test is indeed measuring a single ability or if it is contaminated by other factors.

However, a significant gap remains in the literature regarding the General Training module of the IELTS reading test. The General Training module is designed for different purposes than the Academic module, often focusing on survival English and general workplace contexts, yet it is subject to the same high-stakes pressures. A potential concern in the design of the IELTS reading test is the use of multiple item types (e.g., multiple choice, matching, completion). While Alderson (2000) argues that employing various techniques to assess understanding is a strength that mirrors real-life reading, from a psychometric perspective, such diversity in task format can introduce construct-irrelevance variance. If different item types activate different cognitive processes or require different skills, the test may become multidimensional, which could potentially threaten the validity of the overall score interpretation (Baghaei & Kubinger, 2015).

Given this context, there is a clear need for a rigorous psychometric evaluation of the IELTS General Training reading section to determine whether it functions as a unidimensional measure of reading proficiency. If the test is multidimensional, the raw score may not be a pure reflection of a single latent trait, which would necessitate a reconsideration of how these scores are interpreted. Therefore, the present study aims to fill this gap by applying Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA), specifically the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM), to examine the validity and psychometric quality of the reading part of the IELTS General Training module. By analyzing the item responses of a sample of EFL learners, this research seeks to determine the scalability of the items, the overall dimensionality of the test, and whether the test successfully orders examinees along a single latent trait continuum.

Specifically, the study focuses on three key areas of analysis. First, it examines item and total scalability coefficients to determine the strength of the scale. Second, it investigates whether the monotonicity assumption is violated—which would indicate that some items do not behave predictably as ability increases. Third, it utilizes the Automatic Item Selection Procedure (AISP) to identify any potential multidimensionality within the test structure. By doing so, the study provides empirical evidence regarding the construct validity of the IELTS reading section and offers insights into whether the varied item formats contribute to a fragmented dimensional structure.

The findings of this research are expected to contribute to the broader discourse on language testing and assessment by demonstrating the utility of nonparametric IRT models in evaluating standardized tests. Furthermore, the results may provide valuable feedback for test developers regarding the balance between authentic task variety and psychometric unidimensionality. The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a detailed review of the literature on Mokken Scale Analysis and its application in language testing. Section 3 describes the participants, the instrumentation, and the specific MSA procedures employed in the study. Section 4 presents the results of the scalability, monotonicity, and dimensionality analyses. Finally, Section 5 discusses the implications of these findings for the validity of the IELTS reading section and offers concluding remarks.

segments.text: As noted by Borsboom et al. (2004), a test is considered valid if the attribute it claims to measure actually exists and if variations in that attribute causally produce the observed variations in measurement outcomes. This perspective shifts the focus from simple correlation to a more ontological and causal understanding of validity, emphasizing the processes that convey the effect of a latent trait—such as reading ability—onto the test scores. Within the framework of argument-based validity, Kane (1992, 2013) suggests that validation is not about the test itself, but about evaluating the plausibility of the claims made based on the scores.

segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the cited accounts from Borsboom et al. and Kane review previous research and theory on validity.

segments.text: Therefore, ensuring that a reading test truly measures 'reading ability' and not an unrelated construct (construct-irrelevance variance) is a continuous and necessary process in language testing (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016).

segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit centrality marker “necessary process” establishes the importance of ensuring construct validity in reading tests.

segments.text: Reading comprehension in a second language is a complex, multifaceted process. It is not merely the act of decoding symbols but an interactive process where the reader utilizes lexical knowledge, grammatical competence, and world knowledge simultaneously to construct meaning (Grabe, 2009). Previous research has highlighted the significant role of vocabulary and grammar as predictors of reading success, with vocabulary often showing a stronger correlation with comprehension than grammatical knowledge (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). Furthermore, the cognitive processing involved in reading tests can be highly variable. For instance, eye-tracking research by Bax (2013) has revealed distinct differences in how successful and unsuccessful IELTS candidates process information, suggesting that cognitive validity—the alignment between the intended cognitive operations and the actual processes used by test-takers—is a vital dimension of test quality.

segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews prior research on L2 reading, predictors of comprehension, and cognitive processing through citations to Grabe, Aryadoust and Baghaei, Zhang, and Bax.

segments.text: Despite the criticality of the IELTS reading section, the specific psychometric properties of the General Training Module have received relatively limited empirical attention compared to the Academic Module. While some studies have explored the effect of background knowledge on reading scores (Clapham, 1996) or compared reading requirements in IELTS with those of university study (Moore et al., 2011), there is a scarcity of research utilizing advanced latent variable models to examine the dimensional structure of the General Training reading component.
segments.label: move_2__indicating_a_gap
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the explicit absence signal “there is a scarcity of research” identifies limited work on the General Training reading component.

segments.text: Traditionally, researchers have relied on Classical Test Theory (CTT) or parametric Item Response Theory (IRT) models, such as the Rasch model, to provide validity evidence (Baghaei et al., 2014). However, as Embretson (1996) argues, the 'new rules of measurement' associated with IRT provide more nuanced insights into item-person interactions than CTT. Among these, nonparametric approaches offer a flexible alternative for analyzing dichotomous item responses without the strict distributional assumptions required by parametric models (Mokken & Lewis, 1982).
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews prior measurement approaches and arguments through citations to Baghaei et al., Embretson, and Mokken and Lewis.

segments.text: One such powerful nonparametric approach is Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA).
segments.label: move_1__making_topic_generalization
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the sentence introduces MSA as a general background concept without reporting a specific study, fixing it as a topic generalization.

segments.text: MSA provides a set of statistical tools to explore the relationship between test items and a latent trait, allowing researchers to determine if a set of items forms a unidimensional scale (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). The primary strength of MSA lies in its ability to identify whether items are 'scalable'—meaning that as a person's level of the latent trait increases, their probability of answering any given item correctly also increases monotonically (Mokken, 2011). MSA has been successfully applied across a vast array of disciplines, including psychiatry, health sciences, criminology, and political science, to evaluate the psychometric quality of various scales (Palmgren et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2008). For example, in medical education research, MSA has been used to probe the dimensional structure of educational environment measures, providing a pragmatic way to investigate if an instrument is measuring a single underlying construct or multiple dimensions (Palmgren et al., 2018).

segments.text: Interestingly, while MSA has flourished in other social sciences, its application within the realm of second language (L2) testing remains significantly underdeveloped.

Similarly, Baghaei (2021) applied MSA to the listening section of the IELTS, concluding that while some items formed secondary dimensions, the overall test remained predominantly unidimensional and reliable. These preliminary forays suggest that MSA can be a valuable tool for L2 researchers to verify if a test is indeed measuring a single ability or if it is contaminated by other factors.

segments.text: A potential concern in the design of the IELTS reading test is the use of multiple item types (e.g., multiple choice, matching, completion). While Alderson (2000) argues that employing various techniques to assess understanding is a strength that mirrors real-life reading, from a psychometric perspective, such diversity in task format can introduce construct-irrelevance variance. If different item types activate different cognitive processes or require different skills, the test may become multidimensional, which could potentially threaten the validity of the overall score interpretation (Baghaei & Kubinger, 2015).

By analyzing the item responses of a sample of EFL learners, this research seeks to determine the scalability of the items, the overall dimensionality of the test, and whether the test successfully orders examinees along a single latent trait continuum.

intros.text:
Large-scale standardized English as a Foreign Language (EFL) tests play a pivotal role in the global educational and immigration landscape, serving as gatekeeping mechanisms for academic admission, professional licensing, and migration. Among these, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) stands out as one of the most widely administered proficiency tests, utilized by over 10,000 organizations worldwide, including universities, employers, and immigration authorities (IELTS, 2007). The IELTS is designed to assess the language proficiency of non-native English speakers across four key skills: listening, reading, writing, and speaking. Given the high-stakes nature of decisions made based on IELTS scores, such as university admission or visa approval, it is imperative that the test possesses robust psychometric properties, particularly validity and reliability. Validity, defined as the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses (Borsboom et al., 2004; Kane, 2013), is the most critical characteristic of any educational or psychological measurement instrument. Without adequate validity evidence, the interpretations and uses of test scores may be flawed, potentially leading to adverse consequences for test-takers (Kane, 1992).

The reading comprehension section of the IELTS is a crucial component of the test, requiring candidates to process complex texts and answer a variety of questions that assess different aspects of reading ability. The test is available in two modules: Academic and General Training. While the Academic module focuses on academic texts, the General Training module is designed for those seeking migration or non-academic training purposes, featuring texts drawn from everyday life, work, and general interest topics. Despite the widespread use of the IELTS and the critical importance of its reading component, there is a paucity of research examining the psychometric quality of the reading section, particularly for the General Training module. Most validation studies have focused on the Academic module, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of the General Training module's measurement properties (Baghaei & Tabatabaee-Yazdi, 2016). This gap is concerning given that the General Training module is often used for high-stakes decisions regarding migration, where the stakes for test-takers are exceptionally high.

Reading comprehension is a complex cognitive process that involves the interaction of multiple skills and knowledge sources. According to the interactive approach to second language reading, comprehension is not merely a bottom-up process of decoding text but involves the simultaneous integration of linguistic knowledge (vocabulary, grammar), text processing strategies, and background knowledge (Grabe, 2009). Research has consistently shown that lexical and grammatical knowledge are strong predictors of reading comprehension performance in L2 contexts (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). However, the measurement of reading comprehension in standardized tests like IELTS must ensure that the items used to assess this complex construct are psychometrically sound. This involves ensuring that the test items function as intended, that they measure a single underlying construct (unidimensionality), and that the test scores can be meaningfully interpreted.

In the context of test validation, Item Response Theory (IRT) models have become increasingly popular for evaluating the psychometric properties of test items. Traditional Classical Test Theory (CTT) relies on sample-dependent statistics and assumes that item difficulty and discrimination are constant across populations, which is often not the case in practice (Embretson, 1996). In contrast, IRT models provide item parameters that are invariant across different samples of examinees, offering a more robust framework for test validation. Among the various IRT models, Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) has emerged as a valuable nonparametric approach for evaluating the scalability and dimensionality of test items. MSA is based on the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM) and the Double Monotonicity Model (DMM), which make fewer assumptions about the distribution of the latent trait compared to parametric IRT models (Mokken, 1971; Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). This makes MSA particularly suitable for large-scale standardized tests where the underlying distribution of ability may not be known or may deviate from normality.

Mokken Scale Analysis has been successfully applied in various fields, including criminology, health sciences, psychology, and sociology, to evaluate the psychometric quality of scales and questionnaires (Palmgren et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2008). However, its application in language testing and assessment research remains limited. A review of the literature reveals only a few studies that have employed MSA in the context of second language testing. Tabatabaee-Yazdi et al. (2021) used MSA to examine the unidimensionality and scalability of a 20-item reading comprehension test. Their results indicated that the Monotone Homogeneity Model had adequate fit to all items, and the Automated Item Selection Procedure (AISP) confirmed that the test was unidimensional, providing evidence of validity. Similarly, Baghaei (2021) analyzed the listening part of the IELTS using the monotone homogeneity model of Mokken. The results showed that the listening section was largely unidimensional, although a few items formed a second dimension and were unscalable. These studies highlight the potential of MSA for validating language tests but also underscore the need for more research, particularly on the reading section of the IELTS General Training module.

The present study aims to address this gap by applying Mokken Scale Analysis to the reading comprehension section of the IELTS General Training module. Specifically, the study seeks to examine the scalability, dimensionality, and monotonicity of the test items to evaluate the validity of the reading section. By using a nonparametric IRT model, this study aims to provide robust evidence regarding the psychometric quality of the IELTS reading test, which is crucial for ensuring the fairness and accuracy of the decisions made based on test scores. The findings of this study will contribute to the growing body of literature on the validation of large-scale standardized tests and offer insights for test developers and researchers in the field of English language teaching and assessment. Furthermore, the study will explore the implications of the test's dimensionality for the interpretation of scores and the potential impact of construct-irrelevant variance on test validity (Messick, 1989). In doing so, this research aligns with the broader goal of enhancing the quality and reliability of language testing practices globally.

intros.text:
Large-scale standardized English language tests have become ubiquitous in global educational and immigration contexts, serving as critical gatekeeping mechanisms for academic admission and professional licensure. Among these, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) stands out as one of the most widely administered assessments, used by thousands of institutions worldwide to evaluate the language proficiency of non-native speakers. The stakes associated with IELTS scores are exceptionally high, as they often determine an individual's access to higher education or migration opportunities. Consequently, the psychometric quality and validity of the IELTS are of paramount importance to test developers, educational policymakers, and the test-takers themselves. Ensuring that the test accurately measures the intended construct—language proficiency—and that scores can be interpreted validly for decision-making purposes is a fundamental requirement of modern educational measurement. 

Reading comprehension is a central component of the IELTS, designed to assess a candidate's ability to understand written English in academic and general training contexts. The reading section typically comprises three passages of varying lengths and complexities, accompanied by a set of questions that require test-takers to demonstrate various skills, such as skimming, scanning, and understanding detailed information. Given the interactive nature of second-language reading, which involves the simultaneous processing of linguistic knowledge, cognitive strategies, and world knowledge (Grabe, 2009), the construction of a reading test that yields valid scores is a complex endeavor. Theoretical frameworks in second language reading emphasize that comprehension is not merely a decoding process but an interactive one where readers construct meaning through the interplay of text and reader knowledge. Therefore, any assessment of reading comprehension must account for these multifaceted processes to ensure that the test measures the construct of reading ability rather than extraneous factors. 

Validity is widely regarded as the most critical characteristic of any test or measurement instrument. In the context of educational and psychological measurement, validity refers to the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses (Kane, 2013). Contemporary validity theory, particularly the argument-based approach, posits that validation is an ongoing process of gathering evidence to support the inferences drawn from test scores. This involves examining the construct representation, internal structure, and relationships with other variables. Central to this argument is the assumption of unidimensionality, which posits that a test measures a single underlying latent trait. If a test is multidimensional, it implies that scores are influenced by factors other than the intended construct, potentially threatening the validity of score interpretations (Borsboom et al., 2004). For instance, if a reading test inadvertently measures background knowledge or specific test-taking strategies alongside reading ability, the resulting scores may not accurately reflect a candidate's true proficiency. 

To evaluate the internal structure and validity of tests, researchers have increasingly turned to Item Response Theory (IRT) models. Unlike Classical Test Theory (CTT), which relies on sample-dependent statistics, IRT models provide item parameters that are invariant across different populations and test forms (Embretson, 1996). Among the various IRT models, Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) has emerged as a robust nonparametric alternative that requires fewer assumptions than parametric models. MSA is based on the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM) and the Double Monotonicity Model (DMM), which assume that items are ordered by difficulty and that the probability of a correct response increases monotonically with the latent trait (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). This nonparametric approach is particularly useful in language testing, where data often violate the strict assumptions of parametric IRT models, such as normality of ability distribution. MSA allows researchers to examine scalability, unidimensionality, and monotonicity without imposing rigid distributional constraints, making it a valuable tool for validating language tests. 

Despite its utility in fields such as psychology, health sciences, and political science (e.g., Palmgren et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2008), the application of MSA in second language testing research remains relatively scarce. A review of the literature reveals a paucity of studies employing MSA to evaluate the psychometric properties of language assessments. Most validation studies in the field of language testing have traditionally relied on factor analysis or parametric IRT models like the Rasch model. While these methods are informative, they may not always be appropriate for language data, which can be complex and noisy. For example, Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) applied MSA to a 20-item reading comprehension test and found that the Monotone Homogeneity Model fit the data adequately, with all items showing positive scalability coefficients. Their study concluded that the test was unidimensional, providing evidence for its validity. Similarly, Baghaei (2021) utilized MSA to analyze the listening section of the IELTS. The results indicated that the listening part was largely unidimensional, although a few items formed a secondary dimension and some were unscalable. These studies suggest that MSA can offer nuanced insights into the structure of language tests that might be overlooked by other methods. 

However, significant gaps remain in the literature regarding the application of MSA to the reading section of the IELTS, particularly the General Training Module. While the Academic Module has received some attention, the General Training Module, which is often used for immigration and vocational purposes, has been less scrutinized. The General Training reading test differs from the Academic version in terms of text types and question formats, potentially affecting its psychometric properties. Furthermore, the use of multiple question types within a single reading passage—such as multiple-choice, matching, and true/false/not given items—has been a subject of debate. Alderson (2000) argued that using diverse methods to assess reading comprehension can enhance the authenticity of the test, reflecting the variety of ways readers interact with texts in real life. However, this diversity may introduce construct-irrelevance variance, threatening unidimensionality (Baghaei & Kubinger, 2015). If different question types tap into different sub-skills or require different cognitive processes, the test may measure multiple dimensions rather than a single reading ability. 

Moreover, the validity of the IELTS reading test has been questioned in terms of its construct representation. Some researchers have suggested that performance on reading tests can be influenced by factors such as background knowledge, test-taking anxiety, and familiarity with the test format (Clapham, 1996). If these factors significantly impact scores, the test may not be a pure measure of reading proficiency. For instance, Bax (2013) used eye-tracking to investigate the cognitive processes of candidates during the IELTS reading test, finding differences in reading behaviors between successful and unsuccessful candidates. These findings highlight the complexity of the reading process and the need for rigorous psychometric evaluation to ensure that the test measures what it claims to measure. Additionally, the reliability of the test is crucial for making high-stakes decisions. While the IELTS is generally considered reliable, the specific reliability of the reading section in the General Training Module has not been extensively explored using nonparametric methods like MSA. 

Given the critical role of the IELTS in the lives of millions of test-takers and the limited research on the psychometric properties of its General Training reading section using MSA, there is a clear need for further investigation. The current study aims to address this gap by applying Mokken Scale Analysis to the reading comprehension section of the General Training Module of the IELTS. Specifically, the study seeks to examine the scalability, unidimensionality, and monotonicity of the test items. By utilizing the Monotone Homogeneity Model and the Automatic Item Selection Procedure (AISP), the study will determine whether the test functions as a unidimensional scale or if it exhibits multidimensionality. Furthermore, the study will assess the reliability of the test using various coefficients, including Mokken scale reliability, Lambda-2, Cronbach's alpha, and the latent class reliability coefficient. 

This research is significant for several reasons. First, it contributes to the growing body of literature on the application of MSA in language testing, demonstrating the utility of this method for evaluating large-scale standardized tests. Second, it provides empirical evidence regarding the validity of the IELTS General Training reading test, which has implications for test developers, educational institutions, and immigration authorities. If the test is found to be multidimensional, it suggests that scores may be influenced by factors other than reading ability, necessitating a re-evaluation of how scores are interpreted and used. Third, the study offers insights into the impact of different question types on the dimensionality of reading tests, informing future test design and development. By identifying items that violate the assumptions of the MHM or form separate scales, the study can highlight potential areas for improvement in the test construction process. 

In summary, while the IELTS is a widely used and respected assessment, the psychometric properties of its General Training reading section require rigorous validation using modern statistical techniques. The scarcity of MSA studies in this context creates a niche for the present research. By applying MSA to a large dataset of test-takers, this study aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation of the test's internal structure and validity. The findings will not only advance the theoretical understanding of reading test validity but also have practical implications for the stakeholders who rely on IELTS scores for critical decisions. Ultimately, ensuring the validity and reliability of high-stakes tests is essential for maintaining fairness and integrity in educational and immigration systems.

segments.text: Large-scale standardized English language tests have become ubiquitous in global educational and immigration contexts, serving as critical gatekeeping mechanisms for academic admission and professional licensure. Among these, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) stands out as one of the most widely administered assessments, used by thousands of institutions worldwide to evaluate the language proficiency of non-native speakers. The stakes associated with IELTS scores are exceptionally high, as they often determine an individual's access to higher education or migration opportunities. Consequently, the psychometric quality and validity of the IELTS are of paramount importance to test developers, educational policymakers, and the test-takers themselves. Ensuring that the test accurately measures the intended construct—language proficiency—and that scores can be interpreted validly for decision-making purposes is a fundamental requirement of modern educational measurement.

segments.text: Validity is widely regarded as the most critical characteristic of any test or measurement instrument. In the context of educational and psychological measurement, validity refers to the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses (Kane, 2013). Contemporary validity theory, particularly the argument-based approach, posits that validation is an ongoing process of gathering evidence to support the inferences drawn from test scores. This involves examining the construct representation, internal structure, and relationships with other variables. Central to this argument is the assumption of unidimensionality, which posits that a test measures a single underlying latent trait. If a test is multidimensional, it implies that scores are influenced by factors other than the intended construct, potentially threatening the validity of score interpretations (Borsboom et al., 2004). For instance, if a reading test inadvertently measures background knowledge or specific test-taking strategies alongside reading ability, the resulting scores may not accurately reflect a candidate's true proficiency.

segments.text: To evaluate the internal structure and validity of tests, researchers have increasingly turned to Item Response Theory (IRT) models. Unlike Classical Test Theory (CTT), which relies on sample-dependent statistics, IRT models provide item parameters that are invariant across different populations and test forms (Embretson, 1996). Among the various IRT models, Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) has emerged as a robust nonparametric alternative that requires fewer assumptions than parametric models. MSA is based on the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM) and the Double Monotonicity Model (DMM), which assume that items are ordered by difficulty and that the probability of a correct response increases monotonically with the latent trait (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). This nonparametric approach is particularly useful in language testing, where data often violate the strict assumptions of parametric IRT models, such as normality of ability distribution. MSA allows researchers to examine scalability, unidimensionality, and monotonicity without imposing rigid distributional constraints, making it a valuable tool for validating language tests.

intros.text:
The International English Language Testing System (IELTS) is one of the most widely used high-stakes English language proficiency tests in the world. Its scores are used by universities, professional bodies, employers, immigration authorities, and other gatekeeping institutions to make decisions that may have substantial consequences for test takers’ academic, professional, and personal lives (IELTS, 2007; Pearson, 2019). Because such decisions often depend on reaching specific band-score thresholds, the validity of interpretations made from IELTS scores is not merely a technical concern but also an ethical and social one. If a test score is used to represent a test taker’s ability in a particular language domain, evidence is needed to show that the score is meaningfully related to the intended construct and is not unduly influenced by irrelevant features of the test, the tasks, or the scoring procedure (Kane, 1992, 2013; Messick, 1989; Borsboom et al., 2004).

Reading comprehension is a central component of IELTS and of English for academic, occupational, and migration purposes more generally. In IELTS, the reading module requires candidates to process written texts and respond to a variety of item types under time constraints. In the General Training module, the reading test is designed to assess the ability to understand texts likely to be encountered in everyday, workplace, and general social contexts, rather than the more discipline-oriented texts used in the Academic module. As with other large-scale reading tests, the assumption underlying score interpretation is that responses to the set of reading items provide evidence about a candidate’s reading comprehension ability. However, reading comprehension is a complex construct. It involves lower-level processes such as word recognition, vocabulary access, syntactic parsing, and decoding, as well as higher-level processes such as inferencing, integration of ideas, use of background knowledge, strategic processing, and construction of a coherent mental representation of the text (Alderson, 2000; Grabe, 2009; García & Cain, 2014; Pearson, 2014; Perfetti et al., n.d.). In second language reading, this complexity is amplified because readers must coordinate linguistic knowledge, literacy knowledge, world knowledge, and test-taking strategies in a language that may not yet be fully automatized (Grabe, 2009).

Previous research has shown that lexical and grammatical knowledge are important predictors of second language reading comprehension. Zhang (2012), for example, found that vocabulary knowledge was strongly associated with second language reading comprehension, whereas grammatical knowledge made a weaker but still relevant contribution after controlling for vocabulary. Similarly, Aryadoust and Baghaei (2016), using an artificial neural network approach, showed that vocabulary and grammar measures could classify low- and high-ability EFL readers with considerable accuracy, with vocabulary emerging as the stronger predictor. Other work has highlighted the role of decoding, text genre, and task characteristics in reading comprehension assessment (García & Cain, 2014). These findings indicate that reading test performance may be shaped by multiple interacting abilities and processes. Consequently, the dimensionality of a reading test—whether its items function as indicators of a single dominant latent trait or of multiple traits—is a key issue for validation.

The validity of reading tests has also been investigated in relation to test tasks and cognitive processing. Clapham (1996), in work related to IELTS development, examined the influence of background knowledge on reading comprehension and raised important questions about whether reading scores reflect reading ability alone or a combination of reading ability and topic knowledge. Moore et al. (2011) compared the reading requirements of IELTS Academic Reading items with the reading demands of university study, contributing evidence concerning construct representation. Bax (2013), using eye-tracking and stimulated recall, investigated the cognitive processing of candidates during IELTS reading tasks and found differences between successful and unsuccessful test takers in reading behaviours such as expeditious reading and attention to particular parts of texts and items. Such studies are important because they move beyond simple score correlations and examine whether test takers engage in processes consistent with the intended construct. Nevertheless, psychometric analyses remain indispensable because they evaluate whether the observed item responses support the intended interpretation of scores.

In contemporary validity theory, validity is not considered a property of a test in isolation, but of the interpretations and uses of scores derived from it (Kane, 2013). An argument-based approach to validation requires researchers to specify the claims made on the basis of test scores and then evaluate the assumptions that connect observed performance to those claims (Kane, 1992, 2013). From a latent variable perspective, one crucial assumption is that item responses are caused, at least in part, by the intended latent attribute. Borsboom et al. (2004) argued that a test is valid for measuring an attribute if the attribute exists and variation in the attribute causally produces variation in measurement outcomes. Baghaei and Tabatabaee Yazdi (2016) further explained that fitting latent trait models can provide validity evidence because such models test whether item covariation can plausibly be attributed to a common underlying cause. If the items of a test intended to measure reading comprehension do not cohere around a common latent trait, or if they form several distinct dimensions related to item format, passage type, or subskill, then the interpretation of a single total score as an indicator of one reading ability becomes more problematic.

Item response theory (IRT) models provide powerful tools for examining such assumptions. Unlike classical test theory, which focuses primarily on total scores, reliability coefficients, and item statistics that are sample dependent, IRT models evaluate the relationship between latent ability and the probability of item success (Embretson, 1996). Parametric IRT models, such as the Rasch model and two- or three-parameter logistic models, impose specific mathematical forms on item response functions. These models can provide detailed information about item difficulty, discrimination, and fit, but their assumptions may be restrictive for some real test data. Nonparametric IRT models offer an alternative by making fewer assumptions about the exact shape of item response functions while still allowing researchers to examine whether items order persons along a latent continuum.

Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) is a nonparametric IRT approach originally developed by Mokken (1971, 2011) and later elaborated by Mokken and Lewis (1982), Sijtsma and Molenaar (2002), and Sijtsma and van der Ark (2016). MSA can be viewed as a probabilistic extension of Guttman scaling and is especially useful for evaluating whether a set of dichotomous or polytomous items forms an ordinal scale. One of its main models, the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM), assumes unidimensionality, local independence, and monotonicity. Unidimensionality means that the items measure a single latent trait; local independence means that item responses are independent after controlling for that trait; and monotonicity means that the probability of a correct or positive response does not decrease as the level of the latent trait increases. If these assumptions are adequately met, the total score can be used to order persons on the latent trait, at least at an ordinal level.

A central feature of MSA is the scalability coefficient H, which indicates the extent to which items form a hierarchical and coherent scale. Item scalability coefficients, item-pair scalability coefficients, and overall scale scalability coefficients can be used to evaluate individual items and the scale as a whole. Mokken (1971) suggested that H values below .30 indicate that items do not form a useful scale, values from .30 to .40 indicate a weak scale, values from .40 to .50 a medium scale, and values above .50 a strong scale. MSA also includes diagnostic tools for examining monotonicity and procedures for identifying dimensionality, such as the automated item selection procedure (AISP). The AISP partitions items into one or more scales based on a chosen lower-bound value for item scalability, while also identifying items that do not scale well with others (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). Because MSA is less restrictive than parametric IRT, relatively accessible computationally, and directly relevant to questions of item ordering and dimensionality, it has become increasingly popular in educational and psychological measurement.

MSA has been applied in a wide range of fields, including psychology, health sciences, political science, criminology, sociology, marketing, and educational measurement. For example, Palmgren et al. (2018) introduced MSA as a pragmatic approach for exploring the psychometric properties and dimensional structure of an educational environment measure and showed how it could reveal weaknesses in scale structure that might remain hidden in more routine analyses. In educational assessment, MSA has been used to examine rating scales, test items, and questionnaire data, particularly where researchers are interested in the ordinal measurement properties of instruments (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016). Despite its usefulness, MSA remains underused in second language testing and assessment. Much validation work in language testing has relied on classical reliability estimates, factor analysis, Rasch modelling, or other parametric IRT models, whereas nonparametric approaches have received comparatively little attention.

The small body of MSA research in language assessment suggests that the method can yield valuable validity evidence. Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) used MSA to investigate a 20-item reading comprehension test and found that the items fitted the Monotone Homogeneity Model, had acceptable scalability, and formed a unidimensional scale according to the AISP. Their findings supported the interpretation of the total score as an ordinal indicator of reading comprehension ability. Baghaei (2021) applied the Mokken model to the listening section of IELTS and reported that the section was largely unidimensional, although some items formed a second dimension and several items were unscalable. These studies show that MSA can illuminate the internal structure of language tests and can identify items that may threaten the validity of score interpretations. However, little is known about the performance of IELTS reading items under MSA, particularly in the General Training module.

The reading section of IELTS is especially suitable for such an analysis because it uses multiple passages and a variety of item formats. Alderson (2000) noted that the use of different techniques to assess comprehension is an important feature of IELTS reading and of good reading tests more generally, since real-life reading involves responding to texts in varied ways. From a construct-representation perspective, multiple item types may broaden the range of reading behaviours elicited by a test. Yet from a psychometric perspective, they may also introduce construct-irrelevant variance if performance is influenced by item format, response procedure, or task demands rather than reading comprehension alone. For instance, matching headings, multiple-choice questions, sentence completion, true/false/not given items, and short-answer questions may require somewhat different strategies and may differ in their susceptibility to guessing, memory load, or familiarity with test methods. If such method effects are strong, items may cluster by format or task type rather than by the intended reading construct, thereby weakening the case for a single total score.

Given the high-stakes uses of IELTS scores and the relative scarcity of independent psychometric investigations of the General Training Reading module, further validation research is warranted. Evidence is needed not only about the reliability of scores but also about whether the items form a coherent scale, whether higher-ability candidates have a consistently higher probability of answering items correctly, and whether the test functions as a unidimensional measure of reading comprehension. The present study addresses this need by applying Mokken Scale Analysis to the reading comprehension section of the General Training module of IELTS. Specifically, it examines item scalability, item-pair scalability, overall scalability, monotonicity under the Monotone Homogeneity Model, dimensionality using the automated item selection procedure, and reliability through several coefficients. In doing so, the study contributes to the validation literature on IELTS and demonstrates the usefulness of nonparametric IRT methods for evaluating large-scale second language reading tests.

Bax (2013), using eye-tracking and stimulated recall, investigated the cognitive processing of candidates during IELTS reading tasks and found differences between successful and unsuccessful test takers in reading behaviours such as expeditious reading and attention to particular parts of texts and items. Such studies are important because they move beyond simple score correlations and examine whether test takers engage in processes consistent with the intended construct.

segments.text: In contemporary validity theory, validity is not considered a property of a test in isolation, but of the interpretations and uses of scores derived from it (Kane, 2013). An argument-based approach to validation requires researchers to specify the claims made on the basis of test scores and then evaluate the assumptions that connect observed performance to those claims (Kane, 1992, 2013). From a latent variable perspective, one crucial assumption is that item responses are caused, at least in part, by the intended latent attribute. Borsboom et al. (2004) argued that a test is valid for measuring an attribute if the attribute exists and variation in the attribute causally produces variation in measurement outcomes. Baghaei and Tabatabaee Yazdi (2016) further explained that fitting latent trait models can provide validity evidence because such models test whether item covariation can plausibly be attributed to a common underlying cause. If the items of a test intended to measure reading comprehension do not cohere around a common latent trait, or if they form several distinct dimensions related to item format, passage type, or subskill, then the interpretation of a single total score as an indicator of one reading ability becomes more problematic.

segments.text: Item response theory (IRT) models provide powerful tools for examining such assumptions. Unlike classical test theory, which focuses primarily on total scores, reliability coefficients, and item statistics that are sample dependent, IRT models evaluate the relationship between latent ability and the probability of item success (Embretson, 1996). Parametric IRT models, such as the Rasch model and two- or three-parameter logistic models, impose specific mathematical forms on item response functions. These models can provide detailed information about item difficulty, discrimination, and fit, but their assumptions may be restrictive for some real test data. Nonparametric IRT models offer an alternative by making fewer assumptions about the exact shape of item response functions while still allowing researchers to examine whether items order persons along a latent continuum.

segments.text:
Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) is a nonparametric IRT approach originally developed by Mokken (1971, 2011) and later elaborated by Mokken and Lewis (1982), Sijtsma and Molenaar (2002), and Sijtsma and van der Ark (2016). MSA can be viewed as a probabilistic extension of Guttman scaling and is especially useful for evaluating whether a set of dichotomous or polytomous items forms an ordinal scale. One of its main models, the Monotone Homogeneity Model (MHM), assumes unidimensionality, local independence, and monotonicity. Unidimensionality means that the items measure a single latent trait; local independence means that item responses are independent after controlling for that trait; and monotonicity means that the probability of a correct or positive response does not decrease as the level of the latent trait increases. If these assumptions are adequately met, the total score can be used to order persons on the latent trait, at least at an ordinal level.

A central feature of MSA is the scalability coefficient H, which indicates the extent to which items form a hierarchical and coherent scale. Item scalability coefficients, item-pair scalability coefficients, and overall scale scalability coefficients can be used to evaluate individual items and the scale as a whole. Mokken (1971) suggested that H values below .30 indicate that items do not form a useful scale, values from .30 to .40 indicate a weak scale, values from .40 to .50 a medium scale, and values above .50 a strong scale. MSA also includes diagnostic tools for examining monotonicity and procedures for identifying dimensionality, such as the automated item selection procedure (AISP). The AISP partitions items into one or more scales based on a chosen lower-bound value for item scalability, while also identifying items that do not scale well with others (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016).

segments.text: Because MSA is less restrictive than parametric IRT, relatively accessible computationally, and directly relevant to questions of item ordering and dimensionality, it has become increasingly popular in educational and psychological measurement.
segments.label: move_1__claiming_centrality
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the explicit popularity signal “increasingly popular” claims the centrality of MSA in measurement research.

segments.text: MSA has been applied in a wide range of fields, including psychology, health sciences, political science, criminology, sociology, marketing, and educational measurement. For example, Palmgren et al. (2018) introduced MSA as a pragmatic approach for exploring the psychometric properties and dimensional structure of an educational environment measure and showed how it could reveal weaknesses in scale structure that might remain hidden in more routine analyses. In educational assessment, MSA has been used to examine rating scales, test items, and questionnaire data, particularly where researchers are interested in the ordinal measurement properties of instruments (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016).

Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) used MSA to investigate a 20-item reading comprehension test and found that the items fitted the Monotone Homogeneity Model, had acceptable scalability, and formed a unidimensional scale according to the AISP. intros.text:
Large-scale language tests play a central role in contemporary educational, professional, and migration systems. Among them, the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) is one of the most widely used standardized tests of English proficiency, and its scores are accepted by thousands of institutions and organizations for decisions about university admission, employment, professional registration, and immigration. Because such decisions may have substantial consequences for candidates, the quality of the interpretations made from IELTS scores is a matter of continuing importance. Evidence is therefore needed not only for the overall test but also for each of its component skills, including reading, listening, writing, and speaking.

Reading comprehension is a particularly important component of second and foreign language proficiency. In academic, occupational, and everyday contexts, successful readers must construct meaning from written texts by drawing on linguistic knowledge, background knowledge, strategic processing, and the ability to integrate information across sentences and discourse units. Research on second language reading has repeatedly shown that reading comprehension is not a simple or unitary performance. It involves the interaction of lower-level processes, such as word recognition and syntactic parsing, with higher-level processes, such as inferencing, discourse integration, and the use of background knowledge (Grabe, 2009; Perfetti et al., n.d.). Vocabulary and grammar knowledge have also been shown to predict second language reading ability, although vocabulary knowledge often has the stronger association with comprehension (Aryadoust & Baghaei, 2016; Zhang, 2012). Similarly, decoding, text type, reader characteristics, and features of the assessment task can influence reading comprehension performance (García & Cain, 2014). These findings suggest that scores on reading tests may reflect several interacting sources of ability and task demand.

The assessment of reading comprehension is consequently a complex enterprise. Reading tests typically require candidates to read one or more passages and answer questions designed to elicit evidence of comprehension. However, the particular methods used to assess comprehension may shape performance. Alderson (2000) noted that good reading tests often employ a variety of techniques because real-life reading involves varied responses to texts. Such variety may increase authenticity and broaden the sampling of reading behaviours, but it can also introduce construct-irrelevant variance if test performance is affected by features other than the intended reading ability. In the IELTS reading test, candidates encounter different text types and item formats, and these may require different cognitive operations. Work on IELTS reading has shown that test takers’ processes and performance may vary across items and tasks. For example, Bax (2013), using eye-tracking evidence, found differences between successful and unsuccessful IELTS candidates in their reading behaviours, including expeditious reading and attention to particular parts of items and texts. Moore et al. (2011) also examined the construct validity of the IELTS academic reading test by comparing reading requirements in IELTS items and university study, highlighting the importance of aligning test tasks with the target domain.

Concerns about reading test validity are closely related to broader theories of measurement and validation. Validity is not a property that can be assumed simply because a test is widely used; rather, it concerns the extent to which evidence and theory support the interpretations and uses of scores. In an argument-based approach, validation involves evaluating the plausibility of the inferences that connect observed responses to score interpretations and decisions (Kane, 1992, 2013). From a latent variable perspective, a test may be considered valid for measuring an attribute when the attribute exists and variation in the attribute causally produces variation in test outcomes (Borsboom et al., 2004; Borsboom, 2005). Fitting a latent trait model to test data can therefore provide validity evidence because it examines whether item responses behave as expected under assumptions about a common underlying construct (Baghaei & Tabatabaee Yazdi, 2016). If items intended to measure the same ability do not cohere, or if responses are affected by multiple unrelated sources, the interpretation of total scores becomes less straightforward.

Item response theory (IRT) models are widely used for examining such issues in educational and psychological measurement. Compared with classical test theory, model-based approaches provide more detailed information about the relationship between persons, items, and the latent trait being measured (Embretson, 1996). Parametric IRT models, such as the Rasch model and two-parameter models, specify particular mathematical forms for item response functions and can be powerful tools for evaluating item difficulty, discrimination, and model fit. However, their assumptions may be restrictive for some testing contexts. Nonparametric IRT models offer an alternative when researchers wish to examine the ordering and scalability of items without imposing strong parametric assumptions.

Mokken Scale Analysis (MSA) is one such nonparametric IRT approach. Originally developed by Mokken (1971, 2011), MSA provides methods for evaluating whether a set of items forms a scale that can order persons on an underlying latent trait. Mokken and Lewis (1982) described this approach as a natural generalization of Guttman scaling and classical test theory, based on ordinal assumptions about item response probabilities. The most commonly used model in MSA is the Monotone Homogeneity Model, which assumes unidimensionality, local independence, and monotonicity. Monotonicity means that the probability of a correct response to an item should not decrease as the level of the latent trait increases. When these assumptions are sufficiently supported, total scores can be used to order test takers on an ordinal latent scale. MSA also provides scalability coefficients for items, item pairs, and the whole scale, as well as procedures such as the automated item selection procedure for detecting dimensionality and identifying unscalable items (Sijtsma & van der Ark, 2016).

In recent years, MSA has become increasingly popular in several areas of social and behavioural research. It has been used to investigate the psychometric properties and dimensional structure of questionnaires and tests in fields such as health sciences, psychology, psychiatry, education, marketing, political science, and sociology. Palmgren et al. (2018), for example, introduced MSA as a pragmatic method for exploring questionnaire data and applied it to an educational environment measure, showing how MSA can reveal weaknesses in scalability and dimensional structure. The appeal of MSA lies partly in its relative flexibility: it allows researchers to examine whether items form reliable ordinal scales without requiring the stronger assumptions of parametric IRT models. For language testing, where test performance may be shaped by complex interactions among linguistic ability, task format, topic familiarity, and strategic behaviour, such an approach may be especially useful.

Despite this potential, MSA has received limited attention in second and foreign language assessment. Much of the available psychometric research in language testing has relied on classical reliability indices, factor analysis, Rasch measurement, or other parametric IRT models. Although these approaches have contributed substantially to validation research, the use of MSA remains comparatively rare. A small number of studies have begun to demonstrate its relevance. Tabatabaee-Yazdi, Motallebzadeh, and Baghaei (2021) applied MSA to a 20-item English reading comprehension test and found that the items formed a unidimensional scale, with adequate fit to the Monotone Homogeneity Model. Their findings suggested that the test could order students appropriately with respect to reading comprehension ability. Baghaei (2021) used the monotone homogeneity model to examine the listening section of IELTS and reported that the listening test was largely unidimensional, although two items formed a second dimension and four items were unscalable. These studies suggest that MSA can provide useful validity evidence for language tests, but they also indicate that additional research is required across different skills, modules, and testing contexts.

The need for such research is particularly evident in relation to IELTS. Although IELTS has been the subject of many studies, much of the published work has focused on test preparation, candidates’ perceptions, cognitive processing, score use, or the Academic module. Clapham (1996), for instance, investigated the development of IELTS and the role of background knowledge in reading comprehension, raising the question of whether reading scores reflect reading ability alone or also knowledge of the subject matter. Pearson (2019) examined candidate performance and perceptions of failure in IELTS, showing the high stakes attached to score outcomes and the degree to which candidates may question the accuracy or fairness of results. While such studies contribute to the broader validity argument for IELTS, there remains a need for detailed psychometric analyses of particular test components. The General Training Reading module, in particular, has received relatively little attention compared with the Academic Reading module, even though it is used for important migration and professional purposes.

A further issue concerns the dimensionality of the IELTS reading section. Reading comprehension tests often report a single total score, and such a score is most interpretable when the items primarily reflect a common underlying construct. However, IELTS reading tasks use multiple item formats and text types, and these features may introduce method effects. If items cluster according to format, passage, cognitive operation, or some other task characteristic, the test may be multidimensional even when it is designed to measure general reading comprehension. This possibility does not necessarily mean that the test is unusable, but it complicates score interpretation. A test may be reliable while still containing dimensions that reflect construct-irrelevant or construct-related subskills. Therefore, examining unidimensionality, scalability, and monotonicity is important for understanding what the reading score represents.

The present study addresses this need by applying Mokken Scale Analysis to the reading comprehension section of the General Training module of IELTS. Specifically, it examines whether the 40 reading items form a scalable and sufficiently unidimensional measure of reading comprehension, whether the items satisfy the monotonicity assumption of the Monotone Homogeneity Model, and whether any items form separate scales or fail to scale with the rest of the test. To this end, item responses from 352 EFL university students were analysed using MSA procedures, including item and total scalability coefficients, item-pair scalability coefficients, monotonicity checks, and the automated item selection procedure. By using a nonparametric IRT framework, the study seeks to provide validity evidence for score interpretation in the General Training IELTS reading test and to contribute to the still limited body of research applying MSA in second language testing.

segments.text: Although IELTS has been the subject of many studies, much of the published work has focused on test preparation, candidates’ perceptions, cognitive processing, score use, or the Academic module. Clapham (1996), for instance, investigated the development of IELTS and the role of background knowledge in reading comprehension, raising the question of whether reading scores reflect reading ability alone or also knowledge of the subject matter. Pearson (2019) examined candidate performance and perceptions of failure in IELTS, showing the high stakes attached to score outcomes and the degree to which candidates may question the accuracy or fairness of results.
segments.label: move_1__reviewing_items_of_previous_research
segments.rationale: Move 1 Establishing a Territory: the segment reviews previous IELTS research, including cited studies by Clapham and Pearson.

segments.text: While such studies contribute to the broader validity argument for IELTS, there remains a need for detailed psychometric analyses of particular test components. The General Training Reading module, in particular, has received relatively little attention compared with the Academic Reading module, even though it is used for important migration and professional purposes.
segments.label: move_2__indicating_a_gap
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the niche is established by “there remains a need” and “has received relatively little attention” for the General Training Reading module.

segments.text: A further issue concerns the dimensionality of the IELTS reading section. Reading comprehension tests often report a single total score, and such a score is most interpretable when the items primarily reflect a common underlying construct. However, IELTS reading tasks use multiple item formats and text types, and these features may introduce method effects. If items cluster according to format, passage, cognitive operation, or some other task characteristic, the test may be multidimensional even when it is designed to measure general reading comprehension. This possibility does not necessarily mean that the test is unusable, but it complicates score interpretation. A test may be reliable while still containing dimensions that reflect construct-irrelevant or construct-related subskills. Therefore, examining unidimensionality, scalability, and monotonicity is important for understanding what the reading score represents.
segments.label: move_2__question_raising
segments.rationale: Move 2 Establishing a Niche: the segment raises an unresolved issue about dimensionality and method effects in IELTS reading, culminating in the need to examine unidimensionality, scalability, and monotonicity.

segments.text: The present study addresses this need by applying Mokken Scale Analysis to the reading comprehension section of the General Training module of IELTS. Specifically, it examines whether the 40 reading items form a scalable and sufficiently unidimensional measure of reading comprehension, whether the items satisfy the monotonicity assumption of the Monotone Homogeneity Model, and whether any items form separate scales or fail to scale with the rest of the test.
segments.label: move_3__outlining_purpose
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the phrases “The present study addresses this need” and “Specifically, it examines whether” state the study’s purpose and research questions.

segments.text: To this end, item responses from 352 EFL university students were analysed using MSA procedures, including item and total scalability coefficients, item-pair scalability coefficients, monotonicity checks, and the automated item selection procedure.
segments.label: move_3__announcing_present_research
segments.rationale: Move 3 Occupying the Niche: the methodological details about participants, item responses, and MSA procedures announce how the present research was conducted.

segments.text: By using a nonparametric IRT framework, the study seeks to provide validity evidence for score interpretation in the General Training IELTS reading test and to contribute to the still limited body of research applying MSA in second language testing.

In this changing space of communication, some distinguishing features such as immediacy and dialogicity emerge. In fact, the bidirectional and instantaneous nature of today's interactions differ to a great extent from traditional written communication, many times considered old-fashioned or dysfunctional in our new reality Printed genres offer rather fixed and foreseeable discursive practices which require more time, present limitations of space, and emphasize other features such  as the accuracy of the message. That is why digital genres are taking over in everyday communication, and have set more dialogic ways of interacting in the web.  The Internet has triggered a broader spectrum as regards writing or discursive practices, since the distinctions between the spoken and the written modes are also blurred in digital communication (Mauranen 2016). Thus, paper-based gentes are giving way to digital genres in a great deal of contexts, attracting more and more scholarly attention due to their advantages.  The web engages the users in a digital environment frequently dominated by orality and multimodality. These new modes of communication are reshaping the spoken and written registers and reflect specific lexico-grammatical, discursive and pragmatic features.  In other words, the combination of different codes such as audio, video or pictures has been brought to the fore and is essential in digital gentes (Richardson 2009), including those hosted in travel blogs. Closely related to the spread of digital genres is the use of English as a vehicular language enabling digital communication. More specifically, this research seeks to provide an answer to the following research questions:  1. What is the main communicative purpose of travel blogs posts?  2. intros.text:
The technological developments of the last decades have profoundly reshaped the ways in which people communicate. The Internet, and more specifically the array of digital applications it hosts, has generated new communicative modes that foster immediacy, interactivity and dialogicity to an extent unimaginable in the era of exclusively printed genres. Within this dynamic panorama, the blog has emerged as a particularly rich and versatile space, one where different sub-genres converge and where users from a diversity of linguacultural backgrounds meet, exchange contents and construct relationships. Understanding how such digital environments work, and what they demand from those who write and read in them, has therefore become a pressing concern for applied linguistics and, in particular, for the study of computer-mediated communication.

A defining trait of these online spaces is that the language most frequently mobilised in them is English, employed not so much as a native tongue but as a lingua franca (ELF) that enables speakers with different first languages to interact across borders. Research into ELF has evolved considerably, moving from an early preoccupation with form towards an understanding of ELF as social practice enacted by its users (Jenkins, 2015; Seidlhofer, 2011). Increasing attention has been paid to how ELF operates in academic and professional settings (Mauranen, 2012), and, more recently, to its distinctly virtual manifestations, where transcultural, transmodal and translingual practices come to the fore (Seidlhofer, 2011). Yet the interplay between ELF and the emergent digital genres in which it circulates remains comparatively under-explored, especially regarding how speakers from Anglophone and non-Anglophone contexts alike appropriate a given digital genre and shape its discursive and rhetorical conventions.

At the same time, digital communication is known to reconfigure the linguistic resources speakers draw upon. Herring (2012) has shown that electronic communication often deviates from strict syntactic norms, producing telegraphic or fragmented messages, and that it manifests loosened orthographic practices. Such observations suggest that the study of digital genres cannot rely solely on categories inherited from the description of printed texts; instead, it calls for approaches that are sensitive to the orality, informality and multimodality that characterise online interaction. The blog, precisely because of its malleability and its capacity to host multiple sub-genres, provides a productive site to observe these tendencies in action (Richardson, 2010).

Among the many types of blog, the travel blog stands out as an especially telling case. It is a genre built around the sharing of experiences, opinions and practical information about destinations, and it thrives on the participation of a global readership that is willing not only to read but also to comment, question and contribute. Travel bloggers routinely interweave descriptions of external events—places, sights, festivities—with anecdotes and emotions drawn from their personal lives, blending professional and social dimensions of their online identities. Because travel blogs bring together writers and readers from very different linguacultural origins who communicate through English, they constitute a natural laboratory for examining how ELF is used to build and sustain a virtual discourse community, and for observing whether native and non-native speakers exploit the genre in the same way.

This paper sets out to analyse the sub-genre of the post as hosted in travel blogs, with a threefold aim. First, it seeks to identify the salient linguistic and discursive features that characterise travel blog posts, adopting a data-driven approach in which the corpus itself is the source of hypotheses about language. Second, it aims to uncover the rhetorical structure of these posts through a functional analysis of their moves, purposes and realisations, so as to sketch the prototypical skeleton that both writers and readers implicitly recognise. Third, it examines whether meaningful differences exist between speakers belonging to Kachru's inner, outer and expanding circles, thereby throwing light on how the ELF blogosphere makes use of this digital sub-genre and on what its readership may expect when communicating through it.

To address these questions, the study draws on frameworks from descriptive grammar, speech act theory and metadiscourse analysis, and applies them to a small-scale but linguaculturally diverse corpus of travel blog posts together with their accompanying comments and authorial replies. By situating the travel blog within current understandings of genre as a dynamic and flexible entity, and within accounts of virtual discourse communities and ELF as social practice, the analysis intends to contribute to a better comprehension of the rationale underlying this digital genre. In doing so, it hopes to clarify how communicative purposes are conveyed through specific linguistic and discursive choices, and how a shared rhetorical structure enables users of different origins to participate in one and the same global virtual community.
