intros.text:
The digital world has profoundly reshaped the ways in which people communicate, opening up a wealth of opportunities for more immediate, dialogical and collaborative interaction. Within this ever-shifting panorama, communication is no longer confined to the relatively stable, unidirectional patterns that characterised printed genres; rather, it unfolds through emergent digital modes that are dynamic, malleable and constantly under (re)construction. New communicative technologies do not merely provide fresh channels for messages: they are also reconfiguring language itself, its conventions and the expectations that speakers and readers bring to their interactions. As Herring (2012) notes, how new digital communication technologies are affecting language and language change has excited considerable speculation and inspired a growing body of scholarship, and this interest continues to expand as digital genres proliferate and diversify.

A central feature of these digital communicative practices is that they routinely bring together speakers from distinct linguacultural backgrounds who interact through English used as a lingua franca (ELF). The study of ELF has developed remarkably in a relatively short period, moving from an early, form-oriented focus towards an understanding of ELF as social practice and, more recently, towards a retheorisation of its essentially multilingual nature (Jenkins, 2015). Scholars have explored ELF in relation to culture and identity (Jenkins et al., 2007), academic contexts shaped by non-native speakers (Mauranen, 2012), and the challenges it poses for established linguistic concepts (Widdowson, 2019). Of particular relevance here is the notion of virtual English as a lingua franca (Seidlhofer, 2011), which highlights how becoming an effective communicator online increasingly entails transcultural, translingual and transmodal competences. The digital environment, then, is precisely one of the spaces where ELF is being negotiated and enacted on a daily basis by international users.

Among the many digital genres now available, the blog stands out as a particularly resourceful and sophisticated communicative space. Blogs offer a collaborative platform where a piece of discourse can be composed and simultaneously shared with others who may find it relevant or engaging (Richardson, 2010). They function almost as a tabula rasa, free from constraints of length and open to a wide range of contents, layouts and multimodal resources, and they are characterised by malleability, periodicity and non-linearity. Crucially, the blog is not a single, monolithic genre but a genre colony within which several sub-genres converge and interconnect: the post, the comment and the reply are sequentially dependent, forming genre chains that give the blog its distinctive rationale. It is within this hospitable environment that speakers from inner, outer and expanding circles of English coexist and communicate, building cross-linguistic virtual communities.

Despite the growing scholarly attention devoted to both ELF and computer-mediated communication, the specific discursive and rhetorical workings of travel blog posts as an ELF genre remain comparatively underexplored. Much research has examined the grammar of electronic communication in general terms, yet relatively little is known about how the sub-genre of the travel post is actually realised linguistically and structured rhetorically, and even less about whether and how these realisations differ across speakers of diverse linguacultural backgrounds who share English as their means of communication. If we are to begin comprehending the rationale of the blog as a whole, it seems necessary to start from a close, data-driven examination of one of its most representative sub-genres and of the ways in which the ELF blogosphere makes use of it.

Accordingly, the present study sets out to analyse the sub-genre of the travel blog post along two complementary lines. First, it explores the prominent linguistic and discursive features encapsulated in travel posts through a data-driven approach, identifying tendencies in lexis, grammar, orthotypography and pragmatics and paying particular attention to potential differences between Anglophone and non-Anglophone users, organised according to Kachru's circles of English. Second, it identifies the rhetorical structure of these posts by means of a functional move analysis, relating the moves and their communicative purposes to the linguistic and discursive realisations previously observed. To pursue these aims, a small-scale corpus of eighteen entries drawn from six travel blogs written by bloggers from inner, outer and expanding circles was compiled and examined qualitatively. In doing so, the study seeks to shed light on how travel bloggers and their readers, as members of a shared global virtual community, communicate digitally through English, and on what readers may reasonably expect when engaging with this increasingly oral, dialogical and informal digital genre.

intros.text:
The rapid evolution of the digital landscape has fundamentally transformed the ways in which individuals interact, introducing new modes of communication that prioritize immediacy, dialogicity, and global connectivity. Within this digital ecosystem, the blog has emerged as a sophisticated and versatile genre, acting as a convergence point for various sub-genres and a hub for diverse discourse communities. Because blogs transcend geographical and cultural boundaries, they frequently serve as a primary site for communication between speakers of different linguacultural backgrounds who utilize English as a Lingua Franca (ELF). This phenomenon reflects a broader shift in applied linguistics, where English is no longer viewed solely through the lens of native-speaker norms but as a social practice used by a global community to achieve mutual intelligibility and shared goals (Jenkins, 2015).

The rise of the 'blogosphere' has given birth to what may be termed Virtual English as a Lingua Franca (VELF). In these virtual spaces, communication is characterized by transmodal and translingual practices, requiring users to develop a specific meta-competence to manage rapport within heterogeneous social formations (Seidlhofer, 2011). Unlike traditional printed genres, digital communication often manifests a loosening of established orthographic and syntactic norms, creating a hybrid style that blends written precision with the spontaneity of oral discourse (Herring, 2012). As English continues to be shaped by its non-native users in academic and social spheres (Mauranen, 2012), there is a growing need to analyze how these users negotiate meaning and identity in digital environments (Jenkins et al., 2007).

Among the various types of blogs, travel blogs represent a particularly rich area for linguistic inquiry. These blogs function as collaborative spaces where authors share personal experiences, provide practical data, and express subjective emotions to a global audience (Richardson, 2010). The travel blog post, as a specific sub-genre, is designed to provide trustworthy information and personal anecdotes, blending professional guidance with individual identity. However, despite the proliferation of travel content online, there is a paucity of research specifically examining the discursive features and rhetorical structures employed by a diverse range of ELF users within this genre. While some scholars have questioned the stability of established linguistic concepts in the face of ELF (Widdowson, 2019), the way in which travel bloggers from different "circles" of English proficiency—inner, outer, and expanding—utilize the genre remains under-explored.

Understanding the generic features of the travel blog is essential for comprehending how virtual communities are constructed and maintained. If a genre is defined by its communicative purpose, then the travel blog post serves to bridge the gap between the traveler's lived experience and the reader's desire for exploration. The flexibility of the digital medium allows for a non-linear navigating mode, where the use of hypertexts, images, and a casual register fosters a sense of closeness and trust between the writer and the readership. To fully grasp the rationale of this digital sub-genre, it is necessary to identify the recurring lexico-grammatical patterns and the underlying rhetorical moves that constitute a typical travel post.

Therefore, the present study aims to analyze the discursive features and rhetorical structure of travel blog posts authored by English speakers from diverse linguacultural backgrounds. By employing a data-driven approach, the research seeks to uncover the prominent linguistic markers—such as self-mentions, attitude markers, and non-standard orthography—that characterize these texts. Furthermore, through a functional analysis, the study intends to identify a prototypical rhetorical skeleton that guides the communicative intent of the blogger. By comparing the practices of native and non-native speakers, this paper hopes to illustrate how the ELF blogosphere adapts the travel genre to meet the needs of a globalized, digitally-mediated community. Ultimately, this analysis will provide insights into what readers expect when interacting with digital travel content and how the flexibility of ELF contributes to the dynamism of emergent digital genres.

intros.text:
The contemporary digital landscape has ushered in transformative modes of communication, fostering opportunities for more immediate, dialogical, and interactive exchanges. Among these, the blog has emerged as a sophisticated and resourceful genre where various communicative sub-genres converge. In the globalized context of the internet, blogs serve as vital hubs where speakers from diverse linguacultural backgrounds interact, frequently employing English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) to bridge communicative gaps. This phenomenon reflects a broader shift in linguistic practice, where English is no longer viewed solely through the lens of native-speaker norms but as a social practice shaped by its users in intercultural encounters (Jenkins, 2015).

Recent scholarship has highlighted how digital technologies are fundamentally altering language and language change (Herring, 2012). The emergence of Virtual English as a Lingua Franca (VELF) has necessitated new competencies, including transcultural and transmodal practices, to manage rapport within heterogeneous social formations (Seidlhofer, 2011). Furthermore, the use of ELF in digital spaces often involves a negotiation of identity and culture, as users leverage the language to construct shared meanings across borders (Jenkins et al., 2007). In academic and professional spheres, the influence of non-native speakers in shaping the evolution of English is increasingly recognized, suggesting that the 'norms' of the language are becoming more fluid and data-driven (Mauranen, 2012; Mauranen, 2016). These shifts are particularly evident in the 'blogosphere,' where the flexibility of the medium allows for an intersection of professional and personal discourse, often defying traditional orthographic and syntactic constraints (Richardson, 2010).

Despite the proliferation of digital genres and the growing body of research on ELF, there remains a relative scarcity of empirical studies focusing specifically on the intersection of ELF and the rhetorical structures of digital travel narratives. While much has been written about the general characteristics of computer-mediated communication, little is known about how bloggers from different 'circles' of English proficiency—ranging from native speakers to those in the expanding circle—utilize specific discursive features to achieve their communicative goals in travel posts. It remains unclear whether there are significant discrepancies in the linguistic strategies employed by Anglophone and non-Anglophone users, or if a shared, conventionalized rhetorical framework exists that transcends linguacultural origins. Thus, more research is needed to determine how the functional demands of the travel blog genre influence the linguistic choices of ELF users.

Addressing this gap, the present study aims to analyze the discursive features and rhetorical structure of travel blog posts written in English. Specifically, the research seeks to identify the most prominent lexico-grammatical and pragmatic markers used by bloggers and to investigate whether these features vary according to the author's linguacultural background. Furthermore, the study intends to map the prototypical rhetorical structure of the travel post to understand how its various 'moves' facilitate the communicative purpose of sharing travel experiences and engaging a global audience. 

To achieve these objectives, a data-driven approach is adopted, utilizing a representative corpus of 18 entries from six international travel blogs. These blogs were selected to represent Kachru's Inner, Outer, and Expanding circles of English, providing a holistic view of the ELF blogosphere. The analysis employs a functional approach to identify the rhetorical stages of the posts and utilizes frameworks from speech act theory and metadiscourse analysis to categorize linguistic features. The findings are expected to reveal that while specific linguistic resources—such as acronyms or vague language—may vary by user background, the overarching rhetorical structure of the travel post is largely conventionalized across the global virtual community. This study ultimately contributes to a deeper understanding of how digital genres are enacted in ELF contexts and what readership expectations characterize this mode of communication.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 establishes the theoretical framework, exploring the notions of genre, virtual discourse communities, and the specific nature of the travel blog. Section 3 details the methodology, including the corpus selection and the data-driven analytical approach. Section 4 presents the analysis and discussion of the linguistic and discursive features, followed by a qualitative examination of the rhetorical structure. Finally, Section 5 provides concluding remarks and suggestions for future research.

intros.text:
The rapid evolution of digital communication technologies has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of language use, offering new modes of interaction that are immediate, dialogical, and often informal. Within this digital sphere, the blog has emerged as a sophisticated and resourceful genre, facilitating communication among speakers from diverse linguacultural backgrounds who frequently employ English as a lingua franca (ELF). As Herring (2012) notes, new digital technologies have significantly impacted language and language change, inspiring a growing body of scholarship dedicated to understanding these shifts. However, while the potential of digital genres for intercultural communication is widely acknowledged, there remains a need to explore the specific discursive features and rhetorical structures that characterize sub-genres such as travel blog posts.

The concept of English as a lingua franca has gained substantial traction in applied linguistics, moving beyond a focus on form to consider the social practices and processes underlying communication. Jenkins (2015) argues that ELF requires further retheorisation to account for its essentially multilingual nature, emphasizing the role of ELF users and their communicative strategies. In the context of virtual communication, Seidlhofer (2011) highlights the importance of developing a meta-(V)ELF competence, which involves managing rapport with members of heterogeneous social formations through transcultural, transmodal, and translingual practices. This perspective is particularly relevant when analyzing the blogosphere, where users from the Inner, Outer, and Expanding circles of English interact within a shared digital space.

Blogs, as a digital genre, are characterized by their malleability and the convergence of various sub-genres. Richardson (2010) describes blogs as powerful web tools that can enhance information literacy and facilitate professional development, yet their role in fostering global virtual communities through ELF is less explored. The travel blog, in particular, serves as a platform where personal narratives intersect with practical information, creating a unique communicative environment. This environment is shaped by the expectations of a virtual discourse community that values immediacy, informality, and interaction. As Mauranen (2016) points out, the design and analysis of ELF corpora present both difficulties and triumphs, particularly when capturing the nuances of naturally occurring digital communication.

Despite the growing interest in digital genres and ELF, there is a paucity of research that systematically analyzes the linguistic and discursive features of travel blog posts. Existing studies have often focused on academic ELF or specific professional contexts, leaving the informal, user-generated content of the blogosphere relatively underexamined. Widdowson (2019) suggests that established concepts in linguistics can sometimes be inconvenient when applied to the fluid realities of ELF, necessitating a fresh approach to genre analysis. Furthermore, the rhetorical structure of travel blog posts remains largely uncharted, with few studies attempting to identify the prototypical moves that guide the narrative and engage the readership.

This study aims to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of travel blog posts from a data-driven perspective. Specifically, it seeks to identify the prominent linguistic and discursive features encapsulated in these posts and to determine their rhetorical structure through a functional analysis. By examining a corpus of travel blog posts authored by speakers from different linguacultural backgrounds, this research will shed light on how the ELF blogosphere utilizes this digital sub-genre. The analysis will explore whether there are significant differences in the use of linguistic resources between native and non-native English speakers, and how these differences reflect the communicative goals of the authors.

Understanding the rationale of the travel blog is crucial for comprehending the broader dynamics of digital communication in an increasingly globalized world. As Jenkins et al. (2007) note, culture and identity are deeply intertwined with ELF, and the blog serves as a medium through which these elements are negotiated and expressed. By analyzing the discursive features and rhetorical structure of travel blog posts, this study contributes to the ongoing dialogue about the nature of digital genres and the role of ELF in shaping intercultural interactions. Ultimately, the findings will offer insights into what readers may expect when engaging with travel blogs, thereby enhancing our understanding of the expectations and norms that govern this dynamic communicative space.

intros.text:
The digital landscape has fundamentally reshaped how individuals communicate, offering new modes of interaction that are more immediate and dialogical than traditional media. Within this evolving environment, the blog has emerged as a sophisticated and resourceful genre, facilitating communication across diverse linguacultural backgrounds through English as a Lingua Franca (ELF). As Seidlhofer (2011) notes, effective communication in virtual English as a lingua franca (VELF) is a crucial skill for the twenty-first century, requiring users to navigate transcultural and transmodal practices. Consequently, understanding the linguistic and discursive mechanisms that underpin these digital interactions is vital for comprehending the contemporary communicative landscape. The blog, specifically, serves as a convergence point for various sub-genres, allowing speakers from different backgrounds to coexist and interact within a shared virtual discourse community.

The concept of genre has evolved significantly to accommodate these digital realities. While Swales (1990) originally defined genre as a class of communicative events sharing specific purposes, the dynamic nature of digital communication has challenged the stability of these definitions. Pérez-Llantada (2013) argues that genres and media are now deeply integrated, characterized by flexibility and dynamism rather than rigid structures. This evolution is particularly evident in the blogosphere, where the travel blog post stands out as a distinct sub-genre. Travel blogs aim to provide readers with trustworthy information, personal experiences, and recommendations regarding specific destinations (Lee & Gretzel, 2014). These texts function within a virtual discourse community where members share norms and values, yet they are bounded by the global discourse system of English speakers in intercultural encounters.

Despite the growing interest in digital genres and ELF, there remains a gap in the empirical analysis of how these two domains intersect in specific sub-genres like travel blogs. Herring (2012) highlights that new digital technologies are affecting language and language change, inspiring a growing body of scholarship. However, much of this research has focused on general electronic communication or academic contexts, such as Mauranen's (2012) work on academic English shaped by non-native speakers. Jenkins (2015) further suggests that ELF research needs retheorization to foreground its multilingual nature, yet specific investigations into the rhetorical and linguistic features of informal digital genres remain limited. Furthermore, while Richardson (2010) has explored the pedagogical potential of blogs, the specific discursive features and rhetorical structures that characterize travel blog posts in an ELF context have not been sufficiently examined. It is unclear how bloggers from different linguacultural backgrounds—specifically those from the inner, outer, and expanding circles of English usage—employ linguistic resources to achieve their communicative goals within this genre.

This study aims to address this gap by analyzing the discursive features, rhetorical structure, and use of ELF in travel blog posts. Specifically, it investigates the linguistic and discursive prominent features encapsulated in these posts through a data-driven approach and identifies their rhetorical structure via functional analysis. The research seeks to answer three primary questions: What are the salient linguistic and discursive features of travel blog posts? How do these features vary across bloggers from different linguacultural backgrounds? And what is the prototypical rhetorical structure of the travel blog post? By compiling a corpus of travel blogs from native and non-native speakers, this study provides a contextualized account of emergent writing practices in the ELF blogosphere. The findings offer insights into how the digital sub-genre is utilized and what readership may expect when communicating digitally through it, ultimately contributing to a better understanding of the interplay between digital genres and English as a Lingua Franca.

intros.text:
Digital communication has transformed the conditions under which texts are produced, circulated and interpreted. The Internet has enabled increasingly immediate, dialogic and multimodal forms of interaction, where users do not simply consume information but participate in its production, evaluation and redistribution. These developments have also affected the linguistic shape of communication: electronic discourse often displays informal, speech-like and visually salient features, including syntactic reduction, non-standard orthography, abbreviations and other resources associated with conversational involvement (Herring, 2012). At the same time, digital environments have created spaces where participants from diverse linguacultural backgrounds meet and interact through English, frequently not as a native language but as a shared means of communication. In this sense, online discourse is a particularly productive site for examining English as a lingua franca (ELF), understood not as a fixed variety but as a flexible, situated and multilingual social practice (Jenkins, 2007, 2015; Seidlhofer, 2011; Mauranen, 2012).

Among the many genres that have emerged or been reshaped in digital environments, the blog occupies a distinctive position. Blogs combine personal expression, public dissemination and interaction with readers, and they allow writers to integrate verbal text with images, hyperlinks, comments and other semiotic resources. Their structure is sufficiently recognisable for users to orient themselves within them, yet flexible enough to host a range of communicative purposes and sub-genres. Richardson (2010) highlights the pedagogic and communicative potential of blogs and related Web tools, while research on computer-mediated discourse has shown that such spaces encourage new relationships between author, audience, text and medium (Herring, 2012). Blogs therefore offer a useful vantage point from which to explore how digital genres develop conventions while remaining dynamic, hybrid and open to user innovation.

Travel blogs are especially relevant in this respect. They are built around mobility, experience and intercultural encounter, and they commonly address an audience that seeks both practical information and personal evaluation. A travel blogger may describe destinations, narrate anecdotes, assess accommodation or transport, recommend routes, reflect on cultural practices, and invite readers to respond with their own views or questions. This mixture of information, narration, evaluation and interaction makes the travel blog a rich object for genre analysis. Moreover, because travel is itself associated with cross-cultural contact, travel blogs frequently bring together writers and readers who do not share the same first language or cultural background. English often functions as the medium through which these interactions become possible, making the travel blogosphere a useful context for analysing ELF practices in naturally occurring digital communication.

The study of ELF has moved from an early concern with formal linguistic features towards a broader interest in communicative processes, identity, multilingual repertoires and social practices (Jenkins, 2015; Mauranen, 2016). This shift is particularly important for digital communication, where users draw on multiple linguistic, pragmatic and semiotic resources to establish rapport, express stance and negotiate meaning. Seidlhofer (2011) points to the importance of “virtual English as a lingua franca” as part of contemporary communicative competence, while Widdowson (2019) reminds us that ELF challenges established assumptions about English, norms and ownership. In online settings, such questions become especially visible: native and non-native users may participate in the same virtual communities, adopt similar genre conventions, and at the same time display different linguistic preferences shaped by their repertoires and experiences.

Despite growing interest in computer-mediated communication and ELF, further empirical attention is needed to the internal organisation of specific digital genres and to the linguistic resources through which global users enact them. Blogs have often been described as interactive and informal, but the sub-genre of the post, particularly in travel blogs, requires closer analysis in terms of its discursive features and rhetorical structure. It is important to understand not only what linguistic traits are salient in such posts, but also how these traits contribute to the communicative purposes expected by the virtual community: situating an experience, describing a destination, evaluating events, offering recommendations and inviting reader participation.

This paper therefore analyses travel blog posts as a digital sub-genre used by English speakers from different linguacultural backgrounds. It explores the prominent linguistic, discursive, pragmatic and orthotypographic features of a corpus of travel blog posts, and examines whether these features vary according to the writers’ position as inner-, outer- or expanding-circle users of English. It also identifies the prototypical rhetorical moves through which travel posts are organised and considers how these moves relate to the communicative purposes of the genre. By combining a data-driven analysis of recurrent features with a functional analysis of rhetorical structure, the study aims to contribute to a better understanding of how the ELF blogosphere uses travel posts and of what readers may expect when engaging with this digital genre.

intros.text:
Digital communication has transformed the ways in which people produce, circulate and negotiate meanings. Networked environments enable more immediate, dialogical and multimodal exchanges than many traditional written genres, and they have consequently become a privileged site for observing ongoing changes in language use. As Herring (2012) notes, electronic communication has generated substantial interest because it raises questions about grammar, discourse, interaction and language change. These questions become especially relevant when digital interaction takes place in English among users who do not necessarily share the same first language or cultural background. In such contexts, English functions less as the property of a single native-speaker community than as a flexible communicative resource used across linguacultural boundaries.

Research on English as a lingua franca (ELF) has progressively shifted attention from identifying formal deviations from native-speaker norms to understanding ELF as social practice. Jenkins (2007, 2015), Seidlhofer (2011) and Mauranen (2012, 2016) have shown that ELF communication is shaped by users’ situated purposes, multilingual repertoires and interactional needs. This perspective is particularly productive for the study of online communication, where interlocutors from different backgrounds often collaborate, negotiate rapport and exploit the affordances of digital media. Virtual ELF communication therefore calls for analyses that consider not only linguistic forms, but also the discursive, pragmatic and generic choices through which users build relationships and achieve communicative goals.

Among digital genres, the blog occupies a distinctive position. Blogs offer a flexible space for publishing personal experience, practical information and evaluative commentary, while also encouraging response and interaction through comments and links. They may include other digital resources and sub-genres, and their communicative value depends on the expectations of the virtual communities that use them. Richardson (2010) describes blogs and related web tools as powerful environments for sharing information and constructing knowledge, and their relevance extends beyond educational settings to everyday digital practices. The blog is thus a useful object for examining how genre conventions are maintained, adapted or reconfigured in online discourse.

Travel blogs are especially revealing in this respect. They combine narration, description, advice, evaluation and interpersonal engagement. Travel bloggers commonly present destinations, recount personal experiences, recommend places or practices, and invite readers to respond, plan their own trips or continue exploring through hyperlinks. Because travel itself involves mobility, intercultural contact and the interpretation of unfamiliar places, travel blogs are also fertile spaces for ELF communication. Anglophone and non-Anglophone bloggers can participate in the same global blogosphere, addressing a heterogeneous readership through English and drawing on shared digital conventions to make their posts accessible, engaging and credible.

Despite the growing body of work on electronic communication and ELF, the specific sub-genre of the travel blog post has received comparatively limited attention from a combined discursive, rhetorical and ELF-oriented perspective. Much remains to be clarified about which linguistic and pragmatic features are recurrent in travel posts, how these features contribute to informality, dialogicity and reader engagement, and whether bloggers from different linguacultural backgrounds exploit them in similar or different ways. It is also unclear to what extent travel blog posts display a recognizable rhetorical organization, given the dynamic and malleable nature of digital genres. If blogs are flexible, multimodal and open-ended, it is necessary to determine whether their posts nevertheless follow conventionalized communicative stages that readers can recognize and anticipate.

Addressing these issues, the present study analyses travel blog posts as instances of digital communication in which English is used across linguacultural boundaries. It aims to identify the most salient linguistic, discursive and pragmatic features of travel blog posts; to examine possible differences in their use by bloggers from inner, outer and expanding circle contexts; and to describe the rhetorical structure through which the communicative purposes of the posts are realized. The study is guided by the following questions: What prominent linguistic and discursive features characterize travel blog posts? How are these features distributed among bloggers from different linguacultural backgrounds? What move structure can be identified in the travel blog post, and how do particular linguistic realizations contribute to its communicative purposes?

To answer these questions, a small-scale corpus of 18 entries from six travel blogs was compiled, including blogs written by authors from inner, outer and expanding circle contexts. The analysis follows a data-driven approach to identify recurrent lexico-grammatical, orthotypographic, semiotic and pragmatic features, and it combines this with a functional rhetorical analysis of the move structure of the posts. By bringing together digital genre analysis and an ELF perspective, the study seeks to contribute to a better understanding of how travel bloggers construct experience, engage readers and participate in a global virtual community through English.

intros.text: The issue of whether or not to use the first language in a language classroom seems to stand as one of the most long-standing controversies. The native languages of learners are still finding a great place in practice compared to counter-views in theory. Although the methods and approaches that aim to enhance learners' communicative competence overemphasize the use of target language (TL) in language classes, both language teachers and students go on using the first language (L1) for different purposes and at a changing amount.  Many researchers like Cook (2001) suggesting that “It is time to open a door that has been firmly shut in language teaching for over 100 years, namely the systematic use of the first language (L1) in the classroom” (p.403) try to soften reactions against L1 use. However, several researchers advocate that only L2 should be involved in a second/foreign language learning process. Remarkably suggested by the researchers depending on Krashen’s monolingual approach, the basic reason why language instruction should be based on just L2 is that the more L1 is used by instructors, the fewer opportunity students have to be exposed to L2, which results in detrimental effects on the language learning process (Viakinnou-Brinson, Herron, Cole, & Haight, 2012). Excessive use of L1 in language classes is suggested to have some de-motivating effects on students and minimize their chance of exposure to the target language (Bruen & Kelly, 2017). Furthermore, many language teachers describe the use of “L1 as a hindrance to learning L2, rather than as a resource for making learning easier” (Copland & Neokleous, 2011, p. 278) although their classroom realities showed the opposite (Bilgin, 2016; Copland & Neokleous, 2011; Gaebler, 2014). The opponents of L1 use are also of opinion that the language teaching process should be similar to the process of a child’s language acquisition in which the child learns the language through continuous exposure to the language, and they thus put great emphasis on enhancing opportunities for the immersion of learners in the target language (Jacobs & Kimura, 2013). Besides being inappropriate to be given particularly students who possess a high level of the target language (Debreli, 2016), the excessive use of L1 is believed to lead to laziness or off-task behavior for students (McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Besides, promoting classroom use of L2 forces the students to think in the target language and potentially facilitates language production and comprehension (Lee & Lo, 2017; Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012). On the other hand, based on many arguments to support their position, a great number of researchers suggest that banning L1 totally from an L2 classroom does not seem realistic (Mayo & Hidalgo, 2017; Zhu & Vanek, 2015). Rather than being an obstacle to language learning, L1 use may take place as a useful cognitive tool that helps to connect the new learning concept with preexisting knowledge and thus facilitates the learning process and promotes linguistic production (Codina Camó & Pladevall Ballester, 2015; Zhu & Vanek, 2015). Besides warning about the domination of L1 in L2 classrooms (Chimbutane, 2013), many researchers claim that playing an essential role in diminishing learning anxiety, the use of L1 may also help to create a more comfortable and effective learning atmosphere, particularly for shy or less-proficient L2 learners to communicate in the classroom (Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008; Nation, 2003). Furthermore, the students may have trouble understanding and participating when lessons are carried out in only target language medium since their stress ranges up and naturally, they lose their motivation (Fernandez & Korneeva, 2017; Owu-Ewie & Eshun, 2015; Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012). In this sense, as a pedagogical and instructional tool, the use of L1 is thought to serve many facilitative functions in L2 classrooms (Balam & Perez, 2017; Codina Camó & Pladevall Ballester, 2015; Levine, 2014; Sali, 2014) It has been observed that most English language classes in Turkey are conducted through the native language of learners, Turkish (Balabakgil & Mede, 2016; Bilgin, 2016; Debreli, 2016; Iyitoglu, 2016; Kocaman &Aslan, 2018; Sali, 2014; Şener & Korkut, 2017), although the curricula developed for primary, secondary, and high schools state the opposite (MNE, 2018a, 2018b)  Language learners and teachers are expected to use just English in English classes, but Turkish as the native language of learners has more place in practice for different purposes and reasons  There still seems to be no consensus among researchers, teachers, and students about the use of L1 in L2 classrooms.  This study aims to synthesize the findings of qualitative studies examining the language teachers and learners’ perceptions about and practices in L1 use. Therefore, it intends to reach a conclusion about this last-standing and significant issue in language teaching through a synthesis grounded on the views and practices of language teachers and learners.  Perceptions and practices of learners and teachers, who are the stakeholders of the language teaching process, are to provide valuable insight into the issue about the use of L1 in language classes.  In line with this purpose, the qualitative studies investigating the issue of L1 use in language classes were synthesized to reflect the language teachers and learners’ views and practices, and thus, responses to the following questions were sought: 1. How do students and teachers react against the use of L1 in L2 classes? 2. Which factors affect the use of L1 in L2 classes? 3. For what purposes do they use/advocate the use of L1 in L2 classes?

intros.text:
The question of whether the first language (L1) should have a place in the second or foreign language (L2) classroom is one of the most enduring and unresolved debates in the field of language education. For much of the twentieth century, prevailing methodologies and much of the teaching profession embraced a monolingual principle, according to which the target language should be the sole medium of instruction and the learners' native language ought to be avoided at all costs. This position rested on a set of assumptions that have since been questioned, including a doubtful analogy between second language learning and first language acquisition, an assumed compartmentalization of the two languages in the mind, and the belief that maximizing exposure to the target language necessarily entails excluding the L1 (Cook, 2001). More recently, however, scholars have re-examined these assumptions and argued that the first language, far from being an impediment, can be treated as a legitimate and valuable resource for both teachers and learners (Cook, 2001; Levine, 2014; Nation, 2003).

This reconsideration has been reinforced by the social and cultural 'turn' in language education, which has moved teaching and curriculum design away from many of the more rigid dogmas of earlier generations. Drawing on sociocultural theory and ecological perspectives on language and learning, researchers have increasingly conceptualized the classroom as a multilingual social space in which teacher and learners negotiate and co-construct norms for code choice (Levine, 2014). Related developments in translanguaging and bilingual pedagogy have further challenged English-only ideologies, highlighting the capacity of the L1 to scaffold comprehension, reduce anxiety, and foster inclusive learning environments (Bilgin, 2016). Yet these more permissive views coexist with persistent institutional and curricular pressures towards target-language-only instruction, so that teachers frequently find themselves negotiating a gap between official policy and their own classroom practice (Debreli, 2016; McMillan & Rivers, 2011).

A substantial body of empirical research has accumulated around this issue. Numerous studies have examined the attitudes, beliefs, and practices of teachers and students concerning L1 use, and many have documented that both groups tend to support the judicious use of the native language for a range of purposes. Interviews and classroom observations have shown that lecturers and learners alike value the L1 for explaining complex terminology, concepts, and grammatical structures, and for reducing cognitive overload and learner anxiety, thereby helping to create a relaxed classroom atmosphere (Bruen & Kelly, 2017; Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008). Others have catalogued the functional uses to which teachers and students put the L1, including facilitating understanding of vocabulary and grammar, maintaining discipline, motivating students, giving instructions, and establishing effective communication (Iyitoglu, 2016; Sali, 2014). Still other studies have pointed to contextual and individual factors that shape language choice, such as the linguistic composition of the class, the content being taught, and the language proficiency of both teachers and students (Chimbutane, 2013; Debreli, 2016; Gaebler, 2014).

Despite this wealth of evidence, no consensus has emerged. Some scholars continue to warn that overreliance on the L1 decreases exposure to the target language, limits opportunities for practice, and may hinder learners' development, reporting a high incidence of L1 transfer in learners' output (Copland & Neokleous, 2011; Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). Others report that experimental comparisons of grammar instruction delivered in the target language versus a code-switched approach yield gains for target-language-only teaching, even where students express a preference for L1 support (Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012). At the same time, learner-directed code-switching and shared-L1 use have been found to exert facilitative effects on comprehension and interaction (Bruen & Kelly, 2017; Zhu & Vanek, 2015). The picture is further complicated by variation across educational contexts, ranging from foreign language settings where the classroom may be the only site of target-language exposure to bilingual programmes in which the L1 is officially sanctioned yet met with ambivalence by teachers (Chimbutane, 2013), and by the differing perceptions of native and non-native instructors (Alabakgil & Sede, 2016; Debreli, 2016).

Given the accumulation of individual studies producing seemingly contradictory findings, there is a clear need to bring this dispersed evidence together in a systematic way. Much of the most illuminating work on L1 use is qualitative in nature, capturing the perceptions, attitudes, and situated practices of teachers and learners through interviews and classroom observation. Yet the findings of such studies are scattered across diverse contexts, languages, and educational levels, making it difficult to discern broader patterns or to translate their insights into evidence-based guidance for practitioners and policymakers. A meta-synthesis of qualitative research offers a promising means of addressing this fragmentation, since it can pull together data across different contexts, generate new conceptual understandings, identify research gaps, and put research findings into the hands of those who can make use of them. By treating each research report as an informant and synthesizing findings across studies, such an approach can move beyond the accumulation of isolated case studies towards a more integrated understanding of when, why, and how the L1 is used in language classes.

Accordingly, the present study undertakes a meta-synthesis of qualitative research published between 2010 and 2019 that investigates the perceptions and practices of language teachers and learners regarding L1 use in L2 classrooms. Its purpose is to synthesize the available qualitative evidence in order to shed light on the language choices of teachers and students, the factors that shape those choices, and the functions the L1 serves in the classroom. In doing so, the study seeks to contribute to the ongoing debate by clarifying the conditions under which L1 use is preferred or avoided, and by offering insights that may inform not only teaching practice but also curriculum design and educational policy concerning the role of the first language in language instruction.

intros.text:
The role of the first language (L1) in the teaching and learning of a second or foreign language (L2) is one of the most enduring and contested issues in the field of applied linguistics. For much of the twentieth century, language pedagogy was dominated by monolingual principles that regarded the exclusive use of the target language as the ideal and treated the learner's mother tongue as an obstacle to acquisition. This English-only or target-language-only orthodoxy has proven remarkably durable, standing the test of time despite substantial shifts in the theoretical and methodological landscape of language education (Salı, 2014). Even today, many curricula and institutional policies continue to require teachers to conduct their lessons entirely in the target language, on the assumption that language classes are often the only environment in which learners are exposed to the L2, and that maximising such exposure is essential for developing proficiency.

Yet the justification for banishing the L1 from the classroom has been questioned on both theoretical and practical grounds. Cook (2001) argued that the arguments for avoiding the first language rest on a doubtful analogy with first-language acquisition, on a questionable compartmentalisation of the two languages in the mind, and on the assumption that maximising L2 exposure is incompatible with any use of the L1. Rather than something to be shunned at all costs, the first language can be treated as a legitimate classroom resource that teachers use to convey meaning, explain grammar, and organise the class, and that learners draw on in their collaborative work and individual learning strategies. Building on such reappraisals, a growing body of research has begun to give the effectiveness of L1 use the benefit of the doubt (Salı, 2014), and to conceptualise the language classroom as a multilingual space in which teachers and learners negotiate and co-construct norms for code choice (Levine, 2014).

This reappraisal has generated a considerable literature investigating why, when, and how the L1 is used in L2 classrooms. Numerous studies report that both teachers and students value the judicious use of the mother tongue for a range of purposes, including explaining complex terminology, concepts, and grammatical structures, reducing cognitive overload and learner anxiety, and creating a relaxed classroom environment (Bruen & Kelly, 2017; Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008). Non-native teachers, in particular, have been shown to draw on the L1 for a variety of reasons even when constrained by strong English-only institutional policies (Debreli, 2016; Gaebler, 2014). Classroom-based studies have documented that teachers and learners code-switch to the L1 to facilitate understanding of vocabulary and grammar, to maintain discipline, to motivate students, to give instructions, and to establish effective communication (Iyitoglu, 2016), and researchers have proposed functional taxonomies that distinguish academic, managerial, and affective or social uses of the mother tongue (Salı, 2014; Inbar-Lourie, 2010). At the same time, other studies caution that overreliance on translation and the L1 may diminish learners' interpretive effort and reduce valuable exposure to the target language (Copland & Neokleous, 2011), and some teachers, even where policy permits bilingual instruction, hold negative attitudes towards mother-tongue use (Chimbutane, 2013).

Despite this proliferation of research, the debate remains fundamentally unresolved. There is still no consensus among researchers as to whether language education should be conducted exclusively in the target language or whether the native language can legitimately be enlisted as a teaching tool. Much of the existing scholarship has concentrated on cataloguing the advantages and disadvantages of L1 use within single, isolated contexts, and findings vary considerably according to the educational setting, the proficiency of teachers and learners, and the aspect of language being taught. Individual studies, moreover, differ in their methodological orientation, their participants, and their conceptual frameworks, so that their findings are difficult to compare and are rarely brought into dialogue with one another. As a result, it remains unclear how the accumulated qualitative evidence on the perceptions, attitudes, and classroom practices of teachers and learners might be integrated to produce a coherent, evidence-based picture of language choice in L2 classrooms. What is largely missing is a systematic attempt to draw together the qualitative findings across studies, contexts, and participants in order to identify shared patterns, contextual factors, and the functions that the L1 is reported to serve.

The present study addresses this gap by conducting a meta-synthesis of qualitative research on L1 use in language classes. Its aim is to summarise and synthesise the findings of qualitative studies that offer insights into the perceptions, attitudes, practices, and behaviours of language teachers and learners regarding the use of the first language, and thereby to move towards a more integrated understanding of an ongoing and unresolved debate. Because a synthesis of qualitative research can pull together data across different contexts, generate new conceptual models, and place research findings in the hands of those who can use them, it is a particularly suitable approach for this purpose. To this end, thirty-four qualitative studies published between 2010 and 2019 and retrieved from the ERIC and Web of Science databases were selected against explicit inclusion criteria, appraised for quality, and analysed through a three-phase process in which each report was treated as an informant and its findings were combined to develop first-, second-, and third-order themes. The synthesis was guided by three research questions concerning whether the L1 is used or avoided, which factors influence teachers' and learners' language choices and the amount of L1 used, and which functions the mother tongue serves in the classroom. In so doing, the study seeks to offer language teachers, curriculum developers, and educational policymakers a more comprehensive account of when and why the first language is drawn upon, so that decisions about language choice may take account not only of theories and approaches but also of the lived preferences and experiences of teachers and learners themselves.

intros.text:
The role of the first language (L1) in the second language (L2) classroom has remained one of the most enduring and contentious debates in applied linguistics and English language teaching. For decades, the prevailing pedagogical dogma favored a monolingual approach, emphasizing the maximization of target language exposure to accelerate acquisition and avoid the perceived interference of the native tongue (Nation, 2003). Proponents of this 'English-only' ideology argue that the L1 acts as a hindrance, potentially leading to an overreliance on translation and decreasing the critical input necessary for students to develop proficiency (Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). Indeed, some research suggests that excessive dependence on the L1 can result in interlingual errors and fossilization, as learners may rely on transfer strategies rather than engaging with the target language's unique structures (Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). This perspective is often mirrored in official educational policies; for instance, many curricula strictly mandate the use of the L2 to ensure that the classroom remains the primary site of exposure for learners (Bilgin, 2016; Debreli, 2016).

However, this strict compartmentalization of languages has been increasingly challenged by scholars who view the L1 not as an impediment, but as a valuable cognitive and pedagogical resource. Cook (2001) argues that the traditional avoidance of the L1 is based on a questionable analogy with first language acquisition and suggests that treating the L1 as a classroom tool can actually facilitate the creation of more authentic L2 users. From this perspective, the judicious use of the L1 can serve as a bridge to comprehension, allowing teachers to convey complex meanings, explain intricate grammatical points, and organize classroom activities more efficiently (Cook, 2001). Rather than hindering learning, the strategic integration of the L1—often discussed under the framework of translanguaging—can scaffold the learning process, making abstract concepts more accessible and reducing the cognitive overload that often accompanies immersive environments (Bruen & Kelly, 2017; Bilgin, 2016).

Beyond academic functions, the use of the L1 plays a critical role in managing the affective dimensions of the classroom. Language learning is inherently fraught with anxiety, particularly for low-proficiency learners who may feel overwhelmed or demotivated by a strict L2-only policy (Bruen & Kelly, 2017). In such contexts, switching to the L1 can humanize the classroom, build rapport between the teacher and students, and create a supportive atmosphere that lowers the 'affective filter' (Salı, 2014). By providing a sense of security and confidence, the L1 allows students to express their feelings, ask for clarification, and engage in social interaction that might otherwise be stifled by linguistic limitations (Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008). Thus, the choice between L1 and L2 is often not a binary decision but a dynamic negotiation influenced by the immediate needs of the learners and the pedagogical goals of the teacher (McMillan & Rivers, 2011).

Despite the wealth of research on this topic, a consensus remains elusive. While some studies emphasize the benefits of translation and L1 support for vocabulary and grammar (Kocaman & Aslan Erdinç, 2018), others warn that it may diminish the effort students put into interpreting meaning independently (Copland & Neokleous, 2011). Furthermore, the actual practice in the classroom frequently diverges from official policy. Many teachers, regardless of their ideological stance, find themselves utilizing the L1 as a compensatory strategy, particularly when their own L2 proficiency is limited or when the classroom context—such as a monolingual group—makes L1 use more pragmatic (Debreli, 2016; Chimbutane, 2013). This gap between policy and practice suggests that the 'language choice' in L2 classrooms is governed by a complex interplay of teacher beliefs, student proficiency, and contextual constraints (Bilgin, 2016; Gaebler, 2014).

Given the fragmented nature of the existing literature, there is a pressing need to synthesize qualitative findings to provide a more comprehensive understanding of how and why L1 is used in language classes. While quantitative studies can identify trends, qualitative research offers deeper insights into the perceptions, attitudes, and lived experiences of the participants. Meta-synthesis allows researchers to pull together data across diverse contexts, identify recurring themes, and generate conceptual models that can inform evidence-based practice (Tong et al., 2012). By analyzing the nuances of teacher and learner behaviors through a synthesis of qualitative reports, it is possible to move beyond the simplistic 'L1 vs. L2' debate and instead categorize the specific functions and factors that drive language choice.

Therefore, the present study aims to conduct a meta-synthesis of qualitative research published between 2010 and 2019 to draw broader conclusions about the use of the first language in L2 classrooms. Specifically, the study seeks to identify the primary themes surrounding the avoidance and use of the L1, the factors that influence these choices—such as teacher and student proficiency and the educational context—and the specific academic, managerial, and socio-cultural functions the L1 serves. By synthesizing these findings, the study hopes to provide a nuanced perspective that can assist educators and policymakers in developing more flexible and effective language instruction strategies that balance the need for target language exposure with the pedagogical advantages of the first language.

intros.text:
The question of how to manage the use of the first language (L1) within the second language (L2) classroom has long been a subject of intense scholarly debate and remains a central concern for practitioners in the field of applied linguistics. For decades, the prevailing pedagogical dogma favored a strict monolingual approach, predicated on the belief that maximizing exposure to the target language is the most effective path toward proficiency. This perspective suggests that any reliance on the L1 acts as a hindrance to learning, potentially leading to an overreliance on translation and diminishing the learner's effort to negotiate meaning in the L2 (Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). Indeed, some researchers argue that the L1 can become a crutch that fosters fossilization or reduces the authentic communicative drive necessary for acquisition.

However, in recent years, this rigid adherence to L2-only policies has been increasingly challenged. A growing body of literature suggests that the L1 can be a powerful pedagogical resource when used judiciously. Cook (2001) argued for a re-examination of the views that shun the L1, suggesting that treating the native language as a classroom resource allows teachers to convey meaning more efficiently and organize the class more effectively. Similarly, the emergence of translanguaging frameworks has reframed the L1 not as an interference, but as a tool for scaffolding comprehension and fostering an inclusive learning environment (Bilgin, 2016). Scholars have noted that strategic code-switching can alleviate cognitive overload and reduce the affective filter, particularly for low-proficiency learners who may otherwise experience high levels of anxiety and demotivation (Bruen & Kelly, 2017).

Previous research has extensively documented the various attitudes held by stakeholders regarding this issue. For instance, studies have shown that while institutional policies often mandate an English-only environment, the actual classroom practices of both teachers and students frequently deviate from these mandates (Debreli, 2016; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Many teachers report that they consciously employ the L1 to facilitate the understanding of complex grammatical structures or to provide clear managerial instructions, finding it more practical than attempting these tasks exclusively in the L2 (Iyitoglu, 2016; Salı, 2014). From the students' perspective, the L1 is often viewed as a source of security and comfort, allowing them to express complex feelings or clarify doubts that they lack the linguistic means to articulate in the target language (Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008).

Despite the abundance of studies exploring the advantages and disadvantages of L1 use, a clear consensus among researchers remains elusive. Much of the existing literature focuses on individual case studies or specific educational contexts, which often produce fragmented findings. While some studies emphasize the risks of L1 interference, others highlight its facilitative effects, leaving educators without a unified set of guidelines on when and how the L1 should be integrated into instruction. Furthermore, while there is significant quantitative data on the frequency of code-switching, there is a need for a more comprehensive synthesis of qualitative insights that capture the nuanced perceptions and lived experiences of teachers and learners across diverse contexts.

To address this gap in the literature, the present study employs a meta-synthesis of qualitative research to draw broader conclusions about the language choices made by teachers and learners in L2 classes. By synthesizing findings from multiple qualitative reports, this research aims to move beyond the binary 'L1 vs. L2' debate and instead identify the specific functions and factors that drive the choice of language in the classroom. Specifically, this study seeks to answer three primary research questions: (1) What are the primary perceptions and practices regarding the avoidance of L1 in language classes? (2) What factors influence the decision to use the L1 over the L2? and (3) What are the specific academic, managerial, and socio-cultural functions that the L1 serves in the L2 learning environment?

To achieve these objectives, this study utilizes a systematic qualitative synthesis approach. By treating individual research reports as 'informants,' the study analyzes qualitative data obtained through interviews and observations from the last decade (2010–2019). The methodology involves a three-phase process of analysis, synthesis, and interpretation to develop first-, second-, and third-order themes, thereby transforming disparate qualitative findings into a cohesive conceptual framework. This approach allows for the identification of recurring patterns across different linguistic and geographical contexts, providing a more holistic understanding of the phenomenon of L1 use.

It is anticipated that the findings of this meta-synthesis will offer valuable insights for language teachers, curriculum designers, and policymakers. By articulating the specific functions of the L1, this study may provide a rationale for a more balanced, evidence-based approach to language choice that maximizes target language exposure without sacrificing the psychological and pedagogical benefits of the first language. Ultimately, this research contributes to the ongoing effort to legitimize a more flexible, multilingual pedagogy in the global EFL/ESL landscape.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. The methodology section details the inclusion and exclusion criteria used for the selection of studies, the quality appraisal process via the CASP checklist, and the data analysis procedure using NVivo software. This is followed by the results and discussion section, which presents the synthesized themes regarding the avoidance and use of L1, the factors influencing these choices, and the categorized functions of L1 use. Finally, the conclusion summarizes the key findings and offers implications for future research and educational practice.

intros.text:
The use of the first language (L1) in second language (L2) classrooms has long been a contentious issue in the field of applied linguistics and language education. For decades, the monolingual approach, which advocates for the exclusive use of the target language (TL) in the classroom, has dominated language teaching methodologies. This perspective is rooted in the belief that maximizing exposure to the target language is essential for acquisition, and that reliance on the L1 hinders the development of L2 proficiency (Cook, 2001; Levine, 2014). Consequently, many educational policies and curricula, such as those in Turkey and Northern Cyprus, have enforced strict 'English-only' regulations, positioning the L1 as an impediment to learning (Debreli, 2016; Bilgin, 2016). However, despite these ideological constraints, empirical evidence suggests that the L1 is frequently and inevitably used in language classrooms, raising questions about the validity of the monolingual dogma.

Recent scholarship has increasingly challenged the traditional view, arguing that the L1 can serve as a valuable resource rather than a hindrance. Cook (2001) posited that treating the L1 as a classroom resource opens up various pedagogical possibilities, such as conveying meaning, explaining grammar, and organizing class activities. Similarly, Levine (2014) suggested that the classroom should be viewed as a multilingual social space where learners and teachers negotiate code choice norms to achieve dynamic and pedagogically effective outcomes. This shift in perspective aligns with sociocultural and ecological theories of language learning, which emphasize the role of the learner's linguistic repertoire in the learning process (Levine, 2014; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Studies by Bruen and Kelly (2017) and Copland and Neokleous (2011) have highlighted the complexities and contradictions surrounding L1 use, noting that while overreliance on translation can be detrimental, judicious use can reduce cognitive overload and learner anxiety.

Despite the growing body of literature supporting the strategic use of L1, there remains a lack of consensus regarding the extent and functions of its use in L2 classes. While some researchers emphasize the benefits of L1 for scaffolding comprehension and managing classroom dynamics (Gaebler, 2014; Iyitoglu, 2016), others caution against its potential to decrease target language exposure and limit speaking practice (Şener & Korkut, 2017; Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). This divergence in findings is partly due to the varying contexts in which studies are conducted, ranging from foreign language settings where L1 exposure is limited to bilingual contexts where L1 use is officially permitted (Chimbutane, 2013; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Furthermore, the factors influencing language choice, such as teacher and student proficiency, educational context, and the specific content being taught, are often interwoven, making it difficult to draw generalizable conclusions from individual studies.

Qualitative research has been particularly instrumental in exploring the perceptions, attitudes, and practices of teachers and learners regarding L1 use. Studies by Bilgin (2016) and Debreli (2016) have revealed that non-native EFL teachers often feel restricted by English-only policies, despite their inclination to use the L1 for various pedagogical reasons. Similarly, Gaebler (2014) found that while some students view L1 use as a source of comfort, others perceive it as interference, highlighting the need to consider learner perspectives. However, these individual studies, while insightful, often focus on specific contexts or populations, limiting the breadth of their implications. There is a need to synthesize findings across diverse qualitative studies to identify broader patterns and themes regarding language choices in language classes.

Meta-synthesis of qualitative research offers a robust methodological approach to address this gap. By treating each research report as an 'informant' and synthesizing findings across different contexts, meta-synthesis can generate new theoretical models, identify research gaps, and inform evidence-based practice and policy (Tong et al., 2012; Savin-Baden & Major, 2010). This method allows for the integration of data from various qualitative studies to draw comprehensive conclusions about the use of L1 in L2 classes, moving beyond the limitations of single-case studies. Given the ongoing debate and the lack of consensus in the literature, a meta-synthesis is timely and necessary to provide a holistic understanding of the factors affecting language choices and the functions of L1 use in language teaching.

Therefore, the primary aim of this study is to synthesize the findings of qualitative research investigating the language choices of language teachers and learners. Specifically, this study seeks to explore the factors influencing L1 use, the functions for which it is employed, and the perceptions of teachers and students regarding its role in the classroom. By analyzing qualitative studies published between 2010 and 2019, this research aims to contribute to the ongoing discourse on L1 use by providing a comprehensive overview of current practices and beliefs. The findings of this study will offer valuable insights for language teachers, educational policymakers, and curriculum developers, helping to bridge the gap between theoretical ideologies and classroom realities. Ultimately, this meta-synthesis seeks to clarify whether the L1 should be avoided or utilized in language classes, and under what conditions, to optimize the language learning experience.

intros.text:
The role of the first language (L1) in second language (L2) classrooms has long been a contentious issue in applied linguistics and English language teaching (ELT). For decades, the dominant pedagogical paradigm, often associated with the Direct Method and Communicative Language Teaching, advocated for the exclusive use of the target language to maximize learner exposure and immersion (Cook, 2001; Levine, 2014). This monolingual approach was predicated on the belief that L1 use interferes with the acquisition process, potentially leading to fossilization of errors and reducing the amount of time learners spend engaging with the target language (Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017; Nation, 2003). Consequently, many language curricula and institutional policies have historically enforced strict 'English-only' rules, viewing the L1 as a resource to be minimized or eliminated entirely (Debreli, 2016; McMillan & Rivers, 2011).

However, in recent years, this traditional stance has faced increasing scrutiny and challenge. Researchers have begun to question the validity of the monolingual dogma, arguing that the L1 is an inevitable and potentially valuable asset in the language learning process (Copland & Neokleous, 2011; Levine, 2014). Theoretical shifts towards translanguaging and multilingual pedagogies have further legitimized the use of learners' full linguistic repertoires, suggesting that code-switching can serve as a cognitive and social tool rather than a hindrance (Bilgin, 2016; Chimbutane, 2013). Empirical studies have increasingly documented the pragmatic functions of L1 use, highlighting its utility in explaining complex grammatical structures, managing classroom activities, and reducing learner anxiety (Bruen & Kelly, 2017; Iyitoglu, 2016). For instance, Gaebler (2014) and Salı (2014) found that both teachers and students often view L1 use as a strategic necessity, particularly in contexts where proficiency levels vary or where abstract concepts need clarification.

Despite this growing body of research, a consensus regarding the optimal use of L1 in language instruction remains elusive. The literature presents a complex picture of conflicting findings and divergent perspectives. On one hand, studies such as those by Rolin-Ianziti and Varshney (2008) and Viakinnou-Brinson et al. (2012) suggest that while L1 use is perceived as helpful for comprehension, it may not always correlate with improved grammatical performance or may even be viewed as a threat to immersion by some learners. On the other hand, research by Kocaman and Aslan Erdinç (2018) and Owu-Ewie et al. (2015) indicates that L1 use is often preferred by both educators and learners for its ability to scaffold learning and create a supportive classroom environment. Furthermore, the factors influencing language choice—such as teacher proficiency, student proficiency, and educational context—are frequently cited as critical variables that complicate the debate (Cho & Kim, 2016; Debreli, 2016). Consequently, while individual studies provide valuable insights into specific contexts, there is a lack of comprehensive synthesis that integrates these diverse findings to offer a holistic understanding of the phenomenon.

This gap in the literature is particularly pronounced regarding the qualitative dimensions of L1 use. While quantitative studies have often focused on the frequency of code-switching or its measurable impact on test scores, qualitative research offers deeper insights into the perceptions, attitudes, and in-class practices of teachers and learners (Bilgin, 2016; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Understanding the 'why' and 'how' behind language choices requires a synthesis of these qualitative narratives to identify underlying patterns and themes that transcend individual studies. As noted by Tong et al. (2012), meta-synthesis of qualitative studies can pull together data across different contexts to generate new theoretical models and identify research gaps, thereby putting research findings into the hands of those who can make use of them for evidence-based practice. However, to date, few attempts have been made to systematically synthesize qualitative findings on L1 use to draw broader conclusions about its functions and the factors governing its deployment.

To address this limitation, the present study aims to synthesize the findings of qualitative research on the use of L1 in L2 classrooms. By examining studies that explore the perceptions and practices of language teachers and learners, this research seeks to draw a conclusion about the ongoing debate on L1 use, a topic on which there is still no consensus among researchers. Specifically, this study investigates the factors affecting language choices, the functions for which L1 is utilized, and the general attitudes towards its integration in language instruction. The research questions guiding this meta-synthesis are: (1) What factors affect the choice of language in language classes? (2) What functions does L1 serve in L2 classrooms? and (3) What are the prevailing attitudes towards L1 use among teachers and learners?

To achieve these objectives, this study employs a meta-synthesis methodology, treating each qualitative research report as an 'informant' to synthesize findings across different contexts (Major & Savin-Baden, 2012). Following the discrete steps outlined by Erwin et al. (2011), the study involves searching, selecting, appraising, and combining evidence from 34 qualitative studies published between 2010 and 2019. The data were analyzed using a three-phase process of analysis, synthesis, and interpretation to develop first-, second-, and third-order themes (Major & Savin-Baden, 2010). This approach allows for a critical and inductive examination of the data, ensuring that the conclusions drawn are grounded in the rich, contextualized experiences of teachers and learners. The findings of this study are expected to provide a nuanced understanding of L1 use, offering implications for educational policymakers, curriculum developers, and language teachers who navigate the complexities of multilingual classrooms. By highlighting the conditions under which L1 use is beneficial and the functions it serves, this research contributes to the broader discourse on language choice, suggesting that while instruction should mostly depend on the target language, L1 may be used judiciously if necessary to support learning and manage the classroom effectively.
