intros.text:
The question of which language(s) should be used in second or foreign language classrooms has remained one of the most persistent debates in language pedagogy. For many years, language teaching was strongly influenced by monolingual assumptions which held that the target language should be the sole or dominant medium of instruction and interaction. From this perspective, maximizing exposure to the target language is seen as essential, particularly in foreign language contexts where learners may have few opportunities to encounter or use it outside the classroom. The use of the first language (L1), by contrast, has often been treated as interference, a source of negative transfer, or a practice that reduces learners’ need to process and produce the target language. Such concerns are not without empirical and pedagogical grounding: overreliance on translation may limit learners’ attempts to infer meaning, develop communicative strategies, or build confidence in using the target language independently. Studies of learner output have also associated excessive dependence on L1-based strategies with interlanguage problems and persistent errors (Forteza Fernández & Korneeva, 2017). Similarly, research comparing target-language-only and code-switching conditions has shown that learners may sometimes perform better when instruction is conducted primarily in the target language, even when they express a preference for L1 support (Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012). 

At the same time, the exclusion of the L1 from language classrooms has increasingly been questioned. Cook (2001) argued that the traditional view of the L1 as something to be avoided rests on questionable assumptions, including an overextended analogy with first language acquisition and a compartmentalized view of bilingual minds. Rather than treating learners as deficient monolinguals in the target language, this position regards them as developing multilingual users whose linguistic repertoires can be pedagogically mobilized. Nation (2003) similarly suggested that the first language can have a legitimate role in foreign language learning when used in principled and limited ways. More recent sociocultural and ecological accounts have further reframed classroom code choice as a negotiated practice embedded in interaction, identity, task demands, and institutional expectations (Levine, 2014). In this view, the classroom is not a monolingual space temporarily interrupted by L1 use, but a multilingual social environment in which teachers and learners make situated choices to support learning, participation, and classroom life.

Empirical research has documented a wide range of functions for L1 use in language classrooms. Teachers may switch to the L1 to explain grammar, clarify vocabulary, check comprehension, give instructions, manage discipline, or establish rapport (Iyitoglu, 2016; Sali, 2014). Learners may use it to ask for help, negotiate task procedures, discuss linguistic forms, maintain peer interaction, or express personal attitudes that they cannot yet communicate in the target language (Mayo & Hidalgo, 2017). In classrooms where teachers and learners share the same L1, such practices may reduce cognitive overload and anxiety, particularly when abstract concepts, complex grammatical structures, or unfamiliar terminology are being introduced (Bruen & Kelly, 2017). L1 use may also contribute to a more supportive classroom atmosphere by allowing humor, encouragement, and interpersonal closeness that may be difficult to achieve through the target language alone. These affective and relational dimensions are especially relevant for lower-proficiency learners, who may experience target-language-only instruction as intimidating or inaccessible.

Nevertheless, support for the L1 is rarely unconditional. Many studies emphasize judicious, strategic, or limited use rather than unrestricted switching. Gaebler (2014), for example, found that learners and instructors recognized the value of L1 use but did not regard it as the only or primary classroom resource. Rolin-Ianziti and Varshney (2008) reported that learners attributed useful functions to the L1 in a context designed to maximize target language use, yet also recognized possible motivational drawbacks. Similarly, Debreli (2016) showed that non-native EFL teachers were inclined to use the L1 for various pedagogical reasons but were also constrained by institutional English-only policies. These findings suggest that the central issue is not simply whether the L1 should be allowed or banned, but under what conditions, for which learners, by whom, and for what purposes it may support or hinder learning.

Context is therefore crucial. In foreign language settings, where classroom exposure may be the main source of target language input, teachers may feel a strong obligation to maintain target language use. In multilingual classrooms, a shared L1 may not exist, making target language use necessary for inclusion and fairness. In monolingual classrooms, however, the shared L1 may offer an efficient means of scaffolding understanding, managing time, and maintaining participation. Learner proficiency also appears to shape language choice: lower-level learners tend to need more L1 support, whereas more proficient learners may benefit from greater target language immersion. Teacher proficiency, teacher identity, curriculum demands, institutional language policies, and examination pressures may also influence classroom practice (Bilgin, 2016; Chimbutane, 2013; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). Thus, language choice is best understood as a dynamic pedagogical decision rather than a fixed methodological rule.

Despite the extensive literature on this topic, no consensus has been reached. Part of the difficulty lies in the diversity of research contexts and methods. Experimental studies may examine the effects of L1 use on specific learning outcomes, while qualitative studies often reveal the complexity of teachers’ and learners’ beliefs, classroom practices, and local constraints. Qualitative work is especially valuable because it captures how participants interpret L1 use, why they engage in it, and how it functions in real interaction. However, individual qualitative studies are often context-bound, making it difficult to draw broader conclusions from them separately. A synthesis of such studies can therefore provide a more comprehensive account of recurring patterns across educational settings while still preserving attention to contextual variation.

The present study addresses this need by conducting a meta-synthesis of qualitative research on the use of the first language in language classes. It focuses on studies that report teachers’ and learners’ perceptions, attitudes, experiences, or observed practices concerning L1 use. By synthesizing findings across studies published between 2010 and 2019, the study aims to clarify the major positions on avoiding or using the L1, identify the factors that influence language choice, and categorize the functions served by L1 use in language teaching and learning. In doing so, it seeks to move beyond the binary opposition between target-language-only instruction and unrestricted L1 use, and to contribute evidence for more balanced, context-sensitive decisions in language pedagogy.

intros.text:
The language used by teachers and learners in second or foreign language classrooms has long been one of the most debated issues in language teaching. In many contexts, especially where the target language is taught as a foreign language, the classroom may be the main or even the only setting in which learners encounter and use the target language. For this reason, maximizing exposure to the target language has often been regarded as a central pedagogical principle. At the same time, teachers and learners usually bring to the classroom one or more shared first languages, and these languages inevitably shape classroom interaction, comprehension, identity, affect, and participation. Decisions about whether, when, and how to use the first language are therefore not merely technical choices; they are closely related to theories of language learning, institutional language policies, teacher cognition, learner needs, and the sociolinguistic realities of particular classrooms.

Traditional monolingual orientations have tended to view the learners’ first language as a potential obstacle to target language development. From this perspective, L1 use may reduce valuable exposure to the target language, encourage translation dependence, limit opportunities for production, or reinforce transfer-based errors. Such concerns are reflected in arguments for target-language-only instruction and in educational policies that expect teachers to conduct lessons predominantly or exclusively in the target language. Research has also shown that some students and teachers worry that frequent reliance on the L1 may interfere with learning or weaken learners’ willingness to process meaning in the target language (Copland & Neokleous, 2011; Gaebler, 2014; Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012). In cooperative and communicative classrooms, similar concerns arise when learners use their shared L1 during pair or group work rather than attempting interaction in the L2 (Jacobs & Kimura, 2013).

However, the assumption that the L1 should be avoided has been increasingly questioned. Cook (2001) argued that the first language should not be treated as something to be excluded at all costs, but as a resource that can support meaning-making, grammar explanation, classroom organization, and learner strategy use. Nation (2003) similarly recognized that a principled role for the L1 can coexist with the broader aim of developing L2 proficiency. More recent perspectives on code choice, translanguaging, and multilingual pedagogy have further challenged strict separation between languages, suggesting that language classrooms can be understood as multilingual social spaces in which teachers and learners negotiate appropriate uses of their linguistic repertoires (Levine, 2014). From this standpoint, the question is not simply whether the L1 is good or bad, but what functions it serves, under what conditions it supports learning, and how its use can be balanced with the need for sustained target language engagement.

Empirical studies have identified a wide range of pedagogical, managerial, and affective functions for L1 use. Teachers may switch to the L1 to explain complex vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, or abstract concepts; to check comprehension; to give instructions; to manage discipline; or to provide feedback and encouragement (Iyitoglu, 2016; Sali, 2014). Learners may use the L1 to ask for help, maintain the flow of communication, discuss task procedures, clarify linguistic forms, or express personal attitudes when their L2 resources are insufficient (Mayo & Hidalgo, 2017). In some studies, a shared L1 has been reported to reduce cognitive overload and anxiety, particularly for lower-proficiency learners or when difficult terminology and grammatical structures are involved (Bruen & Kelly, 2017). Other studies have shown that teachers working under English-only policies may nevertheless use the L1 strategically because they perceive it as necessary for comprehension, rapport, or efficient classroom management (Debreli, 2016; McMillan & Rivers, 2011). These findings suggest that actual classroom practice is often more flexible and context-sensitive than formal monolingual policies imply.

At the same time, research findings remain complex and sometimes contradictory. Learners may value L1 use because it gives them comfort and access to meaning, but they may also see it as a threat to immersion or target language development (Gaebler, 2014; Rolin-Ianziti & Varshney, 2008). Teachers may support limited L1 use for grammar or classroom management while still endorsing the target language as the main medium of instruction (Kocaman & Aslan Erdinç, 2018; Sali, 2014). The effects of L1 use may also depend on learner age, proficiency, task type, lesson stage, institutional policy, and whether the class is monolingual or multilingual. For example, L1-supported grammar instruction may be preferred by students even when target-language instruction produces stronger performance gains in some contexts (Viakinnou-Brinson et al., 2012), while translation may or may not facilitate vocabulary learning depending on instructional design and learner characteristics (Codina Camó & Pladevall Ballester, 2015). In bilingual education settings, teachers’ beliefs and practices may also vary according to local language hierarchies and policy conditions (Chimbutane, 2013). Thus, although many individual studies have examined classroom code-switching and L1 use, they have not produced a stable consensus that can guide teachers, curriculum developers, or policy makers across contexts.

One reason for this lack of consensus is that previous research has often been conducted as separate case studies in particular institutions, educational levels, or national settings. Such studies provide rich insights into the perceptions and practices of teachers and learners, but their findings are dispersed across contexts and are not always easily comparable. Another reason is that the debate has frequently been framed in binary terms: target language versus first language, monolingual instruction versus bilingual support, or exposure versus comprehension. This framing can obscure the more nuanced issue of how language choices are made in real classrooms and what purposes they serve. While quantitative studies and experimental designs can examine specific learning outcomes, qualitative research is especially valuable for understanding why teachers and learners make particular language choices, how they interpret classroom constraints, and how L1 and L2 use are embedded in social interaction.

Accordingly, there is a need to synthesize qualitative evidence on L1 use in language classrooms in order to identify broader patterns across studies without losing the contextual richness of participants’ views and observed practices. A meta-synthesis can bring together findings from different qualitative studies, reveal recurring themes, and offer a more integrated account of an issue that remains theoretically and pedagogically contested. Such an approach is particularly appropriate for the present topic because language choice is shaped by beliefs, experiences, classroom events, and institutional conditions that are often best captured through interviews, observations, and qualitative interpretation.

The present study therefore aims to synthesize qualitative research on the use of the first language in language classes, with particular attention to teachers’ and learners’ perceptions, attitudes, and classroom practices. It seeks to clarify whether the studies analyzed support avoidance or use of the L1, what factors appear to influence language choice, and what functions the L1 serves when it is used. By bringing together qualitative findings published in recent years, the study offers a consolidated account of the conditions under which L1 use is resisted, tolerated, or valued in L2 classrooms. The synthesis is expected to contribute to the continuing debate by moving beyond a simple approval-or-rejection position and by providing evidence-based insights for language teachers, teacher educators, curriculum designers, and policy makers who must make practical decisions about classroom language use.

papers.title: Tourism Discourse Revisited: An Analysis of Evaluative Strategies in Tourist Brochures from a Systemic Functional Linguistics Perspective
papers.filename: Tourism Discourse Revisited An Analysis of Evaluative Strategies in Tourist Brochures from a Systemic Functional Linguistics Perspective-Swales_Moves

swales_topic.searched_in: title + abstract + original intro + full body

intros.text: Today, tourism is known as one of the most important businesses throughout the  world.  The  tourism  industry  owes  much  of  its  success  to  the  way  tourist  destinations are advertised, that is, to the content of brochures, leaflets, travelogues, etc. This makes the language of tourism of paramount importance.  Whereas some researchers consider the language of tourism to be general but only more fertile in diction and style (e.g., Gotti 2003), other scholars regard the tourism language to be the language of promotionl and popularization (e.g., Thurot 1989), is a highly organized  and  encoded  system  in  its  own  right  (Said  1991:  21)  which  deserves  careful  consideration.  The  language  of  tourism  is  also  described  as  a  discourse  object (Bhatia 1993) which falls within the broad category of promotional discourse or the study of attitudes in the social sciences (Dillard and Pfa 2002).Due to the significant role that the media play in business activities including the  tourism  industry  (Locksley  2009),  scrutinizing  informative  promotional  media(Choi,  Xinvan  and  Alastair  2007)  such  as  websites  (Burns  and  Robertson  1999;  Doolin, Burgess and Cooper 2002; Hallett and Kaplan-Weinger 2010; Lähteenmäki 2012), publicity programs (Dore and Crouch 2003) and TV commercials (Pan, Tsi and Lee 2011) has contributed to the tourism literature  What constitutes the language of tourism? Which aspects of this language do tourist  text  designers  need  to  focus  on?  Across  the  literature  of  tourism,  various  studies within different theoretical frameworks have tried to reveal different aspects of the language of tourism.  For instance, taking a sociolinguistic approach, certain studies  have  aimed  at  describing  how  intelligently  promoters  in  the  tourism  industry  exert  social  control  over  the  consumers  (Dann  2012)  while  maintaining  the idea that tourists are given absolute freedom (Rokowski 2001). In serving the purpose of promotion here, the language of tourism becomes highly value-laden and ideological biased (Bhatia 1993). Critical  Discourse  Analysis  has  also  been  applied  to  a  number  of  studies  to  uncover the changes that have appeared as a result of new tendencies in tourism sectors (Bruner 1991; Hallett and Kaplan-Weinger 2010;Jonsson and Syssner 2011). For instance, a new positive imagery of Chinatown replaced its demeaning face as a result of the change in the discourse of the brochures promoting this district to attract  visitors  (Santos,  Belhassen  and  Caton  2009).  This  indicates  how  texts  can  camouflage  important  aspects  of  the  places  that  they  purport  to  describe  using  effective rhetorical devices.In  a  review  of  the  literature  on  advertisements,  there  are  studies  employing  Systemic  Functional  Linguistics  (hereafter  SFL)  as  their  theoretical  framework,  such  as  Patpong  (2009)  who  discovered  that  the  use  of  language  in  amulet  advertisements is one example to demonstrate the persuasive use of language. Yet Patpong  deals  with  the  discourse  of  advertisements  in  general,  but  not  tourism  discourse in particular. Among the studies on travel brochures, some tend to focus solely on the verbal content of brochures (Mocini 2009; Cui, Lu and Hong 2012)while  others,  in  line  with  the  idea  of  multimodality  of  travel  brochures  (Kress  and van Leeuwen 1996; Scollon and Levine 2004; van Leeuwen 2004), investigate both linguistic and visual elements deployed in tourist texts to draw an appealing image  of  the  destination  (Ling  Ip  2008).  Some  of  these  studies  (e.g.,  Kress  and  van  Leeuwen’s  1996)  have  suggested  context  bound  patterns,  but  it  seems  that    globalization  has  led  to  outstretch  these  strategies  for  creating  images  even  in  eastern countries. As an offshoot of SFL, the appraisal model (Martin and White 2005) has also been  extensively  deployed  to  study  the  discourses  of  various  genres,  including  academic  discourse  (Hood  2006;  Jalilifar,  Hayati  and  Mashhadi  2012;  Liu  2013;Mei  and  Allison  2003),  journalistic  discourse  (A’Beckett  2010;  Liu  and  Stevenson  2013;  White  2001,  2003)  narrative  discourse  (Macken-Horarik  2003),  as  well  as  the  discourse  of  telephonic  conversations  (Wan  2008).  Demonstrating  a  vivid  interactive  context,  the  above  studies  have  endorsed  that  these  discourses  are  not  value-free  but  value-laden  contextualised,  ideological  and  dialogic.  Tourism  discourse,  however,  has  received  scant  attention  from  scholars  working  within  the  area  of  the  language  of  evaluation.  Thus,  the  present  study  aims  to  partly  bridge the gap in research on evaluative strategies through working on Graduation resources deployed in the language of travel brochures as a promotional strategy to grab the attention of potential tourists  Since tourism discourse is known as a promotional discourse, the main purpose in writing tourist texts is promoting the services and sites in touristic areas. Graduation is related to tourism discourse in that it is concerned with toning the values up. Graduation also comprises toning the  values  down,  but  this  is  of  little  concern  in  tourism  discourse.  Graduation,  as a system within the appraisal model, is concerned with up-scaling and down-scaling of values.  All attitudinal meanings, namely, the values of affect, judgment, and appreciation as well as engagement are gradable resources (Hood and Martin 2007; Martin and White 2005: 135)  Force and focus are the two main areas within which the values are scaled in the system of Graduation. Meanings are graded by either a scale from low to high intensity or from a core to marginal membership. The former scale is referred to as force while the latter is termed focus.  Graduation is  made  either  separately  or  as  infused  with  the  attitudinal  values  (Martin  and  White  2005:  141).  Force  and  focus  are  also  subsequently  divided  into  further  subsystems. Force is concerned with evaluations in terms of the degree of intensity or amount, hence is subdivided as quantification and intensification. Focus, on the other hand, deals with sharpening or softening the boundaries between categories.  Notwithstanding the studies cited above, there is a lot to discover about the language  of  tourism  and  the  lines  of  investigation  are  still  open.  Over  the  last  few decades, tourism industry has been considered as a great source of financial benefit to many countries around the world. This makes the discourse of tourism of paramount importance since a better understanding of the underlying systems for  meaning-making  in  the  discourse  of  tourism  would  aid  the  designing  of  tourist texts which may attract a larger number of people.  Studying the language of tourism from an SFL point of view is justified by the fact that SFL is a broad framework for text analysis, an evaluative tool which helps us to understand the construction of texts. SFL provides us with a comprehensive view of the systems deployed in the language of tourism for the purpose of meaning-making.  This can, in  turn,  lead  the  tourist  text  developers  to  design  brochures  potentially  capable  of  affecting  a  greater  number  of  clients.  Taking  an  SFL  approach  to  the  study   of the language of travel brochures is different from taking other approaches in that  the  former  helps  us  to  view  the  meanings  proposed  in  tourist  brochures  not only in terms of the language choices used for their construal, but also with regard to the functions they serve. The appraisal model is regarded as a discourse semantic  system  within  SFL  for  analyzing  interpersonal  meanings.  Accordingly,  employing this framework for the study of travel brochures helps with knowledge construction  and  locating  interpersonal  meanings  in  such  texts.  This  may,  in  turn,  help  tour  operators  raise  the  power  of  travel  brochures  in  influencing  the  potential  tourists  (Hood  2004).  Furthermore,  the  results  of  the  study  provide  an  assurance  on  the  efficiency  of  the  framework  as  a  useful  tool  for  text  analysis.  Generally,  the  study  reveals  that  appraisal,  due  to  its  comprehensiveness,  has  a  great potential for the analysis of texts within the genre of tourism.  The general intention of the researchers in conducting the present study is summarized in the following research questions: 1. In what ways and through what resources are Graduation values realized in travel brochures? 2. Do  the  identified  resources  and  patterns  through  which  different  values  are graded serve any significant function in the context of tourism? 3. Are  the  frequencies  of  subsystems  linked  to  the  efficiency  of  the  travel  brochures, that is, to their power in attracting potential customers

segments.text: Graduation,  as a system within the appraisal model, is concerned with up-scaling and down-scaling of values.  All attitudinal meanings, namely, the values of affect, judgment, and appreciation as well as engagement are gradable resources (Hood and Martin 2007; Martin and White 2005: 135)  Force and focus are the two main areas within which the values are scaled in the system of Graduation. Meanings are graded by either a scale from low to high intensity or from a core to marginal membership. The former scale is referred to as force while the latter is termed focus.  Graduation is  made  either  separately  or  as  infused  with  the  attitudinal  values  (Martin  and  White  2005:  141).  Force  and  focus  are  also  subsequently  divided  into  further  subsystems. Force is concerned with evaluations in terms of the degree of intensity or amount, hence is subdivided as quantification and intensification. Focus, on the other hand, deals with sharpening or softening the boundaries between categories.

intros.text:
Tourism has become one of the most dynamic and economically significant industries of the contemporary world, and language stands at the very heart of its operation. Long before travellers reach a destination, they encounter it as a text: a brochure, a website, a guidebook, or a television commercial that constructs an image of the place and invites them to become part of it. In this sense, tourism is not merely a matter of movement between locations but a phenomenon that is discursively produced and mediated. As Dann (2012) observes, the language of tourism was originally conceived as part of the modernist project, a largely monological discourse framed within parameters of social control, though it has more recently been transformed by digital communication into a more egalitarian, dialogic exchange between the industry, the tourist, and the toured. Whether monologue or trialogue, however, the persuasive vocation of tourism discourse remains constant: it seeks to attract, to entice, and ultimately to convert the reader into a traveller. It is precisely this persuasive orientation that makes tourism texts a fertile ground for linguistic analysis.

The study of tourism discourse has expanded considerably over recent decades, drawing on a range of theoretical perspectives and methodologies. Some scholars have approached tourism as a language of social control and authenticity (Rokowski, 2001; MacCannell, 1989), while others have examined the psychological and identity-related dimensions of the tourist experience (Bruner, 1991; Thurot, 1989). A substantial body of work has focused on the promotional and marketing functions of tourism texts, investigating destination image, publicity programmes, and the ways in which national and regional tourism organisations construct and disseminate representations of place (Dore & Crouch, 2003; Choi et al., 2006). With the proliferation of the internet, considerable attention has turned to official tourism websites and their role in constructing the identity of destinations, communities, and even nations (Doolin et al., 2002; Burns et al., 1999; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Alongside these text-based studies, a growing multimodal tradition has explored how visual design, layout, and image interact with verbal content to produce meaning in promotional materials (Kress & van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon & Scollon, 2004; van Leeuwen, 2004; Pan et al., 2010). Case studies of particular genres and cultural contexts, such as travel brochures in Hong Kong (Ip, 2008), contrastive analyses of cohesion in English and Chinese tourist texts (Cui et al., 2012), and analyses of tourism discourse in relation to place and community (Santos et al., 2008), have further enriched the field. Genre analysis, too, has offered valuable insights into the structure and communicative purposes of promotional texts within professional settings (Bhatia, 1993; Gotti, 2008), while research on the language of persuasion more generally has clarified the linguistic mechanisms by which texts influence their audiences (Hosman, 2002).

Despite this breadth of scholarship, the verbal content of travel brochures has received comparatively less systematic attention than either the visual dimension of tourism promotion or the discourse of tourism websites. Brochures remain a central genre in the promotional repertoire of the tourism industry, and although they overlap in function with travel guides and web-based materials, their compact, densely persuasive language merits examination in its own right (Molina & Esteban, 2006). More importantly, few, if any, studies of tourism discourse have analysed the evaluative language of travel brochures from the perspective of the appraisal model. This is a notable gap, since evaluation lies at the very core of what tourism texts do: they do not simply describe destinations, but assess, magnify, and celebrate them in order to render them desirable. An approach that foregrounds evaluation therefore promises to illuminate a dimension of tourism discourse that has remained largely implicit in prior work.

The appraisal framework, developed within Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) as an extension of the interpersonal metafunction, offers a particularly well-suited instrument for this purpose. Elaborated most fully by Martin and White (2005), the model provides what Bednarek (2010) describes as the only systematic, detailed, and elaborate framework of evaluative language among critical approaches to text evaluation. Appraisal comprises three interacting systems: attitude, which concerns the expression of feelings, judgements, and appreciations; engagement, which concerns the negotiation of positions and voices; and Graduation, which concerns the scaling up and down of values. The framework has been productively applied across a wide array of discourse types, including academic writing (Hood & Martin, 2005; Hood, 2010; Hood, 2005), narrative and its ethical work on readers (Macken-Horarik, 2003), student argumentative essays (Mei & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), cross-cultural news and media discourse (Liu & Stevenson, 2013; A'Beckett, 2009), and persuasive genres such as advertising (Patpong, 2009). This accumulating body of research demonstrates the versatility of appraisal as a tool for uncovering how writers construe interpersonal meaning and align readers with particular evaluative stances. Yet its application to the promotional discourse of tourist brochures has remained conspicuously underexplored.

Among the three appraisal systems, the present study focuses on Graduation. This choice is motivated by both theoretical and practical considerations. Graduation possesses a distinctive generality within the appraisal architecture: attitudinal and engagement values are themselves gradable, that is, they can be intensified, quantified, or made more or less prototypical, so that Graduation pervades and modulates the operation of the other two systems (Hood & Martin, 2005; Martin & White, 2005). This pervasiveness makes Graduation worth studying in its own right, and it is especially significant in tourism discourse, which is widely characterised as a language of exaggeration, superlatives, and amplification. Graduation operates through two main subsystems: force, which grades meanings according to intensity or amount, and focus, which grades non-scalable categories according to prototypicality through sharpening or softening. These subsystems, in turn, branch into further categories such as quantification and intensification. Given the tendency of tourist texts to magnify the number, extent, and quality of the attractions and services they promote, and given their preoccupation with authenticity, which is closely tied to the resources of focus (MacCannell, 1989; Dann, 1996), Graduation offers a particularly revealing lens on the evaluative work performed by travel brochures. Concentrating exclusively on this system, rather than attempting to survey the entire appraisal model, allows for a more comprehensive and finely grained analysis of the lexicogrammatical resources through which evaluation is realised.

The present study accordingly sets out to examine how Graduation strategies are deployed in the promotional discourse of travel brochures and to identify the lexicogrammatical resources through which these strategies are encoded. Two main questions guide the investigation: first, what statistical variations characterise the use of Graduation strategies, and their constituent subsystems, in tourist brochures; and second, what lexicogrammatical resources are preferred for the construal of these strategies in the texts. To address these questions, a dataset of 50 e-brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013 was assembled, with one brochure drawn from each state in order to ensure a fair geographical distribution and to target an English-speaking readership. The analysis proceeds on two complementary levels. A quantitative analysis, conducted with the aid of statistical software, establishes the frequencies and distributions of the values of force and focus and their subcategories, while a qualitative analysis illustrates the range of grammatical structures through which these values are realised and interprets the promotional functions they serve within their contexts.

In revisiting tourism discourse through the appraisal model, this study aims to contribute in several ways. Theoretically, it tests the descriptive power of the Graduation system as an instrument for text analysis in a genre to which it has not previously been applied, thereby extending the reach of the appraisal framework beyond the academic, narrative, and journalistic contexts in which it has more commonly been used. Descriptively, it maps the specific lexicogrammatical resources favoured in the coding of Graduation in tourist brochures, offering a detailed account of how tourism texts grade and amplify their evaluations of destinations. Practically, the findings hold potential value for those working within the tourism sector, providing a frame of reference for the design and assessment of effective promotional materials and clarifying the linguistic resources through which brochures are made to resonate with the expectations of prospective travellers.

segments.text: In revisiting tourism discourse through the appraisal model, this study aims to contribute in several ways. Theoretically, it tests the descriptive power of the Graduation system as an instrument for text analysis in a genre to which it has not previously been applied, thereby extending the reach of the appraisal framework beyond the academic, narrative, and journalistic contexts in which it has more commonly been used. Descriptively, it maps the specific lexicogrammatical resources favoured in the coding of Graduation in tourist brochures, offering a detailed account of how tourism texts grade and amplify their evaluations of destinations. Practically, the findings hold potential value for those working within the tourism sector, providing a frame of reference for the design and assessment of effective promotional materials and clarifying the linguistic resources through which brochures are made to resonate with the expectations of prospective travellers.

intros.text:
Tourism is one of the fastest-growing and most economically significant industries in the world, and language lies at the heart of how tourist destinations are marketed, imagined and consumed. Long before a traveller arrives at a destination, that destination has already been constructed for them through words and images that create expectations, stimulate desire and promise memorable experiences. The role of language in this process is neither incidental nor merely informative; it is fundamentally persuasive. As Hosman (2002) and others working on the relationship between language and persuasion have shown, particular lexical and grammatical choices are systematically deployed to influence audiences, and the discourse of tourism is a prime site where such persuasive strategies operate. Indeed, the notion of a distinctive ‘language of tourism’ has become a well-established object of inquiry, with Dann (2012) tracing how this discourse, once monological and framed within the logic of social control, has been reshaped by digital communication into a more dialogic, even trialogic, exchange among the industry, the tourist and the host community. Within this framework, the touree and the tourist are addressed through carefully crafted texts whose central aim is to promote, entice and reassure.

Among the many textual manifestations of the language of tourism, the travel brochure occupies a particularly prominent place. Brochures, whether in printed or electronic form, are one of the most enduring promotional genres of the tourism industry, and they have attracted considerable scholarly attention. Molina and Talaya (2006) examined tourism brochures as promotional artefacts, while a growing body of work has investigated tourism texts distributed through the web, including official tourism websites and the images they project. Burns and colleagues (1999) evaluated state tourism websites, Doolin and associates (2002) assessed the use of the web for tourism marketing in New Zealand, Choi and colleagues (2006) analysed destination image representation online, and Dore and Crouch (2003) explored the publicity programmes used by national tourism organisations. Others have turned to the multimodal and televisual dimensions of destination promotion, as in Pan and colleagues’ (2010) study of New Zealand tourism television commercials, and to the discursive construction of place, as in Santos and colleagues’ (2008) reimagining of Chinatown and Hallett and Kaplan-Weinger’s (2010) discourse-analytic account of official tourism websites. Genre-oriented investigations, informed by the traditions represented in Bhatia’s work on genre analysis in professional settings (Huckin & Bhatia, 1995), have further established the promotional character of tourism discourse and its shared conventions across sub-genres such as brochures, guides and websites. Comparative and cross-cultural studies have also emerged, such as Ciu and colleagues’ (2012) contrastive analysis of cohesion in English and Chinese tourist texts and Ip’s (2008) case study of a Hong Kong travel brochure.

What unites much of this work is a recognition that tourism texts are evaluative in nature: they do not simply describe places, they appraise them. To capture how evaluation is encoded in language, applied linguists have increasingly turned to the appraisal framework developed within Systemic Functional Linguistics. This model, elaborated most fully by Martin and White (2005), extends the interpersonal metafunction of language and offers, as Bednarek (2010) observes, the only systematic, detailed and elaborate framework for the study of evaluative language. Appraisal accounts for how speakers and writers construe attitudes, negotiate positions and align themselves with imagined readers through three interrelated systems: attitude, engagement and Graduation. The framework has proven productive across a wide range of discourse types. It has been applied to academic writing, where Hood (2005, 2010) has demonstrated how writers deploy evaluative prosodies to build persuasive stances in research article introductions, and where Hood and Martin (2007) have shown the pervasive role of Graduation in appraising discourse. Appraisal has likewise illuminated the evaluative structure of narrative (Macken-Horarik, 2003), the claims made by student writers in argumentative essays (Mei & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), the characterisation of political leaders in the press (A’Beckett, 2009), stance in cross-cultural disaster news reports (Liu & Stevenson, 2013), and persuasive advertising in non-English contexts such as Thai amulet advertisements (Patpong, 2009). Collectively, these studies confirm that the appraisal model is a versatile and robust instrument for uncovering how evaluative meaning is realised across genres and cultures.

Given both the persuasive, evaluative character of tourism discourse and the demonstrated analytical power of the appraisal framework, one might expect the two to have been systematically brought together. Yet this is not the case. While the language of tourism has been examined from numerous angles—cohesion, image construction, multimodality, genre structure and marketing effectiveness—few, if any, studies have analysed the verbal content of travel brochures from the perspective of the appraisal model. This is a striking omission, because the very purpose of promotional tourism texts is to evaluate destinations positively and to grade the qualities and quantities of what they offer in ways designed to attract holidaymakers. Where appraisal-based studies of tourism do exist, they have tended to concentrate on attitude, leaving the system of Graduation comparatively neglected, even though Graduation is arguably the most general of the three appraisal systems. Attitudinal and engagement values are themselves gradable; they are up-scaled and down-scaled through Graduation resources, which means that this system operates across and upon the other two. Focusing exclusively on Graduation therefore not only fills a clear gap in the analysis of tourism discourse but also permits a more comprehensive and finely delicate account of a system that is worth studying in its own right. The present study addresses precisely this space, examining how the resources of Graduation are exploited for evaluative and promotional purposes in the discourse of tourist brochures, and what lexico-grammatical resources writers draw upon to construe these strategies in their texts.

Accordingly, the study is guided by two main questions. The first concerns the ways in which Graduation strategies, understood as part of the broader appraisal system, are deployed in the promotional discourse of travel brochures. The second concerns the specific lexico-grammatical resources through which these Graduation strategies are coded in the texts. To answer these questions, the study draws on a dataset of 50 electronic brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013, with one brochure selected from each state to ensure a fair geographical distribution and to guarantee an English-speaking target readership. The analysis proceeds on two complementary levels. Quantitatively, the instances of Graduation, together with its subsystems of force and focus and their finer subcategories, are identified, coded and calculated using statistical software in order to reveal the relative frequencies and distributions of the various strategies. Qualitatively, the lexical items and their surrounding contexts are examined in each category so as to uncover the word choices, patterns and functions that these resources serve in the promotional discourse of tourism. The coding scheme is grounded in the appraisal taxonomy of Martin and White (2005) and Hood and Martin (2007), and its reliability and content validity are secured through a pilot study, expert verification and an extensive review of the appraisal literature.

By bringing the appraisal model, and specifically the system of Graduation, to bear on the language of tourist brochures, this study offers a contextualised account of how evaluation is enacted in one of the most characteristic promotional genres of the tourism industry. The analysis is expected to show that the discourse of travel brochures is densely loaded with Graduation resources, and that its subsystems function as powerful tools for promoting the number, distribution and appeal of tourist destinations and the services associated with them. The findings may serve as a point of departure for more comprehensive, corpus-based and cross-cultural investigations of evaluative language in tourism and in promotional discourses more generally. They may also offer a practical frame of reference for staff and students within the tourism sector, helping them to understand the linguistic resources required in developing effective brochures and to assess the persuasive potential of existing ones. In this way, the study contributes both to the theoretical refinement of the appraisal framework as a tool for text analysis and to a fuller understanding of how the language of tourism works to shape the expectations and desires of prospective travellers.

intros.text:
The study of tourism discourse has gained significant traction among scholars of text analysis, reflecting the growing importance of the tourism industry as a global economic force and a complex site of social interaction. Tourism discourse is not merely a vehicle for conveying factual information about destinations; rather, it is a sophisticated form of promotional discourse designed to construct an alluring image of a locale to attract potential visitors. As noted by Huckin and Bhatia (1995), professional settings often utilize specific genres for the purpose of self-promotion and product promotion, and travel brochures serve as a primary example of this generic function. These texts are carefully crafted to persuade readers, employing various linguistic strategies to highlight the desirability of a destination, its accessibility, and the quality of services offered. In this sense, the language of tourism is inherently persuasive, aligning with broader theories on language and persuasion (Hosman, 2002). 

Historically, the language of tourism has been viewed through various lenses. Some scholars have framed it as a monological discourse rooted in social control (Rokowski, 2001), while others have highlighted the search for authenticity as a central motivation for tourists, which in turn shapes the way destinations are represented in promotional materials (MacCannell, 1989). With the advent of the digital age, the nature of this discourse has shifted. Dann (2012) argues that tourism communication has evolved from a monologue into a dialogue or even a trialogue between the industry, the tourist, and the local resident. This shift is evident in the proliferation of official tourism websites and e-brochures, which combine textual and visual elements to foster specific identities for tourist locales (Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). While much research has focused on the multimodal aspects of these texts—analyzing how images and layout contribute to meaning (Kress & Van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon et al., 2004; Van Leeuwen et al., 2004)—there remains a need for a more granular analysis of the verbal content, specifically regarding how evaluative meanings are constructed to influence the reader.

Evaluation is central to the efficacy of tourism brochures. To create a compelling image, promoters must go beyond simple description and move into the realm of appraisal, assigning values to the attributes of a destination. This process of evaluation is not random but follows specific patterns designed to meet tourist expectations and stimulate demand (Dore & Crouch, 2003). Previous studies have explored destination image representation on the web (Choi et al., 2006) and the use of the web for tourism marketing (Doolin et al., 2002; Burns et al., 1999). However, few of these studies have employed a systematic linguistic framework to analyze the precise lexico-grammatical resources used to encode these evaluations. While some researchers have looked at cohesion in tourist texts (Ciu et al., 2012) or conducted case studies on specific brochures (Ip, 2008), there is a paucity of research specifically applying the Appraisal framework to the verbal strategies of graduation in tourism discourse.

The Appraisal framework, developed by Martin and White (2005), provides a comprehensive and systematic tool for analyzing evaluative language. As an extension of the interpersonal metafunction within Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL), the appraisal model examines how writers express attitudes, negotiate alignment with their readers, and grade the intensity of their evaluations. The framework consists of three primary systems: Attitude, Engagement, and Graduation. Attitude is concerned with feelings and judgments; Engagement deals with the writer's positioning relative to other voices; and Graduation focuses on the scaling of values—either increasing or decreasing their intensity or precision (Hood & Martin, 2007; Martin & White, 2005). The utility of the Appraisal framework has been demonstrated across various genres, including academic writing (Hood, 2005, 2010; Hood & Martin, 2005), news reports (Liu & Stevenson, 2013), and argumentative essays (Wu & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), as well as in the analysis of political discourse (A'Beckett, 2009) and narrative texts (Macken-Horarik, 2003).

Among the three systems of appraisal, Graduation is particularly salient in promotional contexts. Graduation allows a writer to amplify the positive attributes of a product or destination, effectively moving from a neutral description to a superlative claim. This process of up-scaling is essential for the 'language of exaggeration' typically found in tourism discourse, where the goal is to maximize the perceived value of an experience. Graduation is divided into two subsystems: Force and Focus. Force relates to the intensity, quantity, or extent of a value, while Focus relates to the prototypicality or the sharpening and softening of categorical boundaries (Martin & White, 2005). In the context of tourism, Force may be used to emphasize the 'abundance' of activities or the 'extreme' beauty of a landscape, while Focus may be employed to underscore the 'authenticity' of a cultural experience—a key driver in tourist motivation (MacCannell, 1989).

Despite the theoretical importance of Graduation, it is often the least studied part of the appraisal system because its meanings can be covert or integrated into other evaluative resources (Yang, 2016). However, studying Graduation in its own right allows for a more detailed understanding of how promoters manipulate the 'volume' of their claims to create a sense of urgency or irresistible appeal. In promotional genres, such as amulet advertisements in Thailand (Patpong, 2009), SFL has been used to reveal how lexicogrammatical choices serve persuasive ends. A similar approach is warranted for travel brochures, where the strategic use of intensifiers, quantifiers, and superlatives constitutes a core part of the promotional toolkit.

This study aims to fill the existing gap in the literature by providing a detailed analysis of Graduation strategies in tourist brochures from a Systemic Functional Linguistics perspective. While previous research has touched upon tourism discourse, few have examined the verbal content of travel brochures specifically through the lens of the appraisal model's Graduation system. By focusing on e-brochures from tour operators across the United States, this research seeks to identify the statistical variations in the use of Graduation and the specific lexico-grammatical resources used to construe these strategies. Specifically, the study addresses how Force (through quantification and intensification) and Focus (through sharpening and softening) are deployed to promote tourist destinations.

The significance of this research lies in its potential to reveal the underlying linguistic mechanisms that make tourism promotion effective. By analyzing a wide range of brochures from different states, the study aims to uncover general patterns of evaluative language that characterize the discourse of tourism in an English-speaking context. Furthermore, the findings may provide practical insights for those in the tourism industry, offering a frame of reference for developing more effective promotional materials that align with the expectations and desires of potential travelers. Ultimately, this study contributes to the broader field of applied linguistics by testing the efficiency of the Appraisal framework as a tool for analyzing specialized professional discourse (Gotti, 2016) and by extending our understanding of how interpersonal meaning is negotiated in the pursuit of commercial persuasion.

intros.text:
In the contemporary era of global mobility, the study of tourism discourse has emerged as a prolific area of inquiry within the field of text analysis. Tourism discourse is not merely a vehicle for providing geographical or logistical information; rather, it functions as a sophisticated form of promotional discourse designed to construct appealing images of destinations and persuade potential visitors to engage with specific services. As noted by Huckin and Bhatia (1995), the language used in professional settings, particularly for product and self-promotion, is characterized by strategic linguistic choices intended to achieve specific institutional goals. In the context of tourism, this involves the creation of a 'destination image,' a process that shapes how travelers perceive the allure, authenticity, and value of a locale (Choi et al., 2006).

Within this promotional framework, travel brochures serve as a primary medium for communicating the attributes of a destination. Whether in traditional print or as modern e-brochures, these texts are engineered to evoke desire and interest by highlighting the unique selling points of a region. Scholars have long recognized that the language of tourism is fundamentally persuasive (Hosman, 2002). For instance, research into the representation of destination images on the web has highlighted the importance of how marketing bodies project specific identities to influence consumer decision-making (Choi et al., 2006). Similarly, Hallett and Kaplan-Weinger (2010) have explored how official tourism websites foster social action and contribute to the reconstruction of national identities through strategic promotion. The goal is often to project an image of 'authenticity,' which is a central motivator for the modern tourist (Dann, 2012).

To analyze these persuasive mechanisms, many researchers have turned to Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). SFL provides a robust toolkit for understanding how language functions in social contexts by analyzing the interplay between the ideational, interpersonal, and textual metafunctions. Previous studies have applied SFL to various tourism-related texts to uncover patterns of cohesion (Ciu et al., 2012) or to explore the persuasive strategies employed in specific advertising registers (Patpong, 2009). Furthermore, the rise of multimodal discourse analysis has led scholars to examine how textual content interacts with visual design—such as layout, gaze, and composition—to create a holistic promotional effect (Kress & Van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon et al., 2004; Van Leeuwen et al., 2004). While these contributions have significantly advanced our understanding of the genre, the specific linguistic resources used to enact evaluation within tourism texts require more granular investigation.

One of the most comprehensive frameworks for analyzing evaluative language is the Appraisal model, developed by Martin and White (2005) as an extension of the interpersonal metafunction within SFL. Appraisal is concerned with how speakers and writers negotiate social relationships and express values through language. According to Bednarek (2010), the Appraisal model stands as the only systematic and elaborate framework for the analysis of evaluative language among critical text-evaluation approaches. The model is organized into three primary systems: Attitude, which deals with feelings and evaluations; Engagement, which manages the alignment of voices; and Graduation, which focuses on the scaling of values. The system of Graduation is particularly vital as it allows for the up-scaling (intensification) or down-scaling (softening) of meanings, thereby modulating the force and focus of an appraisal (Hood & Martin, 2007; Martin & White, 2005).

The application of the Appraisal framework has proven fruitful across various genres. For example, it has been used to analyze the characterization of political leaders in the press (A’Beckett, 2009), the construction of claims in student argumentative essays (Wu & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), and the development of empathy and discernment in narrative discourse (Macken-Horarik, 2003). In academic writing, Hood (2005, 2010) has demonstrated how writers utilize appraisal resources to develop their positions and engage with their scholarly community. Despite the versatility of this model, its application to the specific domain of tourism brochures remains surprisingly limited. While some studies have touched upon the broader persuasive nature of tourist texts or analyzed specific case studies of brochures (Ip, 2008), few, if any, have systematically examined the verbal content of travel brochures through the lens of the Appraisal model, and specifically through the system of Graduation.

This gap in the literature is significant because the discourse of tourism is inherently evaluative. Tourism promoters do not simply describe a waterfall or a museum; they describe it as the 'most spectacular' or the 'finest in the world.' Such expressions are not neutral descriptions but are strategic graduations intended to maximize the perceived value of the destination. Given that Graduation influences the other two systems of Appraisal—Attitude and Engagement—by modulating their intensity and prototypicality, it serves as the engine of exaggeration that characterizes promotional discourse. Therefore, a detailed analysis of Graduation resources is essential for understanding how tourism texts move from mere information-sharing to active persuasion.

Addressing this research lacuna, the present study aims to investigate the evaluative strategies employed in US-based tourist brochures from a Systemic Functional Linguistics perspective. Specifically, the study focuses on the system of Graduation to uncover how tour operators upscale the attributes of destinations to attract potential visitors. The primary objectives of this research are to identify the statistical variations in the use of Graduation strategies—namely, force and focus—and to illustrate the lexico-grammatical resources used to encode these strategies. By analyzing a dataset of 50 e-brochures from across the United States, the study seeks to reveal the patterns of intensification and quantification that characterize the 'language of exaggeration' in tourism.

It is hypothesized that the discourse of travel brochures is heavily loaded with Graduation strategies, with a strong preference for 'force' (quantification and intensification) over 'focus' (sharpening and softening). This preference is expected to reflect the industry's need to magnify the abundance of attractions and the intensity of the experience to appeal to the desires of the holidaymaker. By providing a detailed account of these resources, this study intends to offer a framework for understanding the interpersonal meaning-making processes inherent in promotional tourism texts.

Beyond its theoretical contributions to the field of SFL and Appraisal, the findings of this study may have practical implications for stakeholders in the tourism industry. A clearer understanding of the linguistic needs and evaluative patterns required for effective promotion can assist tour operators and tourism bureaus in developing more impactful brochures. Furthermore, this research may serve as a point of departure for future comparative studies across different cultures and languages, exploring how the 'language of exaggeration' varies across different global tourism contexts.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 details the methodology, including a comprehensive description of the analytical framework based on the Appraisal taxonomy, the criteria for data collection, and the procedures used to ensure the reliability and validity of the coding process. Section 3 presents the results of both the quantitative and qualitative analyses, discussing the distribution of force and focus and the specific grammatical structures used for realization. Finally, Section 4 provides the conclusions, acknowledges the limitations of the study, and suggests directions for future research in the domain of tourism discourse.

intros.text:
The study of tourism discourse has gained significant traction in recent years, as scholars increasingly recognize the pivotal role language plays in constructing destination images and influencing tourist behavior. Tourism is not merely an economic activity but a complex social phenomenon mediated through discourse, where texts serve as powerful tools for persuasion and identity construction (Bruner, 1991; Dann, 2012). Within this context, travel brochures function as primary instruments of promotion, designed to capture the attention of potential visitors and persuade them to choose specific destinations. However, despite the growing interest in tourism discourse, there remains a notable gap in the literature regarding the detailed linguistic mechanisms employed in these texts, particularly from the perspective of evaluative language. While genre analysis has been applied to professional settings and tourism websites (Huckin & Bhatia, 1995; Doolin et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2006), the specific verbal content of travel brochures has yet to be fully explored through the lens of the appraisal model.

Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) provides a robust framework for analyzing how language functions socially and interpersonally. Central to this framework is the concept of the interpersonal metafunction, which concerns the way language is used to establish relationships and express attitudes. Martin and White (2005) developed the Appraisal Framework as an extension of this metafunction, offering a systematic and detailed model for analyzing evaluative language. The Appraisal Framework comprises three major systems: Attitude, Engagement, and Graduation. Attitude deals with emotions, judgments, and appreciation; Engagement focuses on the sources of evaluations and how they are aligned with the reader; and Graduation concerns the scaling of values, either by intensity (force) or by prototypicality (focus). While previous studies have utilized the Attitude subsystem to analyze stance in various genres, including academic writing (Hood, 2005; Hood & Martin, 2005) and news reports (Liu & Stevenson, 2013), the system of Graduation has received comparatively less attention, particularly in the context of tourism discourse.

Graduation is a critical component of evaluative language because it allows writers to modulate the strength and scope of their evaluations. In the context of tourism, where the primary goal is to attract visitors through positive promotion, the ability to 'grade up' the qualities of a destination is essential. As Martin and White (2005) argue, all attitudinal meanings are gradable, and the resources used to grade these meanings are fundamental to the persuasive power of a text. The system of Graduation is divided into two main subsystems: Force and Focus. Force involves scaling values according to their intensity or amount, encompassing quantification (number, mass, extent) and intensification. Focus, on the other hand, deals with the sharpening or softening of categorical boundaries, which is particularly relevant when discussing the authenticity of a destination (MacCannel, 1989). Although the Appraisal model has been applied to various domains, including academic research (Hood, 2010) and advertising (Patpong, 2009), its application to the specific subsystem of Graduation in tourism brochures remains under-researched.

The language of tourism has traditionally been viewed as a form of social control or a monological discourse that constructs a specific reality for the tourist (Dann, 2012; Rokowski, 2001). However, with the advent of digital communication and the internet, the nature of this discourse has begun to shift towards a more dialogic or even trialogic interaction between the industry, the tourist, and the local community (Dann, 2012). Despite these shifts, the fundamental purpose of promotional texts like brochures remains the same: to persuade. This persuasive intent is realized through specific linguistic choices that highlight the positive attributes of a destination while minimizing or omitting negative aspects. Studies on tourism websites have shown that content analysis can reveal how destinations are represented (Choi et al., 2006; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010), but fewer studies have delved into the micro-level linguistic resources that achieve this representation. For instance, while Dore and Crouch (2003) explored publicity programs used by national tourism organizations, and Molina and Esteban Talaya (2006) examined tourism brochures broadly, a granular analysis of the evaluative strategies, specifically Graduation, is lacking.

Furthermore, the multimodal nature of modern tourism discourse, involving both text and image (Kress & Van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon et al., 2004), suggests that language does not work in isolation. However, understanding the linguistic component is a prerequisite for analyzing the multimodal whole. Previous research has often focused on the visual or multimodal aspects of tourism marketing (Pan et al., 2010; Santos et al., 2008), sometimes at the expense of a detailed linguistic analysis. This study aims to address this imbalance by focusing exclusively on the verbal content of travel brochures. By isolating the linguistic resources, the study can provide a clearer picture of how evaluative meanings are constructed and how they contribute to the overall promotional strategy. These strategies serve to construct an idealized image of the destination, appealing to the tourist's desire for authenticity and unique experiences (Dann, 1996; MacCannel, 1989). The present study seeks to fill this gap by investigating the specific Graduation strategies employed in tourist brochures and the lexicogrammatical resources used to encode them.

Moreover, the context of the study is significant. intros.text:
In the contemporary global landscape, tourism has evolved into a multifaceted industry that relies heavily on effective communication to attract visitors and promote destinations. As a result, the discourse of tourism has become a significant area of scholarly interest, particularly within the fields of applied linguistics and discourse analysis. The language employed in tourism materials is not merely informational; it is inherently persuasive, designed to construct specific images of places and influence the decisions of potential travelers. Consequently, understanding the linguistic mechanisms that underpin this promotional discourse is vital for both academic inquiry and practical application within the tourism sector. Scholars have long recognized that the 'language of tourism' functions as a powerful tool for social control and identity construction, shaping how destinations are perceived and consumed (Bruner, 1991; Dann, 2012; Rokowski, 2001). However, while the visual and multimodal aspects of tourism texts have received considerable attention, the specific verbal strategies used to evaluate and grade the qualities of tourist destinations remain an area that requires deeper investigation.

Genre analysis has provided a robust framework for examining language use in professional settings, including the specific conventions of tourism texts (Huckin & Bhatia, 1995). Studies in this domain have explored various dimensions of tourism discourse, from the representation of destination images on official websites (Choi et al., 2006; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010) to the linguistic features of travel brochures and advertisements (Molina & Esteban Talaya, 2006; Patpong, 2009; Ip, 2008). For instance, research has highlighted how tourism texts often function to foster social action and contribute to the reconstruction of national or local identities (Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Furthermore, the shift from monological to dialogic communication in the digital age has prompted calls for new heuristic frameworks to understand the changing dynamics between the industry, the tourist, and the destination (Dann, 2012). Despite this growing body of work, much of the existing literature focuses on broad genre characteristics or multimodal features, often overlooking the nuanced interpersonal resources that writers employ to persuade readers.

A particularly promising avenue for analyzing the persuasive nature of tourism discourse is the Appraisal framework, developed within the Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) tradition (Martin & White, 2005). This model offers a systematic and detailed taxonomy for evaluating language, categorizing evaluative meanings into three main systems: Attitude, Engagement, and Graduation (Martin & White, 2005). The Attitude system deals with emotions, judgments, and appreciation, while the Engagement system manages the sourcing and negotiation of voices. The Graduation system, however, is concerned with the scaling of these values, allowing for the intensification or softening of meanings. As Hood and Martin (2005) note, Graduation is central to the appraisal model because it modulates the force and focus of all attitudinal and engagement values. While the Attitude system has been widely applied in various contexts, such as academic writing (Hood, 2005, 2010), news reporting (Liu & Stevenson, 2013), and student argumentation (Wu & Allison, 2003; Yang, 2016), the specific role of Graduation in promotional discourse has received comparatively less attention.

Previous studies utilizing the Appraisal framework have demonstrated its utility in uncovering the evaluative strategies embedded in texts. For example, Macken-Horarik (2003) explored how appraisal resources create empathy and discernment in narrative discourse, while A'Beckett (2009) applied the model to analyze the characterization of political leaders in the press. In the context of tourism, a few studies have begun to touch upon evaluative language. Ip (2008) analyzed a Hong Kong travel brochure, and Santos et al. (2008) examined the reimagining of Chinatown through tourism discourse. However, these studies often treat evaluation broadly or focus primarily on the Attitude subsystem. There is a distinct lack of research that isolates the Graduation system to examine how tourism writers specifically manipulate the intensity and prototypicality of their claims to maximize persuasive impact. This is a significant gap, as the language of tourism is frequently characterized by exaggeration and maximization, strategies that are fundamentally realized through Graduation resources.

The scarcity of research focusing specifically on Graduation in tourism discourse is notable given the persuasive nature of the genre. Tourism brochures are designed to sell an experience, often promising 'the best' or 'unforgettable' encounters. Such claims rely heavily on the up-scaling of values, a process governed by the Graduation system. As Martin and White (2005) argue, Graduation allows writers to adjust the force of their evaluation, making a difference between a 'good' hotel and a 'superb' one, or between 'many' attractions and 'countless' opportunities. Without a detailed analysis of these gradable resources, our understanding of how tourism texts achieve their persuasive goals remains incomplete. Furthermore, while some studies have addressed the language of tourism websites (Doolin et al., 2002; Burns et al., 1999), the specific lexicogrammatical realization of Graduation strategies in print and digital brochures has not been systematically mapped.

This study aims to address this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of Graduation strategies in the discourse of tourism. Specifically, it investigates how the subsystems of Graduation—Force and Focus—are utilized in travel brochures to promote tourist destinations. The research focuses on the lexicogrammatical resources employed to code these strategies, offering a detailed account of how evaluation is scaled up or down in promotional texts. By concentrating on Graduation, this study seeks to illuminate the specific linguistic mechanisms that enable tourism writers to construct compelling narratives about destinations, thereby contributing to a more nuanced understanding of the interpersonal metafunction in this genre. The findings of this research will not only validate the applicability of the Appraisal model to tourism discourse but also offer practical insights for stakeholders in the tourism industry regarding the effectiveness of their promotional materials.

To achieve these objectives, the present study analyzes a corpus of 50 e-brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013. This dataset was selected to ensure a representative sample of English-speaking tourism discourse while controlling for temporal variables. The analysis employs a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative frequency counts with qualitative textual analysis to identify patterns in the use of Graduation resources. The study is grounded in the theoretical framework of Martin and White (2005), utilizing their taxonomy to categorize instances of Force (intensification and quantification) and Focus (sharpening and softening). By examining these resources in detail, the study seeks to answer the following research questions: What are the statistical variations in the utilization of Graduation strategies in tourist brochures? What lexicogrammatical resources are preferred for the construal of these strategies in tourism texts?

The significance of this research extends beyond the theoretical contribution to the field of applied linguistics. By revealing the specific evaluative strategies employed in tourism discourse, the study provides a framework for assessing the effectiveness of promotional materials. This has direct implications for the tourism industry, where the ability to craft persuasive and engaging content is crucial for attracting visitors. Moreover, the study contributes to the broader discourse on the language of evaluation, demonstrating how the Appraisal model can be applied to specialized genres beyond academic and news contexts. As the tourism industry continues to evolve in the digital age, understanding the linguistic tools used to promote destinations becomes increasingly important. This study, therefore, offers a timely and necessary examination of the evaluative strategies that underpin the discourse of tourism, revisiting the genre with a fresh perspective that highlights the pivotal role of Graduation in shaping the tourist experience.

segments.text: This study aims to address this gap by providing a comprehensive analysis of Graduation strategies in the discourse of tourism. Specifically, it investigates how the subsystems of Graduation—Force and Focus—are utilized in travel brochures to promote tourist destinations. The research focuses on the lexicogrammatical resources employed to code these strategies, offering a detailed account of how evaluation is scaled up or down in promotional texts. By concentrating on Graduation, this study seeks to illuminate the specific linguistic mechanisms that enable tourism writers to construct compelling narratives about destinations, thereby contributing to a more nuanced understanding of the interpersonal metafunction in this genre.
