intros.text:
Tourism is not only a major economic and cultural activity but also a densely mediated communicative practice. Destinations are encountered by many prospective travellers first through discourse: brochures, websites, guidebooks, advertisements, television commercials and, increasingly, interactive online platforms. These texts do more than transmit practical information about accommodation, routes or attractions; they construct places as desirable, memorable, authentic and worth consuming. In this sense, tourism promotion is a form of persuasive professional communication in which linguistic choices participate in shaping destination image, tourist expectation and decision-making. As studies of professional and promotional genres have shown, texts designed to sell products or services typically combine description with evaluation, information with persuasion, and institutional authority with an appeal to readers’ desires (Bhatia, 1995; Hosman, 2002). Tourist brochures are a particularly salient example of this hybrid communicative purpose, since they must present destinations as knowable while simultaneously transforming them into objects of desire.

The language of tourism has therefore attracted sustained attention in discourse studies and tourism research. Foundational work on tourism discourse has argued that tourism develops its own recognizable language, one characterized by euphoria, authenticity, playfulness and the conversion of ordinary places into extraordinary experiences (Dann, 2012). Tourism discourse has also been examined as a form of social control and representation, particularly in relation to the ways in which destinations, local communities and cultural identities are packaged for external consumption (Rokowski, 2001; Santos et al., 2008). From this perspective, tourism texts do not neutrally reflect places; rather, they select, arrange and evaluate features of places in accordance with institutional, commercial and ideological purposes. Such work is consistent with broader critical approaches to travel and tourism that view the tourist encounter as discursively mediated and as implicated in transformations of self, place and otherness (Bruner, 1991; Jonsson & Syssner, 2011).

Research into tourism promotion has also expanded with the growth of digital communication. The Internet has changed the conditions under which destinations are marketed and consumed, moving tourism communication from relatively one-way monologue toward more dialogic and even trialogic exchanges among industry actors, tourists and host communities (Dann, 2012). Studies of destination websites have demonstrated that official and commercial web texts play a central role in representing destination image and constructing local identity (Choi et al., 2006; Doolin et al., 2002; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Other work has evaluated tourism websites as marketing tools and investigated how national and regional tourism organizations use publicity programmes to stimulate demand (Burns et al., 1999; Dore & Crouch, 2003). Although online media have diversified the channels through which tourism is promoted, the written verbal component of tourism texts remains crucial, whether it appears in printed brochures, downloadable e-brochures or official webpages. The verbal text provides the lexical and grammatical resources through which attractions are classified, compared, intensified and presented as uniquely appealing.

Within this body of research, tourist brochures have been recognized as a central genre of tourism promotion. They are relatively compact, highly selective and explicitly designed to persuade potential tourists by presenting destinations, attractions and services in favourable terms. Molina and Esteban Talaya (2006), for example, treat tourism brochures as important promotional instruments, while studies of individual brochures have shown how their linguistic and rhetorical patterns contribute to destination marketing (Ip, 2008). Brochures typically combine factual elements—names of places, distances, facilities, historical references and seasonal information—with evaluative elements that promise enjoyment, authenticity, variety, convenience and distinction. Their promotional power lies partly in this blending of referential and interpersonal meanings: readers are encouraged to view claims about a destination as informative while also being positioned affectively and evaluatively toward that destination.

A considerable proportion of tourism discourse research has focused on content, genre structure, destination image, multimodality and cross-cultural comparison. Multimodal studies have shown that images, layout, colour and typography are integral to the construction of tourism meanings (Kress & van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon et al., 2004; van Leeuwen et al., 2004). Work on television commercials and websites has similarly demonstrated the importance of visual framing in producing destination appeal (Pan et al., 2010; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Other studies have examined cohesion and textual organization across languages, such as English and Chinese tourist texts (Ciu et al., 2012). These strands of research have significantly advanced understanding of tourism as a multimodal and cross-cultural discourse. However, the evaluative mechanisms of the verbal text itself, especially at the level of lexico-grammar and discourse semantics, still merit closer attention. Since the success of a brochure depends substantially on how it evaluates destinations, identifies them as exceptional, and scales the intensity or quantity of attractions, an explicit model of evaluative language is needed.

Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) offers a powerful theoretical basis for such an analysis because it views language as a social semiotic resource organized around meanings made in context. In SFL, interpersonal meaning is concerned with the enactment of social relations, attitudes and value positions. The appraisal framework, developed within SFL, extends the analysis of interpersonal meaning by systematizing the linguistic resources through which speakers and writers evaluate people, things, events and propositions (Martin & White, 2005; White, 2001). Appraisal has been widely used to investigate evaluative meanings in a range of genres, including academic writing, narrative, media discourse and student argumentative essays (Hood, 2005, 2010; Macken-Horarik, 2003; Mei & Allison, 2003). It has also proved useful in cross-cultural and educational contexts, for instance in studies of stance in disaster news reports and appraisal resources in English argumentative writing by Chinese college students (Liu & Stevenson, 2013; Yang, 2016). These studies show that appraisal analysis can reveal not merely whether evaluation is present in a text, but how it is distributed, intensified, negotiated and made persuasive.

The appraisal model comprises three major systems: Attitude, Engagement and Graduation. Attitude accounts for feelings, judgments of behaviour and appreciations of things; Engagement accounts for the ways texts position voices and alternative viewpoints; and Graduation accounts for the scaling of meanings in terms of intensity, quantity and prototypicality (Martin & White, 2005). Graduation is especially relevant to promotional discourse because persuasion often depends on scaling: attractions are not simply described as beautiful, numerous or accessible, but as extraordinarily beautiful, countless, endless, world-famous, the best, the largest, truly authentic or conveniently close. Graduation thus enables writers to raise or lower the force of evaluations and to sharpen or soften category boundaries. Hood and Martin (2005) further argue that Graduation plays a key role in invoking attitude, since values may be amplified, accumulated or made more persuasive even when attitudinal meanings are not overtly stated. In tourism promotion, where exaggeration, distinction and promise are frequent rhetorical strategies, Graduation is likely to be a central evaluative resource.

Despite the relevance of appraisal theory to promotional genres, relatively little work has applied it to the discourse of tourism, and fewer studies have focused specifically on Graduation in tourist brochures. Existing analyses of tourism texts have identified recurrent persuasive strategies, such as the construction of authenticity, novelty, escape, abundance and pleasure, yet these strategies have not often been described through a systematic account of the lexico-grammatical resources that realize evaluation. Moreover, studies of tourism brochures have tended to emphasize general discourse features, destination image or multimodal design rather than the fine-grained linguistic mechanisms by which attractions are graded and promoted. This gap is significant because Graduation resources may reveal how tourism promoters linguistically magnify destinations, quantify opportunities, intensify experiences and present attractions as authentic or exemplary. A systematic analysis of these resources can therefore contribute both to tourism discourse studies and to applied linguistic research on evaluation in professional communication.

The present study addresses this gap by examining the evaluative strategies used in a corpus of English-language tourist e-brochures from the perspective of the appraisal model, with particular attention to the system of Graduation. The study focuses on brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013 and investigates how Graduation resources are deployed to promote natural and cultural attractions, services and tourist experiences. Two main questions guide the analysis. First, what Graduation strategies are most frequently used in tourist brochures, and how are they distributed across the major categories of force and focus? Second, what lexico-grammatical resources are employed to encode these strategies in the verbal discourse of the brochures? By combining quantitative frequency analysis with qualitative examination of linguistic patterns, the study seeks to identify both broad tendencies and specific realizations of evaluative scaling.

In focusing on Graduation, the article does not deny the relevance of Attitude and Engagement to tourism discourse. Rather, it treats Graduation as a particularly productive entry point because it cuts across attitudinal and dialogic meanings and because promotional discourse relies heavily on scaling values upward. The analysis is expected to show how tourist brochures use quantification, intensification, sharpening and softening to construct destinations as abundant, accessible, exceptional, authentic and experientially rewarding. In doing so, the study contributes to a more explicit account of the persuasive language of tourism and demonstrates the usefulness of SFL appraisal theory for analysing evaluative meaning in promotional texts.

intros.text:
Tourism is not only an economic and social activity but also a discursive practice through which places are imagined, differentiated and made desirable. Before tourists encounter a destination physically, they often encounter it textually through brochures, websites, guidebooks, advertisements and other promotional genres. These texts do more than transmit information about accommodation, transport or attractions; they construct images of places, invite particular kinds of experience and position potential visitors as consumers of nature, culture, heritage and leisure. For this reason, the language of tourism has become an important object of inquiry in discourse analysis, genre studies and applied linguistics.

Promotional tourism discourse is especially significant because persuasion is built into its communicative purpose. Like other professional and promotional genres, it combines description with evaluation and information with inducement (Bhatia, 1995). The tourist brochure, in particular, has traditionally been one of the most recognizable genres of tourism promotion. Although digital media have transformed the channels through which destinations are marketed, brochures continue to circulate in electronic form and to function as compact, highly designed representations of tourist places. They condense a destination into a set of memorable verbal and visual cues and typically foreground uniqueness, abundance, accessibility, authenticity and pleasure. As Molina and Esteban Talaya (2006) suggest, tourism brochures remain central to destination promotion because they mediate between tourism organizations and potential visitors at the point where desire and decision-making are formed.

Previous research has shown that tourism texts participate in the construction of destination image and tourist identity. Studies of tourism websites, for example, have examined how places are represented online and how official and commercial texts promote particular versions of local identity (Burns et al., 1999; Doolin et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2006; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Other work has investigated the broader ideological and cultural dimensions of tourism discourse, including the ways in which tourism can reimagine ethnic spaces, reproduce postcolonial relations, and frame encounters between tourists and host communities (Santos et al., 2008; Jonsson & Syssner, 2011). Dann’s influential account of the language of tourism has also emphasized that tourism promotion relies on recognizable rhetorical patterns, such as the search for authenticity, the promise of escape and the use of euphoria to transform ordinary places into extraordinary experiences (Dann, 2012). These studies have established that tourism discourse is not a neutral description of reality but a persuasive semiotic activity shaped by institutional, cultural and commercial interests.

The increasing importance of the Internet has further expanded the scope of tourism discourse research. Tourism communication, once often described as monologic, has been remodelled by digital platforms that allow interaction among tourism providers, tourists and local communities (Dann, 2012). Nevertheless, the promotional voice of the tourism industry remains influential, particularly in official and commercial destination descriptions. Online brochures and travel guides still rely on carefully crafted language to project value, create affective appeal and guide potential visitors toward preferred interpretations of places. In this context, attention to the linguistic mechanisms of evaluation is essential for understanding how tourism promotion works.

Evaluation is one of the major means by which persuasive discourse achieves its effects. Persuasive language depends not only on what is represented but also on how entities, events and experiences are valued, intensified, ranked and aligned with readers’ expectations (Hosman, 2002). In tourism discourse, evaluation may appear in apparently simple adjectives such as beautiful, unique or unforgettable, but it may also be distributed across clauses, nominal groups, comparisons, quantifiers, repetitions and figurative expressions. Through such resources, a destination can be construed as more authentic, more extensive, more exciting or more abundant than competing destinations. These evaluative choices are central to the promotional function of tourist texts because they turn information into attraction.

Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) offers a productive framework for investigating such meanings because it views language as a social semiotic system organized around meaning-making functions. Within SFL, the interpersonal metafunction is concerned with the enactment of social relations, attitudes and positions. Appraisal theory, developed within this tradition, provides a systematic model for analysing evaluation in discourse (White, 2001; Martin & White, 2005). The model has been widely used to examine how speakers and writers express feelings, judge behaviour, appreciate things, negotiate alternative voices and grade meanings. It consists of three major systems: Attitude, which accounts for affect, judgement and appreciation; Engagement, which accounts for dialogic positioning; and Graduation, which accounts for the scaling of meanings in terms of force and focus (Martin & White, 2005).

A growing body of research has applied appraisal theory to a range of discourse domains. Macken-Horarik (2003) explored the role of appraisal in narrative and showed how evaluative resources guide readers’ empathy and ethical interpretation. Mei and Allison (2003) investigated appraisal in student argumentative essays, demonstrating how writers use evaluative resources in developing claims. Hood (2005, 2010) examined appraisal in academic writing, highlighting the ways evaluative prosodies contribute to authorial stance and disciplinary argumentation. A’Beckett (2009) used appraisal to analyse political characterization in the Russian press, while Liu and Stevenson (2013) applied the framework to cross-cultural stance in disaster news reports. Appraisal has also informed studies of persuasive and advertising discourse, including Patpong’s (2009) systemic functional analysis of Thai amulet advertisements. These studies demonstrate the flexibility of appraisal theory as an analytical tool for uncovering how interpersonal meanings are encoded in texts.

Despite this extensive use of appraisal in other domains, tourism discourse has received relatively limited attention from the perspective of appraisal theory. Existing analyses of tourism texts have tended to focus on multimodality, destination image, genre structure, cohesion, ideology or broad rhetorical strategies (Kress & van Leeuwen, 1996; Scollon et al., 2004; Van Leeuwen, 2004; Ciu et al., 2012). Case studies of tourism brochures, such as Ip’s (2008) analysis of a Hong Kong travel brochure, have contributed to understanding the textual organization and persuasive features of the genre. However, comparatively little work has examined in detail how the verbal component of tourism brochures realizes evaluation through the categories of the appraisal system. In particular, the system of Graduation has not been sufficiently explored as a resource through which tourism discourse amplifies desirability, constructs abundance and sharpens authenticity.

This gap is important because Graduation is especially relevant to the promotional language of tourism. Graduation is concerned with the up-scaling and down-scaling of meanings, either by force, which grades intensity and quantity, or by focus, which grades the prototypicality or categorical boundaries of entities (Martin & White, 2005; Hood & Martin, 2005). In tourist brochures, promotional meanings are frequently created by increasing the perceived number, size, extent, intensity or authenticity of attractions and experiences. Phrases such as endless opportunities, the finest museums, truly memorable experiences or one of the most spectacular landscapes do not simply describe destinations; they scale them upward and thereby enhance their marketability. Since the overall aim of tourist brochures is to attract holidaymakers, the resources of Graduation may be expected to play a central role in their evaluative and persuasive design.

Yet it remains unclear which Graduation strategies are most frequently used in tourist brochures and which lexicogrammatical resources typically realize them. A systematic analysis of these patterns can contribute both to tourism discourse studies and to appraisal research. For tourism discourse studies, it can show how promotion is accomplished through recurrent evaluative choices rather than through isolated positive adjectives. For appraisal research, it can test the descriptive adequacy of the Graduation system in a genre where scaling is likely to be pervasive and commercially motivated. Such an analysis can also have practical relevance for tourism professionals, materials designers and students in tourism-related fields who need to understand how effective promotional texts are linguistically constructed.

The present study addresses this niche by examining Graduation strategies in a corpus of 50 electronic tourist brochures released by tour operators across the United States between 2012 and 2013. Drawing on the appraisal framework proposed by Martin and White (2005), it focuses on the verbal content of the brochures and investigates how meanings are graded through force and focus. More specifically, the study asks how frequently different Graduation resources occur in the corpus and what lexicogrammatical patterns are used to encode them. By combining quantitative analysis of frequency distributions with qualitative analysis of representative textual examples, the study aims to reveal how tourist brochures deploy evaluative scaling in the service of destination promotion.

In focusing on Graduation, the study does not treat evaluation as a peripheral stylistic feature but as a central mechanism of tourism persuasion. It argues that the language of travel brochures is densely loaded with resources that amplify quantity, intensity, extent and authenticity, and that these resources help construct destinations as abundant, accessible, exceptional and worth visiting. The analysis therefore contributes to a more detailed understanding of how promotional tourism discourse works at the level of lexicogrammar and discourse semantics, while also extending the application of appraisal theory to a genre in which evaluation is both pervasive and commercially consequential.

segments.text: Tourism is not only an economic and social activity but also a discursive practice through which places are imagined, differentiated and made desirable. Before tourists encounter a destination physically, they often encounter it textually through brochures, websites, guidebooks, advertisements and other promotional genres. These texts do more than transmit information about accommodation, transport or attractions; they construct images of places, invite particular kinds of experience and position potential visitors as consumers of nature, culture, heritage and leisure.

For this reason, the language of tourism has become an important object of inquiry in discourse analysis, genre studies and applied linguistics.

segments.text: The tourist brochure, in particular, has traditionally been one of the most recognizable genres of tourism promotion. Although digital media have transformed the channels through which destinations are marketed, brochures continue to circulate in electronic form and to function as compact, highly designed representations of tourist places. They condense a destination into a set of memorable verbal and visual cues and typically foreground uniqueness, abundance, accessibility, authenticity and pleasure.

segments.text: As Molina and Esteban Talaya (2006) suggest, tourism brochures remain central to destination promotion because they mediate between tourism organizations and potential visitors at the point where desire and decision-making are formed.

segments.text: Previous research has shown that tourism texts participate in the construction of destination image and tourist identity. Studies of tourism websites, for example, have examined how places are represented online and how official and commercial texts promote particular versions of local identity (Burns et al., 1999; Doolin et al., 2002; Choi et al., 2006; Hallett & Kaplan-Weinger, 2010). Other work has investigated the broader ideological and cultural dimensions of tourism discourse, including the ways in which tourism can reimagine ethnic spaces, reproduce postcolonial relations, and frame encounters between tourists and host communities (Santos et al., 2008; Jonsson & Syssner, 2011). Dann’s influential account of the language of tourism has also emphasized that tourism promotion relies on recognizable rhetorical patterns, such as the search for authenticity, the promise of escape and the use of euphoria to transform ordinary places into extraordinary experiences (Dann, 2012). These studies have established that tourism discourse is not a neutral description of reality but a persuasive semiotic activity shaped by institutional, cultural and commercial interests.

segments.text: Appraisal theory, developed within this tradition, provides a systematic model for analysing evaluation in discourse (White, 2001; Martin & White, 2005). The model has been widely used to examine how speakers and writers express feelings, judge behaviour, appreciate things, negotiate alternative voices and grade meanings. It consists of three major systems: Attitude, which accounts for affect, judgement and appreciation; Engagement, which accounts for dialogic positioning; and Graduation, which accounts for the scaling of meanings in terms of force and focus (Martin & White, 2005).
